Quite simply one of the best war films I've ever seen. So much attention to detail in every frame and some excellent character development leads to one thrilling and sometimes emotional ride for audiences. Cinematography is of the highest standard and the documentry feel to it really puts you in the middle of all the action that is occuring. Many of the locations really paint a picture of what three men go through and how you might deal with it The Hurt Locker, shines in incredible dramtic realism, where some Iraq films just hasn't quite got there. As an audience member the realism in this film means that you are going on the journey as the characters area. Consequently, this means that character development is so well done with this realistic style that you really get an understanding of these characters especially, Sgt. James. James is presented as a character who is addicted to the danger and adreanline rush that comes with being a soldier. He is incredibly fearless, much to the amazement of Sandborn and Eldridge. Eldridge is the younger of the three who looks up to his two superiors. Sanborn has much experience behind him but has never quite seen a soldier quite like James. The three actors who play the main three leads are realtivly unknown. I think this is what works in the film; that you can seperate between the actor and the character that is being portrayed. Which is a highlight of this film. Jeremy Renner, who plays Sgt. Jamesis in the role of his life and plays the character with such intense emotion which really brings alive the characters true intentions. I'd love to see him nominated at the Oscars this year because it's one brilliant performance.The film should bag several oscar nominations this year and hopefully such win several. Bigelow has directed one phenomenal films which will be spoken about for years to come. Just Outstanding. May very well be my film of 2009!

Movie trades are so easily dismissive, but Hurt Locker will sooner or later be seen for what it is, an entirely unique war film that is equal parts rock n' roll movie, western and art film -- a combination that I, for one, have never seen before on screen. This film has a physical punch that I defy anyone to find in any Iraq film to date (or any war film for that matter - the closest would be Saving Private Ryan, but this film is so ahead of that one in terms of realism and impact that it's a vague comparison). This gut-punch of a film deserves to be seen, not for any political reasons, but for anyone even remotely interested in screencraft. Nobody wields a camera like KB, and when you add the verisimilitude of writer Boal's experience (he was embedded with a bomb squad), the result is a one-two punch of a film. This is one of those films that you will NOT forget if you see it, and I'm waiting for RT to post some of the better reviews (Richard Corliss in TIME said it was one of the best war films he had EVER SEEN). Quite possibly the most suspensful and heart pounding film I have ever seen, recluse action director Kathryn Bigelow comes out of hiding to blow some minds with her blistering new war flick. The Hurt Locker, which is a term that soldiers coined for war, is about the US army's Bravo Company who have the daunting task of finding and defusing bombs in Iraq. A young upstart cast really made it feel unpredictable, as an interviewer pointed out to Bigelow, "With a relatively unknown cast, you don't know who will get killed off first. Some actors have such big paycheques the viewer will instantly know, 'Oh, he'll last until the end of the movie." He was right, it really helped create more suspense. The three stars Jeremy Renner, Anthony Mackie and Brian Geraghty tore up the screen and left me floored. After a shocking opening sequence that left the crowd in awe, Renner gets brought in as the new leader of the pack. He plays James, who has successfully disabled 873 devices. He's a real wild child, even in the hulking shell of his bomb suit he has a swagger. At first this doesn't sit well with the seasoned intelligence expert Sanborn (Mackie, who is one to watch) and specialist Eldridge (Geraghty), but throughout the film when James prevents them from blowing up they warm up to him. Renner gives such a towering performance that I believe warrants Best Actor consideration, when I told Renner this at the Q&A after the screening he called me ridiculous but was appreciative. It's a star-making performance, brought so many emotions out in me. There's a scene where he attempts to disable a timed bomb that's welded to a suicide bomber but there's too many locks and he has to explain to the man, who can't understand him, that he can't do it. This man is crying and pleading to get the device off him as James is apologizing while slowly backing away, it's brutal. This film has some fantastic cameos from actors Bigelow has used in previous films, Ralph Fiennes and Guy Pearce. Their screentime is short which is a shame but they have really important parts and are a joy to watch. The camera work is insane, there's multiple angle slow motion explosions with people flying all over the place as the camera is zoomed in on shaking gravel. I don't want to spoil much as nearly every scene has something crazy happening and I'd ruin the anticipation factor. I was on the edge of my seat for the whole 130 minutes, the tension level is unbearable. Everything around these men is deadly, everything and anything can be a bomb, and you'd be surprised what is. There was a woman behind me that got really scared and had to leave because she couldn't take it, she eventually came back in but was a real nuisance since she kept gasping and saying things like "oh no!" or "Ahh!" Haha, I'm not kidding. Bar none the most riveting film I've ever seen, and I was shaking and breathless as the credits were rolling. This better get some attention around awards season, it's a true spectacle to behold.

The opening quote of this movie states, "War is a Drug." That statement directly applies to the main character of this film, who is teamed with a bomb squad unit and does things in a mostly brash way because he knows exactly what he's doing and he loves doing it. Set in 2004 Iraq, this isn't really a war film as much as it is just a great action film set during a war. It focuses on characters being put in harms way, while they just try to get their jobs done, regardless of personal motivation. The movie never once focuses on the politics or anyone talking about the situation they are in. It has great amounts of tension, makes good use of its gritty, documentary style film technique, and features a number of good performances.

Sanborn: You realize that every time you suit up, its life or death. You roll the dice and you deal with it.

After a bomb specialist meets an unfortunate end, the bravo unit bomb squad finds a new team leader, Sgt. William James, played by Jeremy Renner. James joins up with the two other members of the teams, Sanborn and Aldridge (Anthony Mackie and Brian Geraghty). On the first mission out, James' style in bomb disposal becomes apparent as he basically disregards common practice and wings it. This shows again on their second time out, but the team still has to endure another 38 days for their tour of duty.

Staff Sergeant William James: This box is full of stuff that almost kill me. 

James isn't necessarily reckless and certainly not suicidal, he just knows how bombs work and likes to get a problem solved. He's just that good. Everyone sees it, including, presumably, the men armed with the detonators. There are some amazingly tense scenes in which James must disarm bombs, while many onlookers stand in the background. Some missions take the men out of the city, one in particular leads to an amazing sniper battle sequence.

During all this time, its not so much about the men growing closer together, but focusing somewhat on each one's state of mind separately. James is of course the main character here, and we learn the most about what makes him tick, but details about Sanborn emerge through his attitude towards James, and we get to know Aldredge through the aid of double sessions with both James and a psych officer.

Director Kathryn Bigelow, responsible for other such films as the adrenaline packed Point Break and the Sci Fi Noir - Strange Days, does a great job at showing us these characters and delivering scene after scene of true and earned suspense. The film captures a wonderful balance in tone, managing to scatter some light moments amidst the tension, and never getting away from the characters in favor of gratuitous action.

Performances are all top notch. Along with Renner, who is just great in this movie and can hopefully emerge from the supporting character actor roles, there are also small parts from Guy Pearce, Ralph Fiennes, and David Morse. 

All these people manage to appear in a great looking film as well. While certainly not a limited budget film, its not a studio picture, and actually having filmed in Jordan benefited and provides for a desert environment that is captured very well through the use of hand held camera work that isn't dizzying and instead, provides a way that captures some of the manic situations and presents it in a well handled way. This is truly a film where the editing is what makes it shine. Handled appropriately to put together a piece of cinema that is structured just right. If there's one Oscar I'm am hoping for this film to win, its for the editing.

The film meanders a bit towards the end of its mid section, the whole plot is fairly episodic, but the way it handles it many tense moments, along with Begelow's direction, and the great work from the entire cast overshadows these aspects and make for a film that will surely remain one of the best of the year.

''The rush of battle is often a potent and lethal addiction, for war is a drug.'' Iraq. Forced to play a dangerous game of cat-and-mouse in the chaos of war, an elite Army bomb squad unit must come together in a city where everyone is a potential enemy and every object could be a deadly bomb. Jeremy Renner: SSG William James The Hurt Locker(2008) is a master stroke from Director Kathryn Bigelow, and superbly written by Mark Boal. An insight into the days of a bomb disposal unit and their time and relationships with each other in Iraq. It has been nominated for 9 Oscars, including Best Picture, Best Director and of course cinematography. Won 3 Golden globes, and won BAFTAs including one for Best picture. Now I have seen it I know why it has garnered these awards. It is simply a masterpiece and study of War, men, people and hurls us into the world of these soldiers. We feel part of this; We feel the tension and suspense with them.
The Hurt Locker is modern-day life in Iraq, shown through the eyes of members of an EOD team. They are put to the test as they spend the remaining 38 days of their rotation together as they encounter some impossible scenarios. The Hurt Locker is not necessarily an action film, but a drama and thriller. As a consequence the realism of the story elevates to pinnacle peaks. Each actor and cast member did an impressive job in their respective roles, never overacting or blandly complying with the script. Guy Pearce, Anthony Mackie, Brian Geraghty, Ralph Fiennes, David Morse and even Evangeline Lilly make appearances with sometimes brief but perfected performances. Although the main character steals the show; Jeremy Renner as SSgt. Will James may portray the typical war hero; Cocky, hotheaded, wild and reckless, but even so, his character is far from perfect, and as his service in Iraq continues, he becomes vulnerable, therefore realizing he is just a man. Renner victoriously impacts this successfully through his acting. ''There's enough bang in there to blow us all to Jesus. If I'm gonna die, I want to die comfortable.'' In addition to the performances, Barry Ackroyd's cinematography is breathtakingly enveloping. He makes the film in such a way that it almost feels as if it could be a documentary made by someone in real time. This includes segments of the shaky camera technique, quick zoom ins and outs, and occasional focus issues. This may seem like sloppy camera work, but it is intentional; It helps put the viewer right in the centre of events, of Iraq. Original Music by Marco Beltrami and Buck Sanders also adds depth in helping make such an intense and realistic journey. Slick editing results in a consistent yet plausible storytelling and insight. On top of this, the ambient effects and sounds, help out in adding suspense, never pushing in being overly used. Director Kathryn Bigelow; I've not seen many of her films, but she has talent, good looks and balls (specifically for the fact that this film was shot in Jordan, just miles from Iraq) for making such an intense, suspenseful, and gripping war film that is not glorifying the military nor is about a moral lesson. She shows the war as it is in Iraq, which includes the chaos of gun battles, the paranoia and racial tensions between the U.S. soldiers and the innocent Iraqi civilians. This is an honest sometimes brutal depiction of life and the World of War. I know this film will win even more awards in the near future, and rightly so. This is one of the best films I have seen this year. It has all the ingredients a good film needs: decent acting, a unique story, wonderful cinematography/composition shots, and a fast-pace. "You'll know when you're in it." Based on recently declassified information and the personal wartime experiences of journalist Mark Boal (who adapted his experiences with a bomb squad into a fact-based, yet fictional story), director Kathryn Bigelow's Iraq War drama The Hurt Locker presents the ongoing conflict in the Middle East from the perspective of those who see the fighting firsthand -- the soldiers. As an elite Army Explosive Ordnance Disposal team tactfully navigates the streets of present-day Iraq, they face the constant threat of death from incoming bombs and sharp-shooting snipers. Review Action woman Kathryn Bigelow returns to form in this intense war drama about an elite Bomb Squad whose job is to disarm and diffuse deadly bombs that plagues modern day Iraq. Her first film since 2002's K19:The Widowmaker, this movie is the best way to make a comeback and I just hope people will notice that. Rarely does a woman captivate the action junkies out there by putting together a series of intense, breath taking scenes and with the lightning fast pace she simply won't let you recover and you'll find yourself glued to the screen for the whole two hours of the movie. Jeremy Renner, Anthony Mackie and Brian Geraghty all gave good performances though not memorable in any way, they carry the sentiments of the soldiers currently serving in the Iraq war and I believe justice is brought to each of their roles. Supporting roles include Ralph Fiennes, who is everywhere right now, Guy Pearce and David Morse. Although much of them are pretty much in only a scene or two, they did pretty well considering. The Hurt Locker is a movie that transcends politics and all that mumbo jumbo. Simply put, this movie is a kickass action pic that grabs you by the throat and won't let go until the end credits roll. If you're into this kind of stuff, then this is a must see.

First movie in nearly 6 years, and Kathryn Bigelow returns cementing her place as one the worlds premiere action directors. An over the shoulder account following a small group of specialists charged with disarming the many traps and unexplded ordnance around Baghdad. Bigelow and her DP Barry Ackroyd approach the enviroment with a no frills energy, hand held cameras but masterfully edited. Moments where characters are forced to explore trapped areas in full sealed armour are made to seem like Astronauts or deep sea divers in a truly terrifying hostile enviroment, which of course they are.It's high tension stuff, the cast and their relationship dynamic make for easy angles on camaraderie and trust, and the film is peppered with a few quality star cameos just to give a little pop to the proceedings but never lifing you out of the moment.Inexplicably the foot comes off the gas pedal just after the halfway mark, but after a dip in the proceedings things get back on track nicely and the film finishes strongly. There's no political message, this is a close up look at specialists survivng by being professional soldiers and all the emotional baggage that comes with that. There's metaphor there if you want it, but mostly this is a great intense war movie.

Jeremy Renner is superb as Sgt Will James, and Geraghty and Mackie make up the other 2 perfect points of the team triangle, highlighting 3 different approaches to how soldiers cope (or don't) within such a dangerous setting.

Without the pacing mistep going into the third act, this for me would've been a classic, as it is it's still exceptional work from a much missed director, and a perfect small cast.

The almost documentary style of the film takes you right into the middle of things and doesn't let go for two very intense hours. The impression of imminent thread hanging over the soldier's heads expands to the audience easily. The few action scenes are well timed and shot, especially the sniper duel across a valley is excellent. And although the topic of the film is as current as it gets and accordingly explosive (literally), it neither preaches any political point of view nor glorifies heroism. Its view on things are realistic and sobering, sometimes even sickeningly so (the body bomb). Exciting and intelligent, one of the highlights of the year 2009, a deserved Oscar winner.

 [font=Palatino Linotype][size=3][i]The Hurt Locker[/i] is something of a rarity, feature war movie set in Iraq that actually works, even though it doesn't tell anything new. Director Kathryn Beigelow ([i]Strange Days[/i]) conters on a highly trained bomb disposal team amidst violent conflict. Scriptwriter Mark Boal was a member of such a team and although the story is said to be entirely fictional, one can't stop wondering if there are any autobiographical elements. Boal's script is unpredictable and challenging offering many unexpected twists and turns. It doesn't try to tell the story, but presents us only with daily routines of the squad entirely doomed with tragic unpredictability. I've always considered Bigelow as a splendid director. In [i]The Hurt Locker[/i] her direction is flawlessly detached when she examines the conflicts between the soldiers and effectively polished when she deals with suspense-ridden sequences. The acting is another highlight. Jeremy Renner as indifferent to death, yet vulnerable Staff Sergeant James gives a complex performance, perhaps the best in his career. Anthony Mackie and Brian Garaghty are totally believable as well. The movie quite effectively shows how the relations between these three soldiers change in the course of time. To conclude, [i]The Hurt Locker[/i] is a suspenseful war movie riddled with sadness and desperation. It deserves to be seen. [b]8.5/10 (B+)[/b][/size][/font]

The first half of this film is tense to the point of being practically a near-war experience.  The script artfully develops characters by simply following them through the streets.  Slowly, it is revealed that on some level, each soldier in the film wishes to die.  Sometimes, the feeling stems from guilt or  fear of failure. "The Hurt Locker" may be one of the only war movies that avoids taking any kind of moral standpoint on the issue; it's a minor miracle that the necessity of USA's involvement in Iraq is never once questioned. Our cast of American soldiers, unapologetic, professional, and battle hardened, goes about the tedium of their duties, counting the days until their rotation is over. Yet this is not a story about the malaise of Marines. Focusing on a bomb disposal unit, their daily encounters with crude roadside bombs take one hell of a toll on the psyche and, best of all, provide a concept rife with suspense in an environment where enemies lurk around every corner and everyone is expendable. It's fucking intense. 

A tight three-man unit is led, in the loosest sense of the term, by Sgt. James, embodied with uncommon gusto by character actor Jeremy Renner. James is a severely troubled soul with a perfect introduction: "relaxing" in his cabin by blasting hard rock music at full volume. If "war is a drug" as the text intro states, this man is a junkie on his last legs. Instead of cleaning out medicine cabinets or his friends' wallets, he foresakes any form of a normal life in favor of the constant, inhuman stress of combat. His addiction may make him absurdly calm under pressure -- helpful when the newbie on the team starts to freak out during an outstanding sniping sequence -- and this may make him a "good leader", but underneath that businesslike exterior lies an ugly, violent, compassionless individual. When there are no visible threats, his rampant paranoia will supply imaginary ones. He's also self-absorbed, throwing away his communication headset at one point, later dragging his poor teammates along on an insane search for the engineers of an oil tanker explosion. James is a compelling character, equal parts protagonist and antagonist. Unfortunately, everyone else can only pale in comparison. 

Not to say Sanborn and Eldrich are underwritten characters, they're just "straight man" and "young kid with PTSD", offering little to save James from his obsessive need for combat stress. His superior rank, and obviously the depth of addiction, render their efforts null and void; ultimately they succumb to his fiery, enigmatic personality, for better or worse. The script also falters by including a questionable subplot with a 12 year old who sells bootleg DVDs. After we think it's paid off, rather gruesomely, there's an inexplicable scene that invalidates those events, turning James into an unapologetic dick to boot. This must be the only unnecessary content in this otherwise drum-tight story. 130 minutes is a bit long, though. There are a couple very minor anachronisms, namely a reference to YouTube and a scene where Eldrich is playing "Gears of War", due to unnecessarily establishing the date as 2004. This is quite ignorable.  

Most of the time you won't notice the time flying by, the bomb disposal and combat scenes are so masterfully done (and plentiful) that you can't help but become immersed. Underrated director Kathryn Bigelow establishes geography, maintains her breathless pace and fluidity of action with a carefree ease. The editing and cinematography are flawless; in the case of the "shakycam" used during a handful of scenes, it doesn't take you out of the action (as Paul Greengrass can't avoid doing) but instead enhances the milieu during moments of chaos and confusion. On the flip side, the camera stays very still, holding shots for considerable lengths during scenes of quiet precision, such as the lengthy encounter with the snipers. The high-speed photography, used sparingly but effectively, is also breathtaking. 

"The Hurt Locker" (title never explained or shown until the end) walks a tautly strung tightrope and makes very few missteps in its lengthy journey. It's neither pro- or anti-war, just a story of men trapped in a hellish climate and the one man who may be insane enough to belong there. The exhilaration of victory, as well as the ugly consequences of defeat, are all there, and Bigelow does exactly the right thing by trusting us to sort it all out. For once, a war movie with a brain and no heart on its sleeve.

Came upon this film quite by accident when I saw a trailer online. An Iraq war story, of which there have been many, but directed by one of my favourites Kathryn Bigelow. And she does so with her usual excellent style. Hardly any of the political grandstanding of many Iraq war films, this focuses on men (and they're all men) doing their jobs, and how that job may become an obsession, the only way some people feel alive. This is told via a three man section of a bomb disposal unit, working the streets of Baghdad. Each day they are moments from death, and they continually scan the windows and doors and rooftops around them. Each day they go out and work on disposing or defusing IEDs, inches from death.

The opening quote is "...war is a drug" and this is what it has become for Staff Sergeant William James (Jeremy Renner, brilliant), newly posted to this Baghdad unit. It would have been quite easy for this character to be the stereotype "gung-ho", but Renner and Bigelow let us see deeper inside of him. Of course his attitude rubs Sergeant JT Sanborn (Anthony Mackie, excellent), a guy relaxed only when things go by the numbers. Between them is the young Specialist Owen Eldridge (Brian Geraghty), who idolises both men but can't decide which side he wants to be on.

In a short part later in the film, Bigelow gives us an excellent portrayal of the confusion and out-of-placeness that some soldiers feel when they get home. Everything feels wrong to the character, and only when he's back in Iraq does he feel comfortable.

Despite some flaws in military procedure (which only people with experience/knowledge would pick up) and a little bit of "spot the guest star" (Guy Pearce, David Morse, Ralph Fiennes all in small roles) and there being little "plot" per-se (which some reviewers take the film to task), this is an excellent character examination piece of men at war.

Caustic and bordering the edge of heroic insanity, Kathryn Bigelow's newest movie, an action drama set on the streets of Baghdad in 2004 just as the Iraqi insurgency was cutting its teeth on American firepower, is really just...intense. There really is no other way to describe it.  For those of you skeptical about a female action-movie director don't stick your noses up just yet...she's the one who gave ya 'Point Break'! Episodic in its structure, gritty and uncompromising in its appearance and generally unsentimental in its morality, HL is one of the purest forms of the war movie I've seen in mainstream theaters for a long while. There is a fair amount of war violence but for the most part it's delicately rendered and wonderfully suspenseful. Everything with this movie lies in the build-up. I was a bit torn at certain times when I was trying to figure out whether or not our director was trying to push an agenda or not (something that irritates the hell out of me). I have my opinions about a potential ivory tower interpretation of the US military, but I decided that ultimately, given the controversial nature of politics in our day and age, this is a pretty politically benign film given the bog standard and what we have here really just tries to look at the rigors of combat with a raw eye for detail and emotion. That said, I can forgive a few scenes that ruffled my feathers when it came to authenticity (there's a sniper scene that was perfectly executed cinematically speaking but still bugged the hell out of me...but don't worry cause as far as I can tell its mostly a purist issue). The overall experience is as anxious as walking through a minefield and sharp as a spool of razor wire. I tip my hat to Jeremy Renner's performance as Staff Sergeant William James: a not-too-crazy but not-too-sane member of a bomb disposal unit handling IEDs. He taps into his character just right, making the depiction something that is utterly unconventional yet wholly controlled. And I don't want to forget the cameos by three big (or at least relatively big) stars that add a richness to an already bold texture-- but I'll leave that as a present for those of you who want to be pleasantly surprised! If you've got the stomach for war movies, or if you're a guy who values what he's got between his legs, then I definitely recommend this!

This isn't one of the best movies of the year, it's one of the best of this decade! Iraq movies are considered box office poison, but this doozy of a film from director Kathryn Bigelow is actually making hefty dough. And for good reason, this is a movie that doesn't settle for easy preaching, preferring instead to get deep inside the heads of men doing life-risking jobs. 

The movie kicks off with an elite bomb-squad unit in Baghdad that watches its staff sergeant die trying to defuse a bomb (Guy Pearce). A new bomb expert William James (Jeremy Renner, who I last saw being scary as hell in Dahmer) is brought in to serve with soldiers J.T Sanborn (Anthony Mackie,excellent) and Owen Eldridge (Brian Geraghty). Sanborn fears James' recklessness and what follows is a taut and combustible thriller in which you feel every bead of sweat and quiet breath that goes along with their situation. All the actors come up aces, especially Renner, who deserves major Oscar consideration. Every look into his eyes is window into the soul of a man who has seen much. And watch out for a cameo from Lord Voldemort himself Ralph Fiennes.

Bigelow, working from a script by former Rolling Stone contributor Mark Boal, who followed a bomb squad unit on assignment, spare no punches. There's action and it's palpable. Bigelow may be a woman, but her films (Near Dark, Blue Steel, Point Break, Strange Days) have the power to make most of her male counterparts look like absolute sissies. This is her crowning achivement, and if Oscar had any brains they'd recognize that. This is a rare miracle of a movie, one that shows that movies that do give a damn do have a place in bloated movie summer.

A war movie utterly lacking in pretense, there is no overriding social or political message, it's the entirely personal story of one of the worst places in the world and the kind of person who could thrive there. Staff Sergeant William James (Jeremy Renner) is one such person. The very definition of a loose cannon. He is a bomb disposal expert in Iraq and he is damn good at his job. In fact, his job is really the only thing he's good at because he has a reckless streak four miles wide and it makes him hard to be around, or hard to feel safe around. He is in his element when his life (and basic physical structure) is inches away from disappearing in a flash of hot light.

The movie is structured in a fairly segmented fashion, with some follow through plot threads, character arcs to connect each segment but the movie is split into scenarios (much like a video game, really), each one involving the team being stuck in the thick of it; there are bombs hidden in the dirt, bombs loaded in cars while hidden insurgents take shots at them, caught in a sniper stand-off in the punishing sun, etc.

Every one of these scenes is intensity magnified, it is the first time in a long time where I was genuinely on the edge of my seat, heartrate jacked, buzzing with nervous energy and excitement with every development. Kathryn Bigelow has built a near perfect construct of tension, it grips you like a vice from beginning to end and you have no idea how it's going to turn out - there is no margin of safety in this movie - anything is possible. The action here is so intense and nerve shredding that I almost feel like I have post-traumatic stress. 

It goes to show that you don't need a huge pyrotechnics budget and overclocked ILM computers to create a great action sequence - you just need a good script, great director and a character you care about.

Jeremy Renner first appeared on my radar in 28 Weeks Later, he wasn't given a great deal to do but he made an impression. It was in The Assassination of Jesse James by the Coward Robert Ford that I really started to pay attention to him. Much like every actor in that film, Renner brought his A-game and made me a fan for life. In a perfect world, The Hurt Locker would represent Renner achieving movie star status. Alas, he's in an indie movie that nobody will see because they're too busy chewing the Transformers cud. There is a cocky/casual ease to his character which makes him joyfully watchable and exhilirating during his bomb disarming scenes, his devil may care attitude to his job brings to mind a more laid back Mel Gibson, with a slow burning intensity running under the surface. He carries this film effortlessly and gives a performance worthy of an Oscar nomination. In fact, given the Academy has increased the number of Best Picture nominations to 10, I would put good money on this being an easy lock for that 10.

The Hurt Locker manages to make a very affecting commentary on a man without purpose beyond his job, but doesn't point fingers or disapprove at the same time, it's almost tragic to watch him utterly fail to connect to civillian life but you cannot help but feel a charge when you see him walk away from it all and back into the fray - because he's the best there is, and the world needs glorious fuck-ups like him to make things safer for everyone else.

The notion of yet another motion picture concerning the Iraq War is probably about as welcome as a knife in the eye. While it may be a pertinent topic in this day and age, it's a flat cinematic subject, with Hollywood producing generally stodgy movies of bloated self-importance marred by various miscalculations (Rendition, The Kingdom, and so on). Thank heavens, then, for Kathryn Bigelow's superb The Hurt Locker. Among the various reasons that Bigelow's flick works where others have failed is that it never endeavours to be "about" the war in Iraq; rather, it accepts the war as a background setting for a fascinating character study regarding the potentially addictive thrills of mortal danger.

Set during the early stages of the post-invasion period in Iraq in 2004, The Hurt Locker follows a group of American soldiers known as Bravo Company who specialise in bomb disposal. With just a few weeks remaining before they are rotated back to the United States, their Sergeant meets with an unfortunate end. This leaves the other soldiers in the unit to serve their final weeks with a new comrade; Staff Sergeant William James (Renner). Much to the chagrin of his fellow soldiers, James is an adrenaline junkie with no qualms about disarming a bomb device manually (and thus breaking protocol). The plot of The Hurt Locker from there is episodic, with the soldiers shifting from conflict to conflict. Tension is a killer during these sequences, because explosive devices aimed at everyone and no-one could be disguised beneath any pile of garbage. Since a bomb would take out anybody and anything within a certain radius, James must approach one of the devices alone to disarm it (with the perimeter maintained by his fellow soldiers). Thus, one of the most repeated images of the film is of the unaccompanied James as he wanders into a strangely deserted space - a fitting visual metaphor for the character's emotional and personal isolation from those around him, both near and far (one even gets the sense his wife and kid back home are never close in his mind).

The Hurt Locker was scripted by Mark Boal; a journalist who based the film's screenplay on his own experiences. Even if you're unaware of this fact before watching the movie, you'll likely suspect it because a clear and unvarnished sense of reality permeates every frame. This is an apolitical, boots-on-the-ground war picture. Not once do the characters stop to discuss why they are there, and they never discuss the wayward politics of the war. In fact, the movie has no political agenda. The filmmakers don't care if the invasion and occupation is right or wrong - all that matters is that the troops are in the country, have a job to do, and are fighting for survival. Much like a number of prior films that have touched on the Iraqi conflict (such as Jarhead), The Hurt Locker portrays a meandering battle that ends up being less about specific offenses and more about maintenance. Unpredictable combat leads to unpredictable schedules, and (particularly for a bomb disposal unit) the call of duty comes when it comes. Right from the opening scene, there's a potent sense that no character is safe, and death can come at any moment. It's this terrifying uncertainty that fuels the story's drama.

Another of the greatest strengths of The Hurt Locker is that it quickly and decisively re-establishes Kathryn Bigelow's position as one of the best action filmmakers in the business. Speaking from a technical standpoint, this film is a stunner from start to finish. Bigelow has always had a knack for directing action in complicated, even abnormal scenarios (like surfers robbing banks in Point Break), and the deserts of Iraq are no different, with the director exhibiting an amazing command for the physical details of filmmaking while shifting through the various set-pieces. A viewer can viscerally feel the danger the characters are in, as most of the film was shot on location in Jordan using an effective documentary style. Interestingly, cinematographer Barry Ackroyd utilised four handheld cameras at any one time, capturing a total of about 200 hours of footage. Even with this handheld disposition, the frame is never rocked too much. However, it must be said that despite this technical competency, the movie fails to resonate as much as something like Saving Private Ryan or Platoon.

The film's cast boasts such names as Ralph Fiennes, Guy Pearce and David Morse, but these big-name actors are relegated to minor roles. This is intentional since, although these well-known stars may entice people to watch the movie, they can detract from the reality of the situation. The main players of The Hurt Locker are instead Jeremy Renner, Anthony Mackie and Brian Geraghty, each of whom pulls off their characters with complete assurance and compelling enthusiasm.

Kathryn Bigelow's The Hurt Locker is not a film that assumes an ideological stand regarding the Iraq War. Instead, it aspires to present viewers with a war film about the ways in which a unit of soldiers react to the pressures of combat. In fact, if a few details were changed, this could be set during any war. To the credit of the filmmakers, the movie only misfires a few times - a major detractor is when the focus leaves Iraq on a couple of occasions to examine William James' life in America, but neither time is necessary. The second trip home provides an explanation for James' risky behaviour that's a bit too on the nose, especially when combined with the music video-style recruitment commercial that closes the film.

If anyone has been close-minded enough to argue that a woman isn't capable of creating an authentic, raw and thoroughly nerve-wracking cinematic portrayal of war, he or she need only watch Kathryn Bigelow's The Hurt Locker to be convinced otherwise.  During this upcoming weekend, millions of people are gonna flock to see the Transformers sequel, which I will fervently stay away from; I saw the first one and thought it was one of the loudest and annoying pieces of crap I'd ever witnessed on a big screen, and now the pundits are saying that the new movie is longer, louder and more annoying.  No, thank you.  Luckily, for those who want a full-on action movie, there's the alternative of The Hurt Locker, which has its dialogue-based moments, but is mostly a compilation of edge-of-your-seat action sequences that are also incredibly realistic.  

War movies tend to go over the top in terms of depicting prolonged shoot-outs and explosion extravaganzas, but The Hurt Locker chooses to exhibit more restraint, with action sequences that are devoid of strident blow-ups and instead focus on the strategic approaches taken by U.S. soldiers who are working as bomb technicians in Baghdad.  The meticulous way in which they handle their tasks and the trepidation they experience whenever they face a dangerous situation is presented amazingly well in the film.

The film begins with a quote by Chris Hedges, who said that "the rush of battle is often a potent and lethal addiction, for war is a drug."  It's a fine way to begin this movie, which does a solid job at showing the range of emotions that can be experienced on the battlefield, from the sadistic euphoria of making a kill, to the remorse upon realizing what that actually means, to the profound fear that these few seconds may be your last.  Though we meet several of the bomb technicians, the story centers around Staff Sergeant William James (Jeremy Renner), Sergeant JT Sanborn (Anthony Mackie) and Specialist Owen Eldrige (Brian Geraghty, who was also in Jarhead, so here's a guy who can actually recognize a strong script for a war movie when he reads it).  One of these three guys shows a humane side when he actually sort of bonds with an Iraqi child who sells pirate DVDs, and the other two eventually comment on "how weird" it is that he developed that sort of relationship with that kid, and this is because, as we eventually note, they don't really see the Iraqis as people, but merely as pieces of the puzzle in this mission they have to be in until their term ends and they get to return to the states.

The Hurt Locker is particularly scrupulous in getting the technical details right.  At one point, one of our characters finds that he can't shoot, but it's not only because of the predictably standard reason of running out of ammo, but because the gun itself is jammed as a result of being stained with the blood of a soldier who was killed, so someone suggests the "spit and rub" approach to solve the issue.  All of this is clear evidence that Bigelow was incredibly resourceful in putting this project together.  There's a moment in the film that is one of those sad-yet-funny things, in which the guys are shooting and one of them asks "What are we shooting at?!" and someone else responds "I don't know!".  While this may seem like a cheap attempt at comedy, I think it's just the script being accurate in terms of showing us the truly chaotic and disorganized nature of shoot-outs, which in real life are certainly not as perfectly choreographed as they are in your standard Hollywood action film.

The opinion that this is the finest cinematic take on the military struggle that the U.S. faces in Iraq is hard to refute.  Recent mediocre attempts such as In the Valley of Elah, The Kingdom and Stop-Loss really gave me the feeling that we probably wouldn't see a good film about this subject until a few years after it was over, which is why I was happily surprised by The Hurt Locker.  Not since Jarhead has such an effective and raw depiction of the arduous life of a soldier in a Middle Eastern desert been brought to the big screen, and even though Jarhead is better, this is still a worthy addition to the elite list of good war movies.  While the film eschews some of the space it had for character development to give more room to its action sequences, those action sequences are so deeply entrancing and eerily authentic that they make the film very much worth seeing.

3.5: This is a fascinating, complex, and laser-focused picture that excels in every area it touches.  The film does not directly concern itself with anything outside of this little world, despite the huge ramifications the war depicted in the story has.  This is the correct approach or at least the approach that has worked best so far.  I haven't seen all the OIF/OEF/GWOT films, but of the many I have, I'm almost certain this is the best.  The simplicity of its style and message is refreshing, when compared to the convoluted and expansive attempts at reaching a deeper meaning in many other OIF/OEF pictures.  By saying less, it actually says and means more.  It is simply non-stop character exploration and action that leaves one breathless and enthralled.  It concerns itself with more than just Iraq, for instance, and extends its message out to encompass the totality of warfare and its varying effects on individuals.  It's all right there in the opening quote: "war is a drug".  Bigelow doesn't get bogged down in the why and doesn't sermonize.  She simply gives the who, what, where, how and leaves it up to the viewer to figure out the rest.  Films almost always fail when they try to teach or explain.  Causing someone to feel, which this visceral and cerebral film has done for me at least, is a far more effective method.  The fast action, elegant editing, prolonged tension, and complete immersion in this environment left me with a strong sense of being viscerally involved in the story.  It also made one stop and think about why they were feeling what they were feeling as well, which is where the cerebral element comes into play.  The manner in which it was filmed really forces one into the environment and into the characters heads.  The performances are superb across the board, with Renner being especially unnerving.  War certainly has many unintended consequences, one of which could certainly be that it is highly addicting, as many have said.  However, as is also clear here, it's only addicting to some.  Some can partake of cocaine, alcohol, gambling, warfare, etc and not be particularly effected, while others have to launch themselves down the rabbit hole once they've gotten a taste. The Hurt Locker begins with a quote, emphasizing on the last part of the phrase: "The rush of battle is often a potent and lethal addiction, for war is a drug." I've heard about that book which the quote derives from... well, y'all can google it for yourself, heh. In a nutshell, The Hurt Locker unfolds like a series of random events strung together. To further generalize the film, it's basically an action picture. The Hurt Locker is a war film that plays like a pseudo-documentary, so expect nauseating camera movements and zooms. However, it's not jarring and kinda transcends the usual spectrum a war film is limited to, not only placing the viewer in the center of it all, but to get a sense of where the characters are coming from. Unlike most Iraq War-based films, there's no politics or sides being taken here. Even being set in the Iraq war, the zone is merely a backdrop and it need not matter to what the film is attempting to show. It's almost like the film could be set in any war. But these series of events need to convey something. We follow our "hero" Staff Sgt. William James (Jeremy Renner) and his escapades on bomb diffusion and other encounters during wartime, completing his tasks with a smile on his face (or more appropriately, showing no fear), smoking a cigarette as a toast to his recent accomplishments, and wrapping it all up by adding another token to his treasure trove of near-death experiences (he finds it interesting to hold something that almost killed him, including a wedding ring). James has other comrades by his side attempting to dissuade his constant disregard of safety by interjecting concerns and protocol. Enter Sgt. JT Sandborn (Anthony Mackie), the one who goes by the book, and Specialist Owen Eldridge (Brian Geraghty), the more uncertain one who's just about reached the tipping point of his stay. During the last days/weeks of their tour, they encounter seemingly random events but all of which are interrelated and revealing for each other. Towards the end of the film, one of the guys asks James how he takes the risk. James' answer is simply, " I dunno... I guess I don't think about it." Simple response... at the end of the film, he comes to a small realization, and perhaps the answer he was looking for: He loves it. Not just a job fulfillment (well, maybe still) but a passion, his only true passion. It's his wife, and it's his life. James isn't inhuman or crazy, he still manages to show emotions (he bonds well with the kid who sells him bootleg DVDs). He finds his role in a world where many people still continue to search, or blindly accept/follow. His job is dangerous and he may be arrogant when it comes to work, but it's something he knows he's good at, and it's the one thing in the world he truly loves. Suddenly, it's not like a film detailing how war is a drug... it's like watching someone withholding a dangerous passion and its effects. Actually, I guess passions and addictions go hand in hand. Mid-way in the film, Sandborn asks James something along the lines of, "You think I could do what you do?" James' response, "Hell no," complete with a smile.

"The Hurt Locker" is a major artistic achievement from director Kathryn Bigelow and is one of the best war films of our time. It is a career-changing film for Bigelow, who has previously specialized in formulaic genre movies. She has finally come into her own and revealed herself to be a filmmaker of uncommon power. 

Equally impressive is the understated yet fierce acting, especially from Jeremy Renner and Brian Geraghty, who give breakthrough performances that deserve to be remembered at Oscar time. Anthony Mackie is also very good. Several well-known actors, including Ralph Fiennes, have brief cameos.

Let's hope that Americans won't overlook "Hurt Locker" the way they have ignored every other serious film about the Iraq War. But then again, this film is not about the Iraq War. It's about warfare. It just happens to be set in Iraq.

Instead of focusing on big explosions and large combat sequences, "Hurt Locker" zooms in almost microscopically on a three-man unit that specializes in defusing bombs. Not only must these three young men deal on a daily basis with the danger of bombs, they are also under constant threat of sniper fire. The non-stop tension is maddening. I've never heard the phrase "hurt locker," and it's not explained in the film. But I suspect it refers to a dangerous situation where you are locked in on all sides. Checkmate, if you will.

Also caught in this hurt locker are the countless innocent civilians trying to live their lives in peace. One's heart especially goes out to the children. Bigelow does a wonderful job capturing the vulnerability of children by introducing us to a boy who sells DVDs to American soldiers. This boy (played beautifully by Christopher Sayegh) has a dazzling personality and befriends Renner's character. When the boy is the victim of an unspeakable atrocity, the tragedy of war is exposed most heart-wrenchingly. 

Renner's character, William James, is the sole member of the three-man unit who defuses explosives. The other two guard him from sniper fire and perform various other essential functions. James is a unique character, to say the least. He at times doesn't seem aware of the danger he is facing, walking almost blithely, for example, into areas littered with explosives. Sometimes he throws off his protective gear if it is getting in the way. James also has an uncanny instinct for bombs. Watching him locate and defuse an explosive is like watching an artist at work. All of the devices are slightly different, so he has to study them with care. He doesn't wear gloves, apparently to get a better feel for them. He touches a live bomb almost with awe.

When James joins the unit, he is initially perceived as reckless, which makes him highly unpopular. But the relationship between the three men evolves over the course of the film in very interesting ways.

I hope Kathryn Bigelow sticks with serious films for the rest of her career. There is no reason a filmmaker of her stature and talent needs to be churning out mindless product for the studios. Please, Ms. Bigelow, stick with work like "Hurt Locker," work that will live forever.

Just saw "The Hurt Locker", and I must say I have mixed feelings about the  flick. I appreciated the cinema verite, moment in time, style of the film. It was a great stylistic choice that suits a subject like the occupation of Iraq. The movie doesn't attempt to explain too much, and soon one is slowly sucked into the debillitating situation that war always is. The performances were outstanding. Renner's a guy quickly on the rise, and as always, Mackey showed  versatility as a performer since his exceptional turn as M&M's rapper foil in the surprisingly good "8 Mile". Director Bigelow did a more than competent job in depicting the surreality  of war. Most flix about the Iraq War are preachy,and therefore the lack of success of those films. In "The Hurt Locker", the angst felt by the members of the bomb squad is as pressurized as it gets. One doesn't need to be told why these soldiers are cracking, because you're along for the ride before you know it.
Now for my problem with the film. It could be seen as a technicality by some. For a movie so grounded in reality, some of the scenes in the film don't jibe with what we know to be the rules of engagement. For instance, in one scene, a car is seen speeding past a roadblock and is engaged by a single soldier when he decides to stop. The guy is then given a chance to slowly back away from the gung ho trooper in front of him. Even one who has a cursory knowledge of the "Army Field Manual" knows that in such a case the man would have been admonished to halt no more than twice before his cab would have been made to look like Swiss cheese. There are several scenes where the the soldiers  appear to be a little slow on the trigger in the face of immediate danger. And too, are there really only three people on a bomb squad crew? There were a few fact-straining moments in the  film, but not enough to keep it from being the best movie yet on the Iraq War. Almost worth seeing just for the cameo by Joseph,(or is it Ralph or "Rafe"?)Fiennes, as a "private contractor" that gets his due. By the way, when did we stop referring to these guys as "soldiers of fortune" or "mercenaries"? IMDB says it's Ralph, pronounced "Rafe", so we'll go with that. In lieu of catching an excellent old episode of the TV show "Combat", see "The Hurt Locker". When you see it, the phrase "casualties of war" may take on new meaning, since most of them are still on, and many will never leave, the fight on the battlefield.

I was pleased to see a film pertaining to this war that didn't seem to have any political idealogy about the war itself, but instead sought to detail what the experience there was like.  It is also interesting because the soldiers aren't ultra idealistic, but real men with their own problems who nevertheless are brave and admirable in the line of duty.  Jeremy Renner does particularly well as the cocky upstart that is at the center of the film, and really evolves as a character by the conclusion of the film.  My central problem with the film is that in its effort to make it as realistic and true to procedure as possible, the film suffered from some pacing issues that dragged slightly in between the really thrilling moments. THE HURT LOCKER has no political messages, no preachy story that its trying to shove down viewer's throats. Its just a raw and very realistic look at the lives of army bomb disposal teams in Iraq, and it's pretty intense for its entire 2 1/2 hour runtime. Jeremy Renner is an actor I've also been a fan of for quite a few years in the various bit parts he's had, but his lead role in this is sure to catapult him to super-stardom. His Sgt. James is a man who appears to be flat out addicted to the constant danger his life is in every time to goes out into the field to disarm a bomb. For an independent movie, THE HURT LOCKER is amazingly loaded with wall-to-wall scenes of tension that make its big-budget brothers this summer look positively boring in comparison. I have never really enjoyed war films. I am by no means a pacifist, but to me all the stories seem to be the same, and until now, I've been uninterested. It wasn't until viewing the Academy's best picture of 2010, The Hurt Locker, that I started to see things differently. In these films, it's not so much the story line that matters, but rather the characters that are featured in the film. The description of The Hurt Locker is just as bland as any other war picture, the story of a unit in Iraq that is responsible for disarming explosives. What makes this film so unique and made it the best film of 2010 was William James, played remarkably well by Jeremy Renner. Renner is known as an action star, so when I saw him nominated for best actor, I couldn't believe it. The truth is Renner's performance in this film was outstanding, because for once, he simply played himself. Renner may have been portraying a Sargent in Iraq, but the personality was his own. Director, Kathryn Bigelow, has become known for letting actors be themselves in developing their characters personalities, to the point where even some of the dialogue was in the spur of the moment. The Hurt Locker is a powerful film, with remarkable events and heartbreaking moments, but it's the films personality that is larger than life. I enjoyed every second of this film and it was truly the best choice the Academy could have made for best picture.

"I hate this place. It's horrible." That seems to be the prevalent sentiment about Iraq from our fighting men and women. And most moviegoers.  In The Hurt Locker, Jeremy Renner doesn't hate Iraq, at least because it allows him to do the one thing he loves most: get his kicks by defusing bombs.  The Hurt Locker centers around the Marines' bomb technicians, who, in a country where everything is dangerous, have perhaps the most dangerous of all missions: to head towards the bombs left behind by Iraqi insurgents and shut them down while everyone else runs the opposite direction.  Renner is part of Bravo Company along side squad sergeant Anthony Mackie and technician Brian Geraghty.  They are all refreshingly real people, screwed up in different ways by the many months of their assignment in Iraq.  Geraghty in particular is excellent in portraying his fear of dying in the desert as he watches his fellow soldiers die often senseless deaths.  The Hurt Locker strives for gritty realism.  This is a movie about defusing bombs were the bombs don't have red digital timers ticking down, if you can believe that.  The characters, Renner especially, struggle against the macho action hero mentality movies and video games ingrain in American males.  His attempts to go beyond their mission and attempt macho heroics end badly.  Renner goes on a side mission to avenge what he believes is the murder of a young Iraqi boy he defended and this is the only sequence of The Hurt Locker that seems inauthentic.  There's a bravura sequence where Bravo Company and a stranded squad are ambushed in the desert, where they have to resort to fighting with sniper tactics that's riveting. Ralph Fiennes, David Morse, Evangeline Lilly, and Guy Pearce also make brief but welcome appearances.

'The Hurt Locker' is an amazing synthesis of two usually separate types of movies: the nail-biter, and the character study.  In fact, many sequences in this movie are brilliant examples of both.  This is an amazing return to the big screen for director Kathryn Bigelow, who has an impressive resume including 'Near Dark', 'Point Break' (yes, that's right), and 'Strange Days', and who has been absent from theatres since her 2002 bomb 'K-19: The Widowmaker'.  The movie, about a U.S. bomb disposal squad in Baghdad in 2004, focuses on William James (Jeremy Renner), a Staff Sergeant who fearlessly walks into each bomb scenario.  This horrifies his company mates, especially his supervisor, Sgt. Sanborn (Anthony Mackie); they're only weeks away from the company rotation, and they certainly don't want this guy to ruin that for them.  However, James isn't a suicidal/death-wish guy: this character could've easily been a recycled version of Mel Gibson in the first act of 'Lethal Weapon'.  Instead, he treats war and danger like a drug (to paraphrase the movie's opening quote), and carries a box under his bed that's full of mementos from several of his 873(!) defused bombs.  Considering the sheer number of bomb scenes, they're never repetitive, managing to up the stakes each and every time.  Plus, they come in surprisingly rapid succession; they occupy a significant amount of the movie's 2-hour, 10-minute running time.  The movie (filmed in Jordan) is refreshingly simple in many ways, which really helps to make the movie as effective as it can be; even in some scenes that don't rely on bombs, like an extended desert shootout, you'll still be on the edge of your seat.  It rarely stumps to long, drawn-out speeches to explain its characters.  Instead, we learn about them mainly through their actions and especially their field behavior.  Also along those lines of keeping things simple, the movie doesn't bog things down by inserting a political agenda about the War in Iraq, which is also refreshing, compared to many of the war-inspired movies of the past few years.  The movie doesn't question the war itself; in fact, this movie didn't even need to be set in this particular war.  Instead, 'The Hurt Locker' focuses on why the characters themselves are there, James in particular.  Finally, I appreciate how Bigelow restrains her style for the movie; from the surfing photography of 'Point Break' to the bravura single-take virtual reality scenes in 'Strange Days', style has been an important component of her films.  However, in this movie, the only stylistic detours are a couple of super-super-slow-motion shots, which are deployed very, very carefully.  Although the main cast members are relatively unknown, Bigelow brings several 'names' into the mix.  First, there's the super-tense opening sequence featuring Guy Pearce as another bomb squad expert. (If you want, you can watch this scene in full here: http://www.hulu.com/watch/81586/)  Ralph Fiennes shows up for the desert shootout that I mentioned earlier.  David Morse appears briefly to commend James on his many defused bombs.  And finally, there's a very brief contribution by Evangeline Lilly (Kate from 'Lost') as James' wife back in the States.  (Her two scenes total less than a minute of screen time.)   However, there are two slight missteps in the movie.  The first is a chunk of the movie where James sneaks off-base to do some investigative work about a vendor kid friend of his.  The second is a scene involving an Army psychiatrist who decides to take a rare trip into the war zone; for a movie that prides itself on suspense and not knowing what will happen next, you pretty much know his fate as soon as he first decides that he wants to tag along.  All in all, this is definitely a hidden gem in this summer season, and it's well worth your time and money if it's near you.

The most cerebral and intriguing thriller since "No Country for Old Men", Kathryn Bigelow's Iraq War film "The Hurt Locker" is as emotionally and psychologically intense as it's phenomenal set pieces. Sgt. James (Jeremy Renner) leads a U.S. Army IED (Improvised Explosive Device) diffusion team in Iraq. As the teams leader, James is reckless, obsessive, and something of a loose cannon. He is addicted to the rush of combat, the thrill of adrenaline coursing through his veins. This causes tensions between him and his two teammates Sgt. Sanborn (Anthony Mackie) and Eldridge (Brian Geraghty), who are very much by the book type soldiers. The film is at once a nail-biting war thriller and a fascinating psychological character study of James. The film's standout strengths lie in the masterful direction of Kathryn Bigelow (likely to become the first woman to ever win a Best Director oscar for her work in this film), the fantastic screenplay by Mark Boal, and a searing performance by Jeremy Renner. I found myself literally sweating and holding on to the arms of my seat for dear life due to the level of suspense the film manages to evoke in EVERY. SINGLE. SCENE. It will not only leave you breathless and beaten, but the emotional, psychological, and visceral intensity of the film does not let up until the credits finally roll. As haunting as it is intense, "The Hurt Locker" hits hard and never stops. I will stay with you for a long time. 

P.S. Michael Bay can suck this film's dick. Kathryn Bigelow made a war film without the kind of military connections Bay always brags about having, and it was 10000000000000000X better than anything he's ever made.

There are a few flimsier moments of movie reality, which may be considered lapses, but they went more to illustrating a character's dilemma in a way that was still beneficial to the movie later on, even if you question why it's happening as it's happening. Kathryn Bigelow's handheld camerawork is jaunty and immersive without being too gimmicky and annoying.  I walked into this film expecting great things, and it delivered. Here's just the film to restore your faith in the war movie again.  The Hurt Locker is a potent, near-perfect blend of heart-stopping suspense and thought-provoking storytelling. This film about the grueling task of disarming bombs in the middle Iraq streets is more than just a war movie. It's a work of art. Combining incredible visuals, mind-blowing heart-wrenching sequences, and superb acting across the board, The Hurt Locker doesn't just pull you to the edge of your seat. It grabs you and forces you into the middle of the action with suspense-building scene after suspense-building scene. 
The film follows an army bomb squad in the current Iraq war and depicts the horrifying effects on one's mind, emotions and actions. The lead character, James- played brilliantly so by Jeremy Remmer- is an addrenaline junkie who gets his fix from marching seemingly unconcerned into the heat of battle to dismantle a bomb and then return to his pack of cigarettes after offering up a satisfying "all done" as if he were simply repairing an air conditioning vent. However, the hostile surroundings of a third world terrorist country catch up to the heroes nearly to the point of all control lost- even for James. It's up to him, even in the most dire moments, to maintain his soldiers' faith and trust.
Complexity isn't this flick's game. Shockingly enough, its the relative simplicity of it that makes it so impressive. How anyone can shake your mind with such powerful intensity takes a creative stroke of genius.
Don't take the first somewhat nonchalant humor moments lightly. The Hurt Locker just flat out causes chills. It wages war against your senses, takes you out of your comfort zone, and never lets you go. This film about an addiction to adrenaline, is absolutely addicting to the eyes. The stunning camera work and editing go hand in hand with outstanding directing creativity from front-woman Katheryn Bigalow, who through perfectly shot sequences and production, earned herself a best director Oscar nomination.
To put it in the simplest of terms, The Hurt Locker is the first of many to be an early front runner for best picture. While many will come along, this film will be very very hard to top. It even outdoes last year's Slumdog Millionaire, which to this point was deemed impossible. The Hurt Locker is the work of art that cinema has been waiting for for years. It stands alone as the most intellectual depiction of combat this side of the 2000s and will go down as one of the best war films of all time.

I had the honor of attending a screening for The Hurt Locker at the DGA (Los Angeles) last night.  The POV visuals and sound design are intense...you stop holding your girlfriend's hand and feel guilty indulging in luxuries like popcorn while watching.  I felt like it was my duty as a citizen to watch this film, almost like a tribute to those who actually live/fight terrifying wars like this.  (Pointless wars, right?  Alas this is a film review not a political commentary)

I know a film is good when I stop watching the framing of the shots, the edits, the lighting...and I simply lose myself in the story.  From the first scene to the final shot, I never felt like a director at a screening...I felt like a fly on the wall during routine explosion missions, which are never "routine."

Director Kathryn Bigelow attended the screening and treated us to Q&A (moderated by Curtis Hanson) after the film.  She explained her writer's first-hand experience with bomb techs as a journalist...the access and knowledge helped them develop the most realistic view of the Iraq war ever created in a fictional film.  She also explained the "profile" approach to the storytelling: the characters don't change throughout the film, instead we as viewers change our opinion of the character as we see them react in various situations.

The film has amazing texture (shot on 16mm) and the actors are believable because they're not A-listers.  I am not usually a war buff, I never watch world news and I don't read novels about combat...but this film exceeds expectations and thrives despite it's small budget and obvious challenges of shooting on-location in the Middle East.  This film is worthy of seeing and discussing after...I look forward to reading other reviews from peer film enthusiasts.

The phrase "edge of your seat" is tossed around a lot (mostly by critics trying to get a quick plug into a commercial), but it's rare to find a movie that actually does make you, if not sit uncomfortably forward in your seat, then keep you continually in a state of tension.  And that is the key word in this film, "tension".  In a film about a crazed, thrill seeking bomb expert disarming IED's in Iraq and the two men assigned to keep him alive, you would expect it, but this film goes far and beyond in making us feel the paranoia and tension of this particular war.   The film stars Jeremy Renner as said crazed bomb expert, who will go to any extreme to put himself in harm's way.  This puts him at odds with Anthony Mackie, who plays the man who's main job it is to keep him alive while he is disarming bombs.  This becomes extremely difficult as a job goes on, as crowds of Iraqis begin to gather, any of whom could be carrying a weapon and could open fire at any moment.  Add to this the possibility of the bomb going off, and you have a recipe for some truly riveting scenes.  Both of these main actors are great, representing two very different points of view about a soldier's mentality in war.  There are also a series of fantastic cameo roles by some great actors, including Guy Pearce, Ralph Fiennes, and David Morse.  The film has some wonderful action sequences, including the best and, I assume, most realistic sniper duel I have ever seen.  But the film isn't an action movie.  In the end, it's a look at a man who is addicted to war.  He's a man who behaves like he's an action star living in a constant action movie, even when the reality of the world around him leads to him getting other people hurt.

War is the most potent of life's possible dramas, it's heightened mortality purifies emotions and adds great consequence to every choice, so it has always been a popular source of setting and inspiration for film-makers. This most recent of wars,Iraq or 'The Gulf War 2 : Electric Boogaloo' has proved no different however the films it is producing have. There has been a consistent attempt to paint this war realistically in fiction, if not in journalism, that has made these films dry and lifeless. The grit, hidden agendas and attempted PC portrayals has lead to a genre that seems to focus more on politics then death, that strikes you as a rant and not a story. Here however is a film that does it right.

Bigelow manages to not only tread a thin and perfect path along the border of realism and entertainment but does so in a completely original fashion. The EOD unit (Bomb squad) which Bigelow has chosen to focus on is unique both to this present war and to this picture. It provides both an insight into what is surely one of the biggest problems faced by the soldiers on that front and a medium in which to further concentrate all that excitement, tension and fear that war alone can evoke. 

From the very first scene in the film there is a tension present that rarely lets up, every face or movement is a threat and every choice is one that could result in either life or death, a fact we soon find out the hard way. You feel instantly as if you too are in this war zone, you cautiously eye the surroundings with even the most innocuous event proving to be beyond ominous. This is all due to some fantastic camera work and editing and works magnificently to amplify the fear you feel throughout.

While the episodic explosive encounters are what draw you into the film there is a well crafted character piece connecting the vignettes. The three lead soldiers are all very well written and performed, they feel human yet they remain interesting managing the perfect character blend. The relationships between these men are vital yet volatile and are almost as fascinating to watch as the missions. It is often spoken of when a male director manages to accurately portray a female character and so it only seems right to here give mention that Kathryn provides a faultless amount of masculinity and emotion in these soldiers.

Of all the films made so far about our current situation i would say that this is the only one that will survive through into the future. It is certainly contextually relevant but it is also timeless, a tale of fine lines with grand consequences and those who tread them.

What makes this regularly watchable are the ambiguous or vague politics compared to those of a Lamentation on the Bare Heights like Jarhead. There certainly aren't any jabs, but the way Bigelow paints her characters wisely leaves it up to the audience to discern where these guys probably stand, as if it matters when the job is dispelling urban chaos caused by IEDs at the high, but noble risk of one's own life. If anything The Hurt Locker (to my own comfort) merely suggests things along the same lines that Jarhead apparently feels obligated to straight-jacket you with and scream into your ears.

The more I watch The Hurt Locker the more it grows on me, not counting the first time I saw it in theaters. What strikes me is the less famous faces are the ones who become more sympathetic with each viewing. While the presence of Pearce, Fiennes, and Morse--with the utmost humility they show in playing such short roles--definitely works toward the film's purpose as an "independent project", Geraghty's Eldridge and Mackie's Sanborn increasingly become the object of my emotional investments. That's in spite of the fact I know what to expect for them.

They become so sympathetic that I root for their survival throughout the film and welcome it increasingly every time they do. Then, after all is said and done, Renner's James becomes a man so sure of himself yet so paranoid that he simultaneously becomes the squad's emotional rock and the very thing inadvertently pushing his men to the precipice of their own minds, not the war and certainly not the bombs. I find myself rooting neither for or against him, as his strengths and flaws leave him as the guy who is simply... there. Knowing the "rockstar roles" he's got lined up, I only grow more impatient to see him go beyond this role and do something even better than what he did in The Town. He's got the... fragile potential for a career as prolific as Jimmy Stewart (one of the extraordinary "average American" actors I admire the most), but for the next few years I guess I'll have to settle for DiCaprio, who's been coming along handsomely.

Early in the film, one soldier says "In Iraq, you're dead" to another who is just starting on the job of being a soldier in a particular unit in Iraq. One might think it a lame line, and it's even mentioned as such right after the character says it. But it is, actually, accurate in a way. The characters, both the soldiers and those who engage in the suicide bombings (whether all willing or totally against in some small cases), are like the living dead, living through the dead that is, every day and every second. It wears down minds and souls, and it sets apart personalities. Some have to stay professionals, others get blown to bits at a second's notice for just not hustling ass or, perhaps, just standing around not on constant alert. Kathryn Bigalow's film is most exceptional at a level of pure suspense, but there's this underlying feeling too, of what this kind of combat does to a person, that isn't underestimated.

Her film is lean and mean. I don't know for certain whether or not it's accurate to all of the details on the streets and in the desert. Some others have already complained about the lack of authenticity (just look at the IMDb negative comments to give some perspective on the inundation of critical praise from the press). While I can figure Bigalow and her writer did their homework, that's not even what makes the film so palpable and worthwhile. It's creating a sense of what it is to be there, the tension that is completely unpredictable even when all appears to be going right. It's essentially about a bomb squad, a unit that goes around checking out and (hopefully) disarming bombs that have been laid out. The hand-held camera and jittery zoom isn't done for ill-used effect (this isn't, for example, Public Enemies again); not a shot in these moments are wasted, and it gives a new urgency to the "ticking time bomb" scenario that actually means something here as opposed to other sources in TV and movies (24 anyone?)

And it's not without some good dosage of characterization as well. True, Bigalow paints with some broad strokes, at least at first; there's the strong-minded leader Sanborn (Anthony Mackie), who pushes down his fear with his professional sniper eye, the weaker link of the group who tries to hold it together but just can't keep going on with it, Eldridge, (Brian Geraghty), and rounding it up is Jeremy Renner as James, the "adrenaline junkie." It would be easy to say James is the antagonist of the group, and I was fully expecting him to be painted as two-dimensional at best. But if anything he's given the most dimension of anyone (compared to him, in fact, Geragthy is given much less to do except to look frightened, not always a bad thing), as we see him break down over little things that turn bigger, like with the 12 year old kid selling DVD's, or his estranged relationship with his ex-wife and little boy. And on top of this, Renner is simply electrifying in the role, going all over the place emotionally but never missing a beat. It's one of those unforgettable characters in recent war movies.

Bigalow also has other tricks up her sleeve casting wise, such as giving "name" actors parts that aren't actually on screen for very long (this isn't quite a spoiler exactly, the three big ones are Morse, Fiennes and Pearce). And as far as person-to-person drama goes, there are some startling moments, such as that drunken fight between James and Sanborn. So with that covered, with the characters in these situations given that sense of danger at any moment anyway (stray bullets can fly through the barracks, of course, as mentioned just in passing), it's the big sequences that steal the show. In particular is a sniper-fire scene, where the bomb unit stops to help a British jeep with a spare-tire fix only to come under sudden fire from miles away. Rarely does one jump and feel such itching tension in one's seat in this scene and, oddly enough, that turns into a long scene where characters have to wait, at the ready at their snipers, sometimes having to do things simply as getting enough fluids into the system. One is reminded of the sniper sequence in Full Metal Jacket and, as high praise indeed, this is just as good if not given fuller dimension with its equal intensity and patience.
