The Hurt Locker is one of those movies that really just comes out of no where. In this day and age, it's rare to see a movie without a massive advertising campaign and whatnot.

The film follows the three men in a squad stationed in Iraq. Early on in the film, the team's leader (a great guest appearance by Guy Pearce...loved him in Memento and I was happy to see him on the big screen albeit briefly) gets replaced by Sergeant Will James played by Jeremy Renner (SWAT, The Unusuals, 28 Weeks Later).

From the get-go, The Hurt Locker mercilessly lets the audience know that the movie is very realistic. Several different factors account for this realism. One is the dialogue. This is less of a dialogue driven film than it is an action driven film (of sorts...i'll get to the action later) but the dialogue is constantly appropriately delivered and it's simple yet effective. The characters (and the film as a whole) is very human.
Next is the film's look. There is no evident computer generation used which is an breath of fresh air to say the least. It's look is gritty, intimate, and it's style of cinematography lends itself well to that feel. It's pretty much all handheld but not like the Bourne movies. You can actually see what's going on. Camera zoom is utilized very well and artistically throughout the film as it is not overdone and works perfectly in a warzone setting. There's even some slo-mo here and there (not "Zack Snyder here and there") and that also adds to the overall look and feel of the movie.

Perhaps the film's greatest strength is the thick layer of tension that it is so effortlessly and smoothly applied to most of the movie. It truly is remarkable. Much of what accounts for this tension also accounts for the realistic feel (namely the minimalistic use of a score and the intimacy and grittiness of the cinematography), but what can be most credited for the film's tension are the main characters: Will James and his squad mates Sergeant Sanborn (Anthony Mackie) and Specialist Eldridge (Brian Geraghty). Sergeant James, a bomb diffuser, is thrown into situations that are rooted in reality and totally believable, but at the same time they are extremely terrifying, haunting, and even disturbing at times. Jeremy Renner does a brilliant job of portraying James as a character who can totally keep his cool while being surrounded by bombs that can kill his and many others. This trait is once again not overdone and utilized well. James isn't Rambo or John McClane. You just get the impression that he's damn good at his job and a spectacular soldier. When the audience is on the edge of their seats waiting for a bomb to explode and even the character on screen is calm, it significantly adds to the level of tension in the film.

With all that being said, The Hurt Locker did have a few issues that were really only present in the end of the film. In the final act, the film seemed to lose focus a little bit. It starts to stray from the bomb diffusals that were used in lieu of major action setpieces and firefights and begins to lose a little bit of its originality and tension. The movie quickly shifts from being about bravo team's missions while getting to know the characters to being about the characters that happen to be in Iraq fighting a war. Fortunately, once this shift occurs it isn't constant; the rest of the film just feels a little bit spotty. There are moments when the final act drags, but there are a couple moments that top some of the beginning/middle's most powerful ones.

Overall, The Hurt Locker is a fantastic film that takes a fresh look at the warzones of Iraq with constant tension, gritty realism, and a great main character. It stumbles slightly in its final act with a lack of focus and questionable character motives.

War is a drug, and 'The Hurt Locker' is a carefully paced and expertly executed film that puts the audience in the middle of a bomb squads day to day jobs.  The film doesn't have any apparent plot or goals to reach other than our featured characters survivng each day.  It shows the guts it takes to do this job, to put ones life on the line every single day, but it also gives a glimpse into what makes these guys tick.  Why they would risk their lives every day and how it affects everything else in their lives.  This is not a big, bang-em up action/war film, it is a character study of three guys: James, Sanborn and Eldridge. The story focuses mainly on Staff Sergeant William James, played with true vigor and a pure heart by Jeremy Renner.  First, it shows us his bad boy side. Leading us to believe he is this kind of "wild-man" personality that has no fear, but the film soon goes past that archetype and gives us a look into a man who fears not being there for his little boy, someone who is scared he has made the wrong decisions in his life so far and is scared about making the wrong decisions every day in the field; but the drug that is disarming bombs is too strong for Sergeant James to walk away from and that seems to be the theme of Bigelow's film, that this is not simply a job one can do and walk away from, this is something that becomes life, it is addicting, controlling and there is nothing like it in the world. James is scared of alot of things, but when he is disarming that bomb, he feels right at home.  The film also develops a good relationship between James and Sergeant JT Sanborn, played by the terrific Anthony Mackie.  It is a love/hate relationship, there is certainly respect between the two, but Sanborn does not approve of many of James' methods.  This creates the excitement of the film, the uncertainty, the consequences everyone faces and the slow build of mystery that surrounds every incident where James is trying to dismantle an explosive.  The film does a great job of making the audience feel a part of this world, one gets sucked into it and the film gets the critical component of making us realize why this is such a rush for people like Sgt. James when on the surface it would appear to be suicide. It is hard to watch at some points, but it is one that is hard to take your eyes away from as well, it is a truly gripping and moving experience, one that will surely get its deserved recognition. One that will go down as the first, great, Iraq war movie.

Easily one of the best films of the year. Well considering the competition was movies like Transformers 2, it isn't saying much. But this movie would have been a stand-out in any year. A movie so visceral, so raw and so involved in the psyche of a soldier in Iraq has been rare to non-existent. 

For me the most poignant moment of the movie has the lead protagonist standing in the cereal isle of a super market trying to decide which one to buy. In his arena of IED disposal, his decisions changes lives. Cereal is well...cereal.

To me, Apocalypse Now is the I Ching of war movies.  The mindless descent into chaos is palpable on the screen.  Martin Sheen is our tour guide for most of it, but it is only when we get an almost god-like Marlon Brando in the last reel that we get a person who truly understands and is omniscient in parts of the human psyche where no one wants to go. 

The Hurt Locker operates on the same wavelength as that great movie.  From the opening scene to end credits, it is a tense, taut, bundle of adrenaline that knows more about the human condition than any other film I have seen in some time. It is by far the best film of the year, and without a doubt one of the best war movies ever made. 

The movie focuses on those patriotic souls who have to defuse IEDs in Iraq circa 2004. An opening sequence involving an accidental detonation so perfectly depicts what occurs that I physically felt the shockwave; rust is knocked off a car frame, gravel is lifted off the ground in a mushroom cloud of dust, and people are knocked over like dominoes, all to the beat of a deafening bass soundtrack. 

The new commander of the unit is Sgt. James- a man that seems to take wreckless actions and thoughtless risks.  As we continue though the movie, we see the increase in the magnitude of the devices, the mindset of how Sgt. James operates, his genius and incredible aptitude revealed and come to comprehend how easy it is to descend into this adrenaline-junky resolve. These men are only alive when they are doing their duty, and when left to ponder the other elements of their lives are broken men. 

I can't speak highly enough about this film.  Kathryn Bigelow has created a film that deserves a place as the greatest Iraq War drama.  She understands the testosterone induced mindset, having previously directed Point Break, and clearly steps up into the A-List with this film.  She deserves an Oscar nomination right now since there is not going to be a better directed film this or the next few years. 

Jeremy Renner is revelatory as Sgt. James. He exudes a cocksure confidence in doing his job, that when we see him completely collapse into isolation and vulnerability, the decline is incredibly steep and heartbreaking. It is one of the breakout performances of the year. 

In a summer where such awful fare as Transformers and other sequels have dominated attention and promotion, a movie as thoughtful, provocative, suspenseful and heartpounding as The Hurt Locker deserves an audience.  If it finds one, it will be one of the biggest films of the year.

The Hurt Locker is a spectacle. 
There are movies that just start off and place you in the middle of something, then just keeps going, but don't actually go anywhere; they end as abruptly as they began without any real ending. Not this movie. You'll be thrust into a stressful situation, then move along with the soldiers as they march through the rest of the movie. It starts out at 150 mph, and rarely lets off the gas. There is a great ending, but one of redundance for me, because I know people in his shoes. I was one of them.
The actors are top notch in their roles. 
The one gripe I have is a scene toward the end was silly, and didn't do the movie justice, but it's quickly forgotten when the director gets right back on track. There are a variety scenarios that help the movie progress along with what happens to the characters as they move along, with the most powerful scenes for me being a couple from the end. Walking down a grocery isle. Sounds easy enough. If you let the movie suck you in, you'll realize it's not.
The Hurt Locker is a powerful experience, and one hell of a ride. Near perfect.

The Hurt Locker is a film about the psychological effects of war, played out through a bomb squad unit. While there is action and suspense, making the movie thrilling at times, Kathryn Bigelow is much more interested in how this action, suspense and pressure is doing to her characters than the action and suspense as spectacle for the audience. This is primarily shown through the good performances from Jeremy Renner (who is ready to get more work), Anthony Mackie and Brian Geraghty. Bigelow also succeeds in the tone and style that she sets with her camera. It is gritty and in tight, but also plays to the nerves of the characters (and audience) as it constantly scanner the parameter, and skeptically looks at everyone as a potential threat. Out of combat, the characters are lost, they drink, punch each other, look for answers, break down, and do not fit. This is most eloquently shown in Renner's brief tour state side (more specifically, the supermarket scene). He is completely lost in civilian life and cannot return to the field. The Hurt Locker is looks at how the stress and exhilaration of being in combat changes one's ability to function. The film does not take sides, there is no agenda, it merely wishes to explore the emotional toll that battle takes on different people as it looks at how the characters handle their situation(s). 8/10

The problem is that the main soldier assigned to do this risky job in the movie is a loose cannon, someone who is reckless, puts his unit at risk, doesn't follow orders and therefore is someone that the military would not want diffusing bombs. This does not mean that this movie is not good or compelling, because it does offer a riveting story, but it must be watched with the understanding that the military does not allow for mavericks who knowingly place their entire unit at risk, like the main character does in this movie. For instance, if a soldier deliberately cuts himself off from communication with his platoon leader, that soldier would soon hear about it, loud and clear. Also, the action is not placed within a larger context, that is, the action takes place in Iraq but that's about all the audience is told, which may cause one to wonder why soldiers are there in the first place. This would be like watching the B-25s dropping their bombs in Thirty Seconds Over Tokyo without knowing why the the United States was at war with Japan or watching Saving Private Ryan without knowing why American soldiers were storming the beach at Normandy. Nevertheless the movie does effectively convey the harrowing and dangerous nature of war and should be shown to persons who are contemplating joining the military.

Beyond war movie and beyond another critically acclaimed movie, The Hurt Locker is the living definition of thriller. Rare is it that I find a movie that has me breathing unevenly whilst gripping my seat wondering what could happen next. The direction is simple but brilliant in its own right, the acting is compelling and the reality of the so-called War on Terror is very real. Director Kathryn Bigelow gets it when it comes to keeping the audience centered on the important things and I look forward to seeing more of her work in the future. Before writing the plot summary I must warn you that this movie is better enjoyed by going into it blindly. The less you know of what you will experience the more immersed you will be in the story. I will attempt to avoid spoilers and any real breakdown of what occurs within this wonderful movie but if you want to truly enjoy The Hurt Locker I urge you to skip my next paragraph within this review.

Plot/Summary: The Hurt Locker is a situation set within the Middle East where American soldiers are forced to find and disarm bombs within the inner city. Sergeant JT Sanborn (Anthony Mackie) and Specialist Owen Eldridge (Brian Geraghty) have a little over a month before the next rotation frees them from their duty. Although the two men eagerly count down the days to escaping the dry and thankless desert, their comrade and leader in Staff Sergeant William James (Jeremy Renner) sees things differently. Battle-hardened, with a hard-on for disarming bombs, James seems to laugh at death and his recklessness alienates him from his peers. However after a few outings the three comrades reach a level of understanding and James emerges as a leader that is much more than a cowboy looking for death.

The most stand-out acting in this movie has to be that of the complicated Staff Sergeant William James (Jeremy Renner). Not only is he believable but he forces you into his world of chaos, confusion, honor and love. Between he and Anthony Mackies Sanborn you are made to feel sympathetic and remorseful to the plight that they are in. Although the movie seemed short, within seconds you are concerned for every single character. The bomb situations are limited but within every single one of them you are holding your breath in anticipation and fright. The cinematography did not look or feel staged and the eery music brings you right into the hopelessness of the jobs these men had to do. Written by Mark Boal, the script felt real, it felt as if it was a day in the life of, with pacing that was relevant and not contrived. There were no forced romances, friendships or atrocities to pull at your heart strings, the events are so seamless that it feels as if there was an invisible other with a camcorder shooting the lives of real men.

Sure you may need to look elsewhere if you are wanting another movie of guts or glory, Rambo-like, one man against the world warfare. But if you want something that feels real, looks real and warrants intelligent thought, you will want to see the Hurt Locker. An absolutely amazing movie.

"The Hurt Locker" is a brilliantly realized action film, expertly directed by Kathryn Bigelow (her finest yet), and certainly one of the best films of the year so far. A war movie without emphasis on war, an ensemble film where the ensemble is clear and easy to identify, a character study whose characters show us their dimensions through the way they approach their job, and an action film that thrill us with suspense and not loud explosions or lightning quick edits. All the more remarkable because the movie is about a bomb squad in Iraq. 

I can't stress enough how incredibly well-made this film is, and how clear the vision of its action is. There is precious little musical score, mostly the sounds of the Iraqi environs and the desert, and we, like the characters, tense at the idea that all the calm could be disrupted any moment with random bursts of violence or, in the case of Bravo company, makeshift bomb explosions. 

Jeremy Renner's central performance as the risk-junkie leader of the squad is a thing of nuanced brilliance, and anchors the fine cast and exceptional performances all around. It didn't surprise me to learn the the writer is a former journalist who was embedded with a similar squad himself - the authenticity of the time and place is palpable: you can taste the baked sand and feel the acridity of the air. My only quibble is with the title, one I didn't understand going in. I think I now know what it refers to - a chest where dogtags of fallen soldiers is kept - but that still doesn't do anything to actually convey what this exciting and unique film is about. Better might be "Beware the Shrapnel", or "Fuck You - You Examine the Bomb!". At any rate, "The Hurt Locker" delivers the goods, and will stick in your head like a ticking bomb long after the credits roll.

The look of the film reminded me of a less severe version of "Blackhawk Down", with the intelligent use of filters & lighting to capture the shocking brightness of the Iraqi sun as well as the pervasive dust.  The sound was... darn near perfect. Minimal music, Blackhawks flying over every few minutes (which was what *really* took me back).  The gunfire and explosives didn't sound "hollywood" at all - it sounded like I was there.  The sound guy needs a booya for this one.

The Hurt Locker is the first war picture Ive seen that depicts battle as a glorified addiction. It doesnt see battle as fun, necessarily, but it does see it as exciting and, for some soldiers, such is the only means for feeling useful. Ive never been a soldier myself, but Im sure there are members of the military who stay on active duty because civilian life simply cant provide them the fix their mind and body crave after experiencing the chaos of war. There have been a lot of movies about the struggles of coming home from war; this one is about the struggle of staying in. 

The film is ultimately anti-war for all the usual reasons, but its main focus is the crippling effects war has on young mens minds. Once youve been in battle, the film argues, everything else can seem small and inconsequential by comparison, which, if you think about it, is tragic because young soldiers wind up hoping for violence and devastation.

Through a series of distinguishable vignettes, director Kathryn Bigelow has crafted one of the most intense films of the year. Not only is it a tour de force on a technical level, but it also contains a story that envelops and convinces us to care about its characters. On paper, a lot of its scenes should be similar, abut Bigelow brings suspense and intrigue to each and every one of them. This is a film whose raw materials and construction all play an especially important role together, from the sound, photography and special effects to the direction and editing. The result is something truly effective as it places us directly in the center of the action. I havent felt this induced in a war picture since Ridley Scotts Black Hawk Down.
 
At the height of the Iraq War (the film was shot in and around the 2007 surge in Jordan), an American EOD (Explosive Ordinance Disposal) team routinely diffuses bombs and struggles with the daily conflicts of their surroundings. Violence and disorder are so commonplace that we, the viewers, can only imagine what its like to be a soldier in this time and place. Such an experience can probably never be fully realized on film, but Bigelow comes about as close as any filmmaker can. Im sure much of the footage was taken right off the streets of the shooting locations and there are particular shots, like a one-legged cat limping across the street, that are brutal to watch but which raise the level of realism. 

There is no traditional plot to follow. Many of the films scenes and situationsbe it a taxi driver going where hes not supposed to; a wisecracking boy selling pirated DVDs; suspicious men gazing down from windows; a fatal, unforeseen attack in the middle of the desertare random and serve to place us in the middle of a hellish and irrational environment. Bigelow and screenwriter Mark Boal also teach us specific things about being a soldier, such as having to clean off blood-stained bullets so theyll fire correctly. 

The EOD team is led by Sergeant William James (Jeremy Renner), a cocky and fearless technician who would probably diffuse bombs all day if he could. Why? Because its what hes good at, its what sets him apart from his fellow soldiers and, for him, its an unparalleled experience. James is obsessive about finding a purpose to his job and he cares little about protocol, which upsets the men he leadsSergeant Sanborn (Anthony Mackie) and Specialist Eldridge (Brian Geraghty). Theyre the more traditional soldier types because they yearn to leave Iraq when their rotation is complete. The curious thing about James is he wants to stay, despite having a wife and baby. We feel sorry for him because of the way war has corrupted him.

Renner, Mackie and Geraghty are all very effective in their roles and their performances are even more impressive because they dont have a traditional formula to work with. For James, Sanborn and Eldridge, everyday is a new conflict and theyre at a loss for a common enemy or purpose. All they know, and all we know, is they hate where they are, as do we, which makes it easy for us to hope they make it out alive. 

Ultimately, what makes The Hurt Locker such a memorable and well conceived film is its ability to place us in another world, a world that happens to be real. Bigelow doesnt hand out rational meanings or make any of the deaths or survivals serve the plot; shes loyal to the films reality and she makes us feel it. Whats also interesting is how the film entertains and excites us. With its piercing sound and visuals, the action has a visceral effect on us, but not the kind that makes us want to experience it action first-hand. One thing were not meant to be is envious of these soldiers.  

The Hurt Locker is a masterful achievement, both technically and narratively. The filmmakers literally shake the ground of the theater we sit in and provide a story and characters that touch us emotionally. The most important thing the film does, and which we leaves the greatest impression, is allow us understand its world and the people who try to survive in it. We gain an insight and perspective of a place and state of mind that most of us only read or hear about through testimonials. At its core, its a human story about young men trying to find their way through chaos, and from the very first scene, we feel we know these men and understand what they go through.

The Hurt Locker is an amazing first-hand look inside the lives of an Iraqi bomb squad unit and the struggles they face in their day to day lives while walking a supposed liberated country. It's not to say these soldiers in this film aren't patriotic or believe in what they're doing, but there is a keen sense of abandonment they feel, and at the end of the day, they're forced to face their own mortality as friends of theirs begin dropping like flies. I imagine it's very difficult to make a movie like this, set in an ongoing military campaign, without upsetting somebody. The director with a political agenda will be lucky if his or her film ever sees the light of day, whereas the director with no worthier goal other than to entertain invites charges of insensitivity, tastelessness, opportunism, etc. Miraculously, Kathryn Bigelow navigates this minefield almost completely unscathed, perhaps because although The Hurt Locker has nothing provocative whatsoever to say about the Iraq War, she says it with such dazzling technical skill that her movie seems more profound than it actually is. Her nerve shredding set-pieces are a veritable master-class in suspense technique and, whether or not dictated by the modest budget, the short shrift given to star names like Guy Pearce and Ralph Fiennes heightens the uneasy feeling that something dreadful could happen to any one of these guys, at any moment.

Kathryn Bigelow said she didn't want to make a film that was particularly dramatic or even cinematic, but experiential. She wanted the viewer to feel and experience of what it is like to be a EOD (Explosive Ordinance Disposal) bomb tech in Iraq, and anything else, politics and thematics included would only be a distraction. 

Which isn't to say the Hurt Locker has no political conscious, it does, but it weaves smoothly in and out of the plot, in lines like, "they changed the name of the base from Camp Liberation, to Camp Victory, they thought it sounded better". to "If he wasn't an insurgent, he is now.", and likewise never serves as a distraction, but as background noise the soldiers, are aware of, but drown out, in order to concentrate on bigger fish. Like "Children Of Men", the film drops us into dangerous situations which erupt mid-conversation and without musical cues, and were left to infer the plot from the surroundings. Though in most of the scenes nothing actually happens the results are electric, because at any moment, were lead to believe, anything really COULD happen. 

The story revolves around three soldiers all dealing with the extreme emotional stress of defusing road side bombs, the difficulty of knowing which civilians to trust, which to suspect, and whether or not they can afford to look to at each person they meet, soldier, foe, and friend alike, as individuals, when it might be more emotionally prudent to see them all as just parts of the job.

Brian Geraghty (who was also in the the first gulf war film "Jarhead")  is morbidly fascinated with death and increasingly fragile, while Anthony Mackie places his faith in his duty, by-the-books, and safety first routine, while the new unit commander Jeremy Renner, is "addicted to war"(as the films opening quotations remind us) and more to the point adrenaline. 

Renner's real risk is a small casual acquaintance of a little boy selling bootleg DVD's and speaking American slang, who appears to have been killed, maybe, so his corpse could be used to smuggle contraband for insurgents. Renner wants revenge, but for who, to whom, and how, are the problem. Renner's doing the most dangerous work in the war, but he's still not experiencing direct combat, and is unable to get the "pay back", the chaos around him seems to demand. 

This is probably the sea-change aspect of the movie for the genre of war films as a whole. Long gone is the heroic calvary charge and now gone seems the days of desolate wilderness guerilla combat, the guerrillas have gone urban now, and like all things urban they have little to no contact with those they are pitted against in a life and death struggle.

A flash of light off of a cell phone and some protrusions in a dirt road are all the sign of attack a soldier might see before disaster, if that, and all the enemy they are confined to do battle with(for EOD techs at least) is a series of wires and inquisitive onlookers (who are either planning to murder them with or just taking videos for Youtube with their cameras). 

As many a current US general has said, the modern soldier, has to be a peace keeper as much as, if not more so, than a warrior. With no one substantial enemy to fight, paranoia, and feeling's of helplessness and rage, are daily bread for most combatants. 

The montage just before the last scene, seamlessly juxtaposes images of war, with those of domestic life, in a way that makes it seem only natural for Renner to re-enlist and return, to the only world which makes sense to him. The red wire, and the green wire, are much simpler choices, in their point blank dichotomy, to make than choosing from the rainbow of cereals in the grocery store, for a distant wife, and child who exists mainly as a nostalgic photograph and pang of guilt. "EOD", tech's often joke, stands for Every One Divorced, because of their extremely high divorce statistics, which can only add to the alienation and stress these men face. 

I once had to put on a suit similar to the one these guys wear, and sit at a desk solving math problems, for a school psychology experiment, to help the designers chart who long it would take for the suits own internal heat and discomfort to effect rational processes. It didn't take long for the sweat to start pouring and plastic visor to get fogged, and I was not in the 100 degree plus heat, defusing live explosives, while under gun fire. All I had to do was remember to carry a one.

This is the truly the most dangerous and I would imagine one of the most difficult jobs on earth, and Bigelow invests just enough plot and character to keep things moving, but it's the sheer suspense, and terrifying difficulty of their duties (a real life absurdity worthy of Werner Herzog films) which the film really hangs on.

Fracois Truffaut said that "action argues for itself", which is why even the most virulent anti-war films fail, as "might" in, cinematic terms anyway, necessarily equals "right". In The Hurt Locker, there is very little "action", in the traditional sense, even the gun fights are drawn out, ducked behind a trench, sniper affairs.  What the film has instead is suspense, which is as new to the traditional calvary charge, machine gun fueled war films genre as it is, to the lives and expectations, of most soldiers, I wager. Suspense, unlike action doesn't argue for anyone or anything but survival, it's a discombobulating experience for all involved, where the only "victor", is he who doesnt die.

The script was based on a collection of stories the author heard while embedded with a EOD team for a few months, and though some seem elaborate all have the jaw shattering ring of truth (the man who had the bomb strapped to him and made to approach soldiers, is one I heard from a few Vet's)

I think the best psychological suspense movie about explosives is "Wages Of Fear", but this is a close second, and for a modern war film, it's top marks. This is a new and critical part of what American warfare looks like today, until such a time comes, as soldiers get super-powered GI-Joe strength enhancing robo armor, which a friend of mine who works in high tech gadgets and rocket engineering for companies he wont mention, tells me is actually closer than you would think.

On the surface, The Hurt Locker is a modern war movie, following in the long tradition of war movies, with ebbs and flows that should be familiar to anyone who's ever seen a war movie.  Except, outside a single combat scene, it's not really a war movie.  Taking place in 2004 Iraq, it follows an EOD (Explosive Ordnance Disposal) team on their daily missions to remove IEDs (Improvised Explosive Devices).  For a little background information on the subject, I've pulled the following quote from wikipedia: "In the 2003âpresent Iraq War, IEDs have been used extensively against coalition forces and by the end of 2007 they have been responsible for approximately 40% of coalition deaths in Iraq.[1]".  Needless to say, the daily threat of these improvised bombs creates an atmosphere of genuine terror.

  Sergeant JT Sanborn (Anthony Mackie) has seen one of his fellow squad members die, and isn't too pleased when the new redneck hotshot, Staff Sergeant James (the excellent Jeremy Renner) comes in and starts behaving recklessly.  I'm sure this sounds like familiar territory, but whereas in the past, the reckless hotshot (as played by Tom Cruise or some other actor of similar caliber) would be incredibly confident and cocky, Sergeant James comes off as almost suicidal (his habitual cigarette smoking seems to be an outward extension of his subconscious deathwish), and yet, he claims he never thinks about death.  It's one of the few movies of this genre where the threat of death of the main character has never seemed more real.  Sergeant James deliberately puts himself into the bomb's blast radius rather than have the unmanned robot go in his place.  The answer lies in the movie's opening quote: "War is a drug".  To Sergeant James, the adrenelin rush he gets from disarming these bombs seems to outweigh everything else, whether it's family back home or even the lives of his fellow soldiers.  At one point, he befriends a young Iraqi boy selling dvds in the street.  When he finds the body of a boy, he's convinced it's his friend and sets out to get some measure of revenge for the boy.  The boy himself is of little consequence to him, though.  It turns out, he's just one performer in the movie plot James seems to have going on in his head.

  Director Kathryn Bigelow never judges the characters she's putting onscreen, she merely presents them and leaves it to the audience to judge.  Likewise, our military involvement in Iraq is also portrayed neutrally; the politics behind the invasion are simply of no consequence to the characters on the screen and therefore are irrelevent to the story.  This movie is wholly character-driven, and not in the way you expect a typical war movie to be, and in the end, I'm left with the question, was Sergeant James a cocky rebel or just a severely disturbed individual?  It's a riveting achievement in film.

The Hurt Locker is an Iraq war movie with no political agenda. It's simply about the life of a guy who disarms bombs and happens to be really good at it. Every single time he goes to work, there's a good 50/50 chance he won't make it out alive.

I know some people may complain about the shakiness of the camera, but it gives you the, "It feels like you're there" feeling. The cinematography is brilliant. Often the film shows you exactly what the soldier can see which makes it even more intense. The soldiers know about as much as we do about who are the bad guys and who are the innocent civilians in Iraq. You can feel the fear that the soldiers are experience. There's moments which include showing us the POV of looking through a sniper rifle. The vision is so blurry, you can't make out what is out there, but it looks like it could be an Iraqi who could be holding a sniper rifle aiming at you...or maybe not. What should the soldier do? The movie shows all the uncertainties of day to day life of serving in Iraq, which adds to the suspense. 

The acting in general is all very good. The dialogue is full of witty zingers, and the main character is very interesting. All the character work is very well done. His backstory, his life back in the U.S, his collection of souvenirs is all great stuff. After a while you kind of want the action to end to show a little more of the soldiers as people.

The best film I've seen about the War in Iraq or any other recent war, The Hurt Locker is a gripping, powerful, and intense war picture that grabs you from first frame to last. The film follows an elite bomb squad in Iraq that consists of three members - Staff Sergeant William James (Jeremy Renner), Sergeant JT Sanborn (Anthony Mackie), and Sergeant Owen Eldridge (Brian Geraghty). 

Bigelow stays out of the way and never takes a side on the political issue, but she does give us an extremely realistic film. Much of the credit goes to screenwriter Mark Boal, who's first-hand experience with a bomb squad as a journalist has allowed him to share what he witnessed during his time in Iraq. 

All three of our leads do terrific jobs, especially Jeremy Renner. All three get more characterization than we've become accustomed to in other films from the war genre - which undoubtedly helped them all out. With that said, all three hold their own and show us a different type of soldier. Each has their own beliefs on what their job is and about the situation at hand, which allows for us to see the war from drastically different points of views. 

Bigelow, the director, does a tremendous job of keeping our attention throughout. With rapid pacing, a handheld camera, and intense, nail-bitting buildups, The Hurt Locker is quite the attention-graber, but for power, it relies heavily on visuals. Overall, this is one of the most engaging war films I've ever seen, and one that is without a doubt one of the best pictures I've seen this year.

I've been wanting to see "The Hurt Locker" since I first saw its promo on Marco Beltrami's website.  That was last winter, and the trailers were only in Italian.  I saw it the other night, and I wasn't disappointed in the slightest.

If you're looking for an action-filled war film like "Black Hawk Down" or "We Were Soldiers," you might be slightly disappointed by this film.  If you liked "The Kingdom," however, you will definitely like this movie.  The feel is the same--but as good as "The Kingdom" was, "The Hurt Locker" is in all ways exponentially better.

I can't even find words to describe it:  it was just incredible to watch.  The combination of both conventional and documentary styles of filming (with two "Matrix"-style slow-motion shots) made the movie intense and very believable at the same time.  The few fighting and explosion sequences were very impressive, but the most gripping were the tense scenes of searching a warehouse or waiting in the desert for a sniper to expose his position.  Those scenes were the ones that made you feel on your toes, or in the case of the latter example, like it was going to last forever.  As my friend pointed out, you really felt like you were there with them.

The acting, as far as I could tell, was next to flawless.  I never felt like something was out-of-place or that there was a weird word.  All of the lead actors especially played great roles.  Anthony Mackie's Sgt. Sanborn was a believer in by-the-books methods and sticking with the plan, and he's obviously learned that that's the best methods from previously doing duty as intelligence in, as he says, "every shithole on this planet," and is constantly trying to first keep Staff Sgt James (Jeremy Renner) in line and also to figure out what his deal is--both end up being more difficult than he anticipated.  Brian Geraghty's Specialist Eldridge is obviously the inexperienced one of the group, and while a good soldier deals with a lot of anxiety and carries some baggage for a young soldier--he feels he is responsible for his previous team leader's death.

But few soldiers of any war film have been as much of an enigma as the main character, Staff Sgt. James (Jeremy Renner).  His entrance shows both the understanding and caring that he shows to his troops in the field as well as his obvious eccentric style.  At the start of the movie, his antics draw some laughs from the audience and scared frustration from his squadmates, to the point that Sanborn even considers killing him, but the audience gets to see both sides--in part, the method to James's madness and the reason for Sanborn's and Eldridge's frustration.  Through the movie, it's obvious that James loves what he does from his manic, adrenaline-rush way of doing it, but another thing that the movie does well is convince you he's just crazy at the beginning, and in a moment less than five minutes from the end of the movie, he's talking to his toddler son and you find out what he's really all about.  And although everything thus far had made sense before, you can then see the real reason.

In a summer where the action genre has been reduced to the mindless schlock we call "Transformers", it's incredibly rewarding to see a film as intelligent, suspenseful, and carefully crafted as "The Hurt Locker". The director is Kathryn Bigelow, whose directorial career has included action pictures like "Point Break", "K-9: The Widowmaker", and, one of my favorite horror films, "Near Dark". She sets her story in 2004 Baghdad and focuses on the lives of the men who risk their lives hourly by defusing, or carefully detonating, insurgent bombs. Some of these are as obviously placed as an illegally parked car with a sagging trunk, and others can be buried under rubble or even nested in a corpse.

Every movie about the Iraq war is bound to have a political agenda, or so we thought. There are brief moments of politics, such as when one character explains that a camp's name was switched from "liberty" to "victory" because "victory" sounded better, but "The Hurt Locker" is largely without bias. It's not a film about the horrors of war or the unjust occupation of Iraq, but rather a film about the soldiers in a war who simply know they have a job to do. 

The film follows the Delta Company, a bomb disposal unit of three men: James (Jeremy Renner), the new reckless addition to the company; Sanborn (Anthony Mackie), the professional who sticks strictly to protocol; and Eldridge (Brian Geraghty), the nervous wreck who is unable to make critical decisions without a sort of fatherly approval by his teammates. The obvious feud is the competitive rivalry between James and Sanborn. Early on in the film, Sanborn considers the possibility of killing James and framing it as an "accident", only to inspire a move towards safer protocol and the removal of the risk-taking James from the Delta Company.

James is the one who gears up in the bomb suit while Sanborn and Eldridge provide cover. He keeps parts of every bomb he's defused, recalling each device and claiming "I like that guy" when one of the set ups is particularly clever. He's an artist of his craft and he approaches each risk without hesitation. When met with a huge trunk full of explosives, he removes his suit because if he's going to die, he might as well die comfortably. Despite his bravado, he has a very tender streak, as when he comforts Eldridge during a startling attack in the middle of an endless desert.

"The Hurt Locker" is episodic, largely drifting between bomb to bomb, and therefore it's pacing is not unlike the suspense classic "The Wages of Fear". Each mission is exciting and intense, and by the end of the film it's remarkable just how much we come to care about each member of the team. It's capable of providing the thrills a casual audience will relate to, and it's enough of a well-constructed character study to appeal to the more picky film-goers. A wonderful film, one of the best so far this year, and certainly the best film made thus far about the Iraq war. Hopefully it won't be forgotten come the 2010 Academy Awards.

The highly respected critic Manohla Dargis began her recent New York Times profile of the filmmaker Kathryn Bigelow by saying: ?The take on Kathryn Bigelow is that she is a great female director of muscular action movies? sometimes, more simply, she?s called a great female director. But here?s a radical thought: She is, simply, a great filmmaker.? The double standard which Dargis points out is well stated, but I would never go so far as to call Bigelow a ?great director? of any kind. This is, after all, a filmmaker whose greatest claim to fame is a mid-nineties Keanu Reeves vehicle (Point Break) which Simon Pegg and Edgar Wright could ridicule with the same breath they mocked Bad Boys II. The other highlights of her oeuvre are a forgettable Submarine movie called K-19: The Widow Maker and a moderately creative vampire movie called Near Dark which was marred by a low budget and a lame tacked on happy ending. The best movie she?d made up to this point was Strange Days, a mostly forgotten science fiction movie which, while solid, was only a minor triumph. As such I?ve been a bit perplexed by the revisionism with which many are describing this career in the wake of the release of Bigelow?s newest film The Hurt Locker. While I?m still not a fan of Bigelow?s career up to this point, seeing this new film does make me excited to see what the future will bring for Ms. Bigelow, because The Hurt Locker is significantly better than anything she?s made before.

Set in the midst of the Iraq war circa 2004, the film covers 20-30 days in the life of a three-man army bomb squad. The newest member is Staff Sergeant William James (Jeremy Renner), he?s the commanding officer and he takes point on the bomb defusing duties. Supporting him are Sergeant JT Sanborn (Anthony Mackie) and Specialist Owen Eldridge (Brian Geraghty) who must watch what he?s doing and look out for possible triggermen looking to set off the bombs. Quickly it becomes apparent that Staff Sergeant James has a very different style than his predecessor, he?s reckless and prone to taking wild risks. With only a couple dozen days left in their tour, the men must try to hold out in spite of the danger that this behavior puts them in.

It is no secret that movies about the Iraq War have mostly been miserable failures both critically and commercially. Granted, a lot of the movies that are lumped into the genre are really either primarily about other Middle-East conflicts (E.G. Lions for Lambs, The Kingdom, Rendition) or they?re about the lives of soldiers after they?ve returned home (E.G. Stop Loss, Home of the Brave, The Lucky Ones). Perhaps the only theatrical film thus far which I would unhesitantly say is about the Iraq War is Brian De Palma?s ballsy but at times terribly executed film Redacted, which came under heavy fire by right-wing ideologues for failing to exult ?the troops.? Many suggest that the problem has been that it?s ?too soon,? that there?s no way to fully assess the conflict until after it?s over. I have trouble buying this explanation, as there have been plenty of documentarians who have proven more than able to assess the situation intelligently as well as some surprisingly superior television projects like FX?s ?Over There? and HBO?s ?Generation Kill.? If nothing else these various projects have more than established the look and feel of the war in Iraq to the point where this film feels more like a return to the setting than an introduction to it, thus allowing Bigelow to hit the ground running.

While this clearly isn?t the first work to tackle the conflict, it is the first one to focus on actual combat? sort of. After all, combat in Iraq doesn?t exactly look like the frontline battles of wars past. Most of the fatalities in Iraq come from hidden bombs which often explode before the victims know what hit them. So in spite of the film?s focus on ?combat,? I wouldn?t call it an action movie as many critics have. In fact, the film only has one scene which I?d classify as an honest-to-goodness action sequence, and even there the thrills are mostly suspenseful rather than visceral. Most of the ?combat? consists of tense situations where the team must deal with live bombs which could go off at any moment. The film avoids most of the clichés of bomb defusing; the characters don?t spend minutes choosing between the red and blue wires (at least they don?t announce their dilemma out loud) and they are never given a large readout counting down to when the bomb will blow. The honest-to-goodness action scene I referred to, a tense Sniper duel, is easily the highlight of the film. In fact it may just be the best sniper face-off since Full Metal Jacket.

The particularly impressive thing about the film?s visual style is its ability to balance both conventional and documentary aesthetics. This is an equilibrium that many filmmakers have been trying to perfect lately, thus making this success all the more impressive. The film is shot handheld, but it is in no way meant to be a mockumentary, and it will not be offensive to those opposed to ?the shaky cam.? The picture oddly looks both washed out and digital, a very gritty look but in an entirely twenty first century way. In spite of this gritty look, when the bombs in the film do go off Bigelow is not afraid to shoot them with all the gusto that Roland Emmerich would. Up until now Bigelow?s style resembled the early work of Tony Scott, it was slick and relaxed. So this film?s docudrama aesthetic is a pretty big departure for her. The is made even more impressive if one compares it to the clumsy way Brian De Palma tried to shift into faux-documentary styling in his Iraq film. 

The film is completely apolitical, I doubt that Bigelow is a fan of the war, but no judgment seems to be made about the conflict other than that it is a highly dangerous environment that can be incredibly trying for those involved. In fact the movie is so neutral that at times it seems to lack even a storyline. The film is completely dedicated to simply showing twenty-some days in the life of these guys and almost nothing else, it goes from set-piece to set piece with only a few scenes back at the barracks to connect it all. In its third act the film threatens to form an actual narrative arc, but then goes back to its slice of life format. This isn?t to say the film is without depth, though it lacks a strong central story the characters are well developed through their actions and their conversations. Though the format is not conventional, this is not some sort of wild Gus Van Sant style experiment, it won?t be confusing to non-cinephiles and its style serves no extraneous purpose other than to support the material.

The Hurt Locker is indeed the best feature length film about the Iraq war, and by quite a distance at that. Still, I feel there are better movies about the war to be made in the future. Perhaps in the future we?ll get movies about this war that are as refined as a Saving Private Ryan, a Thin Red Line, or a Letters From Iwo Jima. This film is reminiscent of the more primitive World War Two movies that were made in the late forties and fifties like Battleground or Twelve O?Clock High. These were very matter of fact films which simply sought to tell a story about men trying to cope with hardships on a battlefield. They were simple stories of survival, no more concerned with the full ramifications of the war then the men on the ground were. I certainly hope that movies will come that can achieve greater ambitions than this, until then The Hurt Locker will have to do.

"War is a drug". This is the main theme behind this exceptional war film, which manages to shine on its own in a summer overpopulated with rampaging machines, talking animals and teenage wizards. 

"The Hurt Locker" is set in modern-day, post-Saddam Iraq. The story is basically a one-month account in the lives of an U.S. Army Explosive Ordnance Disposal (EOD) unit. Their job, in a nutshell, is to look for and defuse bombs, which can be in a pile of garbage or carefully hidden in the gravel roads. The leader, and unlikely hero, of the EOD unit is Staff Sergeant William James (played by Jeremy Renner) who was sent in to fill the boots of a senior Sergeant (played by Guy Pearce) who lost his life while on the job. Helping him is Sergeant JT Sanborn (played by Anthony Mackie of "8 Mile" fame), head of the support team that accompanies James. Throughout the film, their personalities clash since Sanborn follows protocol while James avoids it, but at the same time they know they have a mission to accomplish one way or another.

The film is directed by Kathryn Bigelow (yes, a WOMAN directed it!!) and she does a VERY good job with the subject matter. "The Hurt Locker" takes us deep into an environment where anyone can be a threat and death can happen at anytime. The performances are great, and the script (even though the film is really a documentary-like account and not really a story) is well-written. But what makes this film stand out amongst the many war films of the past is the fact that it relies on tension rather than action. It is the anticipation of disarming the bomb before its detonation time that adds pressure and strain to the EOD unit, and it eventually takes a psychological toll on each of them, especially James. 

"The Hurt Locker" is a unique war film, yet it is quite possibly one of the best films of 2009. It isn't full of explosions and gunfire (though they do exist in the film) but it is a tense, powerful drama of courage under fire. Fans of war films will enjoy this one, and those looking for an action film that will make them think while leaving them breathless should give this one a look. Recommended like reading "The Anarchist Cookbook".

An ambitious project, seeing as all other films dealing with the Iraq war has failed both commercially and critically. The Hurt Locker is neither anti-war, pro-war or war-is-necessary, the film depicts war as a drug, something that keeps them soldiers forever and prevents them for returning to civilian life. Kathryn Bigelows daring direction is what makes this film what it is. For The Hurt Locker is a war film in its style as much as its content. The handheld camera work and the constantly surprising, and shocking action scenes convince the viewer that they are not just spectators. Rather they are participants in the film, scanning the location for insurgents and IEDs. Filled with tense moments in which you seem to know whats going to happen, Bigelow keeps the viewer interested by constantly mixing up the result; sometimes the bombs go off, sometimes they dont; sometimes the Iraqi is a civilian, sometimes they are not; sometimes the soldiers live, sometimes they die. Bigelow uses music sparsely, some scenes the music heightens the tension, sometimes its the silence that create such fear and suspense. In between these tense scenes are scenes of bitter humor and sadness. The soldiers are not just one-dimensional fighters, but we get to know them as people. What makes the film so involving is the honest and heartfelt performances by the three main characters. Learning from film history, bigelow casts unknown actors in the starring roles, and as a result, you never question whether the characters are real. Shot in the Middle East, the film feels as authentic as a documentary, and the explosions are as real as can be. The Hurt Locker is a special film, one that takes full advantage of the type of warfare that exists in Iraq, the lack of clearly identified enemy forces. Spot-on surface details mask a heart of false action-genre cliches. Has it been so well reviewed only because it conveniently confirms the naive misconceptions of movie reviewers?

Boy it sure looks right --the dust, the gear, the flies, the actors. But it's not long before a soldier punches his new team leader in the face. The team leader seems to recognize that he deserved it. At this point they've both acknowledged the gaping hole at the heart of what this story asks us to believe.

But instead of coming into line, for the rest of the movie the team leader proceeds to take ever more boneheaded actions, in which his team inexplicably continue to participate. The movie seems to want to ask Is this man in it just for the excitement, or is he just that good that he can get away with what for others would be reckless? They 
might as well have cast Stallone in the lead role.

It seems the filmmakers stopped at the point of wondering, in awe, what could possibly motivate a person to do this job? And never actually put themselves in that man's shoes. The truth is the two requirements to arrive at the point where we're supposed to believe this individual has
arrived are teamwork and professionalism. Both of which this character seems expressly designed to flout. A military unit, particularly in combat, does not abide such a person any more than nature abides a vacuum.

"War is a drug." So are caffeine and nicotine. Does the fact that soldiers like to pound energy drinks and smoke really shed much light on their humanity? (The fact is most soldiers would probably like this movie, too. That don't make it good.)

Alas, we've seen the pointlessly vicious senior officer before. We've seen the adrenaline junkie before. And we've seen, well, Rambo, before. They're just not usually dressed up so meticulously accurately.

The question is why has this film been received by critics like some great insight into war or warriors? (Why did I go see it in full expectation that that's what it was?) My only guess is that it comfortably fits pre-conceived notions that soldiering of any kind, or in EOD in particular, requires some kind of insanity. But insanity is so often the lazy explanation for that which is difficult to understand, or which we are afraid to try to understand. 

P.S.

Probably of less interest to a civilian are the tactical mistakes made around every corner that any boot would manage to avoid. Suffice it to say that for some reason these guys seem to like to roll around pretty much everywhere with three guys in a lone HMMWV, and they're big fans of the one-man room clear.

The British team in the desert is apparently only there to look at (they do look pretty cool.) Equanimity under fire seems to have been confused in their case with inaction. Did the filmmakers just forget to kill the rest of the team off?

And the point of the US Colonel's order that a medic allow an insurgent to die, rather than try to save him, is what? Maybe this Col. really is a total idiot, and somehow hasn't figured out by now that an insurgent is worth more captured than dead. Maybe he somehow thinks he'll win more points
with his men by seeming to be a hardass than he would win by following the rules in a clear-cut case. But isn't he even interested in giving his medic a golden opportunity for practice? And a full-bird who doesn't cover his ass when it's easy? Come on.

The first scene was convincing. (Then again, I wasn't EOD.) I had high hopes at that point. But with Guy Pearce goes all the credibility of this movie.

Watching Generation Kill first helped me, because this is a war movie about modern warfare techniques. They're not pretty, and they're not flashy, but that's probably how war is these days. People trying to trick people into dying. Even the greatest or rogues or by the book soldiers can die. Then, there are very, very graphic scenes that will make you squirm. That eliminates the pleasure for those two groups.

Once you get over that, and that the movie will not spell anything out for you, you can revel in the beauty of its realism, suspense and acting. These are real people that are forced to change their demeanor, then have it changed in other ways by force. The main character is someone that acts the way he does, but can't really explain why, he just needs to do it. He has the best of intentions, but he needs to do what he does. He needs this transposition and will find surrogates for the things he really needs in life, but in the end, his life is better lived through war.

It is a "fun" ride following him, and it is about as tense as a movie can get. There are great cameos by actors, and superb sets and cinematography for it's documentary style of filming, but it's really the performances of the main three that make this movie so great. Simply put, The Hurt Locker is one of the greatest war films I have ever seen (I have to admit I have many still to see). The cast captures the stresses of war in all aspects, and the writing evokes raw emotion that questions the humanity within all of us.  Every aspect of the film fits within the opening quote "war is a drug." The fighting and chaos of war drives the main character, and pushes the audience along with the rush. The Hurt Locker became my favorite film of the year after just one viewing.

	Jeremy Renner stars as Staff Sergeant William James, a bomb specialist, in charge of disarming all sorts of ordinates. He enters the film as a man apart from his squad by putting them in danger during their first operation together. His two squad partners, Sergeant JT Sanborn and Specialist Owen Eldridge, only have a few weeks left on tour. You can quickly imagine how they feel about this "wild-man" putting them in harm's way. The story charts their days together for a few weeks, tackling their relationships with each other. Without spoiling too much, the ending ties the story together perfectly and leaves you knowing what becomes of these soldiers.

	While the acting creates a certain sense of intensity, the cinematography and camera style complete this depth. Most of the film is shot using the popular hand-held technique, and it is used perfectly for mood and tone of the film. A man who lives on the brink of life or death needs a style to evoke his state of mind, and director Kathryn Bigelow (known for Point Break) hits it spot on.

	You may be asking "What is 'the hurt locker'?" the film doesn't clearly explain what the title refers to, but it hints at the possibilities. Easily put, it could be the mental state when you are between life and death, with adrenaline rushing, and not worrying about death at all. Staff Sgt. James exists only within the hurt locker. He is a man pained by meaningless everyday life, needing to be on the edge. It isn't something the military creates through dehumanization. It is his human nature, and this character study is fascinating. It begs to question how each of our minds is wired, and what makes a man tick. 

	The film moves outside of politics and conventional war themes dealing with humanity and depression, To attempt an understanding of a man himself. By the end, that man never waivers from his true nature, keeping in step with who he is at the beginning. His journey throughout the few depicted weeks is tiring depressing and heart wrenching. One of the most powerful scenes on screen is Sgt. James breaking down while taking a shower in full uniform. This image alone captures what it means to be a victim of war, past or present. That is something Hurt Locker perfects: the psychological effects of battle as the war are happening. The main victim, Specialist Eldridge, has a broken psyche, yet he is forced to suppress it to enter the war zone for each operation.

	The Hurt Locker is not without flaw. The story introduces several characters only to kill them off in the same sequence. Some of these are very intriguing people, yet they get shallow development and fade quickly. The pacing is a little slow at times through the second act, but it builds toward a great resolution. The bomb disarmament scenes are thrilling yet they seem a touch repetitive. These are extremely minor drawbacks to the greatest Iraq war film yet, and it has an actor worthy of an Academy Award.

	Overall The Hurt Locker hits every chord of action, drama, comedy, and suspense to create one emotional ride. The desert firefight is one of the best standoffs I have screened, and I left the theater completely satisfied. As the tagline puts it, "You'll know when you're in it" and once you're in, you're engrossed.

Filmed in documentary style with no political stand point interfering and outstanding performances by the cast, including Jeremy Renner and Anthony Mackie. Another triumph for Kathryn Bigelow ("Near Dark", "Strange Days"). Wihout a doubt a potiential entry for 2009.

Kathryn Bigelow has crafted a complex yet ceaselessly compelling story of war, humanity, and paths of redemption that boasts breakout performances from Renner, Mackie, and Geraghty (three actors who have been around for some time now, but will finally receive their due for their stunning work here). 

One of the film's main strengths is how it avoids any unnecessary temptations regarding war. For example, Bigelow and the script never forget that this is a character-driven story, and focuses on how the suspense impacts them instead of shooting from a more general, action-packed angle. The film is about these three soldiers dealing with war and how it tugs each of their emotions, whether they deal with fear, morality, motivation, obligation, patriotism, etc. Possibly the best move by the filmmakers is the negligence of any Iraqi-War commentary. Unlike (most) of the previous films tackling this subject, no political points are being shoved down the audience's throat. This is a simple story that never forgets it's character essence. 

In addition, numerous small cameos by select, talented actors (Guy Pearce, Ralph Fiennes, David Morse, and Evangeline Lilly) help enrich the cast. Although it seems like few are wasted (Morse only has a few lines!), a solid choice is being made by not distracting from the three frontmen. My one minor complaint would be that because the film does not have a central plot, the soldiers' many episodes seem somewhat fragmented at times when dealing with the sole action & suspense. However, Bigelow's immense dedication and focus strings the film together with the powerful (unpolitical) message and fascinating characters. "The Hurt Locker" is a strong film about war and redemption that deserves to be seen (in my opinion, it's only a few notches below the excellent "In the Valley of Elah", another movie in the same field).

The Iraq War is a title that thrives on a brutal, violent, and chaotic environment. This is something that has yet to be depicted in films. Although Kimberly Peirce's "Stop-Loss" was a good film, it had a lot of cliche's and was endlessly bogged down by an unfocused moral. "In the Valley of Elah" was a much better effort from "Crash" director Paul Haggis. The performances were solid (especially Tommy Lee Jones) and the narrative was strong and emotionally satisfying. But that's just it, I'm sick of being satisfied. I want something more than the dumbed down sequences we see on CNN or Fox News. Coming into "The Hurt Locker" I was hoping for something along the lines of Ridley Scott's "Blackhawk Down." Although the latter was less interested in character development, it nonetheless illustrated an environment that was scary and filled with paranoia. To say Kathryn Bigelow creates the same type of environment I had just mentioned would be a tremendous understatement. Light on a singular narrative and more concentrated on crafting a slice-of-life portrait, "The Hurt Locker" proved to be one of the better war pictures of the decade, perhaps only behind Clint Eastwood's "Letters from Iwo Jima."

The film deals with a trio of soldiers and their involvement in the EOD (Explosive Ordnance Disposal) squad in Baghdad. After their leader is brutally killed, Sergeant William James (Jeremy Renner) is summoned upon to lead the pack. He is quite different from anyone they have seen before, to say the least. In an intense early scene, Jame decides to go after the planted bomb alone. He even puts up a smoke screen to detract the view of his fellow companions. To say he is simply a lunatic would be criminal. After Sergeant JT Sanborn (Anthony Mackie) and Specialist Owen Eldridge (Brian Geraghty) get into a bit a tangle with new comer James, the three eventually begin to form a tight unit. "The Hurt Locker" is filled with a riveting atmosphere scene after scene. From having to disarm multiple bombs, to a life-or-death sniper sequence, director Bigelow is able to capture each scene with excruciating authenticity and intensity.

Each character here is troubled and true to life. Bigelow is not so much interested in who these characters are in a  literal sense, but who they are when occupying their jobs, and how the danger of their job effects their emotional state. Eldridge meets with a doctor who seems to be worried about his sanity. He seems to have already accepted his death destined fate based on the risk and troubling consequences of his duty. Sanborn is juggling whether or not anyone will truly care if he meets his fate in the war, dealing solely with the prospect of having a child with his girlfriend. Thrill seeking James is having a hard time deciding whether he'll be able to operate back home with his wife and kid, or to remain in Iraq and deal with his irrational love for disarming hidden bombs. A scene that depicts this perfectly revolves around the trio and their brawl at night. Although fun on the surface, it explicates the one consistency this job has to offer; violence.

It's a breath of fresh air to see a director who does not have a hidden agenda. There's an opening title card that reads "war is a drug," and "The Hurt Locker" stays firmly on its tracks to keep consistent to this principle. Although mainly a slice-of-life depiction, the film begins to resemble a narrative arc when focusing on the relationship between young boy who sells porn on the streets, and Sergeant James. When James discovers a body bomb that resembles the young kid he had recently befriended, his emotions and feelings begin to emerge. Bigelow carefully ends this arc with beautiful ambiguity, without letting it crowd the bigger picture. Furthermore, Bigelow's greatest accomplishment is her ability to capture the EOD's bomb disarming scenes with endless intensity. A third act scene involving a family man and multiple explosives attached to his body is extremely harrowing. Also, there is a sniper scene so good in quality that it may be fitting to put it in the same class as Kubrick's sniper sequence in "Full Metal Jacket." A brief cameo by Ralph Fiennes was a warm welcome, and his character's conclusion further enhances the atmosphere Bigelow so finely establishes.Her "shaky cam" work is terrific and ambitious, reeling the audience into each and every frightening sequence.

The performances are stellar. Jeremy Renner is simply superb as James. His performance, filtered down to reality through the subtle script, shows a character who is deeply troubled. He knows he has  a responsibility at home, but his irrational passion for his job seems to be gaining control over his cognition. He even keeps spare parts under his bed that reminds him of each and every moment his life was at risk. Supporting work from Mackie and Geraghty is solid while the cameos from Guy Pearce and Raplh Fiennes are dangerously delightful.

It's an examination of any individual walking a fine line in his combat role, and why he does it.  No cheesy Hollywood script, no one-liners, no ridiculous sound-track, no real gimmicks. Kathryn Bigalow, one of the most underrated action film directors ever, uses mostly hand-held cameras, thus putting the viewer right in the middle of the action.

With this one film, he has gone from frequent character actor ("What movie have I seen him in?") to a potential Best Actor Oscar nominee. His love for war is scary. He thrives on the thrill; it's his natural high. He seems more at ease when diffusing roadside bombs in Iraq than choosing a cereal while at the supermarket in civilian life. 

One of the more intense scenes involves a desert shootout. There is no fast moving action; no loud music score or quick editing. We are there with the soldiers, as they take cover from terrorist snipers a few miles away across the open desert. The standoff lasts for hours as both sides wait patiently for the best shot. The best way I can describe this film concisely is by comparing it to another well known war flick.
  "The Hurt Locker" gives the Iraq War that "Full Metal Jacket" gave the Vietnam War. It makes the film personal by focusing in on particular, well defined characters. It makes the story function better on a personal level by sacrificing a broader view of the conflict at large.
This serves the film well.

   The subjects of the story are the three members of an army bomb squad, and their high stress job as they face down car bombs, improvised explosive devices, and suicide bombers. In my opinion, this was an excellent choice as it allows the filmmakers to depict the situations we most often hear about in the news and have come to define the war. It ALSO allows for MANY tense scenes, as one false move could mean death at any instant.

The acting is incredible on many levels. The actors make both the stress, anger, and camaraderie of the soldiers evident, and bring a very human element to the war, without which this film would be lost. You may or may not be able to relate to the characters, but you'll find it easy to empathize and believe that they are in the situations depicted. Regardless of its actual accuracy, it FEELS like the most accurate portrayal of the Iraq war yet put on film.
 
 It eschews political posturing as well, which I appreciated. While it is far from glorifying war, it avoids speculation as to why the war started or whether it was justified or not. Instead you get a straightforward portrayal of life on the ground and the stresses each soldier faces. 

While the film is not lacking in action, the editing is much more patient than your standard action flick, preferring to let a scene develop at its own pace rather than turning into a frantic cut fest and constantly trying to top itself. Its much easier to appreciate a situation when you see it unfold in real time. 

All in all, the film succeeds because it drops all pretense and offers the viewer an honest, no-holds-barred picture of war and warriors with enough humanity to make you care for its characters. Its not perfect, certain elements could have been changed or removed to make the film a more cohesive whole, but it is by FAR the best Iraq War film I have seen thus far.

The greatness of a film can sometimes be realized when you're only part way through. Sometimes it strikes after the last frame transitions into the credits and other times it becomes apparent days later. None of the above applied here. I waited 5 days before writing this hoping to retrospectively decipher why nearly everything written about this film says it's the best of the year to date, but alas, it has not come to me. Nor do I think it'll come to the voters from the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences when the nomination ballots are mailed. That's not to say they won't have it on their short-list though.

The suspense is real when it needs to be and created not by quick cuts and overzealous camera movements, but by the classic method of simplicity. Kathryn Bigelow knows that suspense happens naturally in a story. It doesn't need to be glazed over. In a sequence where snipers are positioned in the desert surrounding our protagonists, the initial gunshot happens so matter-of-factly, it's chilling. The sound of the shot is barely audible. The group takes cover and prepares to retaliate. At one point, Sgt. Sanborn (Anthony Mackie) runs out of ammo. Another magazine has to be retrieved off of a soldier shot down just minutes previous. Sanborn replaces the mag. It jams... too much blood on it. Sanborn hands it back to his Specialist Eldridge (Brian Geraghty). He can't get the blood off. He asks for someone else to help him. There is no yelling and screaming at one another during all of this, the voices are kept cool but with a strong hint of nerves. All the while several snipers sit in a not-so-far-off building. Its scary how it seems to take place in real time.

As promised, there is the dismantling of bombs. But as I look back, it all seems to blur together. With the exception of one instance involving a suicide bomber, there isn't much to distinguish one section of the film from another. There is no big picture (plot-driven nor character-driven) framing the events. We just have the countdown of days until the soldiers are rotated and sent back home. I have a feeling that screenwriter Mark Boal felt he needed some diversity in the action and included a couple sequences where Staff Sgt. James (Jeremy Renner) sneaks off in the night to fulfill his own agenda. I don't have any family or friends in the Army, but I was very curious as to the potential possibility of those occurrences in real life. Can anyone really just get away with sneaking off like that?

Much of the film leaves a veil of mystery over the intent of the Iraqi people that the soldiers encounter. One citizen drives a car straight into a zoned off area and pulls up next to Staff Sgy James while he is preparing to dismanttle a bomb. After a good long minute and a half, maybe two, where James points a gun at the man commanding him to move, the citizen remains in his car and drives away. It's never revealed why this happens. In a sense, this underlines our xenophobic tendencies. I can imagine the soldiers are constantly nervous about the intent of the citizens on the streets and we as an audience are just as nervous throughout the movie.

Renner and Mackie give brave performances. Renner in displaying his character's intense focus but yet apathy towards death and Mackie in his character's frustration with the former. The sound work and editing are nice and the cinematography has the expected level of "grittiness." There are some fascinatingly enjoyable slow motion shots of the explosions.

Ultimately though it all suffers from a lack of depth. What defines a film about war is the strength of the writing between the action. Mostly we see our men just horsing around, drinking, chatting, etc. Nothing new. Not much insight to offer. But then I suppose this isn't about war as much as it is about a man who only enjoys one thing that he does and sticks to doing that one thing. In that case, Robert D. Siegel and Darren Aronofsky do that topic better with "The Wrestler".

"The Hurt Locker" is a brilliant, uncompromising view of what I imagine war must feel like.  The movie follows three soldiers of a bomb-disposal unit as they struggle through the last month of their company's rotation in Iraq.  Virtually plotless, the movie simply follows the three men from job to job, and each experience with these high explosives is intense and agonizing.  Director Kathryn Bigelow gives the movie a documentary feel, placing the audience alongside the unit, and this heightens the anxiety exponentially.  It's not an anti-war film in the traditional sense.  There isn't an agenda here, and certainly no sloganeering.  But the movie does an exceptional job of showing the physical and emotional toll of war, and is as powerful and provocative as anything you're likely to see this, or any, year.
