With Kathryn Bigelow's"The Hurt Locker", the young genre of Gulf War II movies has gotten its first indisputable critical success. The story of an elite Army bomb squad facing a desert full of Iraqi IEDs ("improvised explosive devices") in 2004, Bigelow's movie is like a game of Russian roulette stretched over 2 hours and 11 minutes -- just one near-death experience after another, with nothing else in sight but dust and more suspicious packages. It's so tense, theaters should be obliged to provide decompression areas, with cots, juice and crackers for emerging survivors.

	
The knife blade of a script by Mark Boal ("In the Valley of Elah") focuses on the relationship between Staff Sergeant William James (Jeremy Renner), a talented defuser with a broad reckless streak, and Sergeant JT Sanborn (Anthony Mackie), the unfortunate soul assigned to protect him on the battlefield. Still mourning the loss of his last "blaster" (Guy Pearce, in a brief but memorable turn), Sanborn can only look on in astonishment as James strides into the red zone, protected by nothing but a clumsy suit of armor and his own bravado. It's not that he sees himself as invulnerable. Instead, he seems to regard each bomb as an intellectual puzzle, a peek inside the minds of people he must live beside but hardly understands.


Forget about every James Bond/MacGyver time-bomb scenario you've seen before. A time-bomb, after all, has the decency to tell you when it's supposed to go off. Instead, the guys who tackled IEDs in Iraq had to do their work in the open, potentially in full view of the insurgents who made the bombs, and who might set them off at any time using their cell phones. Add occasional sniper fire, suiciders, and "body bombs" (booby-trapped corpses), and you begin to sense of dimensions of this particular chamber of horrors.

Kathryn Bigelow displays her mastery of exacting tension in this exceptional war thriller about a U.S. bomb squad disarming explosives in Baghdad. It's a big breakthrough for star Jeremy Renner, excellent as a reckless cowboy who is virtually addicted to defusing bombs, hence the film's tagline "war is a drug". During his month-long tour, Renner's character has his eyes opened to the nastiness of the war he's fighting, but experiences internal conflict because he still depends on the adrenaline rush of playing with fire. Tensions are also rampant within the bomb squad unit, especially between Renner and Anthony Mackie, superb as war-weary sergeant furious with Renner's dangerous antics. DP Barry Ackroyd uses handheld camerawork to extremely dramatic effect, particularly for the POV shots that pull the audience right into the action. Ditto to the exhilarating film editing of Bob Murawski and Chris Innis. Be sure to see it on the loudest screen possible, as it's the only way to truly appreciate Paul Ottosson's Oscar-worthy sound design.

"War is a drug." So reads the quotation by American journalist Chris Hedges that precedes Kathryn Bigelow's "The Hurt Locker." The film has a clear thesis, but offers little of substance to extrapolate or back it up. The movie is remarkably effective on the gut level of provoking an emotional response, but relies on a few disappointing action cliches that prevent it from truly being the masterpiece others have been so quick to hail it as.

The aforementioned quote refers to the bomb-diffusing, adrenaline-addled protagonist of the film, Staff Sergeant William James (Jeremy Renner), who deals so intimately with death in his day job, that everything else starts to feel a little bit dull by comparison. Or at least that's the idea. In execution, James comes off more as your prototypical action hero than the fascinating subject of a character study. He behaves like every other Bourne/Bond/Bay superman to grace the screen in recent memory, and the film declines to comment on this condition until the last thirty minutes or so, making what should be the core of the piece feel more like an afterthought.

The pacing is unhelpful as well, broken up as the story is into isolated encounters that neither build in the traditional narrative sense nor offer more than a diverting peripheral glimpse into the lives of the characters. The sequences are so arbitrarily episodic that their order could seemingly be shuffled with little to no detriment to the comprehensibility of the story arc. Ostensibly, "The Hurt Locker" is a film with a clearly defined beginning and end and enough style to keep what's in between from feeling stagnant.

Sure, the bomb diffusion sequences are great. Through the use of ambient sound effects and hand-held camera work (a testament to its correct usage) with an almost Hitchcockian suspense-building prowess, Bigelow is able to masterfully pluck the audience's heartstrings like so many delicate red wires. It's a shame these refreshing, interesting, entertaining pieces of the film are undercut by its vacuous, nearly non-existent story.

And though I'll champion the style in a general sense, the film's pleasing documentary aesthetic is blatantly violated in two auspicious moments, and as far as I can remember, only two. One is a Matrix-esque dancing bullet shell that meets the sand in super-slow motion, and the other, a bomb exploding at an equally fast shutter-speed from multiple angles, letting the audience pause to consider the visual significance of watching the paint peel from the skeleton of a car or a dust cloud rippling in the blast. The moments are pure Hollywood and feel completely removed from the intention of the rest of the film.

The most profound moment comes toward the end, when James is confronted with the one, and really only, consequence of his actions, leading to the serious injury of a squad member. However, the implications are decidedly secondary to the film's conclusion, which has all the subtlety and self-aware military chic of an Army recruitment spot, which sabotages James' only meaningful character change and will likely send you out of the theater with a razz between your lips.

So ignore the hype and the nonsensical title. If you approach "Hurt Locker" looking for a little summer fun, the ingredients are assuredly there. Just don't let the art house fool you into thinking Kathryn Bigelow's latest offers much more than a few cheap thrills.

I didn't know what a "hurt locker" was but figured the movie by the same name would offer an explanation. Welp, I sat through all 130 minutes of the film today, and I still don't know what a hurt locker is.

My expectations for this Iraq war flick couldn't have been higher, given all the buzz it is getting. Oscar buzz even. And, the first amazingly shot, nail-biting sequence where Guy Pearce and crew try to defuse a bomb made me believe this movie would live up the hype. Alas, it was downhill after that scene. And, s-l-o-w-l-y.

If the movie is supposed to say that war is hell and confusing as all get out, it does. I was confused from start to finish. Who just got shot? What was his motivation? Is that guy really an insurgent -- or just an innocent Iraqi who stumbled in to this scene at the wrong time? Hey, what's that kid doing alive? I thought he just got killed. And, what the hell is a hurt locker? It's all a cloudy mess, and it never gets explained. That may well be the reality of war, but as moviegoers, we deserve a bit more.

These characters are so ill-defined, it's hard to tell who's who. It's pretty impossible to care about any of them, when we know so little about them.

My mind kept wandering to that magnificent, three-hour masterpiece about the Vietnam War, The Deer Hunter. In that film, the first hour is dedicated to introducing us to the characters in their hometown. We know where they came from and who they were before war, so we can see what impact war has on them.

The battle scenes and the bomb-defusing scenes in this film feel repetitive. Not only did I feel like I was watching the same scene over and over, but I started to feel nauseous. The hand-held camera used throughout the film does more than make you feel uneasy about the goings-on. It made me queasy.

There is not much about The Hurt Locker that hasn't already been said by nearly unanimous critics and audiences, but being such a feverishly subjective experience, one is bound to have brought one's own relative fears, perceptions and sense of both surprise and inevitability to the experience oneself. Regardless of where those reactions individually come from and the relationship they have with a given scene, that in itself is the experience of the soldier in combat. The actors on screen do not work from prose monologues but through instinctive reckonings of who they are and what they feel. They are not good fighting evil. They see less good and more evil in everyone and everything with each passing day.

Kathryn Bigelow has always been a very skillful director of Hollywood action movies. But this is a whole different beast. She has certainly put her hand to varying themes, settings and subgenres before, but The Hurt Locker is in a class all by itself as the film where she has focused every fiber of her ability into fashioning a unique, unfettered film. Yes, an uber-masculine action film, a film about the Iraq War, but rarely are we so unaware of the distance between ourselves and the screen. It is not just the only film about the war to have been successful thus far, it is an experience she has fought tooth and nail to give us.

There are two name actors in the film. One of them dies in the very first scene and the other appears for a minute or less near the end. Otherwise, we spend the film's protracted duration in the unadulterated presence of actors we may or may not have seen before, unable to comfort ourselves by connecting them with other roles in other films. There are no masks of stardom any more than there are facades of set design or non-diagetic visual effects. We inevitably believe that they are not acting at all, that they are living the very lives and doing the very things on screen.

The film was shot by United 93 cinematographer Barry Ackroyd with hand-held 16mm cameras, usually with four cameras rolling at once. It is gritty, grimy, saturated in sweat, overexposure, underexposure, and the expansion beyond dualism. This is the way we believe the bomb squad's experiences look and feel, because that is the way we undergo our physical day-to-day existence, by looking at the small, representative systems and the entire complex structure at the same time. The eye always has and always will see conflictingly with the lens, though with various focal lengths and an energetic editing approach---indeed you are guaranteed to never feel aware of a cut---the lens gives us that mutual negotiation of opposing perspectives, which inescapably embodies the sense of complete involvement.

It isn't just the self-contained plays depicting the three conflicting sergeants in the bomb unit diffusing improvised explosives that have our hearts in our throats. The building rage and paranoia pervades every moment. One night, the three sergeants, played by Jeremy Renner, Anthony Mackie and Brian Geraghty, who never completely like or hate each other, get more wasted than anybody I've ever seen and take turns smashing each other in the stomach. But this is not quite aggressive enough to satisfy one of them, Renner's Sergeant First Class William James, who lives and breathes confrontation with potentially fatal threats the way a drug addict is never satisfied with more than enough of their substance. He is not bad or cruel. He is not easily offended, he is gregarious and honest. But he is like that in the field as well, such as when he insists on approaching a suspected bomb without first sending a bomb disposal robot on his first mission with this company.

Bigelow will never be the same filmmaker she was before. Near Dark, Blue Steel and Strange Days are exciting thrillers, and they demonstrate her flair for atmosphere, but at the helm of The Hurt Locker, she demonstrates an outright mastery and total understanding of the effects of the camera, the mental creation of the third shot when one shot cuts to the next, and the most unequivocally honest application of life's sights and sounds to those of cinema. She has the brass balls to take a subject matter proved to be box office poison and give it her relentless all.

They do not go out on their own in a single humvee.  They don't go into buildings by themselves and clear the whole damn thing.  An E-5 Sergeant (Mackle's character) would NOT talk to an E-7 Sergeant First Class (Renner's Character) the manner that they do in this movie.  That's called insubordination.  The small things also bug me.  Renner's character is a former ranger, with a Ranger Scroll combat patch, but no ranger tab;  while Mackle's character, a former military intelligence officer has a combat infantryman's badge, something that can only be earned by infantrymen.  Almost no one is wearing an American Flag on their right shoulder.  No one is going to leave a Lieutenant Colonel psychologist out on the street by himself.  I don't mean to go on a rant here, but was the technical/military adviser even working half the time?  It seems like he was taking a nap while the movie was being filmed and scripted.  Or maybe they just didn't have one at all.  All in all, great action flick if you don't want to think about what war really means to REAL people over in Iraq.  Basically, this movie is about as unrealistic as it can be, and doesn't do justice to the men and women serving their country.

THE HURT LOCKER is an electrifying and extremely realistic war film written by a American journalist based in Iraq and Kathryn Bigelow, director of NEAR DARK.  It is the best of the recent influx of Iraq war films, due to the fact that it unrelentingly shows the human and emotional side to the soldiers the story revolves around.  The unit is called the IED, or Bravo Company, a special unit who locate and disarm roadside bombs.  It's a highly perilous job, only those with iron nerves and notable bravery are up to it.  The film is a masterpiece, just as it is hailed to be.  

Jeremy Renner gives a fantastic and emotional performance as Staff Sergeant William James.  A new, rowdy bombs specialist who is replacing the unit's former leader Sergeant Thompson (Guy Pearce).  Sergeant Sanborn (an excellent Anthony Mackie) is speculative on the leadership qualities of William's, especially when the tension is turned on.  38 days are left in Bravo Company's rotation, and Sanborn and his unit friend Eldridge want to be alive by then.  For those 38 days, the three undergo harrowing trials of life-and-death situations, especially in the film's climactic scene (you'll know).  

Director Kathryn Bigelow directs the film with a startling immediacy, pulling you directly into the film's action and conflict as well as pummeling you with situation after situation of fever pitch life-and-death tension.  This could also be one of the best movies of the decade, this decade's SAVING PRIVATE RYAN.  It's that solid and arresting.  Look for an appearance from Ralph Fiennes and David Morse as two squad leaders.  Their brief performances are strong.  All in all, THE HURT LOCKER is an electrifying and extremely realistic war film written by a American journalist based in Iraq and Kathryn Bigelow, director of NEAR DARK. The critics have raved about "The Hurt Locker."  I heard it was an intense portrait of a U.S. army bomb squad in Iraq.  But I think there's two things that people need to understand to truly appreciate this movie:

1.  there is no plot; it unfolds like a fictionalized documentary

2.  almost too subtly, the film is really about the evolving perspective of the central character, Jeremy Renner's shockingly maverick Staff Sgt. Will James; he starts out devil-may-care, the war seems to get to him ... and then the ending throws you for a loop.

The film is beautifully produced to evoke conditions on the ground in Iraq, including the use of shaky-cam that may wear on some viewers.  I loved long, quiet scenes of troops studiously pursuing a target, the way it is in war, in contrast to the wham-bam-thank you ma'am style of typical war movies; that's the same thing I loved about "Saving Private Ryan."

And the cameos.  Awesome.  If you're a "Lost" fan, there's one in particular that will tickle you.

I'm glad I finally went to see this film, but only recommend it to people if they're interested in a more atypical, artistic approach to a war story.

The Hurt Locker manages to be the best movie about the Iraq War by taking the simplest, most direct approach possible.  Director Kathryn Bigelow is at her very best here, and is well within her element, helming what is essentially an action thriller.

Bigelow is one of the most technically proficient directors of this sort of cinema.  The handheld work is rock solid yet visceral.  Where directors like Tony Scott and Michael Bay rely on constant cutting, extreme close-ups, and canted angles to disorient the viewer and convince them they they are experiencing "action," Bigelow is confident enough in her storytelling to let the action occur naturally.  The film's numerous bomb-defusing situations are set up in a series of master shots and explained so clearly without extraneous exposition that the viewer easily slips into the mind of the protagonist and is able to experience the full impact of the ratcheting suspense.

This is not a political movie.  Bigelow isn't shy about her thesis.  "War is a drug" appears on the first title card.  The addict here is an army specialist in bomb diffusion.  He's damn good and he knows it.  Jeremy Renner delivers an incredible performance as a man who comes to the unpleasant realization that there's only one thing he truly loves.  He's backed up by Anthony Mackie and Brian Geraghty, both of whom are also great here.  Mackie's Sgt. Sanborn is competent, professional, and by-the-book.  He wants to do his job well and go home.  Geraghty's Specialist Eldridge is way out of his element.  He's scared and disoriented and scarred by the decisions he's made.  The characters don't feel like stereotypes, they feel like genuine personifications of the men and women drawn into war, and the horrible experiences and emotions they have to deal with.

"War is a Drug"

A great war film. The Apocalypse Now and Saving Private Ryan of the Iraq war. Kathyrn Bigelow's The Hurt Locker makes no apologizes for abstaining from cliches and delivers a visceral and searingly intense experience. The film refreshingly has no interest in a conventional plot, but instead delivers a random series of missions revolving around a group of soldiers that deal with disarming IED roadside bombs. Shot in a documentary fashion with plenty of handheld shots, the viewer can practically taste the dirt, dust, and heat that accompanies the soldiers in increasingly hostile environments.

The film begins with a breathtaking, magnificently paced display of tension dealing with squad commander Thompson (Guy Pearce) and his crew scoping out a potential IED. The scene is crucial for a few reasons: establishing the gritty tone and style of the film, establishing the job of Bravo Company (dealing with IEDs), and setting up one of the recurring themes in the film revolving around soldiers and their gear.

The film trudges on with the coming of squad commander James played by Jeremy Renner. This guy is the real Charles Bronson. Relatively speaking, if commander James has a death wish, Bronson's Kersey makes a living as a children's party mascot. In an early scene, James goes into a life-threatening, uncontrollable situation in which his soldiers have to watch from afar. Wearing a kind of bloated, disarming bomb suit, James diffuses the 1st threat only to realize the situation is exponentially more complex; oh, and at any minute a local could detonate the device using merely a cell phone. 

The soldiers inflate such scenes with occasional dark and twisted humor that would at first seem to cut into the intensity of the scene, but further reflection suggests one must maintain a sense of humor about how absurd and dangerous a situation is in order to bear the potential repercussions.  James, in particular, fuses this easy-going, gung-ho indifference with a daredevil mentality; once his bomb suit goes on, only the Hounds of Hell will get in his way. Post mission visuals are just as interesting, as it is revealed that James will actually sleep in his bomb suit helmet and shower in his fatigues, sometimes blurring the disconnect between where his mission ends and his life begins.

As done in several war movies but without as much depth, The Hurt Locker contains juxtaposition scenes revolving around the war and home life back in America. A particularly interesting scene shows James back with his wife and family shopping at a local food mart. James effectively relays how the gut-wrenching, high stakes simplicity of diffusing a bomb in Iraq pales in comparison to the complexity of finding the right box in the cereal isle.

Bigelow peppers the film with, among Pearce, a slew of celebrity cameos which provides some unanticipated eye candy. While at first jarring given the majority of the film spotlights relative unknowns, the cameos quickly and comfortably dissolve into the frenetic style of the film.

Perhaps only in Apocalypse Now has a war film given such insight into the mentality that "War is a Drug" before The Hurt Locker. It is quite fantastical to believe that the rush of being in near-death situations could eventually become an addiction unsustainable with the friendly confines of home life. Even with with wife and son waiting through constant nerves and inescapable dread, Renner's James provides a powerful case-study example of the mind-altering insanity war inflicts on a malleable mind.

A tremendously suspenseful, exciting and well crafted action picture about diffusing bombs in Iraq.
Jeremy Renner and Anthony Mackie are really great as the leads.
Action scenes are consistently suspenseful and really well shot in a gritty documentary style.  Yet you can still easily follow what is going on in each action scene.
The cameos by Guy Pearce and Ralph Fiennes are great partly because they don't seem like the usual distracting cameos that sometimes happens with more well known actors in smaller roles.  Both Guy Pearce and Ralph Fiennes's characters fit just right in their respective scenes.  David Morse was good in his scene as well.
I thought it was a smart decision to keep the film apolitical and just focus on Bravo squad's operations - doing otherwise would have opened up a can of worms and would have been a pretty big distraction in a film that is probably better off for not having a pro or anti war bent.
The scene where Renner is diffusing the bomb in the car with all the people watching is really great.
Also thought the sniper scene was pretty fantastic.
Although as great as that scene was that does bring me to one flaw that can't be ignored in that scene.  Specifically that Ralph Fiennes's character is hit at one point by the enemy snipers - and then Renner and Mackie end up taking Fiennes's exact same position - and yet the enemy doesn't shoot at them - even though the enemy would know exactly where they are given that they just took up the same position that Fiennes did.  Renner and Mackie are able to stay up in that spot for a pretty long time and yet the enemy doesn't hit them.  An odd decision considering all you'd have to do to fix it is just have Renner and Mackie take up a position different from where Fiennes was and then you'd be fine.  It's not a huge problem but it is a noticeable flaw from a realism standpoint.  Still a great scene despite that though.  Liked the touch with the Capri Sun.
Another somewhat unrealistic moment is the scene where Renner, Mackie and Sanborn all go in after the allleged remote bomb maker w/out more infantry support.  It is a movie after all - and I understand that it wouldn't be as exciting if an infantry group went in that didn't include the leads - so it makes some sense from that perspective.  It is still a pretty great scene despite that.  Also one would think Sanborn getting shot would get Renner in some significant trouble, but that doesn't happen in the movie.
All in all those realism flaws are minor in the grand scheme of things - the fact is the Hurt Locker is a pretty great action picture and one of the best films of the year.

Instead, the movie focuses on the strange little world that war itself creates, and lets the well-acted and well-shaped characters explore the dimensions of brotherhood, comradery, and of course life and death. 

There are few flaws in this movie. Some scenes don't end as predicted, and sometimes the characters behave in unexpected ways without any real motivation to, but these mistakes are easily forgiveable and are off-screen quickly. 

I rather liked the soundtrack as well. Nothing like heavy metal to get the blood pumping. One of the more interesting aspects of this movie has to do with the blaring, chaotic music: it's the main character's favorite. In total silence he quickly and skillfully manipulates pieces of wire and metal to disarm explosives that would shatter his bones and burst his organs. "The Hurt Locker" is undoubtedly the best war film of the past few years. Kathryn Bigelow's film about a team of bomb diffusers in Iraq is a glorious conglomeration of tense set pieces, terrific acting, and original direction. Its plot is loosely connected, more centered on the characters and their job than any overarching story. Instead of some contrived Hollywood story, Bigelow wisely shows only the reality of the characters jobs, their hardships with insurgents and themselves, and their inability to relate to ordinary life. This dehumanization has become a common theme when exploring the Iraq war -- one it shares with Vietnam -- and "The Hurt Locker" subtly fixates on this aspect of Jeremy Renner's Sergeant James. Renner's performance is fantastic, entrancing the audience around his eccentric, adrenaline-obsessed bomb diffuser. He's both charismatic and extremely perplexing, and Bigelow sums up the character in a brilliant final scene; the final shot of Renner eagerly walking out to diffuse yet another IED, his pompous strut, the title on the screen "364 days left in rotation", exhilarates and leaves the audience in thoughtful reflection. Renner's performance is the centre of the film, around which inhabit interesting supporting performances (notably Ralph Fiennes and Guy Pearce in excellent cameos), exhilarating and tense action pieces, and innovative camerawork. "The Hurt Locker" stimulates both the body and the mind, and is one of the best films of the year.

Kathryn Bigelow directs this war movie that is short on staged battles but big on suspense. Sergeant First Class (SFC) James (Jeremy Renner) takes over an Explosive Ordnance Disposal (EOD) squad after their previous leader is taken by an Improvised Explosive Device (IED). James is a good deal more reckless than his successor and the action stems primarily from this, as well as the ever-present hazards of the terrain.

URBAN:
After all of the rave reviews and best film of the year talk, I was expecting this film to provide the summarizing thesis of the Iraq War - A key to grant an understanding of why, what should have been done, that nevertheless endears the viewer to the servicemen who wage this war.

Instead, the film has much more to do with war in general; seen through the particular details of this war. In doing so, it subtly makes a point that will take some time to tease out, but will ultimately provide some of the most remembered images and tensest/darkest meanings of the war.

This film comes as a welcome breath of fresh air for no other reason than that it maintains internal consistency and coherency. The first screen of the film contains with the phrase "War is a Drug". The words eventually fade out and only that phrase remains. This becomes the central tool for understanding the motivations of the characters and of the film as a whole.

The adrenaline rush is the fix that drives these characters. There are really only three: SFC (E-7) James, Sergeant (SGT, E-5) Sanborn, and Specialist (SPC, E-4) Eldridge. Each participates in the adrenaline rush to a different degree and it becomes apparent that SFC James is far and away the biggest junkie of the group. He feeds off of danger, especially the kind that is found while in his bomb suit, separated from the group, and alone with his life-or-death decisions in defusing explosive ordnance.

It is in these situations that the film looks its best. Crane shots that depict the scale of the setting and the isolation of the character compliment the war as a drug interpretation.

At other levels the interpretation stays consistent as well. SGT Sanborne loves the adrenaline, but worries that his draw to it will hurt his chances at promotion, and at life. SPC Eldridge deals with the other side of the rush. He clearly prefers the safety of prescribed work and taking orders, but in his talk with an Army doctor (mental health) he draws his superior in to the fray by relying on the "you have to go outside the wire to understand me" defense. The Lieutenant Colonel (LTC) Doctor, drawn to the thrill and the status it brings, goes out on a mission but doesn't come back.

From my perspective, as someone in the Army, the film may miss in several tactical areas but more than makes up for it by nailing the feel and the mood. First, the most obvious issue is that trucks never travel alone in country. There will always be at least 3 or 4 in a convoy. The second is that the rank of E-7 is very difficult to come by. I know that my platoon sergeant would neither be breaking the rules by drinking downrange or fraternizing with his men. He definitely wouldn't have been the one taking the outrageous risks. At the same time, the strong feelings, the physicality, the empowering of junior soldiers to make difficult decisions, these all seem to ring very true.

Overall, as described above, the film looks great and the form is matched to the content really well. I sometimes felt that the camera panned too quickly and too often in some cases. These scenes generally were accompanied by a fuzziness and blurring of the picture. Eventually I came to understand this blurriness as a sort of visual clue that helps the viewer relate to the confusion present on the battlefield. The only shots I disagreed with was the slow motion shot of the sniper rifle casings hitting the ground. This seemed to directly copy the slow motion casings falling from the helicopter on Black Hawk Down. Not only was it a copy, but it stood out because it was only used that once. It didn't fit the rest of the film's gritty and real-time telling of the story.

This review could go on and on. The few areas of failing really only stand out because the rest of the film is so good. I will end the review by saying that the film is tense throughout and even channels the dark comedy of Catch-22 with a running count of the days left in the deployment and the macabre joke runs full circle when the last scene is viewed. At this point the message of the film becomes overtly simple, just like Snowden's secret.

URBAN: Recommended

The Hurt Locker opens following bomb squad in 2004 Iraq losing it's leader. When the replacement comes, the squad is unhappy with his reckless behavior putting them in danger. Let me get right to the point.  "The Hurt Locker" is the best film I've seen this year, hands down.  I will go further, and side with many other critics in saying that it is the best Hollywood production about the war in Iraq that has been released.  I'm tempted, moreover, to call it the best war film I've ever seen, but although it is a supercharged, visceral experience of a movie, it lacks the epic scale of classics like "Apocalypse Now" and "Saving Private Ryan."  Please understand that this is not a criticism in itself, for "The Hurt Locker" suffers not at all from its low budget and its small, intimate cast of mostly unknowns.  Instead of feeling scaled down and limited, it feels sleek, compact, matter of fact - a personal drama for a war that has not been extensively analyzed by historians, and so still remains mostly on the level of individual experience.  And believe me, those who choose to seek out this movie are in for a ride - "The Hurt Locker" is a film that works almost entirely on the gut level.  It does not have a conventional plot, so much as a backbone of pulse-pounding run-ins with explosives and explosives makers, where tensions build to almost unbearable levels and you are truly, overwhelmingly unsure of what will happen next.  This level of suspense has not been seen in mainstream film for decades.  Not since Hitchcock have filmmakers decided to play games with the audience, daring them to think that they will succumb to cliche, and then sucker-punching them with something so simple, and yet unexpected, as the bomb not going off at the end of the scene.  It sounds anticlimactic, but that's not the point - because the outcome is always in doubt, you're always on the edge of your seat.  And this is only half of the greatness of "The Hurt Locker" - after the suspense, we are brought back to the characters, and the complexity of their reactions to the inherent danger of their job as soldiers serves as the emotional core of the film.  This film speaks volumes about the effects of war on people, and about the kind of people who fight wars, maybe even about the kind of people who need wars to fight - and these wrenching statements are not lost in the action, but heightened by it.  I suspect "The Hurt Locker" is popular compared to other Iraq war films because it has little to say about the war itself; these days, people want to escape from reality, not to be preached to.  It is for the best that this film chooses not to preach; since the war is not even finished, there is really not a lot that can be said about it.  So how, then, can I call it the greatest film about our current conflict?  Because I have never felt so transported into the danger of that conflict - I have never felt a sense of place and time, never felt the sense of being watched by a people that hate you, never felt the sense of being an inch away from death, as vividly as I have while watching this movie.  "The Hurt Locker" wisely does not explain Iraq.  It is Iraq.  And if you feel that your appreciation for our troops abroad is being sapped by grainy images on the news, then you owe it to yourself to see this movie.  It could very well be one of the great films of our time.

On the surface, The Hurt Locker is a modern war movie, following in the long tradition of war movies, with ebbs and flows that should be familiar to anyone who's ever seen a war movie.  Except, outside a single combat scene, it's not really a war movie.  Taking place in 2004 Iraq, it follows an EOD (Explosive Ordnance Disposal) team on their daily missions to remove IEDs (Improvised Explosive Devices).  For a little background information on the subject, I've pulled the following quote from wikipedia: "In the 2003present Iraq War, IEDs have been used extensively against coalition forces and by the end of 2007 they have been responsible for approximately 40% of coalition deaths in Iraq.[1]".  Needless to say, the daily threat of these improvised bombs creates an atmosphere of genuine terror.

  Sergeant JT Sanborn (Anthony Mackie) has seen one of his fellow squad members die, and isn't too pleased when the new redneck hotshot, Staff Sergeant James (the excellent Jeremy Renner) comes in and starts behaving recklessly.  I'm sure this sounds like familiar territory, but whereas in the past, the reckless hotshot (as played by Tom Cruise or some other actor of similar caliber) would be incredibly confident and cocky, Sergeant James comes off as almost suicidal (his habitual cigarette smoking seems to be an outward extension of his subconscious deathwish), and yet, he claims he never thinks about death.  It's one of the few movies of this genre where the threat of death of the main character has never seemed more real.  Sergeant James deliberately puts himself into the bomb's blast radius rather than have the unmanned robot go in his place.  The answer lies in the movie's opening quote: "War is a drug".  To Sergeant James, the adrenelin rush he gets from disarming these bombs seems to outweigh everything else, whether it's family back home or even the lives of his fellow soldiers.  At one point, he befriends a young Iraqi boy selling dvds in the street.  When he finds the body of a boy, he's convinced it's his friend and sets out to get some measure of revenge for the boy.  The boy himself is of little consequence to him, though.  It turns out, he's just one performer in the movie plot James seems to have going on in his head.

 Director Kathryn Bigelow never judges the characters she's putting onscreen, she merely presents them and leaves it to the audience to judge.  Likewise, our military involvement in Iraq is also portrayed neutrally; the politics behind the invasion are simply of no consequence to the characters on the screen and therefore are irrelevent to the story.  This movie is wholly character-driven, and not in the way you expect a typical war movie to be, and in the end, I'm left with the question, was Sergeant James a cocky rebel or just a severely disturbed individual?  It's a riveting achievement in film.

Normal people do not voluntarily approach bombs. They just dont. They run away from them  quickly. They also dont poke at them and cut wires and try to diffuse them. Again, they just dont. War changes a lot of things about normal people.

Im afraid that I lack too much in the ways of communication to accurately convey just how wonderful The Hurt Locker is from start to finish. I havent seen every war movie ever made, so I can only draw on my knowledge of those films I have seen, those that have dealt with The Great Wars, Korea, Vietnam, and now, Iraq. 

Staff Sergeant James (Jeremy Renner) is a cocky but very self-assured US soldier who voluntarily diffuses bombs. He does so in an over-sized protective suit that, in all likely-hood, will do very little in the way of protection. He knows this. He still does his job. Sergeant JT Sanborn (Anthony Mackie) and Specialist Owen Eldridge (Brian Geraghty) are there covering him as he does his job. These men are not friends, but they are a team, and though they are not perfect, they figure out ways to survive. 

Films about the war in Iraq have had very little acclaim. Either they just havent been done well, or people just arent willing to give them a chance. In the Valley of Elah (2007) was a wonderful film and everyone should see it, but it tackles the subject of war from an onlookers perspective. What director Kathryn Bigelow (Blue Steel (1989)) gives us is the perspective of the soldier, the good, the bad, and the ugly.

I was particularly gripped by the realistic feel of this movie. We dont get all the information we need to always know what is happening, but we get enough to understand what is happening. We realize there are good guys and bad guys and neutral guys, but we dont really know a lot about whom is whom, and we dont really need to know, because this film is not so concerned with any kind of cathartic conclusion, rather, it is dealing with a few specific soldiers in Iraq and the turmoil they go through (physically and emotionally) as they do their job in the desert.

This film works with changes in day and night beautifully, and leaves us filled with tension as we follow these men through a barren land in the harshest of circumstances. People are changed by war. The people in this film are changed by war. But they do their jobs and they count the days until they can leave.

Perhaps I give film critics too much credit.  Have you ever had a similar thought as the credits roll on a film that "shouldn't be missed" or is "one of the year's ten best"?  As I walked out of the theater following a showing of The Hurt Locker, the most intelligible statement I could make was "huh?"  What in this particular film so caught the attention and high praise from such a plethora of critics?  Here is a film, after all, about the war in Iraq -- a topic far from the most popular with critics or the general populace.  

My first thought was that somehow I missed an underlying anti-war message, which (whether right or wrong) I could see people rallying behind.  Yet, after racking my brain, I couldn't arrive at a single scene in the film that spoke for or against the war.  I give the filmmakers credit that they rightly let the war be the backdrop for the telling of a very particular story.  Truth be told, one could have chosen the Vietnam War or Korean War and told a very similar story. 

So, where does this leave us?  Why do critics so love this film?  Sure, the cinematography is amazing and things being blown up is definitely a draw.  Yes, the acting is quite good, but not so stellar as to warrant the critics' current love fest with this film.  As for the story itself, it is compelling enough and does have a particular point which the filmmakers make painfully obvious at the beginning (see the quote in the film's first frame).  Still, many films have similar qualities yet don't garner half as much praise as The Hurt Locker.  The movie is entertaining enough, but far from worthy of the critical accolades it has received.

Don't get me wrong, I liked the movie for what it was -- an interesting story about a bomb squad unit during the Iraq War.  The storytelling gets a bit muddled in the middle when the film moves away from disarming bombs and spends a good 20 minutes in the desert with snipers.  Even with this slight hiccup, however, I found myself committed to the story and its characters.  Yet, let's be honest here, the "moral" of the story (if you will) is nothing particularly new or mind-blowing; and the film's images, while beautifully shot, aren't so revolutionary as to warrant special attention. 

At the end of the day, I can only hypothesize concerning why critics have crowned The Hurt Locker their current film prince.  I suspect that due to the recent void of decent war movies, a film with modest qualities like this one appears amazing.  Yet, hold it up to say a Platoon or a Saving Private Ryan and one quickly sees The Hurt Locker for what it is -- an entertaining film that won't much be remembered one year from now.

Gut-wrenching, pulse-pounding, out of this world tension, just mere exterior descriptions of what Kathryn Bigelow's new film, The Hurt Locker is. Written by Mark Boal, The Hurt Locker overflows with intensity, passion, and reverence. In the wake of 9/11, filmmakers have struggled to create a piece that is socially accepted and respected. Only two films have succeeded in this task over the past eight years; Paul Greengrass' beautiful United 93, depicting an open interpretation of the final moments of the doomed plane in it's final moments, and now, Bigelow's film will join the short, elite list.

This character-driven tale tells the stories of three army soldiers who are a part of the most dangerous of jobs to offer in the military, Explosive Ordnance Disposal (EOD), in plainer terms, they disarm bombs. Staff Sergeant William James played ferociously by Jeremy Renner heads up this story as a soldier facing death every moment of the day. With his wife and child at home and often displaying unorthodox behavior, James seems fit for a war soldier. Sergeant JT Sanborn, played by Anthony Mackie is a by-the-book man, living his days at war while incurring losses along the way. Specialist Owen Eldridge played by Brian Geraghty is young, bewildered, and thrust into a situation unknowing of the impact it would have. What these three men bring to their respective roles educates the viewer of the horrors of war. Forget what you think you know on CNN and your local news, Bigelow is running the show with Boal out on assignment and Renner, Mackie, and Geraghty as our anchors. 

The crews of the picture are the tools in building this powerful vessel. Cinematographer Barry Ackroyd uses his four camera use to keep us feeling like a first-person account of the events of the film. The mesh of Marco Beltrami & Buck Sanders score and the sound effects team makes for a more suspenseful experience. Filming in Jordan was the choice of Bigelow to give it a more authentic feel. It paid off big time because I always felt like I was there in the battle zone, enduring pain, torment, and dehydration. 

"If you're going to make a film about the middle east, then film it in the middle east." -- Kathryn Bigelow

The Hurt Locker deserves all the praise its been receiving and should be experienced by any movie lover. The Oscar Prospects might look a little grim based on the summer release but with no real first-half of 2009 contenders, Bigelow and her film have strong chances of taking a spot amongst the final five come end of the year. Renner and Mackie will also be strong contenders in their respective categories. The strongest possibility for an Oscar has to be for writer Mark Boal. The research he did for the film alone will keep Boal in the minds of voters. The Hurt Locker's striking cinematography, crisp editing that keeps it at a heart palpating pace, strong performances, directing, and writing is enough to take this film in consideration for your viewing. Brilliant, simply brilliant.

People may commit the mistake of avoiding this gem thinking that it's just a war film. Don't. It isn't. It's a great, engrossing film about human emotions, not to be missed.

War is a drug. This is the message that The Hurt Locker, a film about an Army EOD (Explosive Ordnance Disposal) team winding down its last days in Iraq, delivers right at the outset. The embodiment of this message is Sergeant William James (played by Jeremy Renner), the man placed in charge of Bravo Company, an EOD team that has just lost its former team leader on a recent mission. James is an adrenaline junkie who appears to have a bit of a death wish, recklessly charging into the delicate life-and-death situations Bravo Company find themselves in and blatantly and nonchalantly disregarding protocol in the process.

As such, he is a stark contrast to the cautious, by-the-book Sergeant JT Sanborn (Anthony Mackie), one of the men whom James now commands and with whom James suddenly finds himself at odds. Bravo Company, you see, has only thirty-nine days left in its rotation, and, while some officers heap praise upon James for his achievements, Sanborn and the third member of the company, Specialist Owen Eldridge (Brian Geraghty), don't take too kindly to James' dangerous behavior. Sanborn even goes so far as to suggest to Eldridge that they initiate an explosion, an "accident" that would take care of their new leader for good. It is merely a joke for Eldridge. For Sanborn, not so much.

The Hurt Locker goes on to follow Bravo Company through these thirty-nine days, James clashing violently with Sanborn even as they grow closer together in the face of the insanity that awaits them on their perilous missions. When they are not disarming bombs, which have the capability of exploding at any moment at the whim of a hidden enemy, they are confronted by insurgents whose bullets strike down the men around them without warning. Here, we see, chaos reigns supreme. As time goes by, tension mounts, the horrors of war reveal themselves, and we see even James, all smiles and cheer in the beginning, start to crack under the pressure, a vulnerable man beneath the cool and collected facade starting to peek through, just a little.

"Do you know why I am the way I am?" A question posed by James to Sanborn near the end of the film, a question that, we discover, James doesn't know the answer to himself. His most desperate moments provide hints, though, the avenging of a boy whose dead body he finds fashioned into a bomb, a hurried attempt to disarm explosives attached to a man pleading for his help, a hunt for an unseen individual or individuals responsible for an oil truck explosion who may or may not even exist.

There seems to be a compulsion present in James to make a positive change in an environment often beyond his control, to triumph over evil at all costs, a need which, perhaps in some part, drives or coincides with his addiction for the rush that comes with the job. This is a man, after all, who keeps a box under his bed full of inert bomb components, souvenirs from his various missions, momentos of the victories he has won. It is when James is at his most helpless, during moments when it appears that his best efforts are just not enough, that we see him start to come apart, endangering not only himself but his comrades as well.

Kathyrn Bigelow's direction here is raw and intense, the writing by Mark Boal, a freelance journalist who once spent time with an EOD unit in Iraq, dramatically powerful, and the acting all around is fantastic. These three aspects combine to forge a film that feels 100% genuine while being both gripping and eye-opening, the viewer transported to a land where each moment in the field could be one's last and where one's basic sense of decency and compassion is preyed upon at every turn.

We see war's detrimental effects on one's mind, body, and soul, and the ability to overcome these effects and aspire to commit acts of selfless heroism. We also see, however, the abyssmal lows to which we as humans are capable. The Hurt Locker is often difficult to watch, but it is also the reality of war, a setting not conducive to pleasantries nor indeed healthy for one's sanity. Everyone involved in the film does an amazing job of bringing this ugliness to light, and I highly recommend it to anyone who wishes to catch a glimpse into this harsh existence where survival is a constant battle.

In war, the men and women who serve our country are often the subject at the center of the debate. One side will hail them as heroes and honor them when they fall. The other side will cheer for their bravery but implore to bring them home. The two sides clash often and passionately. The real truth lies somewhere in between.

What both sides forget is that these are human beings at the center of their hypothetical debate. Often pundits and civilians alike forget that these troops are the few brave people willing to put their lives in harms way each and every day. This takes a special breed of person. There are precious few like these soldiers. It is a calling. It is a job that doesn't forgive. Yet when these men and women are done with their service they don't receive the extraordinary help that they have offered us in their service.

More can be done to help these heroes readjust, but for some this calling is a drug. Counting the days until you go home 
is followed by counting the days until you go back. Navigating the markets of the Middle East are petrifying until you're forced to navigate the farmers market of the Midwest. War is a complicated puzzle. No one man can explain it's effect on a person. No one person can sum up it's hallucinating pain.

The Hurt Locker makes no commentary on war. It simply tries to tell a story. This particular story follows a bomb squad and it's final 30 days of service in Iraq. Each day is filled with multiple calls to disarm IED's in order to save the lives of civilians, soliders, and insurgents alike. Death is a probability. Survival is an uncertainty. 

Staff Sargent Williams James is a Cowboy. He has the hardwired DNA of a bomb technician. Those with fear of Death in the moment need not apply. Sargent James has none.

"What's the best way to go disarming one of these?"

"The way you don't die sir." 

This recklessness or fearlessness drives his small team nearly insane. They don't seem to first understand him, but after multiple sucessful, albeit risky, missions they begin to trust him. He becomes a slightly fantastical character to them. He collects the detonators that could have killed him. He keeps track of all 870 some bombs he's disarmed. He takes off his bomb suit so he can "die comfortably" if he fails. He's Shakespearean in the most tragic of ways.

His most fatal flaw is his belief that he can save everyone from these IED's. He knows if he doesn't disarm these WMD's people will die. Unlike his brothers Hamlet and Othello we don't see the end of Sargent James in a blaze of glory. Rather the tragedy lies within the cyclical behavior that is also hardwired in his DNA. Sargent James tells his son what we already know. That you begin life caring about many things, but that Sargent James only cares about one thing anymore; Not his wife, not his soldiers, not his son, but his bombs. It's man vs. bomb and that is the scenario that will replay itself every day of James' life until one of them wins, whatever the cost.

Don't miss the defining movie of the Iraq war. Democrat, Republican, Libertarian, or Independent. This movies does what amazing art should. Tell a story. Get you to think about someone else's life besides your own. Then talk about what unites us instead of what divides us.

Once in a while a movie comes along that is supposed to be great.  The Hurt Locker is one of those rare films that does not just meet expectations, it surpasses them.

	The Hurt Locker has been out for a few weeks now, but only in a few select theaters.  Week by week it has begun to be played in wider release.  Now it is up to 523 theaters.  To put that in perspective, this weekend, Funny People opened to over 3,000 theaters.  So, most people will have to wait a little longer to see this phenomenal war time drama.  All the hype for this movie has been stunningly positive, and you will not hear anything different from this article.

	The Hurt Locker is based around a small US bomb squad stationed in Iraq.  The group has less than 40 days left in their tour and they are not trying to get killed before their time runs out.  Every day the three soldiers must venture out and disarm a different mess of destruction.  When the newest member of the team proves to be wild and aggressive, it puts the other team-members lives in danger and hostility begins to appear.

	The squad consists of JT Sanborn, Owen Eldridge, and their new team leader, William James.  Sanborn is controlled, by the book, and a realist.  Eldridge is scared, full of guilt, and will not pull a trigger unless he is told to do so.  James is aggressive, reckless, wild, exciting, and addicted to war.  The director goes into depth on each character, and why they do what they do.

	Jeremy Renner (S.W.A.T.) plays William James and did a perfect job as the adrenaline junkie.  Anthony Mackie (Notorious) plays JT Sanborn.  Mackie has been great in almost everything he is in, and deserves more high profile roles.  Brian Geraghty (The Guardian) plays the nervous and scared, Owen Eldridge.  There are a few well-known actors that have minor roles.  David Morse, Guy Pearce, and Ralph Fiennes are just a few of those names.

	The casting was impeccable, and I do not think anyone could have played each character better.  The hurt Locker was directed by Kathryn Bigelow (Point Break).  I want to see more movies by Bigelow.  She has proved herself to be a master of suspense in movies.  When you watch this movie, there are more than a couple times you are holding your seat, because you have no idea what is going to happen to this bomb-squad.  The direction was amazing, and I hope we see more soon from Bigelow.

	The script was written by Mark Boal.  He previously penned the screenplay for In The Valley of Elah (if you have not seen that, go rent it).  Boal dives so deep into each character it becomes infectious.  Not only do you want to know if these guys will survive the next call, you want to know why they actually do what they do.  And throughout the movie, each character is exposed a little bit more.

	It is hard to find a flaw in this movie.  The direction is amazing, the script was written thoughtfully and engaging, and the actors were each significant in their own way.  This is not only the best war in Iraq movie, it is one of the best war movies ever.  This is the best movie of the year so far, and should garner one of the 10 best-picture nominations from the Academy Awards.  If The Hurt Locker finds its way to your theater, do not miss it.

Final Grade: A

While I thought "The Hurt Locker" was an amazingly well-constructed film, very tense, very well-acted, very relevant, my first reaction upon leaving the theater (sadly) was that it wasn't quite as good as "Jarhead" or "Generation Kill." I'm not quite sure why this was my first reaction, because Jeremy Renner gives us a hate-him-even-while-loving-him male character as memorable as any in film history, from Gordon Gekko to Tyler Durden. But the film's themes simply seemed to recap all that we saw in "Generation Kill" (a new type of soldier is emerging, one who feeds on the adrenaline and is desensitized to violence) and "Jarhead" (the inability to function in the regular world after war). 

Of course, I probably approached "The Hurt Locker" with the wrong attitude, thinking that it might unseat one of those two films as the "best" Iraq war movie. It's a great piece of work...tremendous, in fact, with all the grit and unexpected explosive violence of "Black Hawk Dawn," so maybe I should be thinking that it (right now) completes a sort of Essential Iraq Trilogy, amidst a forgettable collection of other war films.

Just as Saving Private Ryan is the most admired World War II film, and Full Metal Jacket for Vietnam, The Hurt Locker will be remembered as the quintessential movie about the Iraq War.
This film is the story of the final thirty days of service for an American bomb squad in Iraq, focusing on Staff Sergeant William James, a man who risks his life daily in his wild and unorthodox approach to disabling bombs.
In the beginning of the film, a soldier remarks how being a soldier in Iraq is practically a death sentence, and with the introduction of Staff Sergeant James, we begin to see how having daily near-death experiences changes one's attitude toward the ending of their life, and the meaning behind it. Perhaps the most intriguing aspect of the film is how James' recklessness seeps into the rest of his squad, and how the weight of James' risk-taking bears down as his service rotation nears its end.
The cinematography of The Hurt Locker is absolutely engrossing. Shot in documentary style for the majority of the film, the way the camera moves instills a feeling of insecurity, a dread of a looming explosion. The audience is thrown into the middle of Iraq, and we feel the frustration of the language barrier, the chaos of not knowing who is an ally, and who is an enemy.
The Hurt Locker is the first successful film about the Iraq War, not because it makes a political point (it doesn't), but because, under the guns, insurgents, and bombs, it is a film about human nature and emotion.

The Hurt Locker is a tantalizing war epic about the struggle of a bomb squad on the last of their rotation undergoing the extremes of near death experiences offered up by war. The film opens up with a quote by Chris Hedges: "The rush of battle is often a potent and lethal addiction, for war is a drug." The words fade out except for war is a drug which puts extra emphasis on the underlying message of the film. 

The movie follows three men, Staff Sergeant William James (Jeremy Renner), Sergeant JT Sanborn (Anthony Mackie) and Specialist Owen Eldridge (Brian Geraghty). William James is the replacement for the former bomb specialist who had died from an Improvised Explosive Device (IED) and a much different character as well, a cowboy with an adrenaline rush on disarming bombs and an opposite to J.T. Sanborn who prefers to do things by the book all the while Specialist Owen Eldridge is just trying to deal with the pressure of warfare. The film follows the three on their 30 day rotation as they disarm or detonate IEDs in the Iraqi streets. 

The film is expertly shot with excellent timing on its action segments, knowing just how to keep your knuckles white as you grip the arms of your seat. You will be kept on edge as seconds count down to what would be inevitable death for our characters as James, the cowboy, refuses to ever leave a bomb un-defused. It is his need for adrenaline that puts his partners on edge when working with him, hes reckless but entertaining, without a doubt the most interesting character in the film whose persona is defined perfectly by the opening quote, war is a drug and further emphasized by the end of the film. 

The movie plays like an action film but weighed down with substance to entertain those looking for thought put into their films and thankfully so. It has sequences of character development that are placed in between scenes of action and a segment dedicated to James return to home and one of the more intriguing scenes when he is in the cereal aisle at the grocery store, helping to shop with his family. A soldier who had defused more than 870 bombs, each instance standing right next to an object that could mean certain death at any minute, now stuck trying to choose which brand of cereal to eat.

The film is further weighed down by an excellent cast who all give great performances. All dialogue is well written and feels authentic as does the scenery and the interactions between the soldiers and the Iraqi people. This is of course speculation that the film is an accurate depiction and from rumor, Kathryn Bigelow had showed the film to soldiers in Iraq first to ensure that the film accurately depicted the situation. Whether or not what the soldiers may have said, an audience here at home will defiantly feel a sense of authenticity, which is important to the excitement of the film. 

Overall, the film is probably the single best depiction of the Iraqi War and one of the best war films as of late. You will feel the rush of excitement staggering each breath you take as the scenes slow down to show dust rise from charred car exterior as an IED erupts from underneath dirt, obliterating everything within its radius. Its an excellent war epic that maintains an important message depicted by James and his addiction to his job while his comrades reflect something else. Each character seems to hold feelings similar to one another but each one has extra emphasis on something particular and endearing about war and its effects. The film maintains an accurate depiction of a multitude of feelings, from excitement to fear to pain, that these soldiers experience. This movie is a must see.

El resultado es una película emocional e ideológicamente incoherente. / Technically well made and tense, with good performances and charismatic characters. However, the screenplay shows its seams in trying to smooth out its presentation of war as an adventure (which, as it deals with the invasion of Iraq, is so questionable) and of its characters as instruments of an oppressive machine. In the opening minutes of The Hurt Locker, we watch as the members of an elite Army bomb squad attempt to defuse an explosive device on a Baghdad street. One guy dons a big suit, akin to something an astronaut would wear, and warily approaches the bomb, while the other two scan the streets for suspicious activity. Its a long, tense, almost unbearable scene, which sets the tone for the entire film. Trust me; this isnt a movie you want to straggle in late for. 

The Hurt Locker follows the men of the Bravo Company bomb squad through the last 39 days of their year long rotation. Their new leader, Sergeant James, is a reckless cowboy who gets off on danger and takes chances not only with his own life, but with the lives of the other squad members as well.

Sergeant Sanborn is a good, solid, by-the-books soldier who does whatever is asked of him but is far more focused on getting home in one piece than in cultivating the adrenaline rush that comes from engaging in unnecessarily risky behavior. 

Specialist Eldridge is a bit of a wuss whose tendency to panic under pressure makes me wonder how he came to be chosen for this job in the first place. 

I think if Goldilocks were to assess the temperaments of the three bomb squad members, she would declare that James is too wild and Eldridge is too timid but that Sanborn is juuuust right. Then shed go off and eat a bowl of porridge.

The Hurt Locker mixes scenes of the bomb squad in action with scenes of them relaxing back at the base. I didnt actually time them, but it felt like there were far more action scenes than getting-to-know-you scenes, a mix that I wish had been reversed. It just isnt possible to sustain such an elevated level of tension for such an extended period, for me anyway. It didnt become boring exactly, but after a while I stopped really caring so much.

Sergeant James reminds me of the Crocodile Hunter, deliberately putting himself into dangerous situations, except with bombs instead of reptiles. Crikey! If I cut the wrong wire Im going to be blown sky high! Its not like I was rooting for the bomb, but my sympathies were squarely with Sanborn and Eldridge, the unwilling parties to James recklessness.   

This film shows us very little of how the characters spend what I assume must be a considerable amount of downtime. Theres no eating slop in the mess hall or tossing around a football a la Hawkeye and Trapper. The closest we see to the guys having fun is when James and Sanborn get hammered and take turns punching each other in the stomach as hard as they can. If movies are to be believed, Korea seems like it was a far more convivial war than Iraq.

We do eventually learn a bit about what makes James tick (heh heh), but his fellow bomb squad-ers are never really fleshed out. As thrillers go, the Hurt Locker is a great one, but for me, the heavy ratio of action to talk was a bit of a letdown.

The movie is boring, cliched and useless.

The first half of this movie is nothing more than diffusing bombs. Guy Pearce tries and (epically fails) to diffuse a bomb. Crazy white guy diffuses multiple bombs at the same time. Crazy white guy diffuses a car bomb. This movie (if you hadn't realized at the first hour mark) is about diffusing bombs.

Screenwriter Mark Boal must have figured that audiences would be bored at this point so, he adds an overlong and ridiculously fanciful sniper shootout. Next we'll go diffuse another bomb, go on a wild goose chase, go on another wild goose chase, try (and fail) to diffuse another bomb, go home, go shopping and head back for more. How interesting. 

Cinematographer Barry Ackroyd tries to make the film realistic with shaky-cam/cinema-veritre style shooting. The cinematography is wholly uninteresting and uninspired. Ackroyd is no Marcello Gatti (of Battle of Algiers fame). It grounds the film in reality. The film could (potentially) be mistaken for a documentary. This ultimately ends up hurting the movie. There are a lot of unrealistic details that take the viewer out and realize how bad the film really is. Certainly Powell and Pressburger's The Small Back Room (which deals with bomb diffusing) must come to mind when watching this film. The Small Black Room proves that 'realistic' cinematography isn't necessary for the subject. As Herzog states, "Cinema-verite is a thing of the 50s and 60s."

The film announces (via epigraph) that it is about the addicting nature of war. It is not about the addicting nature of war. Certainly Jeremy Renner's character has unnatural obsessions with adrenaline rushes, but that doesn't qualify as being addicted to war. That is an addiction to adrenaline; he just gets his fix through war. But, for the sake of argument, I'll bite. His character doesn't become more addicted to war nor does he become less addicted to war. No other character could plausibly be defined as being addicted to war. War is addicting! It only affects one person!

The film is more concerned with the nature of death. You have characters that fear death, welcome death with open arms, contemplate death and state how they'd like to die. Certainly war is one of the best backdrops for exploring death, but that isn't utilized. Remember, the film is about people addicted to war. 

The film has been constantly called suspenseful and tension-filled. Not so much. If anything the film plays up on suspense cliches that no longer work. They even have a lull-the-audience-into-a-false-sense-of-security scene that fails epically because it has been done countless times before. 

The characterization, another unfounded universal plus, is shallow, simplistic and ultimately pointless. The film builds characters quickly. You can easily spot crazy white guy and by-the-books black guy. Hell, this movie could have been Lethal Weapon 5: in Bagdad. The line "I'm too old for this shit" is even said. The film doesn't do anything with the characters they stay the same and for no apparent purpose. 

Let's talk about Beckham now. Beckham is a wiseass local that sells bootleg DVDs and plays futbal. Beckham befriends our crazy white guy main character. Something bad happens to Beckham. Crazy white guy does some crazy white guy shit. Twice. Fully clothed shower scene of defeat and failure follows. It is such an obvious, hollow and manipulative way to evoke some emotion out of the audience.

In-friggin'-tense. This is the closest the Iraq War has gotten to its Deer Hunter or Full Metal Jacket. In the beginning the characters feel invulnerable, but as the movie progresses and their days countdown, it becomes only a matter of time before that one fatal mistake is made. This film is an achievement in more ways than one.

The acting is absolutely breath-taking, especially by those who are aren't acclaimed actors. We're looking at an extremely extremely realistic portrayal of Iraq, and surprisingly the most unbiased one so far.

Using cinema verite techniques, the documentary-esque feel gives the film a heightened sense of realism. While not particularly my cup of tea, the camera is used so economically to the point where it tells the story so efficiently, that you may need to step and ask yourself... is this real?

The film touches on many themes on more than just war. We find the contention of characters as a real character development within each person, growing based on the relationship they have with each other.

With more than 2 hours of movie time, the film exceeds well in escalating the problems without making each consecutive event monotonous or boring. Everything becomes even more dangerous and more emotionally gripping and the tension can spurt instantaneously or rise each second, leaving the viewer at the edge of their seat.

I was not particularly fond of some anti-war nuances that were displayed in the film, not because I'm pro-war,  but it gave some rather sardonic views that leave you with a feeling of "that's just messed up."

Other than that, the film was just so well put together for the relatively small budget it was running on.

However, contrary to some people's understanding of the film, I don't believe that its big message was that war is drug... war is NOT a drug. Based on my viewing, It is an experience that can only satiate the man's apathy towards the world after he's seen his friends and family die in the battlefield. We're looking at how idealistic some people can be, but come out destroyed in the end, and the only way to put a sense of self-worth back into their head is by going back out. (not particularly and accurate portrayal of shellshock, however.)

Director Kathryn Bigelow has crafted a spellbinding war movie that is not so much about the battles themselves, but more about how the soldiers become addicted to the adrenaline rush provided by these battles.  Staff Sgt. William James (Jeremy Renner, in a superb performance) is an example of this.  As leader of a bomb disposal unit in Iraq, he needlessly and recklessly throws himself into harm's way time and time again essentially because he is a junkie, and this is how he gets his fix.  There is also the sad notion that this is basically all he knows, and there are some powerful scenes near the end of the movie that illustrate this perfectly.  Bigelow also does an outstanding job with the battle sequences, perfectly capturing the feeling of what it must be like to be in these situations, as the soldiers desperately try to determine which people on the street are civilians and which are the enemies.  Meanwhile, the timer on the bomb is counting down, and there is always the possibility that one of the civilians will turn out to be an enemy and detonate the bomb him/herself.  The tension in these scenes is unnerving.  The acting is great, with the relatively unknowns Renner, Anthony Mackie and Brian Geraghty giving flawless performances as the main characters, and they're supported nicely by veterans such as Guy Pearce, Ralph Fiennes and David Morse in cameo roles.  This is one of the best films of 2009 up to this point.  It's now starting to get wider release, so go see if it you can.

Movie Review by: FJ -- 4 ½ out of 5 -- 8/13/09

"War is a drug." That is the end of the quote, that they stress the most, in the beginning of the film. That quote also can describe the whole film pretty much. The Hurt Locker is about Bravo Company in the Iraq war doing the most dangerous job, disarming bombs in the middle of the battle. Bravo squad consists of Staff Sergeant William James (Jeremy Renner) the one that actually defuses the bombs, Sergeant JT Sanborn (Anthony Mackie) who acts as the leader, and Specialist Owen Eldridge (Brian Geraghty) the one that is going threw some emotional issues and doesn't really belong in war. What makes this movie great is the heart-stopping intense action scenes, fantastic direction by Kathryn Bigelow (Director of Point Break and Strange Days), and the acting.

Kathryn Bigelow has made one of the best directed movies in awhile. She does the handheld type camera, not an actual handheld, but the shakiness the fast zooms, the far away shots etc. Some movies this works very well and some it makes it horrible. But in The Hurt Locker, it works 100%. It makes a gritty realism to it; it gets in your face and really shows what the characters are going through. Like I said this type of camera doesn't always work, but she still took a risk and went for it, and she succeeds. I see a Best Direction nomination completely possible.

The acting is awesome especially from Brian Geraghty and Jeremy Renner. Brian Geraghty plays a young guy who is in the war but second guesses himself on everything. He couldn't pull a trigger on this guy who killed his original Staff Sergeant. It really screwed with his head and through the movie he is a nervous wreck, and does a fantastic job of acting it. I can easily see a supporting actor nomination. Brian Geraghty isn't in many movies, none of the three are, but he is pretty much tied for top acting award in the movie with Jeremy Renner. Jeremy Renner's character is more interesting which automatically makes his role more difficult. William James is a free living uncaring bomb defuser. He is an unstable man who in the line of danger doesn't care. He isn't scared to die and will do anything for a personal accomplishment. He breaks out the crazy at times and also stays calm cool and collect. Jeremy Renner gives a fantastic Best Actor nominee type performance. I can imagine him getting nominated, just not winning. Jeremy Renner isn't in many movies but I like what I have seen him in (28 Weeks Later, The Assassination of Jesse James, 12 and Holding). He is here and isn't leaving any time soon.

The story is so simple that it is perfect. Mark Boal who wrote the story for In the Valley of Elah, 2007's Iraq movie, writes a fantastic script. The script blends comedy, suspense, drama, and entertainment. At one point towards the late middle it begins to drag, and then you realize that it was a long movie, but everything else is top notch. It think that this is a lock for Best Original Screenplay. He has a talent, and I think he is going to become the next big war movie writer.

I liked this better than 2008's war movie, Stop-Loss (which was very good), but I did like In the Valley of Elah better than The Hurt Locker, even though In the Valley of Elah focused on the soldiers and not the war. The Hurt Locker is one of the best movies so far in 2009, and is one of the best war movies ever. This will be great for anyone that likes actions movies or a good war drama. I would also like to add, the bomb defusing scene's have to be in the top 10 most intense scenes ever. I seriously think my heart stopped at times; nothing can beat the Russian roulette scenes in The Deer Hunter though.
