It's impossible to miss the extraordinary craft Bigelow brings to this film.  Her skill in directing suspenseful action sequences appears to be peaking, and she handles the explosive emotions of her cast with equal aplomb.  The problem with this film, though, is the extent to which it wants to be just an action film.  That would be a meaningless comment, of course, without the context of the film's setting: the Iraq War, circa 2004.  So, is this a war film, or an action film disguised as such?  (That dichotomy is probably false anyway, but hear me out.)  The question nagged at me on-and-off during the film.  At times, the predictable plot twists made me feel like I was watching a very highly skilled, paint-by-numbers genre exercise.  For example, the fate of the Army psychologist will surprise absolutely no one, and thus feels embarrassingly formulaic.  Even the explosion that sets the ball rolling in the film's opening is entirely predictable.  Guy Pearce is not the film's star and was never featured in promotional materials, which gives us a pretty good idea that things aren't going to work out in the first scene.  Moreover, would we even be interested in the rest of the film if that bomb doesn't go kaboom?  (And the same principle basically applies to Fiennes' unexpected cameo.  By the way, in retrospect, is "Strange Days" the best work Fiennes has ever done?  Does anything else shake up his sophisticated Brit routine as well as that warped movie?)

Bigelow's approach appears to be one of political neutrality, but political neutrality is a phantom.  The movie certainly doesn't vilify or demonize Iraqis, but they're mostly spectators here, so Bigelow doesn't exactly give us a fully realized Iraqi character, either.  The closest she comes is with a child actor, and that's taking the easy way out, a la the most dubious tendency of Italian neorealism.  (There is a nice twist with this plot line, however, which initially feels gimmicky but challenges upon further reflection.  Renner's character confronts the psychic dangers of befriending Iraqis, and the psychological distortions of war: all Iraqi children become the same boy he has befriended, potentially compromising his efficiency as a soldier while expanding his compassion.)  

But the movie's true political colors are revealed early enough.  During Renner's first bomb defusion, he needlessly unleashes a can of gas typically used as a smokescreen.  When asked why, he says it's to create a "distraction," but the real reason is crystal clear: because it makes him look ultra-cool and super tough.  And Bigelow can't resist the cinematic luster of her hero emerging from a cloud of smoke.  After his second near-miraculous defusion, David Morse's grizzled veteran calls him "hot shit," and leaves little doubt that we're supposed to deeply admire not only Renner's professionalism, but also his swagger.  Renner's character is, in the end, not very far removed from Tom Cruise's Maverick.  And "The Hurt Locker" comes dangerously close to "Top Gun" in its final moments when the end credits roll and a thundering rock song blares from the screen.  Both of these films could be Army ads.  Bigelow might come closer to the hallowed reputation of a Howard Hawks or John Ford with her interest in men doing a "job of work" well, but her valedictory portrait is also an implicit endorsement of war.

Hitchcock said the way to make any mundane coffee table conversation fascinating is to place a bomb under the coffee table. It's no wonder this film is so fascinating then, because it's set in a place where there's a bomb under EVERYTHING. A hugely successful old-school suspense film comprised of nothing but a series of tense scenarios that could ignite in a split second, with a couple of sparse connecting scenes to tie them together. What makes this film a real winner is that nothing unfolds exactly how you'd expect it to. Sometimes the bomb goes off, sometimes they disarm it and deny the audience that satisfying boom, but you won't know which type you're watching until the scene plays out. I was blown away by the sniper battle with an unnervingly relaxed and methodical pace, or the numerous dead ends and red herrings they toss at you to keep you guessing where the film's going. I'd be giving out five stars, easy, if not for one thing I see as a substantial error. The entire movie is a countdown of 38 days until the end of the unit's rotation, and we're reminded of that every scene change, and yet there's not really anything for us to count down to. It seems like the film's heading toward a final no-holds-barred assignment on day #0 where the audience knows anything goes and no one is safe, where they ratchet up the tension as high as they can. This scene is conspicuously absent, leaving the credit roll as a serious anticlimax. Besides that, there's enough great material in here for five movies, which is good, because we're not exactly swimming in good Iraq War films. I'm going to see every single Kathryn Bigelow film now.

How many female directors do you actually know?  You have Penny Marshall, you have Sophia Coppala.....but really after that, there isnt much.  But what about Katherine Bigelow?  Have you ever seen the movie "Point Break"?  Well to me, that is probably one of the greatest, most high octane, adrenaline fueled action movies i have ever seen.....and what struck me as odd was the fact that it was directed by a woman.....why is that odd you ask?  I mean come on, how many women do you know that could actually pull off a decent action flick?  Well here Ms. Bigelow attempts something that no other woman has tried.....directing a war movie.
Ever since the conflict in Iraq, movies have come and gone......trying to capture the essence.....but none of them have really done that.  The closest movie i have seen thus far, was probably "The Kingdom".  This movie add's that adrenaline element though......something the others do not really have.  Rather than take the approach of the classic term "War is Hell"....they turn to the idea that "War is an addiction".....by following a character who's soul purpose is to defuse bombs.  Needless to say, the film is packed with intense, on the edge of your seat sequences......but trying to understand what is actually happening to the main characters is where it starts to get a little messy.  Yes.....i can see that the main character is an adrenaline junkie, and loves the thrill of defusing a bomb, and that he cannot cope outside of that rhealm.  But this war, something few understand.......so yes, everything that the main characters are experiencing, we do need spelled out for us.  Not only that, there were certain sequences that were a little weird, or didnt make much sense.  Dont get me wrong, i totally get the subtext of the overall plot......but it wasnt as entertaining as it could have been.  From the start of the movie, it was very action packed......and i was kind of hoping it was going to stay that way.....much like Ms. Bigelow's previous works.......but it didnt.  It slowly started to dwindle off and loose its pace with some un-neccessary scenes that didnt make much sense.  I dont know, the best way i can describe it is that it would be up one minute, and then down the next......much like a teeter totter.
Bottom Line.......it was good, but i wouldnt go as far as calling it great.  It certainly had elements that were awesome, and at times, it really started to pull you in.......but it just kept loosing me over and over again.  But would i call this the best Iraq war movie so far.......no, i still think "The Kingdom" is better.

There has been a number of films that have depicted or mentioned the Iraq War, but until now there hasn't been a film that wholly depicts the daily life of our troops in Iraq. The Hurt Locker brings to life the numerous accounts on Iraq that we often read about or see on television, which makes it a truly extraordinary film. Kathryn Bigelow's film is not just one of the best films of the year, it is one of the most realistic war films ever made. The Hurt Locker centers around a bomb squad consisting of three soldiers - James, Sanborn, and Eldridge. Their duty is to disarm the countless number of IEDs (improvised explosive devices) all over Baghdad that are well-hid by insurgents. James is the squad's reckless but skilled bomb technician who uses the war as adrenaline. His impulsive behavior in the field is not well-received by Sanborn and Eldridge, who are convinced that his impetuousness will eventually get them killed. With only a little over a month left before their tour of duty is over, the squad disarms bomb after bomb while looking out for the insurgents, who are watching, waiting for the perfect moment to detonate the explosives. The Hurt Locker captures the soul of the Iraq War. Whether it be the various emotions that the soldiers experience or the danger that lurks at every moment that they're out in the field, it's all there, and it makes the film so real. Never has an explosion been captured on film with so much detail. The resulting shock wave from a detonated explosive lifts gravel and sand off the ground and forces a rusting car to literally shake dust off its doors - and all that is filmed in slow motion. The scenes where the squad is operating out in the field are shot with so much intensity that we feel our hearts beat faster and faster, never knowing if death will decide to take one of their lives. The cast is nothing short of spectacular. Jeremy Renner, Anthony Mackie, and Brian Geraghty - who play James, Sanborn, and Eldridge respectively - bring a certain level of genuineness to their characters by portraying them with so much honesty and sincerity. Geraghty in particular deserves much praise for flawlessly executing the emotions associated with Eldridge - fear, grief, guilt, uncertainty. Guy Pearce, David Morse, and Ralph Fiennes deliver quality performances despite the fact that each of them are only in the film for about five minutes; one can't help but wish that they had more screen time. What makes The Hurt Locker so unique is its lack of plot. I admit that it was an odd experience, watching a film with literally no story, but after thinking about it, it struck me that this is what makes the film so special. Think about our everyday lives - on most days, nothing seems to change; thus, every day is more or less routine. That being said, our everyday lives doesn't have much of a plot. In the absence of a plot, routine becomes the screenplay for The Hurt Locker. Indeed, the daily life of the squad doesn't change because their mission is always the same: disarm bombs. The Hurt Locker is a remarkable film because it achieves authenticity through routine, which is the medium in which reality often presents itself. Unfortunately, I couldn't completely enjoy The Hurt Locker because it's often shot with the dreaded shaky-cam technique. Though I acknowledge that shaky-cam is used to acquire heart-racing sensations and to heighten the tension felt at critical moments, it doesn't make much sense to shoot literally 75% of the film with shaky-cam. Instead, it's often distracting, as it not only wore out my eyes in a short matter of time, it prevented me from concentrating on the subject at hand. Needless to say, The Hurt Locker is by far one of the must-see films of 2009. Bigelow's vision is meritorious, as she succeeds in presenting a war film that deservingly stands next to Saving Private Ryan and Black Hawk Down, two other very raw and visceral films of the same genre. Although the film falls short of being a paragon because of its overuse of shaky-cam, it gains much from its stellar acting, noteworthy screenplay, and the presentation of its central message - to some, war is a drug because it is one of the few things they love. Please watch The Hurt Locker. This is one film you can't afford to miss.

Kathryn Bigelow has the distinction of being one of the few female action directors, and it's hard not to draw comparisons between this and her best-known feature--Point Break.  In Point Break, she gave us some gorgeous cinematography and allowed us to explore the ocean in its terrible, powerful beauty; in the Hurt Locker she does the same with desert and flame.  Point Break was about the type of "adrenaline" junkies who are always chasing the perfect wave; in the Hurt Locker she looks at the same type of man--this time a bomb diffuser in Iraq.  The Hurt Locker asks what kind of man is drawn to such work--each day, a race against an  clock set for death, each job a battle of wits between him and a piece of deadly machinery?  The Hurt Locker, against all odds, is a character study of such a man, and Jeremy Renner does a beautiful job, leading an understated supporting cast.

The Hurt Locker is a Kathryn Bigelow film that follows an IED disposal unit in post-invasion Iraq.  We follow Sergeant Sanborn and Specialist Eldridge as they partner up with Sergeant First Class James as they count down the days until their Bravo unit's term in Iraq is done, but have to survive their encounters with death on the field through their bomb disposals.  James is a bit of a maverick when it comes to bomb disposal as he disarms bombs regardless of how dire the situation is.

The focus of the film lies within Sergeant First Class James's "combat high."  This goes back to the opening quote of the movie in which for some that "war is a drug" and that is all that they live for.  In the course of the movie, you learn that such "adrenaline junkies" endanger their units through their selfishness on the battlefield by trying to cheat death time and again.  It is interesting to see a decent portrayal of such an individual as there are many thrill seekers out there in war.

The movie's strength as I see it lies in its use of tension.  Numerous bomb defusion sequences as well as a long distance sniper battle really set up moments in which you don't know what to expect.  As one should expect in war, one should expect just about anything.  It really did hold suspense so well as you also wonder who will emerge from this and how, if at all.

The movie did seem long and did seem slow at times.  I just felt some of the sequences just seemed awkward like when James broke into an Iraqi house looking for the DVD selling kid, Beckham.  I guess it just goes to show that one shouldn't become too attached to anyone in the battlefield.

It's a decent war movie.  Definitely watchable, but it may be slow for some.

My only reservation with "The Hurt Locker" is the absence of much in the way of counter-perspective. The scene is powerful in its grotesqueness, but Renner plays it just right, performing his job with a dedication tinged with horror, so it doesnât seem exploitative or gratuitous.

At Jamesâ side are Sergeant Sanborn (Anthony Mackie) and Specialist Eldridge (Brian Geraghty). The three men act as a think tank, providing the viewpoints necessary to fully analyze each situation. James has the kind of gung-ho, cocky and mechanical personality that defusing 873 bombs would instill. Eldridge is in counseling and asks permission before he fires on the enemy. Sanbornâs tough exterior is slowly eroding. He canât stand Jamesâ ability to shut the world off, but he envies him at the same time. The men get drunk and punch one another for the feeling of it after spending entire days doing battle and never knowing death.

The movie brings up the question of what it takes to do what James does. Back home, he has a son and a complicated relationship with his ex-wife. He keeps his wedding ring among souvenirs from defused bombs in a locker under his bed, expressing his great interest in grabbing a piece of something that could or has caused him harm. Defusing bombs is what James does. Heâs a robot that never malfunctions. Without a task, he suits no purpose.

Kathryn Bigelow shows great skill in her execution, always letting her shots linger until the right emotion jumps from them. Her camera is always where it needs to be. âThe Hurt Lockerâ is receiving much acclaim for being a sleeper action picture, and it is, but there is more to it than its moments of tension and violence. It is smart enough to refrain from depicting its soldiers as outwardly righteous. These are disturbed men performing disturbing tasks. Like the great war movies, it makes us question how anyone could stay sane under such conditions. It looks for humanity in the chaos of war and finds it burning alive.

This movie is so intense, you won't be able to breathe.  From the moment it begins, the suspense is so high that it's nearly unbearable.  I watched the movie with my teeth gritted, my pulse pounding, and palms sweaty, which makes it stand out as one of the few movies that actually makes you feel like you've been to war.  This also makes the incredibly smart decision to not have a linear narrative as it's plot, but rather just go through a series of days in the lives of a US bomb squad, which gives the film a very documentary-esque feel.  It also can make the film much more disturbing because while it's relatively gore-free for a war movie, you can't help but feel that this what soldiers are going through everyday.  This has the single most unsettling scene I've seen this year and am trying desperately to push it out of my mind where the squad must diffuse a body bomb. Also, casting virtual unknowns to play the leads works terrifically to it's advantage because you know from the get-go that no one is safe.  In regular movies, you know that the superstar leading man will make it at least until the very end of the movie.  Here, you never know.  Only one actor I recognize, Anthony Mackie, who is also the actor who pissed me off the most in "We Are Marshall".  There, he's hammy, over-the-top and makes it so obvious he wants everyone to know he's a Juliard graduate.  Here, it's a much more controlled and subtle performance.  Just goes to show the difference a good director can make. The film takes no stance on the Iraq war or any of the politics, it just tells their story straight, and it benefits the more for it.  Whether you are democrat, republican, pro-bush, anti-bush, you can find something to relate to with these soldiers.  War is hell, but this is the first movie I've seen that acknowledges it's also a thrill and that it's not hard to get addicted to the adrenaline rush.  "The Hurt Locker" is a smart, unbiased look at war and is in my opinion a front runner for the Oscars.  If not, it will almost certainly go down in history as the definitive movie about the Iraq War.

War is a drug, the opening title sequence declares.  And by the end of the film, you could see why.  The Hurt Locker is one of the best war films of the decade and director Kathryn Bigelow has delivered an adrenaline rush of suspense and tension that will have you hooked from the film's very first frame.

Bigelow is responsible for most of the brilliance of this film.  First, she has done well to stand way back and let the events, the actors and the film play themselves out.  The premise of the film, about a team of Army bomb squad troops responsible for deactivating deadly bomb hazards, is itself enough to set the stomach churning from suspense and terror.  Bigelow does little to embelish, shooting the film in a casual hand held style that only heightens the tension.  

Bigelow is also uninterested in laying in to the politics of the war itself.  Carefully observing, avoiding cliches and in so doing, revealing an aspect of the war that goes beyond bravado, machismo and courage.  In her unflinching direction, Bigelow has made the film immensely terrifying and immensely watchable - a conceit she contends, is the addictive nature of the human adrenaline rush, the consequence of a life lived on the edge day after day after gruelling day.  In a way, Bigelow has transcended the usual cliche of war films and its politics, to one that Homer touched upon, that elusive human quest for heroism and immortality and its consequences. Bigelow doesn't judge or forward an agenda, but gently presents the dialectic at once simple and complex.

In the three main characters of the squad, Bigelow has also cast perfect foils in Renner, Mackie and Geraghty, all young men in the throes of discovering their own and each others' survival instincts.  At one point, the three exchange displays of masochistic machismo in a consensual fight that allows them to act out safely both camaraderie and violence - but Bigelow never lets off of the tension, and the scene constantly teeters on the edge.  The conscripted men are boys afterall.  But in an even more brilliant move, Bigelow has chosen to cast A-listers (Fiennes, Pearce, Morse) in cameos that she readily dispenses of, jarring expectation and heightening the sense of bewilderment and volatility to the onscreen diegesis.  Just as our young characters find out in the first scene of the film there are no rules on the warfront, Bigelow expertly sets up The Hurt Locker to dispose of one's usual expectation. Meritocracy is out the window and moral verisimilitude or poetic justice are mere concepts that bear no practical use or, worse, relevance in the film.

There is much much more in Bigelow's intelligent directing that deserves mention but suffice it to say, her most incisive decision, to stand back and allow the honesty of the premise to take centrestage is key.  There is no lack of pathos in a film chockful of suspense, and Mackie, Geraghty and especially Renner deliver in bucketfuls, thanks to an intelligent script by Mark Boal; who clearly understands that suspense arises naturally out of character as much as the situation. 

One of the most honest, thrilling and provocative films in a long long time, genre notwithstanding.  Highly recommended.

Fans of the TV series "Generation Kill" will be delighted that a feature film has finally managed to capture some of the essence of the Iraq conflict. The story focuses on the work of an elite bomb disposal squad who patrol Baghdad defusing IEDs. Heading up the squad is war junkie Staff Sergeant Will James, brilliantly played by Jeremy Renner, for whom war is a drug he cannot live without. As much as he pines for the family he has at home, he knows that (as we see later in the film) the drudgery of the supermarket can never replace the adrenaline rush of coming face to face with a potentially devastating explosive. There are some absolutely stunning set pieces here, expertly crafted by director Kathryn Bigelow. One particularly outstanding scene follows a long and exhausting stand off between James' team, a group of mercenaries (led by a cameoing Ralph Fiennes) and Iraqi insurgents. The performances are top notch throughout, particularly Anthony Mackie as Sgt Sanborn and fine cameos from Guy Pearce, David Morse and Christian Camargo, who was excellent as the murderous boyfriend Rudy in "Dexter". This is a down and dirty war movie with no pat heroics or happy endings. The violence is real and gripping without ever being excessive. One of the best of the year so far, no doubt.

After watching "The Hurt Locker", I noticed that my hands were moist. Intially I was willing to chalk this up to the numerous times I reached for my drink, but then I remembered I brought in a lukewarm water bottle. In actuality, my hands were sweating from the numerous times I was wringing them together and clutching the arms of my chair, as one of the best films of 2009 unraveled before me. From the high octane action to the fantastic performances, I was hooked from the very first frame and it didn't let up until long after the film was over. "The Hurt Locker" tells the story of three men who belong to an Army bomb squad whose sole purpose is to disarm bombs (whether it be roadside or within a cadaver) in Iraq. The three men are only weeks away from being on leave and must find a way to not only survive Iraq, but to survive one another. As alluded to, the first danger is Iraq itself and I must admit, there is a sense of danger presented by director Kathryn Bigelow that no film about Iraq has captured so far. This is not to say I know the danger of Iraq first hand, but I imagine what Bigelow puts on screen is an ample represenation of what soldier's face every day. From the bombs themselves to the suspicious behaviors of Iraqi citizens watching from rooftops, Bigelow creates taut scenes that not only push her characters to the limits, but her audience as well. Yet, the most triumphant part of Bigelow's direction is her ability to draw out fantastic performances from her three protagonists: SSgt William James (Jeremy Renner), Sgt. JT Sanborn (Anthony Mackie) and Spc. Owen Eldridge (Brian Geraghty). The first Oscar worthy performance of the year (aside from Christoph Waltz) belongs to Jeremy Renner, whose SSgt. William James is an adrenaline junkie and the closer he is to the death, the closer he is to living. Renner gives an amazing performance as he creates a charismatic and complex character, whose life is ruined in a way you wouldn't really expect. In some essences, the war is perfect for James because it fills an adrenaline void. Yet, as the war wears on and disarming "typical" roadside bombs no longer do it for him, he needs a "fix" bigger and more dangerous than the last. Where Renner's 'James' is unhinged and seemingly needs the war, Anthony Mackie's 'Sgt. Sanborn' is simply a man on a mission. All he wants to do is serve his time, live, and go home. As you can imagine, the character of 'Sanborn' is pushed to the limit by the character of 'James', as his life becomes relatively more dangerous then it previously had been. Mackie does a terrific job capturing the slow deterioration of his character's confidence in leaving Iraq alive, as well as the growing inquisitive position he has on his own life. With Sanborn and James being stark comparisons to one another, the intensity that Bigelow captures between Mackie and Renner is quite amazing, and at times is far more involving then the disarming of bombs. When combined with a solid performance by Brian Geraghty (Sgt. Eldridge), who plays a soldier with anxiety problems, Bigelow has a trio of characters who not only push one another to the brink of hell, but also force one another to grow in ways they couldn't imagine. Without any political agendas, Bigelow is able to focus on the aforementioned interaction and development of her characters, as well as the perfect execution of taut, action sequences. Because of Bigelow's unbiased approach to the film, she creates a true human drama, where the disarming of character is just as compelling as the disarming of explosives.

Expert bomb disposal unit Bravo Company a month and a half left in their rotation in Iraq, a job of almost unimaginable danger. The unit must enter the very heart of war-torn cities and risk their lives to disable bombs placed by insurgents. It almost beggars belief that people really have this job, I'll steal directly from the film itself here but it can be perfectly summed up as 'every day is a roll of dice with death'. Who knows when the bomb will blow, a sniper could be lurking in any one of the decrepit buildings. How can anyone last more than a day in this job? 

SSgt. William James (Jeremy Renner) is the man responsible for walking up to the bomb itself and disarming it. He is wreckless and hopelessly addicted to adrenaline rush his job provides, seemingly going out of his way to make situations more dangerous than they need to be. It's a top performance from Renner, he doesn't have to deliver any challenging dialogue, it's more a case of the audience needing to believe the character they are seeing. A guy addicted to blowing up bombs? Yeah right. But Renners portrayal makes you believe there are people like him in the real world. 

Sgt. JT Sanborn and Spc. Own Eldrige are the two other members of Bravo Company. They provide the cover, identifying dangers other than the bomb and advising James on what to do (not that he ever listens during the film). Their characters are more grounded in a reality we can comprehend, especially Eldrige who seems to be the one who completely recognises the danger of his job. He is the opposite to James, fearful of every mission and counting down the days till he can leave.

The film is shot wonderfully, giving the subject matter you know what to expect. It's gritty, raw and almost unbearably tense at times. The first bomb we see Bravo Company tackle sets the tone, every person in view could be the man who put it there, it could detonate at any moment, and the suspense crescendos until it literally explodes. There is also a superb sniper encounter halfway through the film which is probably my favourite of the movie, it's a simple set up of two guys facing each other and firing in single shots separated by an almost insurmountable amount of time, you see the smoke as the gun fires and then the half a second wait before knowing if the bullet has missed you or killed you.

I'll stop running through the scenes now, because almost all of them are great. I'll just say I'm very happy I watched this film, when it comes to war movies the bar is set very high but somehow they rarely disappoint. Maybe it's the subject matter, being such a serious concept it makes sense that it shouldn't be taken on unless it can be done right.

This is no mainstream film, and to be honest I am partly glad that it isn't. Still, to me, the purpose of this film remains a mystery. Was it meant to entertain or educate me? Does the fact that it didn't go mainstream have anything to do with the type of audience Kathryn was going for? Otherwise, questions aside, this is a great realist film well worth 130 minutes of your life.

It was certainly interesting to have watched Quentin Tarantino's Inglourious Basterds the night before watching Kathryn Bigelow's The Hurt Locker, as the two films can be put in easy comparison for their strong use of tension in creating powerful scenes. The difference between the two, though, is that Bigelow's scenes of tension are all build-up with no release - unless you count as release the fact that the protagonists didn't die... this time. It's all about Staff Sargeant William James, a man who knows how to handle bombs. He's defused some 800 bombs in his career and with any luck will defuse another 800 before all is said and done. When a bomb squad loses their leader to technical difficulties, James steps in to take the lead and finds himself at odds with another member of his team, Sargeant JT Sanborn. You see, James doesn't play "by the rules". When he sees a car loaded with huge bombs, he takes off all of his protective gear, claiming that he'd rather die comfortable if the bombs explode. When Sanborn's constant worries about safety get on James' nerves, he removes his headset and works without any aid. Bigelow uses a shaky, hand-held sort of style in filming the action, which I suppose was intended for the sake of realism. The movie takes place in Baghdad during the height of the Iraq War, and the idea is to put the viewer in the streets of Iraq... to give the audience that constant fear that any scrap of paper on the street could be concealing an IED. To create the anxiety that every person staring with wonder out of their window at the uniformed soldiers in the neighborhood could very well be the person responsible for planting the bombs. And to a certain extent, that works. Literally or figuratively, the clock is always ticking for this bomb squad, and the desert towns of Iraq seem to be lawless places where a bullet could come flying from nowhere before you have a chance to react. Every day that passes is another miracle - the miracle being that you survived. Or maybe it's just a whole lot of fun, which is the way it seems for James. His carelessness doesn't take the movie anywhere, and even though the camera style appears to be intended for a realistic take, James is treated like an invincible action hero. Near the end of the movie, he actually walks out of an airplane with a look of determination and hard rock music accompanying his departure. Perhaps more interesting, though, is the way that none of it seems very pressing. Even when the boys get into a shoot-out on the side of a sand dune, the thing that registers is not the immense danger but the amount of time that they spend waiting and watching. Other, nameless soldiers are picked off one-by-one, but our three bomb squad heroes calmly keep an eye on the prize. Even when an enemy sniper has them in sight, the sniper politely waits for the good guys to fire at him before trying to retaliate. In a later scene, James and his squad walk through a scene of destruction in the darkest of night, lit only by the flames from an exploded gas tanker. Women are wailing and men are lying on the road with limbs blown off, and yet... and yet it all seems so impersonal. The realism that the movie is striving for just isn't there, and the characters and/or their relationships don't have a lot going in their favor either. Actually, I take that back. There is a B-story about Specialist Owen Eldridge and his reservations about their mission. James' shenanigans serve to annoy Sanburn, but Owen is visibly disturbed by how close the danger truly is. Some scenes show him meeting with an Army therapist to help counsel him on the semi-trauma that he must be going through on a daily basis. Despite some corny explications of his emotions, Owen's story feels the strongest. His worries are mostly internal and the way that his story progresses (especially after his therapist joins him on an outing) is especially rewarding. But then it's all lost in the final act, when Owen begins acting like a totally different person. But aside from Owen's story, there is little of real worth. Yes, there are moments of intensity when the three guys are trying to defuse a bomb, but that tension is unearned and never has any real resolution. It's like when people spontaneously burst into song during a musical - it feels suddenly obligatory, even if the music is quite good. Is that what is supposed to be so real -- a lot of nothing and then the threat of death? Regardless, it doesn't work half as well as it should have. I left feeling as though I had been dragged along by the movie instead of swept up by it.

There have been many Iraq based movies made ever since the first Desert Storm war . Some good , some very average but none outstanding. At last Kathryn Bigelow has made an Iraq war movie that feels so real it can truly be classed as great. 



 


Based on the personal wartime experiences of journalist Mark Boal (who adapted his experiences with a bomb squad into a fact-based, yet fictional story), director Kathryn Bigelow's Iraq War-set action thriller The Hurt Locker presents the conflict in the Middle East from the perspective of those who witnessed the fighting firsthand , the soldiers. As an elite Army Explosive Ordnance Disposal team tactfully navigates the streets of present-day Iraq, they face the constant threat of death from incoming bombs and sharp-shooting snipers. In Baghdad, roadside bombs are a common danger. 


The Army is working to make the city a safer place for Americans and Iraqis, so when it comes to dismantling IEDs the Explosive Ordnance Disposal crew is always on their game. But protecting the public isn't easy when there's no room for error, and every second spent dismantling a bomb is another second spent flirting with death. Now, as three fearless bomb technicians take on the most dangerous job in Baghdad, it's only a matter of time before one of them gets sent to "the hurt locker." 



 


This is simply a belter of a movie .. Using the unsung heroes of Iraq's Bomb Disposal unit and some relentless set pieces this film sucks you in , gargles you, then spits you out leaving you with an emphatic message.. WAR IS A DRUG FOR SOME.... Following one of the most riveting and unsuspecting open sequences I have seen in ages.
 

The dialog flows so naturally, that while we may have never even heard most of the vocabulary here yet we immediately understand what's going on. Visually, I can't remember a film that is both beautiful, and so complete, beautifully composed but never is either self-conscious or without purpose. Midway, there's an extended sequence with three British soldiers that could be used to teach a master class in film schools: We're thrust into an unknown landscape (as the characters are) and what develops is told with such clarity, it's as if we've been given a map prior to seeing the film. 

 


Shot in Jordan, the Middle East looks like Mars. Everything is so alien and no one can communicate with one another because of language barriers. While this isn't any particular political point about our involvement in Iraq, it does point out the grave differences that can exist on two sides of a conflict and how misunderstandingsâcasual and significantâcan perpetuate violence and hatred. 



 


It is so refreshing to see a war film that isn't trying to send some universal message, or trying to preach to the people. This is simply a movie about the soldiers, because when people think about war they should think of the men who are risking their lives day in and day out. The result is an experience is as good as any action war movie I've seen probably since Saving Private Ryan. 

Bigelow's spot on direction and the great sound effects provide us with situations so intense that your heart rate is constantly flying during this movie. 

Highly Recommended

War and defusing bombs has essentially so affected the main character that it becomes the only thing he believes he is or ever can be good at.

Cameos abound, and were done better than any film I've seen in recent memory: no spoilers, but perhaps the way it was done is a tribute to just how war can be. We've known since the early nineties that Kathryn Bigelow is a very good American director specialising in action films. Near Dark (1987), Point Break (1991) & Strange Days (1995) all showed that she has the ability to take a topic with which we feel we are familiar and come up with something fresh, relentless when necessary, and topical. There are always questions of human nature to discuss whether it be the supernatural, friendship and loyalty or censorship. The real problem of choosing to talk about the Iraq War is deciding how much airtime one devotes to the numerous delicate issues which we have seen discussed widely in society for virtually this entire decade. This element of the production proves to be nothing but encouragement for this talented director who delivers a frank, unapologetic and emotionally-charged account of the trials faced by a bomb disposal unit of the United States Army. Bomb detection and disarmourment is clearly a detail fraught with danger at every turn: not only are you trying to avoid trouble but you are also looking for it. Anthony Mackie, Brian Geraghty and Jeremy Renner are the elite bomb squad counting down the forty days until they are out of the rotation. Some members of the group are looking forward to their release from duty more than others and clashes in personality and motivation threaten to bring about complications for the group and provide unwanted hindrances to their efforts. Excellent support is provided by Ralph Fiennes, David Morse and Guy Pearce, all of whom hold senior positions in their respective regiment's ranks. The number of talking points which are touched upon, however lightly, is immense and, at the same time, subtle. That is one of the true pleasures of watching 'The Hurt Locker', along with the intensity of its grip over the audience: seeing each topic raised and commented on with varying importance and focus. The same is true of the direction itself: Kathryn Bigelow shows us the things that she wants us to see (yes, all directors obviously do this but I refer in particular to the strength of focal intensity levied upon separate aspects of the story), giving us her view of things as she goes. There is an auteuristic style to the way she manipulates the camera and our points of view. Undoubtedly the most important American film about the Iraq War 'The Hurt Locker' proposes a thoughtful and studied account of human suffering on all sides and is difficult to watch due to its realism.

In a nutshell, Army bomb-squad in Baghdad gets a new chief tech who's crazy. As the days left on the deployment count down and the violence rises, the other two men of the unit begin to believe that their new tech will get them killed.

This is quite likely the most probing and thoughtful look at the insanity of warfare and the toll it takes on soldiers that I've seen since the Vietnam War films of Platoon, Full Metal Jacket, and Apocalypse Now.

Not only is it thoughtful and dramatic, but the film's suspense scenes add to the drama. The raw tension is so taut, it's impossible not to watch as the men begin to crack under the pressure. Likewise, several high-profile stars are in the film for just one scene and abruptly killed off in shocking fashion to really get the audience concerned with the characters' fate.

In the end, it wasn't as good as the Vietnam trifecta. The small cast added to the personal character development, but at time it felt like these three guys were the only ones in the war, which was distracting.

However, it's still an amazing film, an amazing war film, and the best piece of media made on this war since it started.

Its strange to find such an intense war film directed by a woman that isnt blatantly protesting the war. Thats just what Kathyryn Bigelow did in The Hurt Locker. She isnt new to the genre. She also directed 2002s K-19: The Widowmaker, but to have a woman director, when not many women direct movies, pull off such a gripping, intense, and riveting film such as the Hurt Locker is a site to behold.

Staff Sergeant William James must take over a bomb disposal team when their former team leader gets killed in action. Subordinates Sergeant JT Sanborn and Specialists Owen Eldridge dislike the James different attitude and approach to the job. James is a fucking maverick to say the least. He is a fearless madman that sets out on suicides missions to disarm bombs in the midst of the Iraq war. On a daily basis their team is called to check out suspicious activity or disarm a discovered bomb. James uses a no-holds-bar approach, forgetting protocol and using his balls to get the job done.

James maverick attitude comes with a price. Its as if James has an addiction for adrenaline and the fear rather than doing what he does to get the job done. He likes the fear, he likes the danger, he loves the intensity. He has a complete disregard for the safety of other while he gets his adrenaline fix. Squadmates Sanborn and Eldridge dont approve. Eldridge has a hard time battling with the loss of the their first Sergeant. He is a fickle character desperately struggling with the hypothetical rather than reality. Sanborn seems to be a much stronger character, at least it seems that way for most of the movie. He does things by the book and conflict arises between James and himself.

The movie takes you deep within each characters psyche and shows the turmoils of war that are more than just physical scars. I dont want to ruin the movie for anyone, but I can say that each character struggles to keep themselves together and they all will endlessly fight in this war, even when its over.

The movie was technically brilliant. The camera angles and slow-motion techniques dropped my jaw. They were used to such astounding effects that the drama was multiplied ten-fold. The setting became part of the theatre, it was as if I was there, in another reality. The realism enthralled me as I watched this film grab my balls and twist them with its intensity and brutality. The film was brutal, to say the least. I cant comment on how realistic it may be because I was never there, but it sure seemed good to me.

The cast did a fantastic job, especially Jeremy Renner (James) and Anthony Mackie (Sanborn). Brian Geraghty(Eldridge) had a sub-par performance and did detract slightly from the film. Other than that the film was beautiful. There were subtle undertones that showed American military superiority and Iraqi savagery, but the film played its cards well and made for one intense film that should be seen by all who can stomach a shot to the balls.

There have been two big bummers for me this summer at the movies.  The first was that most of the movies I was looking forward to turned out to be disappointing.  Second, several of the movies that I was really hoping to see such as Woody Allens Whatever Works and Kathryn Bigelows The Hurt Locker were released limitedly meaning that they were only released in big cities like New York and L.A.  Fortunately, I am a patient child and my waiting of over two months paid off because now The Hurt Locker is playing in Tucson.  

It was totally worth the wait!

Director Kathryn Bigelows tale of an Army bomb disarming team is one of the best films I have seen since Slumdog Millionaire.  The movie is two hours and eleven minutes of non-stop, nail-biting action.  

The film stars new talents Jeremy Renner and Anthony Mackie, and Brian Geraghty.  Ralph Fiennes, Evangeline Lilly, and Guy Pearce also have minor roles as well.  

The movie was nearly perfect.   Everything was spot on! Bigelows directing was fantastic and it was great to see another feature length film. The way this film was shot was fantastic! It was so quiet in the theatre that you could literally hear a pin drop and there were some sequences where the tension was building for so long you could practically cut it with a knife.  

The writing as well was superb!  The process with which it was written amazes me!  Writer-journalist Mark Boal actually embedded himself in an EOD Team in Iraq.  The script was great in both the dialog between characters and the fact that the viewer really fees connected to the EOD team.  

And how could I forget the leading team of new-found stars?

Jeremy Renner gives a performance that is so unbelievable for a first-timer.  He really blew me away! It was a very pleasant surprise.  The feud between his character and Anthony Mackies character (who actually thinks about killing Renner) is so believable it adds another complete layer to the movie.

As of today and the movies that have been released to date this year I think, in fact I almost know that The Hurt Locker will be nominated for some Oscars.  I predict Best Screen Play, Best Actor in a Lead Role, and now that the Best Picture list was bumped from five films to ten maybe even a nomination there.  So, if you are looking for something good to see in the theatre, do yourself a favor and go see The Hurt Locker.  Five stars! I cant wait to see the bright, young stars of this movies careers take off!

**********This review may contain minor spoilers**********

 I've seen "The Hurt Locker" three times. On the first encounter I didn't think too highly of this movie. The next two visits were much more amiable.

This movie follows the missions of a bomb disposal team of three from Camp Victory stationed in war-ridden Iraq. The team has just lost their tech team leader Staff Sergeant Thompson while disposing an improvised explosive device (IED). So when Sergeant William James (Jeremy Renner) who is a kind of an adrenaline junkie arrives to replace him, the stage is set for some intense action sequences.

Each character in the movie is defined by half an hour in way that we are able to make complete sense of their actions that follows. Even later new dimensions are added to the characters. What we see here is the pinnacle of character study .In a way each of the character is vulnerable, but at different levels. James is the leader who suits up to disarm the IEDs. His team members Sergeant J.T. Sanborn (Anthony Mackie) and Specialist Owen Eldridge (Brian Geraghty) communicate to him by a radio and cover him from snipers and detonators. So, their first mission arrives when they get a tip-off from a trusted informant. James despite the warnings from his team suits up before sending a bot to examine the situation and then kills their visibility by using a smoke bomb. This obviously shows that James thinks that he himself can prevent the snipers aiming at him without the teams help or maybe he's just getting a kick out of it. By now we know that James gets a high from doing what he does. That, he says, is the only thing he loves. James is the least vulnerable of the characters. James regrets being responsible for Eldridge's injury but only after taking risks which puts his and teams lives in danger.He regrets his actions only when he is alone and doesn't even show a hint of it when he has company.

Eldridge blames himself for the death of Thompson. He has sessions with Colonel John Cambridge. In one of the most rewarding scenes of the movie he talks about how one bullet from his gun could have saved Thompson. He is mostly cynical about his prospects in Iraq and constantly talks of dying in the line of duty.

Sanborn is visibly upset about losing Thompson. Even, James doesn't help him to accept a new leader. He wants to leave Iraq, but doesn't show it much until his final mission where with James he tries to save a man strapped with C4. This near death experience shakes him and what follows is a truly touching scene where he tells James that he wants to have a "boy".

The acting is uniformly great. Jeremy Renner adds depth to his unique character. Anthony Mackie and Brian Geraghty support him well. What's great is unknown actors play the leads and the known actors are given cameo roles. Both, Guy Pearce and Ralph Fiennes are good in their brief roles.

The layered script provides conversations that ring true and pack emotional wallop which I seemed to miss the fist time. What I also missed were some intelligent and hilarious conversations especially the "wild one" conversation between James and his superior. The script doesn't take sides. The Hurt locker is neither anti-war nor pro-war which makes it rather unique. This is not your conventional Hollywood war movie with long patriotic speeches.

It's Kathryn Bigelow's touch that pushes the movie towards greatness and then some more. She is the first woman to win an Oscar for direction and completely deserves it.

The shaky camerawork adds tension to the action scenes. But once or twice it gets distracting even when it's executed brilliantly. This is especially seen when camera focuses on the cat, which almost seems pointless. There is also a scene where the camera constantly cuts between James running and a man carrying meat. There may be symbolic significance to these scenes, but I don't think so. Even with these distractions the action scenes have impeccable attention to detail which is what makes them work. But, these are small shortcomings (about 20 seconds in a 131 minutes film).

"The Hurt Locker" is definitely one of the defining and best films of 2009.

 

Rating: 9.5/10

War films can be very difficult creatures to handle. They can be either too political or too cliched. Kathryn Bigelow, the director of such classics as Point Break and Near Dark, has gone for the approach of telling a simple tale of the men who risk their lives in possibly one of the best movies this year.

Concentrating on an elite Army bomb squad during the Iraq War, we follow the everyday lives of three men, as they face untold dangers from snipers, the locals and, of course, explosives. Nearly arrived Sergeant James has been on tour in Afganistan, and now joins the team, but his methods are both too macho and too dangerous for his two fellow officers, and yet he gets the job done, from discovering explosives in the street, in cars and on human beings. Yet James seems to relish in the danger, but could this affect his relationship with the other men?

Bigalow has done a very clever thing. She doesn't once metion anything about the political views of the war, and as to why the soldiers are there, she simply has set her film smack in the middle of a land torn, and doesn't once question the reasoning. These are men who have a job to do. She gives the film a more realistic viewpoint, as if you are in the heart of the action along with the characters, and she piles on the tension so much so it almost becomes unbearable.

The other clever thing she has done is not used well known names to play the leads. Jeremy Renner has done stuff in the past but you wouldn't know his name if you saw him. Looking like a rougher Daniel Craig, he gives an impressively smoldering performance, as does Anthony Mackie as his fellow Sergeant Sanborn. Brian Geraghty, as the nervous, slightly psychotic Spc Eldridge make up as very strong trio. Guy Pearce, Ralph Fiennes and David Morse all make appearances, but never too long of distracting from the three leads.

If I was to make a criticism, its more of a personal one, as we are in the middle of the action constantly, the camera swings about all over the place, causing a reaction that made me move seats in order not to be sick, but this is a minor problem.

This is an impressive piece of cinema, and one that will stick in teh mind long after it has finished. I wouldn't be suprised if this isn't mentioned in the same breath as Apocalypse Now, Full Metal Jacket or Platoon as being one of the best war films. It certainly is an amazing piece and puts Kathryn Bigalow right back among the best action directors around. If you like your movies to be incredibly tense and nail-biting, then I would highly recommend this stunner. It also has one of the most moving yet perfectly pitched endings I have seen in a film for a very long time.

The Hurt Locker (6 out of 10 Stars)

Star System Breakdown: My father (Antonio Abraira) and I devised a way to get as much of the bias out of our reviews and present what we think exhibits the qualities of a film down to its elements. Therefore there are five categories: Writing, Directing, Editing, Sound and Acting. Each one is capable of gathering a maximum of 2 Stars per category. 0 Stars indicates that the category not only failed to serve the film's function but went to great lengths to hurt the film. 1 star means it was average and nothing got hurt nor glorified. 2 stars is when that category goes beyond the call of duty.

Overview (Synopsis): Iraq. Forced to play a dangerous game of cat-and-mouse in the chaos of war, an elite Army bomb squad unit must come together in a city where everyone is a potential enemy and every object could be a deadly bomb. - from IMDB.COM

ACTING (1): Though the performances ranged from different aspects of the human condition, not one of them really extended to the depths of despair, insanity, hatred, or glory. All of the characters seemed transfixed into their mindsets and therefore, gave the impression that no one had evolved but merely survived the danger.

DIRECTING (1): I was apprehensive in throwing this the one star that it received when I considered that the director Katheryn Bigelow shot this with a 100:1 ratio. For those that don't know what that is, that means for every 100 minutes of footage gathered, 1 minute didn't get cut from the film. With a such a large ratio it is arguable that the filmmaker was excessively careful or worse had no idea what shots she wanted. Nonetheless the right ones were chosen though not extraordinary or very original. Rugged documentary footage shouldn't be lauded.

EDITING (2): The editor (or editors Chris Innis and Bob Murawski) are the true star of this film. With tons of footage it was all too easy to get "edit-happy." This is a slang term for what usually happens in recent Tony Scott films where jumpy cuts are showered throughout the story to the point of distraction. They showed restraint much like the characters in the film. It is because of this duo the film carried fantastic pacing. Without them, many of the director's shortcomings would have exploded on screen like one of those IEDs.

WRITING (1): Screenwriter Mark Boal certainly had an exciting film in his hands. The trio we follow certainly underwent transformative and downright traumatic experiences but offered little opportunity to see their inner world. Instead, a large chunk was dedicated to male-dominant comradery and poker face courage. These elements were vital but so were the vulnerabilities they faced. This story could've easily been two stars, if it had permitted us at least one character to feel scared. One can argue that the character (Brian Geraghty) Spc. Owen Eldridge embodied this emotional stance but not nearly enough to generate empathy.

SOUND (1): Explosions are explosions. Maybe twenty five years ago, I would have been more apt to grant this film another star if I hadn't already been bombarded with explosions for the last decade of truly terrible films (anything by Michael Bay is safe bet). However, it got its star cause it knew when to rely on silence or breath or heart beat. Where the writing couldn't carry the emotional stakes of the experience, the sound was there to at least slow down time and feel the moment by moment terror of dealing with dangerous explosives with a city infested with deception. In short, its what it did prior and after the explosion that mattered most.

Closing Remarks: All in all it was a fun experience and I must admit it got my pulse going a few times there. Time Magazine hailed this movie as a "near perfect film." I would say it was at least a mile away from perfection but certainly well out of the city of mediocrity.

Recent combat in the Persian Gulf has had rather lacklustre representation onscreen. Black Hawk Down practically stuffed the Stars and Stripes down the viewers throat, while the likes of Jarhead and Stop-Loss, while never less than watchable, ultimately proved too preachy.

The Hurt Locker bucks the trend of recent times of presenting war as pure hell. Instead, it shows how certain soldiers can become addicted to the tension and the adrenaline rush. Jeremy Renner, Anthony Mackie and Brian Geraghty are three members of a bomb disposal squad in Baghdad. Renner is a hot-blooded wire-cutter, Mackie the by-the-book leader and Geraghty the worried rookie. Together, they disarm explosive and bear witness to horrific images of war and carnage.

The Hurt Locker is a far more engaging film than previous Gulf War films because these characters are not presumed to be perfect soldiers doing their duty. Renner is basically an asshole, Mackie is too rigid and Geraghty is nervous when faced with potential aggression. However, as they share more and more experiences together, the characters grow, and insight into their personalities flows naturally from the scenarios. Kudos not just to the actors but also to screenwriter Mark Boal for creating more rounded characters than we're used to in these kinds of films.

Director Kathryn Bigelow (she of 'Point Break' and 'Strange Days' fame) can create scenes of extreme tension; this we already know, and tension abounds in The Hurt Locker. However, she also shows an indepth understanding of character development. The handheld camerawork and frequent close-ups serve to accentuate the claustrophobic atmosphere pervading the lives of these soldiers, and combining elegant exposition with explosions proves an excellent narrative move; we care about these characters, and the possibility of their dying in the next scene makes us care all the more.

While a talented supporting cast (including Evangeline Lilly, Guy Pearce and Ralph Fiennes) are given(too) little screentime, the three leads are excellent. Ultimately, this will be remembered as Kathryn Bigelow's triumphant return after mediocre fare such as K-19: The Widowmaker. This is her best film yet, the best war film of the decade and one of the best of the year.

Gritty and realistic, with a surprising amount of dark humour, The Hurt Locker follows the story of a bomb disposal unit in Iraq in 2003. It is the director's unique vision that makes this movie as good as it is and it never once shies away from the realities of wartime. Perhaps most important, however, is the amount of humour to be found, often times about the bizarre confluence of events that occur during war, and it is that humour that both gives the audience a break during especially heady moments and allows them to come down after particularly intense moments. All together, The Hurt Locker is an excellent movie that should be seen by anyone who is truly interested in the human aspect of war.

Scenes are bombastic when they need to be, but mainly so subtly played to ratchet the most amount of tension out of the smallest moments (the desert sniper sequence is almost unbearable).

The small cast is superb, with support by Mackie and Geraghty (playing a similar role to his Jarhead turn) very well played. Of course the most credit must go to Jeremy Renner, a long-term jobbing actor who has always been underrated but yet to get the role to get him noticed... And this is that role. Cocky, borderline psychotic whilst sympathetic and understandable - he is a conflicted character who revels in the job he does but comprehends little else. The notions of war as addiction is well done and not force-fed, and an interesting perspective on the soldier's life. Overall this is quality filmmaking that warrants repeat viewings.

Its very difficult to know what to say about this movie, Im not even sure if I liked it or not. But still I came out having thought it wasnt really a bad film, I still enjoyed watching it and was never bored at any point. Some of the scenes were shot beautifully and as I said before there is a great deal of tension in many scenes.

Call it apathy or desensitization or fatigue or willful ignorance, but irony drips from every film about a major overseas conflict that is produced and released while the war is still ongoing. Or maybe it's just depressing knowing that enough time has elapsed to be able to make a film like "The Hurt Locker"--based on events that occurred 5 years ago--and it's still probably the best record we have of Gulf War II in the post-Saddam-in-a-spider-hole era.

And just like the war keeps clipping along despite the lack of its signature "star," the (relatively) unfamiliar faces and vignette style of "The Hurt Locker" keep the film pulsing with immediacy and a universal pathos. The story begins to fray when it's pushed deeper into character study territory; it's a big challenge to localize the stresses that leave entire neighborhoods, cities, and nations irrevocably changed. Still, "The Hurt Locker" is a gripping manifesto of the modern warrior, a constitution that we are unwilling to discard completely even as we actively try to inch it toward obsolescence.

So rare is it, and so impressive that the definitive film regarding a foreign conflict is produced while that conflict is still ongoing that The Hurt Locker stands nearly in a league of it's own as a contemplative and captivating meditation on the modern war and the modern soldier. 

The characters, particularly those crafted by Jeremy Renner and Anthony Mackie, are labyrinthine in their complexity, yet so subtly portrayed that Bigelow has no need to rely on drastic reveals in order to open them to the audience's compassion. Rather they remain themselves with such underplayed honesty that their brazenness, their scorn, their pain becomes less of a performance and more of a confession. 

Here we have a movie of our time, in our time, imbued with a wisdom beyond itself. There are no blunt politics in Bigelow's film, no one-sided discussions, no heavy-handed summation of what this war has meant. It is, wholly simplified, an examination of fear, obsession and the places that we take refuge in a commonly lethal world.

"The Hurt Locker" is the best American war film since "Three Kings." Its the first successful non-documentary Iraq War movie that shows us the continuous, life-threatening danger faced by an Army bomb squad. Kathryn Bigelow uses her action director skills to maximum effect to create an intense, visceral experience of war. The squad is in constant fear of survival but goes about their routine tasks of trying to diffuse bombs while keeping an eye out for civilians who could trigger the explosive device. There is a phenomenal sequence of the restlessness before a shootout. The movie bogs down a bit near the end when a solider goes on an investigative mission and the trio searches for a suicide bomber in enemy territory. The concluding segment of a soldier's struggle to adapt to life with his family is moving in its simplicity. A great film with terrific performances, most notably by Jeremy Renner. With Anthony Mackie, Brian Geraghty, Guy Pearce, Ralph Fiennes, David Morse, Evangeline Lilly, Christian Camargo. Won Oscars for Best Picture, Best Director, Original Screenplay, Film Editing, Sound Effects Editing, Sound Mixing.

Now I have had my little rant, on to the film. Well, the story doesn't really have a linear structure other than it is a countdown from how many days the three lead men have in the current unit. Without revealing too much (like the telegraph did), it follows a bomb detection squad as they hunt for IEDs (Improvised Explosive Devices) and defuse large bombs. For the first hour, this is the focus. The tension is great and you really do get a sense of fear from all involved. However it is structured like tv episodes. You feel like after the first bomb you could wait a week for the next episode with the another bomb but it continues, much like watching 24 back to back. After the first hour, the story starts to lose pace and focuses more on the characters and their attachment to the war. Jeremy Renner makes an impressive turn in the lead role but you can't help thinking he was inspired by Mel Gibson in Lethal Weapon. The first bomb story is reminiscent of when Gibson talked down the school shooter in the director's cut of LW. For me, I would have constructed the story differently to have this build up of character throughout rather than separating the film into two distinct parts. Also I felt the appearances by more well known, well established actors (names omitted) were a little gratitious. Read a review and you know what happens.
My advice, don't read reviews before a film, read them after. Secondly switch off your phone for the duration of the film. You paid to see a film, not to talk on the phone.

Whenever there is a war there will be war movies. This has been a great thing for cinema, giving audiences blistering action and heartfelt drama all tied in a bullet ridden bow of political subtexts. Of course the last war to supply us with such marvel was Vietnam. The likes of Kubrick, Stone and of course Coppola used such a brilliant but controversial backdrop to explore the devastating impact of war and its general sense of insanity. But where is the Apocalypse Now of, well err now. To date, the most recent conflict, the Iraq war, has yet to inspire such a masterpiece, let alone a plausible effort. So far the only work to achieve anything worth going down in the war roomâs DVD collection is David Simonâs marvellous T.V production Generation Kill. But still nothing for the big screen, which is surely the best place to experience war from a safe enough distance from the actual reality. But now that could all be about to change with Kathryn Bigelowâs latest, The Hurt Locker.
 
Set in the blistering heat of the Iraqi conflict, the film follows a bomb disposal squad whose mission is to rid the Baghdad streets of improvised explosive devices (IEDs). After their team leader is killed in a mission, Sergeant Sanborn and Specialist Eldridge are assigned a replacement, who arrives in the form of William James (Renner). Despite a clear gift for his job, it soon becomes clear that their new team leader has very different approaches to the job. To say James likes to live life on the edge is a slight understatement, his character is addicted to hanging off it! As the story plays out, one white knuckle mission at a time, the date of squad rotation becomes a mission in itself to reach alive.

Avoiding becoming a meaningless action flick or a full tilt political outcry, the films focus is not about the causes or the false justifications of war. Instead, like the great films of âNamâ, Hurt Locker deals with the internal themes of war, in this case, the engulfing effect it can have on its participants and in particular the idea of war being a drug.  To the films credit it does so superbly, holding back on the true emotions and meanings until the very end, by which stage youâre in a fragile state of awe for it to make a true heartfelt impact.

Of course coming straight from the high octane powered vision of Kathryn Bigelow, The Hurt Lockerâs main merits are achieved through its juggernaut supply of action. Every situation the characters are placed in is filled with ridiculous intensity and suspense, whether it be one of the many, but certainly unrepetitive bomb defusing sequences or a stunning patient sniper battle across a dessert plain. Each event is filmed with such a raw quality it truly brings you into them, allowing you to smell the napalm first hand. The technical achievements on show really do blur the boundaries between film and reality for the audience, bringing them to the edge of their seat, with their hearts pounding to every bomb ticking sound.

The film glides relentlessly between these missions allowing the action to only briefly let up in-between. Itâs in these scenes where this film becomes a true combat experience. Because for all the action, the importance of its effect on those submerged within it is where the films heart lies and where conflict has its most devastating impact. Despite never being drawn out for a second too long and without a single emotion or meaning being overemphasised or clear cut, the film manages to delve so deeply into its themes and beyond any expectations for how mature and realistic a film of this nature should be. Of course such emotional depths and meanings could never have been conveyed if it wasnât for the brilliant performances from its cast. Renner, in what will be the breakthrough performance of his career, is simply spectacular. He tackles the task of portraying such a complex and confusing character with such prominent ease, itâs almost too easy to overlook his undeniable achievements on show. The supporting cast certainly tackles easier characters but in no way underperform in comparison to the lead, both the main supporting actors prove this to be especially so in the harder more intense dramatic scenes, ringing out the fears and tears of the soldiers caught up in the hellish world of war.

Of course the films true standout is Bigelow herself who grabbed this difficult and challenging subject by the gun barrels and turned into the rough and ready masterpiece of the year. The film marks an exciting new chapter in her career that will hopefully lead us to similar explosive experiences and allow Bigelow to gain the attention and credit she has now shown she truly deserves. But as for the film itself, itâs hard to predict how it will be remembered and whether it will be listed amongst the likes of Platoon and Full Metal Jacket. Right now it feels it deserves too, but one thingâs for sure, currently The Hurt Locker stands as the torch bearer for not only the Iraq war but for a whole generation of conflict movies.

In this day and age, creating an apolitical movie on war is, in itself, a triumph. The Hurt Locker is immersive, visceral cinema of the highest calibre. From the opening moments, director Kathryn Bigelow throws the audience into the front line task of bomb disposal experts in Iraq. Employing a cinema verite style Bigalow conveys the nerve shredding, adrenaline filled environment without getting drawn into the political arguments behind the war. 

The film isn't a commentary on the Iraq war. It's not even a commentary on the life of a bomb disposal unit. It is simply and fundamentally a portrayal of a particular aspect of the male psyche; machismo. This is a subject matter that Bigelow has explored successfully on numerous occassions in films such as Point Break and Near Dark. 

A bomb disposal unit provides an ideal context in which to explore one man's desire to live on the very edge of life and death and the impact it has on those around him - both in the field and at home. 

The film's production values are universally high and add to the immersive nature of the film. The performances of the largely unknown cast are at times intoxicating and poignant. The film leaves you feeling exhausted and affected by the actions of the characters. 

Bigelow has delivered the most ballsy, macho and nerve shredding movie of the year in a summer dominated by male directed warfare porn such as Transformers 2 and GI Joe.

Now a days it seems very hard to make a tense and smart action-thriller. I am here to declare that The Hurt Locker manages to do that and more. The story is about a group of army men, who upon having their last bomb disarmer killed in a bomb accident, hires a new one. The one they hire is named William James (Jeremy Renner, turning in a fantastic performance.) He does things his own way, much to the dislike of the leader, JT Sanborn. It starts to become intense being in the moment not knowing if William is making the right decision, or if JT is making the right decision. With great hype comes great potential for disappointment, and 'The Hurt Locker' is not immune to this. This visceral, well crafted dramatic thriller also suffers from weak characterizations, repetitiveness, and a touch of predictability and detrimental unbelievability. The 'hero', Sgt. William James (Jeremy Renner) is a fly-by-the-seat-of-his-pants danger junkie, but rather than being an exciting and fascinating character, he comes across more as an annoying, childish prick that cares not a damn for his colleagues. It's intensified by the very real stakes - and that's indicative of the entire film. It sets up the realism so well, that when it incorporates shameless and inelegant Hollywoodism, it sticks out like a sore thumb. Shaky cam is good for a documentary feel, but here it's so gimmicky it's distracting at times.

The cameos are great fun, though, and it's interesting to note that I was most excited when I first heard Ralph Fiennes' voice, before I had seen his face or knew he was in the film. Anthony Mackie is easily the best of the regulars because, while Renner does his job admirably, the writing of his character lets him well down.

The most exciting moment is easily the opening of the film with Guy Pearce, as virtually every major set piece after that is a tad predictable. That said, they are still almost universally taut and exciting (when Renner's Sgt James isn't wrecking things by being a dick, that is), the highlight being the ambush on Bravo company and the British contractors led by Fiennes. The dramatic highlight is easily Mackie's heartfelt breakdown at the end to a Renner who still clearly hasn't learnt his lesson. Mackie's a much more interesting (and believable) hero.

It's a very good film - too long, admittedly, especially without a plot or deep character development (could lose at least 20mins), and certainly not Oscar caliber, but an interesting and insightful viewpoint into the Iraq war and any other example of silly modern day warfare.

"The Hurt Locker" is one of the finest war films I've ever seen.  This is a fearless and extraordinarily frank presentation of an American bomb squad in Iraq.  It is brutally intense, and that's not just critical rhetoric.  It reaches a grade of intensity long forgotten by modern action directors, and herein lies the great value of this film:  it is not an action film and it abandons modern conventions to achieve paramount suspense.  And even then, the suspense seems wholly unmanufactured.  Director Kathryn Bigelow destroys our notion of safety, both in content and technique.  Movies have safety zones:  When a major start enters, they'll be there awhile; when a bomb needs diffused, there will be false alarms, etc.  All these are laid by the wayside.  Bigelow uses each dreadful situation to expose her characters.  This is a dynamic character study, a fascinating attempt at explaining what makes our servicemen walk into danger.  The answer is ...alarming.  If "The Hurt Locker" seems to meander, it's because it does.  That's the point.

"The Hurt Locker" is an insightful and taut look at the insanity of war, with a focus on a bomb disposal unit in Baghdad in 2004.  In order to combat the ongoing insurgency, they have to know who to trust in a country they know very little about.  Who is on your side?  On their side?  But it is never that simple, because most Iraqis are just minding their business, hoping to get through the day.  To illustrate this, director Kathryn Bigelow masterfully uses the shot/reaction shot to illustrate how much everybody watches everybody else with a weary eye.

In such a situation there has to be absolute trust between the soldiers of a unit which troubles Sergeant Sanborn(Anthony Mackie), a seven year veteran, and Specialist Eldridge(Brian Geraghty), a rookie soldier, when the new member of their team turns out to be Sergeant James(Jeremy Renner, of the criminally underrated "The Unusuals").  To them, James is reckless, fueled by adrenaline and therefore very likely to get them all killed.  In fact, with little regard for his own life, James is crazy, and not because he has a wife and child to return to.  And with a little more than a month in their rotation, Eldridge and Sanborn are trying their best to survive while keeping others alive(It is always a nice change of pace for a war movie where the mission objective is to save lives, not take them.), which is the only thing they can do when there is no end in sight for the American occupation at what was once Camp Liberty, now Camp Victory.
