I wasn't entirely conscious, but I have to admit that even then, I appreciated THE HURT LOCKER (Kathryn Bigelow, 2009).

It's a documentary style film about some Iraq War soldiers, specifically "bomb techs," or a unit whose primary function is the defusing of bombs.  The head defuser in this case is a soldier named James (Jeremy Renner), who defuses bombs so often and so well that it actually gets under his skin, becoming like an addiction for him and causing him to defuse at all costs - even if it puts others at risk.  THE HURT LOCKER is thus a complex "war is Hell" story, showing a different kind of psychological state than any I've seen in any other war movie.  But for me, the real appeal of THE HURT LOCKER was in its style.  It's shot so realistically and its characters are so believeable that I actually got woosy and sick watching this film.  Most of it is hand-held, and there's very little exposition (if any - I can't remember any, now that I think about it), so it's more or less just an experience - not of combat, as in SAVING PRIVATE RYAN (Steven Spielberg, 1998), but a mindfuck.  HURT LOCKER is so real that the subject matter becomes really disturbing, which makes it an amazingly effective film.

Why no perfect score, then?  Well, that same technique also makes the film painfully slow and disorienting as well.  As much as I appreciated the technique and how well Bigelow pulls it off, I admit that I got lost in places.  It takes a while to realize where this film is going, and meanders a lot.  Again, I think that all of that is intentional, though.  Though not a pleasant experience, exactly, THE HURT LOCKER is good almost because it's not supposed to be.  Again, war is Hell, and our lead is seriously disturbed as a result of it.  No surprise that we should be too.

It would be an understatement to say that what our troops go through during War is tough. It would be an understatement to say that disabling bombs is scary. It would be an understatement to say that "The Hurt Locker" is a great movie. 

The film, set in Iraq, tells the terrifying story of an elite Army bomb squad that have to disarm deadly bombs while coming together in a city where everyone is a potential enemy. 

The movie's tag line is "You'll know when you're in it." I usually know when I'm in a 100% movie and "The Hurt Locker" is one. Kathryn Bigelow puts the production together perfectly by mixing just the right amount of drama, action, and even a little bit of horror together. Every element of the film is there for a reason and is timed perfectly. No minutes are wasted with tacky romances or overly sugar coated special-effects. There's no excuse for one to take their eyes off the screen at any moment. The film has the best cast I've seen so far this year and Jeremy Renner deserves an Oscar for his work as Sgt. William James. 

The film's outsanding actors not only make us feel as if we're fighting for our country with them, they also add raw emotion to this truly moving cinematic experience. I rarely cry in movies. Many people were saying how I absolutely should not watch last year's "Marley & Me" because I would need too many tissues. I finally watched it and I can't say that I was crying. Maybe it's just me but as I sat in the theater and watched "The Hurt Locker" I got choked up a bit. The story had me feeling its over-bearing elements of sadness, fear, and intensity. 

I honestly could not find any flaws to this film. Bigelow has created a near masterpiece here. The action sequences are perfectly shot and add on to the highly dramatic elements of the film. Not only is "The Hurt Locker" the best film of the year so far, it is also the best War movie that has been released within the last ten years.

The Hurt Locker is a suspenseful ride that not only lacks a plot, but is a better film for it. Think of it as a 'day in the life of' movie, or rather '40 days in the rotation'. The three core characters work very well together, cresting the tensionand feel of a real unit in the field, facing death every day. To one if them though, death is almost disposable, having disarmed 873 bombs, he needs the rush and danger of the life to keep sane.

Shot entirely with handhelds, The Hurt Locker creates a sense of immediacy and danger that few others have mastered, and makes for seriously tense, compelling viewing. It won't be for everyone. Even after six years of Iraq, this film will prove to be topical and possibly painful viewing for some people, particularly Army families. If you can stand the heat though, be sure to give this provocative film a try.

The Hurt Locker follows the action of a bomb disposal squad as they ply their trade on the gritty streets of Baghdad. This is probably the best war film about Iraq so far, as it vividly conveys the tension and stress of combat in the Middle East. It's a reminder of the psychological stress that soldiers suffer in the line of duty, especially the kind of stress that is generated by an unseen & unpredictable enemy. At the same time it does address the fact that for some men war can be a kind of addiction which draws them in.

There isn't much of a story to follow, but that's reflective of the situation the soldiers find themselves in. The count down to when the soldiers finish their tour of duty is the only real indicator of how much time the film has left to run. The action sequences are extremely tense, though the camera work sometimes felt a little forced & claustrophobic - perhaps deliberately so. Overall this is a great war movie; the last time I saw a war movie generate so much suspense was Saving Private Ryan. kathryn Bigelow has certainly done a great job with this.

Gut-wrenching, pulse-pounding, out of this world tension only begins to describe what could well be (at this point) the best film of the year. A fictional story of Bravo Company's Explosive Ordnance Disposal squad in Iraq, the film gives us all a harrowing glimpse of what our troops go through day in and day out in the war torn country. Containing more breathless, nerve wracking sequences of near unbearable tension than most of this years "thrillers" rolled into one, the film is a guaranteed nerve jangler. Jeremy Renner gives a standout performance  as the adrenaline addicted squad leader. Anthony Mackie as the always professional soldier who just wants to get through each day in one piece, also gives a rock solid performance. Directed with a strong, steady hand by the nearly forgotten Katheryn Bigelow ("Point Break", "Blue Steel") and perfectly scripted by Neal Boal ("In the Valley of Elah"), the film doesn't have a single false note about it. Powerful, gripping and supremely intelligent film making of the highest caliber.

If there was ever a serious Oscar contender for Best Picture, this is it. When compared to District 9, which I saw immediately before, The Hurt Locker comes off as a one-trick pony. The movie follows three soldiers in an elite bomb disarmament unit in Baghdad and does a tremendous job of putting you smack into the middle of the action and the white-knuckle anticipation of action that these sodliers actually face every day. What it lacks though, is character development. Sure a selling point of the movie has been that since the cast is mainly unknowns, you never know who is going to get blown up next, but 30 minutes in, that's just not true, and besides, trying to guess who will bite it next does not a good film make. 

The Hurt Locker feels thin to me because there really isn't much going on aside from it taking you from one situation to the next. It's almost more documentary-like in structure than District 9, without actually looking like hand-held news footage. Only one scene about halfway through really shows the three leads doing anything other than their jobs and getting into their lives back home, which doesn't lead to much sympathy for the characters. The situations are quite intense and you will find yourself gripping your armrest without knowing it several times, for instance, the sniper situation, the car bomb and suicide bomber scenes. Director Kathryn Bigelow makes you believe in these scenarios 100%, but that's really all this movie has going for it. While not bad in any way, it could've been a bit shorter and used a bit more emotion.

The Hurt Locker is an action movie on a very human scale. Sure there is a time and place for your Michael Bay-esque action vehicles, the type that scorch square miles and leave recognizable world cities in ruins. However, those kinds of action movies are never the kind where storytelling ever enters the fray beyond a meager question of how to get from Point/Explosion A to Point/Explosion B. In fact, Bay openly admits to planning the story of Transformers 2 by working on various action sequences during the 2007 writer's strike and then tasking screenwriters to connect the dots. The Hurt Locker exists in a frighteningly believable world. This isn't a movie about explosions but about the extinguishing of explosions. It follows the Explosives Ordinance Disposal (EOD) unit, tasked with detecting and detonating bombs and other improvised incendiary explosives (IED) in the field of combat. You will not be restless for loud "booms" while watching The Hurt Locker. In fact, you will be on pins and needles hoping that you never hear another loud "boom."

Delta Company are the men responsible for protecting the other soldiers by disposing of bombs. The new team leader, Staff Sgt. William James (Jeremy Renner) has defused over 800 bombs during his tour of duty. He knows he's the best and he's addicted to the thrill of being so close to death. He will make occasionally reckless decisions putting himself, but not his fellow company men, at higher risk. This does not sit well with Sergeant JT Sanborn (Anthony Mackie), a by-the-book type that doesn't appreciate his officer chasing a thrill. The other EOD unit member, Specialist Owen Eldridge (Brian Geraghty), is a man more accustomed to taking orders than giving them, and his indecision may have actually cost the life of the former head of the EOD. Both Sanborn and Eldridge worry that their new team member is going to get them all killed.

Director Kathryn Bigelow (Near Dark, Point Break) has been directing male-centered action flicks for over two decades; it's been seven years since her last feature, the regrettable Harrison Ford submarine flick, K-19: The Widowmaker. The Hurt Locker is her finest work to date by far. Her action sequences are visceral and downright agonizing to sit through. She is masterful at setting up the geography of the set piece, ratcheting up the suspense, adding organic obstacles and complications, and then makes sure with her camera and editing that an audience knows exactly what's happening to whom for every minute that ticks off the clock. Bigelow takes her time to establish the particulars of her locations and sequences, allowing the audience to, surprise, understand what is happening and better engage in the movie. Bigelow chose to shoot the movie in Jordan, the neighboring country to Iraq, and the locations and actual refugee extras add an unvarnished sense of realism. The movie goes without music during much of the action, which makes it all the more uneasy. There isn't any over eager composer telling you how you should feel, no direction that now things will get even more hairy. You will feel every second of danger, and Bigelow crams in a whole lot of danger. Things can go wrong very, very quickly.

There's nothing to action cinema quite like the bomb that's only a few tick-tocks away from doing its dirty work. Do you cut the yellow wire or the green wire? Never cut the red wire. The bombs found in Iraq are a stark range of death. There's the crude incendiary device just wrapped up in garbage, but then there's also the fiendishly clever devices with multiple charges and there are grotesque devices as well. At perhaps the film's most guttural and shocking moment, Staff Sgt. William James finds the corpse of an innocent stuffed with explosives. The easiest thing would be to simply detonate the bomb, but that would also desecrate the body of someone we have come to know. Watching James snip open the crude stitching and dig inside the chest cavity, if we didn't know then we know now, Bigelow has made sure that The Hurt Locker is the most emotionally resonating contemporary war film in memory.

Bigelow and screenwriter Mark Boal, an Iraq War journalist, create a vivid sense of dread, antipathy, and most of all, paranoia. Is that a kite flying in the air or is that a signal? Is that a nondescript observer with a cell phone or is that a terrorist with a remote detonator? Is that child being friendly or collecting intelligence? Your mind will race through all these possibilities because Bigelow teases out her action sequences to an unbearably taut level. The audience cares about these soldiers and wants to see them make it back home (we're informed how many days Delta Company has left on their tour throughout the film), which Bigelow uses to her advantage at every turn. What happens matters. My nerves were frayed during several sequences, including one where the soldiers are pinned down by distant enemy gunfire. The moment turns into a duel and a chess game, as each side tries to adjust their gaze in the searing heat and measure their long-range shot before the other side beats them to it. Then the sequence turns into a waiting game. This is the kind of movie that keeps you poised on the edge of your seat fearful that at any moment something disastrous will suddenly happen. Every time Staff Sgt. William James went back out to defuse another bomb, my sense of dread intensified. I began to doubt everything that I would ordinarily take for granted in other movies.

While being a top-notch action movie, Boal (In the Valley of Elah) has also crafted a great character study. In between the bomb episodes we learn more about these men, which makes it all the more hard to see them then head out to defuse another explosive. The film opens on a quote equating war as a drug, and we explore this notion through the character of Staff Sgt. William James and the weight his unique duty bears. It takes a special person to volunteer for defusing roadside bombs. The defuser must be extremely intelligent, be extremely cool under pressure, and be able to work in a giant suit that makes them look like a chubby astronaut, while enduring debilitating desert temperatures of 110 degrees. It sounds like a suicide mission. James is an adrenaline junkie and war is his drug. He exudes a Zen-like calm in the heat of the moment and this is now the only life for him. Shopping for cereal back home has lost its meaning. Being a husband has lost its meaning. His life now has one purpose. Renner (28 Weeks Later, North Country) gives a stirring performance laced with cavalier confidence and resignation. Mackie (Eagle Eye, We Are Marshall) is also another standout in the pared down cast. When he laments about the dishonor of having no one to remember you in death, you feel the man's existential sorrow.

Ignore the political cranks that decry The Hurt Locker as another partisan anti-war film from Hollywood. The American public has been mostly indifferent to any contemporary movie that aims to tackle our current military conflicts in Iraq and Afghanistan, but The Hurt Locker eschews the politics of war to focus on the realities and dangers of its characters. These guys are more concerned with surviving the next bomb than the politics of why they're in the Middle East. The public has voted with their wallets and does not want to see the reality of war onscreen, or at least the Hollywood version of war reality, but I pray that those same people give The Hurt Locker a fighting chance. There is no preaching to be found here. The Hurt Locker could just have easily taken place during other wars, though the current Iraq War allows for added cultural dissonance (Is the central goal of bomb-defusing a metaphor for our conflict in the region?). This is a film that transcends politics and genre.

The Hurt Locker is more than an action movie, more than a war movie, more than a psychological study; this is an outstanding movie. This movie is a drug to the adrenaline senses and I need another hit. This is one of the finest films of the year and as it expands across the nation, I highly encourage everyone to seek out The Hurt Locker. 

Nate's Grade: A

'The Hurt Locker' does for Iraq what 'Platoon' did for Vietnam. It makes us AWARE of something we can never fully understand on the homefront. Please, don't be fooled by any of the iffy-looking posters because this is not a fictional political thriller inspired by the middle eastern conflicts; it is a triumphant film about real men in real situations, and it shows absolutely no shame in telling it like it is. You can attribute the Hollywood effect to less-popular faces and low-key budgets if you wish, but movies this powerful don't come around but maybe once a decade.

While the performances are nothing short of Oscar-worthy, the biggest pleasure for me in watching 'The Hurt Locker' is the harsh realism that captivates the structure of the film's atmosphere. Running at about 125 minutes, there aren't a whole lot of words spoken verbally, but there are numerous long shots and lengthy takes that keep the suspense boiling. We know where every person is at all times, and as we sit there right next to James with his tools, we become absolutely embraced by the nerve-wrecking tension resting over his head. To call it "edge-or-your-seat" would be too much of a clichÃ©, but it would also be a complete understatement as we anticipate the results of what could easily become James' last day at any given moment.

An explosive, brilliantly acted, sharply observed film about the lives of the members of a bomb disposal unit in Iraq, The Hurt Locker is by far the best war movie in years.  Director Kathryn Bigelow directs a sharp script by journalist Mark Boal, and wrings out all the tension you'd expect from a movie about such dangerous business.  However, the film doesn't skimp on digging deep into the psychological toll such dangerous work takes on any sane person.  We feel for these guys, and we see the effects it has on them every day; the feeling that they could be blown up at any moment during the course of a day's work.  The acting's uniformly great, with strong performances from Jeremy Renner, Anthony Mackie, and Brian Geraghty, along with memorable (and short) turns from vets like Ralph Fiennes, Guy Pearce, and David Morse.  It's really a shame this had such limited distribution, because it's one that's really not to be missed.

This review contains a minor spoiler towards the end.

"War is a drug" is the pre-text to the film. If you think from this quote that the film will have a political message, you will be disappointed. This is the extent of its political involvement.

Bigelow succeeds in building an amazing tension during the entire film. Contrary to what most reviews say, this film is more about tension than action, which is appropriate given the job of these bomb squad soldiers.

The photography and editing, oscillating between documentary style and big budget, give a degree of realism and accentuate the tension. The film still doesn't have the level of tension of the masterpiece in the genre "The wages of fear" but it's one of the best, which is the reason for the 4 stars rating.

The 3 key characters, the bomb squad soldiers, explore a different facet of the psychology of living in a war environment, although the focus is on the man who actually defuses bombs. He can either be seen as a reckless risk-taking soldier or a daring officer who knows his trade. In any case, he is portrayed as a hero, therefore never really within harm's reach, and this is where one of the film weaknesses is most apparent given the tone of realism adopted by the director. She has created a war hero, and doesn't escape the typical hollywoodian war movie pitfall. Unfortunately, this soldier made hero glorifies war and seems to justify it, if ever to create the heroes who justify any war. It also helps boost the box office.

But given this unbearable and prolonged tension, I couldn't help but wonder: why are these men risking their lives in this particular country? What is the larger context?  What is the political rationale of their presence there?  In order for soldiers to make sense of their mission - wherever they are - I can't believe that no soldier in particular in Iraq is asking that question. But the film remains mute on this.

Although the point of view is admittedly from the soldier's, the local population, here Iraqis, is, as ever, viewed as liar and hostile at best and enemy at worst. There is an embryonic but too timid and awkward exploration of the interaction of soldiers with the local population. The focus is purely on the action and tension, and that makes the film too one-dimensional. The only one Iraqi who seems to be sincere - although one still wonder whether he is not a suicide bomber - is failed by the hero, a master at bomb defusal, in the grand finale. What is the message of that scene? What should we read in this symbol? That Iraq can't be saved by the American hero and doomed? I'm still not sure what to make of that scene, but it is clear that there is a massive cultural misunderstanding between the soldiers and the population, starting with the language, which is at the root of the difficulties in Iraq.

I was expecting an extraordinary story about ordinary men and I saw a good film about an extraordinary man. This is not a thinking movie but an emotional and tense, well built story.

The Hurt Locker is the most entertaining movie that has been made about the Iraq war. Period. No Contest. It is easily the best war movie that I have seen since Saving Private Ryan. Yes, it's even better than Black Hawk Down.

Simply put, The Hurt Locker tells us the story of an Explosive Ordnance Disposal unit (army-speak for 'bomb squad') and their daily exploits. Another war movie, right?

Wrong. I suppose the greatest thing about it, while this statement will be banal, is its ability to blend some many different styles together. In this movie I laughed and I cheered. I was scared and I was shocked. I was grossed-out, and sometimes I even wanted to cry. When someone inflicts pain upon another, he is said to be putting the other 'in the hurt locker.' Which makes for a brilliant title for this movie because of the continuous suspense that Sergeant James puts his fellow servicemen (and us the viewers) into.

This movie sets itself apart from the rest of the pack for many reasons. But what stood out most clearly to me was that it doesn't take sides. It just shows the situation as it is. There's no "the Iraq war is right," nor "the Iraq war is wrong." It shows characters as they are, and what they really care about in that right-here-and-right-now sense. This is in striking contrast to the supposed "realistic" portrayal of a soldier's experience that the cinematic masturbation of Jarhead showed us (based on the first Iraq war). There are parts of the characters that are rather glib though. Why are they doing this? How do they cope? The film's answer to those statements is in the opening text of the movie: "The rush of battle is often a potent and lethal addiction, for war is a drug." That's nice, but it threatens to turn the movie into another American adrenaline-junkie action flick with no answers to any questions.

But we know that the movie is not about that. It's a 'day in the life' story, not a "life" tale. That's what we're interested in seeing anyways, right?

While there are some pretty cliché war-movie scenes in the film, I found it easy to overlook them because the movie makes up for it in so many other original ways. When James suits up in his "blaster" outfit and walks down the empty desert street towards the bomb he is trying to defuse, it feels like an old-western shootout.

There are some great moments though. The first disarming with the new boss, the shoot-out in the desert and the suicide bomber are all nice little scenes. And I really liked the way big name celebrities such as Ralph Fiennes, Evangeline Lily and Guy Pearce have the tiniest roles but still cared to be in the film, allowing the no name actors to steal the show.

But in the end it is still a war movie and whilst Bigelow has done a great job of transcending it from most war films, it doesn't quite go far enough to be an all time classic.

In a time where soldiers are constantly harbored by radicals for their decisions to go above and beyond the call of duty, The Hurt Locker couldn't have come at a more important time for social cinema and American culture. In portraying a man who feels as though war is his "drug", Renner and his men take us through a fear induced journey into a foreign world where the enemies are not clearly marked and could be absolutely anywhere. Because no one is safe, tension is so palpable that it makes the hairs on your hand stand and your fingers clutch the seat.

Your standard war film consists of some pretty traditional bullet points: it's dirty work, no one back home wants to understand, your friends can die in an instant, and so on and so forth.  In different wars these truths remain steadfast and are consistently touted to us, but this latest war in the sandy and dangerous battlefields of Iraq are so infused with politics, confusion, shades of Vietnam and the harrows of a more immediate sense of the danger of the world that it seems difficult to separate the movies from their real-world complexities.  We've been faced with several in the guise of Jarhead, The Kingdom, Three Kings, and several others and none thus far have managed to conceal a serious political agenda despite their compelling stories.  The Hurt Locker makes for a great story, a comment on the human condition of war, and the most intense, gripping, and jaw-biting film I have seen in a long time.  

The film follows the final 39 days in the tour of Bravo Company in Iraq: a bomb squad.  We follow them as their commanding officer is blown to pieces, and his replacement is a veteran having diffused more then 800 bombs.  He's a maverick and, having fully accepted the dangerous parts of his job, throws safety to the wind in favor of the rush.  As their days tick down every encounter is a coin toss as to whether or not they will survive.

Director Bigelow has brought every element to bear.  The sound is busy and frightening as we hear the urban sounds of Baghdad while the camera pans the rooftops looking for snipers, or even a man with a cell phone waiting to detonate.  Our soldiers are human and affected.  The hide their fear or succumb to it and either ride the wave of adrenaline or are taken over by it as their training kicks in and it eats them visibly from the inside out.  

This is a simple and well told story.  It doesn't carry an opinion of the war, or a judgement of its' central characters.  It is harrowing and nail-biting from start to finish and somehow, despite it's distance from the emotional centers of its' characters, makes us care deeply about their survival.  That's a refreshing change of pace from war films where everyone is a casualty that we are unprepared for and thusly we are never given the chance to root for them to survive.

Kathryn Bigelow's The Hurt Locker won a prize at the 2008 Venice Film Festival and its down to earth depiction of war in Iraq is realistic and hard nosed enough to justify more gongs.
Set during Iraq in 2004 it focuses on a group set up to handle improvised explosive device; right from the beginning we are introduced to how awful this particular role is.  Sharp dialogue and camerawork help add to the craziness and the gravity of the world they live in.  Nevertheless the movie is ultimately about the addiction war and this kind of job has rather than what this particular war is about.
The movie ignores politics to the point it could be in any middle east conflict.  Local people rarely speak and tend to be up to no good.  At its most gruesome a local boy?s life is sacrificed for a stomach full of explosives.
To compensate for the lack of politics, the movie gives us the tension of de-activating the IEDs - utterly immeasurable.  Added to that is the tension in the group when a trailor trash techie called James with a wild abandon joins the disciplined group and throws out the rule book.  He lacks fear but is smart enough to stay alive.  In fact he is portrayed as out of control by the army around him, but his ability to deliver results keep him in the team.
Even his male colleagues think he's weird. But nature made him that way - to give him those titanium nerves that enable him to pull bombs apart.
Unconvincingly, he is portrayed as the only one who really connects with local people.  This allows the movie to let him investigate the murder of a boy he befriends but the plot soon gets lost and moves on.
After the thrill of defusing bombs the movie runs out of story and James is seen back home with his family.  But he is simply out of depth in the domestic superstore and we see him for one more time back in thick of battle. 
Bigelow does a stunning job updating movies such as Apocalypse examining the crazed psyche of the soldier addicted to war, but without turning it into Hollywood schlock.

What a ballsy film. And I'm not talking merely about the testosterone of war, or the sheer volume of sound, or the main character's swagger, or Kathryn Bigelow's intensity of direction that built the tension levels here to the sublime and dreadful suspense of an aces horror movie. I'm talking about how this is a hero's movie, old-school propaganda-style. The movie bothers not a whit with why these men, in particular the lead protagonist (played as subtly as could possibly be accomplished given the circumstances by Jeremy Renner), are fighting this war. The frustrations of Renner's fellow soldiers play off his wreckless courageousness satisfactorily for a long time, and then toward the end, things get a little fishy. A scene in a truck in which Anthony Mackie asks Renner, behind tears, how he can be so dauntless. It has the smell of ick, something out-of-place cliche here. Then, there's a scene with Renner's son, and I'm totally scratching my head. But in the last five minutes, I finally got what Bigelow was doing, and it is something very few contemporary directors would have the bravery--or the war-hating conscience--to do. Actually one other filmmaker had it this year: Quentin Tarantino. And two or three years ago Werner Herzog mined it. They made unapologetic yankee-doodle movies about war heroes. Incredibly good ones.

US Army Staff Sergeant Will James (Jeremy Renner), Sergeant JT Sanborn (Anthony Mackie) and Specialist Owen Eldridge (Brian Geraghty) comprise the Bravo Company's bomb disposal unit stationed in Baghdad. I do realize the tediousness of filming about the war in Iraq, and I certainly applaud Kathryn Bigelow's ambitious and documentary-felt intimacy, as it's the most appropriate directorial medium imaginable - in fact, I see 'The Hurt Locker' being a front-runner at the 2010 Academy Awards, maybe for Best Director and Best Picture (unless the end of the year unloads some astonishing work, like the normal Oscar trends). In this Iraq - we have a couple alpha-males, and a few cowardly combatants (i'm not slandering - I would probably fit this role in times of pant-shitting, slow-boiling warfare), who fit the camo-wear of the normal everyday Iraqie war participant we know, hate, or love. They booze it up and spar fights with each other, talk about their hopes, loves, and desires in poorly-written dialogue, and are passionate about their work. The film's goal most likely was not to deliver up anything new or intrinsic to the cinematic table - just to portray suspense in its most blood-boiling and realistic with some artfully-jazzed slow-motion explosion shots and time to kill in between. Thankfully, this doesn't glorify the soldiers like a GoArmy.com commercial, yet there's some shit-grinning, goofy nu-metal rock riffs playing here and there that are truly laughable. Then again - I think I've only met a couple Iraq troops who don't listen to Disturbed or Godsmack. Anyways - my review: this film is visually sharp as a knife, yet lacks in character value where it shines in male brute. The film's lack of linear story (face it, at face value, this film's about this guy's thrill for disarming bombs and what he goes through, yet we learn little about him other than the fact that he loves his job and has a wife and kid) would've been justified by characters playing off each other existentially or in a more heartfelt manner instead of just one sensitive guy feeling weak at the face of war. Its duration would've been dreadful without a realistic pay-off in tasteful action and suspense. The film's ending? Just plain disappointing. **SPOILER** I highly doubt that even the most passionate of individuals would jump at the opportunity to leave their wives and children to go back to disarming bombs.

This is an intense and gritty war drama about an elite Bomb Squad who just has 38 days left in duty rotation and whose job is to disarm and diffuse deadly bombs that plagues modern day Iraq. After their first Sergeant (Guy Pearce) is killed, Staff Sergeant William James (an impressive Jeremy Renner) is assigned to the unit. The team soon discovers that James is flamboyant in his bomb disposing technique to the point of recklessness on the job. He takes more risks in the field than their previous Sergeant and is an adrenaline junkie. He meets his new teammate, the experienced African-American Sergeant Sanborn (Anthony Mackie), a realistic soldier who accepts his dangerous role; adhere to policy, hoping to eventually have a son when he returns home. As for Sgt. "Specialist" Owen Eldridge, war is a killing machine which takes life of a soldier in an instant. He has to live with his fear of being shipped home in a box. Together, they face the experienced, illusive and lethal enemy with exceptional courage.

At the end of the movie, we see a few very brief scenes of James enjoying domestic bliss with his family and then he is back in Iraq, starting all over again his 365-day duty rotation. He needs the rush of battle, a potent and lethal addiction, for "War is a drug". To James, it's all too clear, he is a top professional in his field, and as long as bombs are to be defused, his place is there. Without it, he is as insignificant as a lone shopper picking out cereal in a supermarket.

I bought this movie on DVD from an Iraqi bazaar on FOB Falcon, just south of Baghdad proper and the International Zone, in December 2008 or January 2009.  The cover art did not include any accolades or quotations.  I just thought it looked like it might be an interesting action picture, and, though I was hesitant, for obvious reasons, to watch a movie set in Iraq while I was operating on behalf of the United States Army in this wretched place, I took a chance that it was worth $2.  Guy Pearce usually takes good roles.  

Through a set of lucky circumstances, I was able to take advantage of some free time between missions and watch it completely alone on a standard movie theatre auditorium-size screen with excellent sound quality.  

After my screening, though I knew I had essentially just wasted 2 hours, I reluctantly passed my illegal DVD, which I assumed contained a small-time limited release or straight-to-DVD movie, to a teammate who I thought might appreciate the movie on some level.  I warned him that the movie was, at best, so-so, but potentially not a complete waste of a couple hours for him.  He had injured his legs, so his job kept him confined mostly to base, where he generally had way more free time than I did.  He eagerly consumes a lot of movies, so he vaguely acknowledged my lukewarm recommendation as he slid the disc in his laptop.  At dinner that night he was genuinely angry at me for introducing him to this "terrible" film, as he called it.  

We threw away the DVD.  

Until this past June, I totally forgot about The Hurt Locker; it was a nonentity in my overall personal cinematic experience, except that it represented that one time I got to have full, unfettered use of the FOB's movie theatre.  

I worked an average of 16 hours daily, running an average of 2 missions daily from January to the last week of June 2009, when the Security Agreement and Status of Forces Agreement changed the posture of American forces in Iraq.   With more free time due to the stipulations of the technicality of having the Iraqi Security Forces legally in charge of when and where we operate, movie review Friday became a part of my life again.  NYTimes.com is usually one of the first websites I check when I activate my internet access.  

That's where I saw the beast that The Hurt Locker had quickly become among civilian film critics.  "This can't be," I thought.  

I checked good ole RottenTomatoes.  "Uh-oh."  I checked Salon.com.  "Stephanie Zacharek, no, you fell for it, too?"  

First, I present you the disturbing and error-filled NY Times review, if you care to follow the link: http://movies.nytimes.com/2009/06/26/movies/26hurt.html?scp=1&sq=hurt%20locker%20review&st=cse

Soldiers on a Live Wire Between Peril and Protocol
By A.O. Scott
26 JUN 2009

***********************************************************



I wish I had realized when I first saw it in the winter that this movie would be released theatrically in the United States in the summer of 2009.  I could have tainted some critical opinion before the critics, even my favorites, all made themselves look like a collective jackass.  

And now I present my timely Reader Review response to A.O. Scott's piece, which I see has received some 53 recommendations thus far from NYTimes readers:  

Mr. Scott, for once, is completely wrong.  

A.O. Scott and I have stood on the common ground of some degree of adoration for certain underrated films, including Casanova, Rambo, and Ratatouille, and together in the angry pulpit of disappointment regarding some overrated films, including Seabiscuit, Big Fish, and Kill Bill, but the recent glowing review of a bad film has forced me to take a moment out of my busy day in the life of a United States Army paratrooper and temporarily to take arms against a civilian's glaringly uninformed perceptions rather than against the local threat that lurks in this war zone we call Operation Iraqi Freedom.  An excellent, insightful writer and film critic, with whom I rarely completely disagree, has missed the mark in his review of Kathryn Bigelow's The Hurt Locker.  The critic who has offered witty, acrimonious appraisals of the shortcomings of bad actors ("Mr. Affleck, wielding a Philadelphia accent as thick and inauthentic as low-fat cream cheese") and perfectly succinct praise for masterpieces ("Ratatouille is a nearly flawless piece of popular art.") with equal skill and apparent impartiality has failed me with this recent review.  

Any reviewer who claims expertise on the supposed resemblance to reality of the perspective of the protagonists because he/she claims to be a soldier either does not have the same working knowledge of operations in and around Baghdad that many US Army combat-occupation soldiers possess or is guilty of taking the willful suspension of disbelief a step too far into the realm of deliberate ignorance by shutting down a significant portion of his/her brain while viewing the film.  That method of film viewing has served audiences of Bigelow's oeuvre well, though I agree with Mr. Scott's assessment of her altogether entertaining body of work.  I still recommend Strange Days to everyone.  

Beyond the depiction of bootleg DVD sales at a local-operated kiosk (Indeed, I am guilty of having purchased my copy of this film from a grey market 'Hajji shop,' as we call them here in the desert.), and a few other touches of verisimilitude escaping from the writer's version of the story into the director's final product, lies a film of surprising inadequacy.  Now, if one were swept up in the tension of the set-pieces and the uniqueness of a war story concerning these atypical characters, one could not be blamed.  I, for one, thought Rob Cohen's XXX, with Vin Diesel, was awesome, even as I fully realized its sheer stupidity.  However, to deliver ultimatums concerning the status of The Hurt Locker as the best action movie of the season is to offer evidence of one's inability to care about confounding inconsistency and an accidental or, worse, deliberate evasion of truth-telling by the filmmakers in an otherwise realistic setting.  Unfortunately, the cliches about 'Hollywood getting it all wrong' are applicable concerning The Hurt Locker, in which a 3-man EOD team inexplicably travels independently in its own truck.  The second-ranking man on the team is inexplicably an expert with a powerful sniper rifle, which he employs on a moving human target hundreds of meters away.  The junior man on the team is inexplicably weak-minded and ill-trained for a special operations soldier; he allows enemy activity to continue unhindered when he's not being misguided by equally idiotic friendly forces.  The leader of the trio is just inexplicable, which apparently is what Mr. Scott likes about him; he watches an IED triggerman, a terrorist, present himself within arm's reach of capture, then run away to safety after the Sergeant First Class presents evidence that he has won their little competition by defusing an especially nasty-looking complex secondary explosive device.  Apparently, smirking and holding up a piece of the dismantled device for the terrorist to see is more important than detaining the terrorist.  Is this the work of an artistic genius, "Ms. Bigelow, practicing a kind of hyperbolic realism"?  

I'll add that day-to-day combat operations, if one is performing his job correctly, in this godforsaken place (Thermometer read 120 Fahrenheit today.) leave no room for nuanced contemplation of the relationship among soldiers, as some filmmakers and critics seem to believe.  Mr. Scott notes, "Ms. Bigelows insight is that the tense comradeship of soldiers rests, often tenuously, on barely suppressed erotic and homicidal impulses."  No, her insight is that soldiers in combat at the peak of a war at its most dangerous places have as much time to demonstrate the more confusing aspects of their manliness for the camera as the surfers of Point Break had to ramble about the beauty and catharsis of their preferred escape from the daily grind.  Instead of Keanu Reeves irrationally firing a pistol in personal frustration during an undercover mission, we have a team working toward the end of an OIF deployment while pausing to generate individual goals that no actual soldier in combat would have time to consider.  

******************************************************************


Upon the end of the first decade of the 21st century, a note: 

I have lately noticed that this film continues to receive high praise from most civilian critics & viewers.  Such counterproductive differentiation & such usually pointless partisanship is generally anathema to me, but the dichotomy regarding the opinions of this film among civilians and the opinions of this film among those who have done work in Baghdad this century is strikingly clear.  

I have wrestled with the idea that this is not supposed to be a literal action movie.  For example, I have tried to make something meaningful of SFC James's excursion into the city, when he searches for a target but has neither a mission nor the tactically critical intelligence to match his determination, contorting the sequence in my mind so that it is a microcosm for the entire W/Cheney Iraq War.  This grain of artistic-political provocation makes me nod my head thoughtfully for a moment until I realize how pointless and weak such a political statement it would be in a summer 2009 release, years after countless pages of anti-Iraq War & anti-W articles and musings have already been published and validated by the last couple American election cycles.  And there are other scenes that fail as action and fail as symbols of something more meaningful, so ultimately none of this film provokes or reveals truth.  

There is no mystery to the story, only befuddled decision-making.  There is no fun, redemption, or catharsis in the story, only pointless death and unearned pleas for sympathy.  There is no theme to the story, only cursory examination of thrill-seeking in a high-thrill environment that merits only cursory realization.  There is no meaningful sense of menace, only disposable cardboard bad guys, who may as well be background extras, and the displeasure of witnessing stupidity and incompetence in action until the bomb expert frantically cuts the right wire just in the nick of time.  The twist is, sometimes he fails.  The other twist is, he still kind of likes his job.  I have already been working at an intense combat job myself, but there's nothing cathartic about it that involves special operations soldiers crying and unnecessarily making themselves targets.  Risky behavior in combat is fun and invigorating, in my experience, but we never put our subordinates in danger without knowing there will be severe consequences for doing so.  For those who have never seen this in a film before, it is likely thrilling; they might even think that they have connected with the experience of an Explosive Ordnance Disposal team in Operation Iraqi Freedom.  For those of us who have seen the reality of Baghdad in recent years, this film, barring the outrageous critical praise that has been published lately, is a small, harmless mistake; I can be as upset by its existence as I am upset that my aunt bought me the wrong size sweater for Christmas.  

I shall simply reaffirm that I first scooped this movie in December 2008/January 2009 with no expectations and no laudatory quotations on the DVD cover.  I honestly shrugged off the problems I had with the failed attempts at verisimilitude and noted that it was no wonder the movie had failed to be released theatrically.  I had a fun game going in my head whereby Guy Pearce and Ralph Fiennes each bitch about something in the direction this lousy movie is going until their agents convince the producers to release them from their contracts and minimize their screentime. 

For its performances, despite the script, I regard The Hurt Locker with slightly more fondness than most lousy straight-to-DVD releases, but, to me, that's what it always should have been.

Riveting and disarming in equal measure, acclaimed director Katheryn Bigelow proves that she has a penchant for crafting compelling war films with The Hurt Locker, which surpasses on every account the standard set by 2002's K-19: The Widowmaker.

Using documentary like hand-held cameras - expertly handled by Barry Ackroyd - to inject a healthy dose of realism and attention to detail into proceedings, the film follows the last month or thereabouts in the life of the members of the elite bomb disposal squad within the US army's Bravo regiment stationed in Baghdad,Iraq. 

The action is kept taut and perilously close to the ground as the members cheat death with every wire that they snap. The barren, unforgiving territory and piercing stares of the locals combine to immerse the soldiers into a cauldron of tension. When you're unsure whether the next move you make is going to rattle the ground beneath your feet and even a cursory glance over the horizon could have you making eye contact with adversaries that hide behind expressionless faces, you're battling yourself from within just as much as fighting a war outside. And this undertow of guilt  and insecurity amidst supposed bravado is conveyed perfectly by an ensemble cast in which celebrated faces Ralph Fiennes and Guy Pearce play second fiddle to the winsome triumvirate of Jeremy Renner, Anthony Mackie and Brian Geraghty. 

The Hurt Locker offers the most comprehensive vicarious experience of ground combat in the context urban warfare, an achievement that even actual documentaries dealing with the subject will struggle to emulate.

Jeremy Remmer stars as Staff Sergeant William James the replacement leader of an Army Explosive Ordnance Disposal Unit (E.O.D.) whose last commander was killed in action while attempting to disarm a roadside bomb. His teams consists of Sergeant J.T. Sanborn (Anthony Mackie) and Specialist Todd Eldridge (Brian Geraghty) and the team's current tour of duty has 38 days left.

Unfortunately the team's new leader operates in a most unusual manner. Far from the by the book safety first approach that has been the norm in this particular team, William appears to be cocky, reckless, and wildly dismissive of Army protocol involving almost every aspect of their job. Despite William's casual attitude and friendly demeanor, tension quickly develops between the new leader and his team. The team just want to do their job and stay alive whereas William appears to exhibit strong indications that he is a reckless adrenaline junkie. The team quickly becomes concerned that they might not survive the next 38 days with their new commander and despite some eventual mutual respect and team bonding, the tension continues to increase as their tour of duty grinds on. 

 "A Near Perfect Movie!" "A Full-Tilt Action Picture!" "Ferociously Suspenseful!" After I finished watching the film I stood in the lobby and stared at the comments in near disbelief. It's not that I doubted the sincerity of the their comments, I just found it hard to believe these kind of comments could have been made about The Hurt Locker by major U.S. critics. The near unanimous praise for this film left me somewhat bewildered and confused. The reason? The movie is a unusual abandonment of the typical three act movie structure and the motivations and emotions driving the soldiers are well...subtle. The obvious character reveals aren't hammered into the viewer and their development throughout the film aren't particularly dramatic. It's almost like a film calculated to piss off the traditional movie-goer. 

But then perhaps the reason for all the acceptance is that The Hurt Locker is a film full of masterful contrasts. Right out of the gate the initial scenes are shot and acted out in an almost perfect clinical manner. The commander and his team are the perfect safe and by the book team. They take every precaution, they stay in constant communication, and do everything they can to maximize their survival with their success rate. By contrast when their new commander takes over everything looks and feels vastly different. He barges into enemy territory and into danger zones without an apparent concern in the world. He constantly breaks safety protocol and often refuses to communicate to his team as he appears to be in his own world. These initial scenes are also shot very differently as the camera work is much shakier, active, and manic as quick cuts and tight shots suddenly take command.

The characters themselves follow this pattern of contrasts. On the surface they appear to be typical war stock characters. One is the crazy guy who has suppressed emotional issues. One is the hard-nosed by the book commander that does everything he can to keep himself and his men safe and the last is a young kid that is trying his hardest to be a good soldier but is sure that he's going to die every time he goes on a mission. Yet there is so much that is obviously revealed and then at the same time there is so much left unsaid about all of them. We slowly begin to realize that although we know the men by what how the outside world perceives them, just as much we see a lot that makes us question that character model and begin to realize that the men have far deeper emotional and subtle character quirks and faults that combine to create the whole. 

The environment itself is just as full of these conflicting contrasts. Although their jobs are full of incredible danger and death constantly surrounds them, they are still smack in the middle of a city teeming with life and a vibrant people. Many of these people make very obvious attempts to befriend them throughout the movie and many of these actions seem quite genuine. But the enemy that they fight can look like anybody and the paranoia constantly surrounding them becomes increasingly oppressive as it become very difficult to distinguish enemy from a friendly innocent. 

This becomes more complicated due to the odd dynamic created by William and the people that surround him. Not only does he readily accept the people surrounding him as friends, but he also creates an odd air of respect and admiration towards the enemies that built the very bombs he is dismantling. At times this appears to be reciprocated as some of the people watching him who appear to be possibly in control of the bomb mysteriously do not set it off as if wondering if he can accomplish this feat. I say "if" because it's never completely clear if that is what's going on and this ambiguity only helps to heighten the air of confusion and paranoia. 

Shot in an almost documentary-like fashion the film takes no political stances and tends to just appear to want to show us a series of moments that are happening to these soldiers. There are no impassioned speeches and no false moments of inserted drama. Because of this the film flows in a very organic manner with the interactions between the characters and the action that occurs to them to seem very natural and very realistic.

The film, although highly suspenseful, keeps the violence of the action at somewhat of a distance and actively avoids glamorizing the duty of the soldiers. This is in keeping with a new type of soldier being portrayed in this film's war time setting. Far from the "war is hell" or being full of a macho gung-ho type of posturing, these soldiers view their duty as a job. It's a dangerous job to be sure but it's a job similar to many people who are involved in dangerous situations. As a result the character involved view their "jobs" in very different ways in how they feel about it and how they think their goals can best be accomplished. 

The camera work by Kathryn Bigelow is quite amazing and although she makes liberal use of the handicam to give a typical verite feel to the film, the manic cuts, extreme angles, and short sharp zooms keep the whole affair from becoming a confusing jitter-cam mess wherein the director simply shakes the crap out of the steadicam to denote action and convey confusion. Here the action is sharp and in focus and I never felt disoriented although I very much felt in the moment at all times. 

Overall just a great film and one in which the more I thought about it the more I felt I needed to study my feelings and thoughts about the film. I felt I took in a lot during my one viewing but I think it's really going to take repeated viewings to gather in all the feelings I have about how the film is constructed and how the character are defined and whether I'm way off base or I'm only just scratching the surface. Time will tell I suppose.

The Hurt Locker
/ / / July 8, 2009
by Roger Ebert

A lot of movies begin with poetic quotations, but âThe Hurt Lockerâ opens with a statement presented as fact: âWar is a drug.â Not for everyone, of course. Most combat troops want to get it over with and go home. But the hero of this film, Staff Sgt. William James, who has a terrifyingly dangerous job, addresses it like a daily pleasure. Under enemy fire in Iraq, he defuses bombs.
He isnât an action hero, heâs a specialist, like a surgeon who focuses on one part of the body over and over, day after day, until he could continue if the lights went out. James is a man who understands bombs inside out and has an almost psychic understanding of the minds of the bombers. This is all the more remarkable because in certain scenes, it seems fairly certain that the bomb maker is standing in full view â on a balcony or in a window overlooking the street, say, and is as curious about his bomb as James is. Two professionals, working against each other.

Staff Sgt. James is played by Jeremy Renner, who immediately goes on the short list for an Oscar nomination. His performance is not built on complex speeches but on a visceral projection of who this man is and what he feels. He is not a hero in a conventional sense. He cares not for medals. He could no doubt recite patriotic reasons for his service, but does that explain why he compulsively, sometimes recklessly, puts himself in harmâs way? The man before him in this job got himself killed. James seems even cockier.

âThe Hurt Lockerâ is a spellbinding war film by Kathryn Bigelow, a master of stories about men and women who choose to be in physical danger. She cares first about the people, then about the danger. She doesnât leave a lot of room for much else. The man who wrote âwar is a drugâ was Chris Hedges, a war correspondent for the New York Times. Mark Boal, who wrote this screenplay, was embedded with a bomb squad in Baghdad. He also wrote the superb "In the Valley of Elah" (2007), with Tommy Lee Jones as a professional Army man trying to solve the murder of his son who had just returned from Iraq. Also based on fact.

Bigelow and Boal know what theyâre doing. This movie embeds itself in a manâs mind. When itâs over, nothing has been said in so many words, but we have a pretty clear idea of why James needs to defuse bombs. Iâm going to risk putting it this way: (1) bombs need to be defused; (2) nobody does it better than James; (3) he knows exactly how good he is, and (4) when heâs at work, an intensity of focus and exhilaration consumes him, and heâs in that heedless zone when an artist loses track of self and time.

The most important man in his life is Sgt. J.T. Sanborn (Anthony Mackie), head of the support team that accompanies James. Sanborn and his men provide cover fire, scan rooftops and hiding places that might conceal snipers, and assist James into and out of his heavy protective clothing. Sanborn gives him constant audio feedback that James hears inside his helmet. It is Sanborn who has his eye on everything, who is nominally in charge, and not the tunnel-visioned James.

Sanborn is a skilled, responsible professional. He works by the book. He follows protocol. James drives him nuts. Sometimes James seems to almost deliberately invite trouble, and Sanborn believes that by following the procedure, theyâll all have a better chance of going home. He isnât a shirker and he doesnât have weak nerves. Heâs a realist and thinks James is reckless.

Certainly James behaves recklessly at times, even in his use of protective clothing. He takes risks boldly. But in the actual task of defusing a bomb, he is as careful as if he were operating on his own heart. Bigelow uses no phony suspense-generating mechanisms in this film. No false alarms. No gung ho. It is about personalities in terrible danger. The suspense is real, and it is earned. Hitchcock said when thereâs a bomb under a table, and it explodes, thatâs action. When we know the bomb is there, and the people at the table play cards, and it doesnât explode, thatâs suspense.

"The Hurt Locker" is a great film, an intelligent film, a film shot clearly so that we know exactly who everybody is and where they are and what they're doing and why. The camera work is at the service of the story. Bigelow knows that you can't build suspense with shots lasting one or two seconds. And you can't tell a story that way, either -- not one that deals with the mystery of why a man like James seems to depend on risking his life. A leading contender for Academy Awards.

Blowing Up and Loving It

By now most people have heard that The Hurt Locker is an excellent movie. And guess what, it really is.  On my 15 hour plane ride to Taiwan squished like a sardine in an aisle seat on China Airlines I had the opportunity to watch The Hurt Locker and see what all the buzz was about.

The movie takes place in Baghdad where Staff Sergeant William James (Jeremy Renner) joins the Bravo company's bomb disposal unit after they lost their previous leader when a bomb unexpectedly explodes at the wrong time. James is a tough-guy with a devil-may care attitude who gets his kicks putting his life in danger and flying by the seat of his pants.  He is highly skilled and perhaps his lack of fear is what keeps him alive.   He joins Sergeant JT Sanborn(Anthony Mackie) a boy-scout like soldier who follows orders and sticks to the rules and Specialist Owen Eldridge (Brian Geraghty) a younger guy who appears green behind the ears and seems lost at times. As people around them are dying Sanborn and Eldridge begin to question their purpose and chances of survival. 

The movie excels in providing a realistic story that goes beyond the gun-ho "let's get some" war mentality that Hollywood depicts in the typical action movie. It get's you interested in the war time personalities of these three characters by showing both the strengths and weaknesses of the characters on the battlefield and when the action dies down.   

Director Kathryn Bigelow whose previous experience was mostly television proves that a female can in fact lead a male dominated story and hit all the emotional chords that make a movie solid without relying on cliches.  She pulls the most out of several unknown actors and takes incredible risks with the big name guys including Ralph Fiennes and Guy Pierce.  

The movie has an unfiltered look displaying a grittiness that makes you feel like you are watching a live sequence. The tension throughout the film is palpable and with each bomb that gets diffused you never feel comfortable that the next one will turn out as well.  

Renner delivers an understated performance and while it won't launch him to super star status it definitely will earn him an opportunity to keep working.  His character is the most complex on screen.  He enjoys the camaraderie but he maintains distance not forming bonds or relationships with his fellow soldiers. He loves his job and is an artist at what he does. 

The film is successful because it goes beyond a typical war movie caught up in action and delves into the psyche of the soldiers and focuses on the strengths and weaknesses. Like most of us in the real world the characters are both likable and despicable at different times. 

I recommend this film for fans of movies.

This is not one of the best action movie of the year, but it is viscerally exciting, adrenaline-soaked tour de force of suspense and surprise, full of explosions and hectic scenes of combat.

A three-man crew whose specialty is EOD, or Explosive Ordinance Disposal. For those of us not in the military, theyâre the bomb squad. Their daily routine is much like that of a firefighter, extremely dangerous situations are going to call, and itâs a question of when, not if. Sgt. William James (Jeremy Renner) is the team leader, who seems to insist on doing things the hard way. It so happens that The Hurt Locker takes place in Iraq. But geography is almost beside the point. What makes the film so essential is its pinpoint accuracy in mapping the disorienting roads a man can walk down when his job keeps him so close to death, working for what sometimes feels like a distant principle. Is Sgt. James the reckless hothead he appears to be? Or is he really that good? Whenever he shares details of his personal life, Sgt. James doesnât appear to be the perfect soldier, much less the perfect person. But he continues to dive head-first into the worst situations imaginable, and gets the job done while his crew swears theyâve dodged another bullet.

Screenwriter Mark Boal and director Kathryn Bigelow have made a unique film about war. Other movies have looked and felt the way this one does - hot, suspenseful, as if something could go wrong at any moment. But The Hurt Locker' suppresses the politics of war, particularly this war where the politics always seem to hover, unstable, in the ether. It focuses, instead, on men who exist in combatâs shadow. The bomb squad arrives on the scene in the grace period before daily calm becomes deadly chaos. Troops hang back. Iraqi civilians hide. The bomb squad waxes poetic. Director Bigelow, whose body of work including 'Point Break', 'Blue Steel', 'Strange Days' and 'K-19: The Widowmaker', has been uneven but never uninteresting, has an almost uncanny understanding of the circuitry that connects eyes, ears, nerves and brain. She is one of the few directors for whom action-movie-making and the cinema of ideas are synonymous. You may emerge from 'The Hurt Locker' shaken, exhilarated and drained, but you will also be thinking.

The movie finds unexpected ways to express empathy and sensitivity. Rather than trace the path a bullet takes to its human target, it manages not to glorify war. "The Hurt Locker" works extremely well on two fronts. As a thriller, it packs the most generous servings of nerve-wracking suspense I've seen in a war movie, or most any other movie, for that matter. The uncertain anticipation that precedes before each bomb disarmament scene is sure to keep you at a heightened alertness. And as an expository piece, it brilliantly shows a side of the Iraq War not commonly explored in previous films of the sub-genre. It puts us to the frontline, showing us the different facets of soldiers constantly aware of their mortality. Unlike most Iraq War- themed movies that try too hard to delve into the politics and morality of warfare, often in the perspective of non-combative generals or influential politicians, "The Hurt Locker" is all about the how people cope with the knowledge of an almost certain death. Fueled by strong lead performances, tight direction, and convincing recreations of war zones, "The Hurt Locker" presents us one of cinema's rawest and most human depictions of war ever.

Booze Revooze: A Drinker's Skewed View of THE HURT LOCKER

The Hurt Locker is intense from the instant the curtain rises. The first scene primes you with energy thats explosive for the duration. Magnificently directed by Kathryn Bigelow, the movie never really sinks into those War Is Hell clichés, at least not very often, and also stays away from the politics of the Iraq conflict. The acting is as realistic as the action, so i guess the only thing that really left a bad taste in my mouth was a lack of direction.

You know how you go to the bar and drink until something happens cause if you drink long enough something surely will? Not here. The flick begins full throttle so has nowhere to go from there and i eventually got bored of the bomb disarming scenes. If thats the storys point, that war is repetitive, the characters should have been more blasé than they were at the the end.

When all is said and done, despite this solitary dud, Kathryn Bigelows obvious talent as a director makes The Hurt Locker a blast.

A quote comes up at the beginning that 'war is a drug' and soon we're shown an EOD soldier who is high as a kite. SSgt. William James is an adrenaline junkie who takes unnecessary risks that endanger himself and fellow soldiers, namely Specialist Eldridge and Sgt. Sanborn. While James and his recklessness are the focus of the movie, we get these sidetracks that (with the exception of one) go absolutely nowhere leading one to ask, "What the hell was the point of this?" You wonder if the writers forgot to finish parts of the script and never got around to doing so. One irritating subplot involves a local boy who hangs around Camp Victory where James and the rest of the EOD squad stays. He's called Beckham because of his love for soccer. His body is later found in a building filled with explosives, and just when James shows an inkling of consideration and respect as he covers the body up, we're reminded what a jackass he is. "Ha! Fooled ya! Shame on you for beginning to like James, nyah nyah." - Kathryn Bigelow 

One scene I found offensive was when a colonel (James Morse) is shown gleefully allowing a wounded Iraqi insurgent to bleed to death. Equally absurd is the base therapist counseling Specialist Eldridge with the line, "War can be fun!" I refuse to believe that any soldier, experienced or not, would say that. It is beyond the pale. I knew when director Kathryn Bigelow was popping up all over TV right before this movie's release, crowing in a robotic fashion that it is 'apolitical' and does not preach in any way that it meant there would be some form of that. Mind you, The Hurt Locker is no left wing lecture fest such as Lions for Lambs or Redacted (Movie Makers Are from Mars, Movie Watchers Are from Venus...or Neptune) but there are speckles here and there of that, a little line or two that satisfies the liberal hacks in the smoke filled writing room while they say this movie isn't political with a straight face. 

In another scene, James is on the way by foot to disarm an IED on a road. A man in a taxi runs the roadblock and stops inches from James as he points a 9mm pistol at the guy. The driver backs off after hesitating for a minute, then is pulled out of his car by the other soldiers. "If he wasn't an insurgent before, he sure is now," James quips. Oh, Hollyweird. How you love to be clever. -_- Pricks.

The problem with the Hurt locker is that it is crammed full of Cliches and isn't fresh at all.
Firstly in the Hurt locker you have the standard format for a War Movie. Cliche 1. An independent minded solider is drafted in to replace a well liked member of a team  this solider then is very reckless but goes on to earn respect as a true American HE-R0!
Cliche 2. There is the obligatory solider with the difficult relationship at home and then the phone call in which he rings she answers and he puts the phone down without saying a word.
There are others but I wouldn't want to give too much of the movie away, another thing I didn't like about the movie was its style and the way it was shot.
I understand from IMDB that is was all shot in the middle east using Iraqi extras, well this may be so but it did look (particularly the UN Bomb scene) that it was filmed in the US.
My main problem with the film is however is that the plot is very repetitive once your have seen the team defuse a bomb 5 times then really what is there to keep you watching, I got the feeling of same old,same old and I was wondering if something more interesting was going to happen.
I think this feeling is partly due to the supposed documentary style it was shot in, well as I stated earlier it is shot in a too sanitized way to feel gritty hand true to the conditions in Iraq.
In summary this is a independent movie that makes a mainstream point, it is entertaining but contains old war movie elements that will please many but didn't impress me.

The difference between a great action movie like The Hurt Locker and a poor one like Wolverine lies in director Kathryn Bigelow's understanding that watching stuff blow up is not nearly as tense as waiting for it to blow up, an old Hitchcock mantra. Throughout this movie, Staff Sergeant William James and his crew identify and attempt to diffuse bombs, creating a movie that never lets the audience relax. In scenes back at the base, we see the emotional toll these missions have on the soldiers and that their mental state is just as endangered as their physical being. In removing politics from the film's point of view, Bigelow gives a matter of fact version of the life of an American soldier in Iraq. Kathryn Bigelow does not care what you think.

She is not interested in your flag-waving git-r-done jingoism, and she is not interested in your left-wing apologist psychobabble. What Kathryn Bigelow is interested in is delivering one of the greatest war films ever made. And with The Hurt Locker, she has succeeded.

Most people agree that World War II was the apex of American heroism. At no other time in human history has the USA been held in such high esteem by its allies. As such, films depicting American deployment, combat, and experience in Nazi-occupied France all have the saccharine, yet historically accurate, undercurrent of unshakable bravery amongst its American protagonists.

Thirty years later, America was embroiled in the Vietnam War, a warped return to the battlefield that seemed to turn World War II's noble conquest of evil inside out. Clean-cut PFC Johnny from Iowa City didn't want to serve his country and make it home to his young wife anymore; he wanted to make Charlie bleed and get laid and smoke his painful memories of home away. Americans, just a generation removed from their collective identity as the world's saviors, were killing innocent people, killing women, killing children, killing their own college students in Ohio. As before, the American public educated itself of its country's servicemen through Hollywood, but now, the images were darker, bleaker, angrier. The Thousand-Yard Stare of Colonel Nicholson's heroic lads gave way to Travis Bickle's sociopathic monologue in front of his mirror.

Today, the world--with America invariably entrenched within it--is at war once more. And, as before, the mood has shifted with the passage of time. The recurring theme of the Iraq War, begun in March 2003, is the ebb and flow of emotion and trust. The physical threat to the American soldier is greater than ever--there is no gentleman's agreement between combatants on the battlefield--and the downtime is more customizable than ever. GIs can have protein powder shipped to their bunks, play Xbox 360 off-shift, call their wives at any time. There is no particular routine or arrangement or schedule to military life in the Middle East. And with this new purgatory of the constant switch between duty and simple self-preservation has arisen a new kind of soldier, a new kind of man.

That man is Staff Sergeant William James, our rapscallion hero in The Hurt Locker. He is not charming, he is not particularly handsome, he does not have a snaketongued quip always at the ready. He is a dude, a dude who drinks and swears and defuses bombs, because it's all he's got, dude man. James has a wife and son thousands of miles away, but we do not care about them, because he does not care about them. The compound simplicity and gripping terror that comprise James' life in Iraq also comprise our film experience. The Hurt Locker has two settings: on and off. Movies do not work this way. But this one does, and flawlessly.

The plot of The Hurt Locker revolves around the aforementioned Staff Sergeant James (Jeremy Renner) and his three-man Explosive Ordinance Disposal (EOD) unit during their final 30 days in the stir. James has only just arrived to the unit, and his unorthodox and extremely dangerous style immediately puts him at odds with his two subordinates, Sergeant Sanborn (Anthony Mackie) and the increasingly distraught Specialist Eldridge (Brian Geraghty).

There are more than three people in this film, but you will not be blamed if you only pay attention to Renner. It is difficult to imagine a performance more challenging than one which requires the actor to convey complete sincerity in his boredom and angst. We rightfully praise actors who take on the "difficult" roles--Harvey Milk, Idi Amin, Andrew Beckett--but Renner's task is equally as tall, for nothing--not a covertly wired stash of six IEDs, not a stone-faced suicide bomber, not an unseen sniper--fazes him. Not because he is a one dimensional action hero, like Rambo or the Terminator, but because he is caught somewhere between apathy and insanity. Maybe he doesn't care if he lives or dies; maybe he is just as frightened as Eldridge. He simply has his game face on at all times because he can't afford to remove it, and even if he could, it's likely he's forgotten how to do so. It's truly a brilliant, understated performance that cannot receive enough praise.

The Hurt Locker would be nothing without its sensory accomplishments. You can include all the expository dialogue and giggling drunken bromance you want, but if you make a movie about defusing homemade bombs and you can't pull off a credible explosion, well, you have yourself a worthless film. Fortunately, director Bigelow and English cinematographer Barry Ackroyd beautifully present a dusty land of mistrust and danger. In an filmmaking era in which the mantra seems increasingly to be "make it grittier," Bigelow and Ackroyd have done a simply masterful job of balancing the heat, sand, and wind with the audience's need to actually see what is taking place on screen.

Do not be confused: The Hurt Locker can stand shoulder to shoulder with the grittiest of films. But it doesn't do so at the expense of its stark, exceptional imagery. It won't make you want to visit Baghdad anytime soon, but the photography is beautiful nonetheless. Ackroyd is on an impressive streak, having helmed cinematography duties on the Oscar-nominated United 93 and the Irish independent film The Wind that Shakes the Barley, which won the Palme d'Or at the 2006 Cannes Film Festival. Though Bigelow employs a Canon Phantom HD for the film's handful of slow-motion shots, the bulk of The Hurt Locker was shot on 16 mm Fuji Eterna 250D film stock, which was popular about 25 years ago, through Aaton A-Minima cameras--also about a quarter-century past their peak usage. This unheralded choice of equipment makes a huge difference; the film is crisp and frenetic, like so many modern nailbiters shot on video, but still looks like it belongs on a 30-foot screen.

The lasting image of The Hurt Locker, perhaps, is that of James' bomb disposal suit; it is enormous, bulky, hot, and green; it requires three men just to suit James up; when the camera is inside it, you can hear James breathing heavily, struggling to take his next lumbering step. There is nothing manly or enviable about this suit. Your son will not want an action figure of this suit. Much like that suit is the war which necessitates its use. The camera flits over dead-eyed locals weary of the American occupation of their home and over Eldridge's panicked face as he desperately tries to clean blood off of his rifle's bullets so that he can reload in the middle of a firefight. The Hurt Locker is not a depiction of heroism or cowardice, of nobility or shame. It does not ask its audience to reevaluate its reception of the American military's presence in Iraq. It offers no one dimensional characterizations of villains or champions of justice. It simply invites us to witness and experience the harrowing, exhausting, terrifying, yet encompassingly simple existence of the new American soldier. And that experience just so happens to be one of the greatest films you will ever see.
