I strongly suspect that this film lacks the authenticity it purports to display.  It is easy to portray the chaos ,the suffering and the tensions of war in film.  It takes skill to make a path through the confusion and give it a cohesive storyline, where the penny drops and we are left, not *only* appalled and shocked by the horror, but also appreciative of the other aspects of a soldier's life, the smaller details, the quieter moments, the character developments, which are part of the skillful storytelling and film making that give a film a sense of journey.  On the first point The Hurt Locker makes about par, on the second point it fails.  There are several key ingredients missing that lead to it's disappointing attempt at realism, from my personal perceptions and expectations anyway.  

From a military point of view, there appears to have been little attention given to the non-visual aspects (I mean the things other than equipment and uniforms). The relational dynamics between the characters and different units is just not there, here's why:  

In the military there are very structured levels of accountability and a chain of command, whereas these boys just seem to be three independent "soldiers" that have no accountability to a command structure, no contact with peers in the same profession to mingle with on base, and just go about as they please.  There is no-one overseeing and coordinating their activities at all.  They get a call out, do their job, and then make random "trips" around unknown parts of Iraq for reasons that make no sense to us, because the director has not told us why they are there (unless I missed something).  All things seem to be on the shoulders of Renner's character, and he is apparently not accountable to an officer hierarchy or a unit of which his three man squad is part (a significant failure in the film).  There were no briefings or debriefings by planning staff, which is the norm in the kind of operations soldiers perform.  There is no reference to Standard Operating Procedures, but rather individual bravado is "on call" to create the tension and excitement.  There are certain situations that these boys found themselves in that I doubt would have been the case for the EOD boys in Iraq.  The lines of accountability and command would have prevented these fellas from doing their reckless little unauthorized "missions" that Renner initiated spontaneously several times.

Ralph Fiennes' character and his band were an interesting lot, out there in the desert (why was the EOD (Explosive Ordinance Disposal) squad out there again?).  These guys were either British SAS or perhaps some kind of bounty-hunter mercenaries, but I did get the impression that perhaps they would have better suited being on a putting green at St Andrews Golf Course in Scotland, such gentlemen were they (certainly not from Liverpool or Glasgow evidently), and so incompetent with the powerful .50 sniper rifle in their possession they were also.  And yet these American  EOD boys, with no sniper training, and probably none on the Barrett, somehow manage to be natural snipers too, hitting targets in excess of 800m when the Brits failed(!)- is there nothing these cool US Army EOD boys cannot do?? (This scene was a pretty nasty slight on the British- they produce some hardcore soldiers in reality I understand, Fiennes' band were absolutely soft and very "unheroic", unlike the Americans).

Anyhow, I could go on even longer about this, but will refrain.  In short, I thought that Guy Pierce's character at the beginning was the most likable in the film, his crudity being pretty normal for males in all male work places, especially rougher ones.  The Afro bloke, Anthony Mackie, did very well also.  I liked the brief ironic scene in the breakfast cereal isle of the supermarket back in the US.  On the whole I felt that The Hurt Locker was more an MTV version of the war in Iraq than anything else, and it doesn't compare with the great war films out there, such as The Thin Red Line, etc, etc.

It's a tough trick to make a war movie that portrays its soldiers heroically without turning them into cardboard cutouts, but "The Hurt Locker" pulls it off extremely well.  Eschewing facile commentary on the political aspects of the Iraq War, it focuses instead on the day-to-day challenges facing an anti-insurgent bomb disposal squad in Baghdad, and the psychological toll their harrowing duties take on them, presenting both in a way that humanizes its subjects even as it lionizes them.  The performances are excellent (Renner is particularly good as a brilliant but reckless bomb disposal technician addicted to the adrenaline rush of saving innocent lives at the risk of his own), and the gritty, shaky-cam cinematography is perfect for the material.  This is a tense white-knuckle thriller as well as an outstanding piece of gritty, realistic war film-making, and worthy of its reputation as the first really good movie about the Iraq War.

So, I've been putting off reviewing this one for a while. I needed to reflect a little bit on it because I'm pretty sure this will win best pic at the Oscars despite my thoughts about it. Now before I start rambling I'd like to debunk the one reason that people have complaints about: I did not feel that the film was racist at all and any part that seemed racist was merely a tool of the director's. I was starting to feel that there was something wrong with my perception, something I was missing because the acclaim is pretty much unanomous, but after a bit of reflection and discussions with my friends, whom liked the movie, I realize that though this movie is entertaining enough, it lacks a plot. Absolutely nothing happens with the characters in this seemingly character-driven story. We learn one thing about the protagonist and one thing only: He's addicted to war, whether he get his rush from diffusing bombs or carelessly chasing a terrorist. The makers of this movie trick us into thinking this man is complex especially in certain parts of the movie where he starts to make-up reasons to do things the hard way. We are supposed to be debating whether or not this man is a hero, and i suppose he would be a hero by proxy. He doesn't care about his team, which he endangers on multiple occasions and anytime he saves lives, it isn't intentional. He just loves bombs. The best thing about the Hurt Locker is the suspense and it's not hard to realize why he loves the danger but it's a double-edged blade, for the replay value of the film is null. The second time someone watches this, he or she will not be drawn in by the thrills because he or she knows that nothing is going to happen. No one gets blown up (unexpectedly, that is, which was another problem) and ultimately nothing is resolved. Now, the major determining factor for my rating is hardest part. Do I rate according to how much I enjoyed the movie in the first place, or is the movie actually great in that it got me thinking and analyzing it? Well, I think that since there's no replay value it can't get more than a six added with the lack of plot and development it'd be a two, but the acting, the suspense, and the conversations to be had after the movie is over earn this a five. Now go make Point Break 2!

US Army Sergeant First Class Will James, Sergeant JT Sanborn and Specialist Owen Eldridge comprise the Bravo Company's bomb disposal unit currently stationed in Baghdad. James is the tech team leader. When James arrives on the scene, Bravo Company has thirty-nine days left on its current deployment. It will be a long thirty-nine days for Sanborn and Eldridge whose styles do not mesh with their new leader. James is a renegade for who the thrill of the dismantlement seems to be the ultimate goal regardless of the safety of his fellow team members, others on the scene or himself. On the other hand, Sanborn is by the books: he knows his place and duty and trusts others in the army to carry out theirs as well as he. And Eldridge is an insecure soldier who is constantly worried that an error or misjudgment on his part will lead to the death of an innocent civilian or a military colleague. While the three members face their own internal issues, they have to be aware of any person at the bomb sites, some of who may be bombers themselves.

Kathryn Bigelow (Point Break & Strange Days) directs "The Hurt Locker" and delivers without a doubt this year's most intense and riveting film. From the opening shot to the final frame, the viewer is absolutely capitivated and on the edge of their seat, holding on with very little time to relax or ease the dramatic tension within "The Hurt Locker." Bigelow perfectly presents a realistic and eye opening portrayal of the deadly day-to-day work of a EOD (Explosive Ordnance Disposal) team in Iraq.

Not only is Bigelow's direction flawless, the performances throughout "The Hurt Locker" go unsurpassed. Jeremy Renner is breathtaking as Staff Sergeant William James. His portrayal of a over-the-edge bomb defuser is stunning and his delivery of James's psychological and emotional strain from the war and the years of defusing bombs is Award worthy (Renner actaully won the Independent Spirit Award for Best Male Lead in 2009 for "The Hurt Locker"). Anthony Mackie is also exceptional as Sergeant JT Sanborn, a subordinate of Staff Sergeant William James on the EOD team in Iraq. Mackie also won a Spirit Award for his performance in "The Hurt Locker" and his Best Supporting Male Actor Award was very well deserved. Mackie's performance hinges on his ability to learn and control his new Staff Sergeant and he pulls of the portrayal with hypnotizing precision.

The entire supporting cast of "The Hurt Locker" combine for a stunning cinematic experience. Brian Geraghty plays Specialist Owen Eldridge and powerfully presents a soldier that most Americans can easily connect with, one who is timid and afraid, but does the best he can under the intense conflict he is submersed within. Ralph Fiennes, Guy Pierce and David Morse all provide a small highlights in their minor characters in the 131 minute film.

Mark Boal's fantastic script puts the viewer directly into the emotions and action of the soldiers during the current Iraq War. The film quickly sets a frantic tone that comes with the deadly mission of defusing bombs that could be anywhere, ultimately only giving the viewer brief moments that are not as explosive. Boal was actually embedded with a EOD team in Iraq, which became the source of the screenplay and film. There is no doubt that "The Hurt Locker" takes the viewer places previous war film's have not. "The Hurt Locker" delivers a substantial punch of reality, illustrating the experiences of the soldiers and when you are done watching it, you most definately feel like you've been in war.

One of the best war movies I've seen, and the very best when it comes to a realistic depiction of war from the soldier's point-of-view--we share their limited perspective and only have a vague sense of what's going on, which creates some excruciating suspense and an exceptionally effective sense of chaos. When they pick off the enemy (always depicted as The Other, nameless and faceless), we mostly just feel the relief of tension that the characters must be experiencing--and then we begin to analyze our own response. This narrowing of the dramatic focus also effectively avoids dealing with the political issues--this isn't a film about whether the Iraq war is good or bad, it's a movie about the experience of war, and what it does to people, and it draws its strength from this universality, even as it focuses more on the specifics of life in combat and the physical devastation of war than just about any movie I've seen. The characters are well developed and very believable (kudos to the writing, the direction, and performances), and successfully sidestep obvious war movie stereotypes, and it's interesting the way in which our emotional investment in the characters subtly develops and shifts throughout the film. It's a kind of exhausting experience, but it's more than worthwhile--this is a movie I'd probably show to my kid if they were ever thinking of entering the military, not necessarily to scare them out of it (though that would certainly be one of my main goals), but to give a sense of what they might be getting into.

It's quite a good film in terms of cinematography, dialogue, gritty realism (I'm assuming), but my viewing experience was slightly jarred by my preconceived notion that a war film should say something. At first, I wondered if the film is pro-war or anti-war, pro-instinctual bravado or anti-, pro-demonizing an enemy or anti-, et cetera, but halfway through, I made peace with the fact that the movie doesn't address any of these issues. Every character is at times heroic and douchey; we're not supposed to "root" for any one person. However, the end - namely the soundtrack (I know, really ridiculous detail to gripe over) - reveals the movie's point. War is an addiction like any other; but while intellectual bravery, instinctual bravado, the work that gets you through the day are honorable addictions, is any addiction at all something to glorify? I think it odd that the movie celebrates James' addiction by underscoring his return to the arena with this rousing rock song, more befitting of the flashy cool of G.I. Joe, rather than the respectful ambience that this movie previously exhibited. Now, I've been told that the song underscores James' point of view - his pride at committing again - and I could buy that, if the film wasn't so even-handed with all the characters that I didn't see any one character as the main character, thus finding it problematic to adapt to his point of view just at the end and not throughout.

Theres been a lot of griping about how movies based on our current wars have been mediocre at best. Vietnam cranked out the murderers row of Platoon, Apocalypse Now, The Deer Hunter, Full Metal Jacket, and Born on the Fourth of July. Iraq brought us trash like Jarhead, In the Valley of Elah, and Stoploss. There are two reasons for this. One is enough time passed between the war ending and the movies coming out , so the filmmakers knew why we were in Vietnam. Which is, of course, to do drugs and sleep with prostitutes. The new crop of war movies cant even figure out what the soundtrack to the Middle East should be whereas whenever I hear the Doors or CCR I get flashbacks to Nam.

Second is we had the semi-egalitarianism of the draft so an educated writer like Oliver Stone could find himself in combat and return with stories to tell. Now the military is voluntary which means its only made up of people with no other options. I know life is the best schooling, but without the indoctrination of an education your first instinct after a traumatic experience isnt to write about it.

So  a movie like The Hurt Locker might be were the best were going to do with the war in Iraq. Like the disappointing miniseries, Generation Kill, the script was written by a journalist who spent time following the troops in Iraq. Mark Boal  shadowed bomb squads and recreated their intense experiences. But its more journalistic then cinematic. You get a strong feel for the migraine inducing tension youd feel in combat, but the characters are cyphers. Part of it might be because actors youve never heard of play the main parts. This gives it a bizarre documentary feel except when stars like Guy Pearce, Ralph Fiennes, and Kate from Lost have tiny cameos. It isnt until the end of the flick that you realize who the main character is or the moral of his story.

But then it comes together and you realize Boal came up with a decent hypothesis for what this war is all about and how anyone could enlist for such a meaningless war. Its a chance for soldiers to live out their first person shooter video game fantasies.

War is hell. War is a world of shit. War is our apocalypse (now). War is peace backwards. We get it. We know what war effuses; it inhabits our daily livescourtesy of the media. The Hurt Lockers beauty is that it is not a preachy piece of anti-militant mumbo jumbo. It wants to dramatize war, not chastise it. The Iraq and Afghanistan war has been a fertile subject for intriguing cinema experiments. You have Charles Fergusons No End in Sight (2007) and Sam Mendess Jarhead (2005) which attempted to give war a slower pace and how the lack of battle in a soldiers life is actually emotionally harmful to them. That film worked. This film works even more because of how it is broken down and told. With a premise that revolves around bomb detonation, The Hurt Locker indeed had a big advantage over its predecessors in creating a strong-effective action flick.
	It kills me to classify this film as an action piece, because when we look at action films, we picture Transformers: Revenge of the Fallen or G.I. Joe: The Rise of Cobra. I suppose The Hurt Locker is locked and loaded with the explosions and gun fire, but the effect is more profound and the direction is more exquisite. Kathryn Bigelow, considered to be the oxymoronic director of war films, proves shes got it in her to make our hearts race and feel as if we are on the battlefield (a sensation we need to experience since it is happening to so many of the Canadian and American youth nowadays). The film follows mainly three brothers-in-arms (they arent really nice to each other and they fight a whole bunch, but isnt that what brothers do?): Staff Sergeant William James (Renner), Sergeant JT Sanborn (a convincing Mackie) and Specialist Owen Eldridge (Geraghty). It is important that Bigelow makes them all unique individuals with separate purposes on the battlefieldthey are not just write-offs of each other.
	When in action, the films scenes are not inundated with inane pounding music or tedious drum beats. Bigelow plays her soundtrack always at the perfect moment and lets our palpitating heartbeats do the rest of the work. Most scenes are well-built and unpredictable, mostly because the things we expect to happen (the cliché things) usually dont. Bigelow also has a minor undertone of what other war films have delivered: soldiers losing their wits and how tedious war can be. For example, Sanborn and Eldridge discuss blowing up one of their comrades because they dont like his attitude and the squad has to lie down for several hours, in furnace-burning heat, watching a sniper tower to make sure they have eliminated every single insurgent. Bigelow, most importantly, doesnt linearly state that war is this hell or a place that messes with you, but that war is wara dish best served cold. 
	The film, of course, isnt immaculate (otherwise, itd be in four-star range). Though thematically Bigelow is essentially flawless, her plot feels uncomfortably familiar. The Hurt Locker paces out in checkpoints36 days till the company is dismissed and it counts down from there. We do feel an anxietyhoping the squad will arrive home safely, but ultimately, the ending result slaps on what was once a well-coiled rifle, into a somewhat jammed one. Fortunately, the conclusion of the film does relate to Bigelows thesis: war is a drugno matter how much you want to get away from it, in the end, you always need it.
	Therefore, The Hurt Locker definitely branches off from the typical war movie. Most of the scenarios deliver the dramatic tension you require and the acting is top notch. A final scenario at the end shows the squad having to tell an Iraqi that they cannot disable the bomb that is attached to him. It shows an interesting parallel: soldiers telling an innocent foreigner that he is going to die and (this being at the home front) the man in the taxi cab telling the mother of a twenty year-old son that her boy is KIA. Its unfair and its painful. It hurts. But it is something that we are locked init is a hurt locker.

Even though it's far superior to any other species on the planet (as far as we know), the human brain has always been riddled with its fair share of weaknesses and shortcomings. Even those with tremendous resolve and discipline have fallen prey to the demons of the mind: more specifically, addiction. Everyone either has or had an addiction, be they very mild or incredibly severe.

But what if a something as awful and dangerous as war could be addictive? A drug personified by the constant need to get an adrenaline fix by way of killing enemy combatants? That very conundrum drives Kathryn Bigelow's masterful and emotionally intense "The Hurt Locker", one of the latest films to cover the current wars in the Middle East, but probably the first to actually delve into the psychological frames of mind our troops certainly may be in.

Set in 2004 Baghdad, two members of an Explosive Ordnance Disposal (EOD) unit, Spec. Owen Eldridge (Brian Geraghty) and Sgt. JT Sanborn (Anthony Mackie), have recently lost their leader (Guy Pearce) after he was killed by a remote-controlled IED. Soon enough, his replacement comes in the form of Sgt. First Class William James (Jeremy Renner), a decorated bomb disposal expert with nearly 900 defused bombs under his belt. The problem for Sanborn and Eldridge, however, is that James is a cocksure risktaker who, while highly proficient at his job, performs using unnecessarily dangerous methods. In a dangerous battlezone where insurgents and bombs are anywhere and everywhere, such tactics cause friction between James and his subordinates, with tension and stress building up with every bomb and every firefight.

Unlike previous films about the Iraq War, Bigelow throws politics out the window, instead focusing on the mindsets of these three men going from one precarious situation to another, and how the stress of war slowly but surely cracks away one's sanity, piece by piece.

Rather than the conventional war movie formula where we learn at length about the soldiers' families and home lives, "The Hurt Locker" mainly focuses on the "now": the movie is more like a series of vignettes, rather than a straightforward narrative. Almost every scene is wrought with extreme tension. You can almost literally feel the panic, fear, and adrenaline rush these men experience while under the pressure of not only defusing a bomb (timer or not), but also the threat of Iraqi insurgents hiding in plain sight, ready to strike. And all these scenes run the full gamut of possible outcomes: when it's clearly too late to defuse an IED, especially when civilian lives are at stake, the results are utterly heartbreaking.

Despite the war genre being dominated by men in the past, Bigelow ("Point Break") is no small potatoes when it comes to crafting an emotional, intense, action-packed, and thrilling film experience. Every frame reeks of authenticity, from the production design (Jordan stood in for Iraq for filming), cinematography (the kudos going to Barry Ackroyd for a gritty, realistic, "you are there" element), a solid screenplay by Mark Boal, and manic, heart-pounding editing.

But all of that wouldn't click if it weren't for the fabulous onscreen talent. Mackie and Geraghty are completely convincing as two soldiers reaching their own breaking points in an everyday life-or-death scenario. But it's Renner who steals the show. Calm, steely, with a hint of unpredictability in his eyes, William is portrayed as a man who works on instinct rather than protocol, and it's obvious to the audience that war is more than a mere profession to him: it's becoming an addiction. It's a fascinating, award-worthy performance by Renner that personifies the emotional core of the film.

Far superior to those war films that choose to blindly celebrate hyper-macho attitudes rather than analyze them, "The Hurt Locker" is a one-of-a-kind experience that eschews political discourse and instead focuses on the human side of war. Do not miss this movie.

Its gotta have been two years since I last went to LSC. For those not in the know, LSC stands for Lecture Series Committee. Its a student group that, among other things shows movies on campus. I think the last one I went to was Shooter. They showed Annie Hall a few weeks ago (which is on the AFI list) and I was so pissed that I found out a day too late. There are few other places where admission, a small Sprite, and a bag of Twizzlers only costs you 5.75 Makes it worth dealing with the uncomfortable seats. Back in the day, when I lived in a dorm two buildings over from the screening room, it was not uncommon for me to come in pj's and slippers, with a blanket to snuggle in and a pillow to sit on. Although this time, besides the unpleasantness of the seat, there was this creepy old man who sad down right next to me. Seriously, people, movie theater etiquette. If there's plenty of seats, always leave at least a one seat buffer between you and the stranger beside you. I was scared he was gonna start asking me for my number, saying that the back of my head is ridiculous. 

Now Im in an Athena cluster, waiting for a buddy, typing up this review that I expected would hafta wait til morning. And I really like this keyboard. The keys are really bouncy. Moving on.

Normally, I dont particularly care for war films. In principle, I dont necessarily have a problem with war. I just dont care to pay attention to politics (we're not gonna have the why argument about that now), and these types of movies tend to be uber politcally preachy. Im not informed enough (by choice) to take a stand on one side or the other, but the one thing I damn well know for sure is that I am completely behind our troops themselves. I feel that reguardless of your politics, every American should be able to say that. But lately, something is just drawing me to these films. With Brothers this afternoon and The Messenger last week Im really rackin' them up. And I've been dying to get my hands on Stop-loss, but haven't had any luck. I was actually looking foward to this one all week, since I'd heard so many good things. It made me a little sad that I didnt go last night as originally planned, but I think Bob Saget was a worthy replacement. 

I def enjoyed the film, but I think it mighta been built up too much. I've heard a lot of best picture talk, and while I'd support the nod, I dont know that I'd support a win. There wasn't much story (and we've been over this many times, I like narrative), which made the scenes feel a bit disconnected from each other. However, individually each one of those scenes was fantastic. So the movie centers around a bomb squad team in the army, which means that most of the scenes are these really intense and nerve wracking things where the dude's trying to diffuse a bomb. Needless to say, edge of my seat the whole time.

Great characters, as well. Man guy, Sg james, was played by Jeremy Renner. If your knowledge of the Buffyverse is comparable to mine, you'll know him as Angel's sire Penn. He was a good combination of reckless, badass, and admirable soldier. Although his obligatory big self revelatory breakthrough wasn't quite as epic as they tend to be in these films. Yes, Im actually disappointed in the lack of a cliche. The one I really felt for was Spc Eldridge played by Brian Geraghty. I spent the whole movie trying to figure out where I knew him from. Something told me Jarhead, which IMDB confirmed, but I dont specifically remember him there. He also looked a bit like Corey Feldman in Stand By me, which may have been what threw me. He was the more, for lack of a better word, sensitive soldier. He's really the one I held my breath for whenever they were in a tight spot. Also brief appearances by Guy Pearce, Evangeline Lilly, David Morse (who I so didnt recognize), and Christian Camargo (Dexter's big "ice truck killer" bro), and Ralph Fiennes.

The film was shot documentary style, which was a nice touch (added another level of realism) but there was a lot of shakey cameras. Not quite Blair Witch level of shakey, but enough to annoy my headache-y head. Very happy I did get to see this well before Oscar season, so now I know what all that buzz is about. We'll see what its competition looks like over the next few months

The Hurt Locker is not only one of the best movies of 2009, it is one of the best movies of the decade, and easily one of the greatest war movies of all-time.

The reason that the movie works and is so good is because of how authentic it is.  Not only are the performances entrancing, but the direction, cinematography, and sound editing are all just as amazing.  Director Kathryn Bigelow (ex-wife of James Cameron, can't wait to see which one wins the Oscar) uses camera angles to induce even more tension in scenes where death could be right around the corner.  We as the audience are unaware of where our focus should be and because of this certain scenes become even more nerve-racking. 

Along with the amazing direction come two standout performances from Jeremy Renner and Anthony Mackie. Renner plays the new bomb squad sergeant in charge of Mackie and Specialist Owen Eldridge played by Brian Geraghty.  The team's main job is to report to hazardous areas that are believed to have bombs near by and disarm these bombs.  Renner plays his role with a toughness that a man in his position needs to have.  However, his character who is also an adrenaline junky has a cocky attitude to him that Renner also portrays beautifully.  Mackie's character on the other hand is much more controlled and likes to go by the book.  He doesn't like Renner's cocky attitude, but in a way he is also jealous of it.  He wishes he could be in Renner's position, but unlike Renner he is afraid to die.  

Both Mackie and Renner play roles deserving of many accolades, but there are also great supporting roles from the aforementioned Geraghty, Guy Pearce, Ralph Fiennes, David Morse, and Christian Camargo.  Each character adds something new to the story.

The Hurt Locker does something that no other movie has been able to do.  It portrays the Iraq War in the most real way and shows just how hard it is to be an American soldier.   After watching this movie I have a much better idea of what it's like over there everyday and my respect for the men and women who are a serving our country only increased after seeing this outstanding film.

With a more sedate and thoughtful tone than in any other war film I've seen, 'The Hurt Locker' is less a source of entertainment than a sobering look at how nerve-wracking daily life in a war zone can be.

The Hurt Locker is both a portrait of a man, and a suspenseful exposé on the daily reality for EOD's - the teams of soldiers who diffuse roadside bombs, one of the most deadly elements of the war. The film has both superb acting and excellent camera work. It succeeds at both a visceral portrayal of Iraq, and a though provoking mental probe into the kind of disconnection EOD's need to work calmly while under the most amount of pressure imaginable--tinkering with things designed to kill them. 

I can't help but feel that when people refer to The Hurt Locker as a war movie, an action movie, or a movie about bravery, that they've ALL missed the point. Although all of the above certainly exist within the film, the piece as a whole is more of a character study than an inspirational flag-waving call to nationalism. In a sentence, The Hurt Locker is about a man who's completely comfortable diffusing bombs, but feels completely out of place in the cereal isle of the grocery store; more literally, the world back at home. It's not a film about glory- Sergent James does not want medals. His medals are the hundreds of detonators he stores underneath his bed. It's not about love or family- Sergent James makes it very clear while talking to his baby son that, while his son may love his mommy and daddy, daddy only loves one thing (followed by a scene of James re-enlisting). It's not even about compassion for the innocent- as James was more agitated than overjoyed to see Beckham alive. 

The film is about a soldier who is so good at what he does, so far into his own comfort zone, that he can't help but to be drawn towards the edge he lives on. He loves the edge. When Sanborn puts the knife to his neck, James practically does the deed for him, lusting for the chance to look death in the eye. This is a man who sometimes sleeps in his EOD helmet. He saves the detonators not to learn their lessons, but to look death in the face in quiet defiance. He disarms a complicated car bomb not because he needed to- he was given the clear to leave it. He disarmed it, and risked everyone else's life because it gave him pleasure, evidenced when James said "That was good.." afterward and lit up a cigarette. It's the kind of reaction you would expect after sex. To James, being close to death is an addiction.  "War", as the movie quotes, "is a drug." 

There's almost no confusing the theme whatsoever. James removes the protective covering from his windows, risking death for some sunlight. Instead of stopping one of the bomb planters, he simply holds up the detonation device and looks at him- James was armed and could've apprehended him, but where's the fun in that? During the sniper scene, Sanborn and Eldridge drink juice while James, with flies buzzing in and out of his mouth refuses it- almost as if the proximity of death invited the insects to their feast. This is because James is comfortable there...they need the nourishment more. James doesn't even seem to care when Eldridge warns him of a shooter at his 6 o'clock. He simply says "Well...take care of it." treating life or death as trivial as we treat paperwork. 

Every detail, from James' taste in Death Metal music, to the fact that he doesn't speak to his wife and child  when he calls-- all of this speaks to his character. He's a "Wild Man" as his colonel aptly puts it. He could disarm a bomb in the dark, and that's what gives him purpose- playing with fire and getting away with it. 

The only seemingly selfless moment in the film is when James perceives that Beckham is dead. But is it? Did James go after Beckham's killer because he wanted revenge for the boy, or was it because he failed to diffuse a nearby bomb that killed an officer--because he didn't outsmart the bomb planter this time? Did James diffuse the bomb inside of the boy for Beckham, or for himself? This part of the film is a great juxtaposition of emotion and what has already been established about Sergent James. 

The film is a pressure cooker of good performances, intense- focus camera work, and beautiful shots. There is minimal music, and that seems to add a level of realism. The drama is unaffected by the lack of music, and that should speak volumes about the quality of the writing and acting, since not many films these days forgo the element of music to sell a mood. 

The idea of the solider being at home on the battlefield has been done before, but not so artfully. This may very well win Best Picture.

Realism...that is what makes this movie stand a head above most other war movies & loads better than any of the recent Iraq War movies. With the film following an EOD unit in Iraq, you would think that it would just be one explosion after another but it's so much more. Instead of focusing primarily on the action that's going on around the soldiers, director Kathryn Bigelow focuses more closely on the internal struggles that these men are dealing with. The fact that Bigelow perfectly cast basically three unkown actors as her main characters is even more amazing. Jeremy Renner, Anthony Mackie, & Brian Geraghty all do an excellent job of conveying to the audience three soldiers who each have their own unique struggles that they're internally dealing with while having one of the most dangerous jobs in the military. Renner's character struggles with needing to be in two places at the same time, with his wife & newborn child back in America & in Iraq where he is the best at what he does. Ultimately he must decide what he loves more. The speech he gives to his young son, addresses this issue and is one of the most emotional scenes in the movie.Mackie's character is full of fear & anger because he believes that  no one will care or even remember the sacrifices that he has made by serving his country in Iraq. Geraghty's character has the most basic struggle & that is fear of actually dying in Iraq, and times he is paralyzed by that fear. The supporting cast is equally as good, with cameos by Guy Pierce, Ralph Fiennes, David Morse, & Evangeline Lilly. The tight direction by Bigelow & the excellent cinematography compliment the actors perfectly by creating an atmosphere so tense & suspenseful that your heart will be racing. Overall I was very surprised by this film & wouldn't be the least bit surprised to some oscar nominations come out it. If you haven't scene it check it out!

They always have the same things- gun firing, missile launching, explosions, airplane crashes, men crying and then dying. Why should we see this one? Proceed, and you'll find out.

Director Kathryn Bigelow and Screenwriter Mark Boal are the foundations of "The Hurt Locker." The screenplay is a director's bible. It gives him, her in this case, a story with which he can form a vision and then translate that vision onto the screen. Without such a strong screenplay, it would've been easy to term any war movie at this point of time, a cliche. Especially with Inglourious Basterds being the center of attraction this year. Mark Boal will be honoured with an Academy Award nomination for Writing  Original Screenplay. 

Kathryn Bigelow is simply brilliant, original and has directed this film with utmost care. She employs Cinematographer Barry Ackroyd's evergreen technique, the shaky camera technique. This, being the main reward of the film, gives the film a documentary feel which makes us wonder if what we're seeing is being displayed on the news. Background score is of low importance to her, its the sound effects that are sharp and pronounced, not of the explosions but things to which we pay minor importance, adding to its realistic nature. She uses big actors for cameos and blows them up when you're still glad to see them. Having won most of the precursor awards, its safe to say that she has already won the Best Director Oscar. 

Although the film has no plot, it has an intelligible beginning and a pleasant ending. Its primary focus is on a bomb squad in Iraq that go around dismantling bombs. But we don't hear any bombs ticking, except the ones within us.

Sergeant First Class William James(Jeremy Renner) is the real man on the job who goes face to face with the bombs and defuses them. He is a reckless, carefree and free spirited bohemian. Renner embodies the character without the slightest noticeable effort. He is already a lock for the Oscar. This isn't the Sean penn, Daniel Day-Lewis or Russel Crowe kind of Oscar worthy performance. More like that of Richard Jenkins. There is no getting into character. He doesn't bring to screen something that'll make you go "Wow! Method Acting!." You'll see what you're supposed to see, what kind of a person Seargant William James is. And you'll believe it. This man isn't here to win oscars or steal the show, but to do his job with total sincerity. 

Anthonie Mackie plays Sergeant JT Sanborn who communicates with William James, most of the time via radio during hazardous moments and gets treated as an unwanted accessory rather than as an accomplice. He doesn't like Sergeant James and holds a disapproving glare throughout the first half of the movie. Its intensity increases and ebbs away, but that is subtle acting at its finest. Towards the end he gets weak and breaks down, and that too, is subtle. 

The Hurt Locker is an epic war film. One of the best films of 2009 and will get a Best Picture Nod from the Academy not just because its individual elements distinguish themselves independently but primarily because they all stand together, stronger.

The Hurt Locker is an intense experience throughout, and succeeds where many movies fail as it pulls this off without  relying on typical action gags or cliched, cheesy plot structure. The pace of the movie is such that each moment seems utterly important, and the movie never seems to drag - while watching for the first time, there is never an obvious moment where a scene can be pegged as the "climax" of the film for example, as all scenes remain unpredictable until they are fully resolved. 
The film begins with a quote from Chris Hedges' book WAR IS A FORCE THAT GIVES US MEANING, "The rush of battle is a potent and often lethal addiction, for war is a drug." The point of the quote is a simply stated and unerringly true summary of the point of the movie. The film itself does not insist on presenting itself as a moral statement - it simply tells of the addiction to combat experienced by some. This reservation of judgment and lack of moral authoritarianism make the statement all the more powerful, as there is no convincing to be done; a simple presentation of the facts.
Although I don't like to come up with "Best Of" lists, it is safe to say that The Hurt Locker is one of the best movies I've seen in the last few years, and I would highly recommend seeing it.

With a suspenseful intensity that creates some of the most visceral memories of any film this year, THE HURT LOCKER is one of those movies that people couldn't be bothered with at the time of its release. Folks who missed it-myself included-will soon be clammoring to see what turns out to be one of the finest war films of the almost-finished decade, especially as THE HURT LOCKER begins to create the profile it never had this summer, thanks to a steady stream of awards and accolades.

The current conflict in Iraq has been the subject of some fantastic documentary films in the past few years, such as "Standard Operating Procedure," "Iraq in Fragments" and "No End in Sight," but fictional films on the subject have been mostly limited to homefront conflicts, such as "In the Valley of Elah." Not that I've seen every film made about the current military conflict, but I'd say that THE HURT LOCKER is easily one of the best war films of the decade. It's certainly the best about this military conflict, and joins "Black Hawk Down" and "Three Kings" as a time capsule to represent America's war efforts in the last 25 years.

Perhaps it might surprise some that behind the lens of this intense, suspenseful war film is a woman. Kathryn Bigelow, though, is an action film director, and one used to playing with the boys. Her hits like "Point Break" and "Strange Days" have not been awards fare, but that will change this year. I expect Bigelow to join the very elite club of Oscar-nominated female directors.

But enough about the background perspective...why should you see THE HURT LOCKER? For one thing, it contains a fantastic lead performance by Jeremy Renner, a virtual no-name starring as a specialist who diffuses bombs. He's brought in after the previous man on the job meets the fate that one would expect men in this position to be all too prone to, and this guy almost gives you the impression that his work and situation is fun.

So cocky is Staff Sgt. James (Renner) in his job that he defies orders, disconnects personal communication devices and fights his fellow soldiers for enjoyment. He'd be the loose cannon cop in a buddy movie (like Mel Gibson in "Lethal Weapon") if he wasn't also fully-aware of his situation - and good at it. James might be hard to relate to on some levels, but you know you want him by your side.

There are at least three sequences in the film (one at the beginning, one about a half-hour in and one near the end) that are heart-pounding, and Bigelow relies on the normally motion sickness-inducing and slightly cliched (for war films) tactic of shaky handheld camera work to add to the gravitas of what we're seeing. But Bigelow avoids MTV-style edits and camera trickery. In one very steady and memory-burning moment, she simply pulls the camera back to an overhead shot while James discovers that the wire he's tugging on is attached to not just one bomb, but many, each bomb ominously rising from the sand in unison around him at the urging of his steady and gentle pulling of the wire. It's a terrifying moment.

THE HURT LOCKER has a number of terrifying moments, from the off-putting way that Iraqi civilians (or maybe self-sacrificing terrorists) stand in plain view as the military bomb squad works, to the side-story investigation of the demise of a local boy to whom James has become attached. And to cement the sloppiness of this war and its unfinished business, the film's penultimate scene on the home front is note-perfect in its demonstration of how a soldier like James is actually more in his element at war than in the cereal aisle at the grocery store.

The world of film has done so much to capture some of the famous miltary conflicts in U.S. history. Bet on THE HURT LOCKER to join this list. It's intense.

With a visual treat of raw despair and one of the more effective insights into the current struggles of war in the third world - The Hurt Locker certainly has it's strong points. The issue with the film however, is that these strong points sit on the surface, leaving the blank and sometimes monotonous struggles to push through - with little apparent meaning or purpose for something that has already been established in the beginning of the film. The Hurt Locker begins with a message - the Iraq war is a losing and difficult battle, but the film does very little to build on this.

Finally, a film about the War in Iraq that does not get preachy. And, it is one amazing film. The Hurt Locker follows a bomb squad in Iraq and their existence during that time. It is not so much a story as a narrative about day-to-day life. The film feels real and gives us a different perspective of what war is like. It does not focus on fire-fights which really do not occur at all in Iraq. It focuses on these men in the Explosive Ordinance Disposal unit. Director Kathryn Bigelow employs a shaky cam at different points of the story in order to give it the complete feel of being there with them. There is no focus on a loud score or almost any score at all. They know that the sound of our heart's beating during some of the more tense scenes will be enough. And they are correct. I have never been more alert and tense during a film.
 The main character is Sergeant First Class William James, portrayed in stunning performance by Jeremy Renner. James is essentially an adrenaline junkie. Years of disarming bombs has made is so he loves the feeling of being in harm's way. He is a multi-dimensional character who we see go to many different emotional depths. I deeply hope he gets the honor he deserves for his role. I do not how good of an actor he is overall, but he plays this part phenomenally and deserves a lot of respect.
Anthonie Mackie plays Sergeant JT Sanborn, the man who communicates directly with James while he disarms bombs. His job is to inform James of the situation and keep James alive. As such, he finds James' recklessness to be very frustrating. Both these parts are played with amazing subtlety. Neither of them go over-the-top with their acting. It shows true talent that they can hold back at certain moments of incredibly different emotions. Even when more mainstream actors come on screen, they do not distract at all, and the movie keeps moving.
So, see The Hurt Locker. But know that it will be hard to watch and you will probably sweat a bit.

Worthy of a lot of praise. It's deliberately small in scope and shot like a documentary which removes any Hollywood-esque predictability and keeps the story and the set pieces very tense (whether they stay that way on repeat viewings is a different matter). Jeremy Renner fully deserves an Oscar nomination as the risk taking leader of a 3 man bomb disposal squad in Iraq, as the film solely focuses on their dealings with various tasks over the course of 38 days before they are due to go back home. It doesn't psychoanalyse the mindstate of the soldiers, it surprisingly doesn't question why we are in Iraq and there are no cheap gimmicks to create faux-tension. But it does have one or two scenes which could have been cut (Jeremy Renner's encounters with an Iraqi kid who sells DVD's and calls himself Beckham), there were a couple predictable parts, the limited scope prevents any different avenues or aspects of the effects of war being exposed to these 3 men and whether it is an accurate portrayal can only be known by soldiers currently in Iraq (the film was written by a war journalist but soldiers in Iraq have claimed that it's very inaccurate). But despite some problems it's still one of the better films of 2009 and out of the 3 main contenders for Best Picture (Up In The Air & Avatar being the other 2) I can't call it between this and Reitman's film. 
If you enjoyed the documentary-esque approach to war of this film you have to check out Gillo Pontecorvo's "The Battle Of Algiers", a film on the Algerian Revolution that was looked so realistic there's a disclaimer at the beginning that no documentary or newsreel footage was used in the film.

But after the first hour, you start to see the human side of the story, of the soldier, his true feelings, and this is when the movie shines! I think this might be the year when a woman win Best Direction and for sure, Bigelow is going to be the fourth nominated.

How incredible is The Hurt Locker? What I like most about Independent films is how much they tend to surprise the audience and become classics. The Hurt Locker is no exception. It kicks off with a meaningful little quote that ends in one of the most powerful lines that i have ever read in a movie, "war is a drug." Throughout the course of the film we find out just how much of a drug war can become. Like drugs, war can make a person paranoid, addicted, and give them a rush like nothing else. Director Kathryn Bigelow just did a fantastic job with this indie. She has a very good chance of going home with the Oscar for Best Director, and possibly Best Picture.

She also did a great job at extracting one of the best performances of her young cast's career. Jeremy Renner is nominated for Best Actor for his performance as Will, the one who actually has to get up close and personal with the explosives. He does a great job, coming off as cocky at first, but eventually we get a deeper look into his character's twisted mind. He definitely deserved his nomination, but I do not understand why his co-star Anthony Mackie did not get the same treatment for Best Supporting Actor. He was equally impressive as Sergent Sunburn (I mean Sanborn...bad joke). Both were phenominal, so I appreciate the fact that at least one of them got the recognition they deserved.

Brian Garaghty also delivers as the third member of the Bravo team EOD, Specialist Eldridge. He's not quite as great as his teammates, but still pretty good. In his defense, his performance is not as in focus as the other two. What makes the three lead actors performances so special to me are the three big name actors that took the backseat, and allowed them to shine. I'm talking about Ralph Fiennes, Guy Pearce and David Morse. Who all still managed to standout even though their roles were not any bigger than Beckham's, the kid that sold DVDs. The entire cast did a great job in the movie. I cannot complain about a single person. As far as the film goes, as a whole product, it's damn near perfection.

The Hurt Locker is the rawest fictional film that I have ever seen. It felt like a documentary. I did not really feel the tension that the movie has become known for, but I can still appreciate the gripping suspense of dealing so closely with live explosives. It really is a thriller at heart. The few action scenes deserve credit as well, especially the lengthy desert sniper scene with Ralph Fiennes. The camerawork is top notch. I felt the heat of that desert sun myself, in a cool dimly lit room. You get the feeling that you're along with the team on their missions. Similar to how District 9 puts you in the middle of the action.

I have played dozens of war video games that were alot more hands on and personal than a movie can be. But I got a similar feeling while watching The Hurt Locker, as if I was supposed to be something to help. This is definitely the second best war film that I have ever seen. Saving Private Ryan is my personal favorite war film, but some may even argue that The Hurt Locker is better than that one. For that to even be a discussion means that Kathryn Bigelow and her crew must have accomplished something magnificent. We will just have to wait until March to see if she did enough to beat her ex-husband for Best Director and Picture.

His portrayal of the soldier returning home after the adrenaline rush of Iraq is flawless, and his line to his new son is thought-provoking to say the least: "But you know what buddy? Of his ex-wife Kathryn Bigelow's film "The Hurt Locker," James Cameron had this to say: "I think this could be the 'Platoon' for the Iraq war." 

As much as I admire James Cameron's movies, I really think he's off the mark on this. "Platoon" was an anti-war film whose sole purpose was to show one thing: war is hell. The only thing that "Hurt Locker" shares with Oliver Stone's Vietnam movie is that its about a war and the effects it has on people. "Hurt Locker" goes more in-depth. War is hell, yes. But it's also a drug. You get so into it you don't know what to do when you don't have it anymore.

After Squad Leader Sgt. Matt Thompson (Guy Pearce) is killed in action during a bomb blast, Special Sgt. William James (Jeremy Renner) is called in to replace him. He's almost the polar opposite of what Thompson was, and his other two squad members have a hard time accepting that. James is, as a colonel stationed in Iraq puts it, a wild man. To him, war is an adrenaline fix. He does things his own way. Teamwork is something he's still warming up to.

"The Hurt Locker" is a journey, not a political message. We watch the characters and grow with them as they go about their daily routine. Some die, others are better off dead. In the end, we have a better picture of what it takes to fight for your country.

The Academy has an annoying habit of giving out awards to films which donât really deserve them, in a desperate attempt to cover its past mistakes. When Sean Penn won the Best Actor award for Milk, there was a sense of the Academy atoning for snubbing Brokeback Mountain (with the usual excuse that Hollywood âjust wasnât readyâ for Ang Leeâs film). Similarly, The Hurt Lockerâs victory in the Best Picture category was as much about rewarding the filmâs merits as it was about apologising for United 93 being overlooked.

Of course, to say that this wave of good feeling was the only reason The Hurt Locker won is to do it a disservice. There is much about Kathryn Bigelowâs film which is interesting, arresting or admirable. But it is not as perfect or as revolutionary as many critics have claimed, and in the pantheon of war films it remains in the middling ranks, way behind the likes of Full Metal Jacket or Apocalypse Now.

The Hurt Locker is a thematic continuation of Bigelowâs previous films, in particular K:19: The Widowmaker. All her films are primarily about machismo, about huge quantities of testosterone colliding in a confined space with catastrophic results. Both K:19 and The Hurt Locker have a central relationship built around a massive personality clash, and both address themes of duty and morality against a military backdrop. The Hurt Locker has a stronger script and is a better acted film, but Bigelowâs fascination with men pushing themselves to the limit, often for the sake of it, remains at the forefront. This is, after all, a film in which men relax by punching each other in the stomach.

Oddly enough, the film to which The Hurt Locker owes the biggest debt is not a war film of all. In its character arcs and moments of dark comedy, it is uncannily similar to Lethal Weapon. Our central character, Sergeant James, is akin to Mel Gibsonâs character in that his suicidal tendencies and resulting obsession with death allow him to be the best at what he does. The scene where Jeremy Renner takes off âthe suitâ to defuse a car bomb, saying that he âwants to die comfortablyâ, shows someone with both insane levels of confidence in his ability and an equally insane lack of regard for his own life.

At heart, The Hurt Locker is a strange kind of buddy movie. The three central characters (James, Sanborn and Eldridge) are akin to the Lethal Weapon films in their clashing personalities. James is like Riggs: young and reckless, doing things his way or not at all. Sanborn is like Murtaugh, wanting order and preferring to do things by the book. And Eldridge to an extent is like Getz, a well-meaning individual completely out of his depth who often puts his foot in it. All three characters are struggling with both themselves and each other to do what they consider right in very difficult circumstances.

Beyond the interesting character dynamics, the film is visually impressive. It is shot by Barry Ackroyd, who shot The Wind That Shakes the Barley and United 93 (and recently completed work on Green Zone). This background, coupled with the hand-held camerawork, does make the film somewhat Bourne-inflected, although the use of slow-motion during the opening explosion is not particularly Paul Greengrass. The close proximity of cameras to the actors adds to the tense and desolate feeling of certain scenes, in particular where James and Sanborn are aiming at the snipers hiding out in a stone hut. We see every inch of dirt and sand caked onto their faces, and feel like we are in the trench with them as the flies crawl over their skin.

There are, however, two major problems with this film. The subject of bomb disposal may not have been covered in other Gulf War films, but The Hurt Lockerâs approach to telling this story is not as original as one might have expected. In the Bourne films the shaky camerawork was used not just to make the action scenes more vivid and realistic, but to disorientate the audience so that we are never sure whom we can fully trust. The Hurt Locker attempts such a trick, and it works okay for the first 45 minutes. But when the story attempts to expand with the apparent death of the Beckham character, this is suddenly undermined and the resulting scenes lack both thrill and cohesion.

The plot line involving Beckham hints at the filmâs second problem, namely that certain threads of the story simply donât belong here. We should be praising the film for managing to take a series of loosely connected events and making them something more than episodic. But we end up thinking is that the film could have been more disciplined than it already is, and that cutting the additional scenes would not have undermined either its message or its impact.

As mentioned before, The Hurt Locker is at its most basic a drama about three conflicted men. There is so much potential in these characters, which is explored in the opening act, that it begs the question of why Bigelow didnât simply focus on these men, ripping each other apart while trying not to get blown up. The sub-plots she puts on screen distract us from the tension, and as each one ends the films has to start the character build-up almost all over again.

None of the sub-plots are developed into deeper political points, or used as a means to analyse the war from a different viewpoint. The scene with the private contractors is a passing incident, with no attempt made to explore the nature of such figures, or their relationship with US soldiers, or the deeper moral questions surrounding their involvement. You can understand why Bigelow would want Ralph Fiennes as an incidental character as opposed to a glamorous celebrity lead, but this doesnât change the fact that his character is not used to any real, constructive purpose.

Both the Fiennes character and the useless Colonel fall into the trap of stereotyping. They follow a Hollywood convention that if you have a British accent, you will meet with a sticky end. Sure enough, the Colonel is blown up by an IED just seconds after demonstrating how incompetent he is. Any editor worth their salt would have taken that out, along with the scenes of James going âundercoverâ to find the people responsible for Beckhamâs disembowelling. This sequence is out of kilter with the story, and becomes even more so when we find that Beckham is still alive.

The Hurt Locker is an interesting and technically adept addition to the war movie canon. Despite its flawed storytelling and occasional lapses into caricature, it is a capable account of life on the front line in Iraq, shot with the same combination of humour and nihilistic intensity which Ridley Scott achieved in Black Hawk Down. The film would have been better still if it had focussed solely on the three guys trapped within these circumstances; this would have improved the sense of claustrophobia and made us empathise with the characters to a greater extent. But for all its flaws it is still intensely enjoyable, not Oscar-worthy, but a fine film nonetheless.

Although the Oscar buzz for this movie is on the rise, this likability for this movie depends on one's preference for war movies. There's the traditional war flick that features a linear plot with a predetermined script like Saving Private Ryan and then there's the more documentary type of movie like The Hurt Locker which features unorthodox shooting and more improvised dialog. So for me in appreciating the traditional type of war flick, it was hard for me to give this movie a rating any higher than this. But for those who lean on the more avant garde type of movie making, then this will appease those fans. Unlike most war movies, the camera takes you closer to the action than any other movie I've seen. There's little Hollywood intervention as this movie really depicts the unfiltered and gritty lens of the war in Iraq. The main characters really shine as they accurately reflect the instinct and strategies in fighting an enemy that is in fact, invisible. Also, the fact that the movie was directed by woman, adds to the appreciation that a female can boldly take a step into a genre that has been traditionally dominated by men.

When I saw this movie, I was at a local, single-screen, half-restaurant half-theater eating a giant cheeseburger with a fried egg on the 1/2 pound patty (jealous? yea I know). Needless to say, it was a great night, and not just because of that amazing burger.
The Hurt Locker is one of the best adaptations of the wars in the Middle East through its daunting realism and stressful periods of agony-inducing suspense (I mean that in a good way). The way the locals were portrayed, both the innocent civilians and the malicious, subtle antagonists, was so realistic and unnerving that I felt as though I could feel their distrust and loathing of American soldiers when eye contact was made between the two said parties. Mixed with tragedy and action, the story follows the experiences of an arrogant and humorously cocky bomb defuser as he indulges his life-threatening adrenaline obsession. His personal conflicts fight with his soldier mentality, and forge him into a likeable, relatable man burning with unfiltered passions. 
The only part of this movie I found relatively unimpressive was the scene back in the United States; the brief period of time where his home acted as the setting seemed out-of-place and was uncomfortable to watch, although this is arguably intentional (mimicking the mood of the protagonist with the audience is a fruitful ploy).  

Overall, an excellent, must-see movie. No matter what your take on the wars in the Middle East, this movie portrays what life is really like for soldiers and civilians.

Bigelow is like the female Michael Mann. She has spent most of her career making stylized examinations of violent cultures and macho rituals (Point Break, Near Dark, etc.) Her results have been mixed, at best, compared to Mann's or at least that was the case until now. She delivers a near masterpiece with The Hurt Locker. Examining both the adrenaline rush of combat and the toll it takes on one's nerves, this film says more than the barrage of recent Irag-set films say in total. This is essential viewing and the best war movie in a generation. While American audiences have ignored the previous Iraq war films, this one may just catch on. Delivering some of the tensest moments I can remember in recent years, the film puts the screws to the audience and does not let up for over an hour. Every snip of a wire, every rooftop spectator, every casual conversation carries the constant threat of instant death. It isn't that everyone is dead, it's that everyone is waiting to die. Ostensibly Bigelow intended to make an apolitical film but when one of our bomb disposal experts and an Iraqi civilian suddenly find themselves together in a no-win situation, there is more metaphorical commentary than in all the overtly political Iraq films that have come before. At one point, we are relieved from the stresses of combat and are suddenly thrown into a U.S. supermarket where a returning soldier is completely overwhelmed by an endless aisle of cereal boxes. With this one shot, Bigelow drives home the immense culture shock that these returning veterans must feel. How can they ever be the same again?

From the opening sequence, "The Hurt Locker" gripped me with its intensity and grittiness. The use of hand-held cameras threw me into the middle of events taking place as I watched, with bated breath, one brave soldier make a bold attempt to disarm a roadside bomb. 

Other then it's length, the well-written script and deliverance of the actors provided a peek into the daily lives of veterans overseas better than any documentary, broadcast news special, or war film to date. With this film, I got a deeper sense of the dangers that surround U.S. soldiers on duty everyday. As the movie follows the Bravo Company on their waning days on duty, I was provided a look into the soldiers' minds. Jeremy Renner's character, Sgt. William James, specifically captured the mind of a veteran who's seen enough and felt the rush of threatening situations in many occassions that he's become numb to it.

 That may be what Kathryn Bigelow is conveying with this film. Once soldiers, even we as human beings, grasp the fragility of our own mortality, we become numb; continuing to risk our lives to see if that "adrenaline fix" will finally bring us back to reality. 
If this is certainly true, then, as the film so beautifully illustrates, it takes a special breed to operate inside "The Hurt Locker".

Rather then having an overarching story, "Hurt Locker" operates more as a character piece. It's just three soldiers doing their day to day job, which unfortunately for them happens to be bomb disarmament. Basically, we are given a number of scenes consisting of these guys in some tight situations. Though there are never any outright firefights, the more subtle approach taken instills far greater entertainment value then blatant action ever could. The degree to which tension can build in a scene is absolutely monumental. You can feel it from the beginning that any of these characters could be killed at any moment. A sense of real palpable danger is rarely achieved on film, yet "Hurt Locker" manages to instill in it's audience the same highs that come with being caught in situations of life and death.

Good/very good. I've never been to war, so I can't vouch for its authenticity, but I know a lot of critics have said it's a "great war film." I would imagine that they feel that the film presents a gritty, unsparing view of war (and a soldier's life) in Iraq. At least that's how I would define a great war film.

However, I have seen HBO's spectacular "Generation Kill," and I can't imagine any better portrait of life and combat in Iraq. With seven episodes, GK was able to show the endless waiting, and the inept leadership that defined the early days of the American occupation. Mistakes were made, very little was learned.

"The Hurt Locker" is much more of a Hollywood version of war. There are character arcs, lessons learned, tension and release, and some slow-motion. The first half of the film is pretty excellent, depicting a group of bomb squad techs following an increasingly unhinged leader. While the order of the scenes in this half are pretty much interchangeable, the sense of tension that builds is still palpable.

The second half of the film drags a little bit as some subplots are developed and some (semi-trite) personal revelations emerge. As a Hollywood version of war, it's good, but as a realistic depiction of life during wartime, I would have to say it falls short.

I'm not very big with war movies, specifically Iraq stuff, but I am big with Oscar contenders; so I just had to watch "The Hurt Locker". Like with Inglorious Basterds, I didn't expect much from the movie (which is probably good)...

The acting and characters also stood out, specifically that of Jeremy Renner. Then all this was brought to life by director, Kathryn Bigelow. She did a great job of making it feel realistic and emotionally powerful.

However, as intense and thrilling as everything was, I don't see it as big as an Oscar picture as everyone else does. Maybe I'm really just not supposed to watch war movies because I felt like "The Hurt Locker" was just like every other war movie (though slightly better). The inner fan in me was just screaming for something (anything) more. Maybe it was too serious or maybe it was all the screaming and dizzying camerawork, but for some reason I was left confused at how I felt about the movie.

Maybe it's just me (and it probably is) but I prefer edgier war movies like Inglorious Basterds. I prefer movies that appeal more to the public rather than those that focus on the critics or the war-freaks. Don't get me wrong, the movie was good but it's just not my type of movie... William James, a wild EOD team leader who gets his kicks by de-rigging bombs. Anthony Mackie, who also gives a great performance, plays Srgt. JT Sanbourn, an EOD member who isn't big on James taking over his unit after his former leader is killed in action. The film provides many nail-biting moments that will leave you on the edge of your seat. The film maybe an action-packed thrill ride, but takes you on a thinking trip as well. The movie delves into the soldier's inner psyche. The 3rd member of the EOD team is a soldier who is going through a mild depression of being in Iraq. Sanborn has thoughts of regret as well. It's James who loves every minute of what he does. The film shows you the brawn of the EOD team, but also shows you their deep human sides as well. This is definitely worthy of many Oscars, and as long as either this or "Up in the Air" takes home Best Picture, I'm good. Overall, the first great war movie of the 21st century.

For every generation there is war.  And for every war there is at least one film that helps define it.  Kathryn Bigelow's "The Hurt Locker" has become the definitive film of the Iraqi War.  

The Hurt Locker (2009) - 8.3/10
Director - Kathryn Bigelow
Starring - Jeremy Renner, Anthony Mackie, Brian Geraghty, Guy Pearce, Ralph Fiennes, David Morse, Evangeline Lilly, Christian Camargo

"The Hurt Locker" follows an elite bomb squad as they disarm IED's (improvised explosive devices) scattered about the city.  Staff Sergeant William James (Jeremy Renner) is the leader of the group, having diffused over 800 bombs during his tours.  It's the one thing he's good at which pretty much distorts his view of the outside world.  He's hardened and detached.  His crew consists of Sgt. JT Sanborn (Anthony Mackie) and Specialist Owen Eldridge (Brian Geraghty).  Sanborn is the level-headed vet who wants to keep everyone safe while Eldridge is impressionable and paranoid.  Every day presents a new danger as their tour winds down.

"The Hurt Locker" isn't your typical combat-laced war film.  Instead of non-stop action the film creates an edgy tension as each bomb the squad encounters is potentially fatal.  Adding to the tension is the constant presence of Iraqi bystanders.  You don't know who is a friendly bystander or who may be a sniper.  As James concentrates on diffusing the bombs Sanborn and Eldridge are on guard, surveying potential danger.  Kathryn Bigelow does a fantastic job of putting the viewer in the middle of this chaos.  

The script is relatively simple, but strong.  The focus is on the three soldiers, especially James, and not so much the politics of war.  It does have one unnecessary subplot involving Renner and a young Iraqi boy, but it doesn't detract much from the story.  In addition to the tension Bigelow builds, the film's other main strength is it's acting.  Jeremy Renner has justly recieved accolades for his performance.  It's certainly a career changing role.  But let's not forget Anthony Mackie who is equally good in a less flashy supporting role.  The relationship and tension between these two men is definitely a high point.  Renner is likely to get a Best Actor nomination and I hope Mackie likewise gets a Best Supporting Actor nomination.  

"The Hurt Locker" is definitely deserving of the praise and awards it's recieved, especially in a weak year for film.  And after countless attempts (big and small) at depicting the war in Iraq, it's nice to see someone finally get it right.

The characters are brought to life by stellar performances from Jeremy Renner, Anthony Mackie and Brian Geraghty who all of worthy of Academy attention. There are also some pleasantly surprising apperances from Guy Pearce and Ralph Fiennes and both are very good in their limited time. The real star of the film however is the magnificent directing from Kathryn Bigelow; her gritty, in the action style works brilliantly for creating the tense atmosphere especially during the sniper shoot-out which kept me on the edge of my seat the entire time. Overall, The Hurt Locker is an outstanding piece of film. The movie has an absolutely riveting story, breathtaking action / direction and is top off with three powerhouse performances. Seriously, this is a film that you must see just to understand and obviously Bigelow & crew set out to create a film that opens your eyes to the dangers soliders face in the line of duty. Bravo!

The Hurt Locker is a suspenseful ride.  If not wholly satisfying from a story perspective, it has at least 4 wonderful sequences of suspense to compensate for it.  However, the film's random sequences of events never feel like they are truly leading towards something.  Instead we are just along for the ride with these individuals, for better or worse.  I never got bored, but I also never felt fully engaged in the proceedings.  Do all war films insist on using shaky cam cinematography these days? The rush of battle is a potent and often lethal addiction, for war is a drug. - Chris Hedges

- - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - -

The war in Iraq is starting to become an attractive subject in popular culture. More and more TV shows and movies have started to portray this unfortunate conflict, but not many of them have managed to capture the essence and tragedy present in reality. This is where The Hurt Locker steps into the picture: despite its surprising lack of popularity, it is one of the most critically acclaimed movies of 2009.

The Hurt Locker, directed by Kathryn Bigelow (who was married to James Cameron) and written by Mark Boal, is a war thriller/drama that deals mainly with the psychological consequences of the war in Iraq. Few films have actually dared to meddle with this subject, most of them relying only on action to feed the viewers hunger. The Hurt Locker is different  its not just a war movie, its much more than that.

The plot is centered around a bomb squad led by Staff Sergeant William James (Jeremy Renner) who maybe likes his job a little bit too much. Most of the movie well be following him and the rest of the team all over Iraq while theyre doing their job.

The movie opens with a quote from the book War Is a Force That Gives Us Meaning: The rush of battle is a potent and often lethal addiction, for war is a drug. You may not get it at first (I though it was rather cheesy in the beginning), but by the end of the movie youll realize just how perfectly this quote really fits  it has a deeper meaning, much like the film itself.

While the acting isnt anything special, there is one particular performance that shines: Anthony Mackie as Sergeant JT Sanborn, one of the members of the bomb squad. He plays his part really well and contributes with a lot of emotion to crucial scenes. Another performance that I really enjoyed was that of Jeremy Renner, who plays Staff Sergeant James, the main character in The Hurt Locker. He does really well with his role, but I felt like he overacted at times.

It doesnt seem fair to call Jeremy Renners character the protagonist, since the rest of the team members get pretty much the same amount of screen time. These 3 soldiers (SSgt. James, Sgt. Sanborn and Specialist Owen Eldridge, the latter one not having mentioned before) are the heart and soul of this movie and thanks to a brilliant script they are surprisingly complex individuals, especially for a war movie.

Im glad I saw The Hurt Locker  its far much more than just a war movie. Id pretty much recommend this movie to everyone, even though its a rather melancholic experience. If you want to see something new, daring and thought-provoking then The Hurt Locker is more than just a good choice. Enjoy it!
