a review by M. Alberto Ehrler

"War is a drug," declares the caption on the opening scene of Kathryn Bigelow's masterpiece "The Hurt Locker", and this phrase (written by an American soldier in Iraq corresponding with the New York Times), in its four-word simplicity, summarizes perfectly and shockingly the premise behind this astounding film. Bigelow has gone beyond her trademark film "Near End", and has given us an even deeper and infinitely more intelligent film. Simply stated, "The Hurt Locker" is THE film about the Iraq war we've all been waiting for.

The film follows Staff Sergeant William James (Jeremy Renner, in a possible Academy Award-winning performance) who specializes in defusing bombs as he completes his mission period in Iraq, walking alongside his two specialist companions (Anthony Mackie and Brian Geraghty) in a hostile land where everyone is an enemy and where everything might be a bomb. Unlike his fellow teammates who go about their dangerous jobs with caution and with a terrifying proximity to death, James pursues his missions with such excitement; with such charisma and with such longing that we begin to understand how the soldier who said "war is a drug" was right. James craves the excitement and the sense of self-importance defusing bombs gives him, and he's THE best at doing it. He's untroubled by the danger; on the contrary, that's what makes his job all the more likeable. But even though at first he seems like your typical savage-boy war hero, little by little he begins unveiling a deep and shockingly poignant personality, which he doesn't express through words but through his actions and facial expressions. This is a tough guy who's battling demons within himself and who's torn between life and excitement. This is a character unlike any you've ever seen before.

The film paints a painful, eye-opening and crude portrait of the war on Iraq. We see children used as body bombs, honest civilians used as suicide bombers, we see people gather around the place where James is trying to defuse a bomb against the clock, the faces of women and children expectant and entertained by the violence. We see a country torn by war to its very core; we see simply humans trying to survive with no hope whatsoever and no dreams to uphold. The action sequences are driven by an unbearable tension which makes you gasp in pain; this is definitely THE most suspenseful and tense film of the year. Bigelow has demonstrated in past films that she's an expert at creating tension by submerging her characters in difficult situations and stressing their sanity; with this new film, she turns this on to a sky-high level, not only putting the characters' sanity at stake but wrecking the audience's nerves. The film is violent, but not so much as other war films, and the horror and suspense is gathered from the drama unfolding between the characters. From the first sequence to the last, we find ourselves riveted to our seats, not able to believe our eyes.

The cinematography is excellent, it's fast and cuts to different scenes madly, taking in the entire environment and every single character onscreen giving us a million different points of view and a sense of knowledge of the surroundings. The editing is savagely effective, and never does a scene linger too much or switches too fast- it's always precisely in tune with the emotions and the drama. The score is a cacophony of war sounds which heightens the tension even more and, like I said before, there will be moments when you'll believe you'll die from holding your breath so long. Add a pitch-perfect story written by Mark Boal (who also wrote "In the Valley of Ellah", another movie based on the Iraq war), and you've got yourself the best picture of the year!

The film really has no flaws, and at two hours long it doesn't have a single uninvolving second. Bigelow has taken a intelligent and effective war story, added art and controversy, mixed in exorbitant levels of suspense and therefore created a true masterpiece which will be remembered among the best war films ever made. See it if you know what's good for you!

The Hurt Locker is the multiple award winning war drama from Director Kathryn Bigelow. Do not be put off under the premise that this is just another war film. It is an intense, compelling and consistently interesting look into human emotions, friendship and very real characters. We follow a team of bomb disposal experts on a rotation in Iraq as they go day by day towards the end of their tour, facing danger on and around every street and corner. The film focuses on their relationships together and the dangerous jobs they do. The visuals are stunning with top-notch cinematography, direction and editing that all add a vein of realism that sucks you right into each scene as if you were there yourself. The suspense is relentless and rarely dips apart from the few moments where the team are on down time at the barracks, but even here the suspense comes in different forms as our leads figure each other out and try to have some kind of normality in a situation that is so abnormal to the majority of us sitting here safe at home far far away from the real dangers of war. There are strong performances from all the cast; particular praise goes to the relatively unknown Jeremy Renner whose career has begun to bloom after this film. This film is an amazing character study all tied together in an impressive suspense filled cinema experience. It's definitely worthy of its numerous awards, give it a watch and you'll soon see why.

A very interesting, compelling look at what becomes of men in a war, specifically the Iraq war.  While it's a bit slow at times, and isn't nearly as captivating or lasting as movies like "Saving Private Ryan", it's still a movie worth seeing to, if nothing else, get an idea for what life in modern war is like at times.

The movie is excellent on a few points.  The simple, nerve-racking tension the movie generates is almost palpable at times.  After the opening bomb sequence, each subsequent bomb the men find just becomes that much more tense and anxiety inducing.  Eventually, you come to associate with the soldiers, quickly scanning the scenes for any bit of disturbance or things out of the ordinary.  Eventually you begin feeling the same level of drama that comes with thinking there could be a bomb around every corner or a sniper in every window.  In addition, the character study of the three main soldiers forms a significant, if not the core, of the movie.  And this bit of film-making is particularly well done.  The final ten minutes or so of the film PERFECTLY illustrate one of the central themes of the movie, and form  a perfect ending.  In general throughout the movie, though, the development of the characters is just as potent and realistic.  Finally, the cinematography of the film is quite good too.  A general lack of any score music creates a very real feeling for the film, both helping to increase the tension and to avoid creating a bias for how a scene should be interpreted.  The shaky handy-cam style of filming also works well when it is used, and creates the proper feel for the proper scenes.

The downside to the film in general is a lack of any momentum or clear direction.  The lack of score music for most of the film actually is a bit detrimental, as music can help to move a film and pace it, in addition to gluing the scenes together.  As it was, the scenes in the film felt more than like a bunch of random, unrelated war stories stuck together into a film that uses the same characters in each situation.  While the ending to the film couldn't have been better, the film in general seems to be a bit willy-nilly in some ways, and eventually it starts to be too much about the bomb defusing and the adrenaline associate with it without adding enough humanity or connection or purpose.  Although this in and of itself may form a greater commentary of the war in Iraq and other conflicts like it . . . 

In general, the film was quite well made.  I would recommend it to anyone looking to get an image of what life in Iraq is like.  Excellent use of cinematography, score music, and pacing contribute very well to create a series of anxiety-filled scenes.  In addition, character development and portrayal is nearly perfectly handled, and nothing less than compelling.  However, a lack of clear direction or purpose, odd editing at times, and a failure to include larger, connective elements or true humanity makes a film that just can't hope to become nearly as classic or incredible as "Saving Private Ryan".

It's presented in such a way that you begin to think that even the smallest, simplest items could be a bomb.  The Hurt Locker puts you into a cold sweat, and is probably the most tense movie since No Country for Old Men.  My only problem with the movie is that the characters don't really have much in the way of personality.  They are pretty much soldiers and only soldiers.  Still, the tension is what makes this movie so good and here, it's so good, it is almost perfect.

Bottom Line is this film makes you think, i love all kinds of film but this film (While not my favorite) does something that other films can not, it brings War home....its brings the terror of it and it brings the glory of it in such an artistic and satisfying way....i had goosebumps.

Also on a side note the occasional cameos which are really great to see,Guy Pearce as well as David Morse & Even Ralph Fiennes who really are great to see in a film like this.

One slight problem i had in the back of my head was it was kind of slow, of course since its overall message and its cinematic perfection,Great Story & with its Unique Characters I happily forgave that.

Brilliant. That's the only way I can describe Kathryn Bigelow's masterpiece "The Hurt Locker." Technically, there are no flaws. The fx, while a little artsy, are great. The lack of music and artificial lighting create an inescapable tension that really makes you wonder whether or not the characters will make it. Bigelow's use of budget for the movie is incredible. She wastes absolutely nothing and tells her story of a Iraq war bomb squad perfectly. 

The performances are fantastic and completely believable. Jeremy Renner, Anthony Mackie, and even Guy Pearce and Ralph Fiennes are nearly unrecognizable as actors playing characters instead of just characters. The handheld camerawork and Bigelow's direction are so immersive that I occaisionaly thought I was watching a documentary.

Even though the movie is basically one incredibley tense disarming scene after another, the atmosphere is so well set up that you really realize how this is real life for thousands of Americans. Also, The Hurt Locker finally shows something I thought I might never see again: character development!! 

What else can I praise...? Oh yes: the superb way that Bigelow uses the intensity of the war to develop character studies for each person, and the way the movie shows that everyone fighting in Iraq is crazy and fighting an unwinnable war. And, (listen Michael Moore) for once it doesn't portray the insurgents as misunderstood freedom fighters. Overall, for the first time in a huge while, (seriously, I don't remember the last time I said this) I can't find anything wrong with this movie. I'd say it's pretty damn perfect. See it!!

First of all, I would like to say that I think it is a crime that the "Rotten Tomatoes" web based application does not allow the end user to rate a film at 85%.  This is failure on RT's part and I have to point it out.  To further explain how much I am disgruntled by this, imagine me sitting in my first grade class and being told by my teacher that the hands on the clock only sit on the numbers and move in increments of five to tell the time of day.  My first grade teacher snorted at me when I asked about what time it was when the minute hand was pointing between the numbers...

This film is a 85%.  This movie is very well done and very convincing.

I think that saying this film was "cliche" is definitely not an out of line statement - having seen Patton, Platoon, Saving Private Ryan, Full Metal Jacket and hell -- even Forrest Gump (among others) -- this type of film has been done before and only the subject matter is different.

My Complaints:

1.  Why show a bunch of mangy/sickly cats in the beginning of the film instead of showing mangy/sickly people that have been impacted by war - this might have had greater impact on the audience.  I don't think that the symbolism is necessarily wrong but I do think that there is more to be gained from using mangy/sickly humans to speak to what I think Bigelow was trying to get at.

2.  The movie seemed to drag on in places and there was not enough eye candy.  Occasionally I hear the helicopters flying overhead or the jets/bombers/what have you -- but I needed to see them to feel more like I was in this environment.  The sky - just as much as the ground and the broken glass and the bombs and the people - is part of what we should see too.  Atmosphere speaks volumes in movies like this and we (the audience) might think more about the world that these people live in/work in if we had more to look at.

3.  It seemed farfetched that Special Sergeant William James only loves a couple of different things in life and one of these things is disarming bombs.  I guess I would have to hear it from him -- but having love for life, family, belief system.... Maybe my argument here is that we never knew what exactly was on his mind - this list of things that he loved - and knowing this might have made the film much more poignant.  It seems obvious -- but is it?

4.  My final argument of flaw is of a more personal nature.  Being a hardworking professional workforce member in our great American society (that this trio and many others like them are VALIENTLY DEFENDING) I find myself a little sickened by war - after having endured losses in terms of friends and family of friends to this conflict, after having seen seemingly millions of news broadcasts and read numerous posts and stories I feel like telling a story about Iraq and war is akin to beating a dead horse.  I want to see resolution brought to this horrible conflict and resolve on the table.  This film had no resolve to offer me.

Good resolve might have been that there is improvement in Iraq and that there is a general consensus on value systems between 'us' and 'them' and that a better future is on the horizon.  Seeing people working toward good is one thing, but not seeing change in a much more grand way (which I am sure has happened and will continue to happen in Iraq) leaves an empty feeling in my heart.

I have to admit that this movie had high points but at the same time I have to acknowledge that things could have been a lot better.

Kathryn Bigelow's The Hurt Locker can easily and accurately be summed up with that statement because apparently not just war is a drug, but watching it is too. The Hurt Locker is a total adrenaline rush, it grips you within the first few minutes and never lets go. 
The film tells of a bomb defusing unit set stationed in Baghdad during the (currently ongoing) Iraq War. What makes The Hurt Locker so great is the stark and unflinching realism within every scene. Each shot is engulfed with the same tension that a real soldier in Iraq would have, every day is a fight to survive, not just with the enemy but with oneself. But why do certain soldiers, such as those in The Hurt Locker choose to go even further into harmâs way? Because "war is a drug," there is something they get out of pushing the envelope that also allows these men to stay sane. They figure that if they are going to die in war there might as well be some excitement out of it. However, these men do face extreme mental strain because like with any drug after a high, you must come down. 
Director Kathryn Bigelow puts great detail into The Hurt Locker. The technical features are brilliant and enforce the realistic quality of the film. Bigelow has not just created an excellent war film, but an excellent suspense story. The cinematography is also brilliant; each shot is visual stunning and memorable. It's impossible to look away no matter how brutal the images. Jeremy Renner is great as the "wild man" bomb defusing Sergeant William James. Watching Renner is like watching the documentary and study of a man's ups and downs through the experience of war, and he plays the part beautifully. 
The Hurt Locker certainly stands tall as the best film of 2009, and one that will be remembered for a long time because it covers the issues of a war that has affected many people. Each decade seems to have its own war masterpiece: the 70s have Apocalypse Now, the 80s have Platoon, the 90s have Saving Private Ryan, and now the 2000s have The Hurt Locker.

The hot sun beams down upon deadly streets of Baghdad, one road in particular has been clear of all pedestrians because of suspisios device in the road.  The only thing left on the road is a small tredded robot scurrying towards it.  So begins a relatively normal day for an EOD squad in post Invasion Iraq.  The three men of the EOD team exchange jokes and mess around all the while steering a small robot towards a suspicious package in the middle of the street.  Upon further inspection, the small package contains small IED.  When the robot fails to defused the device one of the men suits up and trots over calmly to the bomb.  The road is deserted and quiet.  All that can be heard is the distant sound of Islamic Worship and gunfire.  The soldier places the explosives on the bomb and heads back towards the "safe zone".  Just then one of the men notices a men who shouldn't be there.  An Iraqi has walked out of his shop window holding a cell phone.  The soldier runs over to subdue him, but in he is too late.  The bomb goes off.  Time slows, as all three try desperately to make it out, one is not so lucky.



So goes the heart pounding introduction to "The Hurt Locker"  an extremely engaging and adrenaline pumping war thriller from director Kathryn Bigelow (of "Point Break" and "K-19: The Widowmaker" fame). What makes this movie click in my mind are three important factors.  



One is the award winning performance (in my opinion) of Jeremy Renner and Anthony Mackie.  Renner's portrayal of a man addicted to war is unnerving.  You want this guy one your team when the shit hits the fan and yet you want to stay the hell away from him.  Mackie provides a stability to the movie which is the ying to Renner's yang, trying to be vigilant and find the safest way to deal with any situation.  When the two of the meet on screen, real Love/hate bromanceal chemistry happens.



Number two is the cinematography by Barry Ackroyd.  His hand held pseudo documentary style grabs the viewer by the throat and drags him into the moment, lending to the suspense.  The camera acts almost like vigilant human eyes, scanning every possible street, alleyway, and rooftop for immediate danger.  You do feel like the situation could literally blow up at any given second.  I think this quote from Kathryn Bigelow sums it up nicely. "That's how we experience reality, by looking at the microcosm and the macrocosm simultaneously. The eye sees differently than the lens, but with multiple focal lengths and a muscular editorial style, the lens can give you that microcosm/macrocosm perspective, and that contributes to the feeling of total immersion."



And number three is the pin pricking score by Marco Beltrami.  An extremely underrated composer who finally got a chance to let his true talent shine instead of getting stuck with snoozer horror movies.  His score almost wanders into the realm of experimental, with just odd sounds and build ups floating around the speakers just waiting patiently to strike.  It makes the viewer sweat bullets, lean in closer to the screen, take in ever detail, run through all the possibilities, and pray to god the red wire is the right one to cut...or was it the blue one?  And the best part of the score is that you notice it in all the right places, it's neither over bearing nor hidden beneath the film.  Kathryn Bigelow gives the score its dues, she knows when to use it and when not to.



If there is one problem I have with an already fantastic movie it's its story, which pretty much isn't there.  Instead of a normal act 1, 2, or 3 we get dropped into Baghdad for a few hours (or 30 plus days according to the movie), try desperately to make it to the next day, and then were out (ironically much like a soldiers tour of duty).  Now I have to admit this didn't bother me one bit.  I was sucked into dangerous and deadly world these men inhabit.  It was a snippet of these three mens lives, where their job description includes staring death in the face on a daily basis.  In the end one might feel that after 2 hours, what was the point?  Why did I invest my time? It was just like it started up randomly and ended randomly.   Ironically enough I hear the same complaints of great films like "8 1/2" and "Wild Strawberries" so I can't fairly divulge into that criticism I feel. Kathryn Bigelow takes viewers right inside the humvee along with 3 American soldiers.  If you go along for the ride, you'll feel your heart race and your head spin from all those bombs planted on the Iraqi streets.  You see, the soldiers in the humvee are looking for I.E.D. to detonate.  They are James, played convincingly by Jeremy Renner who's the most interesting character.  Anthony Mackie (an underrated fine actor) who plays Sanborn as a dedicated solider.  The youngest is Eldridge played by Brian Geraghty as naive.  Their interactions among themselves and with the others are the focus of the movie.

Bigelow, an action director (Point Break) does a remarkable job at engaging the audience.  The screenplay is lean but I wasn't captivated.  Detonating bombs gets repetitive after a while and there wasn't an emotional "hook" to the movie.  Yes, the action scenes are suspenseful but the semi-documentary style and hand-held camera also keeps the audience at a distance.

The movie starts with a quote "War is a drug" and we understand this concept with the James character.  I have a problem with war movies because the conflict is basically will the hero be dead or alive.  If he's alive, will he maimed or suffer post-traumatic stress.  However, I've enjoyed "The Deer Hunter" and "Saving Private Ryan" because they focus on the characters and you get emotionally involved in their growth.  Critics are awarding "The Hurt Locker" best picture awards, but as good as the movie is, I was glad when the end credits arrived. I wasn't exactly entertained but felt that I did my civic duty by watching this movie.  My final wish is that warmongers like Bush and Cheney should be forced to watch this movie to understand how war never resolves conflict but lingers.

The Hurt Locker was a very intense film. The intensity came from all sides: from the acting to the camera work. I was on the edge of my seat even when I had already seen the movie.

What made this film fresh for me is that the situations these soldiers found themselves in seemed relatively isolated. It was not a film about a unit, a batallion or platoon. It was basically three guys doing their thing. That hightened the tension and made the viewer care for those three soldiers all the more.

It really did not focus on the "overall outlook" of the war but was rather a character study about SSgt. William James. The most grabbing idea was that a man can get so caught up in adrenaline and combat that all else feels less important. Usually "character study" war films are about how some kid doesn't want to be there or how war is hell (Platoon, Apocalypse Now, Deer Hunter, most Vietnam films). It was nice to look into the psyche of a true war hawk like Sgt. James.

"The Hurt Locker" is a gritty and real look on war. It's nerve wracking, heart wrenching, and thoroughly convincing. A true masterful achievment indeed.

War is intense. It can change a man. Fear strikes into the eyes of many young men and women who serve daily. Fighting for your country. Going day by day thinking it could be your last. Killing enemies  to protect something worth fighting for. The emotion can get to the people in the line of duty. You account for the people you work with. You get to know them day in and day out. They become your brothers. 'The Hurt Locker' is able to pull all these real-life elements into a spellbinding 2 hours and the end result is summed in one word: perfect. 

The beginning of the movie starts off with the statement: War is a drug. Not for everyone though, of course. Most troops want to get it over with and go home. But our hero of this film, Sgt. William James, who has a  dangerous job, addresses it like it's Christmas every occasion. He has one of the most difficult jobs you can account for in war: defusing bombs. Every time his squad goes in, they risk everything. Their lives are in extreme peril. That account assuring the setting going into the movie alone makes this film worth buying or even renting.  

Jeremy Renner plays Sgt. James. Renner's account of the technician is outstanding. He's cocky, reckless, and at often times insane. But it's all part of him because he knows he's the best at what he does. James' squad partner, JT Sanborn, played by Anthony Mackie, follows the book and protocol. Sanborn is skilled at backing up James. He though thinks his Sergeant (and is right) is insane. One scene depicts James of taking off his bomb squad clothing, putting himself at more risk, and going in to defuse a bomb. Sanborn feels challenged and belittled. But all James is trying to show him is that he's best at what he does. Every time James goes in to defuse a bomb, the moments are suspenseful. The action is filled with adrenaline. Every sequence is so realistic, something only other war movies could only dream of. Director Kathryn Bigelow makes every camera movement worthwhile with the action's pace. It's sometimes fast, but then sometimes slowed down to mere moments. The film's setting in Iraq is grit-filled. 'Hurt Locker' makes everything work together and pulls out one thing that war movies can't resist, but share: politics. Screenwriter Mark Boal first account of writing into a perspective from the war in Iraq clearly shows Hollywood that this is the best movie revolving around the current war we're in. Nothing comes close.

Bigelow has made a crowning achievement. It's not only one of the best war movies ever, but maybe one of the best movies to have come out in recent years. There's nothing negative whatsoever about what maybe one of the defining movies of the decade. It's riveting, exciting, action packed, and emotionally thrilling. 'The Hurt Locker' is the best movie of 2009.

War as spectator sport.  And as in watching an exciting football or basketball game which is counting the seconds to the climatic end, THE HUNT LOCKER is counting down the final days before this three man bomb squad is rotated back to the states. 

THE HURT LOCKER is a solid anti-war film that harks back to memories of Stanley's Kubrink's classic PATHS OF GLORY which also addressed the futility and irony of warfare.  The intense in-your-face sequences do not magically lure you into the action, instead director Kathyrn Bigelow grabs the audience by the back of the neck and forces them to face the absurdity of warfare and dares the viewer to watch, watch and watch more. 

There is no John Wayne-esque romantic gallantry here.  The main character is an adrenaline junkie played "creepily" by Jeremy Renner who enjoys his job just a little to much. His crack-pipe of choice is donning a heavily padded bomb disposal suit and then taking it off when it becomes too uncomfortable to dismantle containers of explosion devices that would take out a city block. WHOA!! He says as much in a scene that if he's going to die he's going to die comfortably.

Noteworthy performances by Anthony Mackle and Brian Geraghty who round out the explosives team that are just trying to make the best of a bad situation. They're job is just to make it to the next day.  And it's damn hard.

Shot is "documentary-style" the richness of the story telling here is in the editorial selections that Bigelow had to work with. With the multitude of cameras used to capture the action, clearly there was bound to be an abundance of material to manipulate accordingly.  This is not to negate the screenplay by Mark Boal. Clearly, the story was on the page.

I do not give away anything here when I mention a moment in the movie when one of the characters is alone on a cereal aisle of a grocery store attempting to decide which brand to get.  This is the great underscore of what war is all about. It's about protecting our point-of-view and the great lengths we as a society will go to do that.  People must and will die to keep the cereal boxes on the shelves on your local supermarket. Talk about your war-theater of the absurd.

Is THE HURT LOCKER the best movie of the year? No.  Is it one of the best?  By all means.

This is a different kind of war movie for a different kind of war that ultimately fails in the same ways the war fails - in that it lacks a singular focus, it has no direction or goal, and the purpose is not clear. It's not a bad movie, I just couldn't find anything to connect to or engage with - and when a moment would arise in which I thought that thing to connect to was coming... it didn't.

The film drags along at a snail's pace at times, which works for some scenes, such as a great scene wherein the main characters are pinned down for several hours by insurgents in the middle of the desert - but mostly the slowness just feels slow. There is no real story here, yet it isn't just a docudrama, either. It doesn't seem to know what kind of a movie it is, or from which characters' view point it is being told. In my opinion the story that it started to tell (and would have made it a much more interesting film) was of the drug-like addictive nature of high risk behavior, and how people who engage in that sort of thing in war will return to civilian life only to find other dangerous, high risk behavior to engage in... which is not dissimilar thematically to another of director Kathryn Bigelow's films, "Point Break". Alas, it seemed as if she forgot about that angle halfway thru the film. The worst part of the film is the ending, which after 125 minutes of slow pacing suddenly races past what should have and could have given the film its purpose. 

If I had seen this film back when it first came out, I think I would have said, "OK. A well-acted, decent film despite its problems."  The thought that this film would be nominated for and would win so many major awards, including being the front runner for any Oscar whatsoever -- would not have even crossed my mind, and it is mindboggling to me now that that is the case.

The best movie I have seen about the Iraq war. But I guess that isn't saying much as there have been very few worth watching (closest thing I have seen to a great movie about the Iraq war was "Charlie Wilson's War"). This is one very tightly knit movie with very few moments to breath. And when it does allow you to breath it is for scenes of quietly devastating pathos involving the soldiers home lives being a mess. Really shows what the effects of a bullshit war have on the people right there on the front lines. But at the same time this is what they signed up for. The politics involving the war are not really at play here during the movie as it is really more about a stranger being in unfriendly waters trying to do a job that puts themselves and everyone they know in said unfriendly territory in danger and the redundancy of having to go through nearly every day for a year. The performances are all just top notch. Espescially Jeremy Renner and Anthony Mackie. I really have no clue who these two are but they are both oscar calliber. Jeremy Renner is introduced as a hot shot know it all douchebag redneck but we slowly get to see the psychology behind him and his motives. The fact that for him this is living. Living any other way is just a alternate form of death. Anthony Mackie plays a man who has seen his best friends be blown to smithereens in a matter of seconds and knows it will happen again. There is just no way of knowing when your time has come or how you'll go. He is world weary to put it is simpler terms. But at the same time it is revealed that he too can't quite face up to the mundane form of life for civilians. Guy Pearce, Ralph Fiennes and David Morse are all great in their bit parts as macho military personnal that live for the moment of being alive. The film runs over two hours but does not feel it. The editing works wonders as the usually annoying use of steadycam is appropiately used here in showing the frenzied crazyness of not knowing what will happen next. Really they are in a hopeless situation and how there is no reason for them to be there. But they are forced to stay there. Yet these acts of senseless violence will just go on and on and there is no way of stopping it. Case in point the diplomatic character portrayed by Christian Camargo. Who is trusting of people in a war zone and doesn't notice the blatent danger near his feet as he talks about his upbringing in New York.  And the situation involving Jeremy Renner's character befriending a little child and the aftermath of it. Kathryn Bigelow, who is being touted as the frontrunner for best director, has done some decent work before this ("Strange Days", "Near Dark") nothing she has done has been this well thought out and executed. A great candidate for best movie of the year and in my book comes close. Though, like "Prescious" and "Inglorious Basterds" , it is a movie I feel is brilliant and well made but it is not a movie I can personally believe in as I have not been in the military or in a war zone and therefore don't feel I have any connections to. But as a movie it is damn near perfect and probably the best action movie I have seen in years. Certainly one of the best movies of the decade. Just not something I feel any personal attachment to.

Lately we've been getting a few Iraq war movies that have been generally disappointing. "The Hurt Locker" attempts to rectify these past attempts to make one see the horrors while giving a somewhat fair view of it, showing that soldiers face incredible danger, both in psychological and physical aspects. The story is about three soldiers in 2004 Baghdad, Iraq, who scout and disable IED (Improvised Explosive Devices). After the team leader of Sgt. Sanborn (Anthony Mackie) and Specialist Eldridge (Brian Geraghty) is killed by said explosive, they are assigned new team leader Staff Sgt. Will James, a very gung-ho and risky soldier, who faces threats head-on. Throughout the film, we see how these soldiers are forced to cope with the danger they face.

What I Liked

It's hard to make a movie create real tension. I have to say that I never felt so much tension in this film than I did with any other in a long time. Not even most horror movies made me stay at the edge of my seat like this did. Every moment the soldiers were on the battlefield I felt the paranoia that the soldiers felt. Anything and everything was possible, and danger waited to strike at the perfect time. The fact that it was possible to connect with the paranoia that the soldiers felt was even harder.

The characters all had very profound depth to them. Each character is given proper development through history, emotions, and their own views on death. This gave each character their own uniqueness as well, both in attitudes and experiences. James shows more concern with others than he does with himself, almost as if he doesn't care about his life anymore. Sanborn is the portrayed as a man who will fight for his life because it is all he really has. Eldridge tries to understand the "ambiguity" of dying or killing to live, only being able to express this to friend and doctor Col. Cambridge (Christian Camargo), who has an over-simplistic view of the war due to his "desk job" position. These different personalities create an even spectrum of ideas on death, although all still fear it regardless.

The direction in this film was spectacular. The shots in this film gave it a documentary feel to it, drawing you into the action while being able to let the audience member get the full feel of what is being portrayed. Thankfully, despite being hand held most of the time, the camera is generally steady and never out of focus. While some shots are grainy to help give it that gritty, realistic feel, there are some shots that are shown in crystal clarity to allow one to see things the way it should be. Right in the beginning, we see the devastation of an IED, showing the raw power of what one can do. It's impossible to describe this shot. It was that well done.

Regarding cinematography, the film felt like it was in war-torn Baghdad. I can only give an over simplistic description of it being desolate, in ruins, etc. All I can say is that there was a very good attention to detail in the surroundings and locales.

The dialogue in this film was also well done. The dialogue was believable almost all of the time and darkly humorous at different points. It came across as "self-comfort" dialogue, which I would expect from soldiers experiencing such tension as they are.

The acting was very strong in this movie. Nothing felt over or under acted and the actors delivered their lines near perfectly, except for a couple of lines with some flat delivery.

What I Didn't Like

If there was one thing in this film that truly bugged me, it was the believability that James would still be in the military after all the things he pulls off. I will simply say that is character is not "orthodox" in his actions and approach to solving problems. It seems that, except for an anger moment from Sanborn, he experienced no disciplinary action at all. Granted, this is a film, but at least make him experience SOMETHING for the trouble he causes.

Regarding the direction, there was one slow-mo shot that felt out of place. It involves a bullet falling to the ground after a shot is taken (and I will not say who was involved, as this was an integral part of the movie). I expect it may have been something to generate more tension, but it just felt unnecessary.

What Can Be a Mixed Bag

I am related to several people who have been in the military, but I know next to nothing about it. However, there are a few continuity things that may bug people who have been in the military regarding weaponry and armor. Because of my lack of knowledge, I was fine with it. Hurt Locker is a perfect example of how a quality low-budget film can be as good as a film that costs over nine figures to make. The film centers on a bomb specialist played by Jeremy Renner (28 Weeks Later, Assisination of Jesse James) who joins an army squad in Iraq after his tour in Afganistan. The movie follows the group through their missions as they count down the days until their rotation ends. He increasingly endangers himself and his squad in order to get his "adrenaline fix" while disarming bombs. He even leads his group off-mission for good reasons on the surface but propelled by his need for a rush underneath.

The acting is excellent, especially by Renner. Small roles and cameos by Guy Pearce, Evangeline Lilly, and David Morse lend some star quality to the film. Morse has one of the top scenes in the film, as a squad leader congratulating but also calling out Remmer's specialist as a "wild man".

The plot is fairly simple following the missions of bravo company. The screenplay does a nice job of intertwining a nice balance of fear from the other squad members and even hate to point of considering to cause an "accident". It is depicted fairly well on the screen by Anthony Mackie and Brian Geraghty. Even with these performances, scenes do tend to drag on at points longer than they seem to need. The movie also has a rapid ending that seemed a bit shallow considering the complexity of the characters that had been presented throughout the film. Not alot of flash if that is what you are looking for. Just a solid, well acted, interesting, war film. If this is your genre, it's worth investing the time.

Thankfully, this movie isn't one of those films. Like "Full Metal Jacket", the war was just a setting. Nothing else. The characters are bomb technicians just trying their best to do their job and save others.

But what makes this movie really cool is that it causes the audience to be just as paranoid as the soldiers. Seeing random people on the ledge watching the main EOD technician try to shut off the bomb can be very suspicious.

On top of that, it didn't even feel like a movie. The script seemed natural, not forced. The scene seemed natural. It was as if you were really there.

The best part for me was the ending, not in a bad way. I just loved how it ended. No spoilers.

Bottom line: this film better win "Best Picture" at the Oscars. That's all I have to say.

I cannot say that this is top of the year material for me but I can say that The Hurt Locker far exceeded my expectations. Let's face it, we are all, no matter how big a war film fan you may be, getting a little tired of Iraq war narratives by now. This feeling towards this type of genre piece may have in many respects lowered my expectations going in. In many ways The Hurt Locker falls squarely within the ranks of its predecessors however, what allows this film to distance itself from other similar films is what lies beneath the surface. Bigelow directs with little artistic flair choosing rather to seek reality and to build tension as one day of bomb diffusion carries into the next for a small squad of U.S. Army soldiers. By focusing on this specialized group Bigelow is able to probe their individual psyches and does so to great effect. Many truths often passed over in war films are revealed; How the most hardened individual can crumble and call out for help, how many confused young men find maturity and a calling in life, how the longevity and constant battles faced in war can lead to a sort of institutionalized frame of mind, and so forth. The pacing of the film and the constant state of action allows the film to move without ever getting tiresome in fact, Bigelow keeps a very tense tone throughout that will keep you on the edge of your seat. I was not blown away by the dialogue or the acting in the film but neither of these are what I would call sub par either. The Hurt Locker has received much praise with some calling it the best war film ever, the best of the year, one of the best of the last decade, yet I don't feel the film quite merits all this praise. I would certainly give The Hurt Locker an honorable mention for 2009 but overall there were far too many superior films for my taste in 2009. Still well worth a look

I was really excited to see this movie. I wasn't disappointed. The Hurt Locker is a real blast, pardon the pun. The hype is totally worth it.

First of all, the plot. The plot is polished, exciting, but most of all, believable. Every scene where they're diffusing a bomb has tangible tension that goes along with it. You can feel your heartbeat rise a little, which is still nothing compared to what it would be like in real life, but is still fairly impressive. All of the lines are realistic, with none of those strange monologues that plague too many war movies.

The characters have a lot of depth for a war movie. The main character, Sergeant Will James, is quite a handful. He isn't fazed by a bomb, and even takes off the bomb suit in one scene. "If I die, I want to die comfortable." Great stuff. Will James is played by Jeremy Renner, who really deserves a lot of credit for his great performance. Another character is Sergeant J.T. Sanborn, who is played by Anthony Mackie, and is a by-the-book, I-must-know-what's-going-on kind of person. It's interesting to see James and Sanborn clash over how to do their jobs over the course of the movie. The other main character is Specialist Owen Eldridge, who is played by Brian Geraghty, and is a bit of a cowardly, "what if" kind of person. I also enjoyed the small appearances of Ralph Fiennes and Evangeline Lilly.

The look of the film is simply stunning. You can tell when you watch this that this is technically an amazing movie. The camerawork is beautiful, and I enjoyed the use of "shaky camera" on some of the scenes, which really accentuated the tension that goes along with these jobs. The first explosion shown is unbelievable. The slow motion of the car disintegrating as well as the pebbles lifting up off the ground is just breathtaking in slow motion.

All in all, The Hurt Locker is a great film that truly deserves to win Best Picture. I'm sorry Avatar, I still find you to be more enjoyable, but The Hurt Locker is technically much, much better.

One of the many things I like about this film is how it subverts not only conventions of the war film but many conventions of narrative cinema.  Granted, Iraq is a different kind of war; unlike WWI and II, the enemy in Iraq (and Afghanistan as well) is not easily identifiable by their uniforms or by their position on a clearly-defined battlefield.  Bigelow effectively uses this ambiguity to maintain the tension and near-paranoia these soldiers experience.  I really never knew who in the film was friend or foe, or what was just trash on the ground or a bomb.  Second, the main character/hero in The Hurt Locker never really changes.  In many traditional films, war or otherwise, a less-than-likeable hero usually has a moment of crisis after which he changes his behavior for the better.  Here, Will James experiences moments of compassion for his comrades, for civilians of Baghdad, and for his family, but they are never enough to alter him entirely.  As he says at the end, he loves "one thing."  I like that.  It's raw and it's real.  Third, the rest of the narrative never plays to expectations.  We might expect Guy Pearce's character, for example, to be a key player throughout the film, yet he's dead twenty minutes into it--kind of like Janet Leigh in Psycho.  The EOD team we follow also does not always save the day, as with the man wearing the vest of explosives.  Again, was this man really forced into wearing the vest or was he lying about that?  We don't know.  Overall, I gained more respect for Kathryn Bigelow; any chick who likes war and guns and violence and machismo is alright with me.  And, even though this is a fictional film, I gained more of an understanding and appreciation for what soldiers do and deal with in Iraq and Afghanistan.  If The Hurt Locker wins Best Picture and Best Director at the Oscars, I'd be happy with that.

It's a challenge to describe The Hurt Locker in a way that hasn't been done before; the realism of this movie must be seen firsthand. Jeremy Renner plays the adrenaline-junkie hero, overconfident at the beginning of his rotation in a group of soldiers reserved for bomb diffusion in Iraq. As the movie progresses, tightly wound and pulse-pounding suspensful, he and his fellow men discover sacrifice again and again in a way that is original and resounding. Director Kathryn Bigelow pulls together what could have been just another war movie, and turns it into a miraculously suspensful ordeal. The raw sequences prove this movies grit, as the smallest gestures in seemingly real-time scenes could result in disaster. This makes for an intensity the audience can relate to, and as the days left in their rotation count down at the bottom of the screen, death could be around every corner. Ultimately, even the rotation countdown gets hearts racing. Everything in this movie is jarring, from the camerawork to the tragic action to the undeniable conclusion.

The Shape of War Films to Come

This is not your average war film. A film that does not rely on action to mask the actual themes of war. It had the similar mood of Jarhead and Full Metal Jacket with the pacing of Platoon. There is action, of course, but it is done in a way that could bore the average pants-wetting bloodthirsty moviegoer. It is a film that portrays conflict in a realistic way, examining human emotion among death.

The story is about a small group of soldiers (basically three men), two of them lost their commanding officer to a roadside bomb in Baghdad, so a new man is called in, William James. He has disarmed close to 900 bombs and is pretty good at what he does... good enough to play by his own rules. His way of dealing with the stressful situation of bomb disarmament is unlike anything his fellow officers have ever seen. He keeps cool despite the looming threat of death everywhere. But despite this, there is an obvious imbalance going on inside James' head. He is not normal, yet maintains his human nature.

In this film, we see no brainwashing techniques or boot camp stories that detail the degeneration of a soldiers' mind. Instead, we get the people who were not expecting to see such horrible sights and envision how affected they are by it. A great example is Eldridge, a soldier who, upon seeing the death of his friend and superior officer goes from a joking young man to a sad and scared soldier of war. His emotions speak so loud that his character cannot be classified as the simple scared soldier, instead we see a man reduced to the utmost regions of his sanity.

Action director and former James Cameron wife Kathryn Bigelow really impresses as a director, further raising the question as to why she would direct low rate action films (although Point Break will always hold a place in my heart), when she really has the potential to direct an actual suspenseful and terrifically meaningful film such as this. Her direction is stellar, giving us that realistic quality of war film with the grainy and sandy look of Three Kings, Black Hawk Down and Saving Private Ryan. It is suspenseful yet the action does not move at lightning pace, it is almost real time combat, and there are a few noteworthy scenes depicting this.

Brilliant. That's the only way I can describe Kathryn Bigelow's masterpiece "The Hurt Locker." Technically, there are no flaws. The fx, while a little artsy, are great. The lack of music and artificial lighting create an inescapable tension that really makes you wonder whether or not the characters will make it. Bigelow's use of budget for the movie is incredible. She wastes absolutely nothing and tells her story of a Iraq war bomb squad perfectly. 

The performances are fantastic and completely believable. Jeremy Renner, Anthony Mackie, and even Guy Pearce and Ralph Fiennes are nearly unrecognizable as actors playing characters instead of just characters. The handheld camerawork and Bigelow's direction are so immersive that I occaisionaly thought I was watching a documentary.

Even though the movie is basically one incredibley tense disarming scene after another, the atmosphere is so well set up that you really realize how this is real life for thousands of Americans. Also, The Hurt Locker finally shows something I thought I might never see again: character development!! 

What else can I praise...? Oh yes: the superb way that Bigelow uses the intensity of the war to develop character studies for each person, and the way the movie shows that everyone fighting in Iraq is crazy and fighting an unwinnable war. And, (listen Michael Moore) for once it doesn't portray the insurgents as misunderstood freedom fighters. Overall, for the first time in a huge while, (seriously, I don't remember the last time I said this) I can't find anything wrong with this movie. I'd say it's pretty damn perfect. See it!!

Positively wrought with tension. What makes fear effective is always the element of things "unknown"; Hurt Locker capitalizes on this with perfect precision. Soldiers in a foreign land, trained to not trust anyone, to kill without conscience--and yet impossibly wrestle with conscience when left to their own devices. Truly remarkable. 

I thought I was going to get an ulcer by mid-way through. Excellent use of sound (and silence) and camera angles to emphasize the stress of each scene. The film is about as well-made as any in recent memory and the sense of desperation, of hopelessness, but also of duty and loyalty is unrelenting. 

A really solid young cast with the always-enjoyable cameos by serious veteran actors too. Fiennes was of particular note. And one can't say enough about the leads: Renner and Mackie and Gegaghty--all three of whom I immediately stopped thinking of as actors, their characters as real as one can imagine. 

The viewer is immediately immersed in their lives without the necessity of heavy back-story--though it is revealed, subtly, through small, key scenes. I imagine this is what military life would be like. Everything in the immediate, the soldier's "home" story not unimportant, but perhaps a liability. And so we move through the story knowing these characters, for the most part, only in the immediate sense. 

For me the film doesn't quite end on a satisfactory note--but this is probably preference more than anything else. I like the absent transition from war-zone to home, the way Renner's character is more out of his element with his family than in the zone. But the closing scenes and brash music felt contrived--not quite macho--but over the top. And something about it all feels unresolved (but not in the "pretty bow" sense). 

Otherwise a great film. .

The intensity factor of "The Hurt Locker" is an amazing thing. Here is a movie that starts with an incredibly suspenseful sequence where it is established anything can happen in such a chaotic environment, and not only does it keep this tone and energy throughout it's ENTIRE running time, but it also uses it to psychologically investigate the mindset of its complex characters. Although it is set in war-time Iraq, and is being released while this war is still going on, it has no political agenda or slant. I wouldn't call it a heroic patriotism movie, but I wouldn't call it a liberal criticism of the Iraq War. There are no sides here. It simply is what it is: a story of an adernaline junkie who finds himself risking his life and the lives around him in the need of a fix. 

"The Hurt Locker" is part character study, part relentless action movie, part gritty realistic war picture, part Hitchcockian thriller. Its sense of realism in the film's combat aspects rank it up there with "Saving Private Ryan" and "Platoon." Everything is rendered in startling detail. Some scenes play out on 20-minute scales, taking their time building the tension up to a crackling level that can be unbearable. Kathryn Bigelow directed the film, and deserves the Oscar for her work her. It's career-best stuff, and she's made some keepers. "Near Dark" and "Point Break" are both incredible cult classics which use the same level and style of real time suspense and visual nerve-wracking; but they are not on quite the same scale at this. In fact, it's hard to find any action or war movie in recent movie to be this effective at maintaining tension. She's made her masterpiece here. I wish this woman made more films. Think of what she could do with some of the slick and boring commerical films that are released weekend after weekend? A real filmmaker, Bigelow goes beyond the action and into the motives of her characters. In a way, it's comparable to "Point Break" in that it features a guy willing to risk everything just to prove himself a badass- to anybody, nobody, it doesn't matter. 

That character is played with skillful, movie-star-in-the-making-magic by Jeremy Renner, who never hits a false note. He's funny, scary, sad, charming, obnoxious, and it all works so well. His Sgt. James is a beautifully rendered movie creation, and his addiction to defusing bombs under stressful circumstances forces the audience to see things from his perspective: that war is a drug. Not all the characters share this insight, and keep the film in check with their own personal demons. Anthony Mackie and Brian Geraghty are the two second leads- and they are equally impressive. Guy Pearce, David Morse, and Ralph Fiennes are the most recognizable faces among the supporting cast, but don't stick around for long. This is Renner's show anyway. He deserves awards attention as well. 

"The Hurt Locker" is not the typical Iraq war movie, and it's not a typical movie period. It could be enjoyed by anyone of any political persuasion, although I would warn you of its rather disturbing impact on your senses and emotions. Like "Saving Private Ryan" and "Platoon," it equals its violent sequences with more emotive moments that ring as powerful as any action sequence. It's one of the best films of 2009, by far.

As I watched Kathryn Bigelow's The Hurt Locker for the first time, I realized that it kept me in a chronic state of anxiety and worry. Suspense such as this is not terribly common nowadays, but it is executed here for nearly the entire running length, and it maintains its effectiveness until the credits roll. Hitchcock's theory of bomb under the table plays out here in its rawest and most potent form. It states that when a bomb under a table explodes, it is a surprise, but when a bomb under table is not exploding, just sitting there ticking away, that is suspense. In the Hurt Locker, there are many bombs under many tables, and boy do they tick away.

Jeremy Renner stars as Staff Sgt. William James, who works with an elite Army bomb squad in Iraq. William is a renegade, a cowboy who seems to greatly enjoy getting into the gritty and clipping bomb wires, and he is damn good at. He is so pumped up by the adrenaline rush of disarming bombs, that his team, made up of Sgt. J. T. Sanborn (Anthony Mackie) and Specialist Owen Eldridge (Brian Geraghty), often times has to try to pull the reigns back a bit. William breaks rules, puts his life and others' in jeopardy, and faces the consequences of his own behavior. 

It is interesting to note that the first thing we see in this film is a quote in which it is highlighted that "War is a Drug." Not only must William face what results from his reckless approach to his job, but he has to live with it as an addiction. "War is a Drug", and it is one that he is fully hooked on. It is one that has effected his personal life, and ruined much of his ability to focus and live and behave in the real world, and in society away from the war. Like all drugs, it distances him from others and forces him into a sort of rebel status. No one else can quite see the things he has witnessed the way that he has witnessed them. It is his gift, this ability to disarm bombs in order to save lives, and to live in the world that he lives in, but it is also his burden.

Renner gives one of the most intensely driven performances ever on screen. William says very little about his life away from Iraq, but tells us everything in a few of complex and visceral scenes that top off this film and edge toward damn near perfect. The sequences in between bombs are short, but they also tell a lot about what being an expert at something that is incredibly unpredictable and dangerous does to someones ability to communicate with others. He is on the fringe of his traditional sanity, and he is pushed over that edge after witnessing something that no person should ever have to see or come to terms with. 

Bigelow takes time with telling us this story. Her shots are very long and deliberate, and make sure that we observe and sweat over the events taking place on screen, and that is why she is able to create such a compelling and emotionally exhausting film. The script is by Mark Boal, who also wrote In the Valley of Elah, another terrific Iraq war movie involving Tommy Lee Jones as a father trying to discover the truth about his missing son. This has a similar feel to Elah, in that it doesn't have any showy, hollywood scenes. War is not glittery and sparkly, and Boal writes with precision and honesty. This is not a film about war heros, it is a film about people who are faced with the job that few people are willing to do.

The greatest thing about The Hurt Locker is that it isn't biased towards the Iraq war. It doesn't settle for a simple message or resolution. There is no 'war is good, war is bad' statement, there's just an honest characterization of the troops and what they are going through. Some love what they are doing, others can't wait to finish. The film acknowledges this and presents us all sides without taking a side. It presents the confusion and madness of war without really saying anything. The actions of the soldiers, especially James (played solidly by Jeremy Rennar), guide the film. There is anger, there is violence, there is sadness, but overall, they are in war. Their actions or emotions are never completely clear. The only thing that is clear is the job they have to do and the consequences of that job. That's the greatest thing of The Hurt Locker- it's honest script. 

Katherine Bigelow, known for such works as Strange Days and Point Break, really shines in this one as a director. Never mind her work with the dedicated actors at her disposal (which is top notch), but the sense of realism and exhilaration she captured is truly something to take note. The film is very suspenseful, never relying on Heavy Metal music to augment a sense of adrenaline. And while the cinematography by Barry Ackroyd isn't that great, it gets the job done in most areas, while also providing some amazing shots from time to time. 

Truly the best Iraq based film yet. Stuff like The Kingdom, Lions For Lambs, Body Of Lies, Stop-Loss, In the Valley Of Elah, Home Of the Brave, etc, don't really do an in-depth representation of the war, just a biased one from the writers and directors point of view. Bigelow and Mark Boal take whatever their personal feelings towards the war aside and create something that audiences would think about and discuss once the film hits the credits, not something that quickly presents itself and leaves. We need more films like The Hurt Locker.

 Although war has become a somewhat overly used subject, there will always be room for new, wondrous looks into the concept of war. The Hurt Locker takes great advantage of that fact and creates a well shot, intense, action packed, thrilling, and well acted war epic. And this is greatly unexpected as well. Kathryn Bigelow directs with enough style to surpass anything she's ever done before. The Hurt Locker delivers emotional quality as well as the intense action of war. This is most definitely, one of 2009's finest films.

    "The rush of battle is often a potent and lethal addiction, for war is a drug."
         Those are the first words you see printed on the screen when The Hurt Locker starts. All that it takes is that very saying to pull you in to the fine narrative style of the film. So....you keep watching, correct? Next, we see an AOD unit in Baghdad. They send Sergeant Thomson, the leader of the unit, to deactivate or dispose of bombs. He finds the bombs via a small robot which was sent to find them. But, there is a man behind these bombs, and via cellphone, this man sets off the bomb, killing Thomson. In desperate need of a replacement, Sergeant William James becomes the new leader of the unit. From then on, the unit carries out missions that they are assigned. You somewhat care about the little characters, because they make connections with even smaller characters. The story is well told and well structured, thanks to the fine writing of Mark Boal. This war story is more on the emotionally wrenching and narrative side, which is a nice little change. I mean, sure. We've had emotional war films in the past, but this is one that actually near perfects the emotional quality. I guess the only real problem there is with the story is the fact that the scenes where the hero is deactivating bombs are the most captivating, despite the nice character moments in between. Altogether, rather intelligent narrative that deserves to be explored. 

      Another thing that makes The Hurt Locker so captivating is how powerful the performances are by the cast. Jeremy Renner(Doyle of 28 Weeks Later) plays the role of Sergeant William James, and he fits absolutely perfectly. His performance is the most powerful of them all. Wow. That's different. I actually like the lead actor's performance the best. Other actors include: Guy Pearce, Anthony Mackie, and David Morse. The performances by the entire cast as a whole are fine.


       The Hurt Locker has some interesting music, although to build the tension, the majority of the film is rather silent. I praise the music from the end titles, though. The sound effects are pretty good.

         What stood out the most to me in The Hurt Locker is the cinematography. This film is shot as intensely as it is unique, which separates it from other war epics. You will get not only unique angles, but shots that increase the tension and the intensity of each scene. I actually think it is the cinematography itself that makes The Hurt Locker experience go by so fast, but that isn't particularly a bad thing. The experience is a good one anyways.

     Wow. What a movie indeed. It deserves ever bit of praise it gets. The Hurt Locker is a classic in both the genre and the world of film, and you can be sure that I'll add it to my DVD Collection soon enough. If you're looking for a perfectly dramatic, intense, crafty, and visually stunning war epic, The Hurt Locker delivers. This is how war was meant to be. Beautiful. Visually stunning. Often times painful to think about. Emotional. And apparently, its also the best kind of drug out there.

Kathryn Bigelow's "The Hurt Locker" is a thrilling human interest story exploring motivation in the era of industrialized military adventurism.

Framing voluntary continued participation in war as an addiction brings to light a method of maintaining sanity that has not been frequently explored in a serious war drama thus far.  In a post-Vietnam era war where the U.S. military doesn't exactly know who the enemy belligerents are, i.e., it could be everybody or nobody, thrill seeking is as good a way as any to artificially maintain an even keel.  The improvised explosive devices exacerbate that problem.  Any object could be a bomb.  Having a faceless enemy elevates the question of just why, exactly, were we fighting a war in Iraq.  Who was the enemy?  What was the real objective?

Jeremy Renner's character SFC James' unconventional approach to war is highlighted by his Bravo Company partners, who take more typical approaches to the situations they find themselves in.  Anthony Mackie's SGT Sanborn is a man who sees the value in sticking to the military structures that SFC James interprets a little loosely and Brian Geraghty's SPC Eldridge has lost much of the insulation protecting his nerves from the constant onslaught of life-endangering situations.  As a result, they have slightly more functional difficulty with war than their team leader.  

This difference in approach also makes for some situational humor spurred by SFC James.  Though it may feel like a humorous vestige of the civil society the soldiers grew up in, the recurring placement of the habitual nicety "please" is reflective of the artifice (questionable integrity of and shallow justification) of the whole Iraq situation.  SFC James is a rogue technician in a rogue war in a formerly rogue middle eastern state.  In this particular situation he is the normal one, not his more tentative team mates.

Though that's not to say he doesn't have an arc.  There is one iconic, but unsubtle scene where he showers after a mission with all his gear on.  One can feel that the man wishes, in this moment, that the water would rinse away the weight of mistakes made, in addition to the blood that leaches off.  The strength of Renner's performance as SFC James makes me want to see more of that character, which is unlikely because this isn't a popcorn film like "The Bourne Identity" or "Casino Royale."

For this story, war mostly takes place in a medium density arid urban setting, rather than a continental countryside or a jungle somewhere in the global south.  For each IED that Bravo Company attempts to disarm, whether successful or not, there is an audience.  Folks of many walks tune into the grotesque magic shows now performing in the Baghdad public square.  Will the magician disappear?  Will the puppet master delight again?

What makes this film so thrilling, in addition to being an engaging drama, is the expert depiction of urgent escalation and suspense.  Using very effective cinematic techniques, Bigelow binds the audience to a fluctuating roller coaster of dread and immense tension.  The editing and stylish speed manipulations help transport the audience to wartime Baghdad.  The action that takes place and the visuals presented carry a wrenching visceral quality, translating the often remote brutality of war to the human body, in varying intensities and degrees of life endangerment.  The pacing is pretty tight as well, responsibly toying with the audience's breath.

The blend of fidget-cam and completely static shots is modulated to the intensity of the action on screen.  It's still and clear when the characters have the luxury of precise examination and shaky and shallow in situations where they don't.  Unlike other films that use constant camera shake to lend "authenticity or grit" constantly, as a baseline, this film uses it to obscure details for the audience when those same details are obscured for our characters by escalating situations.  The constant assessment of where to focus your attention so that you might to fight another day translates perfectly.

The production design is excellent and never looks cheap (to my lay eye).  The weaponry and equipment used looks darn authentic.  It lacks the plasticky/summarized look that many throwaway action films, with much larger budgets I might add, have.  The suit that SFC James wears looks like the real deal, sweltering in the desert sun.

Kathryn Bigelow's Peckinpah-ish chutzpah finally yielded Oscar gold with this film.  She has portrayed macho men doing ridiculous things before, but didn't break through to critical adoration until now.  Just as brilliantly written as "Inglourious Basterds," not in terms of dialog, but in terms of symbolism and historical encapsulation and easily a rawer and less tried and true a story than Avatar, "The Hurt Locker" definitely deserved its Oscar for Best Picture, despite all the grumbling afterward.  Mark Boal's highly detailed and satisfying script is a perfect compliment to Kathryn Bigelow's artful spunk.  As a result, the film is an interesting hybrid of a ballsy and entertaining action film and a serious emotional drama focusing on a select group of people in some of the most intense situations possible.  The film might not be perfectly realistic per se, but it feels completely true in terms of the parts of the human emotion spectrum it covers.  Then again, criticizing a fictional film for its inaccuracy is like criticizing a painting for not being photorealistic.  

Interestingly, it feels much less Hollywood than "Platoon," which, 26 years later, feels more like a counterpart to "Predator" than "Apocalypse Now."  Though it may not be as triumphant as Francis Ford Coppola's "Apocalypse Now," "The Hurt Locker" is just as fitting a portrayal of the Iraq conflict, finding the elusive sweet spot between visceral intensity, intelligent writing, and a resonant topicality that stops well short of the preachiness that is so easy to fall into.

Movies based on current events can be a strange breed. They're often preachy and 

always biased. However, they often get good reviews regardless, so I wasn't putting too much stock into the amazing reviews for The Hurt Locker. I remember when I saw 500 Days of Summer, I had the choice of seeing this instead. Both were only playing in the one theater in Toronto at the time, and it turns out they are both two of the best movies of the year hands down.

The Hurt Locker defies expectations and, instead of being about the war, is a character study. The movie has zero poltical stance. It portrays the bombers as monsters and many other Iraqis as sympathetic. If it had been about the bombers, it would have probably found some sympathy, but this isn't their story.

This is the story of Staff Seargent William James, assigned to a bomb disposal unit in Iraq, replacing their recently blown-up teammate. James is reckless, which pisses off his teammates whose lives are put in danger. This is made explicitly clear during his first job, where he holds up a speeding taxi (and bomber suspect) with a pistol.

James is a static character, and while he learns over the course of the film, he doesn't change per se. The initially unsensible character simply becomes more and more clear to the audience over time. In fact, I would bet his actions early in the film would seem quite natural if seen a second time having gotten to know the character. Renner's performance is absolutely excellent and completely believable and the most realistic and complex badass to cross the screen as of late.

The movie also focuses on his teammates, who do evolve over the course of the film. Veteran soldier Sanborn is the straight man of the film, and at first appears to be the main character. We sympathize with his troubles with James and his position of responsibility. The other member of the squad is Eldridge, representing those who really don't want to be in Iraq. He's not a pansy, but he panicks and desperately wants to go home. Both of these characters serve as foils to James, and as such are often sidelined, but nonetheless add to the film.

Aside from those three, few characters are expanded upon. Guy Pearce and Ralph Fiennes are excellent in small roles, the latter as perhaps the closest the movie comes to commentary, singling the issue of military contractors. Lost's Evangeline Lilly and House's David Morse also make cameos.

While not an action movie, The Hurt Locker is chock full of tension. The situations that James puts himself into are pulse-pounding and the outcome never seems certain. Theres a sniper battle which is excellently filmed (one odd slow-down shot aside), although some parts of it make little sense (notably the accuracy of the enemy sniper). I've also heard some complaints from people who know their stuff about realism, but these are moot to the average film viewer. This is one of the most suspenseful movies of the year hands down, and whether realistic or not, it certainly FEELS realistic.

The Hurt Locker is an excellent movie that only gets better the more I think about it. A great character portrayed with a clearly Oscar-worthy performance with ridiculous amounts of tension add up to make The Hurt Locker one of the best war movies of the decade and proof that contemporary war movies can work without being political.

THE HURT LOCKER lives up to its title.  It is all about HURT as we follow a reckless Army Sergeant during a tour of duty in Iraq where he defuses enemy bombs.  Director Kathryn Bigelow, whose movies include the fabulous vampire movie NEAR DARK and the sci-fi thriller STRANGER DAYS, does a bang-up job capturing the atmosphere and characters caught up in Iraq.  SSgt. William James (Jeremy Renner of 28 DAYS LATER) replaces Sgt. Matt Thompson (Guy Pearce of L.A. CONFIDENTIAL) after he dies trying to neutralize an I.E.D., improvised explosive device, in an Iraq town. Sgt. JT Sanborn (Anthony Mackie of NOTORIOUS) does not get along with SSgt. James at first because James likes his job too much and derives an adrenaline thrill from being in dangerous predicaments.  Spc. Owen Eldridge (Brian Geraghty of BOBBY) does not like the insane risks that James takes.  In one scene, after he discovers that a parked car outside the UN building has been booby-trapped with enough explosives to kill everybody within a block, James shucks his 80 pounds of bomb disposal uniform gear and sets out disarming the home-made but ingenious explosives.  Colonel Reed (David Morse of THE ROCK) personally congratulates James for a job well-done and learns that James has disable over 800 bombs. The picture that Bigelow paints about the war in Iraq and the problems that the bomb disposal teams encounter is powerful stuff.  At another point, James and company find a human bomb--i.e., a corpse with explosives concealed in its stomach--and James defuses it.  Writer Mark Boal was an embedded journalist and he wrote the screenplay that pulls no punches and you will no blink if you get engrossed in this taunt melodrama. This independent production was lensed on location in the Middle-Eastern country of Jordan but an American distributor picked it up for an American theatrical release.
