First and foremost, I'd like to comment on this film's direction.  Kathryn Bigelow, yes, a woman, crafted and directed this film into one of the best war/combat movies of all time.  I'm no sexist, but my jaw dropped when I discovered a woman directed this picture.  Extremely surprised.  

Now, to the movie itself.  It was executed in such a way that, to be honest, sometimes I would loose myself in watching it, feeling as though I am watching an extremely dynamic documentary about real soldiers in real situations in real places.  That said, there is something to be said about lack of any real story.  If I were to try and tell the 'story' of 'The Hurt Locker,' I'm afraid I would not be entirely successful, because the entire story can be summed in one quote cited at the beginning of the film.  'War is a drug.'

Although, I am a fan of a good story, the character development and portrayal in this movie was near flawless.  I only say 'near' flawless because I know nothing is flawless, but I certainly can't think of any character problems off the top of my head.  This film is without a doubt a character study, which more than makes up for lack of linear story-telling, which would seem wildly inappropriate in this movie, and really, in war movies in general.

I've already commented on the acting (phenomenal) and the direction (surprisingly outstanding), but I'd like to touch on the cinematography.  I have very mixed feelings about it to be honest.  In one side of my brain, I find it incredibly amateurish and shaky- unprofessional.  In the other side, however, I find it supremely appropriate.  I think it's the cinematography of this movie that makes it feel so real (like a documentary, as stated earlier) that you do forget you're watching a movie-movie.  When you do remember, however, it's a bit of a 'meh...' moment.

The music was appropriate.  Nothing amazing, and certainly nothing I'd like to carry around on my MP3 player, but it worked for the movie.  

The script, again, was remarkably written.  I could swear most of this was improvised by actual soldiers.  I hate to sound like a broken record, but when you think that these are actors reading a script rather than soldiers in them midst of combat, you just have to stand back and say 'Whoa...'

All in all, 'The Hurt Locker' passed my expectations considerably.  I was expecting an extremely anti-war message, but what I got was a great illustration about how war changes a man, but how much these men and women go through every day while on their tours - God bless them for defending our home.

The ending scene was particularly humbling.  After seeing two hours or combat and hardship in Iraq, after seeing two hours of how dangerous life is over there, after 120 grueling minutes of seeing the conditions of that place, we're treated to five minutes of America.  An entire isle at a grocery store devoted to cereal.  A room full of toys for a child that can't even walk yet.  A kitchen without bugs.  Oh, what we take for granted.  'The Hurt Locker' might unintentionally relay the message that, like the old saying, 'Freedom isn't free.'

'The Hurt Locker' is a great film, filled with action, and character-driven dialog and tension.  Bravo, once again, to Kathryn Bigelow for directing such a movie.  

So just what is the Hurt Locker?  I think it's different for everyone.  For me, it's the restless self - the part of us that wants more.

The Hurt Locker is regarded by film critics as being the best film of 2009. While it is certainly a good film and a cinematical achievement for director Kathryn Bigelow, there are just some things that didn't sit well with me, but let's get to that later. For now, let's relish in what may be the most important film of the year.

From a film maker's perspective, The Hurt Locker is absolutely beautiful to look at, especially on Blu-Ray. The opening sequence alone is a marvel to view, as after the explosive goes off we are treated to a slow-mo sequence of dirt flying into the air and rubble vibrating off of an abandoned vehicle. With the use of S16mm cameras we get a very gritty feel, which works well with the locations and action. Speaking of action, there is barely any of it in the entire film, yet, at the same time, this is one of the most intense and suspenseful films I have ever seen. Not since Hitchcock has someone been able to create real suspense, a feeling that had my on the edge of my seat. The sniper shootout is probably my favorite scene from any film of 2009, as it really recreated what it must have felt like to be in that situation.

Tense, Suspenseful, and Action-packed have all been used to describe this movie. It is all of those things. A war movie set in Iraq, that's not really about the Iraq war, 'Hurt Locker' follows a 3-man elite Army bomb squad led by "loose cannon" bomb diffuser SSgt. William James as they try to save lives and survive their stressful jobs for 40 days before ending their tour.
That's about it for plot. Survive war until you can go home. That's enough. The characters fight and bond while tackling many different bomb diffusing scenarios.

The Hurt Locker grabs your attention from the very opening scene. It is thrilling and full of excitement.  Director Kathryn Bigelow (James Cameron´s ex wife who directed Point Break, the cult classic film for surfers around the world) does an excellent job of putting the viewer right in the middle of the Iraq war. Kathryn doesn´t waste time at introducing the characters, it just puts us right in the middle of a tense situation in where a bomb squad is trying to disarm an explosive device in the middle of an Iraqi street. The tension is felt from that very opening scene and doesn`t stop during the two hours the film lasts. This is without a doubt one of the best movies of the year and recently won best picture at the Critics Awards. This was one of my favorite films of the year along with Inglorious Basterds and Kathryn Bigelow is just as well as deserving as Tarantino for the best director award because she does an excellent job with this war movie. She will have a lot of competition however from her ex-husband Cameron who just made the biggest box office hit of the year with Avatar. I think Bigelow is much more deserving however because she took a genre that has been overused and made an excellent thriller out of it. I know most audiences are tired of watching movies about the Iraq war, but trust me The Hurt Locker is worth your time and will grab your attention from the first minute. I think it is the best war movie made in recent years and I really loved the ending which connects perfectly with the opening quotes the movie presents. 

The film is set in Iraq and we are introduced to the action immediately where an American Army Bomb squad is trying to deactivate an explosive device in the middle of a populated Iraqi street.  The squad is formed by Sgt. Matt Thompson (played by Guy Pierce from Memento) who has the very difficult task of trying to deactivate the bomb, Sgt. JT Sanborn (played by Anthony Mackie) who is Thompson`s eyes in the mission and is in charge of protecting him from the very hostile environment, and Spc. Owen Eldridge (played by Brian Geraghty) who assists both Sanborn and Thompson in the mission. The team first sends a robotic box to try to disarm the bomb, but things go wrong so Thompson has to go in himself. Thompson isn`t able to disable the bomb in time and it explodes taking his life in the process. The team is devastated by the loss, especially Owen who has to see a shrink, but in war there is no time to lose and they have to continue with their mission. They are introduced to the new replacement, Sgt. William James (played by Jeremy Renner from S.W.A.T.) who proves to be nothing like Thompson. In the team`s first assignment he acts recklessly and disables a bomb with a fearless attitude and wastes no time in listening to his teammates. He has an alternative approach and the team will just have to adapt to his new methods. Jeremy Renner gives a terrific performance and one of my favorite of the year. The success of the movie coincides with his performance and the character he personifies. Ralph Fiennes has a small role in the movie along with David Morse and Evangeline Lilly (from the Lost series), but the less known actors are the ones who have more screen time and they all give great performances.

The success of this movie relies on several factors: Kathryn Bigelow`s direction that allowed her to make a great film out of an overused genre, Renner`s cool performance which allowed the audience to identify and care for the character he created and experience how war had become an addiction for him, and Mark Boal`s original screenplay (he had only written one other movie in the past, In The Valley of Elah) which allowed for some good dialogues. These three elements combined perfectly together to make this one of the best films of the year. Another positive aspect about The Hurt Locker is that it combined several different filming techniques allowing for some documentary style shots at times which gave it a more realistic feeling. I`m a sucker for films that have a good ending and I absolutely loved the ending in this movie which tied nicely to the opening quote of the movie which stated: ¨The rush of battle is often a potent and lethal addiction, for war is a drug.¨ We find this to be true for Renner`s character after the final conversation he has with his baby. The Hurt Locker is also one of my favorite war movies so I highly recommend this film to all. I guarantee you that it will have you at the edge of your seat during the entire two hours. It is an excellent and near perfect thriller.

The Hurt Locker is so much more than just another war film. Unlike the obvious war movies that come to mind, this one focuses on the lives of our American Soldiers inside the heat of combat and the ever growing intensity of realizing that anything in this war could be a target or a victim.

This film is unlike most war films that have been released in the past decade. Unlike the Academy Award winning 'Saving Private Ryan', this film does not focus entirely on combat. It dives into the reality of what type of dangers and stress a soldier really experiences out in war.

Potential unknown actors star in this movie, but they do an incredibly believable job in protraying their characters. Every single one of them did an amazing job and I hope their performances grant them bigger projects in the future.

The story follows a US Army EOD squad throughout the Iraq War in 2003. Now for those who don't know military jargon, EOD stands for 'Explosive Ordinance Disposal.' And that's exactly what this team does. They are required to disarm and destroy potential bombs and IEDs (Improvised Explosive Device). Well Jeremy Renner stars as Sergeant First Class James, an EOD squad leader in charge of disarming these located bombs. Anthony Mackie and Brian Geraghty co-star as his squadmates. Now the film follows the daily tasks of these soldiers, locating these bombs and disarming them without causing total chaos, and more importantly; to disarm these bombs before the timer expires or the trigger is pulled.

Now this film is extremely original and perhaps the best military Iraq War film I've ever seen. Watching SGT James take out a bomb in front of hundreds of Iraqi eyes makes the scene extremely tense. Knowing that any of these Iraqis could be an insurgent just waiting for the right moment to pull the bomb's trigger is just nerve racking. I mean there will be several moments in the film where you will be digging your nails into the seat from the anxiety you'll be experiencing. But that is just the suspense/thriller part of the film.

The action is great. Although the film doesn't focus itself entirey on firefights, you'll still see a fair share of some mortar explosions. The camera work reminded me of District 9 sometimes, expecially during some of the frantic action scenes. It made me feel as if I were the soldier looking around for the enemy, which is definitely a plus. There was an awesome sniper scene that totally puts the viewer in the environment of what being a sniper is all about.

The movie really shines when it displays the lives of these three EOD soldiers. It shows a lot of the anxiety they face, the troubles, the drama, the parties, the alcohol, the love, the hate and even the addictions. It really does show the grim reality of what combat can do to a human. What it actually can do to someone thats seen so much war. If i were stick this film to a genre i would say that its a thriller/Drama, but a really good one.

The actors in the flm were absolutely great. They filled their character's shoes to the letter. Their performances were magnificient. The story, like I said, was original. Actually it was adapted from the experiences of a reporter that followed an EOD team throughout the opening months of the Iraq War back in 2003, but that is what made the film so real. I men you really feel what these guys are going through. You actually feel the pressure of having to disarm a bomb with hundreds of lives at stake, and you're the only one that knows the destruction it can cause. 

For those audiences that aren't up to speed on military jargon, the movie does a good job in explaining most things. Some exceptions are some minor stuff that really won't take away from the movie. But the plot is fully explained. There is no plotholes whatsoever, I mean this movie was completely written and shot, absolutely great. 

I remember feeling so much tension when I saw this film. Knowing that my friend is an EOD for the USAF really made me want to see this film. All my military friends have seen this movie, and I definitely recommmend every military family or anyone that is interested in the military to watch this film. But then again, its a great film period. You don't need to be in the military to understand this film. If you're a thriller fan, you should see this, but its mandatory for any service men and women to see this. My military career won't put me in as a bomb specialist but now i have at least a small taste of what some of my brothers-in-arms face on a daily basis.

Definitely a great and I recommend to any thriller or military fan. I give The Hurt Locker 4 Stars.

The film is very strong in every facet, acting, directing, story, writing, and overall effect, but its great at none. Its kind of a jack-of-all trades effort, that left me waiting for that final push to make it great, and for me, it didn't come. Its one of those movies that you can't really say anything bad about, but that doesn't make it great. Hurt Locker falls more into the category of war films like Full Metal Jacket and Jarhead, as it tries to balance the drama with the action.
Hurt Locker follow Sgt. James who is a reckless bomb tech who gets thrills off tempting death, and is an adrenaline junkie. "War is a drug" the film opens with. He replaces the recently deceased Guy Pearce as the bomb tech in the squad, who only has a month left in their rotation, and just wants to get out alive, and play it safe. You can see the oncoming problems.
Jeremy Renner is strong as the lead, not a revelation, but strong. He goes from being a maverick, and borders on unlikable most of the time, if it weren't for the kid subplot, he'd have almost no humanity.  If you're a famous actor in this movie, chances are, you'll die. Ralph Fiennes and Guy Pearce make cameos, and die off quick, and David Morse pops up for a minute. Anthony Mackie gives a strong performance as the buy-the-numbers Sgt. who clashes with Renner's character. Brian Gerarghty is the weak link as his soldier struggling with death, buckles under the odd amount of attention the film gives the character.
The dialogue is sharp, and full of the military-type one-liners and tension easers that you've come to expect.  The film has some odd subplots going on, like the base doctor, and the vengeance sequence that goes nowhere, and was mostly superfluous.  They're both kind of predictable, but don't do much to add to the film.
Some of the direction choices were weird, like showing a slow-mo shell fall to the ground, during a sequence that didn't call for it, because their were 2 other killshots that didn't get the same treatment. But mostly the tension is kept high in the bomb scenes, although they get slightly tedious, as they are just reaction shots of Renner looking concerned and focused, and fumbling around with wires, and we're never explained to how or what he's doing.

"The Hurt Locker" is the definitive movie of the ongoing war in the Middle East. It is one of those rare, unexpected gems that appears every so often in the world of cinema, as it is fitting for its time and effective in its message. "The Hurt Locker" is grim, intense, dark, and not for the faint of heart. It is a psychological study into the mind of the soldier stationed in the Middle East, and the horrors that these brave men encounter on a day-to-day basis. The men portrayed in this movie probably have the worst duty out of anyone serving in the Army, as they are part of a bomb squad unit in a country where almost anything or anyone could be a potential threat. They are the War's unsung heroes, and their great deeds have now been brought to light.

The movie engrosses you and pulls you into its dark and disturbing world. A world millions of miles away from home, and where the unexpected can occur at any given moment in the chaos of the battlefield. The movie twists and turns, and surprises and overwhelms. The bomb squad unit could be walking around in what appears to be a deserted town, only to be confronted by a suspicious object laying in the middle of a clearing. Could it be a bomb? Or is it just what it is and nothing more? It is this element of unsettling anticipation to see what happens next, that drives this film. Much like the War itself, this movie is entirely unpredictable. You just never know what the hell is going to happen next.

My eyes were glued to the screen for the entire two hours. A near-perfect film, I give it 4 1/2 out of 5 stars.

Kathryn Bigelow's action movie sensibilities make some of the setpieces here a lot more fun and suspenseful than they have any right to be, as every new situation William finds himself in keeps getting progressively worse than the previous one, but I found the movie to be a meandering and episodic mess on the narrative side of things. I enjoyed knowing there was someone like Bigelow in the world, a woman director who was interested in making fun horror/action flicks, but based on what she does here she seems to be turning into a Paul Greengrass clone both thematically and aesthetically, and that's just disappointing to me. Seriously, this random zooming and shaky cam bullshit has to stop. Jeremy Renner has a nice screen presence and does alright with his character, but aside from a couple of tense sequences and an undeservingly cool ending, the movie didn't do much for me.

"The Hurt Locker" is the best film I've seen that covers the shaky subject of the current war in Iraq. It feels like a more mature version of "Jarhead", but it's not told through the eyes of a regular soldier making his way through the conflicts of the Middle East. It's told through Staff Sgt. William James, a man with the meticulous job as a bomb defuser. He's good at what he does, and he knows it. But he's cocky and treats his job like an addiction - he basks in the thrill and exhilaration of flirting with death. The film is directed by Kathryn Bigelow, a filmmaker with a knack for creating a tense and intriguing film akin to Paul Greengrass (The Bourne Ultimatum, United 93). It's a suspenseful film, complete with a great plot and some deep characters that you'll come to know and understand more fully the mind of a modern day soldier in Iraq.

Jeremy Renner (who looks like a double for Daniel Craig) plays the protagonist Staff Sgt. William James, a professional bomb defuser whose only place where he truly belongs is in the midst of war. He is accompanied by Sergeant Sanborn (Anthony Mackie) and Specialist Eldridge (Brian Geraghty) who act as bodyguards to him while he is busy defusing bombs. Sanborn just wants to get out of the war safe and sound; Eldridge is an amateur who still has much to learn. But James is cocky and treats everything like a game, and Renner portrays his character like a master, displaying James's psychological makeup not through dialogue, but through his actions. In fact, there are relatively few striking conversations throughout. But when there are moments of dialogue, they are as intense as the times when James is busy defusing bombs. Take for example the conversation between James and Sanborn towards the end of the film. Sanborn breaks down and tells James that he's afraid - of dying, of the war, of never even having a family of his own. James understands what Sanborn is going through, but he himself will never actually feel the emotions Sanborn is feeling. Like the opening quote at the start of the film, "War is a drug".

The scenes where James defuses the bombs are some of the most suspenseful movie scenes I've ever seen. The film is just as intense as "No Country for Old Men", but with less kinetic energy, and instead fixed on one place - on James and his intricate work on tinkering with bombs. And the main character himself is just as intriguing as the plot. He longs for belonging throughout the film, and when he goes home at the end of the movie, you can see he clearly does not belong in normal society anymore. His place is in the red zone in Iraq, gambling life and death every time he puts on his bombsuit. In that way, "The Hurt Locker" reminds me of "The Wrestler" because both deal with characters who need to find a sense of belonging. Micky Rourke finds his home on the wrestling ring. Jeremy Renner, in the middle of war. The ending to the film is gripping and displays the impact of all the violence soldiers go through in an unrelenting way. Some find it hard to accept, some are addicted to it. This isn't just another run of the mill war movie.

The acting is brilliant, the story is compelling, and the camera work makes this film as tense as any thriller out there. Years from now, this will be one of the films remembered for portraying the current War in Iraq. It's one of the best war films ever made, and one of the most memorable films I've ever seen. The character development here is deep and intriguing, offering the most captivating film of the year. Definitely Academy Award gold.

The Hurt Locker is receiving a lot of Oscar Buzz, and after checking it out on Blu-Ray, I can see why. Kathryn Bigelow's Iraq War film is a sort of intimate epic - a look at mainly 3 men whose lives are on the line every day, disarming IEDs on the roads of Iraq. Plenty of explosions rock the screen, as do incredible performances from Renner and Mackie and a tight, terse filming style that adds suspense and tension every minute.

This is a great movie, easily the best of the subject of our current war in the Middle East. Politics are ditched for an objective look at those who are there (some because they want to be more than others), and this lets us see the characters as the heroes they are on a daily basis.

However, this view of the war also seems to leave the film feeling a little incomplete. What is the end result? The level of character growth is minimal - it seems the conflicts between the 3 men who are all vastly different (and stereotypical, one a cowboy, one scared shitless, one the calm silent leader) never leads them to grow or change in anyway. We know who they are, and with no growth at the end, we wonder exactly what we just watched. It left me slightly puzzled at the end of the movie - a minor "what was the point of them being who they were anyways?" moment. 

Despite its issues with character development, calling this movie intense doesn't do it justice. Every minute in the field is filled with suspense and drama, as soldiers scan rooftops and windows, we see Iraqi civilians how they do - who is an enemy and who isn't? These moments are the movie's most terrific scenes - instead of wondering where the characters are, let's see how they act in the field, in their element. It works well.

The visuals of Iraq (actually Jordan, its neighboring country) are superb. The explosions, the gunfights (including one amazing sniper battle, easily the best moment of the movie), they are all shot with incredible skill. 

More on that sniper scene (not to spoil anything) - this is what should have been the turning point of the movie - in fact, it seemed like it until the rest played out. There, we see the 3 men work as a team more than ever, overcoming their weaknesses to take down the enemy as best as they do in the film, but nothing comes of it. This scene, as pivotal as it was, was left empty without  any results. 

Regardless of my feelings, I recommend the movie, and will watch it again down the road to see if I can get a different feel for it. It may just be me, but for all the strengths of the film (cinematography, acting, script), a few weaknesses stop it from being a true classic. It is close, though.

4/5 Stars-The Iraq/Afghanistan conflict now has it's definitive film portrayal.  What "Platoon" did for Vietnam and what "Saving Private Ryan" and "Band of Brothers" did for World War II, "The Hurt Locker" serves as the best (to this point) look at the quagmire in Iraq.  The film is brilliantly shot, and will likely win an OscarÂ® for Best Cinematography.  Kathryn Bigelow deserves serious consideration for Best Director, but will likely lose to her ex-husband, James Cameron.  All of the acting performances are solid, and I liked how none of them were superstars-even Ralph Fiennes and Guy Pearce don't stand out from everyone else.

The story dragged for me in spots, particularly when Bigelow tried to show the tension between the soldiers.  Not a lot of emotion is shown, which is typical for soldiers in combat, so I didn't really care if they got along or not.  I didn't need a knock down, drag out action epic, but it seemed more of a character study, and anytime Jeremy Renner wasn't trying to diffuse a bomb, it wasn't keeping me on the edge of my seat.  However, the long distance firefight between the American/English soldiers and the Iraqis was the best part of the film, and probably is the best overall showcase on how war truly is:  Boring, hot, tiresome, but unbearably intense.

Overall, it is still one of the best films of the year, but the narrative was quite plodding, and at times I wondered where it was going.  We find out by the end (which I enjoyed--war is "better" than real life), but getting there was a bit wishy-washy.

The Hurt Locker probably carries more messages about addiction than it does about any war topic! The fact that its set in the middle of a warzone just makes it more upsetting, real and highlights that while some may not like the conflict or killing, others feed of it. 

I could go on to say more, but basically its an intense and unnerving movie, which makes you think without preaching!

The movie starts off with a quote by Chris Hedges that reads, "The rush of battle is often a potent and lethal addiction, for war is a drug." I did not pay much attention to this quote and how much it relates to the movie until the end. I'll get back to the quote later. "The Hurt Locker" was everything I thought it would be. An intense and suspenseful ride that grabs your attention and makes you focus on the details. I noticed there is no musical score to go with the movie. The pure intensity of the scenes and the wonder of what is going to happen next leaves you on the edge. The movie takes us into a realistic view of modern day warfare and the many danger of being on the battlefield. The main dangers they focus on are bombs and the art of defusing them. 

The movie starts off in Iraq, the year 2004. Sgt. Matt Thompson (Guy Pearce) and his team have received a call about a bomb and it's their job to take care of it. What seemed like a routine bomb disposal goes tragically wrong for Sgt. Thompson. I was recently introduced to Guy Pearce and found him to be a very underrated actor. I've become a fan of his work and would have liked to have seen more of him in this movie but that would have stole Jeremy Renner's thunder. After the unfortunate event they call in a US Army Ranger specialist SSgt. William James (Jeremy Renner) to take Sgt. Thompson's place. He is greeted by Sgt. JT Sanborn, (Anthony Mackie) who was part of Sgt. Thompson's team, to welcome him to his new home and team. On their first call out we find out SSgt. James is either very confident or very cocky. He likes to confront everything head on and is not afraid to express his opinion. Fully suited in his blast suite he finds the bomb, checks it, and defuses the charge. Thinking everything was done and over with he finds seven more. With an Iraqi spectator watching SSgt. James work, time becomes a factor in the equation and the pressure was multiplied by 7. There are a couple of more bomb scenes in the movie but it threw me a curve ball when I saw the sniper fight scene, which was one of my favorite scenes There is a lot more to this movie than defusing bombs so I'll let you experience what the movie has to offer.

I took a look at the mental aspect of the movie and what runs through the soldier's heads. Whether it's dealing with the death of a fallen comrade or staying calm and focused while staring death in the face. The dialogue in the movie is great and from what I've heard very realistic and true to life. There are two scenes that caught my attention. The first was a conversation between Spc. Owen Eldridge and Col. John Cambridge and dealing with what they have seen on the battlefield and having to live with it for the rest of their life. Especially if one of them was a key factors that could have decided whether someone lives or dies. The second is the heart-to-heart between SSgt. James and Sgt. Sanborn about life in uniform and life out of uniform. When you wear that uniform you are not afraid to die for what you believe in but life out of uniform all you want to do is live your life to the fullest and enjoy everything it has to offer. Our mind can only handle so much before we can't take it anymore. 

I give Kathryn Bigelow all the credit she deserves when it came to directing this movie. The cinematography was amazing. All of the actors put on great performances and all had their unique personalities. I expect Jeremy Renner to be nominated and hopefully win the Oscar for best actor. His character has so much depth and so many different shades and it's hard to tell which side of SSgt. James we will encounter in the next scene. Getting back to the quote from the beginning, for SSgt. James war was his drug and he needed his adrenaline fix. I started watching this movie lying down and ended it by literally sitting at the edge of my seat. An overall great film that I would recommend to anyone who likes war dramas or suspenseful thrillers. This is not a full on action movie with mindless special effects, so do not expect to see bullets flying and random explosions every other scene.

The Hurt Locker was directed by Kathryn Bigelow (Point Break) and written by Mark Boal. It stars Jeremy Renner as Sgt. William James, a team leader for a bomb squad stationed in Iraq. The other members of his team are Sgt. JT Sanborn played by Anthony Mackie and Spc. Owen Eldridge played by Brian Geraghty. The story takes place over a 39 day period where Bravo company is waiting to be relieved so they can go home.

This movie's directing is fantastic. The terrifying suspense that builds over time with each bomb wondering if it will be someone's last bomb to attempt to defuse. The terrain, heat, and dust were so well captured, they were making ME thirsty! Emotionally, the life and death situation these soldiers were put into everyday really messed with their psyche and perception of their mortality. James is a wildman, fearless to just jump into any situation recklessly, Sanborn tries his best to keep everyone safe but is afraid of commitment and getting too close to a woman back home, and Eldridge is getting therapy from a Colonel because he so intensely feels the strain that every day he might die.

The actors very clearly defined their characters. All were well developed with layers in their performance, not all bravado or all fear. They just worked amazingly well as a unit. I have a hard time even singling out any of the three because as soon as I attribute something to one in my head, I remember something else one of the others did. Let's just say they handled the heavy burden of this movie incredibly well and I hope to see more from them in the future.

One last note, turns out James' wife back home is Evangeline Lilly, Kate from LOST. My husband and James have something in common, if that was what they had to come home to, they'd be bored too, haha. We're not Kate or Jack fans. We are fans of Locke and Ben!

As I popped "The Hurt Locker" into the DVD player I was anxious. "Is it really as good as everyone says it is?" "Will it live up too all the critical success it has received?" After watching the film, the answer was simple: yes. From the very beginning it grabs its audience by the face and pulls them into the high tension situations that its characters live in. Dragging us at high speeds though desiccated deserts and urban combat zones where almost anything can happen at anytime it both enthralls us and finds the time for good old fashion drama. Masterful director Kathryn Bigelow has created the best movie thus far about our war in the Middle East, possibly the best ever, however only time can tell that fact.

For those who do not already know the film's premise, it follows the story of a bomb squad located in Afghanistan. The squad's members consist of Staff Sergeant William James (Jeremy Renner), Sergeant JT Sanborn (Anthony Mackie), and Specialist Owen Eldridge (Brian Geraghty.) However, looking at the sum of the film's scenes one may not be to consider it much of story at all. It is not that it is incomprehensible, in fact it is extremely pertinent, but it seems to buck general tradition of storytelling. There is no constant, long term goal in the minds of the characters. It has a definite protagonist but the film is much less than solely about him. If I had to describe it I may have to say that it is about three men's reaction to war they are involved in, and I'm not talking about their political reaction. However, looking back on it I feel that Bigelow (or Boal) couldn't have chosen a better method in presenting this film. The character's lack of purpose beyond defusing bombs allows the film to thoroughly explore both their high tension environment and its effect on their minds.

Complimenting its ability to explore, the film's three main characters all contrast wildly to give a wide variety of viewpoints and reactions to the war. For instance, Specialist Eldridge is convinced that he will die before his rotation is over, and thus he is extremely afraid (after all, if "so many people have died already why not [him]?" Sergeant Sanborn is also scared; however he faces his opposition with courage and extreme level headedness. Staff Sergeant James however, seems to lack any fear, or caution for that matter, of the world he lives in. In fact, he every minute of it relishes. There is a quote in the beginning of film explaining Staff Sergeant James: "The rush of battle is a potent and often lethal addiction, for war is a drug." This quote hangs true in every way for James.

On a more technical note, I found the film, and I have no doubt that others will as well, uncannily suspenseful. Note when I say this that I am not talking about ironically predictable trashy suspense, but rather true suspense. When you know something is going to happen, you just don't know when and to whom it will happen to. Even at that, the film will sometimes give us and the characters a sigh relief. It addition to being thoroughly entertaining, it gloriously avoids a political bias. It does not possess thinly veiled monologues or irritating end credit statistics. It neither villanizes Afghanistan nor patronizes our troops. Rather, it simply gives us an unwavering glimpse into the lives of our soldiers. Final Rating: 5/5

One of the best Iraq War movies and one of 2009's great films. It's a deft blend of a war film and an action picture, delivering quiet devastation in its uncompromising dissection of the psychological effects of war and mixing heart-pounding dread with adrenaline-fueled excitement. Brilliantly shot and cut, it puts us right in the shoes of a bomb disposal (EOD) unit. It's grueling work day in and day out, a job that keeps the men on edge since danger can come from any random stranger with a cell phone or a video camera, where the wrong move or slow timing can mean death by explosion. Director Kathryn Bigelow doesn't sermonize us, doesn't add gratuitous subplots. The story's genius lies in her approach: by asking no larger-than-life questions, by taking an apolitical stance, by narrowing the scope to just three main characters, Bigelow makes the men's struggle empathetic and universal. The three actors portraying these men are terrific. Jeremy Renner gives one of those career-making performances built on swagger and recklessness, but eventually reveals layers of depth and humanity. Anthony Mackie is at his best as Renner's straight-laced, by-the-book counterpart. Brian Geraghty is very good as the young guy who looks up to the other two men. Mark Boal's script even attracted great actors like David Morse, Guy Pearce, and Ralph Fiennes to take on bit parts. Bigelow stages several ingeniously heart-stopping and nerve-wracking moments of tension and suspense. It's first-rate entertainment, sure, but its refusal to take the easy road when it comes to the effects of war and how it is "a drug" to some young men makes this linger in the mind long after the credits roll

Ive never understood the concept of war being addictive. Maybe its the adrenaline, the guns, the manliness I just know Id rather not die a brutal death in a foreign country. Im not going to lie, war scares me. War scares me, and I know that I know essentially nothing about it or how it really affects the people that actually fight.

The Hurt Locker brought me some of the reality that revealed how scared I really would be if I found myself in a dessert with a gun and a high percentage rate of dying.

I wasnt too intrigued when I watched the trailer for The Hurt Locker about a year ago. It looked like another boring movie about the war in Iraq, or Afghanistan or wherever it is were fighting at any given moment in time. Im not a huge war movie fan. I then started to hear really good things about the movie, picked it up, and watched it in two parts (I started it late one night; you know youve done it too).

I cant say I loved the movie from the beginning, or that I loved it overall. I did enjoy the movie and it seemed to portray a reality that most war movies do not. This seems to be a goal of recent war movies. Ive noticed that these movies are dealing more with the tolls on individuals than on countries, such as the movie Brothers.

The Hurt Locker follows a group of men in an Explosive Ordnance Disposal (EOD) unit in the Iraqi War circa 2004. Jeremy Renner plays a reckless team leader who puts on a big bomb suit that looks like a space suit, walks in the dust and heat to disarm bombs that have the sensitivity of a guy scared of war watching a war movie and can blow up objects as large as big brick buildings in a foreign country.

Although the premise of the movie does seem intriguing, the movie is more about the affects of war on the characters than just a few guys hanging out in the dessert and disarming deathly bombs. Specialist Owen Eldridge, played by Brian Geraghty is a scared shitless soldier, afraid of death at every corner. Sergeant JT Sanborn, played by Anthony Mackie, provides a straight, confident attitude, hiding the fact that hed rather be at home, making a family.

Whether youre into war movies or not, The Hurt Locker gives a different perspective on war, and allows viewers a chance to really connect with characters that emit real emotions about the affects of war. Its a raw look at the mind of a character that sees war as a drug.

Does this movie have something new to say about war, or is it just an excuse to show how war itself has changed thanks to the nature of our invasion of the Middle East and the technology we've employed there? Set during the early days of the current war in Iraq, The Hurt Locker follows a bomb squad (Anthony Mackie and Brian Geraghty) that goes out everyday and stands at the brink of death, dismantling and neutralizing bombs while worrying that every civilian watching them is holding the detonator. When their squad leader is killed in one such explosion, he is replaced by SFC James (Jeremy Renner) who, as time goes by, takes more and more risks, alienating the rest of his team from himself and culminating in a moment of clarity for their new leader.

You can almost compare to The Hurt Locker to the Saw films. As each bomb progresses into the next one the traps become more and more heinous and disgusting. Each bomb is filled with tension, especially after seeing the horrible way that the original squad leader (played by Guy Pearce) dies. You get to see that just the concussion can cause once head to explode like a melon. The bombs cause tension enough, yet with James taking risks being normal military protocol the team has an element of fear not seen at the beginning of the film. At that point it's like a day at the office. As the film reaches its climax, it's a day in hell. The thing that the squad realizes is that they were in hell the entire time.

Directed beautifully by Kathryn Bigelow (who was encourage to do this film by ex-husband James Cameron), The Hurt Locker really delves into all of the aspects of a soldiers place in Iraq. The film doesn't cast judgement on the war or why we're even there in the first place. It is a brutal account of what is probably the toughest job in Iraq. The soldiers take the center stage in the film, not the conflict. The actors are magnificent, playing their personality types perfectly even to the end of the film. They are relative unknowns that aren't drowning in the excesses of a big name co-star, making you relate to these men as soldiers, not previous characters they may have played. In addition to Pearce, there are appearances by David Morse and Ralph Fiennes, but this is an unknown show and it works great.

Gritty, unrelenting, and disturbing, The Hurt Locker represents and unglorified and star studded look at the Iraqi conflict. If you were to compare this film to another war movie of years gone by, this would probably related closer to Full Metal Jacket. Both films took an unconventional route to telling the story of the men on the ground that weren't covered in brass and war stories. A magnificent, microscopic look of modern warfare.

The Hurt Locker is without doubt the best film based on the conflict in Iraq and one of the best war films in years. Directed by Kathryn Bigelow of Point Break fame, the plot follows the fortunes of an Army Bomb Squad and their day to day tasks. Early in the film one such day goes wrong leading the leader of the squad dead. In steps in SFC William James to take control, a man who is a real dare devil and creates serious tension with the other two members of the squad which eventually leads to some revelations for all three.

The main reason that The Hurt Locker is so good is because of the extreme tension that exists throughout, every single day the team puts themselves in serious danger as they must diffuse bombs while also keeping a lookout for enemies. Everyday they head out knowing that they face a serious chance of dying. It's mostly shot in a documentary style which just adds to the gritty realism, the sound and effects are first class and with a practically on-existent soundtrack it all adds up a top class production.

It by no means covers the conflict in depth, the entire film is based on the day to day activities of the squad, but this just adds to the tension as the characters are fleshed out perfectly eith each one having their own demons. A couple of small sub-plots, one in particular involving a young Iraqi boy, fit in nicely with the main story and the ending is one that is definitely not in keeping with the usual war is bad films churned out by America.

Definitely a tour de force, The Hurt Locker is a must see and an excellent all round film on the realities of war.

When Sgt. William James (Jeremy Renner) dons his protective gear to get ready for a day's work, he looks very much like an astronaut. James could very well be working on the dark side of the moon. 

I don't think THE HURT LOCKER is so much a war film as, say RAGING BULL is so much a boxing film. Rather than being genre films...both serve more as portraits of a man. In the case of THE HURT LOCKER - the story revolves around Sgt. James, who strangely enough considers it a big kick defusing homemade bombs. Addicted to the adrenaline rush of a job well done. Those looking for a more conventional war story may be disappointed. 

Sgt. James seems a bit too cocky to Sgt. J.T. Sanborn (Anthony Mackie) - the leader of Bravo Company, a detachment of soldiers assigned the duty of defusing IEDs (Improvised Explosive Devices). Sgt. Sanborn is more a by-the-books sort of character and is usually put off by Sgt. James' impulsive nature. The third main character of Bravo Company is Spc. Owen Eldridge (Brian Gerhaghty) - who is the polar opposite of the self-assured Sgt. James. Eldridge is second guessing his decision to join the military...and was seeking the help of the company psychiatrist. The interactions of these three men is what THE HURT LOCKER is all about. Being able to set aside or store one's emotions away (as a sort of survival mode) into a "hurt locker" is what I think the title is referring to.

I'm not too familiar with director Kathryn Bigelow. I've only seen and enjoyed STRANGE DAYS (1995) of all her previous films. The use of the shaky cam seems to be de rigueur for action directors these days and it's use in THE HURT LOCKER gives it a documentary-like feel. The subject matter of bombs, naturally will have you on edge the first time you watch this. Watching it a second time, I was able to relax a bit more and enjoy the terrific character interactions.

This is more of a rumination of life at war--and an apolitical one at that--than a film driven by a core plot or mission, so those looking for a flick to "get the bad guy" may be disappointed. I really enjoyed that the cast was relatively unknown, sans a few big-name cameos here and there. I'd like to call this a great "character study" but I feel this film goes deeper, making the mental states of the individuals characters of their own. This one's message is in its silence--and it is deafening.

The Hurt Locker is a staggering film. On strictly a personal level, I've only seen a few pictures in recent memory that have made me reel out of the theater. In the 90's, it was Tarantino's PULP FICTION & Michael Mann's HEAT. In this decade, Christopher Nolan's, THE DARK KNIGHT was another...but Kathryn Bigelow's ode to the Iraq War is extraordinary. To be sure, elements of this incredible piece of cinema can be debated, particularly by our hard working veterans...and that is understandable. Yet that aside, this low budget send off of a bomb squad led by Jeremy Renner is brutally intense. From the opening scene to Fade Out, there is no story that can match the distressing tensions created by Barry Ackroyd's jittery cinematography. I am NOT a fan of displaced, moving camera work. It incites headaches and often causes upsetting confusion. That aside, poor Renner got rolled. While Jeff Bridges is indeed a stud, his performance as an ALHO sucks compared to Jeremy's crooked arrow portrayal of maniacal bomb squad leader. Mackie really shines as a smart, intuitive leader who wisely questions threatening and unecessary situations which James often establishes. By far, the finest depiction of the Iraq War ever captured on film. A vicious, claustrophobic, heart attack inducing, savage film. Very, very intense. Utterly gnarly. To appreciate the value of The Hurt Locker you must overlook the military inaccuracies (do you think its that easy for a movie crew to get access to the details regarding US Army logistics, armament and others?) and judge it by its artistic value as a movie. Its main focus isnt depicting the exact details of a EOD unit in Baghdad, but more of creating 3 relatively different characters that have the role of pretty much illustrating certain situations that a presumed military would go through. 
	The movie is not very abundant of pure action scenes, but it still keeps you connected due to a tension build-up. The very best examples are the stand-off and the attempt of disarming the bomb on the Iraqi civilian. Good editing and cinematographics contribute to that tension and The Hurt Locker could be a winning bet for the Oscar in those categories. Not to be overlooked is also the sound, frequently adding more tension and suspense to the scene. Acting is good tending to very good especially the performance of Anthony Mackie. Jeremy Renner has, of course, been the critics favorite, but certainly not undeserved. It took him several years to get a leading mainstream role, but from now on Im sure well be hearing of him more often (his next movie is Ben Afflecks The Town). A downfall regarding the film is the weak plot. Although it is to appreciate the intention of just depicting the 2004 army-invaded Baghdad through the perspective of a EOD team, I feel that more substance could have been added to the storyline, maybe more development of Renners character. Nevertheless, during the movie you will almost for sure overlook this slight flaw and enjoy the picture.
	All in all, The Hurt Locker is a good film, not as a drama war movie like Saving Private Ryan nor as a action war movie like Rambo, but its still worth the money. Generally good directing make it a candidate for the title of best movie of the year but it still has several bad features that should prevent it from winning that title. So it all comes down to subjectivism and taste, as well as competition.

This tautly wound thriller, directed by Kathryn Bigelow (Point Break, Near Dark) and scripted by journalist-screenwriter Mark Boal (In the Valley of Elah), takes an episodic, "you are there" approach to the material, embedding the viewer with this bomb disposal squad so that you feel every moment of panic and rush of adrenaline they feel. Hell, you can almost feel the beads of sweat forming on their brows. Bigelow and Boal treat war as a drug that James will never kick, and Renner offers one of the more subtly powerful performances seen this year. He finds the humor and right level of energy for his character with the same precision as James uncovers the right wires to cut. James' adrenaline addiction is not unlike that of the literary James Bond, who'd rather die in action than be bored to death leading an average life. Unfortunately, there is a point where the film goes from being "you are there" to "you are in a movie." In what was likely an attempt to give James more of a character arc, the story has him break away from his squad mates for a spell to satisfy a personal mission. This passage doesn't ring as true as all the sequences that preceded it and it breaks the film's narrative rhythm, a misstep that the movie never quite recovers from. It's a shame because up until that point the film had damn near been a perfect thriller.

I saw The Hurt Locker sometime in August 2009. I saw it because I admired Point Break - another film by director Kathryn Bigelow. The rush of adrenalin I felt watching Hurt Locker for the first time was spectacular, but the moment I left the cinema I knew that I had seen the best film in a very long time. When I got home I began to research it on the internet. I watched videos and behind the scenes footage from the movie and became very excited that what I'd discovered was a real gem in the genre, and indeed in all movies.

Although the film was still playing in cinemas around the country for some time, I refrained from watching it because I get a lot of pleasure from the anticipation of a second viewing; so I waited. Four months passed. A lot happened in those four months, I can tell you that. But in the midst of the takeoff and re-emergence of my social life came a second, graceful viewing in dazzling Blu-Ray - oh, what a great experience. Thank you Miss Bigelow.

Rather than what has become convention for a war movie, The Hurt Locker spared us the embarrassment of intensive action scenes and tiresome dialogue and delivered the best film with war as the subject since Apocalypse Now, but presented it in such an exhilarating format that it is impossible not to be swept up in the raw tension.

But rather than other genre classics like Platoon and Full Metal Jacket, The Hurt Locker better resembles the thriller blockbuster Jaws. Both films have a completely different subject matter, but both filmmakers (Spielberg and Bigelow) are two of a rare few that see beyond the spatial dynamics of the theatre and terrify us readily with what we cannot see.

Without an element of tension, a film like this could never work. It is thanks to the sharply written script by Mark Boal and the astonishing directorial bravado of Kathryn Bigelow that The Hurt Locker transcends genre and becomes the best directed film since The Good, The Bad and the Ugly topped my list in '66. And in regards to Boal's script, it is tense and cleverly written - overlooked because of Bigelow's mastery of direction - it draws another line with Jaws by creating dialogue that is as rugged as the lead characters. The Hurt Locker is a treat to behold and pushes the edges of the genre to their very extreme. It is one of the best "Best Picture" winners in many years, earning it's title, it's position and it's reputation.

Yet he is necessary and moral to the core, except to those who love him at home - to whom he confesses his indifference just before the film ends. Yes, he may love his wife and son, yes they may need him for their security, but others need men like him more than they do.

Astonishing in a way that ex-hubby Cameron's Avatar is not -the story and its meaning leave the craft and effects in the dust.

This is the first film about the Iraq War that I've seen, mostly because I don't like war films very much and also stuff like Jarhead and Stop-Loss look very uninteresting to me. While it's not really the life-affirming tour-de-force everyone's saying it is, The Hurt Locker is staggeringly effective in its use of tried-and-true bullshit-free formulas that's been missing in a lot of movies as of late. A story set in the early days of the Iraq war, the personalities that make up the bomb disposal unit were a bit overbearing for my tastes, but at least Jeremy Renner's main character (a shoe-in for the Oscars, no?) is thoroughly engaging, and he himself delivers a subtly complex performance, balancing his "civilized" self with the fearless persona he has developed in the field. And we only get a limited glimpse of how these people cope with the constant sense of danger that surrounds them every minute of the day, but that might be for the better. The Hurt Locker is built on one thing: tension. Most of the movie deals with separate goals that need to be accomplished within a short amount of time or people will be dead. There's the constant paranoia that comes from enemies you cannot identify. There's tension within the disposal unit. The lengthy scenes sort of build on top of one another, each situation more dangerous and emotionally draining than the last. There's almost an old school thriller vibe to these scenes that I totally dug in that it pulls no tricks up its sleeve and the suspense becomes uncomfortably dreadful. These deadly scenarios naturally brings the viewer closer into how Jeremy Renner really is, when he knows that he could blow up in one false move. The suspense and tension becomes the driving force behind the narrative, and it's done in a way that's very realistic while also adding emphasis on character. Blu-Ray Review: a must see if you have an HD rig. It's gritty and occasionally grainy, and for a movie with big explosions and action, just leaves a more jarring effect overall visually. Kathryn Bigelow's The Hurt Locker is one of 2009's best reviewed films. It has gone on to appear on numerous top ten lists, and has been up for many awards in the past and oncoming weeks. So naturally whenever a film of this regard garners a bit of reservation with me after watching it, I like to give it a few days before I get around to reviewing it. Here it is almost a week later, and the few problems I had with The Hurt Locker still linger. I think it is a well made film, and to date the best movie to focus on the current war/conflict that we are engaged in. But there are some kinks here and there I can't get over.

There are two elements that made The Hurt Locker work so well. The first is the way the film builds up suspense, and creates an formidable level of tension throughout its action sequences. The Hurt Locker focuses a small group of soldiers in the Explosive Ordnance Disposal (EOD) field of the U.S. Army. Their job is to respond to reported sites of possible explosives and either disarm them, or detonate them if the situation calls of it. For the first two thirds of the film there are a handful of these bomb disarming sequences, and they are on a "edge of your seat" level of tension. All of these sequences are spectacularly put together and expertly filmed.

The other element to this film that works well is its lead actor, Jeremy Renner. I've enjoyed Renner's work up until now, and have seen him as a very under appreciated actor. Finally he has been given a role that can reach a broader audience, and show off his craft on a larger scale. He plays Staff Sergeant William James, who has become sort of an adrenaline junkie working in this field of the Army. While he is disarming bombs he is filled with this "do or die" attitude, full of life and energy. Whenever he isn't around this stressful work, a different person emerges who seems empty and bored with life. Renner does a fantastic job conveying both sides of this complicated character.

Where the film began to lose me was with certain developments with William. There is a moment in the film that shows his life back home, where he has a wife and an infant son. He seems very apathetic towards this life, most likely due to the "high" created by being in the line of work that he is in. That would be more believable if it weren't for the relationship William forms with a young Iraqi boy (Christopher Sayegh), nicknamed "Beckham," who sells bootleg DVDs on the U.S. base William is stationed at. When the boy's life is threatened, an almost paternal instinct kicks in William, and he goes on an almost revenge kick for a while in the film. I found this a bit inconsistent with the character, and a poor route for the film to have taken.

There were a few other problems I had, mainly with some logic issues (such as the unlikely chance that merchants would be able to set up shop on a military base, especially so close to the living quarters of soldiers), but I won't hark on that too much. I like The Hurt Locker, and yes there are a lot of strong points the film had going for it; Bigelow's direction, Barry Ackroyd's cinematography, ect.. But I see this film as being one of the more overrated movies of 2009. It's an awesome film, but hardly the great film that a lot of people are making it out to be.

There is just something about this movie that makes it the best of 2009. While Avatar is all about effects and is somehow winning best picture awards left and right The Hurt Locker sticks to traditional film making. While it is a low budget war film Bigelow's direction and Renner's performance make this movie my best movie experience of 2009.

Calling this one of last year's best films is not giving into hype or over selling what this film does. The Hurt Locker is easily one of the best action/character studies of the decade and sets a new precedent that Die Hard set almost 20 years ago.
The plot of The Hurt Locker is pretty much non-existent in a strict sense. We are introduced to Bravo Squad and their rag-tag group of War Heroes in the middle of a routine bomb defusing operation. Sgt. Sanborn (Anthony Mackie) and Spc. Eldridge (Brian Geraghty) watch as their leader, SSG Thompson (Guy Pearce) is killed in an explosion, setting up the ground work for just what the film will be covering.
Enter SFC James (Jeremy Renner), a Veteran Bomb squad expert with hundreds of bombs under his belt. He is thrust into Delta Squad during the end of their tour and the tension begins to elevate. James doesn't want to kill anyone, but his thirst for adrenaline is so strong that he constantly puts his team in danger.
The action in this film is very calculated and slow. Nothing occurs at some Keeanu, over-the-top, level or with ridiculous, machismo flare. We get to see an extremely realistic depiction of what war is for the soldiers serving in Iraq.
One particularly outstanding scenes takes place in the middle of the desert with snipers. No one can figure out where the hell the enemy is shooting from and we see about 3 people drop before Bravo squad can even take action. Having to deal with that kind of anguish every day would definitely take a toll on someone.
What elevates that scene beyond normal action fluff is how much James cares about his squad. After what is probably hours of scoping an era, James grabs juice for his sniper and even holds it to his mouth like a mother to a child. It rings very strong with that sense of fraternity that soldiers build during their tours.
This all is made stronger by the superb acting on display. Everyone, even the bit players, perform better than most A-List Hollywood actors. Jeremy Renner gets a nod for being one of the most bad-ass new characters in recent cinema, but you can tell he is hurting and hungering for more on the inside.
Anthony Mackie is very strong as Sanborn and often gives off a vibe of being a by-the-book soldier, something that would make an excellent leader in tough situations. His opening up at the end is very engaging and eye revealing.
Even Ralph Fiennes and Christian Camargo, only being in the movie for about 10 minutes each, draw you to their presence. They just feel like they know what war is, or at least can give us a close guess.
My only main problem with the film is pacing. I know that real war isn't the most speedy thing ever, but this movie takes a bit long in getting to more action or dialog. We have scenes of Bravo Squad taking routine action and calling out positions, etc, but we've already seen that to death in other war films. It just distracts from what the movie is trying to do, show us a great character film.
Regardless of my quibble, The Hurt Locker is not something to miss. It is very rare that an action film comes around that actually makes you think about the things you are witnessing (and not in a, "That's so fake," kind of way). You owe it to yourself to see this film.

"Now I am become Death, destroyer of worlds," spoke J. Robert Oppenheimer after the Trinity nuclear test, quoting the Hindu scripture the Bhagavad Gita.  If there is such a thing as "terrible beauty" that rivals the mushroom cloud Oppenheimer saw, it might be Kathryn Bigelow's filming of an explosion in "The Hurt Locker."  The earth ripples, a man tries to run away in slow motion, and one is stunned by the awfulness of what happens next, yet mesmerized by the clarity and power of Bigelow's imagery and staging.  "The Hurt Locker" just got dinged by NEWSWEEK for being a film with little or no political context, yet that's part of what gives the film its terrible urgency; it's a portrait of men doing a brutal, nerve-wracking job under the worst circumstances imaginable.  Does it matter in the big picture what kind of terrorists (Suni militants? Shia militants?) have wired an innocent victim with a bomb, and sent him out into the public arena to be slaughtered?  No, all that matters for roughly three torturous minutes is, can hotshot SFC William James (Jeremy Renner) get the poor guy free without blowing one or both of them to kingdom come?  James has come to Iraq to replace SSG Matt Thompson (Guy Pearce), who figured in that "terrible beauty" during the first five minutes of the film; over the next two hours we see James carry out his job--methodically, masterfully--yet still slowly get eaten up inside by the horrors he encounters.  The geopolitics are a side issue; James focuses only on what's in front of him--untangling knots of wires and metal which may mean certain death if he makes the wrong move or cut.  "The Hurt Locker" has, to my memory, exactly one scene of sniper fire exchanged, and one foot chase; almost every remaining minute spent outside is one long, stomach-knotting exercise in tension and restraint.  (Note for the physically and emotionally sensitive: there is a very tough scene late in the film which involves the aftermath of a bomb, and the first time James comes face-to-face with the emotional cost of being in Iraq; the gore is almost incidental, compared to the emotional brutality James experiences.)  Jeremy Renner is very good as James, but he has stellar support from Anthony Mackie and Brian Geraghty (and, in tiny cameos, Ralph Fiennes and David Morse).  Uniquely for a war/military film, there is little of the sour mysogeny or homophobia we saw in things like "Jarhead" or "Full Metal Jacket"--these men may challenge each other and, when drunk, do stupid things to "prove" themselves, but there's no doubt that they have each others' backs when things go south.  (This film is also reminiscent of Kimberly Pierce's underrated "Stop-Loss" in that sense.) "The Hurt Locker" could be any film about people--especially men--doing tough, brutal jobs; they get up every day, put on the protective gear, and go out and put themselves on the line, because that is who they are.  It's a film that celebrates a unique kind of courage, the kind that zeroes in on getting the job done and getting out safely--suit up, go in, cut the wire, get out safely, save lives, go on.  Let other male directors overindulge in pyrotechnics and big moments; Bigelow understates and keeps her power in check, and "The Hurt Locker" is that much more remarkable for her artistry and restraint.  Unquestionably, this is one of the best of the year.

what makes this film  is the attention to detail by the writer's, director and actors. What was trying to be achieved here wasn't a political statement and wasn't a propaganda piece. This tackles the very core of the war: The Human Spirit. The film covers the last 30 or so days inside the bravo company bomb squad; an important piece of the military who have saved many lives diffusing bombs in the War in Iraq.

The film has dialogue that is realistic. Almost like a Robert Altman picture, the dialogue between characters will sometime run together, leaving some parts of a characters dialogue inaudible at parts, but this only adds to the effect that the film is trying to achieve. It's not going for a flashy epic tribute, but moreso, telling it like it is with brutal honesty.

The film lacks a score, which leads to more of a focus on the ambient sounds. The wind whistles by in several scenes, and in the bomb diffusing scenes and in the shootout scenes, this adds an extra layer of suspense to the film. Alot of scenes will sometime build itself up only to leave the audience without the "satisfying conclusion". this puts the audience int he soldier's shoes, allowing them to experience the same kind of constant paranoia of not knowing who truly is the enemy. Clever direction and editing make the suspense work to painful effects.

This film should prove to audiences that gore, sweeping scores and a constant hail of gunfire doesnt have to be what a war movie is all about. This is a story that's true to it's word and I can see it going down in time as authentic of a depiction of the War in Iraq as Platoon was to the Vietnam War. While not covering the "frontlines" of the war, the film still rings true to any branch of the military that is fighting in Iraq.

The Hurt Locker is set soon after the 2003 U.S. invasion of Iraq and follows a 3-man Explosives Ordinance Disposal (EOD) team: Sergeant  James, Sergeant Sanborn and Specialist Eldridge.  Sergeant James joins the team near the end of a one-year tour of duty, following the death of Sergeant Thompson. As the senior in rank, James is the team leader. He is also the EOD Tech (i.e. the one who handles the explosive device).  Sanborn is Ranger qualified and acts as a mentor to Eldridge. Eldridge is the young one, fighting his fear of dying in combat.

James has two things against him as a leader.  First, he is a replacement team leader close to the end of a tour of duty. i.e. these are short timers counting the days until the end of the tour.  Second, he is very aggressive, choosing to tackle difficult problems directly instead of conservatively. And this is the defining conflict of the movie.

A lot of things about the setting are very well done. The overall competence of American forces, especially American NCOs, was on full display.  The difficulties in working in insurgent environments where it was hard to tell who was on which side.  The desire to help the Iraqi's against the desire to take the safe way out.  The tension of going into an environment where nothing is secure and everything is fluid and can easily turn deadly without warning. They even showed the tension within the Army between those who viewed their role as security and combat versus those who viewed victory as something that would only be gained by connecting with the population (in the early days, the political leadership was decidedly on the security/combat only view.)  

But in the interest of setting up the story, there are many things that are unreasonable.  An EOD team was a highly valuable asset, and would not have been risked travelling without an escort.  They would not have been employed as light infantry (something alluded to at one point).  A Colonel, (especially one that is not combat arms) would not have been allowed to be outside secure areas without escort (but at least they had the sense to tease him in film about his acknowledged incompetence in potential combat roles). And an EOD tech whose job it was to concentrate intently on a single narrow thing (the explosive device) would not be a team leader with the responsibility for an entire team.  The parts taken from disarmed explosives would have been taken for investigation and study, not allowed to be hiding underneath some soldier's bed.

But all is forgiven with how well the conflict between James and Sanborn is done.  Every scene becomes a way to address this tension in another way.  James aggressiveness versus Sanborn's conservationism (of the "I am a soldier who intends to use my experience to complete my mission and live" variety, not the political variety). James single focus on the technical task and challenge of disarming explosives versus Sanborn's view of situations as a whole.  And with all that, the fact that James is in fact the team leader, even if Sanborn is tactically more competent (note that Sanborn is Ranger qualified, something that is made explicit when he fills the role of sniper in one scene.)

One thing that the director and writer find hard to get is motivation.  The feel of the environment seems pretty good, showing the confusion and lack of clarity in what can be seen.  The characters seem reasonable (the writer spent time with a team, and claims the characters are composites.  Even if he put character qualities that should not be in a single person together).  But we don't quite get the motivations of the characters.  Leaders do not get the luxury of focusing on one technical detail while they ignore their men (the Specialist track is for this group).  People who are highly trained in very technical skills e.g. EOD techs) do not tend to turn into cowboys.  And a Specialist (which usually implies a few years of experience) near the end of a year long combat tour does not get congratulated for not becoming frozen in a combat situation.

Even so, with what they did get right, it is probably one of the better movies on the current wars (see my other reviews).  And the depiction of conflict between James and Sanborn makes it a good film.

The disheartening realization, of the insecure and terrifying minuscule rock we live and fight over, is saddening for anyone who call it home. This is a prime example of the constant wars over peace, that continue to drive it farther away from peace itself. 

After Sgt Matt Thompson dies from an IED in Iraq, SFC William James replaces him in Bravo Company with a month left in their tour. James is a master at defusing bombs and loves the thrill, but for his fellow squad members, they just want to survive the few days of duty they have left. James risk taking however makes the their time left all the more terrifying. 

Kathryn Bigelow has made herself a masterpeice that will be hard to top with any form of media. It was gritty and honest down to its core, with no Hollywood over the top special effects to drag consumers in to a world unrealistic to the one that is present just for a bigger paycheck. Her choice of camera work, and style was perfect for the pacing, and purpose, that made you feel that you were with them the hole way through. While sitting on the edge of your seat and wondering if or when something will go off, and take you out with them.

The acting was fantastic, with no sense of over the top melodramatic scenes, just purposeful genuine acting, that truly made you know the terror and drive, only felt by the people on the frontline. Jeremy Renner played a strong and confident, almost overly cocky Sargent first class in a bomb disposal unit. Anthony Mackie and Brian Geraghty had tough roles within his unit, both with their own personalities, as the logical teammate and fearful follower.

Overall I was totally pleased with this film from beginning to end. The build up was tense and consistant. It left me wondering what was going to happen next all the way to the end. Over all I have to say that it was excellent and a can't miss of 2009.

Kathryn Bigelow's opening sequence is, in every sense of the word, mesmerizing. If you want to know how to create tension and atmosphere then you could learn a thing or two from the first 15 minutes on offer here. Unfortunately the next two hours can't quite replicate its success, falling just short of capturing the same exhilarating levels that set the film in motion. It is still a tightly wound and uncompromising look at life as a bomb technician mind you; the depth afforded to the story drags us into SFC James' unfamiliar and peculiar world - but what an intriguing world it is - and we come out the other end with an understanding of what it takes, mentally and physically, for someone to do such a dangerous and meticulous job. It helps that Marco Beltrami's thumping and pulsating score reverberates through your body with every note and essentially acts as another character.

When Bigelow sticks with the things that go boom, Locker shows why many critics have scored it a chance to the win the big prize at the Academy Awards this year. Gripping is an understatement when describing the numerous tasks undertaken by our risky protagonist, however, there are a few subplots that Bigelow should have left on the cutting room floor, like an unnecessary search and kill assignment at the end of the middle act. It's these small narrative excesses that stop Locker from being an instant classic, instead you'll just have to settle for bloody fantastic. 

Keep an eye out for Jeremy Renner in the future. You may recognize him as the bad guy from S.W.A.T. or seen glimpses of his talent as a supporting player in The Assassination of Jesse James and North Country, but this is his first bona fide chance to show his acting chops. A BAFTA and SAG nomination (and eight wins on the smaller awards circuit) later, Renner doesn't disappoint. His enigmatic and charismatic portrayal of a man forever on the edge, yet always with a casual attitude, is tremendous to witness; the intensity he possesses is electric on screen. Anthony Mackie deserves a mention too as he is impressive in the far less flashy role of the by-the-book SGT Sanborn; arguably providing the only constant throughout the picture which is easily identifiable and relatable.

A powerhouse performance by leading man Renner and assured direction from Bigelow make this an absolute must-see on the big screen.
