War films don't have an easy job these days. Some of the finest films ever made about war have come and gone and appear to have covered most of the bases concerning the subject area. For combat situations, we have the likes of "Saving Private Ryan" and "Black Hawk Down" that give us a gritty, in your face, heart pounding perspective of the battlefield through the eyes of the soldiers who inhabit it. Not that easy to top. At first glance, "The Hurt Locker" seems to be yet another one of those films, which would have been fine if unoriginal. The fact that the film takes place in Iraq during the present climate would seem an innovation, but we've seen gulf war movies that take place in the exact same location and there's nothing much in this movie that would make things seem more contemporary with regards to politics and the like (except the hardware of course) since the film is focused on the soldiers and nothing more. Yes, from purely looks alone, "The Hurt Locker" would seem like a standard combat heavy war flick. But you'd be dead wrong.

Two innovations elevate "Hurt Locker" to one of the most compelling films ever shot about war. One is the perspective. While the protagonists are still soldiers with guns, bullets and cevlar as seen in many other like movies, they come together as an elite bomb squad, whose job it is to seek out and diffuse the disguised booby traps and remote detonated explosives laid out by the local Hajis to send US army troop vehicles sky high. All the while, they must contend with gazing eyes from all sides, not knowing who to trust in a hostile foreign land and not knowing what lays ahead in the rubble and dirt on a seemingly quiet, dusty urban street. This simple conceit (usually reduced to red wire blue wire scenarios in other action movies) leads to one word that sums up most of this film's running length; tense. Everytime the risk of a possible explosive is imminent (which here is all the time) there is a palpable sense of unease and fear of the unexpected. Jeremy Renner (in a stunning performace) plays the hot shot, too confident its scary bomb engineer who's responsible for finding and disarming the bombs and every time your heart is in your mouth not knowing whether he's going to succeed or not.

This masterful handling of suspense by director Kathryn Bigelow translates into other great set pieces; there's an excellent sequence concerning snipers (no surprise in a movie like this but this is at least handled in a way that seems refreshing). The key is in the camera viewpoints chosen to shoot each sequence, aswell as the combination of the ambient sound effects and the low key score. We're consistantly kept on edge during moments of unease and under the impression that anyone can die at any second and that there's always someone watching. This makes for a thrilling ride.

However, great war films are ultimately about the casualties on both sides. Here we get a good idea of the stress and fear that permeates these men with every assignment they have, along with the more long term effects that it may have. We see casualities on the other side too, which is never glossed over or seen as anything less than the loss of human life, whether American or Iraqi.

And through this exploration of war casualties, we see the film's second innovation and probably the one that stays with you the most once the movie's done. This is shown to us in the revealing opening quote from middle eastern war correspondant Chris Hedge, "The rush of battle is often a potent and lethal addiction, war is a drug." The concept of the adrenalin junky is not unfamiliar, but put on the backdrop of intense, traumatic war and combat it becomes something both compelling and unsettling and this is something that has never before been explored on film as far as I have seen, or at least not as effectively as it has here. It's with this, combined with everything else on offer that turns "The Hurt Locker" from an intense, thrilling combat movie into a mesmerising war film that displays one of its most frightening side effects.

After losing their team leader in an explosion two members of a bomb squad must work with his replacement and try to survive the final 39 days of their tour in Iraq.

Katherine Bigelow brings us the best war movie of this Generation; The Hurt Locker follows three members of an elite bomb squad who are called out to clear IED?s out of the way for their fellow soldiers. It is a tense game of cat and mouse not knowing who is placing the bombs, how they are going to be detonated or how much time they will have to defuse them before an insurgent remotely detonates them. Jeremy Renner delivers a phenomenal performance as Staff Sergeant William James the new team leader who appears reckless and without care for his team.  The inside look into what motivates these volunteers to join a bomb squad and perform one of the most dangerous positions in the army is simply astounding the combination of going into an unknown area against and unknown enemy and defusing these crude bombs will make you squirm in your seat as if you are there. The shot?s of the concussive blast from one of these bombs is visually amazing. Bravo Company's sergeant is killed in an explosion and his replacement, Sergeant James (Jeremy Renner, in an Oscar-nominated role), is a former Army Ranger who has disarmed more than 800 bombs and has a penchant for recklessly putting himself in harm's way.  James and the other two members of the team, Sanborn (Anthony Mackie) and Eldridge (Brian Geraghty), find themselves going from bomb site to bomb site, from unexploded car bomb to suspicious pile of rubble to ambushes to people exploding into a fine mist.  Where every person is a possible combatant, every cellphone a trigger, every "present" comes with det cord, all as Bravo Company prepares to rotate out.  And in between, they try to make sense of their actions, in a world where that may not be possible and face the prospect of a civilian life where they donât belong. Like the many Vietnam war films, which seem to only get better with time, so are the Iraq war films finally beginning to take their place within the library of American war films that have become classics. Of course, it is unfair to compare the two, as they are very different wars and these are very different times, but while most notable Vietnam films (like Deer Hunter, Apocalypse now, Platoon and Full Metal Jacket) were made a few years after the conflict was over, Iraq war movies have been emerging throughout the 7 years (and running) that passed since its inception. That being said, one can only guess how these new movies will withstand the test of time. One thing is for sure, the only film that managed to be nominated for as many (nine to be exact) Oscars as the titanic Avatar this year was The Hurt Locker. With the closest second being Inglorious bastards, itself being a war movie albeit with a slightly more idealistic ending to WW2. Perhaps it says something about the American psyche, congratulating at once both wild fantasy and hyper realism. Of course, the fact that Avatar will most likely snatch most of those Oscars is a simple matter of economics (especially considering the crisis) but nevertheless one can see what is on the minds of the nation (of course, with the academy being a very loose, yet at times more accurate, extension of 'the nation' than, let's say, congress). I suppose the only thing that's left to ask now is how Bigelow's past relationship with Cameron plays into Hollywood politics and creative output.

This all isn't to say that "The Hurt Locker" is a bad film...for it's not terrible, but to say it's one of the best of 2009 is over stating what this film really offers.

The Hurt Locker was one of the most realistic and epic war movies I have seen in a long time. When the quote "War is a drug" first appeared on the screen, I thought, how? I have many relatives in the armed forces who can not stand being out there, and this quote made me want to figure out why. Therefore, it hooked me right there. By the end of the film, I completely understood the meaning of the quote, and can now apply it to my thinking. 

But what do I think about everything else? Besides the theme of the film, the gritty realism was overwhelming and amazing in general. It actually feels like the picture was filmed smack dab in Baghdad. Key scenes in the film show a realistic view of gunfire and bomb defusing. For example, when they were sniping, the soldier missed multiple times, the enemy was most likely 3 football fields away, and when he finally succeeded, it was rewarding. They stayed in the prone position just watching, waiting, and what felt like 10 minutes for us, was most likely 2-3 hours for them. 

The filming was very entertaining as well, with Kathryn Bigelow's stylish direction. She uses only handheld cameras, which reminds me of The Bourne Ultimatum in some ways, and she presents slow motion to the audience like she invented it. The editing and sound mixing was phenomenal, I have yet to understand how the sound was edited with such crisp and realistic effects. It completely deserved the editing and mixing oscars, but one award I did not agree on was Best Original Screenplay. I do not think that it had enough lines for the actors to demonstrate for us, and I do not think Jeremy Renner acted to his full potential, but with a realistic war film like this, it does not even matter. The overall prospects of the film's direction completely overshadowed the acting, therefore it can still be a realistic film even though it did not have the greatest acting.

I see other reviews for this film by our Rotten Tomato community, stating things like "It was too boring, and highly overrated." Everyone is entitled to their own opinion, but The Hurt Locker was anything but. Never before have I seen a war film as epic and realistic as this movie was. Comparing this film to other war movies, like Pearl Harbor, The Hurt Locker excels because of its non-cliched war movie framework. In pictures such as Pearl Harbor, the action is shot in the same exact way like every other war film out there, and it gets boring after a while. With this film however, I was completely entertained because of the unique route that Kathryn Bigelow and Mark Boal took, and I think the film will probably be a step forward for cinema in the future, and I strongly believe that. 

This is a great film that completely deserved to win best picture, and I would recommend this movie to anyone who enjoys war films and the war in Iraq as well. It delivers a gritty and suspenseful outlook of the war, and I completely enjoyed the style and direction from Kathryn Bigelow. The realistic view of our boys in the middle east should not be missed. And when the film ended, oh boy, I almost forgot the opening scene, and when the credits started, I actually understood why war is a drug. They use Jeremy Renner's family as a stepping stone rising to the top of his character's outlook on war, and the way the picture ends locks everything together. All in all, The Hurt Locker succeeds on many levels, and pushes the direction of cinema to new heights.

I spent 14 months in Iraq as a Cavalry Scout in the Diyala Province. I am blown away by how many people really think this film was realistic. It was the most far fetched depiction of an EOD squad that one could have made. EOD aren't snipers. A guy can't just hop on a Barrett and take out moving targets at 800 meters. EOD NEVER goes outside the wire without an escort and they wouldn't be rolling around downtown Baghdad without manning their .50 cal. EOD doesn't go charging after trigger men either. And I never once saw an EOD guys suit up and diffuse a bomb. Not to say that never happened, but 99% of the time they drive their robot up to the bomb, drop a C4 charge on it, drive the robot back, and blow it from a safe distance. And security contractors weren't going around hunting high value targets, they were gaurding VIPs, installations, and convoys. And why is the one guys wearing a Combat Infantry Badge? He's not an infantryman, he's EOD and says he spent 7 years in Intelligence prior to that. And one last thing, units in Baghdad weren't wearing the ACU digital pattern uniforms, they were wearing the old desert camo uniforms. This movie was totally ridiculous in so many ways.

The Hurt Locker is a serious character study and a taut, suspenseful action thriller at once.

The subject matter itself - the work of a bomb expert, possibly one of the most nerve-racking jobs on the planet - yields most of the suspense but Bigelow manages to squeeze out every bit of tension of the premise.

This film to me was very apolitical - though set in Iraq, it is distinguished from most of the Iraq-themed war films in that it concentrates much more on the job itself than the political environment. Iraq seemed more like a backdrop - any other war would do, The Hurt Locker does not preach about this one specifically.

The story is deeply emotional, depicting a thoroughly disturbed individual's life in hell. Jeremy Renner gives an incredibly powerful performance as an EOD officer completely hooked on adrenaline stemming from his everyday close shaves with death.

All aspects of film-making are top-notch, from the brilliantly subversive screenplay through vivid cinematography, masterful directing and perfectly paced editing.

In its storytelling the filmmakers wisely break with traditional Hollywood narrative techniques. There is no clear antagonist, no rising action, no obvious character development and no climax. And yet the film manages to be more interesting, tense and suspenseful than any Hollywood action thriller I've seen in years while making a powerful, yet subtle statement about the insane addiction that is war. Kudos for everyone involved for making this film without compromising.

This is pure quality, cinematic storytelling at its best, a thinking man's actioner.

Good movie? Well, yeah, one could say that. Good war movie? Yes, definitely so. Good Iraq war movie? The very best! Actually "The Hurt Locker" has a very peculiar structure. It starts by stating that war is a drug and proves pretty much that in the first act, with mission after mission after mission of a three-man bomb squad, the adrenaline rushing and little time for much else. But as the missions get tougher and the going gets rough (physically and psychologically), then the movie starts to slow down, and show much more barrack-what-am-i-doing-here-war-is-hell-soldier-bonding kind of scenes. It ends up introspectively, the last two missions are darker, but the ending proves the first statement and will surprise. Jeremy Renner very well deserves his Oscar nomination, but Anthony Mackie should be there as well as supporting actor. The movie is surprisingly well held by a woman (well maybe not so, taking into account her resume). Kathryn Bigelow learned the lesson from ex-husband Cameron about action (although the Paul-Greengrass-kind-of-hand-held-shaky-camera-style gave me a freakin' headache), but he should learn from her about unclicheing army soldiers. The way it never showed politicians, or COs, or yelling sargents, but just three plain soldiers was a definite plus in the movie, and these were never stereotyped. It was just plain natural, and the scenes "back home" were great, avoiding all those cliches of other movies. Reality is the best originality. The best movie of the year? Well, looking at the pick, yes, probably, it is one of the most satisfying as a whole. In the war movie genre it delivers. But one may note with sadness that the great movies of today are just great movies. The great movies of yore were much more than that. They stayed with you. The Hurt Locker is a great movie, but really I will not carry it with me.

The Hurt Locker works largely because it's the first dramatization of the war that doesn't force-feed the filmmakers' heavy-handed opinions down the viewers' collective throat.  As a military thriller it's the best since Black Hawk Down (though, that's really apples and oranges), possibly the best ever made. As a character study, the film is never fails to be both insightful and interesting. "The Hurt Locker" is a more or less average film that owes much of its effusive critical acclaim to two factors: its contemporary combat setting, and its ever-so-slight deviation from many of mainstream cinema's hackneyed conventions. In this it shares much in common with another over-praised film from 2009, Jason Reitman's "Up In The Air". 

Unfortunately in "The Hurt Locker", director Kathryn Bigelow employs a rather predictable and tired technique for building suspense--Is the bomb going to blow now? No. Wait, is it going to blow now??? No. And so on--that is to be expected in, say, "Saw III", but not in a film that could be considered anything resembling an enduring achievement.

Bigelow's one-trick-pony is aided and abetted by cinematographer Barry Ackroyd, who here treats us to a reprise of his hurdy-gurdy, sudden zoom-in work from "United 93", but to worse effect.

While ultimately "The Hurt Locker" contains slight deviations from Hollywood norms (melancholy ending, killing off big time actors like Ralph Fiennes & Guy Pearce), it employs too many of the same, tired tropes to be thought of as something special. Perhaps you were in suspense when the Army psychologist went out on a mission with the EOD guys, to see what they went through--what are the odds something will go wrong?--but I was not. And I'm trying to decide if Sgt. James' (portrayed by Jeremy Renner) blind fury at the death of a child is more like Robin Williams in "Good Morning Vietnam", or William Petersen in every other episode of "C.S.I." Maybe Mariksa Hargitay from "Law & Order SVU" is closer to the mark.

"The Hurt Locker" is not a particularly bad film, but nor is it particularly good. Perhaps we need a decade or so of additional ferment over Iraq & Afghanistan before our filmmakers can hit the nail on the head, as was the case with Vietnam. The Great Iraq War Film remains as yet unmade.

Ahem... I'll attempt to justify that statement. The problem with films like The Hurt Locker is that they tread the rather thin line between realistic, tense military thriller and action movie. If such a film is going to fail badly then it's usually in portraying the realism bit (and yes, I'm talking about The Kingdom here). It's nice to see then, that Kathryn Bigelow - she did Point Break - manages to create a solid genre piece that portrays a good sense of the tension and urgency of bomb disposal work in a post war Iraq.

The Hurt Locker has been praised universally by critics as an authentic and dramatically effective war film that avoids the patriotic flag waving and stereotyping of Arabs that many recent Hollywood efforts have been guilty of. The story of a three man team of demolition experts - whose job it is to make safe unexploded bombs planted by insurgents - the movie centres on the squads new leader Sergeant William James (played by Jeremy Renner), who's methods in the carrying out of this task are, to say the very least, reckless.

Despite taking what his squad mates consider to be unreasonable risks to get his job done, James is highly successful at defusing IEDs (improvised explosive devices), and the film follows the team getting involved in various situations of increasing personal danger and shows the detrimental effects that this has on the two other team member's morale. It soon becomes clear that all three member's of the squad are suffering from acute psychological stress and are in danger of cracking under the pressure of being exposed to life-threatening danger on an almost daily basis.

The Hurt Locker does what it sets out to do extremely well. It is well acted and competantly filmed. Mostly, it also seems quite realistic as well (perhaps with the exception of a rather protracted sniper battle sequence which features some quite unlikely shooting at an apparant distance of nearly a kilometre) and certainly portrays war-torn Iraq as a confusing and conflicted place where the American military presense seems quite disorganised and unable to identify who the insurgents are amongst the civilian population.

Unfortunately, the film really isn't as tense as it has been built up to be; at lease it wasn't to me. Though the team get in to several dangerous situations with unexploded devices, I never felt any sense that they were actually going to die and a lot of the sense of battlefield stress that the events were meant to portray somehow fell short. As a portrayal of the Iraq conflict it is by no means a bad film, but HBO's mini series Generation Kill does it much better and feels much more well researched.

All in all a solid effort; but a somewhat overrated one.
In hindsight, this is better than I give it credit for.

Too much buzz can water down a good movie and this film was clearly drowning when I saw it. The subject matter is undeniably interesting, and like all the best war films, it doesn't try to make you feel a certain way about the conflict at hand, but the film suffers most at the hands of its own plotlessness.

That's not to say that the film isn't deserving of praise. All the actors seem to be game for the proceedings and the star power present is impressive, but not too obvious for it to be overpowering. What makes the movie work more than anything else is the direction. Bigelow propels almost every moment with sinister tension to the point that looking at triggers for deactivated bombs makes you recoil in anticipation.

The plot, however, is where the film gets into trouble. In real life, war stories rarely have a satisfying arc beyond the completion of a single mission, and unless you're capturing Saddam Hussein, the catharsis in context of the outer world is fairly small. While it is occasionally fun to see someone play with that convention, the movie just felt like a few tense sequences strung together. It's cool to watch guys rescue a fellow soldier and see one of our heroes behind a sniper rifle, but when the only point the movie goes out of the way to make concerns the mindset of someone who is capable and willing to diffuse bombs in combat situations, these other scenes come across as lacking in relevance. In addition to this, the pacing that at first seemed reasonable also becomes rushed in the final act. Overall, one can't help but feel that this strong effort nevertheless fizzled out.

After finding out that The Hurt Locker won Best Picture, I decided that I had to see it. War films have never been my cup of tea, but this film is quite unique, and it's a totally tense experience. SUMMARY:

After Sergeant Thompson (Guy Pearce) is killed while trying to defuse a bomb on a Baghdad street in 2004, he is replaced by Staff Sergeant William James (Jeremy Renner), who shocks the other members of his team, Sanborn (Anthony Mackie), and Eldridge (Brian Geraghty), with his reckless approach to his dangerous work. James seems oblivious to the fears and concerns of his comrades. REVIEW:

For me, the strongest element of the film was the screenplay. Written by Mark Boal, who was a journalist embedded with a bomb unit in Iraq, it feels absolutely realistic. Throughout the film, we experience these characters' mission - clearing the streets of Baghdad of bombs. It shows us the long and tense process of defusing the weapons. The opening titles state that war is a drug, and it's a major theme of the movie. It's a drug to the character of William James, who is addicted to combat. The ending was a winner for me - it's clever, and it brings you back to the beginning, with the theme of war being a drug. James' character isn't exactly developed, but what they try to do is develop the other characters' opinion on him. Sanborn sees him at first as a 'redneck piece of trailer trash', but during the course of the film his opinion, and ours, undergoes a change. The film doesn't take sides as well, there are no villains here. Other war films tend to potray the opposition as evil people, but they never do this here. Kathryn Bigelow doesn't choose to have bad guys. The acting is terrific. Jeremy Renner excellently plays James, while other members of the cast, including Anthony Mackie and Brian Geraghty, do just as fine in their roles. The supporting actors are superb, with Guy Pearce, David Morse, and Ralph Fiennes, making short, but outstanding, appearances. The problem comes from the cinematography. I did like some of it, I thought some shots were breathtaking, but the problem came from the handheld style of camera movement. It's taken to the extreme here. It's really a shame. It's justified in some scenes, which just shows how good of a director Kathryn Bigelow is, but it becomes overused during the course of the film, and to a certain point it is literally sickening to watch. I felt like throwing up. That doesn't mean I hated the whole of the cinematography - some shots were beautiful, as I said earlier, and the colours of the film were excellent. I thought the explosions were filmed well, which gave the film a wonderful visual edge. The score was good, and it boosted up the suspense in some scenes. Bigelow's main strength is during the scenes where James defuses the bombs. It feels and looks authentic, and it's absolutely tense. Wire cutting, and even looking for the wires, Bigelow gives us a tense experience, filming in the right places, and giving excellent direction to the actors. Despite the handheld camera style, The Hurt Locker is a tense and nail-biting experience. I don't think it's Best Picture - I do think it is quite over-rated. Kathryn Bigelow has done a great job with this, and her direction is amazing - it's no surprise she won Best Director, let alone being the only female to ever win that award.

There's a rock n'roll bravado to Katheryn Bigelow's THE HURT LOCKER, but also a sober sense of duty; it's less horrific than the non-stop shit-show in Sir Ridley's BLACK HAWK DOWN, which nonetheless acts as a kind of recruitment video. Bigelow's film has more of an interest in humanity, but it still acknowledges the adrenaline and addictive element inherent to such dangerous endeavours (think extreme sports with a raison d'Ãªtre). Shot with hand-held cameras, this is nonetheless a carefully crafted film that puts you right in the centre of some extremely intense situations. Jump cuts and strategic camera angles are used with appropriately military precision. At times the suspense becomes almost unbearable, but yet Jeremy Renner's Sgt. James is surprisingly calm and collected. Renner gives a fantastic performance here: as mystifying as James is, he's compelling and we feel his hurt and begin to understand how difficult his adjustment to civilian life is going to be.  The titular locker where he carries around the pieces of the things that almost killed him goes beyond being just a physical thing. The film acknowledges the sense of futility many of us feel about the ongoing occupation of Iraq, but it does so while respecting the people there and why someone would choose to do such a job (EOD team members are volunteers). Unlike many recent films, THE HURT LOCKER ends strongly; the last 20 min of the film defy genre expectations, while giving the film a resonance that moves beyond political boundaries.

The Hurt Locker: Will the bomb explode in his face? Will he accidentally cut the wrong wire? Damnit, whats going to happen!? These were my exact thoughts throughout the entire movie. Not once did The Hurt Locker let up off the gas. Director Kathryn Bigelow's psychological thriller that follows a United States Army Explosive Ordnance Disposal team during the Iraq War almost one-ups James Cameron's Avatar. But not quite. The acting is phenomonal and the non-stop suspense kept me on the edge of my seat the entire two hours. Not only is the film about Sergant First Class William James disarming bombs, but about how his reckless ways of disarming them drives a wedge between him and his teamates. As the film goes into its third act you begin to feel sorry for William and just wish for him to go back to his son and wife. And once he does you realize why he never did. His life at home is just as broken as his life in war. In the end you realize William cant get enough of his own hurt locker and only sees war as a drug where he can get his "adrenaline fix." I give The Hurt Locker an A+.

Being a college student allows for some pretty cool opportunities to brush elbows with famous filmmakers. And who better to get an opinion on the year's Best Picture than from Michigan's (least) favorite son and the screenwriter of Mighty Ducks 3 and The Renaissance Man. The former criticized The Hurt Locker's way of building suspense ("Should I cut the red wire or the blue wire?"), saying it was a lazy way to make a movie. He also pointed out the film's pornographic element and the audience's inability to look away from something that's pretty disturbing. The latter, coming from a screenwriter's perspective, thought that Hurt Locker won the Oscar because it was simply a better script than Avatar, which is tough to argue against. Same reason Annie Hall won over Star Wars. Story prevails over technology and innovation.
My biggest question about the Hurt Locker is this: What exactly was it trying to say about the war in Iraq? So you want the troops to come home. I get that. But are we supposed to believe that everyone who goes to war has the potential to become a deranged lunatic? Or is it saying that all soldiers have problems and the war is their only outlet for aggression? Regardless, the risk and obstacles in filming and distribution are certainly worth recognizing and rewarding.

Besides the obvious action and suspense that you are going to get in a war-based movie like this, you also have a really interesting story. Our main character is addicted to a high caused by adrenaline. It never says how he got this way, if he has always been this way, or if it was his position as a bomb diffuser that made him this way, but regardless the viewer and easily tell that he does what he does because he loves it. 

At once point, we see him go out on his own to figure out what happened to a young boy he had met earlier in the movie. It's easy to believe that he's doing this because he was attached to the child, and that is probably what it was most about. But was it for the adrenaline, too? As he enters the house with a gun, it's intense until the man living there offers him a seat and asks him to stay for a while. That's when our main character decides to leave, with Mamma shooing him out of the house. Did he expect to find a bomb factory leader in the house instead of a normal civilian? Had he unconsciously hoped for a gun to gun stand off, instead of what he got? Maybe, maybe not, but it's a question that ran through my mind having seen his addiction in action.

One of my favorite moments of this film had to be near the end, after the bomb squad had failed to diffuse a suicide bomber's bomb. Sanborn and James are riding back to base from the explosion and Sanborn starts talking about how everything that they have done affects him. He's ready to die, he hates this place, he wants to go home and have a son and live. Then the next scene is showing James do just that, and how unhappy it makes him. To him, that's not living. He's not alive unless he's in that desert with a bomb to diffuse. The juxtaposition of these two characters' mindset of what they do and how they feel about it really spoke to me. It illustrated just how deep James' addiction really is and how having a job like this can really ruin a person for normal life, forever. It's no shock that the last scene is of a smiling James trudging back into a danger zone in that huge bomb-squad suit.

I honestly don't know how to approach reviewing this movie, Yes it was epic but nothing on the Apocalypse Now style, yes it was realistic but not as realistic and telling as Full Metal Jacket was and even the insane main character was done better in Apocalypse Now. That aside this was a suspenseful and realistic look at what the iraq war really is and what actually happens.

This movie is set during the early stages of post-invasion Iraq. The movie opens up with the quote "The rush of battle is a potent and often lethal addiction, for war is a drug" (which is referencing the main character). William James (played by Jeremy Renner)  becomes the sergeant of an Explosive Ordnance Disposal team (basically a bomb squad) when the old leader is killed in action. We then start to follow the Bravo company who are due to finish there rotation in less then a month. We follow them through there missions and watch as there health and mental state starts to decrease as they get in combat situations and bomb defusing situations.

This movie is no near a perfect war film, it just misses its mark by an inch. The suspense is done so well and you really don't know who is going to survive it really adds that edge of on surprise all classic war films have. The one thing that this movie is nearly perfect at is the suspense, the one thing it is lacking in is character development at the start of the film that early stage of the film that would make you connect with the characters in the film that bit more and when they are in life threatening situations your on knife edge because you want them to survive. 

The action scenes aren't Apocalypse Now ones with huge explosions, shots fired everywhere and people being killed left right and centre, The Hurt Locker relies on realistic situations and amazing suspense in fact it only has one 'shoot out'. The bomb defusing scenes really have you on edge and there's one in particular that nearly brings a tear to your eye. One of my favourite parts of this movie is watching all the on-lookers during the bomb defusing scenes and guessing who's going to set it off it, does really well at keeping you guessing until the climax (or anti-climax) of the scenes. Another great thing is that you don't know who is going to be killed and that just adds to the tension and the suspense.

The acting in this is amazing it really feels like a documentary, the cameramen feels like another character and it makes this feel so realistic. Although i have heard there are quite a few minor in-accuracys it still feels realistic, anyway even if it isn't realistic it still is an amazing movie.  Jeremy Renner who plays William James is masterful in his role of a man whose addiction to the adrenaline rush makes him an outcast at him and dangerous in Iraq. All the side characters also feel realistic and you really think they could exist in a real life situation. 

This is probably the best Middle East war film i have ever seen (i haven't seen the Messenger yet although it seems like more of a drama movie then a war film) and it really deserves credit at the oscars which i was very happy to find out that the hurt locker has had nine nominations so there should be at least one or more awards for this movie and hopefully it also gets the attention of people who have yet to to see this fantastic film.

I highly recommend this movie to anyone who has yet to see it but prepare for a emotional trip like you've never felt before in an middle eastern war film before.

The Hurt Locker
People have been praising this like it's a gift from the film gods. It's made plenty of top 10 lists and keeps winning numerous awards, and it's predicted to win Best Picture at this year's Oscars. So what did I think of The Hurt Locker? Read on and find out!
Directed by Kathryn Bigelow, The Hurt Locker follows a U.S. Army bomb squad in Iraq, but mainly focuses on three soldiers: SFC William James (Jeremy Renner), Sgt. JT Sanborn (Anthony Mackie), and Spc. Owen Eldridge (Brian Geraghty) just doing their job trying to stay alive to get out of Iraq. but it's real main focus is SFC William James' life experience serving in a bomb squad in Iraq.
Now I'll first talk about what I liked. The main things I liked about this movie was how intelligent the script was and how three-dimensional the characters are. The script was intelligent for being powerfully realistic and not your average cliche war or action movie. Like having a villain, rising action, and predictable moments. I loved how the three-dimensional the characters were because they all showed who they were and their true emotions and desires. Character-driven movies are always great. Exhibit A: Taxi Driver. Also the raw, handheld camera-documentary-style fell to it really puts a deep impact on the movie, which I like. The realism in this movie is amped up way high, which I think is great (script, dialog, cinematography, costume design, etc.). All the actors are very good as well. They play their characters and reveal their emotions brilliantly. Jeremy Renner was even nominated for Best Actor in a Leading Role for this. 
Now sadly, I have to talk about what I didn't like. Some of the parts in this movie can seem very unbelievable and unrealistic. Like the bit where James goes looking for the people responsible for supposively killing this little Iraqi boy, I feel that that is something an American soldier would never do. And one soldier said "war can be fun." All I have to say to that is: "WHAT?'
Overall, this is an intelligent, character-driven action movie.

It's hard to imagine a place where explosions, death and animosity are as common as a kite in a summer breeze. But right from the start, you feel the oppression, the hatred for the US soldiers. The film offers a real look into the fears of US soldiers and the addiction of war, how some are often unable to give it up after their rotations end. In addition, an ugly, side of the Iraq war not normally seen is revealed; its unpredictable, unforgiving nature. No one is safe and we're right in there, experiencing the tension as these soldiers feel it, hoping that they don't die. It's mundane and routine and and deviation can get you killed. Shot with a "cinema verite" feel, the film shows rather well the intense level of trust each soldier much place on each other, and how one maverick "war addicted" soldier can disrupt the cohesion of the unit. The film also shows how uncontrollably pointless it all is. Soldiers will do anything they can to feel normal, but it's never enough. The performances feel gritty and real, and the soldiers show surprising emotional depth. Actually shooting the film in the Middle East gave it a very authentic feel. War is hell, but a greater hell is the inability to willfully remove ones self from harm's way.

I wanted to see the movie based on numerous reviews that praised its gritty realism as well as Rick Steve's favorable reaction on his blog.  Rick Steves, who was the Washington Post military correspondent and spent time in Iraq, provided an outstanding analysis of the U.S. government and military's missteps in his book, Fiasco.  In the end, I was quite disappointed in the movie, based on my 12 months in Iraq and prior service as an enlisted soldier and U.S. Army officer.  Like any military, the U.S. Army understands that war is inherently risky business and strives to minimize risk.  It does so by building in redundancy whenever possible and ensure that the friendly side can bring overwhelming force to bear on the hostiles.  In this context, an adrenaline-seeking loner like the hero of Hurt Locker would be immediately identified and either court-martialed or receve an Article 15 punishment and be immediately shipped out of theater.  I also would think that the EOD approach, consistent with the preference to minimize risk, would rely on robots or have an SOP to evacuate and blow in place, making many scenes in the movie unrealistic. The Hurt Locker is nothing if not tense.  It drops you immediately into a world of war which wastes no time dwelling on the moments of non-intensity.  Bigelow's directing is evident in every frame of the film, and she draws outstanding performances from her actors, while she milks each moment for its tension, extending and stopping time alternately.  In the end, the quote that opens the Hurt Locker is its undoing, summarizing the theme so well that reflecting on it brings into question what the point of the film is.  I'd give it kudos for skipping the preach while I criticize it for being too sterile.  It's a film too climactic for its anticlimax conclusion.  But war films don't need to preach to be effective views into a moment of culture, and the Hurt Locker is an outstandingly entertaining and engaging glimpse.

In every war film we've seen before, we've been told the same thing: war is hell. "The Hurt Locker" changes our perceptions: war is a drug. And for Staff Sgt. William James, war is an adrenalin-soaked drug that feeds his addictive need to hurtle himself into unknown danger head-on. And that theme of "war is a drug" is a constant, heady reminder throughout "The Hurt Locker."

Set in Baghdad in 2004, "The Hurt Locker" follows the elite bomb squad of Bravo Company, in the last days of their deployment. When Staff Sgt. Thompson (blink-and-you'll-miss-him Guy Pearce) is killed while detonating an IED, Sgt. Sanborn and Specialist Elridge are introduced to a new superior officer, Staff Sgt. James (played by Jeremy Renner, in one of those performances that upon the first second of his introduction, you say to yourself, "this guy's gonna be a star."). It's clearly evident that Sgt. James marches to the beat of his own off-kiltered drum. During a key moment early in the film, when Bravo Company is called into to clear a bomb site, James learns a suspicious vehicle is armed to the gills with the kind of explosive power that'll "send us to Jesus." He disposes of his bombsuit, saying if he's going to die, he'd rather be comfortable. It's this insight that provides a glimpse into James' tranquil recklessness, which causes friction between him and Sanborn and Elridge; James has long figured out that his addiction to the adrenaline rush will inevitably kill him, so he accepts his fate with a Zen-like submission. 

Yet James willingly (or unwillingly) puts his two charges in jeopardy, as he suspects this rash of bomb detonations is a cat-and-mouse game being played by insurgents, and it's a game he's not wanting to lose. 

Under Kathryn Bigelow's skilled direction, "The Hurt Locker" builds upon a slew of tension-and-release sequences, each one ratcheting up tension that becomes more and more paralyzing to the viewer. In addition, her usage of hand-held cameras creates both motion and disorientation, placing you in the footsteps of the bomb squad of Bravo Company. As she's done most notably in "Point Break," Bigelow understands the male psyche and its' need for pulse-pounding action, but unlike the rollercoaster antics of "Point Break," "The Hurt Locker" treats its' subject and its' protagonists with the sobriety they deserve; instead of a thrill-a-minute shoot-'em-up, we're presented with a nerve-rattling meditation on an unfamiliar concept - the concept that, for some soldiers, war provides purpose and meaning, and that purpose and meaning is a powerful, intoxicating drug.

"The Hurt Locker" is a mesmerizing, thought-provoking, claustrophobic thrill ride, and it's easy to see why it's now become the front-runner to win the Best Picture Oscar. And for what it's worth, Kathryn Bigelow, just for simply having the cojones to take on this film as her own vision, richly deserves a Best Director Oscar.

A frontrunner for the Best Picture and Best Director Academy Awards, The Hurt Locker deals with a bomb defusing squad on the field in Iraq. When SSG Thompson (Guy Pearce) is killed when a bomb he is trying to defuse is set off, he is replaced as team leader by SFC James (Jeremy Renner). Things don't quite work out the way the other members of the squad, Sgt Sanborn (Anthony Mackie) and Spc Eldridge (Brian Geraghty), would like as James is an adrenaline junkie who's prone to not listen to anyone around him. As time goes on he detaches himself further from them, and leads them increasingly into more dangerous situations.

Kathryn Bigelow, ex-wife of James "King of the World" Cameron, is a woman who has never rested on her laurels. Each time she steps up to a plate to make a movie she makes something completely different. With Near Dark she hit up horror, with Blue Steel she played with the thriller genre, Point Break took on the action genre, and Strange Days took on sci-fi. Having not made a movie since 2002's K-19: The Widowmaker, Bigelow was looking for a new project. She was trying to determine what movie to make when she sent this script to James Cameron who told her to make this movie. Now Bigelow sits as the front runner for Best Director, only the fourth woman in the history of the Academy to receive a nomination, and may possibly even best her ex-husband for the statuette.

One of the things that stands out about this film, is that it's a war film that doesn't focus on the idea of whether war is right or wrong, whether or not we should be in Iraq, or if our soldiers are doing good things over there. With a job like bomb defusing, one of the great things, is that you're trying to make a safer environment for both your soldiers as well as the inhabitants that reside in the country you're fighting in. Picking this type of job is a masterful stroke, it allows Bigelow to stay out of politics and focus on the true message of the movie: War is a drug. The main character is a junkie, an adrenaline junkie. More and more he refuses to listen to those around him, and seeks bigger and bigger highs.

Really, The Hurt Locker is an excellent character study of how war affects people differently, like drugs, and this war as a drug metaphor is one of the most brilliant things to come from movies based on wars in the past decade or more. On top of that, for an action movie made from only $15 million (that's half the budget of District 9) this movie still looks better than action movies made for over $100 million, with much more to keep you on the edge of your seat. Also, filmed in a style reminiscent of a documentary the film has a certain real life feel to it, like rather than directing actors Bigelow directed a film crew tagging along with soldiers. Unlike many filmmakers these days, Bigelow really knows how to work suspense. Large portions of scenes are waiting for something bad to happen, and you really feel at any moment anyone could die. In a sniper face off, you sit with James and Sanborn on a ridge watching a building kilometers away, worried for your protagonists and hoping that they'll pull of the right shot. The movie doesn't include as much action as you'd expect, but because of the high suspense of the film you feel there's much more action in the film than there really is.

The acting in this film is superb, as can be noted by Jeremy Renner's Oscar nomination. But, in reality, this cast deserved the SAG ensemble nomination they didn't get. While Renner's role doesn't stand out as the "addict" really everyone does such a great job that you honestly feel this could be a documentary where each of these actors aren't actors, but actual soldiers in the field. Of all the things that stand out, there's a great scene that comes later on in the movie, where Renner's SFC James has to diffuse a bomb strapped to a man who's pleading for his life. It's an extremely suspenseful scene that is also touching as James tries to come up with anything he can to free the man from his burden, and the acting in a scene like that is what makes it so suspenseful as you care for these individuals because of their actions and the way that they carry themselves.

I highly recommend The Hurt Locker, definitely one of the best movies of 2009, and one that definitely landed on my top 5 list for that year. If you like war films, suspense, action, drama, and/or a good character study this is definitely one to check out. I know I'll be owning it!

Making a movie about a war that is currently going on is an interesting thing.  Where predecessors to this film have largely failed in attempts to depict the current war in Iraq, usually getting to bogged down in the politics behind the war and losing sight of the real stories taking place, The Hurt Locker abandons politics and focuses on the story of the soldiers and what they have to do day in and day out.  

This film delivers on many levels; story, acting, directing, and gives the movie goer plenty of intense moments.  The story focuses on a group of three soldiers who are basically the army's bomb squad.  These are the guys that get called in to disarm explosives.  Though the subject of the film is pretty large, the script does a good job of keeping the movie very focused on these three guys and what makes each of these guys tick.  No politics.  No pandering.  No heady conversation.  Its three soldiers trying to do their job.  

A strong script is only as good though as the actors who attempt to bring the script to life, and the actors of this film deliver on that potential.  Led by Jeremy Renner the actors give insight into each soldier and what makes him tick.  Sgt. James (Renner) the cowboy who does whatever it takes to get the job done.  Sgt. JT Sanborn (Anthony Mackie) the by the book man who of course clashes with James.  And Spc. Owen Eldridge (Brian Geraghty) who is very eager to please and just be a good soldier.  All three actors play their roles with precision and great heart.  

Finally, Kathryn Bigelow's great direction really pulls everything together.  Technically, she keeps everything focused on what the story is about.  The film never seems to go on any tangents.   The movie pacing is tight and never lags.  The only thing that I found a little distracting is the use of the very shaky handheld camera.  I understand the effect Bigelow was going for and I believe she succeeds in that, but handheld camera techniques like this tend to leave me a little motion sick.    

This really isn't the typical "war" movie.  There are no big, over the top fight scenes.  No massively huge explosions, though there are explosions.  No real "hero" for lack of a better word.  Just soldiers, trying to do their jobs, dealing with their humanity.  The Hurt Lockers is a strong film, the entire package, and a must see from 2009.

The Hurt Locker is a film of tantalizing suspense, gritty realism, and strong character portrayals. The film is not so concerned with portraying war in its entirety and instead focuses on the experiences of a few individuals who are members of a team that disarms bombs. 
Kathryn Bigelow does an incredible job of creating a specific atmosphere and immersing the viewer in it. Bigelow combines the turbulent psychological states of her characters with the grueling physical environment of Baghdad to construct a world that is truly unforgiving and indifferent to its inhabitants. 
The entire cast give strong, convincing performances. I was drawn to the stoic fearlessness of the lead man,Jeremy Renner, although I found his heroism to be a bit unbelievable at times, almost like he was a superhero. However, the film does reveal some of his vulnerabilities, which is important to the development of his character. The two supporting males, Anthony Mackie and Bryan Geraghty, were both well-developed and provide depth to the plot. The differening way these two deal with the struggles of war offer an interesting contrast to the steel nerves of Renner. 
The film differs from many war films in its originality and abstinence from cliches (for the most part). I thought some of the hyper-testosterone moments were a bit cliched, but this could be true to the experiences of males at war. Anyway, one of the most interesting aspects of the film is that it sort of turns the object of war on its head. One thinks, "War is about killing the other side before they kill you." However, in The Hurt Locker, the whole purpose of the characters' team is not to kill, but to prevent killing by disarming bombs. Although Bigelow sort of glorifies her characters, perhaps they ought to be glorified. These are men who immerse themselves in the line of duty solely to prevent violent explosions. While it could be argued that all soldiers play a part in saving lives, they usually take several lives along the way. It's not that the characters of The Hurt Locker are staunch pacifists, it's just interesting to consider that their job is actually the opposite of most of their colleagues. 
I appreciate that Bigelow largely ignored politics. Instead, she focuses on the specific experiences of her characters. Politics have little relevance to people who are in the act of disarming a bomb. The inclusion of an apparent political agenda would likely have bogged the film down and diminished the power of the film's scenes. Bigelow does a great job of showing rather than telling. 
I am curious to see what a soldier with combat experience would think of this film. In this review, I used the word "realism" as if I have a reality that even remotely resembles that of soldiers in combat. The fact is I don't. But The Hurt Locker at least feels real. It seems believable. It holds you on the edge of  your seat. Even though I'm perpetuating the naive judgment of war experiences by ordinary citizens by writing this review, it should be noted that relying solely on war films for developing a concept of war is probably not entirely accurate. Therefore, it is probably most appropriate for me to judge The Hurt Locker on the grounds of how well it tells a story, how well it develops its characters, and how well it holds the viewer in suspense. All combat naivety aside, the film succeeds in these three areas with exquisite precision and momentous intensity.

The Hurt Locker is to the Iraq war what Full Metal Jacket was to Vietnam. A character study on what the rigors of wartime military life can do to some people. Where The Hurt Locker excels, in a way that Full Metal Jacket did not, in my opinion, is it shows the everyday life of a soldier down in the dirt and grime of the battlefield. Sure there was some of that in Jacket, but let's be honest here, the boot camp scene outwashed the later war scenes by a large margin, and there's nothing wrong with that. This film focuses on three members of the Explosive Ordinance Disposal unit of the U.S. Army and their daily tasks of disarming or sapping IEDs and other devices. The main character, Sgt. William James is the leader of the three man group and the one who disables the IEDs they come across. He is introduced after the original lead man was killed in an explosion. It is immediately apparent that he has a much more hand-on approach to bomb sapping than his predecessor and is an adrenalin junkie, and becomes a major cause of contention and animosity among his subordinates, mainly Sgt. Sanborn, who for me comes off as the voice of reason in this film. The film starts out tense and uncomfortable, and stays that way, as it should, war is no joke and it is serious business at all times, much like this movie. The idea that is being conveyed here is that war changes men, and not for the better. Sgt. James, it is revealed is a family man, and when he finally rotates home, just can't shake the monotony of daily life in the safety of mainland America. I'm not going to give away the ending, and to be honest, I don't agree with the ending and I don't want to believe that that is how it is, but the ending works. It works so well that is validates the rest of the film in a way a happy ending never could. I loved this flick for the unrelenting sense of urgency I had the whole time watching it and for the unflinching look at the horrors of war that Kathryn Bigelow has conveyed. Watch this movie and hope that war doesn't do this to as many people as it implies.

Quite frankly, one of the best war movies I've ever seen. "The Hurt Locker" focuses on what it is to actually be addicted to war and the repercussions on those who not only crave it (through the character portrayed by Jeremy Renner), but those who are scared of it (Geraghty) and those who don't understand it (Mackie). Renner, who I've always thought to be a great actor starting with 2002's "Dahmer" and 2003's "S.W.A.T.," takes the lead in this drama as a rebel bomb squad technician who lives on the edge with every bomb he diffuses. An equally impressive Anthony Mackie ("We Are Marshall") plays the spotter on his team, with Geraghty playing the assistant specialist. 

Most might brush this film off as just another war movie made by the liberal media. However, I believe it's anything but just that. What makes this one of the best war films I've seen is that it doesn't so much as focus on just the action as it does on the humanity itself as well as the psychological toll that comes with fighting a war in a country where anyone can -- and most likely will -- kill you. Add the constant unease of being in a job that is as dangerous as bomb diffusion (where every move might be your last) and it's no surprise to see the mental toll it takes on the three central characters. Each moment these guys go into the field, director Kathryn Bigelow easily conveys (with the help of Marco Beltrami and Buck Sanders' on-edge score) the tense moments that fill any soldier's life during war. 

Bigelow deserved the Directors Guild Of America award for Best Director and I think she deserves the Oscar as well. The way this film was shot mostly had the feel of a documentary more than a major Hollywood motion picture. And that (along with using mostly slightly unknown actors) helped the believability of the story. I especially liked that the well-known actors used in the film were more like cameos and were not followed throughout the story (Guy Pearce, Ralph Fiennes, David Morse, Evangeline Lilly). 

For those who don't mind seeing films about war, this should be a must. For those who don't even like war films, you should still give it a try as I find it an essential viewing -- not just in cinema, but also for any film that truly encapsulates a post-9/11 world.

It's built on being very realistic and minimalistic in 'film' like qualities. The low droning score, no title sequence, and fly on the wall style of guerrilla directing all build this sense of character work and suspense that succeeds in every scene on the film. The acting is superb on all aspects (I got really excited to see Guy Pearce and Ralph Fiennes in the cast only to find them as secondary roles) with our three protagonists as our three muses of view points on the stress of their job. 

Sometimes I felt as though the focus of the film gets a little jumbled at times, which is only reason it doesn't get the full 5 starts. With its intensity and subtle side of film making, there are some moments that felt a bit off pace with the rest of the film. I understand that much of this is the 'artistic' side of the film and leaves it up to the decision of the viewer, but these moments tended to make me lose focus on what the general over-arching concept of what the film needed. Every person on the periphery of a scene is a threat; no one is safe here and the anticipation of violence is ever-present. For a film that has a relatively simple narrative, each scene is essentially about the same thing, differently played, itâs still incredibly gripping. For all the war films weâve seen set in Iraq itâs to Bigelowâs credit that she manages to make this seem like something new.
 Jeremy Renner is well cast as the reckless bomb disposal expert whose people skills only come to the fore in stressful situations. We discover with him and his team the sheer horror at the desperate measures that the insurgents will go to to create havoc and destruction, and are completely immersed in the experience of the front line it is so evocative.  The imagery is particularly effective; considering the film is about the thrill of risk and combating death, there are many moments where the sheer beauty of life abounds in a flying kite or a mini tornado whipped up in the middle of the desert, or the heart-break of an injured cat. Now, I watch a lot of war movies. Saving Private Ryan, A Bridge Too Far, Flags of Our Fathers, The Longest Day, Letters From Iwo Jima, We Were Soldiers, and Black Hawk Down, just to name a few. I like to watch them.

Let me say that the Hurt Locker is one of the best. This movie is gripping, riveting, intense, and shocking. Its simply amamzing.

This movie takes you into Iraq and doesn't let you go. The movie will have your heart pounding, your mind racing, and you will be glued to your seat. This movie is unrelenting.

I'm going to compare this heavily to Black Hawk Down. They have a similar setting, a slightly similar feel, but are very different. What they share is their intensity.

The Hurt Locker takes you through the lives of Bomb Defusal Specialists in Iraq. The horrors they have to deal with every day, the intensity and brutality of their lives.

The reason this movie is intense is not because of the fast paced shootouts and explosions of Black Hawk Down, but because of the sheer suspense. The bomb difusal scenes are incredible. The tension in them is very hard to match. The focus of the scenes has you in the moment, where anything could go wrong, leading to disaster.

When I go to a movie, I buy ample popcorn and soda. Its a ritual for me. If I'm going to a theater, I need my popcorn and soda. Usually, all the soda is gone, and I've dented the popcorn heavily. If I'm sharing it, its gone. During the Hurt Locker, I barely touched either of them. I was too tense to move my arm over to the cupholder, to pick up my soda, or to reach into my bag of popcorn. Only in the rare and breif moments of respite did I unfreeze enough to touch them. I was still glued to my seat when the credits began to roll, reeling from the power of the film.

This movie impacts you directly. Its not like most war films, with battles, rifles and machinegun's fireing rapidly. Explosions all around. This is different. The war is between the characters the bombs. There are a few scenes that differ from the formula, but they maintain the tension. "The Sniper Scene" is reminiscent of Saving Private Ryan's sniper scene, and Kathryn Bigelow does her best to match Steven Spielberg's level of tension.

Despite the formula of the movie, none of the scenes feel the same. The movie isn't just bomb after bomb after bomb. There's a lot going on, but it all revolves around a couple of guys, just trying to make it through the day. The movie comes down to that in the end, just a couple of guys trying to make it through their tour of duty.

The Hurt Locker counts down the days until they go home, so the entire movie is like one big ticking time bomb itself. Counting down to the climax that you know must come. 

The comparison to Black Hawk down most often comes in how the movie doesn't let you go. Black Hawk Down takes place over a short period of time. A short period of violent, intense, bloody, chaotic time. The soldiers in Mogadishu have to get out, and they keep on fighting until they are out, or until they die. The characters in Hurt Locker have to just survive each day, because each day is a struggle. Nothing is easy in Iraq for these men, and each day requires a lot of effort just to get by.

The Hurt Locker is not overtly anti-war film. It shows you Iraq and that's all. It has a deep message, but its one people have to discover for themselves. Kathryn Bigelow isn't like her Ex-Husband, James Cameron, who makes his messages very obvious. The Hurt Locker will leave an imprint on your mind, one that will have you thinking for a long time after the credits roll.

The tradgedy of the Hurt Locker was the movie's limited release. There was only one theater that was showing the movie near me, and the theater was nearly empty. Most people didn't get to see this in theaters, the way it should have been seen. I felt trapped in the movie theater, unable to leave, just like the mean unable to leave Iraq, or unable to leave their safe areas.

This Movie is the best of the year, far better than most of the low grade films that came out. If you have to choose between watching this on DVD or seeing a certain movie in Imax 3D that starts with an "A", see the Hurt Locker. This movie is a rare kind of film, one that will stay with you for a long time after you see it.

Maybe It Doesn't Need to Be Realistic  

Graham is trained in demolitions, apparently.  That he does not discuss his war experiences is not, to me, a suggestion that he has PTSD; it is merely that it would mean that he was talking about something, which is completely out of character for him.  I'd be more worried if he talked a lot about his experiences.  If the only real change in his behaviour patterns is that he doesn't have as much of a sweet tooth, well, we can cope with that.  (He also can't handle Terry Pratchett's [i]Monstrous Regiment[/i], because it's a little too close to real.)  I'm also not sure how much I want to know.  Even before he left, of course, he wasn't much into dramas, so even before, he wouldn't have watched it with me and certainly wouldn't now that he's back.  So I am afraid that my one demolitions expert was not inclined to tell me about the realities of war and where the film is coming from, so you won't get those details from me here.  We're going to have to analyze it as just another film, but since that's what most of us are seeing, I'm not sure there's anything wrong with that.

The film takes us inside Explosive Ordinance Disposal--EOD.  Mostly, we are dealing with SSG William James (Best Actor-nominated Jeremy Renner), who actually does the grim duty of disarming all those bombs.  (Though my understanding is that, a lot of the time, they just blow the damned things up and have done with.)  He works with Sgt. JT Sanborn (Anthony Mackie) and Spc. Owen Eldridge (Brian Geraghty) in the hot, dusty streets of Iraq, probably Baghdad proper.  (There is, so far as most people are concerned, no war in Afghanistan.)  Sanborn does not like James's techniques; he takes risks that put himself, and probably the others, in danger.  In some ways, there is no real structured plot to the film.  We are just watching the path of one man through a war zone and through experiences most people will never know.  His interest in Beckham (Christopher Sayegh), a young Iraqi boy, is almost irrelevant except as it moves him deeper into who he becomes.

This is one of the big favourites this year, and it's agonizing to think how many times it's going to lose to the big, shiny one.  Director Kathryn Bigelow still looks like a favourite, though, to win over her ex-husband, which is nice for two reasons.  Number one, it would be nice to have a woman win at all; they are greatly underrepresented in categories like directing.  Studios are less inclined to give female directors the same shot as males, regardless of credentials going in, and a few more wins for women in general wouldn't be amiss.  The other thing is, well, there is the issue of the studios.  This was a relatively minor picture, though that seems to be a theme this year, except for the shiny one.  I'm certainly not going to declare that the major studios are dead; that prediction has been made before, and it's simply not going to come true.  It's also true that every time a so-called "indie" gets a Best Picture nomination, it's supposed to be a revolution in filmmaking, and that isn't necessarily true, either.  It would be a nice change, though.

I believe it was Truffaut who said that there is no such thing as an anti-war film, because the movies make war look too glamorous.  We've discussed before whether he's right or not on that one, but this one definitely falls into that category.  Regardless of what Sanborn thinks of him, James receives nothing but compliments from higher echelon types.  He does his job, and he does it well, and if he's not exactly by-the-book, who cares?  Bigelow worked to capture the look of the explosives--or made her special effects guys do it--as best she could.  There is one amazing shot wherein the shockwave shakes rust off a derelict car.  Similarly, dust and pebbles hang off the ground for just a second until the wave moves past them and they fall.  But James is very much in the John Wayne stripe, only with a little more in the way of obvious psychological damage.  He has become a creature of war, and while he is concerned about Beckham, among others, that doesn't stop him from doing his job and doing it well.

If this wins even a couple of its nominated Oscars next month, and I think it will, it will become that rarest of things, an Iraqi War movie that people will watch.  We are, in this country, less effected by the war than we have been by just about any other.  I am the only person I know, leaving aside Graham's family of course, who has had a loved one overseas.  Yeah, a lot of my friends are too old to draft, even were there still a draft, but some aren't, and most of us aren't too old to join.  However, even in the depths of struggling to find a job, none of us do.  (Well, they wouldn't take me.  But you know.)  We don't get all the propaganda films of even Vietnam--there is no John Wayne charging up the sands of Iwo Jima or through the jungles of Southeast Asia anymore.  Even after all these years, you can probably count the number of major studio releases about the war without even having to take your shoes off, and for the ones which have made a big splash, I'm not sure you'd even have to take off mittens.

War is like a drug.  You just can't get enough.  The Hurt Locker focuses on a small group of soldiers that specialize in disarming improvised explosive devices in Iraq.  Rather than focus on the "big picture" of a full scale war, The Hurt Locker follows several soldiers during their tours of duty.  

Where the movie really shines is in the emotional stress of the individual soldiers.  Why do they do what they do?  What did they leave behind at home?  What consequences occur as a result of the commanding officer's decisions?

The movie unfolds at a slower pace than most war films, but Kathryn Bigelow's direction is superb.  Much like Requiem For A Dream, The Hurt Locker is a movie about addiction.  Whereas Requiem focused on the addiction of drugs, The Hurt Locker instead focuses on the addictiveness of combat, and the insatiable hunger for the next mission.  Definitely worth a watch.

In the Hurt Locker, a small Army bomb squad in Iraq loses their leader in a tragic terrorist bombing a month away from their rotation. He's replaced by "loose cannon" Staff Sergeant James (Jeremy Renner in an amazing performance) whose sadistic love/hate relationship with the war has turned it into a near drug-addiction for him as he disregards all precautions and his safety when handling threatening situations involving bombs or the enemy. Don't get me wrong, the idea seems to set up your standard generic action comedy involving loose cannons getting people in wacky situations, but there's so much more to the Hurt Locker than that. I'm told that this film is heavily unrealistic towards what's really happening over there and I don't doubt that, but the soldier/civilian relationship is already very strained between our two groups. The Hurt Locker serves its purpose of delivering a thrilling, poignant, and dangerous film that is damn-near flawless. Renner and fellow leads Anthony Mackie and Brian Geraghty (as his two team members) provide amazing, breakthrough performances that I hope will get these guys the attention they deserve. Not just that, but we are also provided with some great cameos by the likes of great actors like Guy Pearce, David Morse, Ralph Fiennes, and Evangeline Lilly. A bravo direction from Kathryn Bigelow (Near Dark, Point Break) who is getting the MUCH deserved attention she's should've had for a long time. I can only hope her Hurt Locker film steals the Best Picture Oscar from former husband James Cameron's Avatar. Would be a bittersweet victory! Overall, Hurt Locker is a winner. Movies become subjective as to when you see them. Those who saw this Katheryn Bigelow masterpiece before me have already proclaimed it the best picture of the year and it is in serious contention to beat Avatar for Best Picture at the Academy Awards. Admittedly, I have proclaimed my love of Avatar in previous reviews and do believe it should be considered seriously. However, after watching Ms. Bigelow's gritty, earthy portrayal of Iraqi war, I am not sure Mr. Cameron should be dusting off a shelf any time soon.

I will anger fans of Ms. Bigelow by comparing her film to her ex-husband's, but I am just observing based on the order I saw these films. One thing that struck me with The Hurt Locker was the all-encompassing visceral experience I felt watching this drama unfold. I was swept away by Cameron's 3-D visceral experience, but have to admit, watching the Hurt Locker on demand gave me a similar experience....I can only imagine what those lucky enough to see this gem in the theaters experienced.

Jeremy Renner's subtly gentle, yet reckless, portrayal is mesmerizing and taunt like the best Hitchcokian thriller. Anthony Mackie, unfortunately is unduly robbed in Academy recognition, despite his gritty performance.

Moreover, Ms. Bigelow brought the reality of war to our doorstep like no other movie previously. Millions of Americans sit comfortably in their homes and debate political ideologies. But what Ms. Bigelow reminds us is that war is a dirty, dangerous business by which this freedom is purchased.

We are blessed in 2009 with two films that will change movies forever. We are blessed with the magic Mr. Cameron unfolded in 3-D, and we will certainly have the lasting impression of our immortality with Ms. Bigelow's inspired thriller.

The Hurt Locker comfortably takes its place with important pictures such as Schindler's List, Coming Home, and Boyz In The Hood. And I must admit, I am on Team Bigelow for Best Director and Picture. Sorry James!

Generally I don't go in for war movies sent in the present or recent past, admittedly in large part because I don't feel particularly well-versed in the political subtext accompanying them, so I wasn't sure The Hurt Locker would be anywhere near my wheelhouse; but, not only does the film veer more or less clear of politics, it also succeeds in engaging the full and rapt attention of somebody who doesn't typically have an overwhelming interest in the subject matter simply (that somebody being me). It's a bit of a tough piece to for me to review, however, in the sense that it doesn't have the typical overarching plot or objectives I'm accustomed to (there's no real goal being worked towards outside of "Will they survive to the end of the 130 minutes?"); really, it felt more like a documentary than anything else, and I believe that's a credit, as I have to figure that's what they were going for. This was not a showcase for acting (it's not tossed aside completely, but I also feel it's not particularly flashy because that's not what's being done here), but rather for process, and I found myself appreciating that far more than I'm accustomed to. To that end, I understand and agree wholeheartedly with the praise for Kathryn Bigelow for her directing work as, again, this was an instance where I actually noticed things like camerawork and placement of set and was rivetted by that in the place of over-the-top characters and performances. The use of silence, slow motion shots, shaky cams, lighting, etc. put me totally in the moment as I was utterly engaged in the dangerous situations the characters were placed in even if I found them disposable in large part; Bigelow creates a world and moments that bleed intensity not on the back of your personal attachment to the people inhabiting it/them, but just because, and that feels so much more weighty. The scene that stood out most for me as an example of the film's quality was the face-off in the desert where Bigelow and company demonstrate that a tense lack of noise and quick flurries of discardable violence can be far more effective than explosions and gore in bringing to life the horror of war (I say as somebody who has obviously never experienced it first hand).

Though I said and stand by this not being an actors showcase, that's not to say the leads don't make the most of what they are given and in large part transcend just being believable as soldiers to create memorable performances. Jeremy Renner's charisma and intensity as Will James bring the character above being the stereotypical wild card and make him a fascinating enigma; his turn is extremely powerful, his physical nuances perfect, and he creates a very nice center for his supporting cast, most notably Anthony Mackie and Brian Geraghty, to revolve around.

The movie is certainly not without its flaws, as for as invested I got in the technical aspects of the work being done I never quite got over feeling over my head in terms of understanding it. Also, while the stakes in the moment certainly feel tremendous, as noted I felt no real sense of investment in any of the characters, which was certainly a negative at moments when their survival was supposed to be driving my interest in the film.

But the downside of The Hurt Locker is outweighed by the visual brilliance and technical excellence complimented by one damn fine star turn by its lead actor. For a movie I'm still not quite sure was for me, I enjoyed it a helluva lot.
