The Hurt Locker is a film that follows an EOD (Explosive Ordinance Disposal) team through their everyday lives in the war riddled Iraq. It gives the prospective of three individuals of three different mental states; the maverick, the brave-face, and one who is on the verge of a breakdown. This film shows the action-packed lives these men can lead as well as the emotional turmoil that follows the activities they perform on a daily basis.
        The direction of Kathryn Bigelow (K19: The Widow Maker) was extremely well done as she was able to get the most out of the actors she chose to trust with the task of their seemingly demanding roles. Choosing to shoot the film in a hand-held fashion was a wise choice as it made the film more real to the viewer, almost as if following a documentary at times. Throughout the film, Bigelow is able to capture every aspect needed to make this film complete, which she does with seeming ease.
        Mark Boal (In the Valley of Elah) wrote this film in methodical way that was able to capture a sense of realism. It consumed the viewer from beginning to end as it had a great balance between action and suspense while maintaining the realism of the emotion these soldiers go through. The film's grittiness came across when contrasting the main character's life was shown at home as comparing it to the life he had lived in Iraq. Some aspects were called into question about the realism of this film by some veterans, which is not at all surprising. There were some parts that seemed to stretch the plot to make it more entertaining than real, such as chasing after the car-bombers that Renner suspected of being within the location. Another example is him trying to locate the local boy he had grown to enjoy seeing. It is not unrealistic to think that the entertainment factor was an aspect in making some of this film as some of the action was very close in sequence compared to the emotional connection the men had with each other. Compared and contrasted it could be said there are aspects of truth and aspects of Hollywoodism.
        The acting in this film was well done. Jeremy Renner (SWAT) portrayed a maverick character with a heart that showed the range he has an actor. His convincing performance of a maverick, yet caring soldier was convincing and well deserved of the Oscar-nomination he received. Anthony Mackie (Notorious) and Brian Geraghty (I Know Who Killed Me) helped enhance the character Renner's character portrayed. Mackie played a tough-front type that was guarded and wanted nothing but his team to survive the day, trying his best to keep his emotions in check but sometimes they get the best of him. Geraghty plays the emotionally damaged soldier that comes from seeing his fellow soldiers KIA in front of him, affecting judgment and safety. The chemistry between the three is never forced as they give their expected performances with ease and professionalism.
        This film is one of the year's best. Kathryn Bigelow puts together a brilliant film that depicts many possibilities an Iraqi soldier could go through during their tour of Iraq. It really puts an emphasis on the emotions they go through as well as the inability for some of the soldiers to readjust to a normal life, perhaps leading the viewer to believe that serving in the war as addicting. The action sequences sometimes takes away from the main message of the film as it sometimes could lead into implying that it is just another action film which it is not. It is a must see as it is one of the most complete films of the year, depicting a very difficult subject with poise and nobility.

Director: Kathryn Bigelow
Release Date: February 18th, 2010
Lead Actor: Jeremy Renner
Running Time: 131 mins
Genre: War/Drama
Budget: $15 million

Review by Fraser Green

Director Kathryn Bigelow (Point Break, K19: The Widowmaker, Strange Days) finally delivers us her masterpiece, with the Iraq war/drama The Hurt Locker. The film stars Jeremy Renner (North Country, S.W.A.T.), Anthony Mackie (Million Dollar Baby, Eagle Eye), Brian Geraghty (Bobby, Jarhead), Ralph Fiennes (The English Patient, Strange Days), Guy Pearce (The Proposition, Memento) and David Morse (Contact, Disturbia, The Rock).

Iraq. Forced to play a dangerous game of cat-and-mouse in the chaos of war, an elite Army bomb squad unit, led by SSG William James (Jeremy Renner) must come together in a city where everyone is a potential enemy and every object could be a deadly bomb.

First released in 2008 in Italy, The Hurt Locker's premiere screening finished with a standing ovation from the audience -- and I can easily see why. This film is a masterpiece, using relatively no-name actors as the lead characters, showing depth and emotion to bring a sense of realism, or humanism, to the screen. It is predominantly a war/drama, rather than action, but it works so tremendously well as the characters are thawed out and have a solid script to work with. Bigelow's direction, using mostly the hand-held technique, is sublime making the film feel as realistic as possible, and the tension Bigelow builds in several sequences is incredible, mixed with music that is very similar, if not the same, as the 2007 film There Will be Blood. If it is the same, I don't really care that they 'stole' it, it's just so effective. The slow-pacing of many of the scenes complements the tension that it built, and really gives the audience a different insight to war and what it is actually like in the Middle East -- the characters help this along as the audience is able to connect with them and actually care about them.

Easily one of the best war/dramas to date -- close behind Spielberg's Schindler's List -- Kathryn Bigelow's stupendous film makes you feel everything happening on screen, and with the fantastic work from its actors, you have no option but to remain absorbed in this modern masterpiece of cinema.

Rating: 10/10

90/100.  This is a truly great film, and I'm not just going along with the hype.  There is a reason for this film getting so much praise.  There have been so many war movies, but this movie is more about the inner turmoil of the soldiers in this bomb squad.  There are no huge battle sequences like in Saving Private Ryan, but all of the scenes when they were out on the field on a job were very gripping and added to the character of each character.  I read on someone else's page that this is one of the few war movies that doesn't seem to have a political message- just showed you how terrible and dangerous each day is for the soliders.  It's pretty much a thankless job with no real goal at this point- and this movie finds a way to show that without being preachy and self-righteous.

*** Minor Spoilers ***

I was angry at Jeremy Renner's character for being such a cocky and reckless member of the team.  He was putting his team members lives in jeopardy.  I loved how that guy who was shot in the leg towards the end cursed at Renner- then the black guy started to break down in the hum-vee- it was a very powerful scene.  

My favorite scene was probably the sniper shootout in the desert when the main team was found the stranded team.  Everything from the cautious hello to the enemy sniper's first kill, to the gun jamming- to the capri-sun packets (must be the worst drinks to have in a desert when you're face and hands are covered in sand) - to the shy solider who made a nice kill to save their team with Renner saying "nice job" without even looking.  Lots of respect was earned that day between team members.  

I don't want to give away too much info, but I can't help it here.. the end sequence with Renner's character going back home and looking in the cereal aisle and helping to chop vegatables- none of that was important to him- then his conversation with his son was sad but heartbreaking- Renner's character has a cold, and reckless soul, who is not one to be domesticated and needs to live on the edge- hard to explain his mental state, but it was pretty intense. Not sure if he simply enjoyed the rush or if he truly believed that him being so good at defusing bombs would save lives of his fellow soliders since he sees the death toll on the TV at home.  I'd guess the former, as he said that he only has one love and he really enjoys himself out there on the battlefield... I hated his character early on, and ended up feeling for him big time.  

Very moving movie- and I ended up liking it a lot more than I did at the start of the movie.  I don't think this should win best picture, but it's nice to see it get a nomination (It would have gotten a nom even if the list was only 5 movies in my opinion).

When you hear that a movie has been nominated for several Academy Awards, if you're like me, you get a little excited to see it. This being said, I'm afraid I was disappointed in this film and a little mystified by all the hoopla. I think my major problem with this one is that the folks involved don't seem to know if they want to write something closer to fact or to fiction. I'm sure any kind of service in Iraq -- or Afghanistan, or anywhere else where people are dying in armed conflict -- is tense. This I can appreciate.

Never having been in combat or even near a war zone, however, I'm going to stick my neck out and say that I really don't believe life for a soldier in Iraq is exactly like the soldier's life portrayed here. To be a little more pointed, I don't believe that soldiers in combat at any time or in any place, are quite so stereotypical; I believe they are more like human beings. This movie is very tense -- and that's good. But this movie is full of caricatures, not human beings. I don't for a minute believe any of them belong to the real world -- even the awesomely solid Jeremy Renner. To me they are all types, and for that reason I don't really care about any of them. And it surely doesn't help that they cast the three biggest names -- Guy Pearce, Ralph FIennes, and David Morse -- as almost cartoon-like characters.

Contrast that with the combat veterans who come to my office all the time, and I tell you every one of them is real, and I sincerely care about each one of them.

If you want to see some intense war fiction, this movie may be for you. If you want to see real combat veterans dealing with real combat and its effect on them, then you'll probably do better with a well-done documentary.

Kathryn Bigelow's film does a great job of conveying the isolation of being a foreign army in a hostile land where the further and longer from base one goes the more vulnerable one is, no matter the high power weaponry at your disposal. Also, the constant strain of not knowing how any one day may finish with injury or death high up on the list of probable outcomes, with the end of the rotation a date that can never come soon enough.
Perhaps most successfully, it paints well the psyche of a bomb disposal expert. Here are men who (like mountaineers and rock climbers) get high on risk and who recognise their protective suits are worth zilch against most bombs they may encounter -  it is their ingenuity against that of the bomb maker - this addiction that is greater than any other urge in their lives including a serene home life and a new born son. 
The script by Mark Boal reflects his time as an embedded member of a real bomb disposal squad. Together with Bigelow, they stay clear of Top Gun like silliness and cliché and thankfully avoid making political comment. Through the use of hand held cameras the documentary style of camerawork has a positive effect. 
The shoot-out in the desert is a standout moment of intensity, focus, strain and luck.

"The Hurt Locker" could well be the movie of the year and is definitely in contention for the academy's grand prize. It is very rare for a film to come along in which it is a struggle to find no fault with, yet this is one of them. A movie that is climatic from the beginning till the end is indeed a rare find. "The Hurt Locker" shows the ugly and evil side of war, yet the film is so beautiful. The film is non-stop action and suspense from start to finish, extremely confronting and not for the faint hearted. In Iraq, a group of Americans participate in the bomb squad and are met daily with situations that could end their lives. Each day they are met with different dangerous situations and are faced with the concept of their own mortality. 

	The film itself does not have a straight story line, but is more a way of putting the audience in the shoes of these soldiers. Instead of having a beginning, middle and climatic ending, the whole film is a climax. The audience is completely on edge constantly and there is no sign of the end of the film until the credits start rolling. However, the lack of a whole and traditional storyline does not bother anyone. The film is a masterpiece to watch. The cinematography and editing are absolutely superb. It is a credit to Kathryn Bigelow as a director the way she has constructed her film. It is not a traditional war film, as it is not driven by acting and shooting, but rather by the anxiety of knowing that everyday you wake up in an area where a war is, everyday could be your last. How do they make it through each day knowing this and knowing that this is all part of your job? Some soldiers are completely disturbed by it, while others are oblivious to it. "The Hurt Locker" shows that no one is immune to weakness and it is not possible to be strong 100% of the time. 

	Jeremy Renner, who plays the lead as Will James, is superb and is well deserving of his Oscar nomination. He is witty and smart, and constructs both a strong and weak character. Anthony Mackie and Brian Geraghty play his sidekicks in the field and are both superb in their roles. The character development of the main character, Will James is fantastic. Again, it is not the traditional character development just at the beginning of the film, the development continues throughout the film thanks to a wonderfully written screenplay by Mark Boal. 

	The special effects that are used for the bomb blasts can almost be described as beautiful, if they were not being used for destructive purposes. The first blast in unforgettable and sets the stage for a beautiful, yet horrifying movie. There are many gasps throughout the film and at no moment do you feel safe watching these characters put their lives on the line. There are no guarantees of anyone being spared throughout the two hours. The suspense which the audience feels and the intense emotion felt are indications of how amazing the film really is. Congratulations Kathryn Bigelow, you are a genius.

"The Hurt Locker" opens not with a patriotic hymn, but with a flat statement: "War is a drug."  The film is about just that -- not a soldier fighting for freedom, venturing bravely into battle, forging a bond with his fellow soldiers, or any of the usual sentimental fantasy.  It is about a man who deliberately puts himself in danger to satisfy an urgent need.  We might call it a high, or perhaps a kind of aesthetic satisfaction -- certainly Staff Sergeant James resembles both an artist and an addict on the job, almost disappearing into a trance while he disarms bombs.  He is excellent at what he does -- he has disarmed over 800 explosives and kept the remains of many of them in a box under his bed, saying he likes to be reminded of what has almost killed him.  He is galvanized by that feeling sometimes called "touching the void."  The screenplay, along with Jeremy Renner's performance, manages a perfect balance between James' obsession and his professional expertise.  There are times when the camera cuts away from him to the faces of several Iraqi men and women watching him from windows and balconies, the subtle suggestion being that any of them might be the one responsible for the bomb -- one expert regarding another.  This film must have taken an Herculean effort to complete, especially on the part of director Kathryn Bigelow, who shot the film on insecure territory (Jordan, if I'm not mistaken), on 16-mm film.  I'm no great fan of hand-held "queasy cam" photography -- usually, I find it a nauseating, desperate attempt to create a sense of "authenticity," or to compensate for a lack of energy.  Not so here.  Bigelow knows exactly how to use hand-held to supplement the tension already there, and her editors, Bob Murawski and Chris Innis, understand that you achieve suspense not by rapid-fire music video cutting, but by *holding* a shot until the audience is beside itself with anxiety.  Some of the most unbearable moments in the film happen as we simply stare at the shell of a bomb, or even the side of a building, just . . . waiting.  This film is merciless and visceral, yet somehow, at the same time, it carries emotional undercurrents (there is a reason it is titled "The Hurt Locker").  And considering the way it sees war for the enigma it is -- horrifying, yet strangely compelling to those who participate in it -- it earns a place in the company of "Apocalypse Now."  If I had it my way, "The Hurt Locker" would win this year's Academy Award for Best Picture.

The explosive action thriller is given a much more cerebral redressing in The Hurt Locker. It's being lauded by all and sundry as the best of the films thus far about the current war in Iraq, but I respectfully disagree- this is a film about its characters, not about Iraq. 

Jeremy Renner plays Sgt. William James, a bomb disposal expert drafted in to replace the recent head-sploded leader of a small team of American soldiers, and that's what the film is about. The film could as easily have been about any war, but seeing as how Iraq is the current big warzone, that's where this character study is set. To my recollection, George W. Bush and 9/11 are not mentioned even once in the whole film, because director Kathryn Bigelow is making a film about the soldiers, not the politics.

Bigelow's casting of Jeremy Renner is also a masterstroke. His terrific breakthrough performance deserves the Oscar nomination it received this year. He's the protagonist while the big recognisable stars in this film are all barely in it. Guy Pearce, Ralph Fiennes and Evangeline Lily all make appearances, but not one of them features for more than five minutes. Even David Morse, an actor you probably can't place without looking at IMDB but you'll go "oh, him" when you see him in the film, appears for about three minutes overall. 

In making this film, Bigelow was not about casting Shia LeBeouf as a bomb-disposal nut to sell more tickets and put more posters on billboards. It's all about getting you close to the characters, and it's this approach that makes the whole thing a lot more immersive, not to mention that it puts the film lightyears ahead of any preachy, political or jingoistic film about the Iraq war to date.

Don't get me wrong, by the way- I'm certainly not trying to downplay the explosive element of The Hurt Locker, because I did pick that picture for a reason. In an industry with so few female directors, Bigelow stands out as the best (and possibly the only) female action director, because this film alone is so unbelievably tense. 

The best sequence of the film involves Sgt. James and his colleagues lying on their stomachs in the scorching sun for a whole day, watching their enemies from afar through a sniper scope, just waiting to retaliate if necessary. 

The silence is tense, but the bravado the men try to muster as they wait is worse- it's where the audience is shown what makes these men tick. Why do people who go to Iraq, go to Iraq? 

As a whole, The Hurt Locker is just outstanding- it's the only film I've ever seen to which I can honestly attribute the phrase "The windscreen wiper made me shit myself"- Kathryn Bigelow capably builds the tension throughout, exhausting you at the end of the film. As you come up for air though, I hope you'll agree that it will be a travesty if it loses out on Oscar glory to Avatar on March 7th.

A tense and gripping war-thriller that keeps you on the edge of your seat while highlighting three well-realized characters and several strong acting jobs. This film is worthy of all the buzz that it has received thus far including the multiple Oscar nominations that it recently earned (in the time since I first published this review, the film went on to win 6 of those awards including Best Picture, Director and Original Screenplay at the 2009 ceremony). At first, it may seem as though this has little in common with other grimmer and grittier war films like Platoon, Saving Private Ryan and Black Hawk Down, all of which paint the starkest picture imaginable of modern warfare but ultimately, The Hurt Locker proves to be just as stunning an indictment of the dehumanization that often accompanies life on the battlefield. All the while, it still provides viewers with a jolt of adrenaline that equals or bests many action films. The set-pieces are expertly-crafted and the taut pacing keeps everything on an even keel. Don't be fooled though; this isn't wall-to-wall action. The script takes time to explore the day-to-day drudgery of a soldier in this situation and this adds to its believability.  Of course, knowing that this was written by someone who actually spent time with a bomb disposal unit in Iraq (journalist Mark Boal is credited with the screenplay) enhances the sense of verisimilitude.  Perhaps, the biggest reason why the tension level is so high is that we identify with the main trio of characters which allows us to care about their circumstances. These guys aren't superheroes; they are just ordinary men placed under extraordinary pressure with equal capacity for good or for bad. Credit the performances, as well as the writing, for drawing the audience into this dangerous world. In particular, Jeremy Renner (whose performance earned one of the film's nominations) succeeds in burrowing under the skin of the lead character, SFC William James. Initially, it would be easy to dismiss this guy as just another arrogant, thrill-seeking jackass in the vein of Tom Cruise's Top Gun alter-ego, Maverick, but James proves to be a far more complex individual than such a facile description would indicate and Renner's fierce portrayal fully allows his humanity to emerge. The performances by Anthony Mackie and Brian Geraghty provide a solid counterbalance to Renner's more gung-ho personality. Some of the better known actors to populate the cast include Ralph Fiennes, Guy Pearce and David Morse but none of these performers gets more than 10 minutes of screen time a piece. Lost's Evangeline Lily also has a small but somewhat crucial role. Ultimately, however, its the top-billed trio that catches and holds our attention.  The real star, however, is director Kathryn Bigelow, who is finally getting the sort of serious acclaim that had eluded her for so long. Her first big claim to fame, of course, was marrying and then divorcing filmmaker James Cameron (who, ironically, represented her biggest competition at the 2009 Oscar ceremony for his box-office champ, Avatar - which took that crown from his previous effort, Titanic). She then went on to solidify her action film credentials with her sure-handed direction of such films as the overblown surfer flick, Point Break and the underrated cyber-thriller Strange Days (which was co-penned by Cameron and featured the aforementioned Fiennes in the lead role). She hasn't done much in the intervening years until now...and what a comeback this is! Bigelow proves that her years of toiling in relative obscurity during the early part of this century have paid dividends. Her use of cinema verite film techniques give this film a gritty aesthetic that brings us closer to the action and the on-location shooting in Jordan provides the perfect stand-in for Iraq. 2009 proved to be a surprisingly strong year in cinema and The Hurt Locker has earned its spot amongst the creme de la creme of that year's class.

Almost all of the war movies I've seen can be put into one of two groups: those that glorify war, and those that show the horrors of war.  I can't think of any movie that simply shows war, the good and the bad.  The Hurt Locker breaks this tradition.  This seems to be the overlapping theme of the film, and the moments when we see it are where the film shines.  We see moments where the characters are at their breaking point, seeing friends and civilians die in front of their eyes.  We see them making rash decisions in moments of despair, and we see them wishing death upon themselves.  We also see them in moments of great heroism as well, saving lives, making friends, and bonding with their teammates.  By the end of the film you get the feeling that despite all the shit they go through, they live for what they're doing.

The story is told in an unconventional manner, often seeming more like a series of events rather than a consistent overlapping arc.  I often hate this in movies, but here it works, because that's how war is for an individual soldier, simply surviving day to day.  What we do get in manner of overall story is the tour of duty of three soldiers, Elridge, Sanborn, and leader James who takes the place of Thompson who is killed less than ten minutes into the movie.  James seems cocky and unpredictable, and his methods clash with Elridge and Sanborn, and tensions rise amongst the teammates.  There are a few subplots, namely a friendship developed between James and a local boy who sells DVDs, but we mostly see the day-to-day events this group goes through.  Defusing bombs, stopping suicide bombers, dodging snipers and the like.  All of these events are tense and thrilling.  The sniper sequence I mentioned goes on for over 10 minutes, largely just being the two groups shooting at each other, yet it remarkably never gets boring.  It's a truly gripping experience.

Let's take a closer look at that sniper sequence again.  10 minutes that thing lasted, and I was captivated the whole time.  How many other movies can you think of that could pull that off?  I can't even think of any that have tried.  The Hurt Locker tries and succeeds thanks to the great direction of Kathryn Bigelow, and performances by actors I've never seen before.  Examples such as this can be seen throughout the entire film.  The film is directed and performed in a method so personal and believable that it sometimes feels more like a documentary than a work of fiction.  The shaky cam style can be nauseating and excessive at times, but for the most part it works and enhances the experience.  The style of directing feels so intimate and the performances so real, that I grew to care about the three characters before I even got to know them.
  
This seems to be one of those movies that everyone universally loved (or at least liked), so there's really not much more I've added to the opinions already expressed.  If you've read this far and you haven't already seen it, what the hell are you waiting for?  Go to your local Blockbuster, or Movie Gallery or the house of a buddy with an obsessive DVD collection and rent/borrow it.  I guarantee you won't be disappointed.

Renner steals the film as the 'crazy' William James who is obviously addicted to the adrenalin of the front lines. He is ably supported at each turn and some nice cameos give the film much needed depth.
There are missteps: the US scenes are overwrought, a lot of the scenes are incredibly unrealistic in terms of tactical warfare yet the film seems to expose a more ordinary truth about the men serving there. The film was shot in Jordan and the tension of a place full of Iraqi refugees bleeds into the film.

Baghdad, in 2004, three soldiers of an Army bomb-disposal unit are investigating a report of an improvised explosive device (IED). They use a sophisticated robot drone to examine the device, which consists of several undetonated artillery shells wired together and hidden under plastic/fabric sheets. The unit, led by Sgt. Thompson, decides that they can detonate the IED using plastic explosives that theyll activate from a safe distance. Thompson also says that the explosion won't cause very much property damage and should result in no loss of life.

A small cart is affixed to the back of the robot, which is then sent back into the blast zone. Before it can reach the IED, the trailer loses a wheel. Thompson dresses in a bulky bomb suit and walks down to the trailer. He picks it up and carries it to the IED, rigging it properly. As he walks back, his partners, Sgt. Sanborn and Specialist Eldridge, scan the immediate area for anyone they consider suspicious or who may be in the blast zone. When Thompson is about 25 meters from the bomb, but still in the kill zone, Eldridge notices a man running a butcher shop who is using a cellular phone. Eldridge yells to Sanborn and the specialist begins to run toward the man, ordering him to drop his phone. Sanborn tells Eldridge to shoot the man, who presses a sequence of numbers on the phone. The bomb detonates with Thompson still in the kill zone. The overpressure from the bomb kills Thompson despite the bomb suit; a large splash of blood hits the inside of the clear visor on his helmet.

Thompson's body is packed into a coffin for shipment home, Sanborn supervises the procedure. He looks over Thompson's possessions for a few moments before the coffin is sealed. Back at the base, Eldridge is sitting in the rec room when the base psychologist, Lt. Col. Cambridge walks in and asks Eldridge how he's feeling (in the wake of Thompsons death). Eldridge is still clearly upset over the incident; he dry fires his rifle several times, suggesting that if he'd shot the man with the cell phone, Thompson might still be alive.

A new leader for the team, Sgt. William James, arrives at the base. Sanborn meets him at his housing unit, where James is taking the plywood covers off his windows. When Sanborn suggests that James keep them on because of mortar shrapnel, James tells him that they won't be any good anyway if a mortar shell crashes in through the unit's roof.

The next day the team responds to a report of another IED on a narrow street in the city. After the initial investigation, where they link up with the Army platoon that reported the bomb, James is dressed up in a suit similar to the one Thompson wore previously. As James approaches the bomb site, he tosses a smoke grenade, which agitates Sanborn, who can't see James to instruct him further. James also is uncommunicative with his team members, another factor that Sanborn does not appreciate. James finds an artillery shell buried under a small pile of trash. He disarms it easily, and then notices a secondary wire leading away from it. He unburies the cable and finds it connects to a junction of six more cables. When James pulls on the junction connector, six more shells are uncovered. Another cable leads to a nearby building. James disarms the six new shells; as he does, he notices a man quickly leaving the building, presumably the bomber. James flashes one of the small detonators from one of the shells and smiles at the man, who vanishes from sight. Back at their Humvee, Sanborn tells James that he needs to communicate more during operations and not treat his duty as if it's a solo act. James brushes his teammate off. James does the same later when he and Sanborn talk while grooming themselves for another day's work in the latrine.

The team is again called out for another bomb threat. This time, the bomb is in a car parked in front of a United Nations building. When the building is evacuated, James dons the bomb suit and walks toward the car, which suddenly becomes engulfed in flames. James uses a fire extinguisher to put out the fire and begins to examine the car while Eldridge and Sanborn take up their positions as lookouts. James opens the trunk and finds several of the same type of shells he'd seen the day before. After a few moments, he takes his bomb suit off completely, knowing it won't protect him; there is enough explosive in the car to kill everyone nearby, including his teammates, even if they take cover. James disarms the shells and begins to search the car for the triggering device, a process that takes several minutes. At one point, when Sanborn tries to talk to him through a headset, James pulls it off and throws it aside. A few more very tense minutes pass as James searches the car. Sanborn and Eldridge notice several groups of Iraqis watching them from rooftops and from a minaret. They also see a man filming the incident with a video camera. At the car, James finally finds the triggering device and detaches it. When he returns to the Hummer, he lights a cigarette and is promptly hit in the face by Sanborn, who is again angry that James refused to acknowledge him or any questions he had. James appears strangely unoffended, nor is he angry at Sanborn. A colonel on the scene approaches James and is clearly impressed with James steady nerves and ability to handle such a crisis. When he asks James how many bombs he's disposed of, James gives him an exact number. The colonel is further impressed.

Back at the base perimeter, Sgt. James confronts an Iraqi kid who sells DVDs to the soldiers. The boy, who kicks a soccer ball around and calls himself Beckham, had sold James a movie a few days before; James wants his $5 back because the DVD was poor in quality. When Beckham tries to hustle him further, James is amused and tells him he can keep the money if he's able to block a shot at the makeshift goal area Beckham has set up. Beckham blocks the shot and James agrees to buy another movie from him, mildly threatening him if it's defective.

The team goes out to the desert to detonate some of the explosives they've collected on missions. As they prepare to explode another bomb, James stops Sanborn to briefly drive down to the blast zone to get the gloves he left there. While he's gone, Sanborn tells Eldridge that, with the dangerous nature of the explosives they detonate in the desert, it would be easy to "frag" him by exploding the bomb while James is down there and claiming it was accidental. Sanborn seems pretty intent on doing so but Eldridge tells him not to.

While heading back to the city, the team sees two SUVs parked on their route. They approach them and the occupants standing around as if they were any other threat. The men standing near the vehicles quickly obey Sanborn and his team, dropping their weapons. One of the men reveals himself to be a British commando and the bomb unit relaxes. The British man says they have a flat tire but have broken their jack handle. James offers them equipment from their Hummer. While one of the British men handles the flat tire, the Brit shows the bomb unit members the men he has captured (presumbably high level Iraqi officials) to turn in for a reward. Suddenly, the man fixing the tire is hit by sniper fire and falls before the shot is actually heard. Everyone runs for cover; the British commando mercilessly shoots both of his prisoners as they run away; the reward for capture dead or alive is the same.

The bomb unit and the Brits find themselves pinned down. One of the Brits is killed while manning the Hummer's .50 caliber machine gun. The British team leader takes up a sniper's position on a small, rocky hill and begins to return fire with a Barrett rifle, shooting at a distant stone building where the enemy sniper and a small group are hiding. While adjusting the Barrett's bipod, the man is hit in the chest by the enemy sniper and killed. Sanborn takes up the man's rifle and James spots for him using a powerful scope. They fire several shots back at their enemy and run out of ammunition for the rifle. James has Eldridge search the dead man's pouches and he finds a full magazine. However, the man's blood has leaked onto the rounds and they must be cleaned off to cycle through the Barrett rifle. James helps a queasy Eldridge clean off the rounds. Sanborn is able to continue targeting the building and its occupants and, with James spotting, they're able to kill all the enemy troops. Eldridge notices someone who may be another sniper lurking at a position behind James and Sanborn and he opens fire. Eldridge is unsure of how well he did, but the other man is hit and killed.

The incident seems to create a strong bond between James and his teammates. Having found that they can actually work well together as a team, they celebrate at James' housing unit, taking turns pounding each other in the chest and drinking. After discussing why James seems to be such a maverick teammate and how he got into their line of work, James shows them a box of pieces that he's collected from nearly every bomb he's disarmed. He says he keeps them as reminders of how dangerous his work is. Eldridge and Sanborn are a bit puzzled but now know, after the desert incident, that James is actually a team player.

On their next mission, Colonel Cambridge accompanies the team when they patrol a building where bomb making material has been seen. Cambridge stays outside while the team searches the building. Inside, they find the bomb making supplies and that the bomb makers have just left. James finds the body of a young boy whom appears to be Beckham. He orders Sanborn and Eldridge out of the building spots a large incision in the boy's chest. He opens it and finds several pounds of plastic explosive in the body's abdomenal cavity. He carries the boy outside to the Humvee. Outside, Cambridge is trying to clear the locals from the street, when another IED goes off, killing him. In the immediate aftermath, Eldridge cannot accept Cambridge's death and wanders the area looking for him. He also finds Cambridge's helmet lying in the blast area.

Back at the base, James talks to a man who sells DVDs at the perimeter. James asks the man if he knows Beckham, however the man's English isn't very good and he tells him nothing. James asks the nearby sergeant if the man checks out & the sergeant tells him the man is cleared. Later, when the man packs up his merchandise and leaves, James jumps in his truck and forces him to take him to Beckham's house. James enters the house and finds another man in the kitchen who is scared but surprisingly hospitable. James demands to know where Beckham is at gunpoint, but the man doesnt know. James realizes he's mistakenly entered the wrong home and turns to leave when the man's wife appears and begins to yell and throw things at him. James makes his way back through the city to the base, passing hundreds of angry-looking locals. At the main gate, he announces he's a US soldier and is forcibly arrested. When the duty sergeant demands an explanation for his being off the base at night, James says he was at a whorehouse. The sergeant slyly asks him where it is.

The team responds to a call at night to check out a bomb blast zone. When the get there, they find that a bomb, possibly from a suicide bomber, went off near an oil tanker truck, causing a huge blast radius. James scouts the perimeter of the blast area and theorizes that the bomber didn't commit suicide but stood outside the perimeter and triggered the blast from there. James is furious and vows to find the bomber by ordering Sanborn and Eldridge to search the nearby streets. The three split up; shots are heard and Sanborn and James reconnect, however, they spot Eldridge being dragged off by two unidentified men. The two open fire, killing Eldridge's kidnappers but James hits Eldridge in the leg. James becomes severely upset at wounding his comrade and nearly breaks down in the shower, fully clothed.

The next day, James and Sanborn go to meet Eldridge at the helicopter that will evacuate him. As he approaches their Humvee, Beckham, unexpectedly alive, appears and tries to talk to him, but James ignores him. At the helicopter, Eldridge is bitter with James for shooting him, saying his femur has been shattered and recovery will take months. He also berates James for taking them into a danger zone to satisfy his adrenaline rush. Eldridge is flown off.

Sanborn and James respond to another bomb report and find a man standing alone in the middle of a large plaza. James has the translator order the man to his knees and he suits up and walks to him. When the man opens his coat, James sees he's wearing several pounds of C-4 attached to several steel bars which are locked together with large padlocks. The man pleads for his life, saying he has a family. With only two minutes left on the bomb's timer, James frantically tries to cut the locks. There are too many and James must leave the man behind. Seconds later, the bomb goes off, killing the man and throwing James in his bomb suit out of the blast area. Sanborn rushes to him, thinking he's been killed like Thompson was. James is only stunned and wakes up. As they head back to the base, Sanborn, still shaken by the incident, tells James that he fears he will die in Iraq, having never had a wife or children. James tries to comfort him and convince his friend he'll make it back home and start a family.

The team's rotation ends and James goes back to his home and family. While shopping in a store, he is overwhelmed by the cereal aisle, which has too many products for him to comprehend. He also is unable to adjust to home life and his relationship with his wife and daughter becomes increasingly strained. James decides to return to Iraq and he does. The final scene of the movie shows him beginning a new rotation and approaching another bomb site in his suit.

During the early months of the post-invasion period in Iraq, Sergeant First Class William James becomes the new team leader of an Explosive Ordnance Disposal (EOD) unit with the U.S. Army's Bravo Company, replacing Staff Sergeant Thompson, who was killed by a remote-detonated improvised explosive device (IED) in Baghdad. He joins Sergeant J.T. Sanborn and Specialist Owen Eldridge, whose jobs are to communicate with their team leader via radio inside his bombsuit, and provide him with rifle cover while he examines an IED. James's insistence on approaching a suspected IED without first sending in a bomb disposal robot during their first mission together lead Sanborn and Eldridge to consider him "reckless". Back at Camp Victory, James befriends Beckham, a young Iraqi boy who works for a local merchant operating at the base, selling pirated DVD movies to the soldiers. The team is next called out to the United Nations building in Baghdad, where a parked car has a large bomb in the trunk. While James intensively studies the intricate bomb, Sanborn and Eldridge provide him with cover. Sanborn becomes increasingly concerned about three men watching them from a minaret and another filming them from a nearby rooftop. With the building evacuated, he suggests to James that the they pull out and let a team of engineers come disarm the bomb. James ignores and angers Sanborn by removing his radio headset and his bomb suit, and remains with the car until he disarms the device.

While returning from detonating bombs in the desert, the EOD team encounter a British private military company. They soon come under enemy attack, and three of the British mercenaries are killed in the ensuing firefight, which ends after Sanborn and James shoot the last of the insurgent snipers. For their next mission, the team heads to a warehouse to retrieve unexploded ordnance. While securing the warehouse, James discovers the dead body of a young boy who has been surgically implanted with an unexploded bomb. James is sure that it is Beckham, while Sanborn and Eldridge are not entirely certain. That night, James forces the merchant for whom Beckham worked to drive him to Beckham's house. Upon entering the house to which he is brought, James encounters an Iraqi professor and demands to know who was responsible for turning Beckham into a "body bomb". The professor thinks James is a CIA agent and calmly invites him to sit down as a guest of his household. A confused James is then forced out of the house by the man's wife, and sneaks back into Camp Victory with the help of a sympathetic guard. That same night, Eldridge is accidentally shot in the leg during a mission in which the EOD team successfully tracks down and kills two bomb makers. The next morning, James is approached by Beckham, who is alive and well. Much to Beckham's confusion, he is completely ignored by James. Eldridge blames James for his injury, claiming James unnecessarily put his life at risk just so that he could have an "adrenaline fix", referring to Sanborn's suggestion that the mission, which James had ordered, would be better suited for an infantry platoon.

With only two days left on their current tour, James and Sanborn are called in to assist in a situation where a man was forced to wander into a military checkpoint with a time-bomb strapped to his chest. James cannot remove the bomb nor disarm it in time, and is forced to flee before the bomb goes off. On the ride back to the base, Sanborn becomes emotional and confesses to James that he can no longer cope with the pressure of being in EOD, and relishes the prospect of finally leaving Iraq and starting a family. James is next seen back at home with his wife and child, visibly bored with civilian life. One night he has an internal monologue in the form of speaking aloud to his infant son, where he says that there is only "one thing" that he knows he loves. He is next seen back in Iraq, ready to serve another year as part of an EOD team with Delta Company.

US Army Sergeant First Class Will James, Sergeant JT Sanborn and Specialist Owen Eldridge comprise the Bravo Company's bomb disposal unit currently stationed in Baghdad. James is the tech team leader. When James arrives on the scene, Bravo Company has thirty-nine days left on its current deployment. It will be a long thirty-nine days for Sanborn and Eldridge whose styles do not mesh with their new leader. James is a renegade for who the thrill of the dismantlement seems to be the ultimate goal regardless of the safety of his fellow team members, others on the scene or himself. On the other hand, Sanborn is by the books: he knows his place and duty and trusts others in the army to carry out theirs as well as he. And Eldridge is an insecure soldier who is constantly worried that an error or misjudgment on his part will lead to the death of an innocent civilian or a military colleague. While the three members face their own internal issues, they have to be aware of any person at the bomb sites, some of who may be bombers themselves.

When SFC William James joins Bravo Company in Iraq, they have a month or so left in their tour of duty. He's a bomb disposal expert and he is replacing Sgt Matt Thompson, a long-standing member of the team who was recently killed disposing of an improvised explosive device. To say that James loves what he does doesn't quite capture the emotional high he experiences when he gets to do what he does best. For his fellow squad members however, including Sgt JT Sanborn and Spc Owen Eldridge, they just want to survive the few days of duty they have left. James risk taking however drives them all to the edge.

An intense portrayal of elite soldiers who have one of the most dangerous jobs in the world: disarming bombs in the heat of combat. When a new sergeant, James, takes over a highly trained bomb disposal team amidst violent conflict, he surprises his two subordinates, Sanborn and Eldridge, by recklessly plunging them into a deadly game of urban combat. James behaves as if he's indifferent to death. As the men struggle to control their wild new leader, the city explodes into chaos, and James' true character reveals itself in a way that will change each man forever.

A war movie that critics have labeled "One of the best films of 2009." 

The Hurt Locker was written by Mark Boal and directed by Kathryn Bigelow, who also directed such action films as Point Break and Strange Days. 

The independent film was first released in 2008 in Italy. The next year, The Hurt Locker was limitedly released in the U.S. Soon after the film started receiving positive reviews The Hurt Locker got a widespread release on July 24, 2009 and has so far made more than $16 million worldwide. 

What makes this film different from other past war films is that it does not follow the same concept of displaying high-octane combat and excessive bloody-violent sequences that are predictably shown in the battlefields of almost every war film. But, rather, The Hurt Locker focuses more on a war tactic that's been overlooked in past films that being the Explosive Ordnance Disposal unit (bomb squad). The film's setting is in 2004, during America's early invasion in Iraq. Sergeant First Class William James, (Jeremy Renner), becomes a team leader of a EOD unit that consists of two other army soldiers: Sergeant JT Sanborn, (Anthony Mackie), and Specialist Owen Eldridge, (Brian Geraghty).

The realistic setting can have viewers on the edge on their seats, as these soldiers are under great pressure to defuse these complex, intricately placed bombs before their "enemies" either try to shoot them and/or detonate the bombs. The movie gives two different perspectives on how these soldiers try to survive while in a hostile environment. Sanborn and Eldridge are use to being overly cautious when completing their missions, but their new team leader James throws caution to the wind, knowing that the risks he takes are a matter of life or death but is not over anxious and just focuses on living life day by day. In one scene James goes so far as to take off his bomb suit when attempting to defuse an explosive device, saying to Eldridge "If I'm gonna die, I want to die comfortable." At first, Sanborn and Eldridge become threatened by James' reckless behavior, feeling he is unnecessarily putting their lives in danger too. 

The action and suspenseful moments in this film are worthwhile. The incredible acting is realistic with an added touch of drama without being too melodramatic. 

Personally, the ending of the film is really good. When James returns home to his wife and baby, he tries to find some form of normalcy in his daily life but mentally is still reflecting about life on base. The difficulty in separating these two lives is evident when James makes conversation with his wife by casually talking about a gruesome event that happened during his mission in Iraq. Within a few months later, James returns to Iraq to serve another year with his EOD team. It is to no wonder why the beginning of the film stated, "War is a drug." 

Despite some questioning the authenticity of the film, several critics have praised The Hurt Locker. It has won various awards and has even been nominated nine Academy Awards, including Best Picture, Best Actor (Jeremy Renner), and Best Director. 

Kathryn Bigelow has definitely set the standards for other female action-film directors, and hopefully more female directors will embrace this genre of films in the near future. 

Whatever a person's political views are about the war in Iraq, and whether or not it is a war that soldiers are dying in vain for, everyone can agree on that soldiers put their lives on the line for the sake of their country, doing their job no matter what and for this you can have nothing but respect for the sacrifices they've made. That is what The Hurt Locker portrayed so realistically, a soldier's perspective on fighting the war in Iraq without any political agenda attached to the film. 

The Hurt Locker is rated R and contains war violence and language.

However it isn't the case in either situation.

Granted there are moments relatively cliche considering the war movie genre and there is quite a bit of predictability, but the topic itself is very original. Dealing with a squad whose single task is to sabotage or otherwise destroy enemy explosive device is quite interesting in the first place. Add in the level of fear that the term IED now represents to the world and you have yourself one hell of a movie. A lot of movies try to be suspenseful, and a lot of movies fail miserably at trying to achieve any level of true suspense. I would say this movie is an honest depiction of what American soldiers have to go through to bring peace and security in a war-torn country. 
    The story is about a bomb disposal team assigned to clear roadside bombs that's intended to maim and kill American soldiers. Jeremy Renner plays SSG William James,the main character who seems to have a penchant in diffusing bombs and doesn't care if it blows him up to kingdom come! James gets his adrenaline fix whenever he goes out to diffuse a bomb which almost cost him the life of a fellow soldier in one instance. His expertise in successfully disarming bombs (800+ so far) made him an invaluable asset and have earned him the respect of fellow soldiers and even commanding officers. Like most soldiers,James has a family back home. During the course of the movie,I realized that his "devil may care" attitude  is one way of coping with being away from his family. 
    I like the dialogue between James and Sgt Sanborn(played by Anthony Mackie) when they were inside the humvee. I guess most of us have a proclivity to taking risk without thinking about the reason for doing it. But in the end, it really boils down to what's important to us. The acting is topnotch even though the actors who portrayed them is virtually unknown. If you're expecting to see a war film that's full of guns blazing and massive explosions just about everywhere,then this is not the movie for you. Although there's some action and explosions in this film that was done stylishly(like the opening scene),it's purpose is not only to entertain but to deliver a message to its audience. 
    This is probably one of the best film I've seen in the last couple of years and the kind of film I'll remember in years to come. It deserved to win the best picture for BAFTA. I certainly hope it wins the Academy award as well. I just find it awkward that former married couple Kathryn Bigelow and James Cameron's film "Avatar" is vying for the same coveted award. In the end,itâs still up to the audience to decide which film ranked best in their list. Truly worth watching! 10/10

From the very first scene of this film, it's clear that it's a cut above the cookie cutter action films which Hollywood pumps out on assembly lines nowadays. Just how far is unclear until further along in the film, but if the first scene isn't enough to grip you like a vice, I don't know what is.

Staff Sergeant William James, played with beautiful restraint by Jeremy Renner, is a bomb tech in Iraq, not the best combination. However, unlike most normal people, Will finds bombs a rush, a thrill, almost a turn-on. Each time he goes out, it seems as though he's having more fun than at any point in time. This becomes even more apparent towards the end of the film, where he tries to connect with his wife and child by telling them horror stories of Iraq. He fumbles with his other relationships, with his wife, with his team members, with the local kid selling dvds, though he's solid as a rock when it comes to being less than a foot from a live explosive. Renner plays this role pitch perfect the whole way through the film, whether he's calling his wife or lighting up what might as well be a post-coital cigarette after a hair raising, nail biting experience with a bomb.

The film, though it's war film, steers clear of the politics of why the troops are there in the first place, opting instead to show what's happening to the boys who are over there. And how perfectly it shows this, from Sanborn's emotional breakdown after a particularly harrowing experience (to say any more would mean spoilers), to James' loss of composure during a house raid, the script is a perfect balance between smarmy and heartbreaking.

Brian Geraghty's performance as Specialist Owen Eldridge is worth a special mention. Every time he's onscreen he inhabits his character entirely. When he tells his psychologist what's playing on his mind and when he mourns the victims of a bomb blast, he is perfect in both situations.

But it is the set pieces which make the movie the movie which may actually beat Avatar. Each one is gripping, a thriller movie in itself where the outcomes are unclear, everyone is a suspect and every moment could be someone's last. The movie does little more than follow the everyday movements of Bravo company, but each day is more intense than the last. And the ending is perfect. There could be no other option for how this film could finish. In fact, I would have felt cheated if everyone had lived happily ever after, and the fact that you left wondering not only how crazy Will really is, but whether his luck is still within the best before date.

The Hurt Locker isn't just a film about the war in Iraq but tells a story about how soldiers cope with loss, anger and the constant fear of being killed in any war environment. The film revolves around a squad of bomb defusal soldiers stationed in Iraq in 2004. Within the first few minutes of the film the audience is thrown right into the action as we see the squad's commanding officer get killed by a roadside bomb. Already just less than 10 minutes in, we're given a solid understanding of how dangerous it is to be stationed in such a warzone. The danger of being shot or killed by a bomb is constant throughout the film, and never lets down. This element of danger makes us fear greatly for the three main character's safety and really helps with drawing in the audience into the warzone. SSG William James is soon sent in as the squad's new commanding officer, and the two existing team members Sgt Sanborn and Spc Eldridge quickly become acquainted with James' reckless methods.
The Hurt Locker is a non-stop nail biting ride from start to finish. The bomb defusing scenes not only keep you on the edge on your seat but the film shows off an incredibly impressive sniper scene which highlights the complex process of targeting and firing at an enemy with a sniper rifle. The Hurt Locker also delves into the area of the psychological impact war can have on soldiers, as seen through Spc Eldridge's experience. Director Kathryn Bigalow places large emphasis on how war can be used as a drug and turned into the ultimate thrill ride. The soldier who sees war in this different light is William James. He loves his job so much that he often disregards the safety of his own men, just so then he can get his adrenaline fix. 
The viewer may become thrown off by the constant use of free hand camera work, but this is only a minor flaw of the film. The Hurt Locker is just one of those films which you must watch for it's gripping bomb defusal scenes and refreshingly new perspective on war.

The Hurt Locker, like many movies of 2009, came as a relatively large disappointment to me.  It wasn't a bad movie, it certainly wasn't a great movie, and the national praise it's receiving is surprising.  The Hurt Locker centers itself around three soldiers in the EOD (Explosive Ordnance Disposal) and immerses the viewer into their psyches. This is easily the movies greatest accomplishment as you can really feel what is running through each mans mind as they confront several life threatening encounters between bombs, insurgents and even themselves. However, the narrative is weak as if the storytelling can justifiably be overlooked because of the previously mentioned strength.  In fact, because the movie puts its primary focus into the emotions of the soldiers and very little into the story itself, in the end it all seems forgettable.  A couple of out of place cameos, large gaps of time unexplained and a sense of cockiness from the director all left a bad taste in my mouth.  Just because the Iraq war has not been filmed well in most previous attempts doesn't mean a movie that does it a little better becomes an instant best picture nominee.  Once again as mentioned is a previous review, District 9 and Up are clearly two better films that are almost entirely out of the realistic running for whatever reason.  The Hurt Locker isn't bad, it just gets too caught up in itself to really stand out as a top shelf war epic.

An incredible war film which has garnered deserved praise for both its barbaric realism and exciting action. Bigelow has always been a director of enormous talent, and I am glad to see her find a real gem in this script, a story that lets her utlize her eye for movement and her delightful sense of humor.Using the Iraq war as a backdrop, she explores intense psychological questions without attempting pretentious answers. The cast is one of the best parts of this film- Mackie, Fiennes, Pearce, and especially Jeremy Renner- these are actors of extraordinary power who find real motivation in these parts. The key to the film's success is the way it uses these actors not as pawns or political ideologies, as most contemporary war films do, but as human beings. The violence which occurs is not a result of war as an event but as a result of the people who participate in it. The intensity of an event is only as big as the people who cause it, and Bigelow allows us to see cause and effect relationships, both minor and catastrophic, in a reasonable and unpolitical way.

"The Hurt Locker" was described by one reviewer as "an almost perfect movie".  I feel I need to watch it again to verify this and perhaps make the review 5 stars instead of 4.  What it is is one of the best war movies to come out in ages.  Recent pictures featuring the Middle East conflict have all been politically slanted, and I admire that this isn't a political movie, but a war movie.  It's tense and this tensity is well paced and extremely effective.  Though she hasn't made a lot, Bigelow fashions some great action films.  Even with Keanu, "Point Break" was an exciting and highly fueled action vehicle. My favorite of hers which was mostly panned by critics was "Strange Days"--a sort of mysery noir about the fears surrounding technology.  Anyway, the premise is simple--the effect that war has on the men who fight them.  And Iraq is no typical war. Most casualties have come from makeshift bombs in the conflict and while there are some gunfights, the film lacks any battle scene.  One interesting scene features the bomb-crew on a rare night off entertaining themselves by beating the shit out of each other.  Without a visible enemy, they need to vent their rage on something they can see.  Jeremy Renner is of course the most interesting career.  War is a drug to him in every way shape and form--which is perhaps the motif of the film.

I don't usually like war movies. They tend to be very preachy, leading to 2+ hours of either constantly condemning the evils of war or Wayne/Stallone/etc. mindlessly waving the stars and stripes while gunning down anyone who isn't American. The Hurt Locker partially succeeds by not bogging itself down with politics. The main reason for this film's success, however, is the tension. The various bomb-defusing sequences have just as much tension as any great thriller. 

The Hurt Locker also works because of the cast. The acting is pretty good throughout, and the actors that bothered me (looking at you, Evangeline Lilly; you aren't much better here than you are on Lost) don't get much screen time. Jeremy Renner did a great job playing the adrenaline-junkie William James, who stays fairly likable despite nearly getting a lot of people killed (repeatedly). 

My only complaint about The Hurt Locker is the camera. There were parts that were so shaky that it reminded me of Cloverfield. That style worked in a POV "holy shit, a giant monster" movie, but not so much here. The shaky camera is fine at times, but it just goes overboard. Had it been less erratic in certain parts, this would have been a perfect movie.

Very tense, very well-acted, great cinematography make up the movie, The Hurt Locker. I love the intensity in this movie and I love the angle the filmmakers took with the story. A great screenplay providing a new twist to a war movie, taking the bomb squad unit and putting the focus on a small group of guys who are depended on by so many, both military and civilian. The characters are great, maybe a little cliched  but still very well done. Jeremy Renner is awesome as the fly-by-the-seat-of-his-pants bomb diffuser who has an addiction to being in the war. And the other two men both perform exceptionally well in their roles, especially Brian Geraghty who is extremely timid and feeling guilt about the death of a previous member of the unit. And then he latches onto the bravado of Renner's character and has great confidence that later proves to be false. The camera angles and use of handheld cameras really provide some great theater with the action and tension rolled into one. The interaction with Iraqis and the on-base relations are two things I found interesting. I am curious as to whether or not these situations actually occur or were they just developed to make the movie more interesting and human? One aspect I didn't like or at least understand was the use of Ralph Fiennes and Guy Pearce is such abbreviated cameos that in some ways stole from the purity of the moive and the subject matter. Not sure they were needed; it was almost as if they were helping out a friend (the producer or director) and filling in some roles. The same could be said about David Morse but he isn't as big a star as Fiennes and I felt his role wasn't too bad in the context of the film. That would probably be my biggest beef; the rest of the movie is just really good. The emotions. The acting. The intensity. A great modern war film. And certainly a  movie that should be watched.

It's easy to have high expectations when a movie gets bandied around as being 'near perfect' (usually in its own trailers) and receives almost completely positive reviews. It's also rare to find a movie that can meet those expectations. Whilst The Hurt Locker isn't going to change the cinematic landscape or cause viewers to suffer an epiphany, but it is a masterwork of cinema and difficult to find fault with.

Broken down into a series of sequences following an American bomb disposal squad serving during the Iraq war, mostly centered around group leader Ryan (Renner) who has a reckless and direct approach to his work. Director Bigelow doesn't offer anything original in terms of visual style, dipping heavily into recent action movie trends and cliches, such as shaky camera work, washed out colour palette and split-second editing. What she does do, however, is employ these techniques effectively, using them to rack up the tension in each encounter instead of the over-the-top tangled mess of CGI that most action directors seem to think looks 'cool'. Each scene is in itself an exercise of suspense that no doubt will become textbook learning for a new generation of film-makers.

The cinematic traps and cliches avoided by Bigelow is what elevates 'The Hurt Locker' head and shoulders above its peers. There is no pointless McGuffin to 'motivate' the characters, and there are no scenes of tension killing exposition to pad out the opening act. Viewers are dropped straight into the action and character traits and motivations are not communicated by the actors spending every second scene standing around talking loudly about their feelings (which should give the Oscars a headache finding a scene for their clip show) but rather leaving it up to the characters actions, subtle and crazy, to paint a picture. Even scenes in which one character chats with a military psychologist feels closed off and the soldiers attempts to block the doctor's probing questions.

No doubt the Academy Awards will once again mistake profit with quality and leave the Best Director award in the hands of Bigelow's ex-husband for his spirited remake of 'Fern Gully: The Last Rainforest', but there's no question that this is the better film.

While this to me was not the work of genius that many have touted it as, it is nonetheless a solid, well-directed war film, and perhaps the most complete and watchable piece to focus on the second Iraq war so far.  

The film's strength is it's focus on the job that the protagonists are required to do; the rights or wrongs of the conflict itself are not really explored, and for the film to try and do this would have been too much for it to cover.  Instead we are presented with a faintly obsessive portrait of a bomb disposal team, who are portrayed not as heroes, but simply as men undertaking a difficult job.  The understated performances of a largely unknown cast lend an air of realism and almost complete plausibility to proceedings, with perhaps the desert encounter with a group of English mercenaries led by Ralph Fiennes being the only overtly "cinematic" sequence of the film.  

What comment the film does make about war relates to the direct affect that war has on its participants: Anthony Mackie's turn as the haunted, broken Sgt Sanborn is perfect, as is Jeremy Renner's as SSG James, an adrenaline junkie who by his own admission has been rendered unable to function in the civillian world.  

Bigelow's verite-esque style works incredibly well (parts of the film were apparently brought together from over 200 hours of 16mm hand-held footage), but her occasional use of flashier insert shots - such as the super-slow-motion shot of a cartridge hitting the dirt during the sniper battle - is jarring, and detracts from the measured, down-at-heel feel that she and cinematographer Barry Ackroyd did so well to acheive.  

To my mind, this is a film which could have been truly awful if placed in the wrong hands.  A cast of Hollywood big-hitters, a thumping soundtrack and a CG-heavy look could so easily have been slapped onto the script in pursuit of box office dollar, and created something far less thoughtful and affecting than Bigelow's work.  I hope that this film nets her the recognition she has so sorely deserved for so long: she is simply one of the best action directors working at the moment, and her ability to capture both the unbearable tension of the bomb disposal sequences and the simmering frustrations of the team's downtime is admirable.

We have a bomb disarming specialist enlisted in the Army doing his thing overseas.  Obviously he does it well because otherwise this would be a really short movie.  But barring that obviousness, the film should get a special notice for being the first movie about the current war that isn't half-bad.  It won't change your life and you can telegraph more than a few scenes out ahead of time (one scenario in particular should have anyone remotely paying attention thinking "Oh, you know that guy is about to die") but it's a good time.  And it's probably wrong to call a film that deals with the mental and physical abuse our soldiers face on a regular basis a "good time," but it is a quick two hours that will leave most satisfied.  Our lead guy does well, his team does well , even that soccer-loving kid does well.  There is just something that didn't quite engage me like it should have with this, and I fully recognize I'm in the minority not singing this movie's praises to next Tuesday.  I dug the honesty of the players and of the ending (because, really, how else could it be?) but I felt this was just one bomb disarming incident to another with padding to make you think contrary to "he's our hero, if he dies the movie is over so clearly he'll succeed."  That sort of works in theory (and by "sort of," I mean "not at all" but don't want to spoil stuff) but for all the hype and talk, this falls just short of greatness for me.

The main character in "The Hurt Locker", Staff Sgt. William James, a bomb diffuser, enters the story after his team's previous bomb specialist dies in action. Death in the line of duty doesn't deter Sgt. James. War for him is addictive, and he participates for the effects (I'll leave it up to you as to whether you think the war is "illegal". Even the film shies away from political grandstanding).

"The Hurt Locker" is about Sgt. James and the team assigned to protect him and work alongside him as they scour Iraq for IEDs and other hidden explosives. Documentarian Ken Burns, in creating his recent series "The War", mentioned once that a big difference he found between the World Wars of the early 20th century, and the current war in Iraq is the mission. In World War II, soldiers fought for the cause -- fight off Japanese oppression, end Nazi occupation, etc. Today, in an era when the overall mission can be unclear, soldiers fight for the man or woman next to them on the front line. In the case of "The Hurt Locker", that leads to a very complicated and sticky relationship.

Routinely under-heralded Anthony Mackie plays Sgt. Sanborn, head of the team that goes into the most dangerous zones of the war to uncover and diffuse bombs hidden in the ground, in the walls, in cars, nearly everywhere. Sanborn is counting the days until he leaves the desert, certainly a different mindset than war-addicted Sgt. James., yet it's clear that he and Sgt. James would die for each other. That male bond is brought vividly to life by director Bigelow. She doesn't employ tricky effects like David O. Russell did with his brilliant but different "Three Kings", her direction is more drenched in reality, one I would never want real for me. Jeremy Renner plays Sgt. James with a fiery deliberateness, and he referred to Bigelow's direction as that of "a voyeur". This is a great asset to the film. The movie has top-notch production value, but never announces it. Instead, we get a very credible relationship drama about people under intense pressure.

The film was written by Mark Boal, who wrote the great and very underrated "In The Valley of Elah", also about the Iraq War. That movie (and other Iraq-themed films) tanked, but I'm glad Boal remained undeterred and continued to write about the war. It's paid off, as "The Hurt Locker" is a money-maker, and is destined for Academy Award consideration. An acting teacher of mine often praises work in class when the relationship is "complicated". Too cut and dry, too easily-explained, and we're bored. Boal nails the complicated world of an Iraq soldier, who balances grief, fear, anger and exhilaration on a daily basis. They make life and death choices for themselves and others over and over again. "The Hurt Locker" is the first film to really portray Iraq as the most dangerous place in the world. Nearly everyone these soldiers come across could be guilty of planting bombs. Is it because they hate Americans? Is it because they are tired of Americans in their country? Do our soldiers belong in harm's way? Are they keeping peace? The end result...is complicated.

Film Review- The Hurt Locker

Written by real life war reporter Mark Boal and filmed in Jordan mere miles from the Iraq border, The Hurt Locker is a contemporary war film that largely does without typical sequences of gunfire and bloodshed in favour of gritty realism and psychology. Set in Baghdad during the early stages of the invasion, the film centres around a team of explosives disposal officers, their job being to navigate the hellish terrain defusing bombs constructed by insurgents out of discarded shells. From the very beginning the sense of danger is instilled in the viewer; anything lying in the litter strewn landscape could explode, any civilian could hold a detonator.  Such is the danger that it is only minutes into the film when we see the effect of the devastation, with a bomb detonated by a civilian with a mobile phone claiming the life of team leader Sergeant Matthew Thompson. His two team members, Anthony Mackie as the strong and level headed Sanborn and Brian Geraughty as the inexperienced and anxious Eldridge make up the central trio of characters, completed by new team leader William James, played by Jeremy Renner. 

Compared to the cautious and professional Thompson, Jamesâ methods are reckless and dangerous, his focus seemingly on individual glory and his own desire for an adrenaline rush rather than the safety of the team. It is this conflict between the 3 soldiers as well as the personal demons harboured by each man which is the main story point. Taken close into the action, the viewer is sucked into the tension, whether it be in a ticking car bomb, an intense sniper fight or a heated altercation between the characters. The filmâs âless is moreâ philosophy is an effective one, the sense of dread that surfaces as James pulls a spider-like 6-mortered bomb out of the ground having more impact than any overt display of violence. The character of James is brilliantly complex, at first appearing to be nothing more than a wild glory hound but slowly revealed to be a natural leader who truly loves the thrill of the job. His over-confidence while working juxtaposed with the vulnerability shown in his private moments makes him an intriguing hybrid of hero and villain. The audience may find themselves feeling sympathy for him not only as he reveals his personal issues to his team mates (that being a complicated domestic situation with his ex-wife and baby son), but also that he is so lonely and troubled that he actually takes comfort in danger, that he is seemingly at peace when risking his life. 

The actors do a fine job of conveying the subtle shifts in the relationship between the 3 characters, the dynamic between James and Sanborn being particularly important. Renner and Mackie are equally adept at portraying both hostility and camaraderie, while the fresh-faced Geraughty nails Eldridgeâs innocence, confusion and guilt. The film is fast paced and tight, complementing the urgency of the subject matter. All elements combine to bring the excitement levels to fever pitch, especially the jarring camera cuts and pulsing, heartbeat like score. Every action sequence is a winner, the constant undercurrent of danger and the always rising tension making you believe that anything can happen at any moment. The pinnacle of this is the climactic final sequence. Involving an involuntary suicide bomber, it is an edge of your seat experience and a prime example of visuals, music and dialogue all combining for maximum emotional impact.

At the films conclusion you may find yourself exhausted, having felt that youâve just ran for your life from a ticking bomb. But it is great films that are able to transport you so completely into their environments and the psyches of their characters, and The Hurt Locker accomplishes this soundly. 

****

Kathryn Bigelow focuses on the masculinity issue to uncover a curious concern: what makes a man go to war again and again?  No film has ever done this so impressively.  War films tend to look at the grand scale of war, looking at the humanity and/or inhumanity drawn from its madness, and, we're more accepting that soldiers emotionally crack every so often from this chaos.  The Hurt Locker suggests it's the reverse - the broken emotional self is the constant which can be stimulated to perpetuate the on-the-ground-hyper-violent mindlessness in war.  Soldiers survive by acting and reacting to violence and those who are unable to transcend that in the aftermath - the man unable to heal himself - become agents of the 'addiction to war.'  This is by no means a typical war film, but its compassion in delving into the much neglected broken selves of the foot soldiers makes The Hurt Locker one of the best ever made in the genre for quite sometime.
