One this season's surprise critical hits and Oscar nomination scarfing films, The Hurt Locker flew under most people's radar this past summer. Directed by Katherine Bigelow (Strange Days, Point Break, being James Cameron's ex), this film tracks the lives and exploits of three Army soldiers whose specialty is defusing bombs in wartime Iraq. Jeremy Renner, Anthony Mackie and Brian Geraghty round out the bomb squad in a film that's one part war flick, another part psycho-drama and all parts wonderfully kick ass.

The first thing you notice about the film is how expertly paced and balanced it is. From the first shot to the ending frame, everything is perfectly pitched. Humor is balanced with raw emotion and intense action is intertwined with light hearted joking, all expertly mixed by Bigelow, who deserves top mark for her work in this film. Without her excellent direction, this film could have easily devolved into "just another war flick". Thanks to her, the film brings something new to the table.

Full credit also goes to Jeremy Renner in the role of SSG William James, the leader of the team and the most complex character of the three. When you first meet James, he tends to come off as brash and arrogant, but as the movie develops, you learn how deep the character gets and Renner does a fantastic in this emotional balancing act. If it weren't for Jeff Bridges, he would be the front runner for a Best Actor Oscar.

The other actors do a fine job filling out the triangle. Mackie, playing the hardened journeyman soldier and Geraghty as the young kid just trying to make it though play nicely to Renner's character. The cinematography is also noteworthy as it drops it you into the fray in almost a pseudo-documentary style that not quite District 9, but features a combination of shaky cam, quick pulls and classic filmmaking that compliments the story nicely.

When all is said and done, The Hurt Locker effortlessly balances all the intensity, drama and emotion of modern day warfare in what shapes up as an instant classic. Featuring fine performances by the top three actors, a thrilling story and top notch direction by Ms. Bigelow, The Hurt Locker is one the finest films released this year and is a no-brainer must see film.

The Hurt Locker is an intense, gripping and emotional film which has all the elements put together brilliantly. An excellent war film with characters one can truly invest in, but (for me) it was a very forgettable movie.

This is not a movie I could stand to watch twice. The film's greatest strength was it's ability to build tension and thus do I think a second viewing would be far less enjoyable. The reason I'd call it a 'forgettable' film is because there is no real 'climax' to it, but a series of small ones. Also, there is no overriding story or relationship to hold it together, other than the brotherhood of the characters. There were many long stretches where I found myself losing concentration. However, there were also many moments where I found myself hanging onto every second, curious and terrified of what would happen next. The whole film was rises and falls - very much like war, but not particularly gripping in a filmic sense.

At first I didn't particularly enjoy the film - feeling it to be like any other war movie, but with the introduction of the character James, I began to invest in his character and he made the movie much more enjoyable. Jeremy Renner played his part brillantly, and I largely think that he was the saving grace of this movie. The emotion that he brings into it - with his connection to a loveless family and his unexpected friendship with young Beckham, makes the movie feel less like a macho-domination testosterone fest. However, I feel that the film does lack a strong sense of 'heart', and thus am I surprised that it was directed by a woman!

The sound editing in this film was truly brilliant, although I didn't actually 'like' it whilst sitting in the cinema. The sudden explosions were so loud and unexpected that they put you right in the moment, which terrified me somewhat. It drew me into a world I didn't neccessarily want to be in.

The cinematography was quite excellent, although once again, I didn't neccessarily 'like' it whilst watching it. Hand-held camera is something I can only take so much of, and in this film, it is used so much that we never get a breathing space. However, this so perfectly depicts the situation of the characters in their tension-ridden job. Very effectively used, though uncomfortable for a viewer.

This film is a very (what I would imagine) realistic depiction of war which throws you right among the bullets. A good screenplay overall, with plenty of brilliant moments. A very intense, searing, battle-weary and powerful experience, Kathryn Bigelow's acclaimed Iraq war film is a triumphant piece of filmmaking - never compromising in its reality or focus, all the while keeping its humanity and heart intact.  The previously unknown Jeremy Renner is stunning as a maverick bomb disposal expert in war-torn Iraq, where American soldiers risk their lives for a cause that seems to be as mysterious and potentially dangerous as the faces of the people staring them down as they move on the streets of Baghdad.  The film does not attempt to make a grand guignol statement, nor does it revel in any form of jingoistic excess. It is more concerned with the everyday existence of those men (and women) sent into the eye of the storm, those people who have to do or die with no questions asked.  Bigelow's film is also brilliant in its subtlety, as it poses the big questions about the war within the fabric of its being, with no obvious finger-pointing in its core narrative.  Instead, with the craft and timing of a true maestro, she simply deconstructs the everyday existence of the man of war through the acts of its 'wild man' protagonist - in all its scary, risky, pointless, crazy, druggy, nervy glory.  This is THE film about the Iraq war, and also one about all war.  Brilliant.

In its first scene, THE HURT LOCKER sets the tone for the rest of the movie. From start to finish, it lets you feel the stress, tension, and anxiety of every situation the soldiers have to deal with.

Director Kathryn Bigelow uses her minimalist style to great result: there's no soundtrack to distract us from the urgency of each situation, and no dramatic CGI explosions to take away the realism.

As I watched THE HURT LOCKER, I began to wonder: how far can you push these men until they break? They have constant stress weighing down on them, and they face life and death decisions day after day. Great performances across the board help us stay engaged.

It may be two hours long, but not once does the movie *feel* long. It plays out like separate episodes in a television show- as the team progresses, their personalities change, and we can see it in the way they act.

Engrossing, compelling, and thoroughly entertaining, THE HURT LOCKER deserves the Oscar it's definitely going to get.

So, I saw this movie also as a part of my dedicated Oscarâs week of the films nominated for best picture, although I did attempt to watch this months earlier and fell asleep in the first few scenes of the movie. This movie follows an elite bomb squad and itâs team leader William James, played by Jeremy Renner, during a rotation in war-torn Iraq. During the course of the movie,  the team goes on several different missions as the first responders to evaluate and disarm numerous suspected bombs of all sorts of fashion. 

The plot definitely had a bit of a drag in the beginning. Honestly if this wasnât a part of my Oscar week, I donât think I wouldâve attempted it again as my first attempt did such a great job of putting me right to sleep. I will say that the âplotâ picks up in the latter half of the movie. I say âplotâ because there was no real story line and more of a sequence of events. I actually enjoyed this plot as it felt real. This movie had an almost documentary type feel to it but nothing like a mockumentary. It felt as if we were truly just following this bomb battalion during their normal duties while on rotation in Iraq. The plot didnât have an agenda or a message about war, it was simply just about war. I imagine this is how life feels to a soldier over there; no political agendas or huge conspiracies, simply a job that must be done. 

The camera work fit perfectly with the feel of the movie, with up close hand held film cameras. It really felt like we were watching raw footage from the field. The editing was excellent and well thought out. There were close up shots and unique camera angles thrown in there which really kept the balance of the different filming styles and reminded us that we were watching a movie and not live footage from Iraq. The sound editing was amazing, like most of the best war movies are. A war movie really relies heavily on the realistic sound and this one had it. It wasnât anything ground-breaking but it was on par with other great war movies. The movie used the different camera styles and great balanced editing to provide us with something more than the run of the mill war movie where the camera just follows the action where it goes. 

The performances were good and believable. This was an action driven movie and we werenât given much character development, with the slight exception of Rennerâs character. There was several short supporting characters played by Guy Pearce, Ralph Fiennes, and David Morse.  Jeremy Renner did great with his character and everyone made their characters unique instead of playing the generic soldier-type. Everybody was believable and as the movie was mainly centered around the action/plot, there really isnât much more to say. 

The movie didnât really have a normal storyline with an exposition, rising/falling action, and conclusion. It was more of a deep look into the life of a bomb squad in modern day Iraq. It left the viewer to draw our own opinions, without any political overtones or propagandic agendas. It was unique from most other war movies in which a centralized storyline develops however war is not really like that and therefore this movie felt like a much better account of real life. The film was made on location in Jordan which just gives such credibility to the movie and all of the crew that worked on it. I understand why this film is being revered for its uniqueness and credibility but Iâm not sure if I really see where the best picture nomination came from. I think the people who really will enjoy this film, will be very narrow. I think it will be a great iconic movie for future generations which captured the feel of this war or as James Cameron said it, âthe Platoon of the Iraq Warâ. Although it hits all the right marks and effectively sees through its brief but powerful message--that war is a drug--from start to a slightly depressing and well-done end, The Hurt Locker still feels somewhat generic, indistinguishably lost in the onslaught of war films, and a tad over-hyped. 

The shaky cam, while adding an element of realism, does the film little favor and soon borders on irritating. Certain dialog-heavy scenes are plausible, perhaps a little too much so in that the characters tend to go off into awkward, unnecessarily long silences meant to be touching yet are obvious cues for audience sympathy, The film's main star, Jeremy Renner is a favorite pick to win Best Actor, and while he delivers an overall decent performance, it deserves only the nomination. Subtle though his acting may be, plucked out of narrative context, it is nothing special.

That said, The Hurt Locker has great moments chock-full of realistic suspense that aren't preceded by lame filler scares. In the periphery of the film looms a sense of constant danger that comes with staying in a hostile country; everyone is a suspect. While the hero sets about defusing bombs, he is subject to curious, some maybe sinister, stares of increasingly numerous bystanders that his fellow soldiers can't very well shoot on-sight, thus adding to the ticking tension yet more tension that one of the bystanders might well decide to press the button. 

What's such a breath of fresh air about the film is that it brings under close scrutiny not the politics of war, but its actual participants. On a daily basis, these people have to deal with the all-too-likely possibility of being blown to warm, fleshy bits the next day, and longingly count down the days to the end of their rotation, the latter of which skipped over by the film's main star, who so yearns for the thrills of war that he chooses to re-enlist, even if it leaves his newly-started family hanging.

Put briefly, The Hurt Locker is far from a masterpiece yet still passably decent with a strong premise, which lends the film its strength, but leaves much room to be desired in terms of execution.

From the very first scene of this film, it's clear that it's a cut above the cookie cutter action films which Hollywood pumps out on assembly lines nowadays. Just how far is unclear until further along in the film, but if the first scene isn't enough to grip you like a vice, I don't know what is.

Staff Sergeant William James, played with beautiful restraint by Jeremy Renner, is a bomb tech in Iraq, not the best combination. However, unlike most normal people, Will finds bombs a rush, a thrill, almost a turn-on. Each time he goes out, it seems as though he's having more fun than at any point in time. This becomes even more apparent towards the end of the film, where he tries to connect with his wife and child by telling them horror stories of Iraq. He fumbles with his other relationships, with his wife, with his team members, with the local kid selling dvds, though he's solid as a rock when it comes to being less than a foot from a live explosive. Renner plays this role pitch perfect the whole way through the film, whether he's calling his wife or lighting up what might as well be a post-coital cigarette after a hair raising, nail biting experience with a bomb.

The film, though it's war film, steers clear of the politics of why the troops are there in the first place, opting instead to show what's happening to the boys who are over there. And how perfectly it shows this, from Sanborn's emotional breakdown after a particularly harrowing experience (to say any more would mean spoilers), to James' loss of composure during a house raid, the script is a perfect balance between smarmy and heartbreaking.

Brian Geraghty's performance as Specialist Owen Eldridge is worth a special mention. Every time he's onscreen he inhabits his character entirely. When he tells his psychologist what's playing on his mind and when he mourns the victims of a bomb blast, he is perfect in both situations.

But it is the set pieces which make the movie the movie which may actually beat Avatar. Each one is gripping, a thriller movie in itself where the outcomes are unclear, everyone is a suspect and every moment could be someone's last. The movie does little more than follow the everyday movements of Bravo company, but each day is more intense than the last. And the ending is perfect. There could be no other option for how this film could finish. In fact, I would have felt cheated if everyone had lived happily ever after, and the fact that you left wondering not only how crazy Will really is, but whether his luck is still within the best before date.

The Hurt Locker is a film about some of the unheard of heroes of the US military. The Hurt Locker, directed by Kathryn Bigelow, showcases members of the US army's Explosive Ordnance Disposal team. The job of these soldiers is to disarm bombs. The suspense factor in this movie is ever bearing on viewers as you're thinki. After team leader, Sergeant Matt Thompson(Guy Pearce), is killed during a roadside mission, Staff Sergeant William James(Jeremy Renner) comes in as the new team leader of "Bravo Company" and the story begins. Kathryn Bigelow and writer Mark Boal certainly deserve recognition for what is, in my opinion, a modern masterpiece. The Hurt Locker firmly takes a seat with other great war films like Schindler's List, Saving Private Ryan, The Deer Hunter, and The Pianist. One thing that makes this film so great is the fact that it stars virtually unknown lead actors and features recognizable actors like Ralph Fiennes in brief cameos. Jeremy Renner, Anthony Mackie, and Brian Gergahty may not be "super stars," but their acting in this movie is nothing short of excellence. The Hurt Locker is one of the best films of the decade and certainly the greatest film on the war in Iraq.

I read somewhere that "The Hurt Locker" was the perfect war movie.  Being a fan of Platoon, Paths of Glory, and the like, I was extremely excited to finally get my hands on this supposed new classic.  While I enjoyed the film, I think the marketing of the movie was far better than the product.

This is the first film I know of that focuses exclusively on soldiers assigned to defuse IEDs (Improvised Explosive Devices).  We get to know the three main characters, James, Sanborn, and Eldridge, quite well, although we really only like two of them.  There is no shortage of tense moments as we follow these guys through the rubble-strewn streets of Iraq, plying their trade, staring down death, and counting down the days left in their rotation.  

The conflict in this film is generated by Sergeant James, played by Jeremy Renner.  He's a fearless cowboy that seemingly loves to get right down in the dirt with explosives that will blow a man to tiny bits of sand.  But his bravado doesn't go over well with his two teammates, who think his pursuit of an adrenaline rush is likely to ruin their forthcoming return to loved ones.  

As for me, I really didn't like Sergeant James.  I admired him.  It's hard not to.  But I also doubted the realism of his character.  If a movie is going to claim title as the perfect war film, then their lead character better be believable.  Do the US Army's detonation experts really take these types of risks?  Do they really operate like the freelance posse we saw here?

Now, don't get me wrong.  This is a solid film in many respects, and, except for a couple of standard shaky camera battle scenes that had me half expecting the Blair Witch to pop up with an M16, it will keep your attention.  I loved the ending, where our hero reclaims the place that is truly his, and his alone.  My criticism here is driven more by the annoyance at claims of greatness rather than any pure disappointment in this film.

Great movie. I am not sure if I had even heard of this movie before it received an Oscar nomination for Best Picture. Even then I was reluctant to see it. I have never been that big on seeing movies about Iraq since I thought they would be used to make a political statements and that there was no point in seeing a fictional tale about a real war that is still being fought on TV everyday. But after some strong recommendations from people, I saw it, and I was not disappointed.
The story follows three U.S. soldiers who are simply doing their job before they can go home alive and in good health, even though they know full well that they may not get that opportunity. It pays special attention to Sergeant First Class William James (played by an impressive Jeremy Renner), who is an expert in his field and has a tendency to be very reckless and cocky, but ultimately has the best indentions at heart. However, he soon finds his psychological state in disarray as the impact of war takes its toll on him and he soon becomes addicted to his dangerous occupation. Shot in "documentary-style," it does not really feel like a Hollywood film. There is great suspense, but it does not feel forced. The dialog also feels natural as the characters; it sounds like what "normal" people would say when they are facing a certain situation, whether that emotion be happy, anger, sadness, fear, or depression. The film does not take a political stance; it shows the horrors of war, but it also has the lighter moments when the soldiers are off-duty (and sometimes even on-duty). In other words, it is just trying to tell a story.
The film has been criticized by at least one veteran's group for not accurately portraying the life of a soldier fighting over in Iraq. While I respect their service as well as their opinion, I would like to rebut it. First of all, no film is ever going to depict "what war is really like"; it is a unique experience which cannot be felt second-hand and those who have not served can only be given a general idea of it. That being said, this movie appears have done a better job than most of the other war films I have seen. Yes, there were some parts that were clearly over-exaggerated for the sake of storytelling, such as when he sneaks into the city by himself to find out information about an event that occurred earlier, but intelligent people will hopefully be able to see through this. At the very least, it did not go into overboard like other war movies have done in the past (I am sorry, but am I the only one who thinks that "Apocalypse Now" is overrated?). I thought that the ending was very well done; I would like to go into more detail but I cannot really do this without spoiling it. I will just end this rant with a cliche, which is that the last part, as well as the movie as a whole, makes you respect the soldiers for what they do; I am sorry, but it just does.

The Thin Red Line, original and remake, address the requisite need for fear and valor in war, any war. They were both made long after the end of the war they depicted and so did not require an unnecessary amount of sentimental or patriotic baggage to deliver their unyielding vision of the ambiguous purpose of war.

"The Hurt Locker" uses unsparing realism to attempt to depict unrelenting surrealism. That is like using a lot of orange tint to paint the color blue: in the retinal afterimage there will be an ever fading blue but the painting will continue to scream orange. On Bigelow's canvas the oranges are all yawing cameras (watch "Letters to America" actual combat cameramen are much better than these guys), the sucking sound of tense breathing, and the Hee Haw of men yelling at each other. The subtleties of this film and war are better thought of as "predictabilities".The film "Deer Hunter" runs out its string of personality types and how they reacted to war, variously resigned, withdrawn or aggressive. Yet "Deer Hunter" weaves a story that lets no type win or survive intact. "The Hurt Locker" parses our lead character's aggression into his emotionally frozen adrenaline-high arrogance, forgiven by the cliched "pat on the back" from a random, "out of touch" field commander. I'd have cast Steven Segal in the lead if that were the note I wanted to hit throughout.

Strangely, for a film about a bomb de-fusing squad, what the film lacks is high enough stakes and that is not necessarily Kathryn Bigelow's fault. That is the war's problem. "The Hurt Locker" centers on an individual who is not representative of any soldier in any war: his job in defusing bombs is not to save others lives or advance the column: if he knows there is a bomb somewhere, the people it was intended to harm are probably already gone and the enemy has failed to blow them up. His job then is to preserve his own life while preventing a building that is half destroyed from falling down and hurting whom?

The film works mightily to make that conundrum disappear. It gives him false and lost lives to save or redeem: the soccer kid who conveniently turns up as a dead human bomb, the guy on his knees, a Muslim bowing to the occupier, (a scene made uncomfortable for it's unapologetic demeaning of an Iraqi while we are as yet at war in Iraq).

This film lost me the second I realized that we probably do use little R2D2 robots to look at bombs that we could just detonate with a rifle. My sense is the writer and director are seeking to make commentary from a cliff we have not reached about the moral ambiguity of a war we have neither won nor lost. The irony of Bigelow's realism regarding the destruction of Iraq, homemade or imported, is that there would be no reason to de-fuse a roadside bomb since the only thing it could damaged is something we have already destroyed. www.danteschildhood.blogspot.com

It's quite a daunting prospect. 
Suddenly, your creative baby is open slather for all kinds of judgement/ridicule/praise on a worldwide stage of some of the harshest judges in the business, most often the public themselves. 

I heard the title of this film and was impressed. It reeked of 'oscar pizzazz'. An unobvious, curious title that made you cock your head and think 'hmmmm, I wonder what this is about'. 
I didn't know what I was expecting, and I suppose to be harsh on this film just because the prospect of Oscar glory instantly bolsters expectation may have been a little cruel; but then again, that is the game. 

I had the same expectations for 'up in the air', 'inglorious bastards' and 'Avatar'.     
Now, this isn't going to be one of these spoilt, one sided 'this film deserved it more' arguments because frankly, I didn't walk out of any of the above with great expectations for Oscars, aside from perhaps Avatar for it's impressive effects (although hardly enough for a best picture gong). On the contrary, many times in the past I have watched the Oscars, rooting for one film, only to see the 'other' take the prize. Deep inside, when this happens, I have always had to huff and quietly concede that whilst not my cup of tea, the other film probably deserved it more. 
So was not the case with The hurt locker. 

When I saw this film, I found it quite, for lack on a better word... blah. 
The performances were strong, but the storyline was a little repetitive, definitely predictable and not at all controversial. The concept itself may have been original, but the track the storyline would take was not. Now, had I just seen this as 'another movie' then it would have been alright. I may not have recommended it, but who cares. It is the fact that people will flock to watch this film due to it's Oscar status expecting something that they are not going to get.       

War screws people up, war is tragic, war changes you, war makes everything else seem trivial, war alters peoples lives to the point that they can become dependant on the destruction, war is horrible. These, as well as many other ideas, had popped into my head as the main 'lesson' behind the storyline, but at the end of day, even if you could absolutely pinpoint it, I doubt you would find anything controversial or groundbreaking. The only lesson I really learnt here, is the fact that Americans seem still to find the subject of war so endlessly fascinating. It is, if anything, really quite vexing when there are many more interesting stories in cinema. 

So, if you want to watch the hurt locker, watch it for what it is; the work of another talented director, another talented writer and another talented cast. For all these reasons, I have given the film a positive tomatometre rating. However, don't watch looking for all of those illusive Oscar earmarks that usually have you subconsciously nodding before the credits have rolled; because you won't get them.   

RELIGIOUS COMMUNITY: Hard to say. Nothing directly offensive but it is based around the war in Iraq so It may depend on who you ask. Use good common sense for the audience you are considering. 

CHILDREN: Nope. 

WATCH IT IF YOU LIKED: Forget movies, just watch it if you appreciate anything war/combat related.

Five seconds in and you are there: Baghdad - a hornet's nest. Streets lined with battered cars, animal carcasses, in a once beautiful city (name literally means Given By God) smeared by graffiti, reduced to rubble. Debris and danger is everywhere and you sense it. We feel the sweat, swallow the dust, detect the deception. Kathryn Bigelow leads us to a place where nothing is as it seems. There are long powdered minutes creaking with imminent disaster. Behind the corners,below the flaking Pepsi signs, in the minarets, there is the ever-present whisper of ghosting djellabas; the intense stare of dark eyes - persuasion unknown.
We are given no pointers, intentionally left as clueless as the soldiers in a world where even a goat in the desert can be sinister. This is as close as it will get for non-military personnel. We witness one drama after another.
It is clever stuff. Bigelow focused on a bomb disposal unit. They attempt to unravel the mess that is Iraq, which is as complicated as the coloured wires that connect the bombs to their detonators. 
Making a movie about an unpopular subject is not always recommended - this is a triumph. 
There is nothing pretty about this slaughterhouse of a film. No comment is made, nothing explained. Ultimately that is part of its strength. 
Film-making at its best.

The most meaningful moment in "The Hurt Locker" comes when Sergeant William James discovers a bomb sutured into the cadaver of a child and he must decide whether to defuse the devise or let it blow. It's one of the few political moments in a movie noted for it objectivity, but even in this harrowing scene, director Kathryn Bigelow resists the temptation to preach. The scene examines the choice presented to the United States by the conflicts in Iraq and Afghanistan: should we expend greater effort and risk more lives on a potentially fruitless cause, or should we take the safer and easier route of letting it all explode? 

There are subtle metaphors such as this peppered throughout, but one reason "The Hurt Locker" is the strongest war films in recent years is because it stays off the soap box instead of forcing a prepackaged perspective upon the audience. So many of this decade's war films (and there are many; too many considering the limited scope of history with which we have to evaluate these conflicts) want to tell you exactly what to think by manipulating the characters and events on screen to channel their politics. 

Bigelow takes a more subtle approach by focusing on the everyday life of the Explosive Ordinance Disposal (EOD), an elite unit of bomb squad technicians charged with defusing improvised explosive devices. She expertly captures the stresses and excitement of daily life in a war zone, placing special emphasis on how some are drawn to the adrenaline rush of combat. As the opening title says, "War is a drug," which is especially the case for Sgt. James (Jeremy Renner), who keeps re-upping with the army for additional tours despite a wife and baby girl waiting for him back in the U.S. One domestic scene shows him languishing in a grocery store, smirking at the mundane task of selecting a box of cereal from the rows of never-ending color. It's clear that James feels more at home with the sand blowing in his face as he grips a pair of wire cutters, doing what he does best. Call it duty, excitement, addiction, or meaning, but Iraq fulfills James by satisfying a need that can't be quenched in civilian life. It takes a courageous filmmaker to depict the positive - if that's the right word - of combat, suggesting that something can be gleaned from all this, even if it's a double-edged sword. 

Renner effectively conveys the complexity of his character, preventing him from going too far into the reckless maverick cliche. Anthony Mackie is the real discovery, however, impressing with a heartbreaking monologue that proves he's destined for more serious projects. 

The narrative drones on as we see the unit tackle crisis after crisis in a series of scenes that feel repetitive but are no doubt reflective of the alternating terror and boredom soldiers experience. Each episode has its purpose but with a story centered on character arch rather than plot, it starts to feel endless. Regardless, The Hurt Locker is thought-provoking, intelligent, and well deserving of its Best Picture win.

I only watched the Hurt Locker recently to see what all the fuss was about. I really and truly despised this movie. It had some interesting, shots, good performances (especially from Jeremy Renner), and strong direction from Kathryn Bigelow, but I found it to be quite insipid and excessively violent, such as the scene where the bomb squad discover a child's corpse that has been turned into a human bomb. I realize also that the shakiness of the camera was an esthetic choice but it made me feel queezy, a reaction not even Cloverfield could get out of me. I do not in any way believe this film deserved the best picture prize. While many gripe about the unoriginality of Bigelow's ex-husband's epic, Avatar, Bigelow's themes and story are very familiar and very over-used in our society. I have seen many better and more accurate depictions on the Iraq War. It's not my place to say what is art, and it is not my place to question the need to sometimes understand and visualize the darker elements of human nature, and showcase the darker things going on in our world. Bigelow was duly recognized for having the courage to go to those dark places and create them on film. The film certainly took me to a very dark place in my own mind. I have no problem with trying to understand the real life horror of war, it should be understood and recognized in an effort to stop future wars from happening. My problem with this material was how emotionally detached it was and how bleak and dark it really is. Granted this isn't my type of film, but I think District 9, which was just as dark, conveyed a better message about war, and accomplished what the Hurt Locker was trying to say in a more creative and a more relatable way. Despite my best efforts I found it very hard to connect emotionally with Bigelow's characters, aside from the murdered child and the psychologically traumatized "Specialist." I really think this movie was very dark, very graphic, and attempting to be hyper real, but it came off as distant, and lost. All in all, not worth seeing in my opinion.

Finally, this underrated movie that surfaced up with its critical recognition at the 82nd Academy awards. Not a fare to be "enjoyed". It's a disturbing, yet true to fact picture of the ruthless, inhuman chain reaction that Iraq and the Middle East, have now become.
Seen through the eyes of Sergeant "Will" James (Jeremy Renner), a seemingly reckless dismantler of bombs, we're taken through the streets of the war stricken city, the elements in it that are both hostile and victims and the aimless, cold blooded murder that lurks. James replaces Sergeant Thompson (Guy Pearce, remember "Memento"?) who in an attempt to diffuse a bomb, loses his life. Filling his shoes to lead a EOD (Explosive Ordnance Disposal) squad comprising of Sergeant Sanborn (Anthony Mackie) and Specialist Eldridge (Brian Geraghty), James struggles to strike bonds. But seemingly his cold grit and fearless exploits fascinate his peers and gradually pull them closer. What better role model would a damned soldier want?
The movie captures the sheer numbness that flows through these military men, awakening in surges to their mortality, humanity and fears. It makes you wonder what it must take for someone to "love" a job like that; disarming bombs, protecting civilians in a hostile, foreign territory. And it also makes you wonder, why in this world is there a need for a job like that.
Weapons, greed, power, fanaticism. That realm of thought is dark and endless.
"The Hurt Locker" is a grim picture that has been painted well and has the right strokes to provoke the right thoughts. Well enacted by everyone, and definitely excellent by Oscar nominated Renner. The direction by Kathryn Bigelow is simple, yet admirably brave and has all the raw edges that this picture needed. Her Academy award and recognition is very well deserved, and so are the other technical accolades bestowed on her unit.

I never review a movie until I've watched it twice, once to "feel" the movie, and once to pay attention to how well it was made. 

Overall this movie is a pretty typical low budget film. Its weak and overdramatic script butchers reality in an effort to make a somewhat suspenseful movie. Unrealistic stereotyped characters and bogus random battle scenes caused by the EOD team having no protection (for no reason) make this almost laughably bad. Characters that break protocols and rules just to get an adrenaline rush add to a movie that tries to be suspenseful, but is absolutely predictable. 

While there is some suspense, and there are some cool explosions, what suspense the movie strives for is lost do to a completely unrealistic, yet predictable series of events in each arc. Additionally, the movie has countless disconnects where characters just seem to change (going from overly dramatic to back to just stressed). Time jumps for no reason, and some battle sequences are absolutely unrealistic, but still quite dull. 

If the pacing, characters, and lack of suspense or action isn't enough, a sound track that seems oddly similar to the "left 4 dead" video game series seems to fit this low polish movie. Poor camera angles and shaking cameras don't allow you to connect with characters, as they aimed to show how alone the soldiers feel, but instead just make you feel disconnected from the unit. 

The thing that ruined this movie for me were the over the top stereotype characters. You have characters that are all flawed, and none would be allowed in high stress training environments, much the less real combat if they were soldiers. We make our troops look like psychopathic high school drop outs, and we make EVERY citizen there into bad guys, in a very unprofessional and unrealistic way. I honestly feel that stereotyped characters and unrealistic scenarios killed this movie for me.

I think this movie resembles Reign of Fire in many ways. If you ignore the dragons, the movies are very similarly acted, with almost identical character types and actions. They are both very predictable, and trying to be over the top. And of course, they are both complete garbage because they have poor camera angles and camera work, and a very weak, unrealistic plot.

Kathryn Bigelow's brilliant, guerrilla direction has a startling "You are there" intensity, but "The Hurt Locker" is essentially a top-quality action film with thin characterizations and not much food for thought. The script's episodic structure yields a flat narrative arc, and -- OK, this may be a quirky, personal gripe -- there's a scene with David Morse which didn't fit at all for me and just seemed like a calculated star cameo.

The story initially presents the main character as an unwelcome revival of Tom Cruise's old "maverick" roles, then makes its main attempt to dig deeper via a subplot about a likable Iraqi boy. But the idea that war's impact on a child would cause a soldier to drop his jaded detachment is not exactly the stuff of subtlety. Meanwhile, the character's titular collection of disabled bomb parts does not seem as shockingly macabre as the script suggests, and his alienation from civilian life is wanly depicted with the existential crisis of choosing a breakfast cereal in the supermarket.

I have not seen three of the 2009 Best Picture nominees yet (including Avatar!), but at this point, I would rate Up, Up in the Air and A Serious Man above The Hurt Locker.

I simply had to see The Hurt Locker after its triumph at this year?s Oscars.   If it had not been for this I might have missed it altogether, which would have been rather a pity, because its one of the best war movies I think I?ve ever watched.
 
Directed by Kathryn Bigelow, with a screenplay by Mark Boal, The Hurt Locker stars Jeremy Renner as Sergeant William James, Anthony Mackie as Sergeant J. T. Sanborn, and Brain Geraghty as Specialist Owen Eldridge, members of a three-man bomb disposal team in Iraq during the early stages of the insurgency following the occupation of 2003.  
 
One review I read described the movie as ?anti-war.?  It?s nothing of the sort; it?s just an unremitting and impressive slice of ?war realism.?  It offers no judgements; it just shows things as they are; it shows an uncompromising cross-section of the realities of Iraq, where the enemy is everywhere and nowhere, where there is no frontline, where it is impossible to tell foes from friends.  
 
There is a bizarre unreality to the whole thing, where the conflict itself almost transforms into a larger movie setting, a movie within a movie, with participants and bystanders, actors and spectators, joined together by the unwritten script.  One scene I thought particularly telling was when an IED is being defused by Sergeant James as the other two provide security cover, being watched over by Iraqi civilians, one filming the proceedings, getting ready, as the soldiers say, for his YouTube moment.  
 
James, the team leader, joins after his predecessor is killed.  Soon his reckless and unconventional methods unsettle Sanborn and Eldridge, just as his courage impresses his superiors.  The performances are all good, Boal?s particularly so, for it?s never quite possible to work out exactly what motivates him.  Is he mad, has he been so desensitised that he simply does not care; or is he excited, does war excite him, does the adrenalin rush excite him?  
 
Whatever the answer to these questions it is not just his own life he puts at risk but also those of his colleagues, to the point where they even consider, if half in jest, arranging his ?accidental? death.  In the end it becomes a race to see if the men will all complete their tour of duty and get back to reality, to normality.  In the end we see that for James Iraq is normality.  
 
It is an exciting movie and it?s impossible to watch without feeling the tension, without sharing the adrenalin rush.  The whole thing is thoughtful, intelligent and well-paced.  I imagine it is the kind of depiction of war, and the conflicting emotions of war, that soldiers will understand.  It?s the kind of film that goes a long way to helping those who have never experienced the tensions and the fear of war to understand also.  More than that, it?s as a clever a piece of controlled and precise movie direction as I have ever seen.

But that's the beauty of this movie.

He's so good at this character, if I needed a bomb defused, I'd pick up the phone and ask for him. My heartiest congratulations to Kathryn Bigelow, who became the first woman to win the world's top film directing honour. This review meant to be written last week before the Oscars night, but as the saying goes, better late than never. And perhaps the Oscars buzz was warranted. The film "The Hurt Locker" is a truly remarkable piece of cinema.

Bigelow, the same director who brought us 'Blue Steel' and 'Point Break' has pared down modern war film tropes  to create what can rightly be described  as a masterpiece. The story is based around an elite army bomb squad in Iraq who lose their much loved commander to a roadside bomb.

This brings new commander SSG William James (Jeremy Renner) into the picture. His seemingly reckless methods shake the nerves of the already frazzled Eldridge (Brian Geraghty) and Sanborn (Anthony Mackie), who have the end of their tour in sight. Together these three try to overcome themselves and each other to complete the harrowing daily task of disarming makeshift bombs.

The appeal of this film is driven by the naked humanity of the characters. There is still that sense of cowboys on the new frontier, but the audience is allowed inside lives of these characters after the wires are snipped, and the exhale of relief turns into binge drinking, misplaced aggression and paranoia. 

Renner's portrayal of the foolhardy bomb tech gives the audience plenty to love and hate, and as the story unfolds so do the complex layers of his character. SSG James is the battle-hardened crony with just enough cracks to possibly fall apart, and Renner plays it to a tee. 

This flick purveys the intensity and absurdity of war with unrelenting tension and dynamic production values. And even if the film is exploiting the entertainment value of war, it leaves the audience knowing unmistakably that war is hell, and those who escape it alive will have it seared on their skin long after the dust settles.

Did Jeremy Renner's performance deserve the Best Actor nod? Did the writer deserve his Best Screenplay win? I don't think so - but not through fault of either party, but because this movie's strengths exist elsewhere - in the suspenseful tone, the meticulously crafted set pieces, and the bold pacing. There's something low key about the film, mostly due to the budget constraints and simplicity of the story, but also due to the Paul Greengrass style camerawork. It's a catch 22 because it really works for this movie, much more so in my opinion than in Greengrass' Bourne films. But for me, this style also removes it from that group  of war masterpieces - those that are elegantly designed, less for realism and more for the beauty that a more traditional approach to cinema can provide. That's just my opinion on this particular style of camerawork and probably a reason why I can't put this up there with the Thin Red Line or Saving Private Ryan - both of which don't have a Best Picture Oscar.

Still, criticizing the movie too much on that point would be unfair. This was a great movie, up there with the best of its year, and it has some of the most gripping and well-choreographed action scenes that have ever been put onto film, 16mm or not.

When a film manages to win the Best Picture Oscar before I get around to see it, I naturally go into it with very high expectations. In the case of "The Hurt Locker," I feel like the award was simply given to the wrong film. Although it is certainly a good movie, I would hesitate to call it great, much less does it reach the level of excellence that the title "Winner of the Academy Award for Best Picture" ought to imply.

There are two major strengths of "The Hurt Locker" as I see it. The first of these is outstanding direction by the first female director to win the Academy Award for Best Director, Kathryn Bigelow. Each scene is shot perfectly, and the entire film felt like it was expertly crafted and managed. This leads to what I believe to be the films second strength, the acting. Bigelow gets excellent performances from every actor on screen, including Best Actor nominee Jeremy Renner, as well as his co-star Anthony Mackie. Although Renner was quite strong, I actually feel like the Oscar nod should have gone to Mackie. They make the script believable, and compliment the direction very well.

The glaring issue in the film is inconsistency with reality. Although it might be the best film so far made about the war in Iraq, it is certainly not the most realistic. At many points in the movie, I found myself shaking my head and grumbling about how unrealistic the situations are that the film generates, especially when it comes to the main character, Staff Sergeant William James (Renner). The reaction from real life veterans of the conflict seems to be in line with my criticism, as well. It just leaves a bad taste in my mouth.

Perhaps the most confusing part of the Academy Award results that lead to The Hurt Locker taking home a handful of important trophies is the Oscar for Best Original Screenplay. The weak link, as far as I'm concerned, is the screenplay. Nothing in the dialog or narrative says to me "Oscar." It isn't bad, but the films strength comes from Bigelow's vision, not writer Mark Boal's. It seems that the Academy were voting for Boal's story of getting the story, and not the screenplay itself. It was hardly a dud of a script, and I did like parts of it, but the fact that this screenplay beat out Tarantino's "Inglourious Basterds" is absolutely laughable.

All of my criticisms aside, "The Hurt Locker" has more good to it than bad. The direction and strong performances make it very watchable, and an interesting film. The flaws in realism and only decent script hold it back from being really deserving of its accolades.

War, uh, yeah. What is it good for? Winning Oscars, apparently. Once again, that annual backslapping ritual that is the Oscars has passed, and we find ourselves with an interesting Best Picture Winner - 'The Hurt Locker (2009).' Winner of numerous other awards, this topical feature is gaining acclaim from all directions. But just how justified is the hype?

The opening is an exercise in masterful in tension, with Bigelow creating a grippingly taut and exciting scene that throws the audience right into the action. The horrors and pitfalls of the Iraq war for a US Army bomb squad are made abundantly clear from the very start, highlighting the danger that lies around any corner, under any rock, beside any road. Bigelow also takes her time to carefully depict the fragile mentality of the soldiers, balancing out the explosive action with a softer side. These soldiers aren't depicted as heroes in the conventional Hollywood sense, there's no Rambo style mercenary who can single handedly take control of any situation and come out fighting, no matter the odds. Instead, these are mere men with a job that is required of them, and failure is always an option.

The stars of this film are three men who each have a different reason for doing the job that they do. Brian Geraghty plays Owen Eldridge, who finds himself suffering the most mentally from the affects of the war. Holding himself personally resposible for the demise of his previous squad leader, Geraghty gives his character a firm, tough exterior, but allows moments of inner turmoil and despair to fleetingly shine through. Taking over from the previous squad leader is Jeremy Renner, Oscar nominated for his role as Staff Sergeant William James. He enters the movie with an irritating swagger, pigheaded and arrogant. His recklessness distances himself from his team, but over the course of events he proves himself to be a remarkable leader. Last but by no means least there is Sergeant JT Sanborn, who truly shines thanks to an excellent performance by Anthony Mackie. He's the most level-headed of the team, sensible in difficult situations and harbouring a distrust towards the squad leader, which provides an interesting group dynamic. There's no Captain Willard or Private Joker, no one man that leads the story, this is an ensemble piece and each individual character is handled extremely well.

This is war, but filmed in style. The cinematography is brilliant, bringing the Hellish heat of the Iraq desert to sweltering life on the screen. Deserted hollowed out streets that have been ravaged by war are depicted with acute attention to detail. Meanwhile, the camera reflects the squad, nervously restless as William James tackles various bombs in need of disarming or with a calm stillness in times of quiet tension, such as during an intense sniping scene.

Unfortunately, there are a couple of moments where the film falters - the most obvious being when Staff Sergeant William James recklessly leads his squad into ground combat, searching for the perpetrators of a brutal murder. The scene feels very out of touch with the rest of the film, a gungho foray seemingly placed in the plot as an excuse for some action.

Naturally, with this being an American war film, there is a very clear divide between good and bad. The Americans are portrayed as the heroes, the Iraqis as the villains. That's that. There is no ambiguity, just a black and white portrayal which unfortunately slightly undermines the movie. More could also be explored into the psyche of the soldiers - it's touched upon, but more depth would help give the film a stronger emotional core.

That said, when the film is firing on all cylinders it is great cinema, with some excellent stand out scenes. There are moments of exhilaration, poignant scenes of sadness, and most importantly of all the film allows for reflection and appreciation towards those who are based in the military, fighting a war with no end in sight. Without delving into the politics behind the war, Bigelow portrays the men superbly as soldiers who are there not to be heroes, but because it's just where they have to be. It's simply their job, and nothing more. But even Hell needs heroes.

"The Hurt Locker" will mold itself into the category of one of the greatest war movies of all time. It is arguably the most intense action film in the history of cinema.  As of this date, it has won best picture at the Oscars, a title well deserved.  It is the best live action film of 2009. And it is the second best movie of 2009 behind the documentary "Tyson". 
"The Hurt Locker" is director Kathryn Bigelow's fresh take on a military profession that is not based upon typical cliche, "front-line" gun battles.  The film focuses on soldiers who are in charge of disposing roadside bombs; a job equally as important as any within the military.  "The Hurt Locker" stars Jeremy Renner, a bomb disposal expert who lives vicariously through his job.  He lives life in accordance with the theme of the film which states that "war is a drug"; a very interesting idea about soldier mentality that has never really been explored in war films.  At times he is cartoonishly wild and unpredictable in his methods, forcing co-star Anthony Mackie to try and hold his unit together on a 40 day tour of Iraq.  Mackie wonderfully plays the straight man to Renner's loose cannon.  The two are in conflict with each other, yet at the same time are surrounded by the hell on earth that is the Iraq War.  Their co-existence is key to their survival and to the survival of their unit.
War movies are mostly praised for their realism and "The Hurt Locker" is the most realistic portrayal of war that I've witnessed since the opening scene of Spielberg's "Saving Private Ryan".  We get an accurate glimpse of how intense and scary modern warfare really can be.  This film is gripping and unpredictable.  It is well acted and great to look at.  At times you forget that it's a movie, it feels like your watching something more along the lines of a documentary.  For example, no performance feels like a performance, the acting is that good.  
"The Hurt Locker" is a real achievement in film making and is such a leap above and beyond the crapfest of movies made in 2009.  I take my hat off to Kathryn Bigelow who made a beautiful modern war epic that will stand the test of time.  I would have given this film a perfect rating but I felt the film got really bumpy in its closing sequences and I wanted a bit more in the department of character development. Though you can never really have it all unless your watching "The Godfather". "The Hurt Locker" is a must-see movie, the only must-see of 2009.
Grade: A-

I don't care for war movies, but because this one won six Oscars (Best Picture, Directing, Writing, Film Editing, Sound Editing, Sound Mixing), I figured I'd visit my favorite theatre to see what all the fuss was about.

I still don't care for war movies, but I can understand why this one won most of those awards.  Kathryn Bigelow did a fine job directing actors and action according to Mark Boal's original screenplay (or perhaps Jeffrey Sarver's life: http://www.zimbio.com/Jeffrey+Sarver).  Compelling acting from bit players all the way up to and especially Jeremy Renner in the lead role, combined with edge-of-your-seat action and brilliant sound effects, make for realistically tense and gruesome depictions of bomb activity and combat.

The thing is, there are at least a few well directed, well written, well acted, great sounding films released each and every year, whereas movies that advance the art of filmmaking -- movies that have all of these things and then some -- come along only every once in a while.  Movies like the original "Star Wars" and "The Empire Strikes Back", "E.T.", "Forrest Gump", "The Matrix", and "The Lord of the Rings" trilogy are many, if not most, of these extra special movies that have been released in my lifetime.  "Avatar" is another.  Despite not caring for war movies, I can be objective enough to admit that "The Hurt Locker" deserved five of its six Oscars -- maybe even a sixth for Best Actor had it not been Jeff Bridges' time -- but I think "Avatar", with its incredibly original story and truly mind-blowing visual effects, deserved Best Picture more than just another well directed, well written, well acted, great sounding film.

"The Hurt Locker" is a film that I will have to re-approach once the Oscar buzz has somewhat melted away. Kathryn Bigelow presents the yet-to-be-fully-understood Iraq War exactly the way it should be: the action as it unfolds. Other than the opening epigraph, which states that "War is a drug," this picture does not openly give an opinion on the state of the Iraq war, other than that war in general is inglorious and unromantic. Often the events occur without much explanation, which is fitting, for how can you really explain everything that happens in such conditions? The events seem ludicrous, and have been criticized so, but what 2009 seemed to prove between "The Hurt Locker" and "Inglourious Basterds" is that there is no possible way of presenting war accurately in the cinema. Although the film had some divine thrilling and tender moments, the film suffers from underdeveloped characters, but perhaps we are not meant to completely get involved with the soldiers, because how are we supposed to know exactly how the characters are feeling? Kathryn Bigelow has produced a good film with excellent moments and terrific images and themes, but Best Picture of the Year? I don't think so.

I've never been a big fan of war films in general. "Full Metal Jacket" would probably be the only one that I really liked. A lot of war films just feel the same it can become redundant and boring in watching scene after scene of long sequencing battles and shaky camera movements. What can resolve that problem in making a better film, and not just an ordinary war film is the development of character and strong dialogue. The Hurt Locker has this almost tug of war between making itself out to be like every other war film, but there are times when it truly rises above that to become something special.

There is not much of a concrete plot line to describe. Instead the film focuses more on the theory that those involved in war and dangerous combat, can become addicted to it. The film follows a group of soldiers who have the extremely dangerous job of disarming bombs in Iraq. Early on you see how deadly the job can be, and after that there is a real tension as the group goes from different scenarios in trying to keep things safe, even if it means going beyond reasonable expectations. The dialogue is sparse except for a handful of scenes, but there a number of more meaningful moments that are done with non-verbal messages that say more then any dialogue could.

The film is mildly confusing to follow. As the viewer is thrown into several different situations without knowledge of what is completely going on. Whether that is to demonstrate a chaotic experience of war or if it is incomplete storytelling, I'm not sure, because there are times where it works on both levels. It can become frustrating to feel like you don't "get it," but the the film brings in a lot of high energy and tense moments that move it along.

The film almost seems like it is being played backward as if a lot of what you see in the first 2 hours would make more sense and have more perspective if you were to see the ending sequences toward the beginning. I think it rewards repeated viewings, and in a way it almost becomes more powerful after it is over to reflect back on what was shown previously and to think about it.


While there are scenes where it feels like battles go on longer the necessary to reach it's goal, the film does have a strong yet subtle displayed message of the addictions of war. I personally don't think it is the best picture of the year, but I would say it is above average and I would give it a good recommendation.

"The rush of battle is often a potent and lethal addiction, for war is a drug."

Modern warfare is so much different than the ways of war back in the past (Vietnam, Gulf war etc.) Nowadays the troops biggest challenges are IED's (Improvised Explosive Device) aka roadside bombs for example. 'The Hurt Locker' brings us a different aspect on war, giving us less combat but more adrenaline. But is it realistic?

The film starts with a scene were an EOD (Explosive Ordnance Disposal) team is taking care of a possible situation. It ends with a tragedy and the team leader is replaced by Jeremy Renner's  Staff Sergeant William James, an adrenaline junkie. James has a wife and a kid back home but he tries to cheat death every time possible. Why?

'The Hurt Locker' is a more different film than any other Oscar winner. The film wasn't a box office success but the critics liked it a lot. The film looks realistic but sadly it ain't. And this I can say with experience. I know the ways in the military, have served in Afganistan and know how the EOD teams work. NONE of 'em would take or allow anybody to even try risking their lives in ways that are been showed in the movie. Sure, there's a lot of tension and excitement in the movie but those who don't know how the real men work, can be fooled to believe what they see in 'The Hurt Locker'.

'The Hurt Locker' is not an epic movie. It's more of a small story of how war changes people. Many of those who have served in similar situations have returned back home, more or less different. Some in good ways, by this I mean that they've seen different aspects on humanity and learned a bit more of them selves. Some come back but still something was left behind.

Kathryn Bigelow won an Oscar as the first female director. She deserves it because in the end, 'The Hurt Locker' is a good movie and an important one too. There's not that many films made of Iraq or Afganistan. People should know and understand what the troops are going thru.

'The Hurt Locker' has a very good cast with several well known names that are in smaller roles and then there are these actors like Jeremy Renner, Anthony Mackie and Brian Geraghty, who are making names of them after this movie.

So, 'The Hurt Locker' looks good with excellent camera work, sounds good with blasting sound and has a good story with good characters. But a realistic version of EOD team's work it is not.

Problem is that the tense moments in this film are so few and far in between, and the film doesn't have much to offer plot-wise that would act as filler between the action scenes. Yes, I appreciate that the film subtly avoids making a political statement, and rather keeps the main focus of the story on the three bomb squad members and how war takes its toll on their lives, but haven't we already seen that in "The Deer Hunter" or "First Blood"? The idea of war veterans trying to adjust to citizen life only to find that war is in their blood, as punctuated by "The Hurt Locker"'s last scene? 

And who is the real villain of the piece by the way? Are we led to believe that every Iraqi citizen is a potential bomb-maker, and that all of them have suddenly developed the ingenuity to devise clever tactics of placing and setting elaborate bombs? But without any disrespect to the great work the real world military do, an hour into the movie similar scenes were repeating unnecessarily, for example to me the 15 minute to 60 minute mark could have been quite easily condensed to 25mins, cutting the duration of the movie down entirely whilst retaining the plot. 
 
My explanation of the movies award winning success and overhype is quite simple, patriotism. As it is a movie representing international soldiers and the lengths to which they go risking their lives on a daily basis therefore to some it is only right to award a theme like this highly; political correctness almost. I am left with the perception is this effectively a dramatised observational documentary best shown in military museums but marketed to the mass market movie going audience for financial gain, not to be thrown in amongst the glitz and glamour of Hollywood? Or on the other hand is this what Hollywood needs, to break other variations of cinema into Hollywood amidst all the stereotypical commercialisation?

2010 Academy Award winner for Best Picture. Set in 2004 Baghdad during the Iraq war, the movie follows three members of the U.S. Army's bomb squad- men specially trained to dismantle IEDs (improvised explosive devices).  Low on plot, the movie is basically a series of nicely staged set pieces, with a few sympathetic performances and very fast cameos from well known stars. I enjoyed the craft of the film, and I appreciate Bigelow's design to ruminate on the enormous stresses of war and how it's nearly impossible to inhabit both worlds (war and civilian life), and I very much appreciate how Bigelow steered clear of excessive gore, but I wasn't completely caught up in the story. The film is a bit weak in the character development/character interaction/dialogue department.  And I never like shaky, hand-held camera. For me, it achieves the opposite of the desired effect: Instead of bringing us into the scene, it alienates the audience from the action.  What's present on the screen is nicely done, for the most part, but the movie is not a full, rich experience.

The winner of the 82nd Academy Awards. Gotta go see it, right? At least I had to. I'm not saying I didn't want to, but it's just that war films are not for me. Especially not current-war ones. But I gotta say that I was actually quite surprised about this film. The genre was taken to a whole new level; it had a new approach to the soldiers' lives like, I think, we've never seen before. The experience of watching it was quite disturbing at times, but I can clearly see why it took the big golden statue home.

Like I said, I think that Bigelow gave us a new side of the soldiers that we haven't seen in other movies. She gave us the psychology, the emotions, the human side. How this men live their everyday lives, the effects that daily, small events can have on them, and how they can never be the same once they return home, no matter how hard they want it or try it. And I think that this new vision could be accomplished in great part because the director was a woman. I think that if a man had directed the movie, he wouldn't have gotten the same dramatic impact. I bet he would've focused more on the actual battles, tactics, and shootings, more than in the consequences of these. The direction was awesome, and you could really see it.
I must praise the script as well. I really don't know if it was Oscar material, but, again, we got to see the things that have never been told about what the army men live through everyday while in service. I could clearly see in the movie the reasons of why war is a drug. Great story. Better than most of the ones that come around nowadays.

The acting was also outstanding as well. Jeremy Renner had well deserved that Oscar nomination, but it was just too hard for him to get it. If he can give us such complex performances as this one in the future, I bet we'll be seeing him at the ceremonies more oftenly. The other actors were good as well, but I definitely think he is the one that stands out. I loved his cynism and the total disregard for what he's going through, yet knowing that all of that is the only thing that's keeping him alive and, in his very own way, sane.

The one thing that bothered me, but that at the same time made the film had the impact that it did, was the way it was filmed. It was slow at times, maybe too long, and way too documentarly like. I know that the shaky camera movement adds realism to the story, but by the end of the first hour my stomach was turned upside down. But that's just totally me, and I agree that the camera work was one of the things that made the film so effective. Totally deserved Oscars for Sound Effects, though I'm still debating about the Editing...

The Hurt ?Shocker?. 

If a film wins the coveted Best Motion Picture award at the Academy Awards it?s safe to say that it?s left the realm of average moviemaking and stepped gloriously into the world of great moviemaking. If not, then Huston we have a problem!

This sentiment is a given in most cases but sometimes the unexpected happens, a never saw it coming moment when Tom Hanks announces the winner and somehow an undeserved title grabs the prize leaving the rest of us wondering if someone somewhere made a huge mistake. 

Don?t? get me wrong, I?m not sitting here slating the judgment made by those members of the Academy who thought Kathryn Bigelow?s 2008 release ?The Hurt Locker? deserved the award, I?m just questioning their motives.

Journalist turned screenwriter Mark Boal, who found his inspiration after a trip to Baghdad, scripts a film based thoroughly on reality. During his trip he witnessed first hand the death defying day-to-day lives of those men dedicated to AEOD (Army Explosive Ordinance Disposal), an experience that clearly left its mark.  

Staff Sergeant William James (Jeremy Renner) is known for being a wild card techie who often stares death in the face, and smiles. He is reassigned to a new unit where he leads Sergeant JT Sanborn (Anthony Mackie) and Specialist Owen Eldridge (Brian Geraghty), one struggling to muster the courage to walk the line and the other tormented by the meaningless loss of his brethren. 

Life in the sandpit isn?t what the government made it out to be but it?s become home base for many men who are now too far removed from the normalcy of their lives back home. Sgt James in particular finds it difficult to imagine a world where he doesn?t disarm menacing bombs for a living, a cycle that often lands him in trouble with his superior officers who find his methods unacceptable at best. But, then again, everyone has or is losing their mind so far from home as each day takes them deeper into a world they should never have entered in the first place. 

That last statement could raise debate amongst many who feel that the American infiltration into the Middle East is not only justifiable but also a necessary action. Yet, in contrast, there is a strong contingent that feels that the US involvement in the region is based thoroughly on financial gain; something even Obama can?t stop from happening. 

I?m not trying to turn this film review into a an opportunity to rant on about the pros and cons of American foreign policy, but it plainly shows which films are supported and which are dismissed come the Oscars. 

Director Kathryn Bigelow who has, since the 1980s, proven her worth as a fine storyteller and a master of the technical craft of filmmaking delivers one of the, so-called, surprise hits of the year. Her film is true to life and tells an honest story, one that those who live through such circumstance could well appreciate. 

Yet, her offering doesn?t stand out from any of its predecessors. Personally, I think Hollywood is trying to cover every aspect of the American Army?s involvement in Iraq and this time we get a day in the life of those men who disarm explosives on the streets of Baghdad. 

Don?t expect a deeply moving character study of a man who, in an attempt to deal with being thousands of miles away from his family, finds his calling as a bomb techie and with every successful disarming begins to test the limits of his mortality only to realise that the life he once led is no longer an option. 

Though the film touches on these existential issues, it certainly doesn?t explore them with enough vigor for ?The Hurt Locker? to become a poignant portrait with the same flair as ?Apocalypse Now?.   

Her ability to truthfully create an atmosphere of suspense is aided heavily by the fact that whenever there?s a situation that involves disarming a bomb, you?re almost guaranteed an atmosphere of suspense. It?s a similar effect achieved by those films that involve domestic animals. Put the animal in mortal peril and the audience is guaranteed to respond emotionally. I find these party tricks a cop out at best making ?The Hurt Locker? a shallow experience.

Yes, the style in which she has told the story, and the way in which it is shot, is worth mention. But, it is clear that her method of filmmaking is not the focus of the film. She has genuinely attempted to tell a story that possesses a deeper meaning and sadly I feel she has failed. Perhaps if Guy Pearce and Ralph Fiennes, who make cameo appearances in the film, had been offered leading roles instead of bit parts we?d be speaking about a milestone of modern war drama ripened by award winning performances.

Unfortunately she made the decision to cast Renner as her leading man, an actor who made his leap into stardom alongside Colin Farrell in 2003?s ?S.W.A.T?. If a film critic has to search your name on IMDB, having been nominated for Best Actor at the Oscars, then there?s a serious problem. 

The fact of the matter is, ?The Hurt Locker? isn?t everything it?s made out to be. Technically it?s an above average release that speaks to the class of fan who enjoyed ?Jarhead?, but in terms of storytelling and award winning presence this film offers nothing new. The Academy?s decision to award Kathryn with Best Director and her film with Best Motion Picture seems utterly contrived. She deserved none and, having held onto the film since late 2008 for a 2009 sneak release, it seems she?s merely tried to show up her ex-husband (James Cameron) who spent 10 years developing the next phase of cinematic entertainment only to watch ?Avatar? play second fiddle to a half-wit war piece.

The Hurt Locker is a film that is very well executed. Kathryn Bigelow is a competent director, Jeremy Renner is a fine actor who is perfect for the role, the cinematography is great, and the film provides some moments of well-crafted suspense. Unfortunately,  this movie is surprisingly conventional. While it is interesting to see the war in Iraq through a different occupational lens (the bomb-tech), the movie sidesteps into conventionality. 

As a character driven piece of cinema, The Hurt Locker almost works. Jeremy Renner's representation of Sergeant William James is, for the most part, quite convincing. "War is a drug" an opening screen tells us, and for William James, this couldn't be truer. Consider the scene where James obsessively hunts for a detonation device in a dusty Hyundai. Tension mounts as Iraqi men suspiciously eye and videotape James desperately searching the car, while James's comrades vainly order him to abandon the search. It is a wonderfully tense scene, and gives us good insight into James's obsession. Unfortunately, this scene is undone come the climax of the film. James inevitably comes across a bomb that he cannot defuse. What disappointed me here was the fact that following this scene James shows little to no remorse at having not diffused the bomb. Where is the emotional fallout that the movie so wonderfully suggests James should suffer in such a scenario? If this is supposed to be a character driven war film, this is too glaring of a problem to ignore, and detrimentally effects the film. 

The Hurt Locker becomes conventional when we consider the representation of the Iraqi people. Yet again, they are clearly established as 'the other'. They are unintelligible, villainous, and are blatantly dehumanized. Had the film included a central Iraqi character, this could very well have been avoided. Indeed, we are given the character Beckham, a young Iraqi boy who uses a vernacular lifted straight out of 8 Mile. However, Beckham is intensely Americanized. He is in tune with American pop culture, and even adopts a name associated with European/American society (Beckham, as in the soccer player David Beckham). James takes a liking to the boy, and they develop a charming little relationship. SPOILER AHEAD. When James mistakenly believes Beckham to have been killed, he embarks on the standard 'army of one' revenge mission. What is curious here is that James only concerns himself with one Iraqi character, a Iraqi character who is intensely American. 

I was troubled that at no point does the film acknowledge civilian casualties as a result of American occupation. The only civilian casualties we see are in the two 'body bomb' scenes, whereby Iraqi extremists are clearly to blame. I suppose, then, I was disappointed that there was no sympathy by the film's central characters towards the Iraqi people, the one exception being James's retrieval of the first 'body bomb'. For all I know, this may very well be the case with soldiers currently in Iraq. If this is the case, this film then seems to endorses it, which is a troubling consideration. 

The Hurt Locker is by no means a bad movie. That said, The Hurt Locker is by no means a great movie. Essentially it is a film that is conventional in its Americanization, and invariably does not provide anything new. Consider the closing shot of James confidently walking towards a unseen bomb, electric guitars blaring in the background, a self-assured smirk on his face. How many times have we seen this? That being said, I'm still glad that a film with a 11 million dollar budget beat out the 255 million dollar monstrosity that was Avatar.
