The Academy has an annoying habit of giving out awards to films which don't really deserve them, in a desperate attempt to cover its past mistakes. When Sean Penn won the Best Actor award for Milk, there was a sense of the Academy atoning for snubbing Brokeback Mountain (with the usual excuse that Hollywood "just wasn't ready" for Ang Lee's film). Similarly, The Hurt Locker's victory in the Best Picture category was as much about rewarding the film's merits as it was about apologising for United 93 being overlooked.

Of course, to say that this wave of good feeling was the only reason The Hurt Locker won is to do it a disservice. There is much about Kathryn Bigelow's film which is interesting, arresting or admirable. But it is not as perfect or as revolutionary as many critics have claimed, and in the pantheon of war films it remains in the middling ranks, way behind the likes of Full Metal Jacket or Apocalypse Now.

The Hurt Locker is a thematic continuation of Bigelow's previous films, in particular K:19: The Widowmaker. All her films are primarily about machismo, about huge quantities of testosterone colliding in a confined space with catastrophic results. Both K:19 and The Hurt Locker have a central relationship built around a massive personality clash, and both address themes of duty and morality against a military backdrop. The Hurt Locker has a stronger script and is a better acted film, but Bigelow's fascination with men pushing themselves to the limit, often for the sake of it, remains at the forefront. This is, after all, a film in which men relax by punching each other in the stomach.

Oddly enough, the film to which The Hurt Locker owes the biggest debt is not a war film of all. In its character arcs and moments of dark comedy, it is uncannily similar to Lethal Weapon. Our central character, Sergeant James, is akin to Mel Gibson's character in that his suicidal tendencies and resulting obsession with death allow him to be the best at what he does. The scene where Jeremy Renner takes off 'the suit' to defuse a car bomb, saying that he "wants to die comfortably", shows someone with both insane levels of confidence in his ability and an equally insane lack of regard for his own life.

At heart, The Hurt Locker is a strange kind of buddy movie. The three central characters (James, Sanborn and Eldridge) are akin to the Lethal Weapon films in their clashing personalities. James is like Riggs: young and reckless, doing things his way or not at all. Sanborn is like Murtaugh, wanting order and preferring to do things by the book. And Eldridge to an extent is like Getz, a well-meaning individual completely out of his depth who often puts his foot in it. All three characters are struggling with both themselves and each other to do what they consider right in very difficult circumstances.

Beyond the interesting character dynamics, the film is visually impressive. It is shot by Barry Ackroyd, who shot The Wind That Shakes the Barley and United 93 (and recently completed work on Green Zone). This background, coupled with the hand-held camerawork, does make the film somewhat Bourne-inflected, although the use of slow-motion during the opening explosion is not particularly Paul Greengrass. The close proximity of cameras to the actors adds to the tense and desolate feeling of certain scenes, in particular where James and Sanborn are aiming at the snipers hiding out in a stone hut. We see every inch of dirt and sand caked onto their faces, and feel like we are in the trench with them as the flies crawl over their skin.

There are, however, two major problems with this film. The subject of bomb disposal may not have been covered in other Gulf War films, but The Hurt Locker's approach to telling this story is not as original as one might have expected. In the Bourne films the shaky camerawork was used not just to make the action scenes more vivid and realistic, but to disorientate the audience so that we are never sure whom we can fully trust. The Hurt Locker attempts such a trick, and it works okay for the first 45 minutes. But when the story attempts to expand with the apparent death of the Beckham character, this is suddenly undermined and the resulting scenes lack both thrill and cohesion.

The plot line involving Beckham hints at the film's second problem, namely that certain threads of the story simply don't belong here. We should be praising the film for managing to take a series of loosely connected events and making them something more than episodic. But we end up thinking is that the film could have been more disciplined than it already is, and that cutting the additional scenes would not have undermined either its message or its impact.

As mentioned before, The Hurt Locker is at its most basic a drama about three conflicted men. There is so much potential in these characters, which is explored in the opening act, that it begs the question of why Bigelow didn't simply focus on these men, ripping each other apart while trying not to get blown up. The sub-plots she puts on screen distract us from the tension, and as each one ends the films has to start the character build-up almost all over again.

None of the sub-plots are developed into deeper political points, or used as a means to analyse the war from a different viewpoint. The scene with the private contractors is a passing incident, with no attempt made to explore the nature of such figures, or their relationship with US soldiers, or the deeper moral questions surrounding their involvement. You can understand why Bigelow would want Ralph Fiennes as an incidental character as opposed to a glamorous celebrity lead, but this doesn't change the fact that his character is not used to any real, constructive purpose.

Both the Fiennes character and the useless Colonel fall into the trap of stereotyping. They follow a Hollywood convention that if you have a British accent, you will meet with a sticky end. Sure enough, the Colonel is blown up by an IED just seconds after demonstrating how incompetent he is. Any editor worth their salt would have taken that out, along with the scenes of James going 'undercover' to find the people responsible for Beckham's disembowelling. This sequence is out of kilter with the story, and becomes even more so when we find that Beckham is still alive.

The Hurt Locker is an interesting and technically adept addition to the war movie canon. Despite its flawed storytelling and occasional lapses into caricature, it is a capable account of life on the front line in Iraq, shot with the same combination of humour and nihilistic intensity which Ridley Scott achieved in Black Hawk Down. The film would have been better still if it had focussed solely on the three guys trapped within these circumstances; this would have improved the sense of claustrophobia and made us empathise with the characters to a greater extent. But for all its flaws it is still intensely enjoyable, not Oscar-worthy, but a fine film nonetheless.

The Hurt Locker represents a turning point for Hollywood: it not only marks the first time a woman has been awarded the Oscar for Best Picture, but also for Best Director, and anyone who has seen this film will surely agree it deserved them both. Bigelow's direction demonstrates a natural command over her subject, despite never having been to war. Her battle scenes deliver tense moments of suspense and terror in this story about a bomb disposal unit, Bravo Company, serving in the Iraq War during 2004.

Mark Boal's award winning script offers an authentic angle as it draws on his experiences as a journalist embedded with a bomb disposal unit in Iraq. Bigelow manages to bring out this authenticity and maintains a sense of realism and intensity throughout the action sequences. One of the ways this is done is by keeping the camera alongside the action at all times, so the viewer feels drawn in. At times the camera jiggles along beside the soldiers as they chase after insurgents, and the viewer feels as if they are holding a portable camera and running with them. At another moment, the team engages in a gun battle in the wilderness, and the camera focuses and refocuses on the distant targets, making you feel as if you are trying to sight through the scope of the gun yourself. This technique helps to build the suspense in the heat of the battle.

Jeremy Renner, who plays the unit's leader, Staff Sergeant William James, is seen by his men as a reckless thrill-seeker, obsessed with cheating death and getting his next adrenaline fix. His two subordinates, Sergeant Sanborn (Anthony Mackie) and Specialist Owen Eldridge (Brian Geraghty) feel that he is putting their lives at risk, and the audience also begins to question James' sanity. However, before long, we come to realise that James does have a conscience, and that underneath his façade of bravado, there is a man trembling with humanity. We later come to realise that Sergeant James is driven by more than just his job; he has become addicted to war. All three men give excellent, unflinching, performances.

Unlike many of the epic war films that comes before it, 'The Hurt Locker' neither glorifies war, or focuses on the senselessness of war. In fact, the film has no political agenda and avoids making any explicit statements about whether the United States military's presence in the region is legitimate or justified. It simply focuses on the day to day dangers faced by the men who are posted there to do a job, disarming dangerous bombs. But what makes the film, ultimately, is how it approximates the soldiers' feeling of utter anxiety as they fight a war in a place so hostile and hateful of their presence, in which everything and everyone is a potential enemy, and when at any moment, even the ground before you can explode and annihilate you forever.

The first time I saw The Hurt Locker I paid more attention to my brand new surround sound than I did the movie itself. It wasn't a complete waste of two hours; the film's Academy Awards for sound design and sound editing are well deserved. The Hurt Locker has so much more worth seeing, however. After watching the film for a second time with open eyes, I felt compelled to write a review focusing on its outstanding visuals.

The first visual symbol that I remember seeing (and believe me, there are many that I have forgotten about or missed) was the flies on the eyes of the sniper and spotter of both sides of the shootout towards the middle of the movie. The fly doesn't discriminate. There are two human beings, neither of whom's life is more important that the others.

In that same scene, we see an empty shell-casing falling unnaturally to the ground contrasted with a naturally occurring sand cyclone. We are drawn to the sight of the swirling desert cyclone. We are equally attracted to the visual of the manmade shell falling lifelessly to the ground. The cyclone is natural; the shell is not. War is not natural.

Another striking visual was of the protagonist Staff Sergeant William James sitting alone in his room late at night putting on his bomb suit helmet. He is physically and emotionally shut-off from everythingânot only in the world back home, but everyone and everything around him at war.

The tanker explosion scene that takes place at night reminded me of Kubrick's Full Metal Jacket as the soldiers walked through a fire-drenched hellscape. Shortly after that, when Specialist Eldridge gets shot in the leg by SS James, I was reminded of the "Humpty Dumpty" nursery rhyme. The physical injury of his femur being shattered in 9 places mirrors the mental break from the post traumatic stress disorder that is sure to follow him. And all the king's horses and all the king's men...

Through a combination of handheld camerawork and Academy Award winning editing, The Hurt Locker does an excellent job of putting us in the middle of war. As the three soldiers clear a building room-by-room, we sit at the edge of our seats and peek around corners with them. We feel as alienated as Staff Sergeant James does as he walks through the corporate-painted supermarket to the sound of satirical elevator music. How trivial our lives seem when the toughest choice we face is what brand of cereal to buy.

It is SS James's alienation that leads the film to its ending that, foreshadowed by the opening Chris Hedges quote, ends the only way it can.

These few short paragraphs give only a glimpse into what a great film The Hurt Locker really is. The nail-biting opening scene gives us a good idea of how well shot, designed, and edited Kathryn Bigelow's masterpiece is from beginning to end. To top it all off, we're left with three equally intriguing character studies by the time the credits roll. I'm quite interested in seeing how this one plays ten years down the road.

One of the finest motion pictures ever made dealing with a controversial war, The Hurt Locker sets itself above the rest because it does not take a pro/anti-war stance, nor is it swayed by any political motives.  No corruption, no Washington D.C. officials, nothing objectionable.  The movie itself is best summed up by the opening quotation - War is a drug.  The story follows a US Army Explosive Ordnance Disposal unit led by the seemingly reckless Sgt. First Class William James (an Oscar-nominated performance by Jeremy Renner).  Not helmed by any huge names, the movie is easier to get behind as you don't see someone like Bruce Willis or Denzel Washington - you have less-recognized actors delivering powerhouse performances.  There are some supporting roles from bigger names like Guy Pearce, Ralph Fiennes, and David Morse, but the majority of the movie deals with Renner's troubled James, and his impact on his fellow squad-mates played by Anthony Mackie and Brian Geraghty.  Not filled with epic battle sequences like Saving Private Ryan, the movie is more about the characters and war's impact on them, rather than the war itself.  Despite this, the movie is still filled with suspense and tension, and for the Michael Bay in all of us, there are plenty of explosions.  Well-deserving of its 6 Academy Awards, including the first ever Best Director win for a woman by Kathryn Bigelow, the Hurt Locker is one of the finest motion pictures in years, and one of the few times I have completely agreed with the Academy's choices.

The Hurt Locker opens up with a quote informing the audience that âwar is a drug.â To Sergeant William James, this quote rings unnervingly true.

The horrors of war, to James, are merely high-stakes games to be played. James does not merely enjoy war, however; he thrives in this environment because itâs exhilarating and adrenaline-fueled.

James also flourishes in Iraq because of how impersonal it is. A pivotal moment of the film occurs when a young Iraqi boy James thinks he knows is found dead; when the boy is proven to be someone else, James realizes that the emotional breakdown he suffered because of the incident is proof enough that emotional attachments are deadly during war.

But Jamesâ love of the impersonal stems also to his family at home. When he gets a chance to return and visit his alienated wife and child, he become conscious of his war âaddiction.â All he can think about is returning to Iraq, and becoming part of the game again.

Directly paralleling James is Specialist Eldridge, whose emotional conflicts come not from a need for war; indeed, quite the contrary. Eldridge blames himself for the death of a teammate, and desires nothing else than to get out of Iraq; his desperation is (purposely) reminiscent of an unwilling addict caught in the snare of drugs, trying his best to escape. The excitement proves to be too much for Eldridge, and he realizes that he needs to get out fast.

Drug metaphors aside, The Hurt Locker succeeds admirably even when it strays from its more thematic elements. Even if it didnât pack a fascinating emotional punch, the film would still be an amazingly taut, powerfully suspenseful action movie. Kathryn Bigelow directs the movie to perfection; you can almost see her talented hand guiding every element of the film into its ideal place, making sure every cast and crew member performs their respective jobs to sleek perfection.

Now, detractors of The Hurt Locker typically say two clichÃ©d things: 1) that the movie is unrealistic and 2) has no plot. Referring to the former argument: Itâs a movie, not a documentary. Get over yourself. As for the latter, more legitimate argument: I defend the filmâs situation-based, seemingly-unstructured narrative by simply saying that it works. War does not have a linear, straightforward âplot,â so why must a war-based movie have one? The Hurt Locker doesnât need a larger storyline, because its strong thematic elements carry through every incident of the movie.

Overall, The Hurt Locker is absolutely worthy of all the praise and acclaim it has received. Itâs a perfect film, and will be remembered as one of the best of the decade. Itâs definitely more deserving of the Best Picture Oscar than that brainless waste of money known as Avatar.

Not a fan of the Middle East as a setting for a war movie, at first I overlooked "The Hurt Locker" but after it's triumph at the Oscars I gave it a second glance and I'm glad I did. Jeremy Renner plays Staff Sergeant William James, the leader of a three man team of bomb disposal experts on the front line of Iraq.  He does a good job of playing a character who seems addicted to war and is unable to function properly out of it.  Anthony Mackie is the perfect foil to Renner, playing a charcter who hates Iraq, hates the war and is very downbeat but at the same time acts the sensible to Renner's maverick.  The cast has small roles for David Morse, Ralph Fiennes and Guy Pearce, all of whom take their opportunities to shine, especially Pearce and Fiennes and the whole production is extremely well shot by Kathryn Bigelow who deserved Best Director for the movie at the Academy Awards.  

The headlines have been dominated over the last 12 months with roadside bomb and IED casualties, making "The Hurt Locker" is a very relevant movie.  For this reason I can see why the Academy rewarded it with so many Oscar nominations and that could be part of the reason that it won so many awards.  I don't think the film deserved Best Original Screenplay, Best Editing or Best Sound at the Oscars, I think all three of these awards should have gone to Tarantino's Inglourious Basterds which demonstrated better writing and was more of a feast for the senses.  

I think "The Hurt Locker" was the best picture of 2009.  It certainly deserves a lot of the praise that it has been given and I didn't want it to end as I was watching it.  Avatar was visually stunning but definitely an example of style over substance.  The performances here are strong and the story is not bad at all.  If you are a fan of the action genre this is definitely worth a look, Bigelow has made the best film of her career so far in "The Hurt Locker" and I will certainly keep an eye out for her future work.

A brutal movie.  This movie disturbing on numerous levels.  

The supposed attempt to create a film about daily life in the early days of the Iraq War for a military bomb squad without editorializing is merely an ethically deceptive 'punt.'

This is, I think, why it is so warmly received.  Like the War(s) themselves, this movie massages the immature instinct of an unthinking culture to remain at arms-length from the ethical conflicts.

Now, I understand the lesson from the movie is that war can create monsters.  Adrenalin-addicted, psychologically mangled sociopaths who need to "stay in the shit" because the moral corrosion of war has killed their inner light.

I liken it to attempting to make a neutral movie about gang rape.  Irresponsible. (Obviously this analogy is imperfect, but you get my point.)

As a victim of a family member post-war suicide, I understand the overall message of this film. But if that is the morality tale, then there is no reason to, say, represent Iraqis as one-dimensional cartoons as this movie does.  Indeed, the film would actually work if the humanity of the Iraqi people was shown.  (Don't tell me that the little boy selling DVDs is a character that accomplishes this.)

If you want a documentary about the soldier's perspective of Iraq, fine.  Just don't attempt to create a morality tale out of a narrative about something as opaquely immoral as the Iraq War without treating this backdrop as such.

I give it a 10% based on the technical quality of the film making. War movies about current wars carry a responsibility.  This film punted.

You get a 100 for the story but a 0 for technical accuracy.  I was a Military Analyst in Baghdad from 2004 to 2005.  At the beginning the movie say Baghdad 2004.  They should have said Baghdad 2006 and maybe you would been better.  In 2004, we weren't wearing the Advanced Combat Uniforms, we were in the Desert Camouflage Uniforms.  The soldiers or even elite soldier didn't have M4 MWS (Modular Weapon System) most just had the M16 some had the plain M4 with the carrying handle without a scope.  We didn't drive up-armored HMMWV's (HUM-V's), we had basic issue HMMWV's.  Then we took steel plate and strapped it to our vehicles, we called it Hillbilly Armor.  Up-armored HMMWV's until the middle of 2005.  Then one thing they got totally wrong that didn't change with time was t name of the camp.  There was a time when Camp Victory grew expanded and grew into two camps North and South Victory, South being the original Camp, the huge PX going into the North.  Later they changed the name of the camp to Camp Liberty.  In the movie they said the opposite, the name went from Camp Liberty to Camp Victory...Wrong.  Next time get a technical advisor who is either a Military Analyst or was there.

Here's a film I've been meaning to see since about November that I just today finally got around to seeing. Unfortunately, the quality of the film did not correspond too well with my desire to see it. Hurt Locker is far from a bad movie, but it's also not at risk of being a masterpiece.

If I could describe Hurt Locker in as few words as possible, I would just call it a fantastic war movie. However, that's much different than calling it a fantastic movie. Apocalypse Now! is a movie set during a war, but I would never think of it as a war movie, because the inner struggles of the lead characters are so much more important than the actual war story. Same goes for a movie like The Thin Red Line or Rescue Dawn.

That isn't the case with Hurt Locker. The characters are all pretty well rounded, but almost all of the character development is saved until about the last half hour when all the characters have to suddenly come to terms with various issues. When resolution for the lead character finally comes, it's delivered in an unfortunately heavy handed speech to an infant while holding a jack-in-the-box. Best Picture material, naturally.

So, war movie. Under this criterion, the film shines gloriously. The audience never has to deal with dull generals, no scenes depict officials trying to create the perfect plan to defeat the enemy, nothing of that sort occurs. Instead, there is the simple concept that everyday brings new challenges, and in war, this means life or death. That makes the movie tense, as it often is. The movie follows a unit that neutralizes bombs (which the opposing forces seem all too willing to take their time in detonating).

I don't really know much about Kathryn Bigelow, but her direction here is pretty top notch (a quick glance at Wikipedia informs me that 1) she directed that surfer movie with Keanue Reaves, and 2) she was married to James Cameron, no doubt 2 mistakes). The cinematography is really quite excellent, and even the firefight scenes aren't especially dull thanks to the camera work.

As a film, I have no real complaints about The Hurt Locker. It's not a bad movie. I would even call it a good movie, but nothing more. It's not incredibly unique in its approach, but at least it isn't entirely riddled with cliche. Also, any movie that takes awards away from Avatar is fine by me. I think it fails in its lofty attempts to be a brainy war flick, but succeeds in separating itself from the glut of action heavy war movies. I would put it on par with a movie like Jarhead, which I actually thought was surprisingly good.

«The Hurt Locker» se centra en el quehacer de tres soldados, que conforman el equipo especial de desactivación de bombas en Irak post ocupación estadounidense. La historia comienza unas semanas antes de que expire el tiempo de servicio obligatorio de este grupo.
Hay dos elementos en esta película que merecieron mi principal atención:
(a) La dirección. Gran parte de «The Hurt Locker» ocurre en las misiones mismas. Por ello, tiene un alto grado de suspenso. Hay considerables momentos de tensión donde el espectador no sabe cuándo alguno de los protagonistas sucumbirá a la amenaza de muerte que se cierne sobre sí. Entre misión y misión, las secuencias son acotadas, con un valor diegético conciso. En lo personal, me sorprendió la capacidad de esta directora (Kathryn Bigelow) para abordar tan excelentemente un filme de guerra. (Debo admitir que no estaba familiarizado con su trabajo anterior)
(b) La posición del filme en relación al tema. No es cosa ociosa preguntarse por la posición que toma «The Hurt Locker» en relación al conflicto bélico, en especial al tema de Irak. Toda película de guerra tiende a tomar parte acerca del fenómeno de la guerra y se la puede ubicar tentativamente como a favor o en contra; si la promueve o la denuncia. For the first time since I've been writing this blog, I struggled to meet my self imposed weekly deadline. Not because this film didn't move me, but because it moved me in ways that I found difficult to articulate. 'The Hurt Locker' is a confronting movie about the Iraq War directed by Katheryn Bigelow (the ex wife of Avatar's director James Cameron). The opening quote from Chris Hedges (who was a war correspondent for the New York Times during the Iraq War) sets the scene perfectly - "The rush of battle is often a potent and lethal addiction, for war is a drug". And "War is stoopid" should've been the concluding quote I say.

'The Hurt Locker' follows an elite army bomb squad in Iraq during the chaos of war. And if watching several bomb detonation scenes in slow drawn out detail isn't enough to build suspense, the film is also shot in documentary style which contributes to the tension even more. I read somewhere that the way the camera continually zooms in and focuses on close ups of the bomb detonation is designed to have the audience focus on the detail and prevent a focus on the bigger questions such as "why war?". Interestingly, it had the opposite effect for me -watching someone obsess over the detail of a single bomb when people were dying all around him seemed to amplify the feeling that war is pointless, futile, and almost ridiculous.

The film focuses on three soldiers each with very different personality styles and comfort levels with the war. The main character is Sargaent Will James (Jeremy Renner), the leader of the squad who is called in to replace his predecessor (played by Guy Pearce who made an all too brief appearance). Will is a solo operator who is fearless, arrogant, and seems to only care about himself but he has a unique talent for defusing bombs. In fact he's a bloody genius. Then there's Sargeant JT Sanborn (Anthony Mackie), the second in charge - a brave, reliable, and honorable soldier, who at times is quite torn about the war in Iraq but even so, his loyalty to the cause is boundless. The third key member of the bomb squad is Special Agent Owen Eldridge (Brian Geraghty) who is young, inexperienced and always scared but still performs his duties to the best of his abilities. For this reason he may be the bravest of all three. And whilst the bomb scenes are certainly gripping to watch, it is the interactions between these three very different characters that made the film so compelling to watch.

In particular, Will's character had me intrigued. Upon first impression he comes across as a reckless cowboy but as the film progresses you find yourself more and more confused about his character and what makes him tick (pardon the pun!). Is he just a reckless adrenlin junkie or is he sacrificing his own fears to save the world? Is he doing this job because he is good and selfless or is he a selfish jerk? Did it make him brave that he consistently threw himself in the face of death, or was he just too scared to face himself in normal life? And then it got me thinking about why I needed him to be one way or the other. In fact I needed him to be one way or the other so badly that I couldn't even write about it!

And then I concluded that it was because I needed him to make sense.

It made me realise how much we do a similar thing in real life. That we need to categorise people as good or bad, jobs as interesting or boring, relationships as right or wrong - because we need life to make more sense. But ironically maybe life would make more sense if we accepted that the same person can be callous in one situation and tender in another. That the same job can make you feel both energised, and exhausted. And that losing something can be make you weaker and stronger all at the same time. As the 'Hurt Locker' develops, all three characters show parts of themselves that make it more and more difficult to make sense of them and actually that's what made them so interesting.

Another interesting theme was related to fear and in particular, conquering fear. It's impossible not to admire the bravery of all three characters in 'The Hurt Locker" but while fear seemed to be paralysing for Special Agent Eldridge, it was like a lifeblood for Sargeant Will. There's a great scene towards the end of the film when Will finally makes it home and he's hanging out in a very domestic scene in the kitchen with his wife and son.

And for the first time since the film had started I felt relaxed.

He was finally safe and home! But the stability and the security of being home seemed to suck the life out of him. For his own sanity, I felt like he needed to be sent back to a place where his life was at risk. And I was almost expecting that I might be able to make sense of him once I saw him at home but even Sanborn doesn't get any closer to understanding him when at one point on their way back from battle, he turns to Will and says: "Will, how do you do it? You know, take the risk? ...and Will says "I don't know, I guess I just don't think about it".

I highly recommend 'The Hurt Locker'. Action filled war movies don't usually leave me feeling anything much after the credits roll but the Hurt Locker stayed with me for days. It makes you think about the kind of person you are - Am I a Will? Or a Sanborn? Or an Eldridge? Truth is I think I'd like to think I'm the kind of person who is energised by the excitement, the fear, and the riskiness of the choices one faces when detonating a bomb, but I think that maybe I'm the kind of person who prefers to be faced with the choices in the cereal aisle.....And for a few days that felt like an uncomfortable conclusion to write but maybe the point is to just accept the one that you most resemble, or at least get comfortable with the fact that you might be bits of both.

As it has been built up to be, so 'The Hurt Locker' has quite quite possibly attained the status as the antithesis of the 'Avatar' colossus: with a budget of $15m (one-twentieth that of 'Avatar's'); an almost-documentary feel; pro-American outlook and the much-discussed ex-partner intrigue, the lightweight has not only landed the knockout blow in the top-trump battle of critical acclaim, but more importantly the 2009 Oscar scoop. However hard objectivity can be, 'The Hurt Locker'-'Avatar' comparison is one that cannot be avoided and therefore will not be.

Opening with the now-famous quote "War is a drug", 'The Hurt Locker' follows the exploits of Sergeant William James (Jeremy Renner), leader of a three-man bomb disposal unit comprising himself, Sergeant J.T. Sanborn (Anthony Mackie) and young Specialist Owen Eldridge (Brian Geraghty). A newly-formed team, Sanborn and Eldridge struggle to acclimatize to James' need for a battle-rush born of his often suicidal actions. 

The sole reason this film will not be receiving the full 100% lies with what lacks in my plot overview, namely a central story with which the pace of 'The Hurt Locker' is dictated. The result is (an admittedly wonderful) a film feeling as close to documentary as movie. Personally this adds an edge to the already razor-sharp tension, however the lack of central story can just as easily confuse an audience and some may regrettably discover the film loses its appeal without the story that is so-often the enticing power lurking omnipresent throughout a film. 'The Hurt Locker' does feel slightly at times that we are forced to shift time sequences from one masterful action sequence to another, interspersed with slightly awkward character development between where many audience members might decide to relieve themselves of the drink downed through the film's tense and nervous energy.

Without doubt 'The Hurt Locker' is a film with sharp, slick scripting with the obvious abilities,enthusiasm for and understanding of the Iraq War belonging to, Mark Boal (who's prior credits included one small adaptation and several regular magazine contributions-most notably 'Playboy'), 'The Hurt Locker' never descends into formula or cringed-cliche. However, to say 'The Hurt Locker' deserved Best Original Screenplay over 'Up' (the only other nominee I can speak for) was a mistake. 'Avatar' did not deserve it for an unoriginal storyline and less than stellar writing, 'The Hurt Locker' did possess the masterful writing  but (arguably) did not even possess a storyline, only half of the criteria fulfilled for the title of Best Original Screenplay.

A major contributing factor to the economically prudent production lies with a cleverly constructed cast whose reputation stood predominantly in television. Renner, Mackie and Geraghty portray their respective roles with strength and conviction which conveys strongly the sense that they are soldiers but with the intended extra sentimental and emotional edge in place of the all-too-often, embarrassing G.I archetypes. The chemistry between the trio, be it friendship, necessity or hostility, is always as palpable and sharp as the tension of events around them. Renner in particular depicts James' hidden awkwardness brilliantly.

Shot on location in Jordan and Kuwait, 'The Hurt Locker' certainly feels, to the armchair tourist at least, like the real thing. 'The Hurt Locker's' cinematography earned it the highest academy accolade, the full range of techniques and opportunities exploited cunningly with the use of slow-motion, hand-held, wide-angle and intimate shots that both force the audience into the heart of proceedings and drag them back to a distance offering a terrifyingly clear view to oversee the larger-scale. Despite the brilliance, the documentary-confusion should have reversed the Oscar decisions on Editing and Cinematography ('Avatar' and 'The Hurt Locker' respectively); where 'The Hurt Locker' excelled in the choice of shot but whose confused feel should not have put-performed any, more obvious movie.

Music and musical score have rightly earned 'The Hurt Locker' praise, the key ingredient in the concoction of the movie's incredibly tense ambience. Composer Marco Beltrami did not shy away from periods of silence broken by sudden moments of comparatively harsh white noise. 

The final questions that nobody has asked are inevitably whether 'The Hurt Locker' deserved to be entitled both Best Picture and its director, Kathryn Bigelow, the Best Director, for which 'Avatar' was the only genuine contender.  Rarely has a film been so tense and absorbing, with the ability to shock and suspend an audience effortlessly with the constant, life and death gamble of its characters. The gritty realism, magnificent script, casting and palpable score all combine to create a breathtaking movie-the reason for rightfully claimed her award as the figure through which a simple vision, deep commentary and story-lacking script deserved such high honour. However the few faults of 'The Hurt Locker', however small in my eyes, can be seen and detract some from entertainment that 'Avatar' can sustain. In spite of better scripting and direction, 'The Hurt Locker' simply should not have triumphed over the revolutionary, entertaining Titan for the Best Picture throne and instead serve as the pinnacle of films for which the director deserves such high praise.

There's an underlying theme both in front of and behind the camera in the explosive war thriller The Hurt Locker -- and that is craft. The story follows bomb squad Staff Sgt. William James (Jeremy Renner) as he comes to terms with the fact that nothing much else matters in his life other than being the best at what he can do -- which is strap on a 100-lb. suit in 110+ degree heat and walk into a dangerous situation that he knows he can handle. With 873 successful bomb diffusions under his belt, James doesn't blink, he just does. The same goes for director Kathryn Bigelow, who has already proven herself capable of standing shoulder to shoulder with the big boys of action, but hits yet another confident stride with this exercise in high-pressure filmmaking. The reason to see the engrossing Hurt Locker isn't so much to soak in the politics of war or be overwhelmed by an overblown Hollywood budget, but to be taken on a journey of one breathless scene of tension after another. On the way, the heart of the picture makes itself apparent, but until then, this is an exemplary display of craft that's sure to take your breath away.

The year is 2004, and the picture begins with a disastrous bomb-disarmament scene, laying the groundwork for just how dangerous a locale Baghdad really is for these troops. As if disarming bombs weren't enough, the soldiers have to keep on constant alert for insurgents who could be anyone around them. For this, the Army needs a three-man squad -- the Explosive Ordnance Disposal (EOD) crew -- a small force consisting of a point person and two others supplying lookout for trouble that can come from all sides. Such is the case for Sgt. J.T. Sanborn (Anthony Mackie) and Specialist Owen Eldridge (Brian Geraghty), who after losing their previous leader, are assigned to work under Staff Sgt. James (Renner), a maverick soldier whose efficient ways don't always end up on the right side of protocol. As the men's tour winds down, the pressure gets higher and higher for the crew, with one dangerous day leading to the next. Nerves are shot; people live and die at the switch of a button or the pull of a trigger -- thus it goes when you live in "the hurt locker."

Some have labeled The Hurt Locker an action film, but that's a bit deceiving. What it lacks in traditional combat scenes, it more than makes up for in nail-biting tension. With each and every set piece, Bigelow amps up the pressure in precise ways that keep the audience nailed to their seats, as if they are right there in the midst of the war zone. The absence of a score in key scenes adds to the realism, as does the handheld cinematography, complete with the same kind of slight shake and quick zooms used to best effect within documentary filmmaking. And when the picture isn't ramping up your heart rate, it switches gears and becomes an intimate character study in what war does to humankind. Whether it's facing deadly obstacles that you live to overcome or being saddled with a crew member whose adrenaline addiction has put you directly in the line of fire, the hardships of war don't leave you with a lot of easy ways to return to normality in its aftermath. Though apolitical in much of its intentions, the film does nail home that fact -- which might end up being one of the strongest wartime messages of all. Not bad for such a meager little (by today's standards) action film. Not bad at all.

This film won 6 Oscars, including Best Director for Kathryn Bigelow and Best Film. It has also picked up a further 72 Awards around the world and had 46 nominations. Given that kind of attention, there must be something really good about it, either that, or everything else was really bad. I decided it must be the first option, so I decided to get the DVD and give it a spin. I wasn't disappointed; it's a really good, well made film about the Iraq war. But more of my thoughts later, here's a short summary.

The leader of an Explosive Ordnance Disposal (EOD) unit with the U.S. Army's Bravo Company, Staff Sergeant Thompson is killed in the line of duty. With just over a month of their tour to go, the Sergeant is replaced by Sergeant First Class William James. The rest of the team, Sergeant JT Sanborn and Specialist Owen Eldridge are not put at ease by their new CO's cavalier attitude to his work. It seems that James, although a very talented explosives expert, is also addicted to the danger. This puts his team on edge and arguments inevitably ensue. Things calm down when they come across a group of men from British private military company in the desert. They have just captured two wanted Iraqis but their vehicle has broken down. Just as the EOD team offer to help they come under fire from insurgents. Three of the British team are killed before the EOD team get it together and manage to neutralise the threat. This brings them closer and back at base they celebrate before the reality of the war hits them again the next day. I won't say any more, don't want to give too much away.

I found it a really compelling film to watch. Some great cinematography, the explosions, in particular, looked really impressive. Some great performances too, in particular, Jeremy Renner as Staff Sergeant William James, Anthony Mackie as Sergeant JT Sanborn and Brian Geraghty as Specialist Owen Eldridge. Honourable mentions go to the supporting cast, including, Guy Pearce as Sergeant Matt Thompson, Ralph Fiennes as Contractor Team Leader, David Morse as Colonel Reed and Evangeline Lilly as Connie James.

I'm quite surprised this film didn't do as well at the box office as its critical acclaim might suggest, however I do remember it coming to a local multiplex and only being on show for a week. But over all I really enjoyed this film, it kept you guessing where it was going next but also allowed you to engage with the characters. The, kind of, documentary style put you right in the centre of the action which made it a more exciting experience. Definitely one of the films of 2009 and I recommend it very highly.

There's a lot to like about The Hurt Locker, which manages to be a good war film and a good character study, but could have been great had it focused on only one of them. There's no denying the incredible tension the film creates, firmly placing the viewer in the tense, violent world of bomb disposal units in Iraq, and watching the way Bigelow and company toy with the audience makes you appreciate how hard they worked to put you into the dangerous world of Iraq. By contrast, there's Jeremy Renner, the main focus of the film, whose need for adrenalin/heroism pushes him to take risks and increasingly stray from the military's prescribed techniques and methods. I don't come to the movies looking for realism, but I can't help but feel frustrated by the conflict here; while Renner is clearly not intended to be totally realistic, instead creating a complex character and using him to explore ideas about warfare and human nature, there's no denying that his actions (specifically a couple of off-base excursions) feel jarring and implausible, especially when contrasted to the gritty, brutal realities of the rest of the film. Had the film focused on one or the other - either entirely focused on bomb disposal or let the film be a more subjective, less "realistic" take on the war that followed Renner - it could have been a masterpiece. As it is, it's a solidly good film with two conflicting ideas that don't quite mesh together as well as hoped.

The little film that could, Kathryn Bigelow made history with this film, as it became the lowest grossing film to win Best Picture at the Oscars, and she became the first woman to win the Best Director Oscar. Set in Iraq in 2004, it follows the work of a U.S. Army Explosive Ordnance Disposal working in and around Baghdad. It has Sergeant First Class William James (Jeremy Renner) joining the unit after Staff Sergeant Thompson (Guy Pearce) was killed in action by a bomb. James served in Afghanistan, so he is very well used to situations like this, but he is a maverick, chosing to do it his own way, rather than follow the correct procedures, much to the ire of his superiors Sergeant J. T. Sanborn (Anthony Mackie) and Specialist Owen Eldridge (Brian Geraghty), but they just get on with it. It's a minimal plot, but it manages to stay gripping, taut and suspenseful for the duration, shot documentary style by Barry Ackroyd, Bigelow puts you at the centre of the most nerve-wracking and most difficult job in the world. It is not a bible verse, but it is one for whom is watching The Hurt Locker to remember: 
"War is a drug". Well that is what the movie's point is.

The Hurt Locker, which won six Oscars including Best Picture, is simply situated in Iraq while they are in the War On Terror. The story starts as Senior Sergeant Thompson, who is leading the bomb squard of the US Army was killed while diffusing a bomb in what would be an iconic snapshot of the movie of him (played by a cameo of Guy Pearce) running from an exploding bomb and also an amazing opening sequence. So Segeant James (Jeremy Renner) is the new leader with support from Sgt. Sandborne (Anthony Mackie) and Sgt. Eldridge. But his unorthadox methods frustrated his mates especially Sandborne who does his best to fight off bombs. During their 39 days on duty, the trio encountered killings of their allies including a 12 year old from Iraq who was a mutual friend with James.

As expected of this movie, Jeremy Renner is incredible as Sgt. James who's character is addicted into war himself. Anthony Mackie is explosive as his fellow mate critical of James' reclessness who over the process in this movie begin realising the fate of Iraq. 

Much of the movie is totally dynamite with its robust sound and cinematography and also its well-written screenplay by Mark Boal who was in Iraq with the bomb squad, when he was a journalist. Dialogue in shows the attitudes of soldiers in Iraq and also is well on the mark of being objectiveness meaning that they don't take sides. The theme of this movie is 'men in war'.

However, The Hurt Locker is not quite perfect. The fact is that director Kathryn Bigelow, who won an Oscar for Best Director becoming the first woman to do so, takes the handheld camera or as I call it 'shaky' camera to a very high extreme causing me, the reviewer, to feel nauseous then throw up. It explores feelings of hopelessness and longevity in war situations, similarly to Jarhead, but shows them not through the central character, but the situations they're put in. For example they get stranded in the middle of the desert for about a day waiting for a pick up. After they've killed some snipers firing on them they have to wait and stare at their position just in case there's someone else they haven't shot yet. They wait like that, in the same positions for hours on end. The main character is an abrasive redneck named Sergeant James who comes into the story about 10 minutes in as the new bomb disposal technician. Now I'd assume the guy is supposed to be abrasive and a bit of a tool otherwise Bigelow massively misjudged the character. However there are times when his cocky attitude is more of a help than a hinderance, and this only seems to be in war-time situations where he risks his own neck to save everyone, but when he's play fighting with his army buddies and takes it too far, he ends up with a knife against his throat. This exemplifies the idea that soldiers are a different breed of human, who can't function in society, something which is touched upon when he returns home and does the shopping, finding it difficult to decide which cereal to choose. Another point worth mentioning, is that the whole scene that takes place in James' room where they all drink and punch each other, seemed completely stupid and just made me like all the characters less. I sort of understand that the idea was to make them the jocks of the working world, but it just made them seem overly-violent for no reason. Other than that, I did really quite enjoy the film, despite my reservations. There were some harrowing moments, and these were delicately balanced by uplifting ones. The film ends on a high but questionably immoral note, as James makes the decision to do what he loves.

There are no big actors in this movie, besides Guy Pearce and Ralph Fiennes, who both play very minor roles.  If Christian Bale were casted as the main character, you would know that he'd survive the whole way through. It would releive the effect every bomb scene has with the lesser-known actors that are actually in the movie.  You never expect these actors to have too much screen time, you expect them to die off quickly. There are many more aspects of this film that make it great, like the score, the screenplay, and the acting.  It's the first great modern war movie.  It shows the war in its true colors, and shows us the real problems soldiers are facing.  It shows us our addiction to war, just as Cameron does with Avatar. I worked in a supply platoon in which its ammunition delivery people, driving HEMTT M985 cargo models, would take part in transporting for EOD (explosive ordinance disposal) the UXO (unexploded ordinance)--things like IEDs (improvised explosive device), small arms ammo, large bombs, etc., anything impounded by EOD--after they had been difused.  On a side note, the only fatality from my battalion was due to a roadside IED.  My own military occupational specialty, fuel supply specialist, with an H7 identifier, because I also attended the fuel truck driving school, fuel being combustible material and hazardous itself, even more hazardous than ammunition for the fact I dealt with liquids and spills, is literally like driving bombs around.

After my return, I, too, would be caught in the grocery store cereal box aisle as depicted in this film.  I, too, would be caught with my loved ones as depicted in this film.  And, I, too, had learned not to love.  As I said, these things happened before my army service, but I used it to get me through it, because I had a job to do, because I was trained, and because I had to earn those paychecks and military benefits.  This raises some questions for which, in my own disjointedness, have no complete answer.  I'm guessing it must be a question about life.  But, this film seems to point in the right direction for addressing the distinction of what makes a military person unique.  The subject matter is important and the cinema realistic, almost documentary, but the story's end makes logical sense specifically because of its disjointed and oblique view.  It seems like the only way to address the issue: exploring the intensity and careless lack of intensity to what it feels like in ordinary human terms.  This puts a high value on this film and does so without the stereotypical cliche results of this genre.

Kathryn Bigelow's Oscar-winning thumbscrewer doesn't necessarily have any radically new or fascinating insights into the physical and psychological toll of warfare, but her masterful control of tension and visual space makes "The Hurt Locker" a notable entry into the burgeoning Iraq War genre.

Focusing on a three-man Army bomb squad in the final month-and-a-half of their tour, Bigelow's film (from Mark Boal's taut script) is prefaced with a heavy-handed pronouncement: war is a drug. We are not for one moment allowed to lose sight of the clear adrenaline rush that Sergeant William James (more on this character's conspicuous name in a moment) gets from his high-risk work investigating and defusing bombs. Jeremy Renner's Will James oozes cocky machismo and sucks on quasi-post-coital cigarettes after each mission, but even this embodiment of American masculine swagger can't shake the demons of war for long. The soldier's inability to adjust to civilian family life has been a war movie cliche since the post-WWII "The Best Years of Our Lives", if not longer, and Boal and Bigelow trot out the well-worn trope with little concern for its expiry date.

But "The Hurt Locker" is not about reinventing the brain of the war movie; it's about giving it a lean, muscular, proportioned form. Bigelow indulges in flashy but undoubtedly poetic slo-mo shots of dust rising and settling after a blast, brief, zen-like snapshots of environments shattered by man. The various extended combat sequences are the true directorly tours-de-force, however, though they might more properly be called anticipation of combat. Bigelow keenly establishes the geography of her settings with initial sweeps and cuts (Jordan poses for war-torn Iraq, helped along by the casting of actual Iraqi refugees), so that when action begins to ratchet into motion, the audience knows precisely how close to deadly peril everyone stands. The superlative adjectives have been overstrained already on this film, but one still holds true: riveting.

Although a bit more displayed awareness for the film's place in the war movie canon might have been preferable (an Iraq film with cultural knowing of "Jarhead" and the action set pieces of "The Hurt Locker" would be a formidable beast indeed), the lead character's name hints at a veiled resonance embedded in Bigelow and Boal's work. William James was, of course, one of the great minds of early psychology, and the founder and leading proponent of functional psychology. 

This school of psychology emphasizes the human mind's active, ongoing adaptation to external environmental stimuli, precisely the sort of stimuli that cannot be replicated in controlled experiments. In a like mind to his famed namesake, Sergeant James has little patience for official attempts to tame the rabid monster that is war, and believes it needs to be confronted on its own terms, in its putrid, bone-strewn lair. He is repeatedly called a "wild man" by his more professional peers, but James feels instinctively that war itself is wild, and that any attempt to approach it as anything else is counter-intuitive. What he is, he only really is in the theater of war; his behaviour is his identity, and his identity is tied to war. Civilian life cannot engage him, for its adaptation are too proscribed, not active or extreme enough. Inscribed in Boal's naming of the character, then, is a fixed psychological standpoint, in the academic sense, a clever nod to the film's deeper possibilities.

Still, as entertainingly-staged as "The Hurt Locker" is, it has its weaknesses. It loses its momentum as the second hour winds on, and the various big-name actors in minor roles prove more distracting than anything else. Furthermore, those not of a mind to agree with my William James-functional psychology leap might find it lacking in intellectual heft and too invested in narratives of masculinity. But when Bigelow tightens the vice on us (and she does so often), such concerns are moot, and the edges of our seats bear our weight.

After six years of mediocre, Oscar-trolling prestige films that failed to impress audiences or critics (Rendition, In The Valley of Elah, Lions for Lambs, etc.) the first true masterpiece of the Iraq War sub-genre has finally arrived. The Hurt Locker is filled with tense scene after tense scene, including multiple IED-diffusing scenarios -- when we know an onlooking insurgent could press the button at any moment -- and a desert shoot-out sequence that goes on for what seems like hours. But the film is as heartbreaking as it is nerve-wracking, especially in an epilogue sequence that recalls the "I'm an average nobody" scene at the end of Goodfellas. "War is a drug," the film tells us in an opening title, and takes that almost literally. What makes this film truly great is that it's most interested in telling us an honest story about these soldiers and this war, without servicing any type of political agenda. The film, refreshingly, is politics-free, and isn't aimed at provoking a reaction one way or another about the political ramifications of the war. The soldiers aren't depicted as soulless killing machines, as tools of a corrupt government or as pure saints. They're honest, flesh-and-blood human beings (what a concept!). For this we can largely thank the script and the actors, especially Jeremy Renner, who deserves every acting accolade in the world. Kathryn Bigelow has always had a great eye for action, but with The Hurt Locker, she not only has made her masterpiece, she has set a new standard for which every modern day war movie should be judged against.

Great cast, great story, great dialogue, great everything. But why, then, does this movie feel like its missing something? 

The Hurt Locker is a war story, obviously set in Iraq, focusing on an elite bomb squad unit. When Sergeant First Class William James (Jeremy Renner) is called on duty to disarm dangerous bombs located all across the sweltering country, the audience follows his various objectives and struggles. 

First, let me begin by saying I totally respect this film: it's fantastic that the underdog of the list of nominees (for those who don't know, The Hurt Locker wasn't "stellar" in box office) was highly respected by everyone. 

That being said, let me launch into the actual review. The cast in The Hurt Locker aren't exactly fantastic, due much in part to the movie's lacking character development. We don't know much about who the characters are. However, most of them take their roles very seriously: Anthony Mackie (who plays Sergeant JT Sanborn) definitely delivered a stunning performance when it came to all the emotions he had to deliver in the film, from happiness to hopelessness. The problem with some of the scenes is that there isn't emotion where emotion lies. Overall though, the performances were great.

The dialogue in the film is very realistic. There's a scene in the movie where Jeremy Renner delivers a speech to his new baby, which is very powerful and which makes the scene very memorable. There's also many conversations between the bomb squad group that are memorable, and then there's an intense scene where Renner talks to a guy who has a bomb strapped to his chest. 

Some of the scenes in the movie however feel very dragged out. There are times where Renner finds a bomb and tries to disarm it. At first, the audience is wondering "Oh my gosh, is he gonna die? Will this detonate?". But the anticipation is slowly transformed into impatience as the audience is sitting there saying "Okay, is it going to go off or not?"
 
So plot line and character wise, there's only slight improvement. That's why this movie definitely doesn't deserve a "Best Picture" winner at the Oscars. Sure, I'm glad that the production crew won "Best Editing", "Best Sound", and of course "Best Screenplay". But the movie has too many small flaws to have won 6 Oscars. Oscar winning movies like this should have excellent character development and just the right amount of suspense to keep the audience on the edge of their seats. But therein lies the problem with this movie. 

With 10 nominees up for Best Picture, this one shouldn't have one. There are plenty of other nominees (for example, Up, District 9, and The Blind Side. I would also say Precious, but I have yet to see that) that would have deserved the Best Picture winner. 

8/10 - There are several small flaws with the film, such as character development and dragged out scenes, but overall the film delivers a very emotional feeling and rich dialogue.

Okay, I'm back. I haven't written any reviews in a while and now I'm getting re-started with The Hurt Locker. I was quite interested in the film for a while, and it's best picture win naturally made me more curious, so here's my review.

  In case you don't know, The Hurt Locker tells the story of an American bomb squad in Iraq. When their team captain is killed, he is replaced by the totally wild Sergeant James, who shocks his two team members by his extreme confidence and lack of hesitation in his job. The film has an amazing and authentic realism that truly does put you there like no other war film has. It's like District 9, but real, and never stops being that way. But while that is a major positive for the most part, it's also a bit of a negative as there isn't much of a story arc, and definitely no hollywood ending, I can do without the latter, but even in realistic movies, I like it when events are connected somehow.
 I was glad to discover that the film doesn't just depict bomb-disarming after bomb disarming, you get to see all forms of modern combat, with the highlight being a spell-binding sniper duel in the middle of the dessert. And it's told so well, because it's shown through the soldiers' eyes. You only see the enemy snipers from a distance, mostly through the soldiers' scopes, so you can never be more sure than the characters about a hit or a kill. It's not like most action movies where you're the omniscient bystander. Nonetheless the bomb disarming sequences are unflinchingly suspenseful, and there are some great little bits like the main protagonist pulling a wire from a car-bomb and having the wind-shield wipers activate, a little bit of comic relief that isn't at all forced or distracting from the situation.
But when it comes down to it, The Hurt Locker is really about the soldiers, the three men put through all these intense encounters. And thankfully for that it is perfectly cast.
Jeremy Renner, who plays James, does a fine job and creates a very fascinating character, at first you can't tell whether he's over-confident or just really really good at his job, or even just plain nuts, but all these questions are firmly tied off in the end. The other leads are perfectly convincing, and there's also some fine cameo work from David Morse, Raph Fiennes, and Guy Pearce.

  The only issue I have with the film is the story arc. In the second half of the film, some scenes venture away from the every-day-sweep-of-the-area thing and seem to be leading toward something bigger going on, or finding the main bad guys behind everything or something, but it all goes nowhere. That could've been what they were going for, but it's kind of depressing to say that in real life things don't tie off or get resolved.
   
  Overall, The Hurt Locker is a great film and is deserving of all the praise it has received. It's a must-see for it's presentation of the depicted situation alone, but there is also fantastic character development and great performances that really make it stand out in the genre 9/10.

Director Kathryn Bigelow ("Point Break") became the first woman to win the Best Director Oscar for her 2008 film "The Hurt Locker" (ignore what this says, it was '08, not '09 when released, one of 3 films in history to win Best Picture the year after release, including "Casablanca" and "Crash").

The story follows an Army bomb squad unit as they patrol Irag (filmed in the neighboring Jordan) looking for explosives that always seem to be up the road.  Several characters come and go, but we mainly follow James (Jeremy Renner, "S.W.A.T."), Sanborn (Anthony Mackie, "Notorious") and Eldridge (Brian Geraghty).  I'm not an expert, but frankly I'd want more then 2 guys watching my back while hostile territory.

Bigelow makes good use of hand-held Steadicams to put the viewer into the action (likely with props to "Saving Private Ryan"), everything always seems to moving about from building to bomb to building, etc, random civilians walking in and out of places, never knowing exactly who's just walking by and who's gonna blow the street up.  It's effective process and ya never quite know whether things'll be okay or someone about to burst into a million pieces.

Jeremy Renner of all people runs the show as the cocky explosives expert and his slow building friendship with Anthony Mackie seems realistic enough.  His performance would garner him a nomination for a Best Actor Oscar, a feat I consider hilarious considering he played Dags in "National Lampoon's Senior Trip".  That's not a Paul Giamatti rise to a fame, but more a "played the lead in a badly received movie, do nothing, years later be the bad guy in "S.W.A.T.", then get nominated for an Oscar".  Talk about a sudden rise in quality of acting.

A few random notable actors make brief appearances in the form of Guy Pearce, David Morse and Ralph Fiennes, though their roles are as big as Paul Giamatti's or Ted Danson's in "Saving Private Ryan".  Certainly one of the better war films out there, especially dealing with the Iraq war ("Jarhead" I always found highly underrated) and it's definitely worth checking out.

I'll admit he was looking way too smug at the awards, but at the end of the day he has made the better film.

The film itself does an excellent job at building tension and is shocking in places, mostly due to the main protagonist's crazy antics. Jeremy Renner was an excellent lead right from his first appearance about 15 minutes in. He is a character that leaves you wondering whether you like him or hate him all the way through the movie. He can do something heroic, but then something very stupid, but then play with a young child in his spare time when he's not defusing bombs and then do something stupid that could result in everyone's death. He is a complex and unpredictable character, but he is the film's centre point and his cocky personality can annoy but somehow generate respect and sympathy. His decision at the end of the film to return to the war, is a way that completes his character and allows the audience to fully understand why he appears so insane and dangerous, and it is right down to his character and his lust for excitement in his life that connect us to him. James is a well developed character, and for that reason alone, The Hurtlocker is a great movie.

The film's pacing is about right, its exciting but not unrealistic; we see the same amount of downtime for these soldiers as we do 'bomb time'. The script is expertly written  and interactions between characters remain interesting even in the longer conversations and one sequence that sees our heroes pinned down by snipers for a good 20 minutes.

The real issue with this film is simply it's lack of something extraordinary. On its own, the film succeeds in everything it is trying to be; a suspenseful and emotional war themed thriller. However, give it so much hype that audiences view the film expecting something original and incredible, they will not be able to help feeling disappointed, as The Hurtlocker is a good film, but nothing particularly special, nor does it contain anything particularly memorable minus the solid leading man.

The film that blew me away back in the summer of 2009 remains my favorite of the ten Best Picture nominees, and also my favorite film of the entire year. Directed by Kathryn Bigelow, "The Hurt Locker" is an intense, drama-filled portrait of U.S. soldiers fighting in the war in Iraq, and it couldn't have been more flawlessly crafted, in my opinion. Since November, this small film has been gradually building awards attention and momentum, winning many awards within critic circles and the various "Guild" awards, and it is now a favorite to win the top prize at the Oscars alongside "Avatar," and for good reason.

"The Hurt Locker" follows a three man Explosive Ordnance Disposal team (EOD) in the U.S. Army's Bravo Company stationed in Baghdad, Iraq, with the new man on the team, Sergeant First Class William James (Jeremy Renner) replacing a fallen soldier previously on the squad. Will's job is to disarm and dismantle IED's (improvised explosive devices) scattered around the city, hiding in places such as cars or buried down in the dirt. His teammates, Sergeant J.T. Sanborn (Anthony Mackie) and Specialist Owen Eldridge (Brian Geraghty), are given the job of keeping Will safe as he disarms the bombs, looking out for present threats and communicating with him via headset. Bravo Company's rotation in Iraq is nearly up, witha little over a month to go, and they are quite anxious to finish up and go home.

This is not a story with a linear, A-to-B style plot structure, which might turn some people off. However, it doesn't need to be. It focuses mostly on the different experiences that these men have to together in the war, and the horrors they face. Watching the very different methods each of these three characters uses to perform their duties and deal with the incredible pressures of their daily jobs is fascinating, and the way they interact with each other and put up with their different attitudes and styles makes the film something very special. On one hand, you have Will, who is a "wild man," as he is called in the film. He is a reckless individual that seems to have no concern for his own safety....or the safety of his teammates. He does things his own way, taking irresponsible and inappropriate actions such as discarding his headset while in the process of trying to disarm a bomb, or taking off his protective suit. The main conflict in the film lies in the danger that Will is putting his teammates in, when they understand exactly what could be in store for them if they continue working alongside him.

Will is a man addicted to the thrill of war, and the adrenaline it gives him. He can't get enough of it, and his addiction could possibly end up leading to the demise of the brave soldiers accompanying him, which forces the other two to count down the seconds until they're free to leave their rotation. J.T. is a man who takes the experience of war and contrasts it with the beauty of a normal life, striving to escape the horrors he faces and emerge on the other side as a better man. Owen has seen the dangers of war and knows that in any second, a life can be taken, and that terrifies him to his very core. He is the character that you can tell immersed himself in something that was too complex for him to fully comprehend, and in every action he takes and every breath he breathes, you can sense his fear and longing to exit untouched.

The great character development and emotional connection is beautifully complemented by some of the most intense scenes available in cinema, and I truly believe this is one of the most suspenseful films I have ever seen. "The Hurt Locker" is basically a series of bomb-diffusing scenes, and every single one brings its own level of insane intensity, keeping you on the edge of your seat until you finally reach either a quiet, relieving conclusion, or a loud and deadly one. Kathryn Bigelow used a somewhat shaky, documentary style for this film that doesn't annoy you, but immerses you so deeply into the action that it literally places you in Iraq, right next to our three main characters. We feel every explosion, understand every character's decisions and reservations, and cringe and shake our heads every time Will takes action to exemplify his personality and further define the identity of his character. 

"The Hurt Locker" succeeds in evoking extreme emotion from its viewers, and it manages to remain incessantly entertaining throughout with the help of three dynamic main characters, flawless direction, and a screenplay that paints such a vivid picture of human emotion, addiction, and fear, altogether fused with the unfortunate and horrifying circumstances of the Iraq War. I was exhaustively invested in this film, and I am unashamed to say that this has instantly taken its place among my favorite war movies.   This film had an incredible impact on me when I saw it in the theater, and I definitely feel that it is a theater-driven movie, due to the effects that the giant screen and loud sound system can have on you, but the home-viewing experience of the film is jaw-dropping as well.

"The Hurt Locker" is an undoubtedly wonderful film, and in my opinion, it's the very best that 2009 has to offer.

The Hurt Locker is a film about the psychological effects of war, played out through a bomb squad unit. While there is action and suspense, making the movie thrilling at times, Kathryn Bigelow is much more interested in how this action, suspense and pressure affects her characters than the action and suspense as spectacle for the audience. This is primarily shown through the good performances from Jeremy Renner (who is ready to get more work), Anthony Mackie and Brian Geraghty. Bigelow also succeeds in the tone and style that she sets with her camera. It is gritty and in tight, but also plays to the nerves of the characters (and audience) as it constantly scans the parameter, and skeptically looks at everyone as a potential threat. Out of combat, the characters are lost; they drink, punch each other, look for answers, break down, and do not fit. This is most eloquently shown in Renner's brief tour state side (more specifically, the supermarket scene). He is completely lost in civilian life and cannot wait to return to the field. The Hurt Locker looks at how the stress and exhilaration of being in combat changes one's ability to function. The film does not take sides, there is no agenda; it merely wishes to explore the emotional toll that battle takes on different people as it examines how the characters handle their situation(s). 8/10

For present situations we currently face in the Middle East, it's hard to make movies based off of those events. However, The Hurt Locker has broken that cold streak and for me, is the best film of 2009. The Hurt Locker takes place during the post invasion period of the Iraq War, where we follow one of the most elite teams in the U.S. Army, the EOD (Explosive Ordnance Disposal) unit in the Bravo Company. The job description of this unit is to dismantle IEDs (Improvise Explosive Devices). A new leader takes over after the former leader dies in and IED incident and the two other members are challenged by his unorthodox and reckless techniques. This movie is a near-perfect war film for many reasons but most of the credit must go to director Kathryn Bigelow. She almost tricks you into thinking that you're watching a documentary because of the countless number of quit cuts and first person shots. She also does a great job at building up the suspenseful tension the film offers and she surprises you at every twist the story takes. To add onto the suspense comment I made, you will be on the edge of your seat for over eighty percent of the movie because of how tense the action gets. Because of how great of a job Bigelow did directing this film, she could most likely be the first woman to break the feminine barrier and win Best Director at the Oscars. Another pair of honorable mentions go out to writer Mark Boal and actor Jeremy Renner. Boal, who was an investigative journalist during the early days of the Iraq War, traveled with an EOD team in Iraq, which is where he got the inspiration for the story. He also portrays Marines in a good way and doesn't make them too far-fetched but still gives them some good comedic lines, too. Jeremy Renner plays Sergeant First Class William James, the leader of the EOD team, who unlike the past leader, has unorthodox and reckless techniques for how he does this job. You want to not like him but as the film progresses, you see that he has a strong heart for those around him. His performance has received a lot of praise and he might be the underdog to possibly receive a Best Actor nomination at the Oscars. Overall, The Hurt Locker is one of the most realistic films on the war in Iraq and certainly one of the most memorable. A white knuckle action film that also provides an interesting look at the psychological effects at fighting a war we never know that we'll win.

The Hurt Locker (2009)

Directed by : Kathryn Bigelow
Starring : Jeremy Renner, Anthony Mackie, Bryan Geraghty, Evangeline Lily


The good news is...the Hurt Locker is good...really good.


The bad news? It aint great. 


I've seen a ton of flicks based on the U.S. occupation of Iraq & while many of them are really good...pretty good...they aint great. This one...well...it just mystifies me that everyone pulled their panties over their heads & gave up the holiest of holies for it. For real...& I aint just cryin' cause it booted Avatar outta the running. This movie aint worth all the hub bub. 


The Kingdom...now that one was worth the hub bub & it pretty much got panned. 


Anywho..."the Locker" follows the members of "Bravo Company", the U.S. Army's team of elite Explosive Ordnance Disposal & the days that count down to the end of their 38 day rotation. 


The movie starts out with Jeremy Renner coming in as a replacement for the team's leader who takes one for the team during the first five minutes of the film. You gotta give credit to Bigelow as she sets quite an intense pace with little effort. 


The one thing that really got me? 


30 minutes into the film...I actually began to picture a war torn Iraq in my head...& buddies...this was it in front of my face. 


The effects & settings are just astounding, but it's the acting (fantastic on all fronts) that makes the movie. 


Jeremy Renner makes the movies as Staff Sergeant Will James just as easily as he runs the team. Playing second fiddle to Renner are Anthony Mackie as  J.T. Sanborn & Brian Geraghty as Specialist Owen Eldridge. Although these two boys are back up players they more than pull their weight. It'd be a crime if all three of these boys don't get bigger & better roles off of this one. Sanborn & Eldridge are taken aback with James & his way of dealing with Iraq, his role, & his skills. 


The one question that needs to be answered for Sanborn, Eldridge, & we the viewers? 


Does this fool James have a death wish? 


By the end of the movie...I really couldn't answer the question...but it sure was fun wondering. For his team mates...it didn't seem all that fun. At one point during the film Sanborn & Eldridge even contemplate detonating James & passing it off as an accident. This movie's got a shit pot load of stuff going on. One of the most stirring images for me was near the end of the flick. When Sanborn & James are driving down the street just after a rather explosive scene passes. They pass by a handful of kids on the street & get pelted by rocks. Kind of makes you wonder just what in the hell are we really doing over there. 


In the end...the movie's good...but it aint great. If anything...the acting's the great part of it all. While I'll give it a fresh rite of passage...it's just not the "bomb" (heh heh heh) that everyone makes it out to be & it surely, in my humble opinion, didn't deserve the Oscie nod.
