I only give this movie a 10 on here because as a movie, it's pretty good. But as for it being an actual representation of soldiers in Iraq, it isn't. I spent two tours in the sandbox, OIF 1 and 3, the first being 14 months, the second being 13 months, and this movie is beyond unbelievable.
First, the uniforms. The digital grey ACU was not issued to Army soldiers until 2006. Up until then, we wore the brown DCUs. That in itself doesn't ruin the movie, it just bugs the hell out of me.
Second, from the beginning of the war up till I ETS'd in 2008, you could not leave base with 3 soldiers in 1 humvee. 3 humvees with at the very least 12 soldiers were required for anyone to leave base. I spent my first tour going off post 6 days a week, and we never went with less than 15. Also, if you ran into a combat situation, the odds had to be at least 2 to 1 to stay and fight. If there were more of them than us we had to do everything we could to get back to base, if not, call the QRF for back up.
Third, pinned down by a sniper in the middle of nowhere? Not so unbelievable. But, when everyone is being taken out by the sniper, don't grab a rifle and go all Enemy at the Gates. You call in artillery, or an air strike, that's what they are there for.
Fourth, any high ranking officer almost never leaves the protection of their overly protected areas. When they do, it's with a whole lot of infantry to protect them.
Fifth, sneaking off base, and sneaking back in. Not possible the way it was shown in the film. Every vehicle going in or out is inspected so no one can get in that's not supposed to be, and out that's not supposed to be. This is done to ensure that no one is sneaking out, but also to protect the soldiers from being kidnapped. Had any normal soldier come strolling back to base as portrayed in the film, he would have been arrested, interrogated, and given at least and article 15, and at his rank, he probably would have been booted out of the Army.
Sixth, the soldier getting shot due to them running off on their own to find who set off the truck bomb. There are Intel teams that do that, I know because I was on one of them. I can see a squad of infantry going off to check the surrounding areas, but if 3 soldiers went off on their own and one ended up shot like that, it's safe to assume that the Sgt would have been arrested and been put into Leavenworth for a few years for needlessly endangering the lives of the soldiers under his command.
Finally, the getting drunk scene where they were carrying him back to his room. I'm not going to say there isn't drinking going on over there, I'll be the first to admit that we drank whenever we had the chance (going off post into the city everyday did have its advantages), but they would have been stopped by the officer that they talked to and been busted, and dealt with harshly.

Has there ever been a time when you watch a movie where you can feel the intensity of a scene building up inside you? Well, that has just happened to me after viewing Kathryn Bigelow's Iraq war drama, "The Hurt Locker." This is the kind of war I haven't seen since "Saving Private Ryan." It's because of the fact it's one that doesn't involve political issues, but one that gets us to know who the soldiers really are.

The movie is set in present day Iraq. In the beginning, we get an intense example of what is to come throughout the movie. The story focuses on a bomb squad group, who counts down the days of finally going back home where they want to be. They are, of course, ready to get rid of another bomb hiding under the rocks of the Iraq town. Here, their enemy could be anywhere. Surrounding them is the towns-people, looking awfully suspicious. It seems any of them could be the enemy (cue the suspense). With of them operating a cellular device, the bombs go off. When the bombs go off, we see the entire explosion in slow-motion, feeling the full impact of it, with the dust falling off a rusty car, to the shock wave striking the bomb squad leader, Sgt. Matt Thompson (Guy Pearce). 

After the death of Sgt. Thompson, the squad needs a new bomb squad expert. Joining their crew is the fearless, SSgt. William James (Jeremy Renner). This is the kind of soldier that loves doing what he does. He loves going out, defusing bombs. He defuses them like they were nothing. Who would've known there could be someone like this? He doesn't flinch, he doesn't feel fear, heck, he even takes off his protective suit, quoting, "If I'm gonna die, I want to die comfortable." Sheesh. Now I don't know too much about defusing bombs, but I'm sure that would be up in my top jobs I would never want to do list. William, however, thinks the opposite.

The rest of the action sequences and most of the scenes get the exact gut-wrenching feeling like the explosion scene. What's great about it is that they use no visual effects tricks. That's what stunned me the most. How was Bigelow capable of pulling off these nail-biting scenes without even using green-screen technology? Well, I guess she's just wanted to make the movie as realistic as possible, which is a good thing for a war film. With realism film-making, we get to actually experience what these soldiers must be feeling.

What is it about defusing bombs William loves doing? Is it because he accomplished something? Is it because he wants to escape reality? Is he trying to make his other squad members jealous? For me, there are endless questions, yet I don't know if I can answer them for myself. I guess war has a tendency to drive a person out of the real world, making them feel good about doing these dangerous jobs I don't want to come in range of. What I loved about the film is that it isn't one that isn't making social statements, it's one that tells the story of being a soldier, out on the field of duty, knowing what it's like to feel fear surrounding them, unknowing where an enemy, an attack, or an explosion could happen. "The Hurt Locker" is one of the greatest war films to come out in a very long time. It builds high tensions through out each scene, with great direction from Bigelow, the use of hand-held camera work through out a lot of the movie, an emotional screenplay by Mark Boal, and terrific cast appearances from actors such as Ralph Fiennes, David Morse, Anthony Mackie, and Brian Geraghty. It is the war film of our generation, and it was one that was meant to be told of what it's like being a soldier, and the dangers it possesses.

Kathryn Bigelow has the best filmic sense of any working American director. She seems to have some sort of advanced natural sense of exactly where the camera should go, exactly how long to hold a shot, exactly where you'll want to see the next bit of motion come into frame. She knows when to hold the camera still, when to let you see handheld jitters, and when to twiddle zoom back and forth. 

You never feel like she's roughhousing you, either. You feel like you're watching the events of the movie unfold right in front of you--she never steps back for a fancy camera trick or some ironic twist to events to remind you that it's all just a story with her as the teller and you as the audience. She kicks you out of the back of the plane for your tour of duty and then she scoops you back up at the closing credits.

Nobody else in this country, except for Spike Lee, is in her league at taking visual energy and cutting it together into a story. This is why she won the Oscar. People make a big deal about how she made a movie about the war without commenting on the political discussion surrounding the war. She does avoid political discussion, but not because she's such a deft storyteller that she can find ways around it. She avoids it because she's telling the story of soldiers in the field, and stays true to the events of combat as they happen to them. She's organized and focused about showing you what's happening, and doesn't bog herself down trying to get any points across outside the story. She makes you wonder why more people don't make their movies this way. Maybe they would if they could.

She has in the past as well, especially with Point Break. That movie always made you wonder why it was so watchable, especially with the three leads it had--Swayze, Busey, and Keanu don't exactly make for a trifecta of Shakespearean complexity, but she got good use out of all of them. Even with some of the most howlingly bad line readings of the last 25 years (especially from Reeves), that movie is fun to watch over and over. Hurt Locker has the same skill on display except in even more concentrated dosage. 

This time, she gets much more interesting dramatic work. She has some big names (or skillful contributions) in bit parts--Evangeline Lilly, Guy Pearce, Ralph Fiennes, David Morse. But the three leads here are less known. Renner in particular shows all kinds of interesting emotional subtlety, and his scenes are the engine of the movie. You almost can't believe how fast the movie flies by when it's just him staring at an IED and cursing under his breath. 

In the end you don't feel like you've watched much of anything in the way of an epic, even though the movie is over two hours long. Some people probably knock her for not showing a more complicated internal emotional life for the characters. But what she shows feels like a convincing portrayal of combat rotations--soldiers deploy, tour, and come home, sometimes more than once. Some of them freak out, some go by the book, some of them get hooked on the adrenaline. You see them all here but they don't feel like types at all. They want to do their jobs, and their interactions with civilians, officers, and the enemy (when they can find them) are intense but usually brief and quickly set aside for the sake of getting through the next day. 

To my mind there's no doubt that this movie was Oscar-worthy, though it's hard to find ready connections to the events for the audience. Most of us haven't been through anything remotely like these events, and even for recent combat veterans, the point is made over and over that what we're seeing is unusual even by the standards of a war, and a war that's unusual to some degree among wars. Somebody has been someplace and brought it back here, and with Bigelow helping get it fully back into the observation chamber for us we feel like we get to see it while it's still alive. 

Nobody in this movie ever calls for the cavalry and then greets them with fresh new dialogue like "boy, are we glad to see you guys!" Everything they get into, they gut out on their own. Not because they're a bunch of little Rambos who can't be stopped, but just because they follow their orders and do their jobs all the way to the end. That's the same way Bigelow and her crew made the movie.

The Time magazine review quote on the dvd box calls The Hurt Locker "A near-perfect movie" and by the end of the film you will believe it. The film earns points right off the bat for being the first major war movie about the Iraq War without a political message but it will keep you on the edge of your seat most of the way through this emotional roller coaster.

The first thing to mention is that the acting in this movie is absolutely superb. All three of the main leads do their jobs just as well as their characters do theirs. In fact I really didnt notice any scenes where I thought I was looking at actors portraying soldiers instead of actual soldiers. Each character has their own hopes and fears and this is brought across well. Only complaint I have is that the characters could have had a bit more back story for the main characters but what we do get works well enough.

As for the setting, this movie probably portrays 2004 Iraq better than any currently out there. The audience gets a real sense of the paranoia, knowing that any of the hundreds of foreign faces looking at you might be planning to kill you and its a wonder our soldiers don't crack under the pressure and just start shooting people if that is actually how it is. The man in front of you might really be a concerned family member or he may be lying through his teeth. If he is you cant do anything till he makes the first move and then there is no guarantee you will still be able to move. This kind of intensity is present in several scenes throughout the movie and the camera work does a fantastic job of getting it across.

The story works for this movie but it does seem to lack a clear beginning middle and end. Still if Avatar, which had virtually no story in comparison, can get nominated for best picture, then its justice that Hurt Locker should win best picture. Again this is a war story told from the soldiers point of view and like the soldiers were aren't always given the full story beyond what the mission is. 

Of the 2010 oscar nominees for best picture, as of this review I have seen Avatar, District 9, Blind Side, Up, and The Hurt Locker. The last three movies are the only ones that truly deserve their place on the list of best movies of 2010. My recommendation, buy The Hurt Locker and watch it if you haven't already. This is the best Iraq War movie out there and will likely remain so for a long time to come.

The Hurt Locker is a extremely tense and thrilling portrayal of a bomb squad deployed in Iraq. Directed by Kathryn Bigelow, starring Jeremy Renner, Anthony Mackie, Bryan Geraghty and Evangeline Lilly. This is a brilliant and realistic look at what is happening right now in regards to the war on Iraq.

The Hurt Locker focuses on a team of men whose priority it is to defuse bomb threats around Baghdad. Jeremy Renner is brilliant, as adrenaline junkie William James who replaces the old team leader after his initial death due to the bomb sitation that opens the film. His team J. T. Sanborn and Owen Eldridge, played by  Anthony Mackie and Bryan Geraghty respectively are the perfect contrast to their somewhat crazy team leader creating alot of tension not only when defusing bombs but also between the team.

All performances are brilliant but my main reason I scored this film so highly was without a doubt down to Kathryn Bigelow and Barry Ackroyd for creating some beautiful visuals of desolate Iraq. Their use of slow motion makes this film a wonder to watch and the way she has directed this film only makes the situation even more tense. This combined with the great music score.

My favourite scene is without a doubt William James' first mission with his new team in which he finds a bomb at the side of the road and the stand off between an Iraqi driver and himself, only to discover there is more than just one bomb. My mouth dropped when he pulled the bombs out from the rubble and he was directly in the middle of them.

I think this film should of definitely focused more on the bomb defusal aspect and the ties between the team (which it did to some extent) than James' 'addiction' to war. However, its interesting to see how war can affect men in this modern day and age and knowing that with all the technological advances, being on the front line has never changed.

I can personally see why Kathryn Bigelow won the best director award but the films strength doesn't just rely on her. Overall, this is a thrilling film which really is very, very tense.

Better answer than it's different because it's illegal, immoral and begun upon false pretenses, but equally hollow. The best war movie I've ever seen. First off The Hurt Locker is so unlike any other war movie by being much much less violent than most. Saving Private Ryan was an incredibly forceful and emotional movie because of the massive amounts of violence, which mirrored the terrible violence of WWII. However, The War in Iraq is different. We fight a different enemy. There are no bloody charges and enemy lines. We're constantly behind enemy lines in Iraq, and the suspense of being behind enemy lines is captured all too well in Kathryn Bigelows epic. Soldiers rarely see action in the form of shootouts (fucking 3 Kings) but they do see many IEDs, the main killer of American soldiers in Iraq. So to get a realistic depiction of the War in Iraq while still being able to capture action and suspense, we follow a bomb diffusal squad.

Makes sense right? And for God's sake, this movie brings the suspense by the cubic fuck ton. Our protaganist is Seargent James, (Renner) who is the one who must put on the giant Juggernaut suits from MW2 and diffuse the fuck out of any bomb incapable of being disarmed by an unmanned robot. The role is very interesting. James is addicted to disarming bombs. He cannot stop the joy he is overcome with by the adrenaline rush which accompanies being in the face of Death (in the form of bombs). Renner does a great job, the role is not anything incredibly hard to play, but again he still does great. Of course, James's addiction often puts his troop in danger. Make no mistake, the two other members of James's squad (Sanbourne and Eldridge) play a vital role in the movie. Sanbourne wants to serve his country, but doesnt want to die. And Eldridge just DOES NOT want to die. So imminent confrontation between the Russian Roullete Sarge and his squad arise.

I could talk about the movie's characters and all their multi-faceted levels of emotion and the movie's great script, but the star of the show in this film is the cinemtography. Bigelow's camera direction makes this movie. This script was not designed to be as goddamn suspenseful as it was. This script was designed as a character study of the brave men serving our country, and Bigelow managed to keep this concept while turning the movie into an ass kicking heart fucking mountain of suspense which leaves the viewer feeling what James must feel like after a bomb diffusal. This film wrings your adrenal gland absolutely dry. The shots in this movie create a sense that the viewer is a part of Jame's squad, and that the viewer is in as much danger as them. By making all the shots close and POV from the ground, the viewer is surrounded by an unfriendly country trying to kill you and everyone else not wanted. I swear the scene where James diffuses the car bomb and the guy with the camera appeared on the roof I though I was going to have a heart attack. It's awesome.

An important film - presumably it gives the US public a fiction to help them structure certain aspects of what they hear about the experience of the military in Iraq. Well acted and, by Hollywood standards, adventurous in the way it tells its story. However, it is haunted by the need to have at its centre the superman whose almost magical powers depend on repressed inner conflict - this is a well-worn motif in the genre. It also doesn't quite know how to handle doubt - Hollywood movies are usually defined by the need to "show all", to minimise events that do not have a sufficient explanation - this film strays into the depiction of uncertainty but with a certain reserve.

I saw a programme recently about films made with the cooperation of the US Navy which revealed that they only cooperate (understandably enough) with projects that portray what they do sympathetically and that they often put recruiting teams in the foyers of cinemas which show the approved films. I'm not convinced that The Hurt Locker could be used in the same way - but it's not beyond the bounds of possibility.

There is one absence which is more than ususally disconcerting: any attempt to portray the mindset of the Iraqi people. Does this mirror a US cultural bewilderment at the fact that all too many Iraqis failed to react to the intervention in the way that the political script that made the war possible had suggested?

After watching The Hurt Locker I was unsure how to write my review, as I didn't believe it had enough action to make it an action film, it didn't have enough climatic sequences of emotion to make it a drama, and thriller is such a wide topic now that it could cover anything. It was with an unwilling heart that I decided to renegade the movie to the most unliked of all classifications, the heading of War. 

The only people who enjoy war films are (dare I say it) men, they love to see something fantastic that they would never personally have the guts to be in themselves. Men enjoy death.  They also enjoy action; it's in our genes, reaching as far back as Roman times when the Roman army's motto was "Death And Glory". With all that in mind, what is a women doing directing was is obviously a mans film? 

Kathryn Bigelow is directing The Hurt Locker because, she knows how to capture sentiment and strong characters with complicated relationships while keeping the overall feel of the movie action orientated (if anyone would like further proof of this please watch Point Break). While her style of directing does work for The Hurt Locker it can at times make the movie feel like its carrying dead weight. There are misused moments and the last minute inclusion of a poignant reflection on life could be seen as clichéd and confusing. 

Bigelow wants to make us feel on edge with The Hurt Locker, she wants to give a feeling that these people might actually die, as appose to most films where as soon as you see the "big" names you know they will last till the credits, no ones going to kill an Arnold Schwarzenegger or Chuck Norris, no ones that dumb. However, Bigelow creates the mood desired by making us feel paranoid for the characters, Bigelow doesn't care if you are a big Hollywood name like Guy Piece (who is killed in the opening sequence) or a total unknown, if she wants you dead, you're dead. 

This attitude gives the films an uneasy frame to it, that anyone could die at anytime, but then that's what war is like, real war I mean. Something we forget so quickly is that there are people dying all the time because of war. We are made to care so much that someone famous has popper there clogs when the real people of the world could all drop dead and we wouldn't know the difference. Here....I'll prove it to you, we all remember Michael Jackson dying and where we where when we found out the tragic news but how many of us remember the horrific story that there were a string of teenagers who took their own lives in Wales?

The Hurt Locker is a symphony of destruction and pain, comparable to The Devils Last Gallop by Charles Williams, any silence we experience is only to make the next sound more powerful.

The Hurt Locker is an uncompromised look at the real horrors of war and how there have more lasting effects then any of us can imagine. The Hurt Locker is like a sonic boom for our emotions, we are shown the initial explosions to start but then we feel the tremors for weeks afterwards. The most realistic depiction of war from Hollywood in years.

Rather than feeling an emotional attachment to the characters and empathizing with their conflicts, I felt like I was watching a documentary... and that was another problem with this film.  The film was shot in documentary style with first-person camera angles, shots zooming in around corners, and a shaking camera, and yet it was not intended to be a documentary.  I was excited to see Guy Pearce and Ralph Fiennes' names on the credits, but their involvement cannot be considered more than a cameo.  Jeremy Renner was okay but I would've rather seen the aforementioned actors.  This unending display of machoism did not provide any twists or surprises.  A few scenes made me hold my breath but other than that, I was indifferent to what might happen next.  I felt a tiny bit of emotion in the last 10 minutes of the film but aside from that, I felt removed from the plot and waiting for something new to happen.  Instead, I seemingly watched the same scene 4 times with a few random fights thrown in to split them up.  If you want to enjoy this film more than me, be sure to walk into it with a low level of expectation.

The Hurt Locker, Best Picture winner of the 2010 Academy Awards, is a stylized and wildly filmed and edited war movie. If you love you're war movies with thrills and drama, The Hurt Locker is great. But if you've seen 1 war movie, then The Hurt Locker is nothing speacial.

Set in Iraq War, Jeremy Renner plays Sergeant Willam James; a bomb specialist. His job is the most dangerous job of any soldier. His life is on the line constantly. The Hurt Locker follows William and a band of soldiers through many different, life threatening situations where you never know what's going to happen or who's going to die. Well.... that's almost the truth. The fact is this movie builds itself to be a really suspenceful movie, but you know that the main character isn't going to die. Jeremy Renner plays his character cool and very well. His character is an antisocial, adrenaline addicted soldier who doesn't seem to care about his life that much. Renner's acting is very good, but his character's depth is not all clear, his character's background makes no sence, and his character, overall, just seems tragically doomed. There's an amusing bit with a little kid that makes you see his softer side, but his character is so secretive, you can't really analyze him in a way that doesn't seem like melodrama. And it's not like any of the supporting characters make this movie any smarter. The dialogue is so cliche and doesn't make for an insightful story about war or their character develpoement.

The Hurt Locker is a very wild movie, and you gotta give it a lot of credit for it's crazyness. Multiple, handheld cameras surround the Iraq-set location. And when you edit all these different, shaky-cams together, it really builds up the suspenceful moments, even when nothing is happening. The narative is done in a 'realist' style, so the movie looks like you're right in the action. There's little to analyze as far as what you see in realist films, you only see character driven drama. But the filming locations set in this movie is fantastic, and shot very well. The sets look very gritty and realitic, using all the real military weapons and vehicles and armor, ALTHOUGH, some of it is bullshit. The Hurt Locker is known for its compromising realism for thrills. The tactical strategies used in the real army is nothing like what you'll see in The Hurt Locker. Example: No one cuts fucking wires on Bombs anymore, they use liquid nitrogen, and they use robots, not soldiers.

There really isn't any war movie that is 100% accurate, and the fact is The Hurt Locker is a well made and directed movie. But alas, this movie's inaccuracies for the sake of making a war movie more thrilling is not forgivable, and the unexplained and contradicting character developement makes The Hurt Locker, in my opinion, not worthy of its Best Picture Winner title.

Unlike any other war film, there isn't a body count or taking over any property or land that determines the winner of this war. Instead, the priority of this war focuses on defusing bombs. The Hurt Locker only follows three main characters in this film, as they are members of a United States Army Explosive Ordnance Disposal (EOD) unit in Iraq. We travel their tour together as they contend with defusing bombs, the threat of insurgency, and the tension that develops among them.

The Hurt Locker is perfect for what it is; but it doesn't have any re-watch value as this is a very uneasy movie to watch, similar to the film United 93. The only plot is for the characters to stay alive. What works in the film is the directing, photography and its cinematography. With how this film is shot gives you the experiences of how the soldiers are exactly feeling as they are in constant dangers. This film ends perfectly, as it takes one sentence to explain your respect & sympathy for the American soldiers; including our awareness of their fight within an unwinnable war.

Australia then realised how special the film was so once again changed their minds, canceled the DVD release & reset the cinema date for February/March this year just in time for oscar season! What a journey indeed!

The Hurt Locker is without doubt the best film based on the conflict in Iraq and one of the best war films in years. Directed by Kathryn Bigelow of Point Break fame, the plot follows the fortunes of an Army Bomb Squad and their day to day tasks. Early in the film one such day goes wrong leading the leader of the squad dead. In steps in SFC William James to take control, a man who is a real dare devil and creates serious tension with the other two members of the squad which eventually leads to some revelations for all three.

The main reason that The Hurt Locker is so good is because of the extreme tension that exists throughout, every single day the team puts themselves in serious danger as they must diffuse bombs while also keeping a lookout for enemies. Everyday they head out knowing that they face a serious chance of dying. It's mostly shot in a documentary style which just adds to the gritty realism, the sound and effects are first class and with a practically on-existent soundtrack it all adds up a top class production.

It by no means covers the conflict in depth, the entire film is based on the day to day activities of the squad, but this just adds to the tension as the characters are fleshed out perfectly with each one having their own demons. A couple of small sub-plots, one in particular involving a young Iraqi boy, fit in nicely with the main story and the ending is one that is definitely not in keeping with the usual war is bad films churned out by America.

Definitely a tour de force, The Hurt Locker is a must see and an excellent all round film on the realities of war.

War is his life and he is damn good at it! James replaces Staff Sergeant Matt Thompson(played  by Guy Pearce) after he dies from not getting away in time from a ticking bomb. His team: Sergeant JT Sanborn(played by Anthony Mackie) and Specialist Owen Eldridge(played by Brian Geraghty) both hate James, but they can't help but be influenced by him. Sanborn tries and tries to make peace with James and try to understand him, but hey, he is a maniac who loves the thrill of war....there's not too much to relate to when Sanborn is at war for his country, not thrill seeking. Owen Eldridge is the newbie. He takes advice(given and not given) from both Sanborn and James. He hates the affects of war and he wants to help out as much as he can, but he still has a lot to learn, like if he really wants to be a part of the bomb squad. Although it may seem like Sanborn and others are better for this job of theirs, James is the only one who has the guts to do it over and over and over again without slipping up and losing it. He constantly leads his team into the battle with bad-assness and nonchalance. He is the man to go to if you need any type of bomb diffused quickly, with percission, and ease. Katherine Hardewickle did an AMAZING job directing this movie, and I am so glad that Avatar did not beat The Hurt Locker when it came to Best Picture. The film is wonderfully gritty and dark, yet light enough to not dampen your mood. I can watch this movie again and again, and I will never be dissapointed! The Hurt Locker is, without a doubt, a tense, thought-provoking, and beautifully filmed epic by Bigelow, who deserved her Best Direction Oscar, and then some. However, the film as a whole, like many of the films nominated this year, was not Best Picture material. 

Yes- the acting was top-notch, with Renner pulling off a terrific performance as the Bomb Squad Specialist with an addiction to the adrenaline rush that comes with the anxiety and suspense that surrounds him at every turn. Accompanied by a stellar supporting cast, it is an impressive site to survey these men as they delve within the harsh landscape and the uncontrollable, dangerous atmosphere that surrounds them. It is indeed a taut, engrossing, powerful film and certainly deserved a nomination. 

Best Original Screenplay winner Mark Baol has molded a modern war film unlike others that have been presented before it: he offers no preachy sentiments, nor does he write with a stylized, melodramatic nature. War is simply presented, as it is- nothing more. It is a brutal, honest and ultimately, unbiased account of what occurs within the confines of those serving in the Iraq war. In that respect, the film is a standout. But there is a flaw that keeps the film from being a perfect war film. Baol has written his opus in such a fragmented way, that the audience (or maybe just myself) can really only appreciate the film as sections of dramaturgy, rather than a flowing, directive screenplay. Whilst interesting, it creates a thin but apparent barrier that keeps one at bay from fully connecting to what we are seeing, and it is really the inspired and ballsy direction of Bigelow and the solid characterization of Renner, that moves this film to one of connectivity and memorability.

So.... *this* is what beat "Avatar" at the Oscars? Well, it wasn't a bad movie by any means. In fact, I found it suspenseful and I thought Jeremy Renner was fantastic and I liked watching him. That said, I honestly don't think it deserved to beat the most innovative film (technologically-speaking) to date. 

I was happy that Kathryn Bigelow was the first female "Best Director" winner, but come on: "Best Picture"? There's nothing here that is any different from any other war movie I've seen. The only difference is Bigelow was playing in a boys' sandbox. After all, it's *always* dudes directing war films and guys dominate film direction, period. To me, it's just a confirmation of what women always knew, which is we're just as good as the men are when given a shot. 

If Bigelow was a guy, I hate to say it, but I don't think this film would have been such a big deal and I don't think it would have won "Best Picture". In fact, looking back at the Oscars and after watching this film, I even think that win may have been borderline condescending, to be honest. I now see it as more a vote of, " 'The Hurt Locker' was directed by a woman and she did pretty good, for a chick. Let's give her best director and/or Best Picture." Read the way reviewers talk about Kathryn Bigelow's direction and you'll see what I'm talking about. It all sounds like, "Dude, she did pretty good for a girl." And call me ungrateful, but I'm not cool with that.

I can appreciate "Best Director" for what it means for other up-and-coming female directors out there and the fact that it lets people know we mean business-- but "Best Picture" was totally undeserved. This movie was good, but it wasn't fantastic and there was nothing unique about it as far as its genre goes. Nothing at all. I refrained from saying "Avatar" was robbed until I saw "The Hurt Locker". Now I can safely say it.

Title: The Hurt Locker
Starring: Jeremy Renner, Anthony Mackie and Brian Geraghty
Directed By: Kathryn Bigelow
Genre: Action/Adventure, Drama, Thriller
Running Time: 131 minutes
Release Date: 07.10.09
Rated R - For war violence and language
Review:

     If you've read my review of Transformers: Revenge of the Fallen, you'll probably remember that one of my complaints about the film was that it was tiring and exhausting. Well same goes for The Hurt Locker. But while Transformers felt assaulting and not the least bit entertaining, The Hurt Locker captures exhaustion by showing the viewer what the brave men and women in the Army face everyday; near certain death. The Hurt Locker is a reall
y terrific film, filled with enough action and drama to satisfy any action film fan and or, pretty much, anybody that likes a good, well made, well acted film. Without further ado, I give you my review of The Hurt Locker.
     Unlike Michael Mann's Public Enemies, The Hurt Locker has a very engaging, raw shaky cam, that while Mann's film's shaky cam was very distracting, The Hurt Locker's only enhances the visual stimulation of all of the action and suspense transpiring on screen. Another thing I appreciated is the real attention to detail in all of the action sequences. One that stands out in my mind, is actually the first scene. When Guy Pearce's character makes his way across a small town to defuse a bomb. Little does Pearce know that there is a man with a cellphone, ready to detonate the bomb, which he does, (promise that's not a spoiler). Not only is the explosion a true spectacle, but all of the extra little nuances like the bombed out car shuddering from the immense explosion, seeing individual grains of gravel rise of the ground in ultra slow-motion; just breathtaking. If any complaints can really be leveled at Kathryn Bigelow's direction, I guess you could say that they're are some scenes that might not have needed to be done using a handheld camera and some of the quick zooms can be a bit nauseating. But this is almost a complete none-issue because Bigelow shows both expert knowledge behind the camera, and also how to get great performances out of her actors.
     The Hurt Locker follows three army men in the Iraq war. Their job, defuse bombs, and neutralize enemy threats if necessary. Jeremy Renner's character, Staff Sergeant William James, is the leader of the squad, and while a pretty easygoing guy, also has quite a few problems, starting with the fact that he is a major adrenaline junkie. There is a quote that begins the film, about "war," being, "like a drug." This is focused on for much of the film and almost seems to be the underlying theme. Besides Sergeant Williams, the squad consists of Sergeant JT Sanborn, played quite effectively by Anthony Mackie, and Specialist Owen Eldridge, played by Brian Geraghty. While the bulk of the film is basically different types of action sequences strung together, there is an extra layer of both humanity and depth to the characters and situations presented, that you don't usually find in other war films. Williams, as I mentioned, is an adrenaline junkie. Sanborn is struggling with the loss of his friend and previous sergeant, played by Guy Pearce. And Eldridge is having serious issues due to the horrible things he witnesses almost everyday. But what seems to triumph in terms of plot and script, is the idea that all of the men and women, currently in the Iraq war, put their lives on the line almost everyday. None of the violence or action is set up like an action film but rather, raw and brutal; almost documentary like. This was a very wise choice by the filmmakers. It adds a lot more gravi-tas to the plot and characters that inhabit the film. Overall the plot and writing of The Hurt Locker is very engaging and very entertaining. It is as eye grabbing as it is eye opening. Besides the opening quote at the beginning of the film, which tampers with the effectiveness of the film's ending, there is very little to complain about here. 
     I'm starting to notice a trend in Hollywood these days; if a film has less music than the average flick, than all of the regular sounds inside the film are cranked way up. The Hurt Locker easily does this better than most of the films out there right now. All of the explosions sound amazing. Everything feels very realistic and raw. All I can say, is that if you don't see this movie in with really great dolby digital surround sound, you my friend, are missing out!
     I find it very funny that neither of the really recognizable names of this film, Guy Pearce and Ralph Fiennes, last particularly long. Both have very short amounts of screen time, which almost seems odd considering that both of them are such fantastic actors. But, I have to say, that I'm glad director Kathryn Bigelow went with a more unknown cast. Don't get me wrong, you'll probably know Jeremy Renner and Anthonie Mackie when you see them up on screen, they just aren't necessarily household names. Both Renner, Mackie and Brian Geraghty give very strong performances, as the rag tag group of soldiers. Mackie, in particular, gives a star making performance as Sergeant JT Sanborn. Renner leads the film with a considerable amount of emotion and depth, showing that he is a more than capable leading man. Geraghty is quite good as the brave, yet, slightly damaged, Specialist Owen Eldridge. Of course both Fiennes and Pearce are good in their little parts in the film. Even David Morse has a brief cameo as Colonel Reed, who is also pretty good in his small part. Bigelow really did leave this film up to her actors, and she did a wise job in doing so. Everyone, from the almost unknown Mackie, to the the widely know Fiennes, shows a true mastery of their craft.
     The Hurt Locker is definitely one of the best films of the year, and I would not be surprised if it's nominated for best picture this year. Be it the directing, the writing, the sound or the acting, The Hurt Locker is a truly remarkable film, that will have you talking long after the ending credits roll. Definitely a film that should not be missed.

The biggest flaw of The Hurt Locker is how there was hardly any plot or story, it was just a bunch of scenes thrown in. First off, as many have rightly said, this is NOT an Iraqi war film. This is a film about the "rush" of war, and the flirtation with danger, and that fragile catalyst which can send you over the edge and into an early grave.

Never, in my opinion, has this subject been covered so concisely, with such passion or detail. This is simply as study of the men and women, but in this case men, who not only put their lives in danger for others, but for themselves.

The performances were first rate across the board, with an inspired choice and use of cameos, such as Ralph Fiennes, who was pitch perfect, as well as the ever likable and reliable Guy Pearce, and an amusing turn by David Morse.

But all these were far from through away, in fact each demonstrated a different aspect of the war junkie, with Fiennes British soldier, being one of the best. War is tough and each solider must face their own horrors of it in there own ways, but this offered a take on the horror as something that some men are bred for, but not in a monstrous way.

The genius of this film is in its lead, Jeremy Renner, who is portrayed as a headcase of sorts, constantly seeking and reveling in moral danger whilst being very intelligent, skilled, disciplined, whilst given at times going too far, and most importantly, with a strong moral sense; a true soldier.

This is a respectful and yet revealing war film, that deserves the kudos which it has received, and is up there with the best. The reason that I only scored it 9/10 is due to its only real flaw and that is in its pacing.

It does take its time, and for the most part that is not bad thing but there are moments in which it does move a little too slowly and the narrative is quite episodic in nature, and slightly fails in fully engrossing you all of the time.

'White knuckle intensity' does not begin to define this year's finest and most harrowing drama thus far. Rather, the ferociously explosive The Hurt Locker comes at you like a white knuckle sandwich, cold-cocking viewers with a corker of an opener and then never letting up. Even when there's downtime between characters, filmgoers are kept poised well beyond the edge of their seat with an emotional back-and-forth. The film might pull a balancing act comprised of both social commentary and character study, but the trappings are all-in can't-take-your-eyes-off-of-it captivating. Were it not for its 2004 Iraq War setting and sobering ending, one might accidentally call this an action film. Action simply proves to be the by-product of this timely and tragic tale, expertly told and acted with a gritty realism.  
 
In the R-rated war drama The Hurt Locker, the members of an elite Army squad (Mackie, Brian Geraghty, Jeremy Renner, Guy Pearce) battle Iraqi insurgents and each other while disarming roadside bombs in Baghdad. 
 
Director Kathyrn Bigleow has locked down her masterstroke. Bona fide movie stars Ralph Fiennes and Guy Pearce make brief appearances, but the true star wattage is provided by Brian Geraghty, Anthony Mackie, and, especially, Jeremy Renner. Ironically, Fiennes and Pearce have gained reputations as actor's actors, but bomb disarmer Renner's risk-addicted cocksuredness gives the film's most telling and damning lesson in acting-especially in the film's final moments. When the all-too-true reality of this soldier's fate hits screens, his gripping performance truly puts the hurt on filmgoers' sympathies. 
 
Bottom line: So great it hurts.

But, while you're watching the movie, it feels plausible enough. Jeremy Renner is quite good as the focused but reckless bomb disposal expert, and Anthony Mackie is convincing as his by-the-book sergeant. Guy Pearce, Ralph Fiennes, David Morse, and Evangeline Lilly from Lost are all in the movie, but only long enough for you to notice their presence. Kathryn Bigelow became the first woman ever to win an Oscar for directing with this movie, and overall it is definitely a director's picture. It's the way everything is co-ordinated that makes this movie impressive. The movie makes no attempt to preach about the Iraq war. This was one of the better movies of last year, but I don't know if I would have given it the Best Picture Oscar. Avatar will ultimately be remembered longer, and Inglourious Basterds was more fun, but I guess this movie is more serious than those two (plus it was made on a comparatively low budget).

Some examples include; the straight shooter who follows the book (doing so makes him think nothing can harm him), the rookie who continuously second guesses himself (and is beating himself up over it), and the rebel who thinks every day could be his last and there's nothing he can do to stop it. I have never been to war or had to experience a fraction of what these men went through, but Bigelow was able to shine a light into the everyday lives of soldiers so that I may bear witness to the horror and strange beauty behind war. Upon watching The Hurt Locker, I realised that I had watched every movie nominated for Best Picture this year apart from the actual winner. So all this time I have kinda been fuming over the fact that my favourites Inglourious Basterds, District 9 and Up in the Air didn't even get a look in, but I had never actually seen the film that beat them.
The Hurt Locker follows the story of an elite Army bomb squad who are centered in Iraq. Everything they do is done with extreme care as everything and everyone are potential threats and enemies. William James (Jeremy Renner) has seen a lot of bomb disposals in his time, and has found out that war and adrenaline are drugs to him. But while he is off at war, he has a family back home. Does he love war more than that?
I can see why this movie won Best Picture. It is, for once, an interesting look at the war in Iraq. Because of it's tough topic, bomb disposal, it has a lot of adrenaline, which is helped by some fantastic direction from Kathryn Bigelow. She makes the film in a way that draws the viewer in to what's happening. Too often I found myself lost in it's world because of this. 
The performances are pitch perfect, especially from Jeremy Renner, who exudes greatness as the tough guy James. Anthony Mackie, also, delivers an underrated performance as Sanborn. Even Brian Geraghty is great, and I have already forgotten him in Open House. The cameos from Guy Pearce and Ralph Fiennes don't detract from the film as many other cameos do, and they just fit in so well. It's hard to picture this movie as a movie, because we have become so used to films so dumb and flat, whereas this acts like a real-life piece that could have been filmed as a documentary in Iraq.
It sure is a great film with shattering direction from Kathryn Bigelow; her direction is enough to match twenty men, and I found it so hard to believe that a woman was directing this; however, I didn't enjoy it nearly as much as Inglourious Basterds, District 9 or Up in the Air. I do think it was better than Avatar, though. The film will probably go down in history as one of the best portrayals of war in Iraq.
A masterful war film with some amazing direction from Kathryn Bigelow. A definite must-see.

The message is harder to swallow because despite all the claims this is a film that "doesn't take sides", its portrayal of the Iraqi people and society as ciphers clashes with the very internal depiction of the American protagonists. By making the other so impenetrable, our only sense of them is filtered through the (understandable) paranoia of the US soldiers. We are embedded in their world and not allowed to grasp the possibility of an outside except through their prejudices. In a sense, Bigelow is playing the same role as uncritical journalists reporting from inside tanks and helicopters, tied to a war machine whose existence and actions are never interrogated, only assumed. A very powerful piece of filmmaking in the service of a very poisonous cause.

With restraint, honor, and humility, director Kathryn Bigelow and her cast, led by Jeremy Renner, Anthony Mackie, and Brian Geraghty take a step into the less-documented aspects of warfare, where soldiers delicately toy with their emotions, duties, responsibilities, and their lives. Jeremy Renner shines in his Oscar-nominated (and well-deserved) turn as Sergeant First Class William James, the leader of an Army bonb squad charged with investigating claims and (if necessary) disarming bombs. His cool, collected, carefree, yet cautious performance drives his character James as he does his job, ignorant of whether his actions may have potentially lethal consequences. And Renner has strong support behind him, with Anthony Mackie and Brian Geraghty watching his back as he disarms those bombs. But most of the credit goes to director Kathryn Bigelow and her talented production team, led by screenwriter Mark Boal, film editors Bob Murawski and Chris Innis, Director of Photography Barry Ackroyd, sound designer Paul N.J. Ottosson, and composers Marco Beltrami and Buck Sanders. With her taut and delicate Oscar-winning direction, Bigelow shows how tough soldiers have it, particularly when they have to deal with those explosive death traps. The intensity and draw comes from the tense editing job of Murawski and Innis. The reason the film feels so real and gritty is because of the lighting fast, clever, and suspenseful edits and cuts. Another Oscar-worthy effort. The beautiful documentary-style cinematography by Oscar-nominee Ackroyd further heightens the danger and reality, and the sound effects by Oscar-winner Ottosson are prominent and restrained when they need to be to compensate for the pulsating score from Beltrami and Sanders. Oscar winner Mark Boal crafts his script very simply, with an easy-to-follow storyline. But the strength here is the believable dialogue. Very natural and relevant. Long story short, this Best Picture winner is definitely a must-see.

Although The Hurt Locker is certainly an interesting and above average war film, addressing many issues facing the world within modern conflicts, I could not fathom why it deserved the Oscar for Best Picture. The story of an US Army bomb disposal unit trying to act as a cohesive group despite various setbacks, personal problems and daily danger of death is certainly interesting, but it doesn't move at such a speed where you are constantly kept on the edge of your seat. The acting is also proficient, with Renner managing to be equally fascinating to watch but also bringing across a character who seems vaguely friendly yet disturbed. Intense, suspenseful, and gut-wrenching, The Hurt Locker is one of the better films made on the over done War in Iraq. Superb camera work, and gripping action keep the viewer on the edge of their seat for the entire 130 minute run time.

Director Katheryn Bigelow follows a three man EOD team through the twists and turns of the War in Iraq. The viewer sees each men from a physical, intellectual, and emotional level, so much so you feel as if you knew the men personally. Jeremy Renner is fabulous as Sgt. Will James, the commander of the EOD team. Sgt. James is a fearless, but strong team leader who truly loves his job as a bomb tech. Never once does he back down when in harm's way, and in some cases actually intentionally finds danger. While Sgt. James might be a macho tough guy on the outside, we see his softer side when he meets a young Iraqi boy named Beckham. A touching, yet gut wrenching scene shows James' reaction to seeing who he thought was Beckham dead. Anthony Mackie plays Sgt. J.T. Sanborn, who is critical of how James runs the team and at one point is so impartial to James he thinks about intentionally killing him. Sgt. Sanborn seems to fear more for his life than James, and it comes to light later in the movie how much he despises Iraq, and all he wants to do is live through the final days and have a son. Brian Geraghty is specialist Owen Eldridge, a young, frightful and emotional soldier who can't get over his first EOD team leader's death. Eldridge throughout the movie is hesitant to fire his weapon, or engage in danger in fear of death. As the film progresses Eldridge seems to be developing more invincibility, until an unfortunate friendly fire accident takes place, leaving him wounded and medically discharged from duty.

While the portrayal of the characters is fascinating, the actual basis for the movie is quite flawed. Numerous current and former soldier of the Iraq War have criticized the way the film portrayed both bomb-tech's and EOD teams. Also, certain parts of the story are unbelivable, most notably when Sgt. James leaves base alone to go after Beckham's killers, and when the EOD squad leaves the aftermath of an explosion to go search for the people responsible. The film also shows the Iraqi people as angry for the armed forces engaging in their city. While it is likely not all Iraqi's are partial to the US being over there, many feel safer and grateful for the soldiers present.

While The Hurt Locker contains great action, splendid camera-work, and solid performances, it falls a little short of bringing justice to the men and women serving overseas. Still it is arguably the best film depicting life in Iraq, and deserved it's critical praise and success. It's a step in the right direction to making this country aware of the importance of this war, and might be the first non anti war film out there. Though it might have some flaws it's still a fantastic movie and deserves to watched by all Americans.

Esa noche, Bigelow le arrebató el Oscar a su exmarido y realizador James Cameron, quien participaba en la misma categoría con Avatar. En ese sentido, The Hurt Locker rompió con todas las expectativas al ganar también en la categoría de "Mejor Película", cuando todas las apuestas estaban dirigidas hacia Avatar. Apenas hace poco acabo de ver The Hurt Locker, y si bien no me ha parecido esa clase de grandes películas que uno siente deben ganar el Oscar, me siento a gusto de que haya sido esta película, y no Avatar, la ganadora.

Al ver The Hurt Locker, lo que menos puede pensarse es que esté dirigida por una mujer, y una tan atractiva como Bigelow. Pero si uno revisa su filmografía (Near Dark, Point Break, Strange Days), la mayoría de sus películas son así, muy masculinas, tanto en los temas como en el reparto. The Hurt Locker no es la excepción, una película ambientada en Irak, durante la invasión del ejercito norteamericano. Como sucedió con Jarhead, esta película está lejos de ser una película bélica convencional. No hay batallas, o violentos enfrentamientos, salvo uno en medio del desierto, entre un pequeño grupo de insurgentes y marines estadounidenses. The Hurt Locker trata igualmente sobre la desesperación de los soldados de verse atrapados en un país desértico, del otro lado del mundo y  atestiguando los horrores del terrorismo, con  sus ataques usando coches bomba y bombas humanas.
Como personaje, Will no es tan interesante más allá de sus habilidades técnicas para los explosivos, su adrenalínica personalidad y ese lado humano que demuestra con la amistad que le ofrece a un niño que vende películas pirata. El no es más que un vehículo para que Bigelow logre un intenso reflejo de la paranoia que se vive en un escenario afectado por la guerra, en el que todos los que miran desde ventanas y balcones, o que simplemente sostienen una cámara pueden ser sospechosos.

Like a latter day Ayn Rand, Bigelow is la major muy macho in her depiction in the film of a few tough American hombres stuck in Iraq defusing roadside bombs set by the ruthless, relentless, child-killing Arab terrorists. As Bigelow posits the Iraq war as the backdrop of the grand stage of human drama, one veteran bomb expert gets blown up and another shows up to replace him in the dusty, hot, ugly rubble that is Iraq, and a new hero is born.

The new guy is what John Hershey described in his book, and later the movie, The War Lover, as a sadistic wingnut who actually isn't fit for civilian life, and requires the stimulation of war to sublimate and suppress his errant sexual desires. The war lover can only fully function in war, peacetime suffocates him. While Hershey chastised the war lover, (played in the film by Steve McQueen in one of his greatest roles) Bigelow glorifies him. The army needs war lovers, they are the bulwark of defense against our enemies. We can't handle the truth, that it is war lovers who are the best soldiers, the toughest men. According to the unironic Bigelow, regular men are pussies, the war lover is a special breed, the last of the cowboys. So what if he wants to bare-back his men, or fondle an Iraqi boy? He is a throwback to the sex-and-death cult of war. In war, sex is a thankless, loveless, don't-ask, don't-tell kind of male bonding. Bigelow has no opinion on this; she just limits the options of masculinity in this ham-fisted attempt at realism. Only a war-lover can win the moral struggle between right and wrong, between American innocence and Arab perfidy. Bigelow disguises her racism and arrogance behind the ingenuous facade of journalism. She's just another gung-ho yahoo depicting a brutal war against civilians as a moral triumph of the spirit.

On the political front, Bigelow returns to the western genre and its relentless clichés again and again, ad nauseam: the wonderful world of the open frontier, which happens to be some one else's country. ("You can shoot people here" says a soldier ); the tough but human black guy companion, the soldier with a premonition of death, the gruff, possibly crazy commanding officer, the college-educated fool who tries to befriend the enemy. You name it, Bigelow resurrects it.

The man-boy love is palpable in scenes with the cute Arab boy who befriends the war lover, but Bigelow plays it straight; she doesn't consummate the sex, just sanitizes it. What Bigelow really wants to show us is the ugly, sneering face of the Arab enemy. Any Iraqi who isn't pure evil is either demented, hostile or up to no good, anyway. They all deserve to die for their impudence, and many of them do in this glib gore-fest film. The Iraqi women are all hysterical, they only make their presence known by screaming. They could be male stunt men in drag for all I know, you never see their faces. There is no female presence at all on base or in battle, although female casualty rates in Iraq would certainly disprove this.

Bigelow goes through all the motions one by one. She glorifies war, she canonizes the sadist nut-case hero. The cowboys, surrounded by the subhuman Indians, prove their mettle by doing God's work and subduing the wretched terrorist-infested hellhole with sheer bravado and suicidal mania. Toward the end, I felt like rooting for the Indians. In Bigelow's world, though, no mercy or understanding ever makes it through. The Iraqis are dehumanized par excellence. The slaughter of civilians is just the dramatic backdrop to our hero's psycho sexual struggle. Every U.S, bullet finds its mark. You have to love the guy, the war lover. It's just his way, he is the true hero. He's just a guy trying to get things done the hard way, and so what if he lusts for boy tang on the side.

The story itself is not drastically different from a lot of the other war films put out; war is hell and you'd have to be crazy to fight it, see Catch-22.  However, this movie chooses to follow a small team of IED disposal experts and the particular stresses such a role puts them under.  This presents a unique take on the war and allows director Kathryn Bigelow to hone in on smaller moments.

This contrast of the action-war picture versus the small character piece such has been done before with Sam Mendes's Jarhead.  However, the action is more intense and the tension is really built around the set pieces which goes against the purpose of Jarhead as it was the absence of action that defined that story.

Bigelow definitely knows how to ratchet up tension and shoot action from her past credit with Point Break and Near Dark.  The action scenes are fantastically sweat-soaked that you can feel the heat from the blasts.  She is also able to draw very gritty performances from her cast.

Jeremy Remmer is a real find as the maverick bomb disposal expert and gives honesty to his performance that could have so easily slipped into a parody of the character Tom Cruise played in Top Gun.

The rest of the cast with nice guest slots from David Morse, Guy Pearce, Evangeline Lilly and Ralph Fiennes all acquit themselves well, but this is truly Remmer's film.

The Hurt Locker is a bold and striking film, but does not teach any new lessons about war.  However, it must be said that we certainly do not seem to be learning that lesson despite how many times we are taught it.

The cinematography truly captures the most intense moments of the film, and seems to embody the claustrophobia and paranoia in the film. Even though the film isn't action packed, it has the same effect; the adrenaline flows, tensions build, and you constantly catch yourself holding your breath.

There was great acting and great cinematography; let nobody tell you that this is not a beautifully made film. What really makes this film shine is Kathryn Bigelow's Oscar-winning direction, which is enhanced greatly by the terrific performances from the cast (especially Jeremy Renner). At its core The Hurt Locker is an action film, but it's an atypical one at that. What makes it atypical? Well, because the film centers around a bomb squad, we actually are made afraid of the very thing that defines an action film: the explosion. Renner's character puts his life on the line every day, so if a bomb goes off it's game over. Not wishing for an explosion to happen is really what makes this film so intense, coupled with the incredible cinematography and sound design.

What also makes this film so great is the fact that it's a expertly-written character study. It explores the effects war can have on a solider. We see a "tough guy" soldier eventually shed tears due to his fear of being killed. We see the same soldier consider killing Renner's character and making it look like an accident because he is afraid that his unorthodox style might end up getting everyone killed. Another member of the same squad has trouble coping and seeks counseling, only to have it end in disaster. We see Renner's character get attached to a local boy and nearly get in a heap of trouble thanks to rash decision making. I could go on, but I'll stop there to avoid spoiling too much.

The Hurt Locker is well-deserving of the acclaim and awards it has received and it one of the best war movies ever made. Had Bigelow been male she would have still deserved to win Best Director at the Oscars. The Academy definitely did not give the award to her because this is a woman. She truly earned it.

Watching The Hurt Locker can be as troubling as the thud of a bullet piercing through the skull or as pulsating as blood running through the veins of a male in danger, in heat, or on a high.   Whether to react with fear and loathing or rate it (to quote the storys commanding officer) as hot sh*t is entirely up to the viewer.  But few would walk away unmoved or underwhelmed.

The films catch tag, war is a drug, was culled from a sentence written by journalist Chris Hedges, but the idea first found eloquent expression in William Broyles Jr.s 1984 piece about the Vietnam War in Esquire magazine, Why Men Love War.

I finally saw the movie seven months after it won the Oscar Best Picture award of 2009 and a year of critical acclaim.  Being embedded among a few hundred young adults was a bonus because it placed me among a highly responsive audience, people who are only beginning to ask questions about peace, war and death, in between mall trips, video games and the next college exam.  This is a post-Cold War generation who has nevertheless witnessed war, conflict and terrorism on some vicarious, media-sustained level. 

Its easy to accept director Kathryn Bigelows and war witness/screenwriter Mark Boals claim of not having any political agenda, since the film is the clear proof .  It bears no trace of sermonizing or polemic on the war in Iraq. They simply set out to capture the reality of bomb disarmament experts lives.  And capture it they did in scene after gritty scene. But in doing so, they also managed to shed light on the bigger picture, of the wars raw brutality and the zones of hell it has engendered.  In some subversive way, thats a statement in itself.    

Their success hinges on that of Sgt. 1st Class William James and his two partners in the bomb disposal squad.  Bigelow found a perfect James in actor Jeremy Renner, his face still with a layer of baby fat, half-innocent, half-neurotic and solidly stoic.  His eyes twinkle with childish glee as he jokes about male sperm and his dream of setting up a grass business (lawn grass, not the type that creates a high) in Iraq.  Those same eyes stare with glints of excitement and fascination on the tangles of wiring and ignition contact points that he must cut off if he is to cheat death, for the 871st time. They convey exactly the lust of the eye that Broyles cites in his essay (he also uses an X-rated word). 

The bomb suit is Jamess defining look, like an astronauts gear on the lunar landscape of the war zone, and akin to a decontamination worker fighting toxic blight or a virus that has mutated from some fanatical political and religious ideology.

Bigelow and editor Chris Innis may not have had the frame-by-frame blueprint of a Hitchcock or a Kurosawa film, yet the editing in The Hurt Locker has the same effect. Choosing from the raw footage generated by four cameras simultaneously filming any scene must have been intimidating.  But the result is thrilling in its pacing, orchestral in its mix of quick cuts, slow pans, shifting points of view and slow motion.

To these, the audience of Generation Y-ners reacts with surprising honesty.  The single sequence in the movie that is set in a desert -- where the bomb removal techs encounter a Western mercenary group followed by an ambush by local insurgents -- is a virtuoso performance in direction, camera work and editing, producing one of the finest examples of fusion between audience and film that I have seen.  The simple close-up of a fly alighting on an eyelid at a nail-biting moment drew gasps. Every bulls-eye gunshot elicited either a groan (for the allies) or a burst of applause (against the terrorists).  Rather than being a sign of taking sides, the glee was really more an expression of relief and wonder.

The enemy is clear, ever present and even more dangerous but he unhinges viewers precisely because hes shadowy, shown only in paranoid glimpses, and even then no one is ever sure who the bad guys are. We never get close enough to a single bomber, only to the victims and the bomb removers who stand between them. The closest contact with the enemy is through their obscene instruments of mass destruction, metallic, bathed in granite black and often phallic in form.

Surprisingly good with the Mideast cast, Bigelow has less success in her patchy handling of Jamess colleagues, the doctrinaire Sgt. J.T. Sanborn (Anthony Mackie in a solid performance) and emotionally fragile Specialist Owen Olridge (the promising Brian Geraghty).  Sanborns sudden urge to kill James during one operation strains the psychological profile of his character.  But the muscular trio shares several perfect ensemble moments, especially near the end in that crazy, drunken rite of male bonding.

Motivation is never explicit in this movie, but it rears its timid head now and then.  What propels this movie to the status of an instant classic is the same impulse that gives James steps extra swagger as he walked, cowboy-like, in his new bomb suit at the close of the movie:  the lust to stare at death squarely in the eye.

A pure, thrilling, and raw war film; Katherine Bigelow proved to her ex-husband and competitor James Cameron that budgets and box-office grosses don't matter when it comes to movies.
Writing and acting do.

Deserving to sit besides classics like Platoon, All Quiet on the Western Front and Saving Private Ryan, this movie abandons the common escapist cliches and reaffirms that in war, there is no pot of gold at the end of a rainbow: it is, more than often, a dank hell of dirt and shrapnel. And, if the right man is in the military; the fear before a mission is nothing compared to the thrill of success.

Even with the odds stacked against it, it beat out most films that gained a lot more publicity, winning best sound design, best original screenplay, best sound mixing, best picture editing, best director (the first award of such ever won by a woman) and best picture.

Some people don't like that it beat Avatar in most respects, but to me, that's like Halo fans who don't like to play Call of Duty: Modern Warfare because it doesn't have any Needlers or Arbiters. Another gripe some had was the way it handled the depiction of the Iraq war. If anything, that quagmire needed more attention, not less when it came out.

My only problem with this film is that it sometimes attempted to "Hollywoodize" parts of the war in order to make it more appealing to mainstream audiences with lower expectations. These are the same people who made Transformers: Revenge of The Fallen a $402 million hit yet also made GI Joe: The Rise of Cobra a loss of $25 million. 

Aside from that, this is still a riveting whistleblower of a movie that gives the same effect as reading Moby Dick for the first time-the feelings of one person do not always match the feelings of a group or belief as a whole. The Hurt Locker is a 97 out of 100.

I will give credit to The Hurt Locker where it is deserved, but one thing it was not deserving of was the Oscar win for best picture. While it works as a great action and war film, it just doesn't work the way that I think critics say it does.

In the movie, Jeremy Renner plays William James, a reckless and cocky bomb squad technician in Iraq. After the leader of a small squad is killed in combat, he is sent to replace him. He soon puts the entire group at risk with his unorthodox methods of disarming the bombs, such as not wearing his suit.

I'll talk about what I liked first before I go into my rant. The visuals are actually very good for a war movie. The film as a whole is very well shot, with certain camera angles adding intensity to every scene. The desert is also strangely beautiful, and the film really captures this environment of Iraq and the Middle East very well.

The acting on display here is particularly great, and the characters are very well fleshed out. Renner is entertaining and thrilling to watch. The other actors also bring a very human touch to their characters as well. But despite all this, I didn't really care about these characters that much, other than "will he live?" or "will he die?". The main hero is just unlikable and the other characters aren't much better.

Critics have praised the film for it's disarming sequences and the raw intensity that is created in these sequences. And they are pretty intense, I'll give them that much. Your nerves are constantly on edge as James takes more and more risks to disarm the bombs. They are very well done. However, it never seems like there is a real satisfying payoff to all this tension. It just seems to go nowhere. Other action sequences not as involving as bomb disarming (and there are a few) are also good and thrilling.

WARNING: Incoming Rant

However, what does it all mean if there's no real plot to tie it all together? That's the way I felt when I watched this movie. It seemed like there were no real motives or anything to keep the characters going in this movie. There just never seems to be anything to drive the plot forward, but somehow it keeps chugging along. Sure, there's some part where James is angered by the death of a small boy he befriended at the base, but that's about it. I felt very little for this story or it's characters and I just didn't care what happened in the movie very much. The ending also left me cold. It seems like it's trying to tap into some kind of deep-seeded human trait about violence and war, but it doesn't follow this in a satisfying or meaningful way.

Critics have praised this movie to no end about how intense and well-made it is. I just don't see it. The action sequences are intense and thrilling, the acting and script are decent, but the story and characters were seriously lacking. I felt like it was trying to convey some deep philosophical message, but never knew what that message was. As I stated in my recent blog, people slam Avatar for not having a plot, but it had way more going for it plotwise than this movie. At least Avatar made me care. The Hurt Locker is just an extremely well-made and pretty action movie with little soul.

The opening scrawl of the film sets out the basic underlying theme of the whole movie very clearly.
Set during the Iraq war, the film follows the fortunes of a team of young EOD (Explosive Ordnance Disposal) tec's, who are lead by the borderline psychotic William James (played brilliantly by Jeremy Renner).
The film doesnt concern itself with any of the politics behind the war or the ongoing debate about whether US/British forces should even be there in the first place, instead it focuses entirely on getting the viewer in there with the troops, generating the nerve-shredding tension that makes the film so good and giving the constant feeling of 'are they gonna make it through the day?'
The performances are strong.  Jeremy Renner gives a star-making turn as hero/villain/fuck-up hybrid William Renner, a man so addicted to the adrenaline rush of combat and diffusing bombs that he treats every situation as a sort of life-or-death challenge that has to be overcome, he is more at home in these situations and yet struggles awkwardly when at home with his wife and child, and he regularly puts the lives of his team-mates at risk in pursuit of his next combat-based adrenaline fix.
The camera work is superb, and director Kathryn Bigelow does a magnificent job of capturing the paranoia of the situation, where any man, woman, child or even goat could potentially be the trigger that will blow the next hidden device up, obliterating the whole team.
That said, I have to disagree with certain claims made.  I dont think this is 'the best war film ever made' as some have claimed, I think it is without doubt 'the best film about the Iraq war' in the same way that Saving Private Ryan is 'the best film about The Second World War'.  It is not one of 'the greatest action films ever made', but it is indeed a great action movie.  I'm not even sure it should have won as many Oscars as it did (Best Film and Best Director for starters), but then again Im hardly surprised that it did, considering its subject matter and how topical it is at the moment, given the situation in Afghanistan, and the Academy do love that sort of thing.  I think its a future classic, and should definitely be seen, I just dont think its as good as some of the rave reviews say it is.  You may disagree!

The smoke has cleared and all the Avatar haters have skipped merrily into the sunset, so.... it's time for me to have my say.

The Hurt Locker is a very good film.  Note I didn't say "great".  Is it Oscar worthy?  Considering some of the past winners - (Life Is Beautiful comes to mind - a film, like this one, that I enjoyed, but didn't knock my socks off) I have to say sure, why not?  Is it a classic film that defines a genre, or revolutionizes filmmaking in general?  Nope.

Having not been in Iraq, all I can do is say that based on several other films this seems to do a very good job of portraying the hell that is war.  It shows the claustrophobia of all the streets where you never know who is watching and may have a gun pointed your way.  Similarly, due to the language barrier, you get several scenes where you just aren't sure of the home folk's motivations.  Are they innocent bystanders, or insurgents just waiting to make a move?  This makes for great tension and good theater.

The storyline tells one story while really being about something else. It concerns Bravo company, a special forces unit whose soul purpose is to disarm bombs.  You get to see the procedure in the film's first set piece, which is important because when a new munition's expert (read bomb disarmer) enters the mix, it is easy to see that he is NOT into following procedure.  From this you gather that he either has a death wish, or is an adreniline junky.  Either way he is constantly putting the rest of the squad in harm's way.  But since he is the ranking officer, the rest of the squad has to follow his lead.

There is a tenseness to many of the street scenes, but others fall flat (like the drunken fight scene in the barracks - I have no idea what the director was trying to say there, and it certainly made no lasting impression on me) - or the too long scene where the squad has the task of investigating a bomb site (which leads to the adreniline junky leader once again putting the rest of the squad in harm's way and ironically then having the leader shoot one of his own squad in a firefight).  

The film then rallies in the final Iraq scene where an innocent Iraqi is strapped with C4 which the disarmer is unable to difuse in time.

Some pretty compelling stuff here, so why not a higher rating? Scenes that went on too long, like the bonding scene where the squad is pinned down in the desert after helping some Brit mercenaries.  All the waiting after they finally take out the snipers in the building didn't rachet up the tension at all. 

Secondly, the bit of contrivance where the company psych is challenged by one of the squad to get out from behind a desk.  Of course he takes up the challenge and - gee I didn't see this one coming - steps on a mine and goes boom.

Thirdly, and probably the most important - The HBO mini-series Generation Kill did the whole Iraq thing equally as well, if not better.  If a film cannot surpass what you can see on TV, then perhaps garnering an Oscar for best film is a sad indictment on the state of filmmaking - or a realization that television, especially when given the time to develope charactors and a story, can exceed its big brother.

If given the choice of watching either the Oscar winning Hurt Locker, or Generation Kill over again, I'd go for GK hands down.
