I know two things about director Kathryn Bigelow.

1/ She made Near Dark, a vampire classic that has unfortunately dated just a wee bit since it's 80s release.

2/ She made Point Break, a fact I only was reminded of with the passing of star Patrick Swayze. Point Break was a bizarrely over the top yet entertaining 80s movie.

That's it, two films both made in the 80s. Both rarely mentioned but at the very least thought of in generally positive terms when they were.

Now she has made a totally different movie, one I had also never heard of until it was mentioned in an online column as being a great film, and it actually is.

Bigelow should either make more movies - or get a better agent... Either that or comparisons to Deuce Bigalow have killed her name in the industry.

The Hurt Locker is a film that follows a unit of explosive disposal experts through Baghdad, where booby traps and mines are plentiful, and spread randomly about the place to kill soldier or Iraqi with seemingly no care as to who is the victim.

The opening scene neatly encapsulates the film: It is nearly 9 minutes of building suspense, is never tacky or showy, and creates real characters that are in constant peril. It also shows that this will be a movie with no favourites as Guy Pearce makes sure he won't be in Hurt Locker 2.

It seems in The Hurt Locker, the more famous and known you are as an actor, the sooner you will be killed.

The replacement for Pearce is Will, he is gung-ho and reckless but apparently always gets the job done. This is a shock to the system of the remainder of the team who were by the book, diligent and careful.

Sanborne is the personification all of those things, and he sees himself and his other partner Eldridge, a younger soldier who is almost the team dogsbody, as being put at risk by Will's carefree attitude.

Without going into detail the film follows the team through various events that occur over their tour, all of which are hazardous due to the key role they play.

Each event is allowed to play out in real time, and each participant, and their reactions and thoughts, are shown as the pressure builds. The viewer also feels the pinch, as the tense scenes are allowed to build, and there are long stretches with little or no dialogue.

Oh, and of course being bomb disposal guys they are almost always near a live bomb which may or may not go off at any time.

It seems Will has some sort of death wish, which he explains as "well if the bomb does go off, I'm toast anyway", though there are times when the three are off duty and letting off steam when reality kicks in and we learn more about his background.

This is the kind of film that even with the large explosions that happen periodically is not a boom-boom bang-bang A Team affair with stuntmen bouncing off unseen trampolines and cigar chomping boneheads spitting witty dialogue in between narrowly cheating death yet again.

This is a realistic film showing three guys in ultra-high pressure roles as they strive to get through each day on the job, and also how they deal with it once they do. You actually care about the soldiers, even when they are being d*cks, and feel real concern as they go about their business.

You don't want them to die. But being a film about real life people in conflict, you always know that there is the chance that they will. If that is what Ms Bigelow set out to achieve then she succeeded.

If nothing else you get far more appreciation of what soldiers go through daily in what is largely thought of as a "kiddie's war" than you would in 100 Arnie or Stallone shoot-em-ups.

Not a happy film, not a big action film, just one that deserves to be watched by a far wider audience.

Final Rating - 8.5 / 10. Hard to watch, easy to recommend.

Generally well-acted and well-directed, the film remains quite flawed, being hurt (pun intended) by an extreme lack of development, expendable moments, overdrawn points and abrupt events. As for the action sequences, I feel that the tensity falls flat, as the quietness and dragging goes too far. It doesn't help that Bigelow fails to escalate the tension during the body of the action sequences. Also, a consequencial atmosphere soon fades due to the action sequences being overused. Still, with all of my complaining, I'm sure you just want me to cut to the chase and answer the question on everyone's mind: "Do I think this film is overrated or even bad?" Well, just in case the 90% didn't tell you, the answer is an emphatic "no". I disagree with a lot of the majority's points and though Bigelow's direction is very flawed, she has still produced a fine work of art.

The film is supported by an effective hook, (that is admittedly tense the last 10 seconds) a rare, but good score, fine production designs, fairly good sound charming character chemistry, good dialogue and a reasonably smooth pacing. As for the cinematography, it's more of that shakey-cam bull, but with its own distinctive quality, being crisp and gritty. There is a climactic point in this film where the soldiers walk through a burning area at night and the sight of the pitch-black darkness, barely illuminated by the roaring flames is near-breathtaking. That's why if I'm going to get any version of this film, then it is going to be that awesome steelbook case with the cover that references that beautifully shocking scene. As for the performances, what little development you get is made up by the compelling performances. You really get the roles that the characters play in all of this, but it's never really emphasized, giving them that aura of mystery. Like I said, if they were fleshed-out more, then we could invest ourselves more into them, but that's not to say that you're hanging on these characters.

As for Bigelow's direction, it is flawed, - as I said - but still solid nonetheless. She creates one of the most authentic war simulations in modern cinema and in a film like this, where tensity is debatable, it works to great affect. Though the film does get too authentic with its overdrawn and underwhelming action sequences, the film is rarely, if ever really dull. The tensity falls flat, but what keeps the movie going is its authenticity, which is deeply fascinating and gets you feeling for the people in this scenario, not just onscreen, but on the real battlefield right now. The authenticity - complemented by the solid performances - keep the film compelling and at some points, emotionally resonant.

Ultimately, though it - to me - falls flat on creating tensity, "The Hurt Locker" remains a well-crafted, compelling dramatization of the Iraq War, carried by the solid performances and fascinating authenticity.

The Hurt Locker is an intense, well shot, superbly acted and suspenseful war film. The Hurt Locker is also a brilliantly made film that is gripping and can be painful to watch, but the question of Is The Hurt Locker a realistic look at war is a good one, but is it possible to make a accurate and realistic war film?

The Hurt Locker follows a team of bomb disposal experts, as they try to disarm the bombs in a chaotic Baghdad, however risk taker Staff Sgt William James (Jeremy Renner) puts lives in danger as war is drug to him, and he needs the adrenaline rush to keep his life going.  

The Hurt Locker is a very powerful film, the suspense reaches unbearable levels every time the team attempts to disarm a bomb, everyone is aware that one tiny slip could result in devastating consequences, there is a very thin line between life and death. The bomb disarming scenes, in my opinion, are superbly done and the level of tension results in these heart pounding scenes to be immensely gripping. The first bomb disposal is a terrific and a powerful scene, it is also suspenseful and effective. When the bombs do explode they are impressive on a technical level, a slow motion shots can come close to showing the power of a bomb.

Intensely shot, the documentary style film making adds to the realism of the proceedings, the shaky camerawork also adds to the gritty portrayal of war and adds a great deal to action and the levels of suspense. The question of Is the Hurt Locker realistic is again raised, perhaps The Hurt Locker is more realistic then many war films, but again I do not have the experience to judge. The film was shot in Jordon, barely miles away from the Iraqi border; the cinematography is without a doubt totally stunning. 

The Hurt Locker is also brilliantly acted Jeremy Renner (Staff Sgt William James) Anthony Mackie (Sgt JT Sanborn) and Brian Geraghty (Specialist Owen Eldridge) all give a fantastic and charismatic performance, plus some impressive, but small roles, from Guy Pearce and Ralph Fiennes. All performances are powerful ones, and you care a great deal for the characters. The script is a decent one, but the actors work wonders with it making the script seem better then it is.

The action is brilliantly shot, the defusing of the bombs are superbly done, they are gripping and suspenseful and the supreb sniper duel is also fuelled with immense levels of tension. What makes The Hurt Locker a good film is the unbearable levels of tension that is present ib almost every scene, they are nerve-racking and effective, the camera works add to this, and you can quite clearly feel your heart pounding inside you.

The most powerful scene in the whole film is one nearing the end, on the second from last day of duty, an innocent family man has several pounds of explosives tied to him, it's a powerful, moving and shocking scene, and this tactic is employed throughout warzones. I heard a story that the same horrible, disturbing thing happened to a 10-year old child in Israel. If this scene does not move you in anyway, then I seriously doubt you have a heart. The reason why this is so powerful because this does happen in real warfare and this is terrifying and disturbing.

Kathryn Bigelow excels in a typically male dominated genre, creating one of the greatest films on the Iraq war granted it does not touch the likes of Platoon and Apocalypse Now, but the Hurt Locker is great war film, a question however is did it really deserve to win Oscar for Best Picture? I for one am glad that it beat Avatar, but films such as District 9 deserved the award far more then The Hurt Locker.

The subplots are not really developed enough to have a strong enough influence to the story and the vengeance quest that Sgt William James embarks upon seems to be rather forced in and really does very little apart from add to the running time, there are moments where the Hollywood influence creeps in for example the quest of vengeance previously mentioned, and when the bomb disposal quest go on the hunt for those who planted and detonated the bomb, however this Hollywood influence is present in many war films. According to many veterans The Hurt Locker inaccurate portrayal of war, but do concede this is a more realistic effort. 

Overall, The Hurt Locker is more than effective look at the Iraq war, powerful, moving and brutal. Full of dramatic tension, brilliantly choreographed action scenes (The sniper sequence is a highlight). The Hurt Locker looks more at the physiological aspect of war; the film starts with a quote "The rush of battle is a potent and often lethal addiction, for war is a drug" which goes a great distance in explaining why Sgt William James takes huge risks and why he returns to war so soon often arriving back home, the return to normal life is difficult for all solders who have returned from the front line. The Hurt Locker is good, gripping and keeps most on the edge of their seat, but the question of whenever it deserved award for Best Picture is a debateable one.

I can't give the movie more than 3.5 stars because I'm pretty sure that a lot of the big-picture view of serving in the army was wildly inaccurate.  There was almost no emphasis on the omnipresent chain of command, the movie replaced the large amounts of boring down-time soldiers wade through with near-constant tension, and the principle actors hardly interacted with anyone but each other. When I watched Avatar, I was blown away.  It is the only movie I have ever watched multiple times in the theater.  When it lost the Academy Awards in almost every category to The Hurt Locker, a movie I had not seen, I assumed it was because The Hurt Locker must have been beyond awesome.  I had heard that there was some politics behind it since the director of The Hurt Locker, Kathryn Bigelow is the ex-wife of the director of Avatar, James Cameron.  I now firmly believe that Cameron was robbed in some sort of popularity contest.  I was excited as I started the DVD.  That excitement turned, quickly, into sighs. 
 
The Hurt Locker follows a three man Explosive Ordinance Disposal (EOD) team based out of Camp Victory in Baghdad (October 2004, year after I was there) as they are called out to diffuse numerous Improvised Explosive Devices (IED).
 
Let us start with the things the movie did well.  The cinematography is well done.  The sets featuring Iraqi streets were done fairly well.  The best I have seen in a movie set in Iraq to date.  Jeremy Renner delivered a very good performance as the lead character William "Will" James (great name!).  That is about it.
 
Now for the things that were just beyond ridiculous.  The three-man EOD team moves about Baghdad in an HMMWV (Humvee) by themselves.  Not in convoy, etc.  In fact, there are scenes where they do not even have someone in the turret.  Like they are out for a nice leisurely Sunday drive.  We did this in blacked out civilian vehicles working with the Iraqi Police, but never in a Humvee.  That is just asking to be ambushed which is why standing orders were (and probably still are) three vehicle convoys minimum.
 
Then amazingly, they seem to be out on long distance patrols for no apparent reason.  While out on the patrol they come across a bunch of private contractors (think Blackwater) who happen to have had a flat tire in the middle of the desert while transporting two of the Playing Card members of Saddam's regime.  Amazingly, the soldiers cannot tell that they are contractors so they get out of the Humvee, and advance across a great deal of open terrain without cover to disarm one of them.  Then they finally realize what is going on.  Amazingly, an Iraqi sniper team ambushes them from a distant building.  So far distant in fact that the American's can barely make out the enemy through the scope of the Barrett .50 sniper rifle.  The Iraqi sniper is using what appears to be a Draganov and has channeled the spirit of Carlos Hathcock, rarely missing a shot.  After killing the sniper, they sit watching for the rest of the day, in the sun.  They never get reinforcements, air support, etc.  When one member tells Will that he sees movement behind them (in the middle of a bunch of goats) the team leader does not look, instead he tells the guy it is his call.  The guy shoots (and kills an insurgent), and Will the psychic knows that the insurgent is dead and says good job.
 
The scene that throws all logic to the wind is one of the first.  Will and his crew go to diffuse a bomb.  They cannot find the soldiers who called for them.  They find their Humvee empty, soldiers nowhere to be seen.  Will spots someone waving a small American flag out of a building.  He walks over and the entire squad is hiding in the entryway of a building and says that the bomb is down the road.  The soldiers fear is plainly evident.  Will shuns the use of the robot, and instead suits up.  He walks out and deploys smoke on the way.  Okay, I could possibly see deploying smoke to obscure your movement so an insurgent does not see you getting close to the bomb to diffuse it, but you would need to put smoke in all directions the guy might be watching from.  He then continues down the road, the only ones not able to see him, are the troops.  Iraqi's are everywhere watching.  Oh, and this is a magic smoke grenade.  He keeps walking through smoke even though the grenade is far behind him and not being blown forward.  He then walks into an intersection with Americans guarding it.  So I guess the cowardly soldiers he is disgusted with, are also the ones furthest from the bomb.  Suddenly an Iraqi in a taxicab drives around the roadblock (without being shot at all) and nearly runs Will over.  Will draws his US Army issue Beretta.  Amazingly it is a Beretta 92 which has not been manufactured since 1976 (obvious because it has no safety) instead of the 92FS.  He then gets the driver to back up to the soldiers who promptly take him into custody.  He then continues down the road, now probably about 1/4 mile from where he started.  He finds and diffuses a bomb.  Then realizes it leads to multiple more.  He quickly diffuses them all while the insurgent who buried them watches.  The insurgent waits to go downstairs and blow the bombs until Will is almost done.  By the time he gets down the two flights of stairs, it is too late and Will is finished.  Will shows him the blasting cap in victory and lets him go.
 
Shortly thereafter, a Psychologist Lieutenant Colonel decides to go on a mission with them.  An IED in a rice bag goes off and vaporizes him, leaving only his helmet.  He is so obliterated that there is no blood, and apparently no body, because one team member is desperately trying to find him.  The three-man team is called to collect unexploded ordinance from a building.  Amazingly the troops who called them had not actually cleared the building yet.  I'm still unclear how the psychic troops knew that there were bomb making materials in the building if they hadn't gone in it yet, but hey this is Hollywood right.  Therefore, the three-man team clears the whole building by themselves while the dozens of infantry stay outside.  I guess EOD is trained to act as Delta operators in their spare time or something.
 
The Hurt Locker is Hollywood's extreme left wing biased view of what war is and soldiers are.  The most telling moment is the scene where there is a wounded insurgent and the soldiers are ordered to execute him despite the medic's assertions that his wounds are survivable.  If this were the case in reality then we would not have to have any debates about Guantanamo Bay because there would not be anyone there.
 
In short, this movie was so frustratingly illogical that I found it impossible to enjoy.  Even looking back at it and trying to imagine watching it as if I was never a soldier, nor an OIF vet, I still do not think I could get past the total lack of logic.  Amazingly nearly all the top critics love it.  Reading up on it, it seems that many OIF veterans and EOD Techs are quite disgusted with it.  I totally agree with them.  I give it a 4.5 / 10, which places it on par with GI Joe Rise of the Cobra, which seemed more realistic.

This movie basically feeds off of the emotional attachments that people have towards the Iraq war. None of the characters are likable, original or relatable. The lack of chemistry between the actors makes many scenes dull, awkward, and forgettable. Critics and people everywhere claim that this film realistically portrays the war in Iraq but I can definitely tell that is not the case from reading several comments from actual people who served in the armed forces about how bogus the premise of the film is. By no means is this film horrible but by no means is it great. It is just an okay war movie. I expected way more especially when being treated to great war movies like Saving Private Ryan, Apocalypse Now, and Full Metal Jacket. My thoughts; If you see this with no expectations, you will probably enjoy this film enough to recommend it. However if you're a war film buff/movie geek like I am, you will probably see the many flaws that plague this film.

The film may have been released in 2009 but thanks to successes this year at the BAFTA's and Oscars Kathryn Bigelow's Iraq war film has received a short cinema re-release.

The strength of "The Hurt Locker" is it's unremitting tension from beginning to end as we watch a bomb disposal unit battling against a variety of unexploded bombs in Baghdad. A largely unknown cast (aside from cameos from Guy Pearce, Ralph Fiennes and Evangelina Lilly) stokes up the tension with strong performances creating likable characters that you increasingly care about.

It avoids the obvious route of apportioning blame or attempting any kind of politic comment, instead purely concentrating upon their efforts of surviving each day and returning home intact at the end of each tour of duty.

In many ways the monotony of each day helped to increase the tension although the undoubted find of the film is Jeremy Renner. It was his ability to convey his character as a man who only came alive through the adrenalin rush his job provided that made the film its focal point.

Not my idea of the best picture of the year but still an interesting and riveting film.

When I heard that Kathryn Bigelow had directed a war film that was a likely front-runner for Best Picture (which it eventually and deservedly won), I was very excited.  I grew up loving her vampire/western classic, Near Dark, which still stands as one of my favorite vampire films (Let the Right One In being the other).  I didn't get to see it in theaters because it didn't exactly blow the top off the box office so it wasn't in theaters for very long (especially if you live in Kentucky).  So I waited for the blu-ray release and sat down to watch what I expected to be a super cool, possibly very violent war movie.  I knew it was about a bomb disposal team in Iraq and about the cavalier expert of the group, so this seemed a fair assumption.
I won't say I was exactly wrong about those expectations (except about the violence part).  I think I was just not thinking high enough.  This movie is super cool, in a sense.  The main character Sgt. William James (Jeremy Renner) is magnetic, but his obsession which is likened to a drug addiction is obviously disturbing, particularly because he also has a reckless streak a mile long which his two team members are afraid will get them all killed.  Still, as much of a cowboy as he is, his exacting technique with bomb disposal is equal to that of a heart surgeon.  You feel like you're truly watching an expert at work, and working against the unseen foes who plant these devices in their places.  He isn't working against them to save lives, at least that doesn't seem his foremost concern, he's working against them in a dangerous game.  The better the bomb, the more Sgt. James is determined to dismantle it, even long after those endangered have been evacuated.  He knows the stakes, that these devices can kill him, but with him you wonder what he'd say to the bomber if he couldn't dispose of one and it was about to actually kill him.  "You win" perhaps?  
In the final act of the film, however, Sgt. James begins to realize (or perhaps remember) what can happen to men and even children in a war.  He is humanized, not just to us, but to himself.  It doesn't change his addiction to his job, but rather, it shows him the tragedy of it.  He knows now what he is, but he is what he is.
I know I've spent a lot of time on this one character, but don't let that fool you.  It's about him and his team, but to understand them it helps to understand him, because that's what they're trying to do.  One is by the book, because he believes that going by the book is the best way to stay alive.  The other is becoming more and more convinced that he will be killed, and is shouldering the blame for a choice he regrets making.  How these two cope with someone who cares little for the book and may very well get them killed is fascinating to watch, and depicted excellently.  Bigelow is far beyond the top of her game here, she's redefining it.  She most definitely deserves being the first female Best Director.
This is easily the best Iraq War film, and one of the best war films in general.  It's not a tear jerker like Saving Private Ryan or a farce like Inglourious Basterds, both of which are excellent films.  No, The Hurt Locker is about men doing a very dangerous job in a very dangerous place, and whether or not they can survive doing that job.  It's enthralling from start to finish and shouldn't be missed.

(SPOILER ALERT)

I was trying to think of the last action film where they killed off a popular actor early in the script, and the first that came to mind was Executive Decision (1996) where they killed Steven Seagal in the first act.  That may not sound like a big deal now, but '96 was the end of a pretty long run of Seagal as an invincible super action hero - I mean, only six years earlier he was literally Hard to Kill (1990), "and you can take that to the bank!"  So Executive Decision's Seagal-dropping early on in the film was a moment of cinematic entropy in action films - and more immediately, it set a tone in the film that no veteran on-screen ass-kicker is safe anymore.  

I don't know if Kathryn Bigelow had Executive Decision in mind when she killed off Guy Pearce in the opening scene in The Hurt Locker, but there was certainly a similar function.  In a film about defusing bombs, we need to clearly know the stakes early on - blow someone up - someone recognizable.

But Hurt Locker is significantly more realistic than Executive Decision.  I went to bed the night I watched this and had dreams of Improvised Explosive Devices (IEDs) only to be startled awake by my alarm clock in the morning - not a typical anxiety-ridden reaction to my BlackBerry alarm - but fortunately no wire snipping or bomb blast suit was necessary.

It's the first war dream I've had in a long time, probably since I first watched Saving Private Ryan (1998).  I've never been in the military (and I don't play Xbox), so I only know war through massively replicated media like blown-up YouTube-quality camcorder wide shots of seemingly distant roadside explosions edited into newscasts - something Kathryn Bigelow brilliantly and consciously turns the camera on to reveal conspicuous Iraqis watching impending explosions from Mosque towers and balconies with handicams in hand.  

The perspective of these local death voyeurs is infused with the paranoia of Bravo team's monitoring of surrounding activity, fingers hovering over triggers at the sign of a cell phone that might repeat what happened to Guy Pearce's character earlier on.  And Bigelow even extrapolates that element of trigger-hesitation when later they find themselves in a sniper standoff out in the desert.  With several men down, Specialist Eldridge is dehydrated and unsure of some activity behind their position on some railroad tracks near some animals.  Without confidence, it's only after consulting with his team, and still seemingly unsure if the target on the tracks is even armed, does he shoot and kill.  Bigelow makes much clearer to the audience that this was the right choice than to the characters in the frame at the moment.  This is akin to the classic wire dilemma - snip the red or blue wire - and what is an ultimate 50/50 in defusing the larger ticking time bomb of battle.  A moment or two more of hesitation and Eldridge most certainly would have been shot and killed.

Time bombs are no stranger to the screen and they very effectively enhance anxiety.  The use of time bombs as a tension device for suspense have been around since early Hollywood, like in Alfred Hitchcock's, Sabotage (1936).  Hitchcock creates a terrifying experience for the viewer and our knowledge of this concealed ticking bomb on a bus full of people - it's a completely nail-biting scene.  

But the best ticking time bombs in film history came along with the aforementioned defusing "Wire Dilemma" we've seen over and over.  A personal fav of mine is in Leathal Weapon 3 (1992), where it doesn't take itself too seriously with lines like, "Grab that cat!" in the famous Danny Glover bathroom bomb scene.  Likewise, we've all seen the end of The Abyss (1989) - interestingly enough a film by Bigelow's ex-hubby, James Cameron - where Ed Harris's character is precariously faced with deep sea climactic wire dilemma under poor lighting and depleted air supply.  

But is it even possible to do the red wire/blue wire waffle without eye rolls anymore?  Maybe in the context of an obvious parody, but we're unlikely to take this scenario very seriously these days.  Kathryn Bigelow proves that you still can, and she is deserving of the Best Picture Oscar just for this.  The film itself is the world's biggest and baddest wire dilemma in the history of cinema, riddled with ticking time bombs in all forms, from metaphoric character arcs, to ACTUAL ticking time bombs, the most obvious being the climactic forced-suicide-bomb defusing - a terrifying moment that has brought us a long way since The Abyss with an outcome that doesn't end in underwater vagina castles and the world being saved from an angry ocean.

Bigelow literally makes the entire film a ticking time bomb by graphically inserting updates on how many days remain in Bravo Company.  In a filmic sense this is reminiscent of Danny Glover's retirement countdown in Lethal Weapon 3, likewise it's very aware of news media's graphic domination of war in a genre-sense.  Bigelow abducts title overlays from news, like superimposed Chyrons and tickers injecting us with stats and info.  It's very important for us to know that war is a violent countdown to going home - or not going home.

It's choices like this that are courteous on the part of Bigelow, because we've seen it.  We know the expert will come in and defuse it with 007 seconds on the clock like in Goldfinger (1964), we know that despite only having 5 of a required 6 pairs of wire cutters with John Lithgow in The Manhattan Project (1986), the bomb will not go off.  And we finally laugh at a self conscious jab poked by Tyler Durden to Ed Norton at the snipping of the green wire in Fight Club (1999), "Oh, heavens, no, not the green one, anything but the green one."  This to me, marked the end of 50 years of cinematic wire dilemmas on a parodic note.

But Bigelow brings on the goods, shattering a logical film history progression of bomb defusing that was supposed to end in 1999 with Tyler Durden in celebratory parody as the towers of capitalism crumbled to the Pixies.  But Kathryn Bigelow has snipped the right wire to defuse any lingering primary label of "the ex wife of James Cameron" - she's dropping that character faster than Steven Seagal in Executive Decision.  The Hurt Locker is terrifying and fantastic.

Remember...this is a movie, which in my opinion needs to either entertain or challenge.  So perhaps I came into Hurt Locker with way too high expectations (I was thinking this was going to be a challenging movie, showing a facet of the lives of soldiers, or a facet of war in general), but I felt the movie was fairly disappointing.  Technically (cinematically) it was good.  You can't help but draw comparisons with other recent "gritty" war movies, and Hurt Locker did a decent job.  There were a few "iconic" moments, which I feel are hallmarks of really good movies.  But what the visual couldn't make up for was the lack of real impactful storytelling.  I didn't care much for (nor believe in) the characters (although not for want of acting skills...the acting was good).  There wasn't really a unified issue (remember, this is a Hollywood movie).  Was it how the team worked together?  Was it finding the bombers?  Was it the fact that the were fighting a faceless, invisible enemy?  Was it reconciling with the Iraqis?  Was it dealing with death?  Was it dealing with the tension/contrast of being home versus being at war?  Each of these themes seemed to be touched on slightly throughout the movie, but none were really dealt with in any thoughtful manner.  Was the movie simply a vehicle to produce tension (an obvious facet of war)?  Perhaps. but that requires caring about the characters (which I didn't...I was just waiting for the explosion).  So was the message that war isn't really that simple, and that it's a bit aimless?  The movie did emphasize that at times, and I suppose it works to an extent if you take that perspective.  But none of the high points and areas that "worked" warranted a Best Picture win.  Blackhawk Down is still the standard for urban warfare movies (and was much more deserving of a Best Pic nomination...it was snubbed of course), despite that movie having its own flaws.

I'm not a huge fan of the post-modern war movie.  Shaky camera angles, stilted heroes, and ambiguous moral messages aren't really my cup of tea to begin with (see: No Country for Old Men), and when you throw in the political concerns of a real-life war you have the potential for a level of preachiness and/or forced gravity (see: The Kingdom) that turn me off as an audience member.  Happily, The Hurt Locker avoids these pitfalls and provides a visceral cinematic experience that feels authentic and sincere throughout without throwing the message in your face every five seconds.  Jeremy Renner leads an outstanding cast featuring several prominent cameos from some of the finest character actors of this generation (David Morse, Guy Pearce, Ralph Fiennes, etc.).  Renner plays the role to perfection, and Bigelow manages to establish some continuity with the character that elevates him from the "cocky badass" archetype that Morse's character makes him out to be.

The tension builds brilliantly throughout the film, with the sniper scene around its mid-section providing some of the most intense depictions of modern combat on film.  Each actor responds to his surroundings in a way that seems organic, rather than simply rehashing the anti-war sentiment seen in films of the post-Vietnam era (I'm looking at you, Full Metal Jacket).

My concerns mainly lie in the cinematography, and the lack of development for the secondary members of Renner's squad.  I felt like their "maturation," so to speak, occurred at a pace that seemed unrealistic.  Sanborn had his head his shoulders the entire film, but loses it in the last ten minutes on the way home?  Eldridge is five seconds from a nervous breakdown, but putting one between a guy's eyeballs is supposed to settle him down completely?  I will never know what war is like (thankfully), but these characters developed in a way that didn't seem real to me.  Also, I cannot stand over-use of the shaky camera.  Jason Bourne directors and Katheryn Bigelow-see Saving Private Ryan for a perfect illustration of the effective use of shaky camera.  Using it in every scene doesn't make your film seem gritty, it makes it seem as though you're co-opting a fad for the purposes of your film.  You've crafted some very post-modern characters to frame your war story, we don't need the camera to remind us we're in the 21st Century every second.

Now before you all say "Dude, The Hurt Locker is that stupid movie that beat out Avatar!" just realize that in the end, The Hurt Locker was the better film. The Hurt Locker follows SFC William James (Jeremy Renner), a seasoned veteran to the USA EOD units. He is crazy, cynical, and a risk taker. His fellows companions, Sgt J.T Sanborn (Anthony Mackie) and Specialist Owen Eldridge (Brian Geraghty) seem to have an almost instant dislike for his, especially his recklessness. However, they begin to grow more attached to the man who has almost gotten them killed on numerous occasions. The Hurt Locker shows corruption in soldiers, and how these little things such as serving in Iraq can put them over the line. Jeremy Renner's performance as James is phenomenal, and a performance I think should have won the Oscar for Best Actor. He shows complexity, wit, and most of all, he is very realistic. With Anthony Mackie and Brian Geraghty as the films supporting cast, the movie has a near perfect three leads. The scene where Sanborn breaks down after watching a man be killed really shows amazing acting and how well chosen these people. Not to forgot, Kathryn Bigelow does a fantastic job of creating this kind of hell hole of a place and makes it so we feel like we are there. Whether we see DVD salesmen or just families, the portrayal of Iraq is extremely realistic and it is very well put together. That, and the fantastic action and suspense sequences. So, if you watch the trailer and like it, go rent the movie. It isn't for everyone, but if you think you can take it, watch it. 5/5 Stars

It is very rare that I find a movie that I don't like. But, Hurt Locker is one of those films, not only because it wasn't good, but because the critics hailed as some sort of masterpiece. Screw critics.

Now, first of all, this movie was said to be incredibly suspenceful. It. Was. Not. I knew the guy in the beginning was going to die. Maybe others weren't but I did. So, his replacement, who turns out to be the main character, is introduced. Now, while there are exceptions, it is a pretty good rule that the main character will usually not die. With that realization, and the fact that the main character is the ONLY OTHER PERSON TO ACTUALLY DISARM THE BOMBS, all the tension that this film should have had vanished. And I was left there, bored, thinking to myself, "When is this just going to end?" I mean, the sniping scene just drags on and on and FREAKING ON!

Now, I can handle boring films. King's Speech could be considered as "boring". However, the strengths of that film lie in the great acting, characters, and script. None of which Hurt Locker has.

The characters in this film, well, let's just say that the "main character never dies" rule didn't play out here, and that the main character did indeed die. I wouldn't have cared. Why? Because he is an extremely unlikeable character. He is the stereotypical "rebel" with no regard toward safety or protocol when disarming bombs. And apparently, his superiors are okay with this, seeing as how he disarmed 873 bombs. Uh, bulls**t. You are telling me that the first bomb squad commander, who did it by the book, dies and yet an adrenaline junkie is better suited for the job? That's stupid. .

And that's this films main problem: It's script is so remarkably flawed with "that doesn't happen" type moments. For example, the main character (named James) abandons his post TWICE and is not repremanded for it at all, and then there is the above mentioned sniper scene. But I think the most insulting thing is the doctor. Now get this. The doctor is a Lieutenant (making him an officer) who graduated from Cambridge, and yet, he seems completely oblivious that he is in Iraq. And so, the first time he goes out on a mission, he dies. Now let me put this in perspective. Frankly this movie doesnt live up to its hype.

It is certainly generally quite entertaining, it is fairly acted, it does come up with a slightly new perspective on the wars in the Middle East. On those counts the movie works pretty well.

However, the way it is shot, it claims  to be some sort of a war documentary, wrapped in a fictious story. And this is where the movie literally blows itself up. It lacks that certain degree of authenticity that would be mandatory for such a type of movie and that you would find with masters like Steven Spielberg or Stanley Kubrik.

For instance at the very beginning, where that remote controlled robot is supposed to take a pile of explosives to a roadside bomb site. Its highly implausible that any EOD technician short of a complete retard would risk his life due to a broken wheel and try to defuse such a bomb manually. Or that someone acting that suspicious, being arab and having a mobile phone in his hand in the vicinity of a roadside bomb, would last as long as 5 seconds after being spotted. 

But it gets even worse, when the EODs meet a group of private military contractors, according to the accent probably former SAS operatives who are stuck in the middle of nowhere due to a breakdown. There all of a sudden they get attacked by snipers, and contrary to their training, since they cant spot anyone they dont take immediate cover, but stand around, providing a fantastic target, and spray their ammo all over the place, in the middle of a desert. And then it turns out that those badass mercenaries though equipped with a state-of-the-art sniper rifle, totally suck at sniping, but need to be saved by our brave EODs, who probably never have fired a Barret before. Laughable.

However,the climax of Bigelowresque incredibility and ridicule is found somewhere towards the end of the movie, when EOD technician James is asked by a superior officer how many explosive devices he has defused so far and comes up with a staggering 800 and something. Considering how reckless and outright stupid this technician defuses bombs, it is outright insane and ludicrous at best, to imagine this guy would even last a few days in Iraq let alone defuse over 800 bombs and live.

Unfortunately this picture is loaded with such flaws, what clearly reveals that Ms Bigelow exhibits a gross lack of comprehension when it comes to warfare and military related issues in general. While you cant expect everyone to have been with the Marine Force Reconnaissance, it is mandatory that a good director minutely does their homework. It is simply entirely inconsistent with serious film making to build such an implausible screenplay and claim authenticity, because that is absolutely nowhere in evidence in this picture.

I urgently request Ms Bigelow to return to film academy and anyone who hasnt watched  this movie yet, to just take a 2 hours nap instead of watching this imposition of a movie.

Now before you get angry and say I'm being picky because I am in the military please read the entire review.

At first this movie poses as a "realistic" account of what happens in an Army EOD team.  Hence the "fact-based" aspect.  As far as fact goes the only realism this movie had was the scenery and the concept that EOD is responsible for dismantling bombs.  None of the procedures or actual events that EOD would use were portrayed in this movie.  I know everybody has a friend who has a friend that went to Iraq and destroyed 15 tanks and captured 25 insurgents and dismantled 100 bombs, but I am telling from personal experience that all that is FALSE.  This movie has absolutely no realism...from rolling out the FOB(forward operating base) in 1 vehicle with 3 guys who are barely armored...I don't even know of Special Forces operators that would do that unless the mission is absolutely requiring it...  EOD is not Special Operations...EOD is training in disarming bombs, mostly through the use of robots nowadays.  The fact that this guy decided he can roll out the FOB whenever and however he pleases is completely false.  ESPECIALLY when it involves going on a mission and chasing insurgents in 1 Hum-Vee.  This action would INSTANTLY result in going to Fort Leavenworth and serving a prison sentence for endangering the life of junior soldiers.

On a realism scale this movie gets a 3/10 for great scenery!

Characters development in this movie is NIL.  None existent.  You meet a guy, who happens to be a raving lunatic and yet somehow is allowed to be in the army...Not likely, believe or not ladies and gentleman but the army is so concerned about their image nowadays they would never let that slide.  Never in the movie do you find out why he is the way he is, all you see is a brief glimpse of his cliche domestic life as a soldier...comes home argues with family and yada yada....Yes it does happen to soldiers, but its been so played out in movies and done so much better that this movie seemed like it just slapped it in their for public appeal.  As far as other characters...well they don't even play any significant roles in the movie...

Character Developement gets a 2/10 because they showed him at home ...

Overall plot:
The overall plot was not THAT bad.  A guy is in the Army for a long time, Army trains him to be EOD, guy is so used to Army he doesn't see himself as civilian, guy decides Army is only thing right for him...Very simple, yet EOD is a very highly sought after field in the civilian world because of their security clearances and experience with demolitions, so it can be argued that it is a simple transition from EOD to civilian as opposed to infantry or cavalry scout or tankers which have very little application in civilian life other than law enforcement.

Overall plot gets a 6/10 because it is a slightly above average concept.

Final rating: 4/10

I don't particular care for war movies, but I discovered upon watching this that it wasn't a war movie at all.  You know were at war, but it doesn't focus on that aspect of it.  What it does very well is it focuses on one man's position during the war efforts.  He diffuses bombs.  This film was shot in a way that gives you a documentary feel as if its really happening.  This makes it all the more unsettling.  We follow the role of a bomb tech guy who straps on an 80lb suit in 100 degree weather in the desert.  He then goes to a location where a bomb has been discovered and he dangerously pulls the wires from it so it doesn't go off.  We watch with fearful anticipated anxiety as he carefully pulls each one out.  Onlookers by those that live in the area look on as these soldiers move into their territory in hummers with guns.  You don't know if the onlookers are good or bad and it's brilliantly captured.  This is a realistic portrait of the feeling of what it would be like if you were a soldier rolling in there or if you were living there and these guys were coming in.  Jeremy Renner plays the bomb tech guy and developed a three dimensional character with neurosis and faults.  His performance is incredible and it makes the movie all the more interesting.  The guy is cocky and has to be out of his mind to be able to perform a job such as this.  One of the better movies I've seen these days.

With any major conflict, sooner or later, someone is going to make a film based around it.  Platoon has come to be known as the defining movie of the Vietnam war and it's likely that The Hurt Locker will do the same for the war in Iraq.  It's hefty Oscar haul almost guarantees it.
It's well worthy of its accolades though, Kathryn Bigelow's near documentary style movie following the count down of remaining days in a battle zone for a bomb disposal team is gripping and from the off has the palms wringing in sweat.
Jeremy Renner delivers a performance which is both entertaining and tragic in equal measure as the new Sergeant assigned to the unit who's unorthodox and risque methods do nothing for his comradeship with his team mates.  The film then charts several missions the group are sent upon as Renner's character becomes detached from the world back home.  Renner's portrayal under Bigelow's direction is heart breaking by the time the credits role, leaving a lasting and haunting impression.
Bigelow turns the tension grinder on in many of the mission scenes.  The documentary style of filming she employs, with no use of music to heighten the dramatic tension, means that the film has it's viewer on constant tenter hooks.  The constant threat that at any moment something could bang is amazingly powerful under Bigelow's direction.  She's shown she can direct testosterone fuelled action with aplomb before but she's never shown such an ability to put her audience through such a real feeling of danger as this.
The Hurt Locker is a supremely powerful movie which gives a glimpse of what it must be like to have to out yourself in these situations and the, from one point of view, devastating effects it has on the people who do and those around them.

There's no Stalone's or Bond's, just everyday people who have been thrown into a situation beyond their control, where they are not fighting some great evil, but other human beings in the same circumstance as themselves. With a suspenseful intensity that creates some of the most visceral memories of any film this year, THE HURT LOCKER is one of those movies that people couldn't be bothered with at the time of its release. Folks who missed it-myself included-will soon be clammoring to see what turns out to be one of the finest war films of the almost-finished decade, especially as THE HURT LOCKER begins to create the profile it never had this summer, thanks to a steady stream of awards and accolades.

The current conflict in Iraq has been the subject of some fantastic documentary films in the past few years, such as "Standard Operating Procedure," "Iraq in Fragments" and "No End in Sight," but fictional films on the subject have been mostly limited to homefront conflicts, such as "In the Valley of Elah." Not that I've seen every film made about the current military conflict, but I'd say that THE HURT LOCKER is easily one of the best war films of the decade. It's certainly the best about this military conflict, and joins "Black Hawk Down" and "Three Kings" as a time capsule to represent America's war efforts in the last 25 years.

Perhaps it might surprise some that behind the lens of this intense, suspenseful war film is a woman. Kathryn Bigelow, though, is an action film director, and one used to playing with the boys. Her hits like "Point Break" and "Strange Days" have not been awards fare, but that will change this year. I expect Bigelow to join the very elite club of Oscar-nominated female directors.

But enough about the background perspective...why should you see THE HURT LOCKER? For one thing, it contains a fantastic lead performance by Jeremy Renner, a virtual no-name starring as a specialist who diffuses bombs. He's brought in after the previous man on the job meets the fate that one would expect men in this position to be all too prone to, and this guy almost gives you the impression that his work and situation is fun.

So cocky is Staff Sgt. James (Renner) in his job that he defies orders, disconnects personal communication devices and fights his fellow soldiers for enjoyment. He'd be the loose cannon cop in a buddy movie (like Mel Gibson in "Lethal Weapon") if he wasn't also fully-aware of his situation - and good at it. James might be hard to relate to on some levels, but you know you want him by your side.

There are at least three sequences in the film (one at the beginning, one about a half-hour in and one near the end) that are heart-pounding, and Bigelow relies on the normally motion sickness-inducing and slightly cliched (for war films) tactic of shaky handheld camera work to add to the gravitas of what we're seeing. But Bigelow avoids MTV-style edits and camera trickery. In one very steady and memory-burning moment, she simply pulls the camera back to an overhead shot while James discovers that the wire he's tugging on is attached to not just one bomb, but many, each bomb ominously rising from the sand in unison around him at the urging of his steady and gentle pulling of the wire. It's a terrifying moment.

THE HURT LOCKER has a number of terrifying moments, from the off-putting way that Iraqi civilians (or maybe self-sacrificing terrorists) stand in plain view as the military bomb squad works, to the side-story investigation of the demise of a local boy to whom James has become attached. And to cement the sloppiness of this war and its unfinished business, the film's penultimate scene on the home front is note-perfect in its demonstration of how a soldier like James is actually more in his element at war than in the cereal aisle at the grocery store.

Let's get this out of the way right now: The Hurt Locker isn't genius filmmaking or anything breathtakingly fresh. The fact that it's based in Iraq and is one of the few films to focus on the action during The War in Iraq is what made this film ten times as noteworthy as it should have been. Focusing on the personal conundrums of the characters mixed with action isn't a breakthrough; in fact, for action-oriented director Kathryn Bigelow, The Hurt Locker is probably tame in comparison to some of her other works. What is impressive is how Bigelow goes about filming each scene without any kind of sugarcoating or hyperbole.

Immediately, the danger and uncertainty of the film's moments stands out. Unlike many dramatized works of the past, there's no hinting at disaster or death just like there's no background music to set a mood. Scenes can be quiet and calm one minute, loud and chaotic the next and all of a sudden someone is laying dead on the ground. There's no cinematic suspense, just real-time, heat-of-the-moment suspense. The truth is never pushed and neither is the reality. There are miraculous saves and there's never the feeling where one character might feel more safe than the other. The battleground is seemingly endless; you never know when everything could fall apart.

Sequences of peril certainly account for much of the film's success, but the way in which it impacts the film's respective characters is just as important. In opening with the line "war is a drug," Bigelow acknowledges right off that bat that war becomes something larger to a lot of the soldiers. It becomes a part of your life; whether it is something you learn to love and appreciate or something you learn to see the evils of and can't wait to leave it behind you. There is an undeniable level of pride that comes with the situation you're thrown in to, but how you harness these delicate, sometimes life or death moments can define you, for better or for worse. The Hurt Locker doesn't limit itself to one mold. Pride, stupidity, fear, anger, and revenge are only a few ways you can be defined and a lot of men and women find out just the kind of person they are just from how they act in certain situations.

The Hurt Locker is the most entertaining movie that has been made about the Iraq war. Period. No Contest. It is easily the best war movie that I have seen since Saving Private Ryan. Yes, it's even better than Black Hawk Down.

Simply put, The Hurt Locker tells us the story of an Explosive Ordnance Disposal unit (army-speak for 'bomb squad') and their daily exploits. Another war movie, right?

Wrong. I suppose the greatest thing about it, while this statement will be banal, is its ability to blend some many different styles together. In this movie I laughed and I cheered. I was scared and I was shocked. I was grossed-out, and sometimes I even wanted to cry. When someone inflicts pain upon another, he is said to be putting the other 'in the hurt locker.' Which makes for a brilliant title for this movie because of the continuous suspense that Sergeant James puts his fellow servicemen (and us the viewers) into.

This movie sets itself apart from the rest of the pack for many reasons. But what stood out most clearly to me was that it doesn't take sides. It just shows the situation as it is. There's no "the Iraq war is right," nor "the Iraq war is wrong." It shows characters as they are, and what they really care about in that right-here-and-right-now sense. This is in striking contrast to the supposed "realistic" portrayal of a soldier's experience that the cinematic masturbation of Jarhead showed us (based on the first Iraq war). There are parts of the characters that are rather glib though. Why are they doing this? How do they cope? The film's answer to those statements is in the opening text of the movie: "The rush of battle is often a potent and lethal addiction, for war is a drug." That's nice, but it threatens to turn the movie into another American adrenaline-junkie action flick with no answers to any questions.

But we know that the movie is not about that. It's a 'day in the life' story, not a "life" tale. That's what we're interested in seeing anyways, right?

While there are some pretty cliché war-movie scenes in the film, I found it easy to overlook them because the movie makes up for it in so many other original ways. When James suits up in his "blaster" outfit and walks down the empty desert street towards the bomb he is trying to defuse, it feels like an old-western shootout.
Oscar Winner cranks up the suspense and tension while maintaining an intense story.

The story of "The Hurt Locker" is about soldiers, bomb specialists to be exact, and their journey on the field of battle. It's about the power of a team and how they should work together. Personal vendettas are not worth it in war because not only are you putting yourself, but your whole team in danger. It is also about how war can be like a drug, how even if you hate it, it pulls you back because it becomes hard to adjust to normal life. It is a story that is very important to our generation. It helps us get a feel for what it is like for soldiers out there and the constant threat they face each and everyday.

"The Hurt Locker" is a very well directed movie. The environment Kathryn Bigelow creates is both gritty and very real. There is always a sense of tension in the film, it really does feel like we as the audience are in a real war zone. Danger feels like it's lurking in every corner and we don't know if the characters will be able to get out of the situations that they are in. Nice camera work helps escalate the vibe and feel of a war zone. From deserted landscapes to cramped spaces, the camera aids in what the story is trying tell. Writing is also really well done. Dialogue between characters is engaging and edifying. Humor helps ease some of the tension that is present throughout the film. It isn't laugh out loud funny, but manages to make it easier to cope with some of the harsher and tense moments.

Acting is top notch with compelling and characters that very much feel real. Jeremy Renner does a great job of portraying a cocky soldier. His emotions are raw and his character is a  likable douche-bag. But I feel his character is a little to over the top, which clashes with the real environment that they set up. Anthony Mackie is superb in the film. He is the more realistic character that only wants to get out alive. We sense his experience and knowledge of the war zone, but also we can feel his fear and worries. Another great performance is by Brian Geraghty, who plays a worrying soldier, who is in constant fear of dying.

The sound of the film is very raw. It sounds as if we are on the battlefield with planes/choppers flying overhead, gunshots being fired, and bombs exploding in the distance. The score weaves you through the intense and more subtle scenes; It is perfectly orchestrated.

Overall "The Hurt Locker" is an incredible work of cinema. The story feels true and subtle things can make you emotional especially during a sniper sequence. Well balanced action with subtle humor and drama make the film very impactful. However, the film does get a little slow in the third act and some the believability seems to stray away, I give it 4.5/5, incredible performances and smart script bundled with intelligent direction.

"The Hurt Locker" is a must watch, at least once. It is significant to our generation and truly does give us a sense of what war is like.

After finding out that The Hurt Locker won Best Picture, I decided that I had to see it. War films have never been my cup of tea, but this film is quite unique, and it's a totally tense experience. SUMMARY:

After Sergeant Thompson (Guy Pearce) is killed while trying to defuse a bomb on a Baghdad street in 2004, he is replaced by Staff Sergeant William James (Jeremy Renner), who shocks the other members of his team, Sanborn (Anthony Mackie), and Eldridge (Brian Geraghty), with his reckless approach to his dangerous work. James seems oblivious to the fears and concerns of his comrades. REVIEW:

For me, the strongest element of the film was the screenplay. Written by Mark Boal, who was a journalist embedded with a bomb unit in Iraq, it feels absolutely realistic. Throughout the film, we experience these characters' mission - clearing the streets of Baghdad of bombs. It shows us the long and tense process of defusing the weapons. The opening titles state that war is a drug, and it's a major theme of the movie. It's a drug to the character of William James, who is addicted to combat. The ending was a winner for me - it's clever, and it brings you back to the beginning, with the theme of war being a drug. James' character isn't exactly developed, but what they try to do is develop the other characters' opinion on him. Sanborn sees him at first as a 'redneck piece of trailer trash', but during the course of the film his opinion, and ours, undergoes a change. The film doesn't take sides as well, there are no villains here. Other war films tend to potray the opposition as evil people, but they never do this here. Kathryn Bigelow doesn't choose to have bad guys. The acting is terrific. Jeremy Renner excellently plays James, while other members of the cast, including Anthony Mackie and Brian Geraghty, do just as fine in their roles. The supporting actors are superb, with Guy Pearce, David Morse, and Ralph Fiennes, making short, but outstanding, appearances. The problem comes from the cinematography. I did like some of it, I thought some shots were breathtaking, but the problem came from the handheld style of camera movement. It's taken to the extreme here. It's really a shame. It's justified in some scenes, which just shows how good of a director Kathryn Bigelow is, but it becomes overused during the course of the film, and to a certain point it is literally sickening to watch. I felt like throwing up. That doesn't mean I hated the whole of the cinematography - some shots were beautiful, as I said earlier, and the colours of the film were excellent. I thought the explosions were filmed well, which gave the film a wonderful visual edge. The score was good, and it boosted up the suspense in some scenes. Bigelow's main strength is during the scenes where James defuses the bombs. It feels and looks authentic, and it's absolutely tense. Wire cutting, and even looking for the wires, Bigelow gives us a tense experience, filming in the right places, and giving excellent direction to the actors. Despite the handheld camera style, The Hurt Locker is a tense and nail-biting experience. I don't think it's Best Picture - I do think it is quite over-rated. Kathryn Bigelow has done a great job with this, and her direction is amazing - it's no surprise she won Best Director, let alone being the only female to ever win that award.

The Hurt Locker tells its story by breaking it up into different episodes. Each one is titled by telling us how many days are left in this groups tour in Iraq. This is a war film about the adventures of three men during the Iraq war. It doesn't have much in the way of an overarching story, except that its characters remain (mostly) consistent throughout. While some come and go, our three men generally are always present. We begin with the death of man tasked with defusing a bomb. It's a long scene that ends when his squadmates fail to shoot a civilian with a cell phone which ends up being the trigger. This man's replacement ends up being Sergeant James (Jeremy Renner), an overconfident young man with a wife and child back home. His group consists of Sergeant Sanborn (Anthony Mackie) and Specialist Eldrick (Brian Geraghty). Most of the time we spend with them involves one mission or another, with downtime being skipped. They have forty days left until they can return home. Any suspense generated is typically done in one of two forms. Either the group will be dealing with a bomb that could go off due to an error or because any random civilian could detonate it, or because snipers could be everywhere, and the group constantly has to be on guard for that. Road mines are also common, and the group's Humvee could be blown to smithereens at any moment. A quote opens the film, and it tells us that war is a drug. In many ways, I can see that's true. The Hurt Locker certainly presents itself to make sure that point gets across to the audience. The episodic format that the narrative is told through actually works for something like this. When we just get done with one tense scene, going back to base and waiting a few days before the next one could harm the pacing. By simply skipping those parts and fast-forwarding to the next thrilling part of the solders' lives, we are always involved. There are enough character moments thrown in, but this is mostly an action-thriller. It certainly does a good job at filling both genres' expectations. As the group goes on more missions together, tensions begin to rise. At one point, Sanborn and Eldrich contemplate killing James, making it look like an accident. It makes sense why they'd want him gone -- he is, after all, a danger to their group thanks to being an overconfident man who works with bombs for a living -- but James never finds out that they thought about it, which is surprising. There's a scene in which all three characters get drunk together, which seemed like the perfect moment to increase the tension by having it slip from one of their mouths. No such luck, I'm afraid. The tension of the group doesn't actually last all that long, and it's eventually forgotten that they even fought. Only through a very stupid decision does it get brought up again, and even then, it's only for that one scene before it's deemed "water under the bridge." I get that the film wants the characters to come together and become friends, but doing it as early on as it happens here doesn't help the already-disjointed narrative. It gives us one less thing to think about, and despite director Katherine Bigalow's attempts, the characters (especially in the case of Sanborn and Eldrich) fade into the background. Sergeant James is really the only character that gets enough development to make him relatable. He's an adrenaline junkie, someone else says, and that's a pretty apt description from where I'm sitting. But he's also funny, a risk-taker, and generally a likable guy. He even becomes friends with one of the Iraqi children who tries to sell him bootleg DVDs. But once he starts working on the bombs, he becomes focused and we get to see a real craftsman at the top of his game. It's enjoyable to watch him wherever he goes, and it makes sense for the film to focus on him. Jeremy Renner's performance is what really makes the Sergeant's character work. It's a very subdued job, although he's pretty much the perfect actor for this type of role. He can be cocky, he can be confident, and he's athletic enough to perform in the actions. But he's also kind of an everyman. Mackie and Geraghtly are relegated to supporting detail, but despite that, they're strong and make what little character they're given work. Other supporting roles -- in these cases, the characters usually appear once and then aren't seen again -- go to Guy Pearce, David Morse, Christian Camargo, Ralph Fiennes, and Evangeline Lilly. If nothing else, The Hurt Locker feels very authentic. I don't know if it actually is -- I have a hard time believing some of the things these soldiers get away with could actually happen -- but the way it looks and feels makes you feel like you've just experienced war. It's a very gritty filming style, primarily consisting of handheld shots, but it works well in this case. The action scenes are all very intense, and you feel that, at any point, the lives of these people could be at an end. The Hurt Locker is a very exciting movie about the Iraq war. It contains a solid lead performance from Jeremy Renner, has nerve-racking action scenes, and works well telling this one man's story, even if that means the supporting cast is ultimately inconsequential. It feels real, it looks real, and it's a fine journey to experience. I was never bored while watching it, and while it has a few flaws, they're easy to look past both while watching and afterward. Definitely give this film a watch.

Okay so here's the second movie that I was borrowing from my youngest brother along with Gladiator. So without further intro, let's get into The Hurt Locker.

Plot: Sergeant First Class William James becomes the leader of a  Explosive Ordnance Disposal unit during post-invasion Iraq after the units former leader was killed by a bomb. Throughout the film, the other members of the unit, Sanborn and Eldridge become concerned about James because his methods in how he does his job as they try to find and disable or destroy bombs, and encounter other missions and danger in Iraq.

This was a very well done war movie. And I actually have a friend who was in the military who has told that this movie really hits it pretty accurately with the war in Iraq. It really displays the suspenseful things that soldiers out there face out there with the hard relationships between the troops and the Iraqis, how hard some of the choices they make can haunt them, and altogether trying to survive long enough to go home. The actors really do an extremely good job at giving us these characters and what each one of them goes through throughout the movie.

Actors/Characters
Jeremy Renner/Sergent James: James was a very interesting character. He did have an interesting sort of 'I prefer my own way' kind of methods with disabling or destroying bombs, and I especially liked his line "If I'm gonna die, I want to die comfortable." But he did have his more serious side where he was determined to get the job done and he did really care for his unit and some times was dramatized about some pretty harsh stuff that was happening and Renner displayed all of that really well which makes it little surprise that he was nominated for Best Actor at the oscars and has make a breakthrough in his career since this movie.

Editing: I particularly liked the editing from the first scene of this film. Mostly because during one editing class I took at film school a couple of years ago, the teacher showed that particular scene and roughly took it apart and showing how every since choice of shot and time of cutting from one shot to another worked really well and I liked how much sense that makes even watching it not sometimes.

And that's my review for The Hurt Locker. It's an excellent Iraq war film that displayed a lot of things that happened around that time with very well made and acted characters that makes it probably the best Iarq war movie ever made.

Well, I tried again to watch this riveting Oscar winner. 

I don't know why it's shot like a music video - I don't know why so many music videos are shot in a way that is antithetical to the way the human brain takes in information through the eye - and I don't know why it doesn't seem to bother so many people - but it makes the screen unwatchable for me. 

It is not an intellectual choice on my part, although I can use my intellect to analyze the problem.

I might even be able to manage if it was just the fast cutting...or just the faux-photojournalist stitching, as in let's pretend that the audience is the cameraman, and so we see the camera zooming in and out as if it were trying to choose its focus...but these two together completely pull me out of the story - makes me want to scream - stop playing with the camera and let me see what is going on!

Greenblatt says it makes the viewer feel like he is in the war zone, and I guess Bigelow feels that way too, but no one I know who's been in a battle agrees with them.

The brain always tries to settle in on a picture so that it can figure out what is going on - yes, that is difficult to do in battle, but the brain makes an effort, and effort that is made impossible here, because the camera (via the camera work itself and the multi-angle cutting) forces, as it were, the eye to flit quickly from one impossible angle to another.

On the other hand, if I have to watch this kind of camera work and editing, in its style it seems to me about as well done as is possible, on its own terms.

In every other way, for my money, it's a stunning film. In particular, I like the use of silence, the composition of the story itself, the utterly natural dialogue that yet moves the story along without showing its stitches at all (completely opposite from the camera work in that regard), as well as the oft-praised acting and directing.

My friend and excellent young filmmaker Alex Keipper in his review made an interesting point about the theme, which is explicitly stated at the film's outset, and well developed. I have many thoughts on the subject, which I won't go into here, except to say that for me it is a little too pat an explanation to say that some men are attracted to battlefield as a 'drug'...Robert Capa was famously disdainful of the comment.

There is truth in it, no doubt, but it smacks a little of the bourgeois, of the outsider looking in. 

If a man feels more alive in the face of danger, a feeling I've experienced myself, perhaps the problem is not in the so-called addiction, but in what is missing in the world 'back home'. Something starkly and poetically suggested in the supermarket scene, shelves stuffed banally with ridiculous deserts masquerading as childrens' breakfasts. 

Which scene, indeed, is the more surreal?...the young Iraqi boy hawking pirated DVDs, or the blandness of abundance such that food itself has been made into entertainment, and American popular music, one of the great cultural gifts to the world, is reduced to the dullest possible orchestration to create a Muzak to shop by?

A very specific selection from the quote that opens the film, taken from Chris Hedge's "War Is a Force That Gives Us Meaning", sums up the next 133 minutes of Kathryn Bigelow's The Hurt Locker in just four words: "war is a drug." It's a sentiment that mirrors the mindset of Jeremy Renner's Staff Sergeant William James, who is fearlessly calm in coordinating his EOD squad. Too calm, perhaps, to the point where his actions continuously risk his own life, and the lives of his fellow squad members, including Anthony Mackie's by-the-book Staff Sergeant JT Sanborn and Brian Geraghty's emotionally naive Owen Eldridge. It's a war film, but at its core, Mark Boal's screenplay is a character study of how war affects everyone: as their tour of duty winds down, these three soldiers and their worldviews are changed quite drastically as tensions continuously rise. The film lacks a single, overarching plot, which occasionally hurts the film's pacing, but allows for plenty of character moments between Renner, Mackie, and Geraghty, all of whom give strong performances.

Kathryn Bigelow directs the film with a sense of raw and gritty viscerality, especially when the story necessitates intense action sequences. Bigelow understands how the war works: there's no huge shootouts with running-and-gunning and constant explosions from entire militaries here. Between the handheld camerawork and the general lack of a noticeable musical score, the EOD bomb disposal scenes are filmed in a way that feels like a guitar string is being wound too tight, and could snap at any minute. They're slow paced, but deliberately, and effectively so. It's as if we're stuck down in the sandy streets of Baghdad with these soldiers, and there's no telling who's going to come out of each mission in one piece.

This Best Picture and Best Director winning film (Bigelow is the first, and currently the only, female to win both of these awards) is simultaneously a phenomenal war film, with perhaps the strongest onscreen portrayal of the Iraq War to date, and a fascinating character study of the effects of said war. The Hurt Locker is a must-see.
